p-v-glob: Peter Vilhelm Glob was born on 20 February 1911 at Kalundborg on the Danish island of Zealand, the son of the painter Johannes Glob. He studied archaeology at the University of Copenhagen and was awarded his PhD in 1944, after publishing his dissertation. He married Harriet Roepstorff, and they had five children, among them the ceramic artist Lotte Glob.

Glob worked for the National Museum of Denmark from 1937 to 1949 and then taught as a professor at Aarhus University until 1960. From 1960 to 1981 he served as the state's Director General of Museums and Antiquities, the Riksantikvaren. He also co-founded the Scandinavian Institute of Comparative Vandalism, which studied the history of graffiti.

In Denmark his best-known work concerned the bog bodies, the mummified remains of Iron and Bronze Age people preserved in peat, among them the Grauballe Man and above all the Tollund Man. Abroad he led several scientific expeditions to the Middle East. In the 1950s he discovered and excavated ruins of the ancient Dilmun civilization on Bahrain, and in 1954 he and his team uncovered the Barbar Temple, considered part of the Dilmun culture. The Danish expeditions to the Arabian Gulf were later described by Flemming Højlund in Glob and the Garden of Eden and by Geoffrey Bibby in Looking for Dilmun (1969).

His Danish book on the bog bodies, Mosefolket, appeared in 1965 and appeared in 1969 as The Bog People: Iron-Age Man Preserved, in a translation by Rupert Bruce-Mitford. Mound People: Danish Bronze-Age Man Preserved followed in 1974. His survey Danske Oltidsminder appeared in translation in 1971 in two editions, Denmark: An Archaeological History from the Stone Age to the Vikings and Danish Prehistoric Monuments. Glob died at Djursland on 20 July 1985.
p-v-narasimha-rao: Pamulaparthi Venkata Narasimha Rao was born on 28 June 1921 into a Telugu Niyogi Brahmin family in Laknepalli village in present-day Telangana, then part of Hyderabad State. At the age of three he was adopted by Pamulaparthi Ranga Rao and Rukminamma and taken to the village of Vangara. He studied at Osmania University, took a master's degree in law at Hislop College and completed his law studies at Fergusson College in Pune. In 1931, aged ten, he was married to Satyamma, who died in 1970.

He was an active participant in the independence movement and joined full-time politics after independence as a member of the Indian National Congress. He sat in the Andhra Pradesh assembly from 1957 to 1977 and held ministerial posts from 1962 to 1973. As chief minister of Andhra Pradesh from 1971 he applied land reforms and land ceiling acts strictly; President's rule had to be imposed to counter the Jai Andhra movement. In the union government he later held the Defence, Home Affairs and External Affairs portfolios.

In the 1991 general election the Congress under Rao won 244 seats, and with outside support from other parties he formed a minority government. India was then close to bankruptcy. I. G. Patel declined the post of finance minister, and Rao chose the economist Manmohan Singh, a former governor of the Reserve Bank of India. The reforms advanced furthest in opening to foreign investment, reforming capital markets, deregulating domestic business and changing the trade regime. In 1992 the Controller of Capital Issues was abolished. Some socialist nationalists criticised the liberalisation at the time.

On 6 December 1992 members of the Vishva Hindu Parishad demolished the Babri Mosque at Ayodhya. The act led to large-scale communal violence, the most extensive since the Partition of India, in almost every major city. His government introduced the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, India's first anti-terrorism legislation. In 1993 an earthquake at Latur in Maharashtra killed nearly 10,000 people, and Rao's relief operation drew applause. Voters turned the Congress out in the 1996 election, and Atal Bihari Vajpayee became prime minister on 16 May 1996.

Rao published a novel, The Insider, whose rise of a man through Indian politics resembles events in his own life. He spoke 17 languages, and translated a Telugu work by Viswanatha Satyanarayana into Hindi and a Marathi novel into Telugu. He suffered a heart attack on 9 December 2004 and died 14 days later, aged 83, and seven days of state mourning were declared. Biographies by Vinay Sitapati and studies by Sanjay Baru and Jairam Ramesh examine his role in the reforms of 1991. He was awarded the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian award, posthumously in 2024.
pa-sak-river: The Pa Sak rises in the Phetchabun Mountains, in Dan Sai District of Loei Province, and runs through Phetchabun Province as its backbone; its valley through the mountains is the dominant feature of that province. It then crosses the eastern parts of Lopburi Province and Saraburi Province and joins the Lopburi River northeast of Ayutthaya Island, before running into the Chao Phraya southeast of Ayutthaya near Phet Fortress.

Its basin of 16,291 square kilometres is part of the Chao Phraya watershed, and its annual discharge is 2.4 cubic kilometres, though its water levels vary with the seasons. Besides the Lopburi River, its tributaries include Khlong Muak Lek, Huai Pa Daeng, Lam Sonthi, Khlong Wang Chomphu, Khlong Saduang Yai and Lam Phaya Klang.

Within living memory the stretch of the river in Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya Province was a waterway known for its Khanom chin, rice noodles, and was called Khlong Khanom chin after them. Its water was clean and clear enough to drink, and it was home to the zig-zag eel, a fish prized as a delicacy. Wat Mondop, across from the Hua Ro quarter, was an important pier for boats bound for Bangkok, and rafts and boats there sold Khanom chin and Thai sweets such as Khanom thuai, Khao lam, Lot chong and Thong yip, many of them made by people living along the river.

A natural channel links Khlong Bang Kaeo in Maha Rat District with the river at Nakhon Luang District. On its banks stand two Buddhist temples, Wat Khot Khema Pitaram and Wat Tan En, where flying foxes gather. In the 11th and 12th Thai lunar months, after the end of the Buddhist retreat at Wan Ok Phansa, when the waters rose and the paddies flooded, the stretch between them was a place for courting, boat song festivals and boat races.

Of those customs only the boat races between the two temples are still kept, and the Khlong Khanom chin section still produces Khanom chin and Lot chong for the market at Hua Ro. The Pa Sak Cholasit Dam in Lopburi Province, built in the 1990s to meet drought in the lower valley, is 4,860 metres wide and 36.5 metres high, holds 0.785 cubic kilometres of water and supplies about 6.7 MW of electricity.
pablo-escobar: Pablo Emilio Escobar Gaviria was born on 1 December 1949 in Rionegro, in the Antioquia Department, and grew up in poverty in the neighbouring city of Medellín. He was the third of seven children. His father was a small farmer and his mother a teacher.

Escobar began his criminal career with a gang that stole tombstones, sandblasted the inscriptions and resold them, and then joined gangs that stole cars. He also had people kidnapped for ransom. His best-known victim, the businessman Diego Echavarria, was kidnapped and killed in 1971.

In May 1976 agents of the Colombian Security Service (DAS) arrested Escobar on his return from Ecuador and found 39 kilograms of cocaine in the spare tire of his car. He changed the first judge in the case and bribed the second, and was released. The agent who had arrested him was killed the following year. His method of bribing officials and murdering those who refused became known as silver or lead, meaning money or death.

With Carlos Lehder he developed a transshipment point on Norman's Cay in the Bahamas, used from 1978 to 1982. He bought some 20 square kilometres of land in Antioquia for the Hacienda Nápoles, which had a zoo, a lake and a private bullring. He also spent millions on housing, parks, football pitches, hospitals and schools in poor districts of Medellín, and was known as the Paisa Robin Hood.

In 1982 he was elected an alternate member of the Chamber of Representatives for the Liberal Party, which gave him parliamentary immunity. The Liberal leader Luis Carlos Galán expelled him from the party, and Escobar announced his retirement from politics in January 1984. The justice minister Rodrigo Lara-Bonilla, who had accused him of criminal activity, was murdered three months later.

In 1991 Escobar surrendered and was held in his own self-built prison, La Catedral, under a deal with President César Gaviria that excluded extradition. He escaped in 1992 when authorities tried to move him, and a nationwide manhunt followed. On 2 December 1993, a day after his 44th birthday, Colombian special forces traced him to a house in Medellín after he made a call to his family. In an exchange of gunfire he was shot while trying to escape over the roof, and a bullet to the head killed him. Whether he killed himself or was shot has been debated.

Over 25,000 people attended his funeral, and some of the city's poor, whom he had helped, consider him a saint. After his death the Cali Cartel came to dominate the cocaine market until the mid-1990s.
pablo-morillo: Morillo was born to a peasant family in Fuentesecas and joined the Spanish Royal Marine Corps at 16. He fought at the Siege of Toulon in 1793, was taken prisoner when the San Isidro was captured at the Battle of Cape St. Vincent in 1797, and was wounded at the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805. When the Peninsular War broke out he joined the army, fought at the Battle of Bailen, and won fame at the Battle of Puente Sanpayo, where his troops forced Marshal Ney's French force to retreat and leave Galicia. He rose to field marshal during the war.

On 14 August 1814 Ferdinand VII gave him command of an expeditionary army, publicly bound for the Río de la Plata but secretly redirected to Venezuela and New Granada. It sailed from Cádiz on 17 February 1815 with 18 warships and 42 troopships carrying some 10,400 troops, most of them Peninsular veterans; the flagship San Pedro Alcántara exploded and sank on 25 April with a thousand crew. His 105-day siege of Cartagena earned him the title Count of Cartagena. In Santa Fe he revoked an amnesty granted by Miguel de la Torre, and more than a hundred republican officials were executed, among them Camilo Torres Tenorio, Francisco Jose de Caldas and Jorge Tadeo Lozano.

Back in Venezuela he fought Simón Bolívar to a stalemate and defeated him at the Third Battle of La Puerta in 1818, where he was wounded, earning the title Marquess of La Puerta. After the uprising of Rafael del Riego on 1 January 1820 stopped the reinforcements assembling at Cádiz, Morillo was ordered to have the colonies obey the Constitution of 1812. He met Bolívar at Santa Ana on 26 November 1820 and signed a six-month armistice and a second treaty on the conduct of the war.

In Spain he became Captain General of New Castile, supported the constitution during the Liberal Triennium, prevented a coup against it in 1822, and was defeated in the north in 1823 by the French invasion under the Duke of Angoulême. When Ferdinand VII restored absolute rule he went to France, later returning to serve in the Carlist Wars. He died at Barèges on 27 July 1837. His contemporaries knew him as El Pacificador.
pablo-neruda: Ricardo Eliécer Neftalí Reyes Basoalto was born on 12 July 1904 in Parral, about 350 km south of Santiago. His father, José del Carmen Reyes Morales, was a railway employee. His mother, the schoolteacher Rosa Neftalí Basoalto Opazo, died two months after his birth. He grew up in Temuco and composed his first poems in the winter of 1914.

His father opposed his interest in literature, but others encouraged him, among them the future Nobel laureate Gabriela Mistral, who headed the local school. On 18 July 1917, aged 13, he published an essay in the daily La Mañana under the name Neftalí Reyes. By mid-1920 he had adopted the pseudonym Pablo Neruda and was a published author of poems, prose and journalism. He is thought to have taken the name from the Czech poet Jan Neruda.

Neruda held diplomatic posts in Buenos Aires and Barcelona, then succeeded Mistral as consul in Madrid, where he became the centre of a literary circle that included Rafael Alberti, Federico García Lorca and César Vallejo. He later served as Consul General in Mexico City from 1940 to 1943. Back in Chile in 1943, he toured Peru and visited Machu Picchu, which inspired the 12-part poem Alturas de Macchu Picchu, completed in 1945, and later Canto General (1950).

Like many left-leaning intellectuals of his generation, Neruda came to admire the Soviet Union of Joseph Stalin, and he received the Stalin Peace Prize in 1953. His friend Octavio Paz later criticised this loyalty. When President Gabriel González Videla outlawed communism in 1948, a warrant was issued for the Communist senator's arrest. Friends hid him for 13 months, and in March 1949 he crossed the Andes on horseback into Argentina. He returned to Chile in August 1952 to support Salvador Allende's presidential campaign.

Under President Allende, Neruda served as ambassador to France. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1971, though some committee members had not forgotten his praise of Stalinist dictatorship. In September 1973 he was diagnosed with prostate cancer, and after the coup led by Augusto Pinochet he planned to go into exile in Mexico. He died at a clinic in Santiago on 23 September 1973, the day before he was to leave. The official cause was complications of prostate cancer, but the circumstances of his death have been investigated since 2011.

Neruda is often considered the national poet of Chile. His three houses, La Chascona in Santiago, La Sebastiana in Valparaíso and Casa de Isla Negra, are museums, and he and Matilde Urrutia are buried at Isla Negra.
pablo-picasso: Pablo Ruiz Picasso was born on 25 October 1881 in Málaga, Andalusia, the first child of José Ruiz y Blasco and María Picasso y López. His father was a painter of birds and other game and a professor at the School of Crafts. According to his mother, his first word was "piz, piz", short for lápiz, the Spanish word for pencil. From the age of seven he was trained by his father, a traditional academic artist, in figure drawing and oil painting. The family moved to A Coruña in 1891, and an apocryphal story relates that his father, seeing the precision of the thirteen-year-old's technique, felt his son had surpassed him.

His career as a painter can be said to have begun by 1894. The academic realism of the mid-1890s appears in The First Communion (1896), and a Modernist period followed in 1899–1900. After 1906 the Fauvist work of Henri Matisse pushed him towards more radical styles, beginning a rivalry between the two. The commonly accepted periods are the Blue Period (1901–1904), the Rose Period (1904–1906), the African-influenced Period (1907–1909), Analytic Cubism (1909–1912) and Synthetic Cubism (1912–1919). His works include Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907) and Guernica (1937). From 1909 to 1928 he made sculptural constructions from diverse materials, such as Guitar (1912) in sheet metal and wire. In 1944 he joined the French Communist Party, and he remained a member until his death.

Picasso died on 8 April 1973 in Mougins, France, of a heart attack, having painted until 3 a.m. the night before. He died without a will, which led to a feud over his estate. At his death there were more than 45,000 unsold works in his estate, among them 1,885 paintings, 1,228 sculptures and 3,222 ceramics. In 1971 he was the first living artist honoured with an exhibition in the Grand Gallery of the Louvre, for his 90th birthday.
pachacamac: Pachacamac lies about 40 kilometres southeast of Lima in the valley of the Lurín River and covers about 600 hectares. It was named after Pacha Kamaq, the Earth Maker, a creator god worshipped by the people of this part of Peru before the Inca conquest. The Inca took him into their pantheon, but never as an equal of Viracocha, whom they held to be more powerful. The surviving myths of Pacha Kamaq are sparse and confused. In one he made the first man and woman but forgot to give them food, and was later thrown into the sea by the hero Wichama and became the supreme god of fish.

The site flourished for about 1,300 years until the Spanish invasion. Its oldest building, the Old Temple, was raised in massive adobe brick under the influence of the Lima culture in the 3rd to 7th centuries CE. The Huari, around 600 to 800 CE, rebuilt the city, probably as an administrative centre. After the Huari empire collapsed Pachacamac kept growing as a religious centre, and most of its common temples and buildings date from about 800 to 1450. Ancient DNA and isotope analyses of feather ornaments from elite tombs show that the Ychsma, the rulers of the site, obtained live macaws and Amazon parrots from the Amazon basin, which points to long-distance trade that predated Inca rule.

The Inca took over the site around 1470. They made it an important religious and administrative centre, built five additional buildings including a temple of the sun on the main square, and allowed its priests to work independently of the Inca priesthood, including the oracle, whom the Inca presumably consulted. After the Battle of Cajamarca Francisco Pizarro sent his brother Hernando Pizarro with fourteen horsemen to collect its gold. Hernando left Cajamarca on 5 January 1533 and returned on 14 April 1533. According to Cieza, the priests had removed more than four hundred cargas of gold and hidden it, and it has never been found. Spanish settlers later pulled down the temple walls for building stone.

Archaeologists began exploring the site in the 1890s and found many large buildings and burial grounds already looted. Its sacred sector holds the Painted Temple, the Temple of the Sun and the Old Temple. The Ychsma pyramids of the second sector were long thought to be religious embassies for delegations from distant communities, but Peter Eeckhout concluded from his excavations that they were palaces of the Ychsma rulers. An Inca cemetery in the Temple of the Sun held women set apart as mamacuna, who had been strangled and buried with offerings from the highlands. Looting and El Niño have damaged the Temple of the Sun and many other pyramids.
pachacuti: Pachacuti was known as Cusi Yupanqui before he took his throne name, which in Quechua evokes pachakutiy, the turn of the world. According to the Spanish chroniclers he was born in Cusco at the palace of Cusicancha and was the son of the eighth ruler, Inca Viracocha. The historian María Rostworowski concluded from Andean customs of succession, which let the most able take power, that he was probably not Viracocha's son. His brother Inca Urco was the appointed co-ruler and heir. In the early 15th century, in the version most Spanish sources support, the Chankas invaded the Cusco confederation. Viracocha and Urco fled, while Cusi Yupanqui rallied the army and defended the city.

At the battle of Yahuar Pampa the Chankas were beaten. When Viracocha gave the honour of trampling the captives to Urco, Yupanqui refused, and Viracocha went into exile after a failed plot against him. Urco died in a short civil war and Yupanqui was crowned Sapa Inca as Pachacuti. Since the early 1980s most scholars have treated the Chanka war as largely mythical, following Pierre Duviols, and some regard Pachacuti himself as a representation of the start of imperial expansion.

The Incas did not count years systematically, so the dates are approximations. Pachacuti conquered the chiefdoms around Cusco and took Chincha on the south-central coast. His army defeated the Colla at Ayaviri and received the submission of the Lupaca, Pacasa and Azangaro peoples, and his generals pressed north to the Cajamarca chiefdom, bringing tension with the Chimú Empire. Local lords were bound by reciprocal gifts, and women from Cusco were given to chiefs as principal wives so that their children would rule.

He ordered painted panels to record the history of earlier rulers, and is credited with irrigation networks, terraces, roads and hospices. He moved hundreds of thousands of people to colonise remote edges of the empire. These forced settlers were called mitimaes. Most archaeologists now believe Machu Picchu was built as an estate for him.

Pachacuti named his son Amaru Yupanqui co-ruler, then replaced him with Tupac Yupanqui as lacking military ability. He died in 1471 of a terminal illness. His deeds were kept in genealogical histories and quipus near his royal mummy. He is also credited with the Sacred Hymns of the Situa ceremony.
pachamama: Pachamama, or Mama Pacha, is the Andean deity representing space-time, revered by the peoples of the Andes. In Inca mythology and religion she is a mother goddess, linked to space, time, the universe, life, fertility and nature. The word comes from Quechua: pacha means world, universe, space-time or cosmos, and mama means mother. In various myths she is the wife of Pachacámac and the mother of Mama Quilla, the goddess of the moon, and of Inti, the god of the sun. She was commonly worshipped in her earthly form as Allpamama, or goddess of the earth; her shrines consisted of sacred rocks or tree trunks, and artists showed her as a woman bearing harvests of potatoes or coca leaves.

Pachamama is normally loving and generous, but she can be terrible and destructive when she is upset or hurt. She is said not to need temples or specific places of worship, since she is everywhere, though she likes springs. Fertility is a vital matter for Andean people, extending to the flowering of crops, the arrival of spring and the reproduction of animals. In exchange for her help, the shepherd of the southern Puna is obliged to offer part of what he receives, establishing a kind of reciprocity known as ayni. Allpamama is often hungry, and if she is not fed with offerings or is offended, she can cause a cosmic imbalance.

The central ritual is the Challa or Pago, meaning payment, carried out during all of August, when ritual is especially abundant before the sowing season, and in many places also on the first Friday of each month. People spill a little chicha on the ground for the goddess and drink the rest. Another day of worship is Martes de challa, which coincides with Shrove Tuesday.

After the Spanish colonisation of the Americas, the native populations were converted to Roman Catholicism, and through religious syncretism the figure of the Virgin Mary was associated with Pachamama for many Indigenous peoples. Many rituals are practised together with those of Christianity, so that many families are at once Christian and pachamamistas. According to the scholar Manuel Marzal, in Peru the cult has in some cases taken on Christian characteristics, and for some Andeans Pachamama has become a symbol of the providence of one God.

Pope John Paul II, in two homilies delivered in Peru and Bolivia, on 3 February 1985 and 11 May 1988, described homage to Pachamama as an ancestral recognition of divine providence. Many Indigenous peoples in South America base environmental concerns on these beliefs, saying that problems arise when people take too much from nature because they are taking too much from Pachamama.
pachomius-the-great: Pachomius was born around 292 in the Thebaid, near modern Luxor, to pagan parents. According to his hagiography, at the age of 21 he was swept up in a Roman army recruitment drive and put on a ship down the Nile with other youths. At Thebes he met local Christians, who brought food and comfort daily to the conscripts, and he vowed to investigate Christianity once free. He left the army without having to fight, moved to the village of Sheneset in Upper Egypt, and was converted and baptised in 314.

He then studied for seven years under the hermit Palaemon, and afterwards lived as a hermit near Anthony of Egypt, whose practices he imitated. According to the Bohairic Life, he heard a voice at the deserted village of Tabennisi telling him to dwell there and build a monastery, for many would come to be monks with him.

Pachomius established his first monastery between 318 and 323 at Tabennisi. His elder brother John joined him, and soon more than 100 monks lived nearby. Until then Christian asceticism had been solitary, with monastics living in individual huts or caves and meeting only for occasional worship. Pachomius created the cenobitic community, in which men or women lived together and held property in common under an abbot or abbess. A second monastery was founded at Pbow, which became the centre of the monasteries rising along the Nile in Upper Egypt, and after 336 he spent most of his time there.

He was the first to set down a written monastic rule. It began with prayers in general use, such as the Lord's Prayer, and was later elaborated with precepts from the Bible. It sought to balance prayer with work and communal life with solitude, the day being organised around the liturgy with time for manual work and devotional reading. Fasts and work were apportioned according to each monk's strength, and each received the same food and clothing. Jerome translated the rule into Latin, and Basil the Great and Benedict of Nursia adapted parts of it.

Neither Pachomius nor his monks became priests. Athanasius visited in 333 and wished to ordain him, but Pachomius fled. Pachomius continued as abbot for some thirty years. During an epidemic, probably of plague, he called the monks together, strengthened their faith and appointed no successor. He died on 9 May 348. By then eight monasteries and several hundred monks followed his guidance, and the number of monks, though not of monasteries, may have reached 7,000. Within a generation cenobitic practice spread from Egypt to Palestine, the Judean Desert, Syria, North Africa and eventually Western Europe. Coptic churches keep his feast on 9 May.
pachuca: Pachuca, formally Pachuca de Soto, is the capital and largest city of the state of Hidalgo, about 90 kilometres north of Mexico City. It lies in a small valley almost surrounded by hills, and its nickname, La Bella Airosa, refers to the strong winds that blow through the canyons to the north. In the Otomi language it is Nju̱nthe. Its official name honours Manuel Fernando Soto, a congressman credited with founding the state, and Benito Juárez declared it the capital of Hidalgo in 1869. The origin of the word pachuca is not agreed.

People mined green obsidian in the Sierra de Pachuca, at Cerro de las Navajas, as early as 12,000 BCE. Artifacts from between 200 and 850 CE show Teotihuacan influence, and it has been argued that Teotihuacan monopolised the deposit to control the obsidian trade of central Mexico. The obsidian was prized in pre-Columbian times and traded as far as Spiro Mounds in the United States. The Spanish began mining silver here in the mid-16th century, and the city remained a major mining centre until the mid-20th century.

From 1824 Cornish miners and English investors came to Pachuca and nearby Real del Monte; some founded the Compañía Real de Monte y Pachuca. Ships carrying 125 passengers and about 1,500 tons of equipment sailed from Falmouth and reached Veracruz three months later, and the trek inland killed about half the miners and their families, many from malaria and yellow fever. The survivors brought high-pressure steam pumping engines of the kind designed by Richard Trevithick, which turned flooded mines into large silver producers. They also brought football and the pasty, known in Pachuca as pastes, which became defining features of the city.

A manufacturing sector, set up in the 1950s, has changed the city's mining image. The last Pachuca mine to close was El Álamo, in 1993. The Universidad Autónoma del Estado de Hidalgo, the state's oldest educational institution, began in 1869 as the Instituto Literario y Escuela de Artes y Oficios. The Monumental Clock, 40 metres high, was donated by the Cornishman Francis Rule and inaugurated on 15 September 1910 for the centennial of Mexican independence. The English Cemetery holds about 600 graves, mostly of Cornish miners and their families, and many of their descendants still live in the area.
pacific-ocean: The Pacific is the largest and deepest of Earth's five oceanic divisions. It covers about 165,250,000 square kilometres, taking the definition with an Antarctic southern border, which is about 46% of Earth's water surface. Its mean depth is 4,000 metres, and the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, at 10,928 metres, is the deepest known point in the world. More than 25,000 islands rise above its surface, many of them the remains of volcanoes, and the Ring of Fire, a belt of explosive volcanism above subduction zones, surrounds it.

Modern humans first reached the western Pacific around 60,000 to 70,000 years ago. They crossed from Sundaland to Sahul, a sea journey of at least 80 kilometres, to reach Australia, probably on large bamboo rafts, although the level of maritime technology is not known with certainty. Settlement of Buka by 32,000 years ago and Manus by 25,000 years ago confirms their seafaring skill. Their descendants include the Negritos, Melanesians and Indigenous Australians.

In 1513 the Spanish explorer Vasco Núñez de Balboa crossed the Isthmus of Panama and sighted what he called the Mar del Sur, the Southern Sea. The present name was given by Ferdinand Magellan during the Spanish circumnavigation of 1520, when he met favourable winds and called it Mar Pacífico, the peaceful sea. From 1946 to 1958 the Marshall Islands served as the Pacific Proving Grounds designated by the United States, where 67 nuclear tests were conducted.

The Pacific is divided by the equator into the North and South Pacific. Its marginal seas include the Philippine Sea, the South China Sea, the East China Sea, the Sea of Japan, the Sea of Okhotsk, the Bering Sea, the Tasman Sea and the Coral Sea. The Bering Strait joins it to the Arctic Ocean, and the Drake Passage and Strait of Magellan link it to the Atlantic. It is the only ocean mostly bounded by subduction zones.
pacific-war: The Pacific War was the theatre of the Second World War fought between the Empire of Japan and the Allies in East and Southeast Asia, the Pacific and Indian Oceans and Oceania. It was the largest theatre geographically and included some of the largest naval battles in history. War between Japan and China had begun in 1937, and Japan had invaded Manchuria in 1931, but the Pacific War is more widely held to have begun in 1941, when the United States and the United Kingdom were drawn in. Japanese strategists had concluded as early as 1935 that the oil of the Dutch East Indies was crucial to expansion, and Japan invaded French Indochina in 1940.

On 7 and 8 December 1941 Japan struck simultaneously at Pearl Harbor, the Philippines, Guam, Wake Island, Malaya, Singapore and Hong Kong. At Pearl Harbor eight American battleships were put out of action and 2,403 Americans were killed, but the three American aircraft carriers were at sea. Over six months Japan took the territories it had attacked, together with the Dutch East Indies, Burma and parts of New Guinea.

The Battle of the Coral Sea in May 1942 turned back an invasion force bound for Port Moresby, and the Battle of Midway in June is considered a key turning point. Allied offensives began in August 1942 on Guadalcanal and New Guinea. The Allied strategy of island hopping followed, with landings in the Gilbert and Marshall Islands, the Marianas and Palau, Iwo Jima and Okinawa. After the Battle of Leyte Gulf in October 1944 the Japanese fleet turned to kamikaze attacks. Of the 117,000 Okinawan and Japanese troops defending Okinawa, 94 percent died.

The United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 and Nagasaki on 9 August, and the Soviet Union invaded Manchuria on 9 August. Japan accepted the Potsdam terms on 15 August and signed the surrender document on 2 September. It lost its possessions in Asia and the Pacific and was occupied by the Allies until 1952. Total American losses were 161,000 killed and 248,000 wounded. About 2,121,000 Japanese military personnel died between 1937 and 1945, according to a 1964 Japanese report. Japanese forces killed millions of non-combatants, including prisoners of war, and at least 20 million Chinese died during the Second Sino-Japanese War.
pact-of-biak-na-bato: The pact was signed on 14 December 1897 to end the Philippine Revolution. It was concluded in San Miguel, Bulacan, in the house of Pablo Tecson, a revolutionary captain who served as a brigadier general in the Brigada Del Pilar of General Gregorio del Pilar. Aguinaldo and his fellow leaders were granted amnesty and a money indemnity, and Aguinaldo had decided to use the money to buy firearms and ammunition for a later return to the islands.

Writing in 1899, Aguinaldo said that he and any associates who wished could live in any foreign country, and that he chose Hong Kong. An indemnity of $MXN800,000 was to be paid to him personally in three instalments: 400,000 when the arms at Biak-na-Bato were handed over, 200,000 when 800 stand of arms had been surrendered, and the rest at 1,000 stand, with a Te Deum sung in Manila Cathedral for the return of peace.

Two Spanish generals were to be held as hostages until he reached Hong Kong and received the first payment. He added that the expulsion of the religious corporations had also been agreed, but that Primo de Rivera asked for it to be left out of the treaty to spare Spain criticism.

The historian Teodoro Agoncillo describes three documents, known together as the Truce of Biak-na-Bato, which also promised a further $MXN900,000 to the families of non-combatant Filipinos who had suffered in the fighting. Sonia M. Zaide names them the Program, the Act of Agreement and a third document on the indemnity, a total of 1,700,000.

Under the first part of the pact, Aguinaldo and twenty-five other leaders of the revolution left for Hong Kong carrying $MXN400,000. The men who stayed behind received 200,000, but the third instalment was never paid. No general amnesty was ever declared, and sporadic skirmishes continued in the islands.
pact-of-steel: Germany and Italy had fought on opposite sides in the First World War. Italy at first opposed German designs on Austria, signed the Rome Protocols of 1934 and joined the Stresa Front. Its isolation after the Abyssinia Crisis left it without major allies, and on 23 October 1936 Italy and Germany signed a secret protocol aligning their policies on the Spanish Civil War, the League of Nations and Abyssinia.

The pact was first drafted as a three-way alliance with Japan, which wished it to be aimed at the Soviet Union, while Germany and Italy wanted it directed at the British Empire and France. Germany feared that an anti-Soviet alliance would risk a two-front war before it could conquer Western Europe, and Japan stood aside. The original name, Pact of Blood, was changed to Pact of Steel when Mussolini was told it would be badly received in Italy.

The foreign ministers Joachim von Ribbentrop and Galeazzo Ciano signed the pact on 22 May 1939. Under the third article, if one party became involved in military complications with another power, the other would come to its side as an ally with all its military might on land, at sea and in the air. The fifth bound both to conclude any armistice or peace only in full agreement, and the seventh set its first period at ten years. A secret supplementary protocol urged closer military and economic cooperation and joint work on the press and propaganda. The treaty rested on the assumption that war would not come within three years.

Together with the Anti-Comintern Pact and the Tripartite Pact, the Pact of Steel was one of the three agreements that formed the main basis of the Axis alliance. When Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, Italy was not prepared and had difficulty meeting its obligations. It entered the Second World War only in June 1940, with an invasion of southern France.

The pact did not last its ten years. After the invasion of Sicily in July 1943 Mussolini was overthrown, and the new government under Marshal Pietro Badoglio signed an armistice with the Allies in September, ending Italy's real part in the pact. The Italian Social Republic, a puppet state under Mussolini in northern Italy, remained a member in name only.
pact-of-umar: Scholars disagree about where the text comes from. Anver M. Emon notes intense discussion over whether it dates from the reign of Umar ibn al-Khattab or was a later invention tied to his name to give the contract of dhimma greater weight, and some historians see it as a compilation that grew over several centuries. Bernard Lewis judged that the document itself can hardly be authentic. Its versions are addressed to different people: some to Umar, others to Muslim generals such as Abu Ubayda.

Norman Stillman wrote that many of its provisions were elaborated only over time, some going back to the early conquests and others added as Muslims settled more permanently. A. S. Tritton, who printed several versions in Caliphs and Their Non-Muslim Subjects, thought it a later construction because other early treaties lack it, while Daniel C. Dennett argued that the version kept by al-Tabari could record a genuine early agreement. Abraham P. Bloch held that Umar's name was wrongly tied to the restrictions, and Thomas Walker Arnold that later generations added to them.

In the best-known version the Christians of a city write to Umar as Leader of the Faithful. Besides the bans on new churches, crosses in public, weapons and saddles, they promise not to restore places of worship in need of repair, to lodge Muslim travellers for three days, not to teach their children the Qur'an, and not to prevent any of their own people from becoming Muslims.

They also undertake to give up their seats to Muslims, to ring church bells only quietly, not to raise their voices at funerals or carry torches through Muslim streets, not to bury their dead beside Muslims, not to sell liquor and not to buy captives taken by Muslims. The text ends by declaring that if they break these conditions their protection is void.
pact-of-zanjon: The Ten Years' War, the armed struggle of Cubans for independence from the Spanish Empire, had gone on since 1868. General Arsenio Martínez Campos arrived in Cuba as Spanish commander two years before the pact and at once sought to come to terms with the rebels. On 10 February 1878 negotiators for the rebels gathered at Zanjón, a village in Camagüey Province, and signed the document he offered. The end of hostilities was no military victory for either side, but a recognition by both of their mutual exhaustion.

The pact promised Cuba the same status under Spain as Puerto Rico, notably some representation in the Spanish parliament, and greater freedom of the press and of assembly. It granted a general amnesty for political offences since 1868, freeing those imprisoned for them and Spanish deserters, though freed leaders had to leave Cuba, and guaranteed everyone the right to leave the island. Among those released were José Martí and Juan Gualberto Gomez; Calixto Garcia, freed from prison in Spain, went to Paris to raise funds for the next phase of the independence movement. The pact also promised an eventual end to slavery in 1888; in the event slavery in Cuba ended in October 1886.

In the years that followed many new political and fraternal organisations were founded, union activity developed, a liberal autonomist party that sought reform without independence grew, and new Black organisations pursued civil rights. The peace proved more a truce than a treaty. Maceo's group in Oriente argued its case without success at Baraguá on 15 March, and hostilities ended on 28 May 1878, after Maceo had left for Jamaica. The rebellion was briefly renewed in August 1879, Spain abandoned most of its commitments, and a guerrilla war simmered until the Cuban War of Independence broke out in 1895.
pacta-conventa-croatia: After Petar Snačić, the last Croatian king of Croat descent, was killed in battle in 1097, the Croats refused to submit, and an agreement was made, probably in 1102, to end the war. The Croatian nobles are said to have concluded it with King Coloman before his coronation as king of Croatia in Biograd. The document, also called Qualiter after its first word, was found in a library in Trogir and is kept in the Hungarian National Museum in Budapest. It names the twelve noble tribes, among them the Čudomirić, Gusić, Kačić, Šubić and Snačić families.

Under its terms the signatory nobles kept their possessions undisturbed and were exempt from tax and tribute to the king. In return each of the twelve tribes was to answer the king's call when his borders were attacked and send at least ten armed horsemen at its own cost as far as the Drava River, Croatia's northern boundary with Hungary; beyond it the king paid the expenses.

Whatever the text's origin, the relationship it describes held in practice. From 1102 until 1918 the kings of Hungary were also kings of Croatia and were represented there by a ban, while Croatia kept its own parliament, the Sabor, and considerable autonomy.

Historians have disagreed over the document since the 19th century. Milan Šufflay first called it an outright forgery and later a 14th-century addendum to the manuscript of Thomas the Archdeacon; János Karácsonyi and Nada Klaić judged it a 14th-century forgery, Ljudmil Hauptmann dated it to the 13th century, Miho Barada and Marko Kostrenčić to 1102, and Stjepan Antoljak called it an incomplete source but not a forgery. Klaić held that the Trogir text described relations between king and nobles in the 14th century and traced them back to an original agreement.

The question is tied to the wider dispute over the union. Croatians long held that their kingdom remained a separate state sharing a ruler with Hungary, a view some Hungarian historians accept, while some Hungarian and Serbian historians hold that Hungary annexed Croatia outright in 1102. Matjaž Klemenčič and Mitja Žagar argue that the story of the pact served later to support Croatian claims to statehood within the Habsburg monarchy.
pactolus: The Pactolus, in Ancient Greek Pakṭōlos, was also called Chrysorrhoas, streaming with gold. Its modern name, Sart Çayı, means the Sardis stream, after the ancient city through whose ruins it runs on its way from Mount Tmolus to the Gediz River, the ancient Hermus, near the Aegean coast of Turkey. The electrum it once carried was the basis of the economy of Lydia, and the first coins were minted from this natural alloy of gold and silver under Alyattes of Lydia. The historian Herodotus held that the gold in the river's sediments was the source of the wealth of King Croesus, son of Alyattes.

Pseudo-Plutarch, in De fluviis of the second century CE, wrote that the river was first called Chrysorrhoas because, according to legend, Chrysorrhoas, a son of Apollo, threw himself into its waters. Later Greek mythology explained the change of name through Pactolus, son of Leucothea, who at a festival of Aphrodite failed to recognise his own sister, Demodice of Lydia, and ravished her; overwhelmed by grief when he learned what he had done, he too threw himself into the river.

As a river god, Pactolus was said to be the brother of the river Hydaspes and so a child of the Titans Oceanus and Tethys, and the father of Euryanassa, one of the women named as mother of the children of Tantalus. The only myth in which he takes an active part is told in the Dionysiaca of Nonnus, in the account of the young Dionysus and his Indian campaign. In the Philoctetes of Sophocles the chorus hails Gaia as ruler of the golden stream Pactolus, and the Roman poet Sextus Propertius has the waters of the Pactolus staining the Lydian fields.
padishah-khatun: Padishah Khatun, whose name was Safwat al-Din Khatun, was born in 1256, the youngest daughter of Qutb al-Din, who died in 1257, and Kutlugh Turkan. She held her own fief of Sirjan after her mother attended the coronation of Abaqa in 1265, and on 22 May 1272 she married Abaqa Khan, a match her mother arranged to secure Mongol support. She converted from Islam to Buddhism on her marriage and was granted the household of Abaqa's late mother Yesunjin. She backed her mother against her siblings Muzaffar al-Din Hajjaj in 1276 and Suyurghatmish in 1280.

After Abaqa's death in 1282 she stayed at court with her mother, who died in 1283, and sent her sister Bibi Khatun to guard her interests in Kirman. Through her influence on Arghun she won a share in the rule of Kirman in 1284, but the vizier Buqa favoured Suyurghatmish, had her married to Gaykhatu and removed her to Anatolia in 1286. When Gaykhatu was elected in 1291, she asked for Kirman as her personal fief, and he agreed.

She imprisoned her half-brother Suyurghatmish in October 1292; he escaped with the help of his wife Kurdujin Khatun, was imprisoned again and was strangled on 21 August 1294. She was granted the rule of Yazd and Shabankara as well, and in Ormus replaced the prince Rukn al-Din Masud with Sayf al-Din Ayaz. Her coins struck in Kerman named Gaykhatu as overlord with the title Padishah-I Jahan, ruler of the world.

After Gaykhatu was assassinated on 21 March 1295, she was imprisoned on the orders of Kurdujin Khatun and Shah Alam, Suyurghatmish's widow and daughter, and strangled on her way to Baydu's court at Kushk-e Zar in June or July 1295. She was buried in the Gonbad-e Sabz Mausoleum. Marco Polo described her as an ambitious and clever woman who put her own brother to death as a rival. She wrote Persian poetry under the pseudonyms Lala Khatun and Hasanshah and was skilled in calligraphy.
padmasambhava: Padmasambhava, whose name means Born from a Lotus, is described as a tantric Buddhist master whose life is known largely from later tradition. One of the earliest chronicle sources is the Testament of Ba, which records the founding of Samye monastery under King Trisong Detsen. Manuscripts from Dunhuang also mention a tantric master of that name who tames demons. Earlier Tibetologists questioned his historicity; according to Lewis Doney it is now cautiously accepted.

His life story grew mainly from the 12th century. The first full biography, the Copper Palace, is a treasure text said to have been revealed by Nyangrel Nyima Özer (1124–1192). It tells that he appeared as an eight-year-old child in a lotus blossom on Lake Dhanakosha in the kingdom of Oddiyana; other accounts have him born from the womb of Queen Jalendra.

In the Testament of Ba the Indian abbot Śāntarakṣita, invited by Trisong Detsen to Tibet, helped plan the first monastery at Samye, but a flooded temple and a lightning strike on the palace convinced some at court that the local gods were angry. The later hagiographies tell how Padmasambhava was invited, subdued the spirits and demons of Tibet and made them guardians of Buddhism, the deity Pe har becoming protector of Samye. He is also said to have initiated the king into tantric rites.

Because of his part in founding Samye he is regarded as the founder of the Nyingma, the Ancients, school of Tibetan Buddhism. Tradition names Yeshe Tsogyal and Mandarava among his students. Bhutan has many pilgrimage places linked with him, the best known being the Tiger's Nest monastery at Paro, built around a cave where he is said to have meditated.

Tradition holds that his teachings pass down as an oral lineage and as hidden treasure texts, or terma, concealed for later discoverers called tertöns, to whom he is said to appear in visions. The Bardo Thodol, the Tibetan Book of the Dead, is held to be one of these, found by Karma Lingpa (1326–1386). He is closely associated with the kila dagger, and the Vajra Guru mantra and the Seven Line Prayer, which many Tibetans recite daily, are addressed to him. His life is shown in masked cham dances, and he is venerated in Tibet, Nepal, Bhutan and the Himalayan regions of India.
padmavat: Padmavati, princess of the Singhal kingdom, is friends with the talking parrot Hiraman, who flees her father's anger and becomes the pet of Ratansen of Chittor. Inspired by the parrot's account of her beauty, Ratansen crosses the seven seas with 16,000 followers, and after the god Shiva advises him to attack the fortress of Singhal, he wins her from her father Gandharvsen. On the way home a sea storm, sent to punish his pride, kills his followers. In Chittor Padmavati and his first wife Nagmati vie for his attention, and the Brahmin courtier Raghav Chetan, banished for cheating in a contest, goes to the court of Alauddin Khalji.

Alauddin besieges Chittor, glimpses Padmavati by deceit and carries Ratansen to Delhi; the vassals Gora and Badal free him, Gora dying in the escape. Ratansen and Devpal Singh of Kumbhalner, who had proposed marriage to Padmavati, then kill each other in single combat, and the women of the fort commit jauhar before Alauddin takes an empty fortress.

Padmavat is the oldest extant text among the important works in Awadhi, and was first written in the Persian Nastaʿlīq script. Its earliest surviving manuscript is a Nastaliq copy made in 1675 at Amroha by Muhammad Shakir, found in Rampur with interlinear Persian translations; others are in Kaithi and Nagari, and the Kaithi copies add many verses. Mataprasad Gupta published a critical edition based on five manuscripts. Historians differ on its history. Kishori Saran Lal held that only Alauddin's capture of Chittor and the jauhar of its women are historical, while Banarsi Prasad Saksena thought even the jauhar a fabrication, since Amir Khusrau does not mention one at Chittor.

The earliest known adaptation is Prem Nama (1590) of Hansa Dakkani, a court poet of Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur, and twelve adaptations exist in Persian and Urdu, among them the Rat-Padam (1618) and the Shama-wa-parwanah (1658). Hemratan's Gora Badal Padmini Chaupai of about 1589 was the first popular Rajput version. The poem shaped Alaol's 17th-century Bengali epic Padmavati and was the ultimate source of Albert Roussel's opera Padmâvatî (1923) and of the 2018 film Padmaavat.
padri-war: Islam had been spread in the Minangkabau lands from about 1692 by Sheikh Burhanuddin Ulakan of the Shattari Sufi school. Many students of the Sufi scholar Tuanku Nan Tuo, appointed religious head of Koto Tuo in 1784, were returning pilgrims influenced by the ideals of the Wahabi movement, and they called themselves Padri. Around 1803 three scholars back from Mecca, Haji Miskin, Haji Sumanik and Haji Piobang, called for stricter Islamic law, and with Tuanku Nan Renceh and others they became known as the Harimau Nan Salapan, the Tigers of Eight. The Padri forbade cock-fighting, gambling and opium, forced women to cover themselves and punished dissent with death.

Tuanku Nan Tuo rejected their violence, and the Padri burnt Shattari villages, killed scholars and waged war on Koto Tuo from 1815. In the same year they attacked the Pagaruyung Kingdom, forcing Sultan Arifin Muningsyah to flee; Thomas Stamford Raffles found only the burnt remains of the palace in 1818.

On 21 February 1821 the nobility made a deal with the Dutch at Padang, ceding Simawang and Sulit Air, and on 4 March 1822 Lieutenant Colonel Raaff drove the Padri out of Pagaruyung. The Padri won several battles, among them Baso in 1822 and Sulit Air in 1825, and the Treaty of Masang ended the fighting for some years while the Dutch dealt with the Diponegoro War in Java. Christine Dobbin sees the war as largely a trade war, driven by Dutch wish to control the expanding coffee cultivation of the interior.

From 1831 the Dutch took Lintau and the Agam region and pushed the Padri back on Bonjol. In 1833 nobles and Padri began to make common cause, and on 11 January Dutch posts were attacked and many soldiers killed. Governor General Johannes van den Bosch demanded that Bonjol fall in 1833, but the assault failed. After a long siege and a final campaign under Major General Cochius with troops from Java, Madura, Bugis, Ambon and Africa, Tajadi Hill fell on 15 August 1837 and Fort Bonjol the next day, though Tuanku Imam Bonjol escaped with some followers.

The victory tightened Dutch control of West Sumatra. After the war traditional and religious leaders drew closer, and their reconciliation spread the principle adat basandi syara', syara' basandi Kitabullah: custom founded upon Islamic law, and Islamic law upon the Qur'an. The Padri movement is regarded as one of the precursors of the 19th-century Salafiyya and influenced the Muhammadiyyah movement of South East Asia.
padua: Padua lies on the banks of the Bacchiglione, 40 kilometres west of Venice and 29 kilometres south-east of Vicenza, in the Venetian Plain. The Brenta River, which once ran through the city, still touches its northern districts, and the Euganaean Hills to the south-west appear in poems by Petrarch and Percy Bysshe Shelley. The origin of the Roman name Patavium is uncertain; it may be connected with Padus, the ancient name of the Po, or with a Gaulish word for pine.

According to a tradition at least as old as Virgil and Livy, the Trojan prince Antenor founded Padua around 1183 BCE, leading the Eneti or Veneti to the Euganean plain. When a stone sarcophagus was dug up in 1274, officials of the medieval commune declared its remains to be Antenor's. Attila sacked the city savagely in 450. It then fell to the Gothic kings Odoacer and Theodoric, was reconquered by the Byzantine Empire in 540 and passed to the Lombards in 568. The Magyars sacked it in 899.

In the early eleventh century the citizens established a constitution with a general council and an executive body, and in 1138 the government was entrusted to two consuls. Jacopo da Carrara was elected lord of Padua in 1318, and nine members of the Carrara family ruled until 1405, apart from short periods under the Scaligeri and Giangaleazzo Visconti. Padua came under the Republic of Venice in 1405 and stayed under it until 1797, except for a few weeks in 1509 during the wars of the League of Cambrai.

After 1797 the city passed to the Habsburgs, then to the Kingdom of Italy in 1806 and, from 1814, to Lombardy-Venetia under Austria. It was annexed to Italy in 1866. Padua was the Italian army's main command in the First World War, and the armistice with Austria was signed at Villa Giusti in Padua on 3 November 1918.

Padua is the capital of its province, with 208,202 inhabitants. It has two UNESCO World Heritage entries, its Botanical Garden, the world's oldest, and its fourteenth-century frescoes, among them Giotto's cycle of 1305 in the Scrovegni Chapel. The University of Padua, founded in 1222, is one of the oldest in the world; Galileo Galilei observed Jupiter's moons from Padua in 1610, and in 1678 Elena Lucrezia Cornaro Piscopia became the first woman in the world to graduate from a university.
paekchong: In the Goryeo period the groups later called paekchŏng were known as the yangsuch'ŏk, such'ŏk, hwach'ŏk or mujari. They are said to have descended from Jurchen or Khitan peoples present since the start of Goryeo, lived in temporary dwellings as they moved about, were concentrated in Pyongan and Hwanghae provinces and were left out of the national register. The scholar Chŏng Yagyong recorded the theory that they were of Tatar origin, a general name for northern peoples, and described the yangsuch'ŏk as a people hardly assimilated, who made and sold willow baskets, slaughtered animals and liked to hunt.

King Sejong's settlement did not change their lives easily: many settled but did not farm, and went on making wicker goods, slaughtering, singing and dancing, while officials ignored the king's instructions and others regarded their customs as despicable and even criminal. Throughout much of the Joseon dynasty they were forced to serve as executioners. Near its end they formed a mutual aid body, the Sŭngdongdoga, which at times represented them in legal matters. After the Kabo Reform their family registers remained separate, marked with the word for butcher or a red dot, and rules of 1896 let others become licensed butchers, cutting into one of the few trades open to them.

The Tonghak rebels of 1894 demanded among other things that the paekchŏng no longer be forced to wear discriminatory hats, and in 1900 leaders from 16 counties petitioned the mayor of Jinju to be allowed to dress like others.

The Hyeongpyeongsa was formed by wealthy or educated paekchŏng and non-paekchŏng reformers, calling for the abolition of classes and of contemptuous names. In 1925 leadership passed from its original Jinju faction, which stressed education, to Seoul intellectuals more concerned with economic reform, and after members were arrested in 1927 over an underground nationalist group it moved to the socialist left. Young radicals were later charged with founding a secret communist Hyeongpyeongsa Youth Vanguard and acquitted after a four-year trial, a case that appears to have been constructed by the Japanese authorities. The movement then shifted to the right before disbanding. Today the word is used in the names of Korean barbecue restaurants without a negative sense.
paestum: According to Strabo, Poseidonia was founded by Achaeans from Sybaris; Solinus calls it a Dorian colony. No ancient source gives a date, but the archaeological evidence points to about 600 BCE. When Croton conquered Sybaris in 510 BCE, Poseidonia probably sheltered refugees. Strabo says the Lucanians conquered the city late in the fifth century BCE, and the evidence suggests that the Greek and Oscan cultures then thrived side by side.

The city became the Roman Paestum in 273 BCE, after the Pyrrhic War, in which the Poseidonians had sided with King Pyrrhus of Epirus against Rome. It stayed loyal to Rome during Hannibal's invasion and was rewarded with special favours, including its own coinage. It became a bishopric around 400 CE. Decline began between the fourth and seventh centuries, probably through changes in drainage that brought malarial swamp, with pirate raids perhaps also a cause. The site was abandoned in the Middle Ages and left largely forgotten until the eighteenth century.

Its fame rests on three temples in the Archaic Doric order, dating from about 550 to 450 BCE and in excellent preservation. The first Temple of Hera, about 550 BCE, is the oldest and was long called the Basilica by eighteenth-century scholars who thought it Roman. The Temple of Athena, about 500 BCE, mixes Doric and Ionic features and was used as a church in the Middle Ages. The second Temple of Hera, about 460 to 450 BCE, keeps most of its entablature. Walls about 4.75 kilometres long, a Roman forum and a small amphitheatre also survive; of about 120 hectares, only 25 have been excavated.

The Tomb of the Diver, found in 1968 and dated to about 470 BCE, is the only known Greek tomb of its period with frescoes of human figures, and it is displayed in the site's national museum. The ruins came to wide notice in the eighteenth century, and Piranesi's etchings of 1778 spread their influence on Greek Revival architecture.
pagan-min: Born Maung Biddhu Khyit on 21 June 1811, he was the ninth king of the Konbaung dynasty. His father Tharrawaddy made him Prince of Pagan in August 1842, and he became king when Tharrawaddy died on 17 November 1846. He won the struggle for the succession by having his rival brothers killed, and his chief ministers, Maung Baing Zat and Maung Bhein, enriched themselves by executing wealthy subjects.

In 1851 Maung Ok, the governor of Pegu, charged the captains of two British merchant ships with murder, embezzlement and evading customs, fined them 500 rupees and kept them until their debts were paid. Lord Dalhousie, the governor-general of British India, sent Commodore George Lambert to demand £920 in compensation and Maung Ok's dismissal, and Pagan Min replaced the governor. On 6 January 1852, after Lambert had seized a Burmese royal ship and the new governor refused to meet a British delegation, British subjects were evacuated and Lambert blockaded the coast at Rangoon, which his warships were soon bombarding.

Pagan Min protested to Dalhousie on 7 February, and on 13 February Dalhousie demanded the equivalent of £100,000 for the cost of preparing for war, to be paid by 1 April. The ultimatum went unanswered, British troops entered Burmese territory and quickly routed the king's forces, and Britain annexed the province of Pegu in December.

His half-brother Mindon, who opposed the war, fled with his brother Kanaung to Shwebo and raised a rebellion. After a few weeks of fighting the chief minister Magwe Mingyi went over to Mindon, and Pagan Min gave up the throne to him on 18 February 1853. Mindon spared his life, released the European prisoners and sought peace with the British, though he refused to sign a treaty giving up Burmese territory. Pagan Min died of smallpox during the reign of King Thibaw.
pagaruyung: Pagaruyung lies in Tanjung Emas subdistrict of Tanah Datar regency, near the town of Batusangkar. Its name derives from a Minangkabau name for the nibung or ruyung tree, and the kingdom it named was also called Malayapura; the seal of Sultan Tunggul Alam Bagagar calls it Pagaruyung Darul Qarar. The highlands around it were long reputed rich in gold. In 1684 the Portuguese explorer Thomas Dias, sent by the Dutch governor-general in Malacca, reported, probably from hearsay, a palace entered through three gates and a people who lived by gold panning and agriculture.

An inscription carved on the back of the Amoghapasa statue records that Adityawarman proclaimed himself king in Malayapura in 1347. He is believed to have ruled central Sumatra until about 1375, at first as a vassal king of Majapahit and most likely to control the gold trade. Inscribed stones and statues of his reign were found at Bukit Gombak, a hill near the village where a royal palace is believed to have stood. By the 16th century royal power was shared by three kings, of the world, of custom and of religion, known together as the Rajo Tigo Selo.

Islam spread through teachers from Aceh and Malacca, and in the 17th century the kingdom became a sultanate. Early in that century it was forced to recognise the Sultanate of Aceh, but the west coast rose against Aceh's governors around 1665, and the Dutch Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie (VOC), which had opened a trading office at Padang, drove Aceh from the coast in 1666. Pagaruyung's rulers then dealt with both the Dutch and the British, and congratulated the British when they took Padang during the Fourth Anglo-Dutch War in 1781.

The palace on Batu Patah Hill was burned during the Padri War in 1804. When Thomas Stamford Raffles came in 1818 he found that the capital had been burned three times and abandoned, leaving little more than waringin trees. On 10 February 1821 Sultan Tunggul Alam Bagagarsyah and 19 other traditional leaders signed an agreement with the Dutch against the Padri, which the Dutch took as the kingdom's submission. The last king, Sultan Arifin Muningsyah, returned in 1824, died in 1825 and was buried at Pagaruyung. Bagagarsyah, made only Regent of Tanah Datar, was arrested for treason on 2 May 1833 and exiled to Batavia.
pagasae: Pagasae, also called Pagases or Pagasa, was a town and polis of Magnesia in ancient Thessaly, at the northern end of the bay named after it, the Pagasaeus Sinus. Strabo put it 90 stadia from Pherae and 20 from Iolcos. Its acropolis stood on rocky heights above Cape Angkístri, and copious springs rise at the foot of the rocks. Some ancient writers derived the town's name from these springs, others from the building of the Argo.

Myth made Pagasae the port where Jason built the Argo and from which he set out on his voyage, a setting Apollonius of Rhodes describes in the first book of his Argonautica. Philip II of Macedon conquered the town after the defeat of Onomarchus; in the account of Diodorus the place is spelt Pagai. When Demetrias was founded, the inhabitants of Pagasae were among those moved to the new city.

After the Roman conquest Pagasae was restored and again became an important place, and in the time of Strabo it was the port of Pherae, the principal city in that part of Thessaly. Because its springs were rather saline to the taste, the city was supplied in Roman times with water brought from a distance by an aqueduct, whose ruined piers are still a conspicuous sight.

The site is now a suburb of Volos, which has given the bay its modern name, and in the nineteenth century the ruins of the ancient city could still be seen near the town. The accepted site is in the village of Nees Pagasees in the municipality of Volos, though the most recent excavations suggest that Pagasae may be the ruins at nearby Soros.
pago-pago: Pago Pago lies at the narrowest part of Tutuila, the main island of American Samoa. Tutuila is a basaltic volcanic dome built by five volcanoes along two or possibly three rift zones. The central feature of its geology is the Pago Volcano, active between 1.54 and 1.28 million years ago, whose caldera, about 6 miles long and 3 miles wide, collapsed 1.27 million years ago. The harbour formed in the partly submerged remnants of that caldera, and the village stands near its centre. Rainmaker Mountain, also called Mount Pioa, shelters the eastern side and helps give the harbour very heavy rainfall.

The area was first settled about 4,000 years ago by Polynesian navigators. The people of Tutuila made a plain clay pottery known as Samoan Plainware, found at sites such as Vaipito, which ceased to be made about 1,500 years ago. Tutuila was part of the Tuʻi Tonga Empire from an invasion around 950 CE until the Tongans were expelled in 1250. Samoan tradition credits a warrior from Pago Pago, Fua'au, with leading the revolt, after his fiancée Tauoloasi'i was kidnapped and taken to Tonga.

Among the early names of the place were O le Fagaloa, or Long Bay, and O le Maputasi, the Single Chief's House, a compliment to the Mauga, the senior chief of the area. The first European ships arrived in the late 18th century, and in 1830 a man from Massachusetts living in the household of High Chief Mauga translated parts of the Church of England Prayer Book into Samoan.

The initial American interest in Tutuila was the use of the harbour as a coaling station, and its strategic position played a direct part in the political separation of Western and Eastern Samoa. On 17 April 1900 the first American flag was raised on Sogelau Hill above the new wharf and coaling facilities at Fagatogo. The Deed of Cession of Tutuila and Aunu'u, written and signed by the chiefs, formalised the relationship between the United States and American Samoa.

Pago Pago is the capital of American Samoa and its main port, the seat of the territorial government and the centre of its commerce. Greater Pago Pago consists of six villages strung along the harbour, among them Fagatogo, the downtown area, which holds the territorial legislature, the Fono, and Utulei, which holds Government House. Sixteen buildings of the former United States Naval Station Tutuila are listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The National Park of American Samoa lies immediately to the north.
pagoda-of-fogong-temple: The pagoda stands 85 km south of the Liao capital at Datong and was built by Emperor Daozong of Liao, Hongji, at the site of his grandmother's family home. Following the Khitan custom, Hongji had been raised in Ying County, and he was a devout Buddhist. The historian Nancy Steinhardt suggests that the 1050s, which marked the end of a Buddhist kalpa, made the pagoda an ultimate death shrine to the Buddha of the age. The Yingzhou zhi, edited by Tian Hui under the Wanli Emperor, credits a monk named Tian with funding it; later texts claiming an earlier pagoda of 936–943 on the site are not supported by the dating of its timbers.

The pagoda was renovated and expanded in 1195 under the Jin dynasty and repaired again in 1471. Its temple, called Baogong Temple until it was renamed Fogong in 1315 under the Yuan dynasty, was vast under the Jin but declined under the Ming.

The tower rests on a 4 m stone platform and carries a 10 m steeple, reaching 67.31 m in all. It uses fifty-four kinds of bracket arms, more than any other Liao structure. From outside it seems to have five stories, but inside it has nine, the four hidden ones marked by terrace balconies, with bracket arms on mezzanine layers between the outer stories. A statue of the Buddha Sakyamuni sits at the centre of the first floor beneath a carved caisson ceiling, and gives the pagoda its name. On a clear day it can be seen from 30 km away.

The Yingzhou zhi records seven earthquakes between 1056 and 1103 that the tower survived, and before the 20th century it needed only ten minor repairs. During the Second Sino-Japanese War Japanese soldiers fired more than two hundred rounds into it. Repairs in 1974 uncovered Liao dynasty texts, among them the 12-scroll Liao Tripitaka printed with movable type in 1003 at Yanjing, as well as a Buddha tooth relic hidden in a statue on the fourth level. In 2013 the pagoda was placed on China's tentative list for World Heritage status.
pagondas: Pagondas was the son of Aeolidas. Little is known of his life: Pindar mentions him as born to a noble Theban family, and he was in his early sixties at the time of Delium. Apart from a brief account in Thucydides, almost nothing survives about him, so that he appears in the record only for this one battle. He was evidently a forceful and persuasive speaker, said to have moved the separate Boeotian contingents to unite and attack the Athenians by his words alone.

At Delium the Boeotians faced an Athenian army led by Hippocrates, charging down a hill while the surprised Athenians re-formed and charged up it. Men of Thespiae held the Boeotian left and Pagondas's Thebans the right, massed twenty-five shields deep instead of the usual eight, the first recorded case of a Greek general changing the standard depth of a hoplite unit. The Thebans broke the Athenian left, but the Thespians, facing the best Athenian troops, were surrounded and killed almost to a man. Pagondas then sent in a reserve of several hundred horsemen, itself without precedent, to support them.

The Athenian right fell into confusion and fled, and with the Thebans already in their rear the whole army was routed. The victory kept Athenian forces out of Boeotia for the rest of the Peloponnesian War.

Most historians agree that his deeper phalanx and his use of reserve cavalry are the first recorded use of formal military tactics. They foreshadowed the victory of his fellow Theban Epaminondas at Leuctra in 371 BCE, though Epaminondas was not yet born at Delium, and it is unknown whether the deep phalanx became part of Theban military tradition or had to be devised again; Pelopidas used it at the Battle of Tegyra four years before Leuctra. Philip of Macedon, raised as a hostage in Boeotia, developed these ideas further, and his son Alexander the Great built on them. Victor Davis Hanson, among others, argues that Pagondas thereby set the stage for the military history of the West.
pahang-river: The river's headwater, the Jelai River, rises on the upper slopes of the Titiwangsa Mountains near Cameron Highlands and flows south-east past Kuala Lipis to meet the Tembeling River, which comes down from the Pantai Timur Mountains on the border with Terengganu. From their confluence near Kuala Tembeling the Pahang runs south past Jerantut Feri and Temerloh, turns north-east at Mengkarak and then east through the floodplains of Paloh Hinai and Pekan to the South China Sea.

Its basin covers almost every district of Pahang, Rompin alone excepted, and the districts of Jelebu and Jempol in eastern Negeri Sembilan. Its tributaries include the Lipis, Semantan, Lepar, Bera and Triang rivers, and Temerloh stands where the Semantan joins it. Seven bridges cross the river, from the Abu Bakar Bridge at Pekan to the Sultan Abdullah Bridge at Jerantut Feri.

The river has changed course, and there is evidence that it once reached the sea by way of Muar. Its banks were settled as early as 1400 by warriors and seafarers from Aceh, Riau, Palembang, Sulawesi and elsewhere in Maritime Southeast Asia, and the earliest records of its people are in the Malay Annals and the Hikayat Abdullah. At Jempol in Negeri Sembilan the Pahang and Muar systems nearly met, so that trading boats from the Muar could travel on to Kuala Pahang, or to Kuala Lipis and on towards Terengganu, Kelantan or Perak.

About 10,000 years ago, when the sea stood some 120 metres lower than today, the Sunda Shelf was dry land and the Pahang belonged to the system of the North Sunda River, which also joined the Mekong, the Chao Phraya and the rivers of Sarawak. When the ice melted and the sea rose the rivers were cut apart, and the DNA of their freshwater catfish still shows the old connections.
paide: Paide is the capital of Järva County, one of the 15 counties of Estonia. Its German name, Weißenstein, originally Wittenstein or Wittensten in Low German, means white stone and comes from the limestone used to build the castle; a Latin translation, Albus Lapis, has also been used. The Estonian name was first recorded in 1564 as Paida and is thought to derive from the word paas or pae, meaning limestone.

Konrad von Mandern, master of the Livonian Order, ordered a castle built at Paide in 1265 or 1266. It was constructed from the beginning around a central tower or keep, locally called the Tall Hermann tower or Vallitorn, which has six storeys and has always been the core of the complex. The fortress was strengthened in the 14th and 15th centuries, when the walls were enlarged and towers added, and it was modernised to meet the threat of firearms. In the 16th century outer bastions were added.

During the Livonian War the castle was repeatedly besieged by Russian troops, and in 1573 troops loyal to Ivan the Terrible occupied it. It then changed hands several times and was involved in the fighting of the Polish-Swedish War of 1600 to 1611, in the so-called Siege of Weissenstein. The central tower was restored in 1895 to 1897. In 1941, during World War II, retreating Soviet troops blew it up, and it was not repaired until after Estonia regained its independence, in 1990 to 1993. The church dates originally from the 16th century but was badly damaged by war and fire on several occasions, and the present building is mainly a reconstruction of 1909 to 1910.

The restored central tower houses a part of the Järva County museum. Among the town's natives are the composer Arvo Pärt, born in 1935, and the Baltic German novelist, poet and painter Alexander von Ungern-Sternberg, who lived from 1806 to 1869.
paigc: The party was established in Bissau on 19 September 1956 as the African Party of Independence. It grew from a movement founded in 1954 by Henri Labéry and Amílcar Cabral, and had six founding members: Cabral, his brother Luís, Aristides Pereira, Fernando Fortes, Júlio Almeida and Elisée Turpin. Rafael Paula Barbosa was its first president and Cabral its secretary-general. After Portuguese soldiers fired on protesting dockworkers at Pidjiguiti in 1959, killing 50, the leadership turned to armed struggle and moved its headquarters to Conakry.

The armed struggle began in March 1962 with an unsuccessful attack on Praia, and on 23 January 1963 the party opened the war in Guinea-Bissau by attacking a garrison at Tite. Fighting was concentrated on the mainland, and on the Cape Verde islands the party worked clandestinely. Cuba sent artillery experts, doctors and technicians after Cabral met Fidel Castro in 1966, and the Soviet Union and China supplied weapons. By 1967 the party controlled two thirds of the colony.

Cabral was assassinated on 20 January 1973 by the naval commander Inocêncio Kani, in a plot within the party; Kani and at least ten others were executed. Independence was declared on 24 September 1973 and recognised by the UN General Assembly by 93 votes to 7 in November, before Portugal recognised it. By the end of the eleven-year war some 1,875 Portuguese soldiers and about 6,000 of the party's troops had been killed.

After independence the party was the sole legal party of Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde, with Luís Cabral as president of Guinea-Bissau. A coup led by João Bernardo Vieira in November 1980 ended the plan for union, and the Cape Verdean branch became a separate party. Multi-party politics began in 1991; the party won in 1994, lost power in 1999-2000 and returned to government after the elections of 2004.

During the Cold War the party received support from China, Cuba, the Soviet Union, Senegal, Guinea, Libya, Algeria, Poland, Czechoslovakia and Ghana. It was also the first African party to establish a comprehensive cooperative programme with Sweden.
painted-grey-ware-culture: In its region the Painted Grey Ware culture followed the Cemetery H culture and the black and red ware culture, which continued alongside it in the eastern Gangetic plain and Central India. At some sites its pottery is found together with Late Harappan pottery; at Bhagwanpura in the Kurukshetra district of Haryana excavations revealed an overlap between the two. The archaeologist Jim Shaffer noted that the record shows no cultural break separating it from the indigenous protohistoric culture, while Chakrabarti and other scholars trace the origins of its farming and most of its other traits to eastern India or even Southeast Asia.

Some 1,576 sites were known by 2018. Most were small farming villages, but several dozen grew into towns, the largest defended by ditches and earth embankments with wooden palisades. Fresh surveys by Vinay Kumar Gupta suggest that Mathura, at about 375 hectares, was the largest site, and Ahichatra covered at least 40 hectares. People kept cattle, sheep, pigs and horses, ploughed their fields, worked ivory and built houses of wattle-and-daub, mud or brick, from small huts to large houses of many rooms. Jakhera in Uttar Pradesh shows a proto-urban stage, with ornaments of gold, copper and ivory, grain bins, stone weights, paved streets and water channels.

The pottery is highly standardized, mostly shallow trays and deeper bowls decorated with lines, rows of dots, spiral chains and concentric circles. Terracotta figurines and incised discs that probably had ritual meaning survive, as do a few stamp seals with geometric designs but no inscription, unlike the Harappan seals before them and the Brahmi-inscribed seals after.

The culture probably corresponds to the middle and late Vedic period and the Kuru-Panchala kingdom, the first large state in the subcontinent after the decline of the Indus Valley Civilisation. It was followed by the Northern Black Polished Ware, linked with the rise of the Mahajanapada states and the Magadha Empire, and many of its settlements grew into that period's towns and cities. Radiocarbon dates from recent excavations at Ahichhatra, Kampil and Alamgirpur have been read by some archaeologists as pushing its beginnings back.
paisius-of-hilendar: Little is known of the life of Paisius. He was born in the Samokov eparchy into the family of a merchant, Bilyu Baanov, and scholars name the town of Bansko as his birthplace. His own account gave his birth year as 1722.
