His family was wealthy, and one brother, Lavrentiy, became abbot of the Hilandar Monastery while another, Valcho, was a merchant who patronized the Hilandar and Zograf monasteries. Without a formal education, he entered the Rila Monastery as a novice and in 1745 established himself at Hilandar on Mount Athos, where he was a hieromonk and deputy abbot. As a travelling monk he visited villages and towns to collect donations and attract pilgrims.

In 1758 Paisius travelled to the Sremski Karlovci Monastery to seek historical sources. He consulted the Russian translation of Cardinal Caesar Baronius's Annales Ecclesiastici and Mavro Orbini's Kingdom of the Slavs. After he returned to Hilandar in 1761 disagreements with other monks forced him to move to the Zograf Monastery, where he completed his Slav-Bulgarian History in 1762. It was the first attempt at a complete history of Bulgaria, and the third modern work of Bulgarian history after those of Petar Bogdan Bakshev in 1667 and Blasius Kleiner in 1761.

Its best-known passage asks why a Bulgarian should be ashamed of his name, language and great history and turn himself into a Greek. The historian Roumen Daskalov saw its main aim as exposing Greek spiritual domination and rousing his compatriots against it. Richard Frucht calls the book as polemical as it is factual and says it is filled with self-serving errors. It glorified the medieval Bulgarian tsars, called for relief from Ottoman and Greek ecclesiastical oppression, and set negative stereotypes of Greeks against flattering ones of Bulgarians. It blamed the Greeks for the Ottoman conquest and used Greek as a term for Byzantine in an ethnic sense it originally lacked.

The book had little influence in his lifetime. Sophronius of Vratsa made the first copy after meeting him in 1765 at Kotel, Aleksi Popovich of Samokov made another in 1771, and sixty copies by hand are known. Scholarship generally accepts that he died in 1773 on the way to Mount Athos, near Ambelino, now a neighbourhood of Asenovgrad. The book was first printed in 1844 as Tsarstvenik. The historian Marin Drinov popularised Paisius in 1871 as father of the Bulgarian National Awakening. The Bulgarian Orthodox Church canonised him on 26 June 1962, and a state university in Plovdiv bears his name.
paithan: Paithan lies 56 kilometres south of Aurangabad, on the left bank of the Godavari River, in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district, at an elevation of about 458 metres. Its old name, Pratiṣṭhāna, means standing firmly. It is one of the few inland towns named in the 1st-century Greek Periplus of the Erythraean Sea. The mounds round the town have yielded prehistoric and protohistoric remains and, from the historical period, beads, terracottas, bangles and coins of the Satavahana age, along with punch-marked coins older than the Satavahanas and foreign coins that show its links with the western world.

Pratishthana was the capital of Simuka, the first Satavahana king, and the town kept its importance until the time of the Yadavas. The Puranas say it was founded by King Sudyumna, son of Manu, who as Ila established the Somavamsa there; his son Pururavas ruled after him. Under the name Pishtapura it was taken by the Chalukya ruler Pulakesin II, who had the event recorded in a poem. Buddhism, Jainism and the Vedic religion all flourished there, and the medieval saints Dnyaneshwar and Eknath, who wrote in simple Marathi, made it a centre of the bhakti movement.

The Marathas of the 17th century valued Paithan as a place of pilgrimage and trade. In 1679 Chhatrapati Shivaji halted there on his way to Jalna and issued a charter making Kawale, a leading priest of the town, a royal priest, an arrangement his successors long honoured. The Peshwas kept close ties: Peshwa Balaji Bajirao married into the Wakhare family, moneylenders of Paithan, in 1761, and Peshwa Madhavrao's letters show his regard for the town's textiles.

Paithan is a town with a municipal council. Pilgrims gather each year at the shrine of Saint Eknath for the Paithan yatra, and its Digambar Jain temple of Munisuvrata, the 20th tirthankara, is an old place of pilgrimage. The Jayakwadi Dam nearby holds a bird sanctuary.
pakistan: Pakistan is bounded by the Arabian Sea on the south and shares land borders with India to the east, Afghanistan to the west, Iran to the southwest and China to the northeast. The Wakhan Corridor, a narrow strip of Afghanistan, separates it from Tajikistan. It lies where the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates meet, a region of high seismic activity.

The country is divided into three major geographic areas: the northern highlands, the Indus River plain and the Balochistan Plateau. The highlands include the Karakoram, Hindu Kush and Pamir ranges and five of the fourteen peaks over 8,000 metres, among them K2 at 8,611 metres. The 1,609 km Indus River and its tributaries cross the country from Kashmir to the Arabian Sea and sustain the alluvial plains of Punjab and Sindh.

The earliest known stone tools in the region, about 2 million years old, were found in the Soan Valley. The Neolithic site of Mehrgarh dates from 7000 to 4300 BCE, and the Indus Valley Civilisation included Mohenjo-daro and Harappa. After its decline, semi-nomadic Indo-European Aryans migrated into the subcontinent around 2000 BCE, and the Gandhara civilisation later flourished at the crossroads of India, Central Asia and the Middle East.

The western regions became part of the Achaemenid Empire around 517 BCE, and Alexander the Great conquered the region in 326 BCE, defeating King Porus at Jhelum. The Mauryas ruled from 322 BCE to 185 BCE, and Ashoka introduced Buddhism. The Indo-Greek Kingdom founded by Demetrius of Bactria included Gandhara and Punjab, and Greco-Buddhist culture flourished under Menander. Later powers included the Kushan, the Ghaznavids, the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals, and the British Raj from 1858 to 1947.

Pakistan gained independence in 1947 through the partition of British India, which was accompanied by mass migration and loss of life. It adopted a republican constitution in 1956, and East Pakistan seceded as Bangladesh in 1971 after a nine-month civil war. The 1973 constitution established a parliamentary system. Military rule governed in 1958 to 1971, 1977 to 1988 and 1999 to 2008, and the first successful democratic transition took place in May 2013.

The 2023 census counted 247,541,947 people, and the population grew more than sevenfold between 1951 and 2023. The country is ethnically and linguistically diverse and has a very young population, with a median age of 19. Its legislature has a 96-member Senate and a 336-member National Assembly.
paku-alam-viii: He was born on 10 April 1910, the son of Paku Alam VII and Gusti Bendara Raden Ayu Retno Poewoso, with the childhood name Gusti Raden Mas Harya Sularso Kunto Suratno. The Pakualaman, dating from 1812, is an enclave within the Yogyakarta Sultanate. He came to its throne on 12 April 1937 under the official name Kanjeng Gusti Pangeran Adipati Arya Paku Alam VIII.

On 19 August 1945 he and Hamengkubuwono IX congratulated Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta on the founding of the Republic of Indonesia, and after the sultan declared his readiness to join the republic he did the same. On 5 September he decreed that the Pakualaman was an integral part of Indonesia, and by a joint declaration of 30 October the two rulers united their realms as the Special Region of Yogyakarta, with the sultan and the prince serving for life as governor and vice-governor.

From 1946 to 1978 he often acted as governor while Hamengkubuwono IX held posts in the republic's cabinet and served as vice president. He led the elections commission in Yogyakarta for the local elections of 1951, 1955 and 1957, was elected to the Constitutional Assembly for the League of Supporters of Indonesian Independence (IPKI), and sat in the People's Consultative Assembly from 1997. On 20 May 1998, in response to the riots of that month, he and Hamengkubuwono X issued a joint declaration supporting a peaceful Reformasi.

He died in office on 11 September 1998 and was buried in the family graveyard at Girigondo, having served longer than anyone as an Indonesian vice-governor and as prince of Pakualaman. He was credited with helping to found several universities, among them Gadjah Mada University and Yogyakarta State University, and in 1979 the Notokusumo Foundation, which opened academies of state administration and nursing. On 7 November 2022 he was named a National Hero of Indonesia.
pal-pronay: Prónay was born on 2 November 1874 into an old aristocratic family at Romhány in Nógrád County, northern Hungary. He attended the Lahne Military Institute but advanced slowly as an officer, partly because he was abusive and violent toward his own men. After the Communist coup of March 1919 brought Béla Kun's Hungarian Soviet Republic to power, he considered emigrating but went instead to Szeged, where he was one of the first officers to join Admiral Miklos Horthy's counter-revolutionary National Army and took command of Horthy's bodyguard. He also became a close associate of the right-wing politician Gyula Gömbös.

In the summer of 1919 Prónay formed the first partisan militia of what became the White Guard. His men chose their targets among Communists, Social Democrats, peasants and Jews. They kidnapped and blackmailed Jewish merchants, tortured and mutilated prisoners, and fed the bodies of prisoners, some of them alive, into the boiler of the battalion's armoured train; Prónay later described these acts with relish in his writings. After Romanian troops left Budapest in November 1919, the unit was quartered in the Hotel Britannia and grew to a battalion, and Horthy put a stop to its plan for a citywide pogrom.

Tolerance for the violence waned as it drew hostile foreign press before the ratification of the Trianon Treaty. After his men were implicated in the murder of a Budapest policeman in November 1920, Prónay was tried in the summer of 1921 for extorting a wealthy Jewish politician, found guilty and stripped of his command. Refused reinstatement by Horthy, he moved to the Austrian border, and in the autumn of 1921 he joined the second failed attempt to restore Charles IV to the throne. The government dissolved the battalion in January 1922.

In the 1930s Prónay tried and failed to build a Hungarian fascist mass movement on the Nazi model, and in 1932 he was sentenced to six months in prison for incitement and stripped of his rank of lieutenant colonel. In October 1944, aged 69, he assembled a death squad in Budapest and again hunted Jews. He was long believed to have fallen in the siege of Budapest, but the Soviet archives showed that he was captured on 20 March 1945 and sentenced to twenty years of forced labour for sabotage and espionage, and that he died in the Gulag. He is considered the most brutal of the officers who led the White Terror, though Iván Héjjas, Gyula Ostenburg-Moravek and Anton Lehár led similar squadrons.
palace-of-nestor: The site lies on the hill of Epano Englianos, beside the road 4 kilometres south of Chora, at 150 metres above sea level, and covers an area of 170 by 90 metres. In the Odyssey, Telemachus tells of going to Pylos and to Nestor, shepherd of the people, who received him in his lofty house and welcomed him as a father would his own son.

The palace was the main building of a larger Late Helladic settlement, probably once surrounded by a fortified wall. Besides storerooms, workshops and baths, it had light wells, reception rooms and a sewage system. The settlement had been occupied for a long time; most of the objects found date from 1300 BCE, and the complex burned around 1250 BCE. The site reopened to visitors in June 2016 under a new roof with raised walkways.

Two tholos tombs north of the Bay of Navarino were excavated in 1912 and 1926. Trial digging at Epano Englianos began on 4 April 1939 and from the first day found stone walls, fresco fragments, Mycenaean pottery and inscribed tablets. The frescoes later proved to be egg tempera murals, among the oldest known uses of that paint. The tablets were cleaned in Athens, photographed by Alison Frantz and then kept in the vaults of the Bank of Greece until 1950 to protect them from the war.

Excavation resumed in 1952, and between 1952 and 1966 the palace was uncovered and the area around the acropolis explored. In 1952 the English architect Michael Ventris found that Linear B was an archaic form of Greek, and the reading of the tablets in the following years identified them as part of the royal archive. In 2015 the University of Cincinnati found nearby the undisturbed burial of a warrior, called the Griffin Warrior, with gold rings and bronze weapons whose imagery mixes Minoan and Mycenaean culture.
palace-of-the-grand-master-rhodes: The palace, also known as the Kastello, is one of the few examples of Gothic architecture in Greece. Recent study suggests that the foundations of the ancient temple of the sun god Helios lay on the same spot, probably where the Colossus of Rhodes stood in antiquity. A Byzantine citadel was built there in the late 7th century. After the Knights Hospitaller occupied Rhodes in 1309, they made the fortress their administrative centre and the palace of their Grand Master, repairing it and making major changes in the first quarter of the 14th century.

The palace was damaged in the earthquake of 1481 and repaired soon afterwards. After the Ottoman Empire captured the island in 1522 it served as a command centre and fortress. In 1856 lightning struck a gunpowder magazine under the nearby Church of Saint John, possibly stored there since the siege of 1522. The explosion killed many people, destroyed the church and brought down most of the palace's upper floors, though the ground-floor rooms survived.

Under Italian rule the Ottoman-era structures were demolished, and the architect Vittorio Mesturino was asked to design the reconstruction of the palace and of the nearby Street of the Knights. With few remains or records of the earlier building, he created a structure that also met the authorities' need for a working government building drawing on the Hospitaller legacy. The works took place between 1937 and 1940. Critics have faulted its lack of historical accuracy and its changes to the authentic remains; one scholar called it "horrendous fascist taste". It became a holiday residence for King Victor Emmanuel III and later for Benito Mussolini, whose name remains on a plaque near the entrance.

The Treaty of Peace with Italy of 10 February 1947 transferred the Dodecanese Islands to Greece, and the handover took place in 1948. The palace was then turned into a museum. In 1988, while Greece held the rotating presidency of the European Economic Community, Prime Minister Andreas Papandreou and the other leaders of the community met there.
palace-of-westminster: The site may have been used by Cnut during his reign from 1016 to 1035, and from about 1045 to about 1050 Edward the Confessor built a palace and the first Westminster Abbey. The oldest surviving part, Westminster Hall, was erected in 1097 for William II, when it was the largest hall in Europe. The palace was the principal residence of English monarchs in the late medieval period. After a fire destroyed the royal apartments in 1512, Henry VIII moved in 1534 to the Palace of Whitehall, and from then on the two houses of Parliament and various courts of law were its main occupants.

On 16 October 1834 a fire broke out when an overheated stove, used to burn the Exchequer's stockpile of tally sticks, set alight the House of Lords Chamber. Both Houses were destroyed. Westminster Hall was saved by firefighting and a change in the wind, along with the Jewel Tower and parts of St Stephen's Chapel.

Charles Barry won the competition to design the new palace and chose the Perpendicular Gothic style, aided by the Gothic architect Augustus Pugin. Work began in 1840 and lasted thirty years, with delays, cost overruns and the deaths of Barry and Pugin. Pugin, displeased with Barry's symmetrical layout, remarked that it was "All Grecian, sir; Tudor details on a classic body". The stone is Anston limestone, carried by canal, sea and river. The Victoria Tower, 98.5 m high, was the tallest secular building in the world on its completion in 1858.

The building has over 1,100 rooms and 100 staircases. It is planned around the Central Lobby, from which corridors lead north to the Commons Chamber, south to the Lords Chamber and west to Westminster Hall.

In the Second World War the palace was hit by bombs on fourteen occasions. In the raid of 10 to 11 May 1941 three people were killed and the Commons Chamber was destroyed, because firefighters could save only one of it and the roof of Westminster Hall; they chose the hall. The chamber was rebuilt in a simplified style and completed in 1950.

The Gunpowder Plot of 1605 aimed to blow up the House of Lords at the State Opening of Parliament, and since then the Yeomen of the Guard search the cellars before each opening. The palace became a Grade I listed building in 1970 and part of a World Heritage Site in 1987. Tsar Nicholas I called it "a dream in stone", and Westminster is now used to mean the UK Parliament and government.
palaikastro: The town lies at the eastern end of Crete, about 2 km west of a steep promontory 65 m high called Kastri, from the Latin castrum, a fort. The promontory runs along the sea between Kouremenos beach to the north and Chiona beach to the south, and it has no flat ground. Above the town rises Mount Petsofas, with the ruins of a Minoan peak sanctuary. Since the Kallikratis Programme of 2011 Palaikastro has been a local community of the municipality of Sitia in the regional unit of Lasithi.

Already in Minoan times the region was a centre of trade. The large Minoan settlement of Roussolakkos, behind Chiona beach, was excavated by English archaeologists and shows that this was one of the main commercial centres of the Minoan culture in the far east of the island. The ancient port of Itanos to the north now lies several metres below the sea. A farmer found the Minoan moulds of Palaikastro in October 1899, 150 metres north-east of the town, and the Palaikastro Kouros was recovered in fragments between 1987 and 1990.

The name, meaning old fort, dates from the Middle Ages, when Crete was ruled by the Republic of Venice and a walled and turreted fort stood on the ridge of Kastri. The promontory was too steep and dry to live on and served chiefly as a lookout. Once cannon had made the fort useless it was abandoned, and much of its stone was taken for building, though sections of its battlements remain.

Palaikastro has about 1,100 inhabitants, most of whom live from farming olives and vines, with a few fishermen and tourism as a further source of income. In 2017 it took over the settlements of the former community of Mitato, which had lost its permanent residents.
palaiologos-dynasty: The Palaiologoi were a Byzantine Greek noble family whose origins are unclear. Their own medieval stories traced them to Roman patricians who accompanied Constantine the Great to Constantinople in 330, but they more probably arose in Anatolia. The earliest known member, possibly the founder, was Nikephoros Palaiologos, a commander in the second half of the 11th century. In the 12th century the family belonged to the military aristocracy and often intermarried with the ruling Komnenos family. When the Fourth Crusade took Constantinople in 1204, the Palaiologoi fled to the Empire of Nicaea, ruled by the House of Laskaris, and held high office there.

Michael Palaiologos, born in 1223, was mistrusted by the Laskaris emperors. After Theodore II Laskaris died, Michael led a coup against the regent George Mouzalon, seized the guardianship of the child emperor John IV Laskaris and was proclaimed co-emperor. After the recapture of Constantinople from the Latin Empire in 1261, John IV was deposed and blinded. Michael VIII and his successors ruled the empire at its weakest, with decline caused partly by Bulgarians, Serbs and Ottoman Turks and partly by civil wars within the family. The war between Andronikos II Palaiologos and his grandson Andronikos III lasted until 1328.

In 1394 Manuel II stopped paying tribute to the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I, who besieged Constantinople for more than a decade. Manuel signed a peace with Mehmed I in 1403. By the 15th century the empire was effectively a client state of the Ottomans. The dynasty ended in 1453, when Mehmed the Conqueror took Constantinople and the last emperor, Constantine XI Palaiologos, died in its defence. His brothers Thomas and Demetrios kept the Morea as Ottoman vassals until a civil war between them led Mehmed to annex it in 1460.

The Palaiologoi were not well liked by their subjects, partly because of their religious policy. Michael VIII achieved a union of the Orthodox and Catholic churches at the Second Council of Lyons in 1274, which the Byzantine people opposed passionately. It broke down in 1281 when Pope Martin IV excommunicated him, and he died condemned as a traitor and heretic. Constantine XI's death in battle, however, led Greeks to remember him as a hero and improved the dynasty's reputation.

A branch in Italy, the Palaeologus-Montferrat, ruled the March of Montferrat until 1536. The senior imperial line probably died out in the 16th century, and many later claims of descent were fabricated. Thousands of people, particularly in Greece, still bear the name.
palanan: Palanan is one of four remote coastal towns of Isabela that face the Philippine Sea and are separated from the rest of the province by the Sierra Madre. No road links it to the rest of Isabela: it is reached by a short flight from Cauayan to Palanan Airport, by boat from Divilacan or from Dingalan and Baler in Aurora, or by a hike of three to five days over the mountains from San Mariano. Its name is said to come from the Ibanag warning palanammu, a word of caution used because the area was surrounded by Aetas.

Unlike other towns of the Cagayan Valley, Palanan was founded on 22 July 1609 by Spanish forces who came by boat from Baler on the Pacific coast. It therefore belonged in turn to Pampanga, Laguna, Tayabas, Nueva Ecija and Nueva Vizcaya before passing to Isabela, and it was served by Franciscan missionaries rather than the Dominicans who worked elsewhere in the valley. Its people were at first Paranan, later joined by local Negritos, Tagalog migrants from Baler and outlaws from the Cagayan Valley, and Tagalog rather than Ilocano or Ibanag became the common language.

From 1900 Palanan served as the last capital of the First Philippine Republic. The capture of President Emilio Aguinaldo there on 23 March 1901 by an American force under Frederick Funston, who had gained access to his camp by a ruse, was one of the final chapters of the Philippine–American War.

In 1978 President Ferdinand Marcos proclaimed the area around the town part of the Palanan Wilderness Area, a protected conservation area that President Fidel V. Ramos expanded in 1997 into the Northern Sierra Madre Natural Park.

Palanan is divided into 17 barangays and had 18,091 inhabitants in the 2024 census. Work began in March 2016 on an 82-kilometre road from Ilagan to Divilacan through the Sierra Madre, following an old logging road, to open the coastal towns to the rest of the province.
palapye: Palapye is a growing town in Botswana, about halfway between Francistown and Gaborone, 170 kilometres from Francistown and 240 kilometres from Gaborone. Its position has made it a convenient stopover on one of southern Africa's principal north-south rail and road routes. It lies by the Lotsane River nearly 70 kilometres north of the Tropic of Capricorn, towards the central-eastern edge of the country. Summers, from mid-September to mid-April, are very hot, with daytime temperatures up to 40 °C and plentiful thunderstorms, and winters are mild and dry. The name is a form of Phalatswe, said to mean the place of the impalas.

The Bamangwato people under Kgosi Khama III are widely believed to be the first people to have settled near present-day Palapye. Their capital was Phalatswe, also called Old Palapye, at the western end of the Tswapong Hills, and it was the capital from 1889 to 1902. Its remains lie about 20 kilometres east-southeast of Palapye, close to the village of Malaka.

The ruins of the church, built in 1892, can still be seen a few kilometres from the town centre. Khama contributed some 3,000 pounds to its construction and took a keen interest in church affairs. The Bamangwato's houses were at first clustered around the church, but they found its vicinity too rocky and moved away.

The Morupule Colliery near the town supplies the Morupule Power Station, an important source of Botswana's electricity. The A1 highway, which connects Gaborone and Francistown, passes through Palapye, a secondary road leads to Serowe, Orapa and Lethlakane, and the national railway also runs through the town. Preliminary results of the 2022 census gave a population of 52,398, up from 37,256 in 2011.

The Botswana International University of Science and Technology began construction of its campus in December 2009, on a site of 2,500 hectares on the Tswapong Hills, and enrolled its first students in August 2012; it was intended to ease the burden on the University of Botswana in Gaborone. Visitors come to the Tswapong Hills, the Moremi Gorge with its permanently flowing water, and the Khama Rhino Sanctuary, about 50 kilometres away near Serowe.
palar-river: The name Palar means milk river in Tamil. The river flows 93 kilometres in Karnataka and 222 kilometres in Tamil Nadu, with a shorter stretch in Andhra Pradesh, and reaches the Bay of Bengal at Vayalur, about 75 kilometres south of Chennai. For a long distance it runs underground, emerging near Bethamangala, from where it gathers water and flows east down the Deccan Plateau. Of its seven tributaries the chief is the Cheyyar River.

Among the towns on its banks are Kuppam, Vaniyambadi, Ambur, Gudiyatham, Vellore, Katpadi, Arcot, Ranipet, Walajapet, Kanchipuram, Chengalpattu and Kalpakkam. Rainfall across the basin is low and droughts are frequent.

The sharing of its water was settled in 1892, when Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh were part of the Madras Presidency and the upper basin lay in the Mysore kingdom; the Palar was one of the rivers named in Schedule A of that agreement. A plan by the Andhra Pradesh government for an irrigation dam at Ganeshpuram near Kuppam caused agitation in the northern districts of Tamil Nadu.

The former Chief Minister Jayalalitha opposed it, arguing that under the 1892 agreement an upstream state should build no new dam to obstruct, divert or store the river's water without the downstream state's consent. In 2008 the documentary En Peyar Palar, directed by R.R. Srinivasan, traced the harm done to the river by sand quarrying and industrial effluents.

Water diverted at the Palar anicut feeds the Poondi reservoir and Chembarambakkam Lake, two major sources of Chennai's supply, though the Telugu Ganga project, bringing Krishna water to the city, has much reduced the dependence on the Palar. Karnataka and Tamil Nadu have built many minor and medium irrigation tanks in the basin. In Karnataka the reservoirs of Bethamangala, long the main source of drinking water for the Kolar Gold Fields, and Ramasagara lie within seven kilometres of each other.
palatinate-neuburg: Palatinate-Neuburg was a territory of the Holy Roman Empire founded in 1505 by a branch of the House of Wittelsbach, with its capital at Neuburg an der Donau. It covered about 2,750 square kilometres and had a population of some 100,000. After the Verdict of Cologne ended the Landshut War of Succession, the duchy was created from the territories north of the Danube for Otto Henry and Philipp, the sons of Ruprecht of the Palatinate. While they were minors their grandfather Philip, Elector Palatine, ruled it until his death in 1508, followed by Elector Frederick II.

In 1541 Count Palatine Otto Henry converted to Lutheranism, and his palace chapel at Neuburg Castle, consecrated on 25 April 1543 by the theologian Andreas Osiander, was the first newly built Protestant church. In 1556 he became Elector Palatine and the next year ceded the duchy to Wolfgang, Count Palatine of Zweibrücken. Wolfgang's eldest son Philipp Louis founded the elder line of Palatine Zweibrücken-Neuburg in 1569, and the Sulzbach line separated from it in 1614.

Palatinate-Neuburg joined the Protestant Union in 1608. When the Duchies of Jülich-Cleves-Berg fell into dispute in 1609 after the death of the childless John William, Count Palatine Wolfgang Wilhelm claimed them and fought in the War of the Jülich Succession, converting to Catholicism midway to secure alliances. Neuburg and the Duchies of Jülich and Berg were then held in personal union, formalized in the Treaty of Xanten. Philip William became Elector Palatine in 1685, as did his successors Johann Wilhelm and Charles Philip.

When Elector Charles Philip died in 1742, all his territories, Palatinate-Neuburg among them, passed to the Palatinate-Sulzbach line of the House of Wittelsbach, in the person of Charles Theodore, a descendant of Augustus, Count Palatine of Sulzbach, a brother of Wolfgang Wilhelm. In 1800 France invaded the duchy, and on 26 June a Habsburg, Württemberg and Bavarian force fought a battle there and withdrew after most of a day. General Ney then made his headquarters in the castle at Neuburg. The duchy was abolished in 1808. After the partition of Bavaria in 1837 it was joined with Swabia, and it became part of Upper Bavaria in the 1970s.
palatinate-region: The Palatinate, in German Pfalz, occupies most of the southern quarter of the German state of Rhineland-Palatinate, with an area of 5,450 square kilometres. It borders Saarland in the west, the Hunsrück range forms its north-western border, and the Upper Rhine marks the eastern border with Hesse and Baden. In the south the German-French border separates it from Alsace. One-third of the region is covered by the Palatinate Forest, Germany's largest contiguous forested area. Its highest mountain is the Donnersberg, at 687 metres, and the German Wine Route passes through its wine region. Most of its major towns, among them Ludwigshafen, Speyer, Landau, Frankenthal and Neustadt, lie in the lower eastern part, down to the Rhine.

A Celtic region, the area was conquered by the Roman Empire under Augustus about 12 BCE and became part of Germania Superior. Alamannic tribes settled there in the decline of the Empire, and Francia under King Clovis I conquered them about 496. From the Middle Ages until 1792 the Palatinate was divided into 45 secular and ecclesiastical territories, the largest being the Electorate of the Palatinate. By the late 12th century its count palatine had become a prince-elector, as the Golden Bull of 1356 confirmed. The Bishopric of Speyer was the major ecclesiastical territory.

French revolutionary troops occupied the left bank of the Rhine in 1794, and in 1798 the Palatinate largely became the French department of Mont Tonnerre. The Congress of Vienna in 1815 and a treaty of 14 April 1816 ceded most of it to Bavaria, which made it a district with Speyer as capital, first called the Rheinkreis and, from 1835, the Pfalz. Because the Bavarians kept the Napoleonic Code, it kept a distinct legal status. The Hambach Festival of 1832 near Neustadt became a milestone in German liberalism, and a separatist uprising in 1849 was suppressed by Prussian troops.

After the First World War French troops occupied the region, and French-backed separatist attempts between 1919 and 1923 ended in January 1924 with a treaty that guaranteed it would remain in Bavaria. Under Nazi rule it was merged with the Saarland into the Gau Westmark. In 1947 the French occupation authorities combined it with Rhenish Hesse and part of the Prussian Rhine Province to form Rhineland-Palatinate.

The Palatinate has about 1.4 million inhabitants, known as Palatines. The Diocese of Speyer and the Evangelical Church of the Palatinate still follow largely the boundaries of the old Bavarian district. Many Pennsylvania Dutch are descendants of Palatine immigrants, and the Pennsylvania Dutch language derives primarily from the Palatine German that Mennonite refugees brought to Pennsylvania between 1717 and 1732. Its best-known dish is saumagen, a sow's stomach stuffed with pork, potatoes and seasonings.
palatine-chapel-aachen: Charlemagne began the chapel around 792, together with the other buildings of the Palace of Aachen, and Pope Leo III consecrated it in 805 in honour of the Virgin Mary. Charlemagne visited Ravenna three times, first in 787, and in that year he wrote to Pope Hadrian I asking for mosaic, marbles and other materials from the floors and walls of Rome and Ravenna for his palace. The architect, Odo of Metz, is named in a tenth-century inscription around the dome; nothing more is known of him. Of the palace itself nothing remains, but the chapel survived and became the central part of Aachen Cathedral.

The chapel is a centrally planned building whose octagonal dome, a double shell resting on heavy piers, is encircled by a sixteen-sided ambulatory with a gallery above. It was entered from the west through a monumental atrium, its east end had a square apse, and two basilican buildings, now known only from archaeology, once flanked it. Its plan simplifies that of San Vitale, and its barrel and groin vaults follow late Roman practice rather than the Byzantine techniques of Ravenna. Coloured marble veneer, ancient spolia, which Einhard said came from Rome and Ravenna, and bronze doors and railings of very high quality furnish the interior.

The dome bore first a fresco and then a mosaic of the twenty-four elders of the Apocalypse, replaced with stucco in the Baroque period and reproduced in the 19th century. Christ in Majesty faced the royal throne in the upper gallery, the king's space, which opened both onto the church and onto the atrium. The westwork at the entrance is one of the Carolingian contributions to Western architecture.

In 936 Otto I used the chapel's bond with Charlemagne by holding his coronation as King of Germany there, and rulers went on being crowned in it until 1531. In 1000 Otto III paid homage to Charlemagne's remains in the chapel, most likely as a symbolic display; the original tomb, probably a niche later called the Karlsmemorie, was destroyed in 1788. The chapel is a central monument of the Carolingian Renaissance and part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
palatine-chapel-palermo: The building mixes Byzantine, Norman and Fatimid architectural styles, showing the tricultural state of Sicily in the 12th century, after Roger I and Robert Guiscard conquered the island. Roger II of Sicily commissioned it in 1132, building upon an older chapel, now the crypt, constructed around 1080. It took eight years to build, and its mosaics were only partially finished by 1143.

The sanctuary, dedicated to Saint Peter, is reminiscent of a domed basilica. It has three apses, as is usual in Byzantine architecture, and six pointed arches, three on each side of the central nave, resting on recycled classical columns. According to European historians, Roger made the throne room and chapel equal in the main part of the building to tell the papacy and other European rulers that he was going to stay in Sicily.

The oldest mosaics are probably those of the ceiling, the drum and the dome, and the Pantokrator is at the apex of the dome, with rows of angels, prophets, evangelists and saints. The mosaics of the transept, presumably from the 1140s and attributed to Byzantine artists, include five saints, among them the Three Hierarchs. The rest, dated to the 1160s or 1170s, are cruder, bear Latin rather than Greek inscriptions and are probably the work of local craftsmen. A few show oriental flora and fauna and may be the only substantial passage of secular Byzantine mosaic extant.

The nave, built under Roger II, had no Christian images; his successors William I and William II added them. The royal throne stands against the west wall, up six steps, with two heraldic lions over its frame. The muqarnas ceiling of the nave has about 75 inscriptions invoking regal power, many in Kufic script, and scenes of hunters, drinkers, dancers and musicians, with two crowned rulers, one of them Roger II. Twenty eight-pointed stars are set in octagons, and clusters of four stars form a Christian cross. The ceiling is the earliest surviving example of wooden muqarnas.

The origin of the muqarnas is unclear. Scholars have proposed North Africa, citing Zirid fragments from Qal'a Beni Hammad, Syria, though Sicily's examples precede the earliest Syrian ones by 30 years, and Egypt, where Fatimid artists may have fled unrest in Cairo; this last is the leading theory but lacks tangible evidence. A newer theory holds that skilled Islamic craftsmen already worked in Sicily. Some scholars claim Roger chose wood to allude to Solomon's palace in Jerusalem.

Slobodan Ćurčić considers the chapel a reflection of Middle Byzantine art, set against Sicily's melting-pot culture. It forms part of the UNESCO-listed site Arab-Norman Palermo and the Cathedral Churches of Cefalù and Monreale, recognized in 2015.
palau: Palau is an archipelago of about 340 islands in the western Pacific Ocean, the western part of the Caroline Islands, with a total area of 466 square kilometres. Its most populous islands are Angaur, Babeldaob, Koror and Peleliu, and about two-thirds of the people live on Koror. North of them lies the coral atoll of Kayangel, and west lie about 200 uninhabited Rock Islands. A remote group of six Southwest Islands, some 604 kilometres away, make up the states of Hatohobei and Sonsorol.

The Palauan name for the islands, Belau, derives from the word for village, beluu, or from aibebelau, meaning indirect replies, which relates to a creation myth. The name Palau came into English from the Spanish Los Palaos through German. An older English name was the Pelew Islands.

The islands were first settled in the 3rd or 2nd millennium BCE by Austronesian peoples, most likely from what is now the Philippines or Indonesia. In December 1696 sailors from the Caroline Islands were stranded on Samar, where the missionary Paul Klein met them. They showed him with pebbles the position and size of their islands, and he drew from this the first European map of the Palau area.

The islands became part of the Spanish East Indies in 1885. After Spain's defeat in the Spanish-American War they were sold to Germany in 1899 and administered as part of German New Guinea. After the First World War they fell within the Japanese-ruled South Seas Mandate of the League of Nations. In the Second World War American and Japanese troops fought in the Mariana and Palau Islands campaign, including the major Battle of Peleliu.

In 1947 Palau became part of the United States-governed Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. A referendum in 1978 rejected joining the Federated States of Micronesia, and Palau adopted a constitution in 1981. It gained full sovereignty in 1994 under a Compact of Free Association with the United States, and the United Nations General Assembly admitted it on 15 December 1994.

The Republic of Palau is a presidential republic with a bicameral Palau National Congress. Its capital, Ngerulmud, is on Babeldaob, the largest island, and its most populous city is Koror. The official languages are Palauan and English, and the currency is the United States dollar. Palauan society follows a strict matrilineal system, seen in funerals, marriages, inheritance and the passing of traditional titles.
palawan: Palawan is an archipelagic province of the Philippines in the region of Mimaropa and the largest province in the country by area, at 14,649.73 square kilometres. Its islands stretch between Mindoro in the north-east and Borneo in the south-west, lying between the South China Sea and the Sulu Sea. The province takes its name from its largest island, 450 kilometres long and 50 kilometres wide. It comprises roughly 1,780 islands and islets, including the Calamianes group in the north-east, Balabac Island off the southern tip and the Cuyo Islands in the Sulu Sea. Unlike most of the Philippines, Palawan belongs biogeographically to Sundaland, with fauna and flora related to those of Borneo.

Researchers led by Robert Bradford Fox found evidence in the Tabon Caves that humans have lived on Palawan for more than 50,000 years, along with the bone fragments of an individual known as Tabon Man. The oldest inhabitants are the Palaw'an, Batak, Tagbanwa and Tau't Bato of the interior and highlands and of the Calamianes Islands, who traditionally practise animist anito religions. Later groups settled the coasts. In the 1200s Palawan, Calamian and parts of Luzon came under the nation of Sandao, a vassal of the more powerful Ma-i in Mindoro. The Molbog of the south, and the Cuyonon and Agutaynon, arrived later.

The northern Calamianes Islands were the first to come under Spanish authority. In the early 17th century Spanish friars sent missions to Cuyo, Agutaya, Taytay and Cagayancillo, but met resistance from Moro communities, and churches enclosed by garrisons were built against Moro raids. The Spanish census of 1818 recorded 4,486 native families and 29 Spanish-Filipino families on Palawan, then called Isla de Paragua. In 1902, after the Philippine–American War, the United States established civil rule in northern Palawan as the province of Paragua. In 1905 the province was reorganised to include the south, renamed Palawan, and given Puerto Princesa as capital.

During the Japanese occupation guerrillas, called Palawan's Fighting One Thousand, resisted, helped escaping American prisoners of war and guided the landings of the 8th Army. Palawan also felt the effect of martial law, declared by Ferdinand Marcos in 1972. Later settlement from Luzon and elsewhere changed the island's population and languages.

Palawan has about 968,795 people, according to the 2024 census. The capital and largest city, Puerto Princesa, is administered independently of the province. Tagalog is spoken by more than half the people, and the native Cuyonon and Palawano are also used. The economy is basically agricultural, with palay (rice), corn and coconut the main crops, along with fishing, logging and mining. The Puerto Princesa Subterranean River National Park, listed by UNESCO in 1999, and the Tubbataha Reef Marine Park, listed in 1993, are World Heritage Sites.
palazzina-di-caccia-of-stupinigi: Stupinigi is now a frazione of the town of Nichelino, 10 kilometres south-west of Turin. The original castle there belonged until 1418 to the Acaja line of the House of Savoy, Lords of Piedmont, was sold to Marquis Rolando Pallavicino in 1493, and was acquired by Emmanuel Philibert in 1563, when he moved the ducal capital from Chambéry to Turin. He also took from the Pallavicini family almost 1,700 hectares of land and woods around it as a hunting estate. Work on Filippo Juvarra's new lodge went far enough in two years for the first formal hunt to be held in 1731.

Juvarra's plan follows the arms of a St Andrew's Cross: four angled wings, holding the royal and guest apartments, spread from a double-height oval hall, aligned with a tree-lined avenue from Turin. The hall was finished in 1730, and from 1731 to 1733 the Bolognese brothers Giuseppe and Domenico Valeriani painted its vault with the Triumph of Diana, goddess of the hunt. Francesco Ladatte made the bronze stag on the dome in 1766; the original was moved into the Portrait Gallery in 1992 and a copy now stands on the roof.

Under Charles Emmanuel III and Victor Amadeus III the lodge and its park kept growing, first under Juvarra's assistant Giovanni Tommaso Prunotto and then under architects such as Benedetto Alfieri, until it had 137 rooms and 17 galleries. The French gardener Michael Benard laid out the walled park in 1740. The interiors are Italian Rococo, with lacquer, porcelain, gilded stucco and mirrors. The French engraver Charles-Nicolas Cochin criticised their abundance of decoration, and Jérôme Lalande called the hall the dream of an architect.

The House of Savoy preferred Stupinigi for celebrations and dynastic weddings: there, in 1773, Princess Maria Theresa of Savoy married Charles Philippe, Count of Artois, the future Charles X of France. Pauline Bonaparte, Napoleon's sister, fitted out a cabinet with a marble bath while her husband Camillo Borghese was governor of Piedmont. The building now houses the Museo di Arte e Ammobiliamento, with furniture by Pietro Piffetti and Giuseppe Maria Bonzanigo, and since 1992 the surrounding woods and farmland have been protected as the Parco naturale di Stupinigi.
palazzo-della-pilotta: The complex stands between the Piazzale della Pace and the Lungoparma in the historic centre of Parma, and takes its name from pilota, a ball game once played there by Spanish soldiers stationed in the city. It was begun in the last years of Duke Ottavio Farnese and grew up around the corridor that linked the Rocchetta, a keep beside the river Parma, to the Ducal Palace. Its three courts are the Cortile della Pilotta, the Cortile del Guazzatoio and the Cortile della Racchetta, and the façade on the Piazza della Ghiaia was never built.

The Pilotta was meant to hold a great hall, later turned into the Teatro Farnese, along with the ducal stables, the grooms' lodgings and an Academy Hall. Elizabeth Farnese, later Queen of Spain, was born there in 1692. When Farnese rule ended, Duke Charles I, later King of Spain, took much of the palace's movable contents to Naples in the 1730s, and the Biblioteca Palatina had been founded there by 1769. The Reinach Theatre, opened in 1871 on the site of the church of San Pietro Martire and renamed Teatro Paganini in 1939, was almost wholly destroyed with parts of the palace by aerial bombing in May 1944 and then pulled down.

Besides the library, the building now houses the National Archaeological Museum, the Teatro Farnese, the Galleria Nazionale di Parma, a museum devoted to the printer Giambattista Bodoni and an art school named after Paolo Toschi. Between 1986 and 2001 the Piazzale della Pace beside it was redesigned by the Swiss architect Mario Botta, with a garden and a fountain tracing the outline of the lost church of San Pietro.
palazzo-farnese: The palace was designed by Antonio da Sangallo the Younger, one of Bramante's assistants on St. Peter's, for Alessandro Farnese, who had been made a cardinal in 1493 at the age of 25 and lived in princely style. Work was interrupted by the Sack of Rome in 1527. When Alessandro became Pope Paul III in January 1534 the palace was greatly enlarged, and the later work used architecture to express the power of the Farnese family. Michelangelo, Jacopo Barozzi da Vignola and Giacomo della Porta all worked on it, and della Porta's porticoed façade towards the Tiber was finished in 1589.

The main façade has alternating triangular and segmental pediments over the windows of the piano nobile, a central rusticated portal and Michelangelo's projecting cornice, which casts a deep shadow across the top. In 1541 Michelangelo revised the central window and added the largest papal coat of arms Rome had ever seen, so that the façade became a setting for the pope when he appeared on the balcony. The courtyard is ringed by the Doric, Ionic and Corinthian orders in ascending order. Michelangelo also proposed a bridge across the Tiber to the gardens of the Vigna Farnese, which was never built.

The palace held the Farnese collections, including the Farnese Hercules. Annibale Carracci painted the Hercules cycle, the Room of Maps and, from 1597 to 1608, The Loves of the Gods in the Farnese Gallery, whose central scene is the triumph of Bacchus and Ariadne. After the death of Cardinal Odoardo Farnese in 1626 the palace stood almost uninhabited for twenty years. Queen Christina of Sweden later lodged there, and after she left, papal authorities found that her servants had stolen silver, tapestries and paintings. It inspired the Reform Club in London and appears in Puccini's Tosca. Today it is the French Embassy in Italy under a 99-year lease.
palazzo-madama-turin: At the beginning of the first century BCE the site was occupied by a gate in the Roman walls of Augusta Taurinorum, the ancient Turin, from which the decumanus maximus, the main east-west street, set out. Two of its towers, though restored, still stand as witnesses of this original core. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the gate served as a fortified stronghold in the city's defences.

The building then passed to the Savoia-Acaja, a secondary branch of the House of Savoy, who enlarged it into a castle in the early 14th century. A century later Ludovico of Acaja rebuilt it as a square with an inner court, a portico and a cylindrical tower at each corner, a form still clearly visible at the back of the palace. When the Acaja line died out, the castle became a residence for guests of the House of Savoy.

In 1637 Christine of France, aunt of Louis XIV and regent for Duke Charles Emmanuel II, made it her own residence, roofing the court and refitting the apartments. Sixty years later the second regent, Marie Jeanne of Savoy, known as Madama Reale, lived there and fixed the name Madama on it. She wished to turn it into a sumptuous royal palace and brought in artists, among whom Domenico Guidobono decorated the first-floor halls named after him: the Madama Reale's Chamber, the Chinese Cabinet and the Southern Veranda.

Juvarra's plan was for an entirely new palace in white stone, but only its front section was built. During the Napoleonic Wars the palace housed the provisional French government. In the 19th century King Charles Albert made it the seat of the royal picture gallery, the Pinacoteca Regia, called the Galleria Sabauda after 1933, and later of the Subalpine Senate, the parliament of the Kingdom of Sardinia, and of the High Court.

Juvarra's front on Piazza Castello is a scenic façade only one bay deep, screening the older building behind it. A high piano nobile with arched windows is joined to a mezzanine by a giant order of composite pilasters on a rusticated ground floor; the three central bays have full columns before a glazed hall, and a balustrade with marble vases and statues crowns the whole. Since 1934 the palace has housed the City Museum of Ancient Art, a collection of paintings, statues, church ornaments, porcelain and decorative art mostly from the late Middle Ages to the 18th century. In 1997 it was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site with other residences of the House of Savoy.
palazzo-schifanoia: The name is thought to come from schifare la noia, to escape from boredom, and the palace was one of several pleasure houses where the Este court relaxed. It began as a single-storey building without wings for Alberto V d'Este, a retreat for suppers and diversions with an urban front and a garden front, long before the first such villa of Renaissance Rome, the Belvedere of Nicholas V. Under Borso d'Este the architect Pietro Benvenuto degli Ordini added a ducal apartment on an upper floor with a hall for receiving ambassadors, and in 1493 Biagio Rossetti designed a terracotta cornice and extended the palace for Ercole I d'Este.

The frescoes of the Hall of the Months were made for the expected investiture of Borso d'Este as Duke of Ferrara in 1471 by Pope Paul II, and celebrate the right ordering of mankind and nature under his rule. Olympian gods ride cars drawn by their own beasts above figures of the zodiac and scenes of the year's labours and the court, the larger figures from cartoons by Cosimo Tura. The learned scheme probably came from Borso's circle, perhaps the court astrologer Pellegrino Prisciani, with details from Boccaccio's Genealogia deorum. In the nearby Hall of Virtues the sculptor Domenico di Paris made a stucco frieze of putti and the Virtues.

After the Este left Ferrara in 1598 the palace passed through heirs to the Tassoni family, the frescoes were whitewashed, and under the Papal States it became a tobacco warehouse and manufactory. When the comune of Ferrara acquired it after World War I only seven of the months remained legible. In a lecture of 1912 Aby Warburg used the cycle to show how visual motifs pass from one culture to another. The palace belongs to the Musei Civici d'Arte Antica di Ferrara and holds antiquities, coins and medals cast by Pisanello and others for the Este.
palazzo-te: The palace takes its name from Il Te, the suburb where it stands, a name most likely derived from the Lombard tejee or tejé, a linden grove that once grew there, or from the Latin attegia, a hut; Giorgio Vasari spelled it Palazzo del T. The site was that of the family stables which Federico II Gonzaga, Marquess of Mantua, had built as early as 1502 at Isola del Te, on the edge of the marshes just outside the city walls. Giulio Romano, a pupil of Raphael, was commissioned to design the building, and its shell was put up within eighteen months.

The palace is basically a square house round a cloistered courtyard, with a formal garden enclosed by colonnaded outbuildings that end in a semicircular colonnade, the Exedra. Like the Villa Farnesina in Rome it mixes the architecture of a palace and a villa. The façades have flat pilasters against rusticated walls, the piano nobile is on the ground floor, and the façades are less symmetrical than they look: the spans between the columns are irregular. In the courtyard, deep niches and blind windows stand among surfaces of broken, blemished plaster.

For ten years after the shell was finished, plasterers, carvers and fresco painters worked until barely a surface of the loggias and salons was left undecorated, with local painters such as Benedetto Pagni and Rinaldo Mantovano under Romano's direction. The frescoes range from Olympian banquets in the Sala di Psiche and horses in the Sala dei Cavalli to the giants of the Sala dei Giganti. The Casino della Grotta was a small suite round a grotto where courtiers bathed under a little cascade.

Emperor Charles V saw the rooms on his visit in 1530, when he raised his host Federico II Gonzaga from Marquess to Duke of Mantua. In July 1630, during the War of the Mantuan Succession, an Imperial army of 36,000 Landsknecht mercenaries sacked Mantua and the palace over three days, and the plague the invaders brought struck those who remained. The palace was looted from top to bottom and left an empty shell with its painted gods and giants. Part of it now houses the Museo Civico del Palazzo Te, endowed by the publisher Arnoldo Mondadori, with a collection of Mesopotamian art.
palazzo-vecchio: In 1299 the commune and people of Florence decided to build a palace worthy of the city's importance and more secure for the magistrates in times of turbulence. Arnolfo di Cambio, architect of the Duomo and of Santa Croce, began construction on the ruins of the Palazzo dei Fanti and the Palazzo dell'Esecutore di Giustizia, once owned by the Uberti family. Giovanni Villani wrote in his Nuova Cronica that the Uberti were rebels of Florence and Ghibellines, and that the palace was built to ensure their homes would never be rebuilt on the site. It was first called the Palazzo della Signoria, after the ruling body of the Republic of Florence, and also the Palazzo del Popolo, the Palazzo dei Priori and the Palazzo Ducale.

The cubical building is made of solid rusticated stonework, with two rows of two-lighted Gothic windows, each with a trefoil arch. In the fifteenth century Michelozzo added decorative bas-reliefs of the cross and the Florentine lily. Projecting crenellated battlements on small arches and corbels crown it, and under the arches are nine painted coats of arms of the Florentine republic. Some arches served as embrasures for dropping heated liquids or rocks on invaders.

Michelangelo's David stood at the entrance from its completion in 1504 until 1873, when it moved to the Accademia Gallery; a replica of 1910 stands there now, beside Baccio Bandinelli's Hercules and Cacus. The first courtyard was designed in 1453 by Michelozzo, and its walls carry views of the cities of the Habsburg monarchy painted in 1565 by Giorgio Vasari for the wedding of Francesco I de' Medici and Archduchess Johanna of Austria.

The Salone dei Cinquecento, the largest chamber, was built in 1494 by Simone del Pollaiolo on the commission of Savonarola as the seat of the Grand Council of 500 members. Vasari later enlarged it so that Grand Duke Cosimo I could hold court there, and unfinished works by Michelangelo and Leonardo da Vinci, the Battle of Cascina and the Battle of Anghiari, were lost. A legend holds that Vasari built a false wall to preserve Leonardo's work; attempts to find it behind the fresco have been inconclusive.

The building acquired its current name when the Medici duke's residence moved across the Arno to the Palazzo Pitti. From 1540 Cosimo moved the seat of government to the palace, and the apartments of his wife Eleonora of Toledo were richly decorated, including a chapel frescoed by Bronzino. Vasari designed a small secret study for Francesco I between 1570 and 1575. In the chapel of the Signoria Girolamo Savonarola said his last prayers before he was hanged in the Piazza della Signoria and his body burned. The palace is today the town hall of Florence.
palden-thondup-namgyal: Palden Thondup Namgyal was born on 23 May 1923 at the Royal Palace, Park Ridge, in Gangtok. From the age of eight to eleven he studied under his uncle, Rimpoche Lhatsun, to be ordained a Buddhist monk, and he was recognised as the reincarnated leader of both the Phodong and Rumtek monasteries. He graduated from Bishop Cotton School in Shimla in 1941. He hoped to study science at Cambridge, but his elder brother, the crown prince, an officer in the Indian Air Force, was killed in a plane crash in 1941, and Palden trained instead for the Indian Civil Service at Dehradun.

He served as adviser for internal affairs to his father, Sir Tashi Namgyal, the 11th Chogyal, and led the negotiating team that established Sikkim's relationship to India after Indian independence in 1949. In 1963 he married Hope Cooke, a 22-year-old American graduate of Sarah Lawrence College, and the marriage brought worldwide media attention to Sikkim. His father died soon afterwards and he was crowned Chogyal on an astrologically favourable date.

In 1975 the Prime Minister of Sikkim appealed to the Indian Parliament for Sikkim to become a state of India. In April the Indian Army took over Gangtok and disarmed the palace guards. He had financed Satyajit Ray's documentary Sikkim (1971) and was an amateur radio operator with the call-sign AC3PT. A referendum on 14 April 1975 voted 59,637 to 1,496 for Indian statehood and the removal of the Chogyal, who was under Indian army guard in his palace.

Namgyal and Hope Cooke divorced in 1980. He died of cancer at the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City on 29 January 1982, aged 58, and 31 members of the State Legislative Assembly offered khadas in respect. His elder son, the former crown prince Tenzing Kunzang Jigme Namgyal, died in a car accident in 1978. His second son, Tobgyal Wangchuk Tenzing Namgyal, was named the 13th Chogyal, though the position no longer confers any official authority. His honours included India's Padma Vibhushan in 1954 and the Order of the British Empire in 1947.
palembang: Palembang occupies a wide lowland east of the Bukit Barisan Mountains in southern Sumatra, at an average elevation of about 8 metres and some 105 kilometres from the coast at the Bangka Strait. The Musi River, one of the largest in Sumatra, runs through it and divides the city into Seberang Ilir, the downstream bank, and Seberang Ulu, the upstream bank. The city stands where two major tributaries, the Ogan and the Komering, join the Musi, and in the rainy season the tide of the river floods many areas.

The oldest inscription found in Palembang, the Kedukan Bukit Inscription, is dated 682 CE. It tells of a king who acquires magical powers and leads a large force over water and land, setting out from the Tamvan delta and arriving at a place called Matajap, and, in the reading of some scholars, founding the polity of Srivijaya. Matajap is believed to be Mukha Upang, a district of Palembang. George Coedes wrote that in the second half of the 9th century Java and Sumatra were united under a Sailendra ruler reigning in Java, with his centre at Palembang.

Prince Parameswara fled the city after Javanese forces crushed it, and pirates then plagued it. In 1407 the returning treasure fleet of Admiral Zheng He confronted the pirate Chen Zuyi there. A local Chinese informant revealed Chen's plan for a surprise attack, and in the battle that followed the Ming fleet destroyed the pirate fleet and killed 5,000 of its men. Chen was taken to Nanjing and executed, and Shi Jinqing was installed as Palembang's ruler.

Islam became the dominant religion after a Demak nobleman, Geding Suro, fled to Palembang with his followers and founded a new dynasty. The Sultanate of Palembang was proclaimed in 1659, and its Grand Mosque was built between 1738 and 1748. The Dutch abolished the sultanate in 1825 and made the city the capital of the Residency of Palembang. It was chartered as a city on 1 April 1906.

Palembang is the capital of the Indonesian province of South Sumatra and the second most populous city of Sumatra after Medan. It is known for songket, a hand-woven silk or cotton cloth patterned with gold or silver thread, which was used at court under Srivijaya. Local cooking relies on freshwater fish and prawn from the Musi, and pempek is among its best-known dishes. The city co-hosted the 2018 Asian Games with Jakarta.
palencia: Palencia lies on the left bank of the Carrión river, near its confluence with the Pisuerga, in the north of the Meseta Central at an altitude of 749 metres. It is about 190 kilometres north of Madrid and 40 kilometres north of Valladolid. The old city stands on the left bank, on higher ground, and the modern suburbs on the right; the first inhabitants probably settled on the right bank and moved because of frequent flooding. A 21-metre statue of Christ, the Cristo del Otero, stands on a hill north-east of the city.

As Pallantia, the town was a fortified Celtiberian settlement and the chief town of the Vaccaei. The Romans starved it into submission in the 2nd century BCE and incorporated it into Hispania Tarraconensis. According to the chronicler Idatius, it was all but destroyed in 457 in the Visigothic wars against the Suevi. The Catholic bishopric was founded in the 3rd century or earlier. Under Visigothic rule the Arian bishop Maurila, installed by Leovigild, followed King Reccared's conversion to Catholicism in 587 and attended the Third Council of Toledo in 589.

After the Moors arrived in the early 8th century the see was a title only, until Froila, Count of Villafruela, retook the area in 921; Sancho III of Navarre was the true restorer of Christian power, and Bernardo, said to be the first prelate of the restored see in 1035, rebuilt the cathedral over the crypt of Saint Antolín.

Alfonso VIII founded a studium generale here in 1208, which did not long survive him; Saint Dominic and the poet Gonzalo de Berceo studied there. Jews are first documented in Palencia in 1175, when Alfonso VIII brought 40 Jews to the town, and most moved to Portugal in 1492 after the expulsion. In 1212 Bishop Tello took part in the battle of Las Navas de Tolosa, where the city won the right to put a cross over its castle emblem.

Palencia is the capital of its province, on an economic axis with Valladolid and Burgos. Its Gothic cathedral, dedicated to San Antolín, was built from 1321 to 1504 over a Visigothic crypt, and its museum holds a twelve-panel retablo by Juan de Flandes, court painter to Queen Isabella I of Castile. Thirteen kilometres south, at Baños de Cerrato, stands a 7th-century basilica built by the Visigothic king Reccaswinth, the oldest church on the peninsula. The Roman villa of La Olmeda, a 4th-century house with 27 rooms, is known for its mosaics. The Canal de Castilla runs close to the city, and lechazo, roast suckling lamb, is the local speciality.
palenque: Much of Palenque's history has been reconstructed from the hieroglyphic inscriptions on its monuments, which give a long sequence of rulers. The first king known to the inscriptions, K'uk' Bahlam I, governed from 431. The city's kings competed with the states of Calakmul and Toniná. Under Yohl Ik'nal, troops from Calakmul invaded and sacked Palenque in 599, and in 611 the king of Calakmul entered the city in person, a disaster followed by political disorder. An inscription records that annual ceremonies went unperformed in 613 and laments the loss of the divine lady and the king.

The city recovered under K'inich Janaab' Pakal, who came to the throne at the age of 12 and reigned from 615 to 683. His mother Sak K'uk' had ruled for about three years and remained a force in his early reign. Most of the palaces and temples were built in his time, and the Palace was enlarged and remodelled in 654, 661 and 668. In 711 Palenque was sacked by Toniná and K'inich K'an Joy Chitam II was taken prisoner, and for some years the city had no king; K'inich Ahkal Mo' Nab' III was crowned in 722.

In the 8th century Palenque came under increasing stress, as did most Classic Maya states. There was no new elite construction in the ceremonial centre sometime after 800, an agricultural population stayed for a few generations, and the site was then abandoned.

Palenque, known in the Itza' language as Lakamha, meaning big water, stands in the Mexican state of Chiapas near the Usumacinta River, 150 metres above sea level. It is a medium-sized site, smaller than Tikal, Chichen Itza or Copán, but holds some of the finest Maya architecture, sculpture and bas-relief carving. The Palace, the largest complex, measures 97 by 73 metres at its base and has a four-story tower. An aqueduct with a three-metre-high vault diverts the Otulum River under the main plaza.

The Temple of the Inscriptions holds the second longest glyphic text known from the Maya world. In 1952 Alberto Ruz Lhuillier lifted a slab in its floor and found a stairway to the tomb of Pakal, whose sarcophagus held the richest jade collection seen in a Maya tomb, including a mosaic mask. John Lloyd Stephens and Frederick Catherwood visited in 1840. Archaeologists estimate that only about 10 percent of the city has been uncovered. Palenque National Park was designated in 1981.
palermo: Palermo lies in a basin formed by the Papireto, Kemonia and Oreto rivers, which the Arabs named the Conca d'Oro, the Golden Basin, in the 9th century. A mountain range forms a cirque around the city and faces the Tyrrhenian Sea, and historically it made the interior of Sicily hard to reach. Monte Pellegrino, which stands apart in front of the sea, is the historically most important of the mountains, and Goethe called its cliff the most beautiful promontory in the world. Cave drawings at nearby Addaura show settlement perhaps around 8000 BCE.

The original inhabitants were the Sicani, who according to Thucydides arrived from the Iberian Peninsula. In the 8th century BCE the Phoenicians built a settlement on the natural harbour, one of their three main colonies in Sicily along with Motya and Soluntum, and the city later passed to Carthage. As Panormus it was part of the Roman Republic and Empire for over a thousand years. The Vandals under Geiseric took it in 440 CE, and in late 535 Belisarius laid siege to the city, which had refused to surrender, and eventually prevailed. From 831 to 1072 Palermo was under Arab rule and for the first time the capital of Sicily.

After the Norman conquest it became the capital of the Kingdom of Sicily, which lasted from 1130 to 1816. Spain ruled the city from 1479 until 1713, with brief interruptions, and Austria from 1720 to 1734. Charles III chose Palermo for his coronation as King of Sicily, but the royal court resided in Naples. In 1866 Palermo was the seat of a week-long popular rebellion against annexation by the Savoy kingdom, which was crushed under martial law, and the Teatro Massimo opened in 1897.

Allied bombing in 1942 and 1943 destroyed the harbour and much of the city, with heavy civilian casualties, until the Allied invasion of Sicily captured it on 22 July 1943. In 1946 Palermo became the seat of the Regional Parliament, and in 1948 the element technetium was discovered at its university.

Palermo is the capital and largest city of Sicily. Its inhabitants speak Italian and the Palermitano dialect of Sicilian. The city is the main seat of the World Heritage Site Arab-Norman Palermo and the Cathedral Churches of Cefalù and Monreale, and its markets of Vucciria, Ballarò and Capo are known for fruit, vegetables and fish. Its patron saint is Saint Rosalia, whose feast day is 15 July.
palermo-cathedral: The cathedral is dedicated to the Assumption of the Virgin Mary and is the church of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Palermo. Walter Ophamil, the Norman archbishop of Palermo and minister of King William II, had it erected in 1185 on the area of an earlier Byzantine basilica. By tradition that church was founded by Pope Gregory I, and the Arabs turned it into a mosque after conquering the city in the 9th century. A Qur'an verse is carved on a column of the southern portico, which belonged to the original basilica and the mosque. Ophamil is buried in the crypt.

The building mixes styles because of centuries of additions. The upper orders of the corner towers date from the 14th and 15th centuries, and the Gothic-Catalan southern portico was erected around 1465. Charles III and Victor Amadeus II of Sardinia were both crowned in the cathedral, the latter in December 1713.

The present neoclassical appearance comes from work between 1781 and 1801, supervised by Ferdinando Fuga and Giuseppe Venanzio Marvuglia. Marvuglia's changes were more radical than Fuga's plans, and the great retable by Gagini was destroyed, its sculptures moved elsewhere in the building. In 1801 the astronomer Giuseppe Piazzi, who discovered the asteroid Ceres, built a meridian line on the floor, where an image of the sun, projected through a small hole in a dome, crosses a bronze line at solar noon. It was meant to standardise time and to fix the date of the spring equinox for Easter.

In the first two chapels of the right aisle stand the tombs of Roger II, his daughter Constance I of Sicily, her husband Emperor Henry VI and their son Emperor Frederick II, with the burials of Constance of Aragon and Peter II of Sicily. The four main sarcophagi are of porphyry and are described as the first medieval free-standing secular tombs in the West. Odo of Bayeux, half-brother of William the Conqueror, was buried in the cathedral in 1097. The chapel of Saint Rosalia, patron of Palermo, holds a 17th-century silver urn that is an object of devotion.
palermo-stone: The Palermo Stone is one of seven surviving fragments of a stele known as the Royal Annals of the Old Kingdom. The stele listed the kings of Egypt from the First Dynasty through to the early part of the Fifth Dynasty and noted significant events in each year of their reigns. It may originally have been about 60 centimetres high and 2.1 metres wide, and is made of a hard black stone, probably basalt. The Palermo fragment is irregular and shield-shaped, 43.5 centimetres high, 25 wide and 6.5 thick at most.

Its front has six horizontal registers of hieroglyphs. The first lists the names of predynastic kings of Lower Egypt, identified by the Red Crown. Later registers give the annual events for kings of the First to Fourth Dynasties, and the back continues down to Neferirkare Kakai, third ruler of the Fifth Dynasty. Where a king is named, his mother's name is also recorded, such as Betrest, mother of Semerkhet, and Meresankh I, mother of Seneferu.

The annals record the height of the annual Nile flood, festivals such as the Sed festival, taxation, sculpture, buildings and warfare. They name pharaohs including Djer, Den, Semerkhet, Nynetjer, Peribsen, Khasekhemwy, Djoser, Huni, Sneferu, Khufu, Djedefre, Shepseskaf, Userkaf, Sahure and Neferirkare Kakai, and they preserve names of royal family members of the first five dynasties not otherwise recorded.

New Kingdom king lists such as the Turin Canon and the Abydos king list name Menes, probably Narmer, as the first king of the First Dynasty. The top register of the annals names at least fourteen earlier rulers, which may be preserved through oral tradition or may be fictitious; their identification with historical persons is controversial. The historian Manetho may have used information like that of the stele for his chronology.

The stele's original location is unknown, and no fragment has a secure archaeological provenance. A Sicilian lawyer, Ferdinand Guidano, bought the Palermo Stone in 1859, and his family presented it to the Palermo Archaeological Museum on 19 October 1877. Five fragments are in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, four acquired between 1895 and 1914 and one bought in 1963, and one small fragment is in the Petrie Museum in London. A visiting French archaeologist recognised its importance in 1895, and Heinrich Schäfer published it fully in 1902.

The date of the text is uncertain. It was probably made in the Fifth Dynasty, but it has been suggested that it was carved much later, perhaps in the Twenty-fifth Dynasty, though it would still rest on an Old Kingdom original. It is also unknown whether the fragments come from one stele or from separate copies, and some small Cairo fragments may not be genuine.
palestine-liberation-organization: At its first summit meeting in Cairo in 1964 the Arab League initiated the creation of an organisation to represent the Palestinian people. The Palestinian National Council convened in Jerusalem on 28 May 1964, and the PLO was founded on 2 June 1964, with the stated complementary goals of Arab unity and the liberation of Palestine. It initially sought an Arab state over the entire territory of the former Mandatory Palestine, and launched guerrilla attacks on Israel from Jordan, Lebanon, Egypt and Syria. In 1968 the founding charter was replaced by a revised version calling for a Palestinian state in which Christians, Muslims and Jews would have equal rights.

Fatah's founder, Yasser Arafat, was elected chairman in Cairo on 4 February 1969. In September 1970, in the events known as Black September, Jordan assaulted the PLO's armed groups, and by July 1971 it had been expelled to Lebanon. Israel drove it out in the 1982 Lebanon War; about 8,000 fighters evacuated Beirut, and the PLO moved to Tunis. In 1974 the United Nations General Assembly granted it observer status, on 22 November. In 1988 the National Council proclaimed a Palestinian Declaration of Independence in Algiers, and the PLO endorsed a two-state solution.

In the Oslo Accords of 1993, signed on 20 August and publicly on 13 September, the PLO recognised Israel's right to exist and accepted United Nations Security Council Resolution 242, and Israel recognised the PLO as the representative of the Palestinian people. The accords created the Palestinian Authority, with Arafat at its head, to govern Gaza and Jericho. In 1996 the PLO nullified the parts of its charter that called for Israel's destruction.

The PLO is formally an umbrella organisation of resistance movements, political parties and popular organisations. It was designed as a government in exile, with a parliament, the Palestinian National Council, as its highest authority and an elected Executive Committee. The Council has 740 members and the Committee 18. The Oslo Accords created a separate Palestinian Authority for the occupied territories, which came to replace the PLO as the prime Palestinian political institution.
palghar-district: Palghar district lies in the Konkan division of Maharashtra and forms the northernmost part of the state's Konkan lowlands. It runs from Dahanu in the north to Naigaon, between the Arabian Sea and the slopes of the Sahyadri, and borders Thane and Nashik districts, the Valsad district of Gujarat and Dadra and Nagar Haveli. Its hilly east, the jangalapatti, takes in Jawhar, Mokhada and Vikramgad, while the coastal bandarpatti includes Vasai, Palghar and Dahanu.

The main river is the Vaitarna, the largest of the Konkan rivers, 154 km long, which rises in the Trimbakeshwar hills and reaches the sea through a wide estuary off Arnala. The district receives about 3000 mm of rain a year, and dams such as the Tansa Dam send its water to Mumbai, an arrangement that is debated among scholars.

Vasai taluka shows the cultural mix left by the Portuguese, above all in its nine or so large churches, and forts such as Vasai Fort, Arnala Fort and Mahim Fort stand in the district; a stupa of the Buddha in the same taluka is another of its historic places. Until 1 August 2014 the talukas of the present district were part of Thane District. After a demand for division lasting almost 25 years, the Cabinet of Maharashtra approved the new district on 13 June 2014, and Palghar became the 36th district of Maharashtra on 1 August that year.

The district headquarters is the town of Palghar, and the district comprises eight talukas: Palghar, Vada, Vikramgad, Jawhar, Mokhada, Dahanu, Talasari and Vasai. At the 2011 census these talukas had 2,990,116 people; Marathi was the first language of 61.96%, and Scheduled Tribes made up 37.39% of the population. Satpati is the largest fishing port of Maharashtra, Dahanu is known for its chickoo, and India's first atomic power plant stands at Tarapur.
palk-strait: The strait stretches for about 137 km and is between 64 and 137 km wide. Its waters are shallow: around the shoals of Ram Setu they are typically only 1 to 3 metres deep, the central part is typically around 20 metres deep, and the greatest depth is 35 metres. To the north, in the Bay of Bengal, the waves are mostly swells, while in Palk Bay to the south they are mostly smaller wind waves. In the Hindu epic Ramayana the shoals are part of a bridge built by the vanara army of Rama to rescue his wife Sita from the Asura king Ravana.

During the Last Glacial Period, when sea levels fell to as much as 120 metres below their present values, the whole of the shallow strait was dry land. It was submerged again as the sea rose during the Holocene, by around 7,000 years ago.

The construction of a shipping channel through the strait was first proposed to the British government of India in 1860. Pamban Island was linked to the Indian mainland by the Pamban Bridge, opened for traffic on 24 February 1914. Trains ran from Madras to Dhanushkodi at the southern tip of the island, where a ferry crossed to Talaimannar on Mannar Island and another train carried passengers on to Colombo. The railway line to Dhanushkodi was destroyed in the 1964 Dhanushkodi cyclone together with a passenger train, killing around 200 people. A ferry between Rameswaram and Talaimannar continued into the 1970s and was discontinued by the Indian government in 1984.

The shallows, small islands and reefs make the strait difficult for large ships, though fishing boats and small craft navigate it.
