The city's decline began with the conquest of Sher Shah Suri, and earthquakes in the 19th century and the monsoon climate brought down much of its architecture; only raised mounds mark the royal palace. Francis Buchanan-Hamilton rediscovered it in 1808, Sir Alexander Cunningham studied it in detail, and the Archaeological Survey of India surveyed it from the air in 1931. Its surviving monuments include the Adina Mosque, the Eklakhi Mausoleum and the Qutb Shahi Mosque.
pandukabhaya: In the traditional account, Pandukabhaya was the only child of Princess Unmadachithra, daughter of King Panduvasdew, and Prince Dighagamini. Astrologers had foretold that the princess would bear a son who would kill her brothers, so the king shut her away, but Dighagamini broke in to see her and they met in secret. To protect the child he was exchanged for a girl and raised in the village of Doramadalawa, escaping several attempts by his uncles' forces to kill him. A brahmin named Pandula, who knew who he was, taught him the skills of a king and gave him an army, which he stationed at Kasagala.

Pandula foretold that Princess Pali, daughter of the prince's uncle Girikandasiva, would be his queen, and Pandukabhaya took her; Girikandasiva and five more uncles made war on him and were defeated. Camped at Dhooma Rakha and Ritigala, he drove other uncles across a river and, with the support of the Yaksha woman Chathiya, defeated them all. Legend tells that when Pali first served him food on a lotus leaf the leaf turned golden, so that she came to be known as Swarnapali.

He made Anuradhagama, named after Vijaya's minister Anuradha, the seat of his kingdom, appointed Pandula's son Chandra his chief advisor and gave his allies high rank. He is credited with deploying scavengers to keep the city clean, building one of the oldest hospitals and the first reservoir of the kingdom, the Abaya Wewa, and creating the office of nagara gutthika to govern the city, to which he appointed his uncle Abhaya. In his tenth year as king he ordered the demarcation of all the villages of the island, the first king to do so.

Many historians consider him the first truly Sri Lankan king, the ruler who ended the conflict between the Sinha clan and the local clans and reorganised the population. His legend is the subject of Aba, a film of 2008.
pandulf-ironhead: Pandulf was the son of Landulf II and Yvantia, and from 943, when his grandfather Landulf I died, he ruled jointly with his father, and from 959 also with his brother Landulf III. About 955 Pope John XII led Romans, Tuscans and Spoletans against Landulf II and Pandulf, but Gisulf I of Salerno came to their aid and the pope made peace at Terracina, beginning a lasting alliance between Gisulf and Pandulf. After their father's death the brothers were in principle joint rulers of one indivisible principality, but in practice Pandulf held Capua and Landulf Benevento.

When a revolt in Rome drove out Pope John XIII late in 965, Pandulf sheltered him in Capua; the pope made Capua an archdiocese, and after ten months Pandulf sent him back with a Capuan escort. In 967 Emperor Otto I granted him the Duchy of Spoleto and Camerino and charged him with the war against Byzantium. On his brother's death in 968 he made his own eldest son Landulf co-prince at Benevento. Left in charge of the siege of Bari, he was captured by the Byzantines at the Battle of Bovino in 969 and held in Constantinople, while his wife Aloara and Archbishop Landulf I of Benevento governed. He was freed in the agreement that gave Theophanu in marriage to Otto II.

When his cousin Landulf of Conza deposed Gisulf of Salerno in 973, Pandulf restored Gisulf as his vassal, and on Gisulf's childless death he succeeded in Salerno as they had agreed. He then held all three Lombard principalities, with lands from Tuscany to the Gulf of Taranto. In 978 he confirmed the Sanctuary of Monte Sant'Angelo sul Gargano to the archbishopric of Benevento.

His sons fought over the inheritance. Landulf IV took Capua and Benevento and Pandulf II Salerno, but when Otto II came to Rome in 981 Spoleto went to Thrasimund IV, Benevento to Pandulf's nephew, and Manso I of Amalfi took Salerno. Another son, Atenulf, died at the Battle of Stilo on 13 July 982.
pandulf-iv-of-capua: Pandulf IV ruled first from February 1016 jointly with his cousin Pandulf II. After the Byzantine catapan Basil Boioannes destroyed the army of Melus of Bari and his Norman allies at Cannae in 1018, Pandulf became the most ardent of the southern princes in support of the Byzantines, and in 1020 he helped Boioannes take the tower of Melus' brother-in-law Dattus on the Garigliano. This brought an imperial army from Germany. Pilgrim, Archbishop of Cologne, besieged Capua and took the prince in 1022; Emperor Henry II almost executed him, and he was imprisoned in Germany for two years.

Emperor Conrad II released him in 1024 at the request of Prince Guaimar III of Salerno. With Guaimar, the Norman adventurer Rainulf Drengott and later Boioannes, Pandulf besieged Capua, which fell in 1026 after a siege of 18 months. In 1027 he deposed Sergius IV of Naples, but Rainulf restored Sergius in 1029 and received the county of Aversa, the first Norman toehold in the Mezzogiorno. Pandulf imprisoned Theobald, the abbot of Montecassino, and in 1032 conquered Gaeta from John V and took its ruler's titles. The chronicler Aimé of Monte Cassino called him a man of "wily and wicked deeds".

At the request of Guaimar IV of Salerno, Conrad came south and at Troia in 1038 ordered Pandulf to restore stolen property to Monte Cassino. Pandulf offered 300 lbs of gold and a son and daughter as hostages, but when the son escaped he took refuge in his castle of Sant'Agata de' Goti, and Conrad gave Capua to Guaimar. Pandulf fled to Constantinople, seeking the protection of his old Byzantine allies, but was imprisoned there, and he was released only after Guaimar became an enemy of Emperor Michael IV.

Pandulf returned to Italy in 1042, and for five years he and his few followers threatened Guaimar. In 1047, a watershed year in the history of the Mezzogiorno and the Lombards, Emperor Henry III, Conrad's son, came south, made the Drengot and Hauteville possessions his direct vassals, and restored Pandulf at Capua for the last time. Pandulf died in his own princedom, after a third reign.
panduranga: Panduranga, known to medieval Chinese sources as Bīn Tónglóng and to Vietnamese annals as Phan Lung or Phan Lang, was long an autonomous princedom within Champa. A southern dynasty called Panduranga rose in 757, unified Champa and ruled from Virapura, near modern Ninh Phước; Javanese raiders burned a Shiva temple near Phan Rang in 787. Prince Jaya Harivarman I fled there during the Khmer occupation of 1145 to 1150 and led the resistance from it. According to the Panduranga annals its own line of princes began with Po Sri Agarang, whose reign began in 1195 or 1205, and it kept a tributary tie to the kings at Vijaya.

After the Lê army of Emperor Lê Thánh Tông took Vijaya in 1471, Vietnamese sources say a Cham general, Bố Trì Trì, fled to Phan Rang, set up his own rule and submitted to Lê Thánh Tông seven days later; the emperor divided the Cham remnants into smaller polities. Scholars now see this less as the end of Champa than as a sign of its many centres. The Cham stopped paying tribute when the Mạc dynasty usurped the Lê throne in 1526, and in the 16th century Panduranga prospered from trade; in 1594 its king sent 400 warships to help Johor against the Portuguese at Melaka.

The Nguyễn lords invaded repeatedly, in 1629, 1653 and 1692. In 1692 Lord Nguyễn Phúc Chu arrested King Po Saut and renamed the land Trấn Thuận Thành, but Cham revolts that began in 1693 led him to restore the Cham monarchy as a vassal, confirmed by a treaty of 1712. From the early 17th century until 1832 its capital stood at Phan Rí Cửa.

Cham merchants traded with Siam, Manila, Macao, Malacca, Johor, Pahang, Patani and Makassar, and Cham textiles were widely sold. Most historians agree that the Cham began converting to Islam in large numbers only after the fall of Vijaya, and Pierre-Yves Manguin argues that it came through the Malay world. King Po Rome, who reigned from 1627 to 1651 and had studied in Kelantan, brought the Muslim Cham Bani and the Ahier closer together, and is still venerated by the Cham. By the 1670s European missionaries described a mostly Muslim population and court.
pandya-dynasty: The Pandyas, also called the Pandyas of Madurai, were one of the three great kingdoms of Tamilakam, with the Cholas and the Cheras; their rulers were known together as the three crowned rulers, the mu-ventar. The dynasty existed since at least the 5th to 3rd centuries BCE, and its origin and timeline are difficult to establish. Early Pandya chieftains ruled Pandya Nadu, which included the inland city of Madurai and the southern port of Korkai. Greek accounts, the edicts of the Maurya emperor Ashoka and Tamil-Brahmi coins and inscriptions suggest their continuity from the 3rd century BCE.

Tamil legend tells that three brothers, Cheran, Cholan and Pandyan, ruled together at Korkai, and that the two others then left to found their own kingdoms. The Silappatikaram says the Pandya emblem was a fish. Medieval Pandya kings claimed descent from the Lunar Race, and tradition holds that the Sangams, the academies of Tamil poets, were held at Madurai under their patronage.

The early Pandyas faded into obscurity with the rise of the Kalabhra dynasty. Kadungon revived the kingdom in the late 6th century, and from the 6th to the 9th century the Chalukyas of Badami or the Rashtrakutas, the Pallavas of Kanchi and the Pandyas dominated south India, often invading the Chola country, the Chera country, Venadu and Sri Lanka. The Pandyas declined with the rise of the Cholas of Thanjavur in the 9th century and were in constant conflict with them.

They entered a golden age under Maravarman I and Jatavarman Sundara Pandya I in the 13th century. Jatavarman I, about 1251, expanded the kingdom into the Telugu country as far as Nellore, into south Kerala, and conquered northern Sri Lanka. Maravarman Kulasekhara I defeated an alliance of the Hoysalas and the Cholas in 1279 and invaded Sri Lanka, from where the Tooth Relic of the Buddha was carried away. Rule was shared among several royals, one holding primacy.

An internal crisis coincided with the Khalji invasion of south India in 1310-11. Sultanate raids followed, with the loss of south Kerala in 1312, of north Sri Lanka in 1323 and the establishment of the Madurai Sultanate in 1334. Later Pandyas ruled from Tenkasi and Tirunelveli.

Early Pandya rulers are traditionally associated with Jainism and later with Shaivism. Pandya Nadu was home to major temples, among them the Meenakshi Temple in Madurai, which were large employers and landowners and also served as banks, schools and dispensaries. The Pandyas issued silver punch-marked and copper coins bearing the fish, their emblem. The dynasty is considered one of the longest-ruling in the world, in power from roughly 500 BCE to 1618 CE, though its extent varied greatly.
panfilo-de-narvaez: Pánfilo de Narváez was born in Castile and was a relative of Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar. Bartolomé de las Casas described him as tall and somewhat blonde inclined to redness. He took part in the Spanish conquest of Jamaica in 1509 and went to Cuba in 1511 to join its conquest under Velázquez. He led expeditions to the eastern end of the island with Las Casas and Juan de Grijalva, and Las Casas, an eyewitness, reported that Narváez presided over the massacre of Caonao, where Spanish troops killed a village full of people who had come to meet them with food.

In 1519 Velázquez sponsored Hernán Cortés's expedition to Mexico but, doubting his loyalty, recalled it. Cortés disobeyed. Velázquez named Narváez governor of Mexico and sent him with 1,400 men in 19 ships to intercept Cortés. Narváez landed at Veracruz and made camp at the Totonac town of Cempoala. Cortés returned to the coast with perhaps as few as 250 men. Although Narváez's remaining 900 outnumbered them three to one, he was outmanoeuvred, lost an eye and was captured at the Battle of Cempoala on 27 May 1520. After two years in prison he was sent back to Spain.

Charles V then appointed him adelantado of Florida. He sailed from Sanlúcar de Barrameda on 17 June 1527 with five ships and 600 men, and after a hurricane in Cuba set out again in February 1528. Storms drove him to Florida's west coast, where he landed in April 1528 with 300 men near Tampa Bay, among hostile people. The party divided, with about 100 men and 10 women on the ships and 300 men and 42 horses marching north. Narváez never saw the ships again.

Finding no gold, his men built four rafts near the St. Marks River to reach Pánuco. A storm drowned most of the remaining 240 men near Galveston Island, and Narváez and a small group were carried out to sea and never seen again. Four men survived: Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca, Andrés Dorantes de Carranza, Alonso del Castillo Maldonado and the Moroccan slave Estevanico. Cabeza de Vaca's account of their journey on foot across the present-day southwestern United States and northern Mexico was the first book to describe the people, animals and plants of inland North America.
pang-juan: In the traditional account, Pang Juan and Sun Bin studied military strategy together under the hermit Guiguzi in the mountains, became close friends and swore brotherhood. Pang left for the state of Wei when he heard that King Hui of Wei was recruiting men of talent. He impressed the king with proposals to strengthen Wei and with the claim that he could help it conquer the other six major states, and was put in command of Wei's armies, leading them to victories over smaller states such as Song, Lu and Zheng.

Pang later invited Sun Bin to serve Wei, but was secretly jealous because Sun had learnt more from their teacher. He framed Sun for treason before King Hui, who ordered Sun's execution; Pang then pretended to plead for him, and the sentence was reduced to face-tattooing and the removal of his kneecaps. Pang hoped to have Sun write down his knowledge of strategy and then kill him, but servants warned Sun, who feigned madness and escaped with the help of officials from the state of Qi.

When Pang led Wei's army against the state of Zhao, Zhao asked Qi for help. Sun Bin and Tian Ji answered with the strategy known as besieging Wei to rescue Zhao, drawing Pang back to defend his own state, and ambushed his forces at the Battle of Guiling.

Later Pang attacked the state of Han, and Sun Bin again invaded Wei to relieve it. Feigning defeat, the Qi army seemed to shrink as it retreated, and Pang pursued with light cavalry into a narrow valley at Maling, where he was ambushed. The Wei army was crushed, the Wei crown prince was captured, and Pang Juan killed himself. Folklore adds that Sun Bin carved the words Pang Juan dies under this tree on a tree there, and that when Pang lit a torch to read them the hidden Qi troops attacked. Pang Juan sometimes appears as a door god in Chinese and Taoist temples, usually paired with Sun Bin.
pange-lingua-gloriosi-corporis-mysterium: The opening words recall an older Latin hymn from which this one is derived, the Pange lingua gloriosi proelium certaminis of Venantius Fortunatus. Two plainchant settings survive. The better known is a tune in the Phrygian mode, Mode III, from the Roman liturgy, which was originally part of the Gallican Rite; the other comes from the Mozarabic liturgy of Spain.

The hymn expresses the doctrine that the bread and wine are changed into the body and blood of Christ during Mass. It tells of the mystery of the body and the precious blood shed for the world's redemption, of Christ born of a virgin, and of the Last Supper, at which he gives himself as food to the Twelve with his own hands; where the senses fail, faith alone suffices.

Its last two stanzas, beginning Tantum ergo, are sung at Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament and close with a doxology to the Father, the Son and the Spirit. There are many English translations, among them one by Edward Caswall, and in English it is often sung to the Latin tune under the title Of the Glorious Body Telling.

Josquin des Prez based his Missa Pange lingua, one of his last works, dated to between 1515 and 1521, on the Roman tune, and many commentators count it among the high points of Renaissance polyphony. Juan de Urrede, a Flemish composer active in Spain in the late 15th century, set the hymn many times, mostly on the Mozarabic melody. The theme of its third line in Josquin's Kyrie was later used by composers from Johann Jakob Froberger to Johann Sebastian Bach, and Anton Bruckner's first composition was a setting of the first strophe.

The Tantum ergo has been set separately by Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina, Franz Schubert, Maurice Duruflé and others. An organ reharmonisation of the hymn by Beethoven was found in October 2012 by the musicologist Barry Cooper. In 1818 Pius VII granted an indulgence of 300 days for each recitation of the whole hymn and 100 days for the Tantum ergo. A Syriac translation was used at benediction in the Syro-Malabar Catholic Church of Kerala until the 1970s.
pangeran-antasari: Antasari was born in 1809, the son of Prince Mashud and grandson of Prince Amir, in a line of the Banjar royal family whose power had been usurped in the 18th century. In 1859 the Dutch backed the coronation of Sultan Tamjidillah, rather than Prince Hidayatullah, as successor to Sultan Adam, a choice that troubled Antasari. Wishing to drive out the Dutch, he made common cause with the leaders of Martapura, Kapuas, Pelaihari, Barito and Kahayan, and was aided by Hidayatullah and Demang Leman.

The Banjarmasin War broke out on 18 April 1859, with Antasari's alliance able to field some 6,000 armed men. The fighting took place mainly in South and Central Kalimantan. His forces attacked the Dutch at Gunung Jabuk and the Dutch coal mines at Pengaron, while his allies struck other posts and ships; in December 1859 they sank the ship Onrust, killing Lieutenants Van der Velde and Bangert. Antasari rejected Dutch offers of wealth and power in exchange for his surrender.

In early August 1860 his forces were at Ringkau Katan, where they were defeated on 9 August after Dutch reinforcements arrived from Amuntai. Hidayatullah was exiled to Java, and Antasari succeeded him as sultan. With Prince Miradipa and Tumenggung Mancanegara he defended the fort of Tundakan on 24 September 1861, and with Gusti Umar and Tumenggung Surapati a fort on Mount Tongka on 8 November 1861. On 14 March 1862 his people gave him the title Panembahan Amiruddin Khaliful Mukmin, which made him their religious leader.

In October 1862 Antasari was planning a large attack when an outbreak of smallpox killed him on 11 October. He was buried in Banjarmasin, where other resistance leaders of different periods were later laid to rest, and the place became known as the Antasari Heroes' Cemetery. His son Muhammad Seman carried on the struggle against the Dutch until his own death in 1905.

President Suharto declared Antasari a National Hero of Indonesia by presidential decree No. 06/TK/1968. A documentary on his life was made in the mid-1990s, and he appears on the obverse of the 2,000 rupiah note of the 2009 series, which shows traditional Bornean dancers on the reverse.
pangkor-treaty-of-1874: Perak was a major tin producer, and Britain, already holding Penang, Malacca and Singapore, valued it highly. The Larut Wars of 1861 to 1874, fought among Malay chiefs and between the Chinese secret societies Ghee Hin, led by Chin Ah Yam, and Hai San, led by Chung Keng Quee, disrupted the supply. When Sultan Ali died in 1871, the heir Raja Abdullah missed the funeral and Raja Bendahara Ismail was proclaimed sultan instead. Abdullah turned to the Singapore businessman Tan Kim Cheng and the merchant William Henry Macleod Read, who drafted a letter for him asking Governor Andrew Clarke to place Perak under British protection.

The conference opened as the Chinese chiefs arrived on 13 January 1874, the Mantri Ngah Ibrahim the next day and Abdullah with the Malay chiefs on 15 January. Clarke heard the chiefs one by one before choosing a candidate, and the documents were signed on 20 January aboard the Colonial Steamer Pluto off Pangkor island. Frank Swettenham and Mohamed Said prepared the Malay text.

Abdullah was recognised as Sultan of Perak, and Ismail was to keep the title Sultan Muda with a pension and a small territory. All revenues were to be collected and appointments made in the sultan's name, but under the Resident's advice; an Assistant Resident was attached to the Governor of Larut, and the cost of both was a first charge on Perak's revenues. The boundaries of Pulo Dinding and Province Wellesley were adjusted in Britain's favour. A separate agreement bound the Chinese leaders to keep the peace under a bond of $50,000, made Chung and Chin Ah Yam Kapitan Cina, and renamed Larut Taiping, everlasting peace.

Of the three possible claimants only Abdullah was present: Ismail refused to come, and the British seem not to have known of Raja Yusof. The chiefs of Perak held that Ismail had been elected three years earlier and kept the royal regalia, so in their eyes Abdullah's accession was not valid. The historian Tate judged the Larut settlement satisfactory to both sides and the succession agreement unsatisfactory from the beginning. Sir James W. W. Birch became Perak's first British Resident. Residents followed in Sungei Ujong in 1874 and Selangor in 1875, and Pahang came under protection in 1888; with Negeri Sembilan these states later formed the Federated Malay States.
panglao-island: Panglao lies in the north of the Bohol Sea, in the Central Visayas region, south-west of Bohol and east and south of Cebu. It covers 91.12 square kilometres and is divided between two municipalities of Bohol Province, Dauis and Panglao. Its land runs from plains to hills and higher ground, and it is built of Maribojoc limestone, the youngest of the limestone units of western Bohol.

Because coralline limestone dissolves in water, the island is marked by caves and sinkholes, which delayed the building of its international airport. It has no rivers or lakes, and the Hinagdanan Cave, with its underground water, is an important source of fresh water. Several small islands belong to the group, among them Gak-ang, Pontod and Balicasag, and Pamalican lies close by.

Before Spanish rule Panglao was known to Chinese, Malay, Siamese and Indonesian traders. It was the seat of the Kedatuan of Bo-ol, a precolonial polity that fell to an attack by the Ternate Sultanate and was later rebuilt under Spanish protection at Dapitan. The census of 1818 counted 2,055 native families in Dauis, then the island's chief town, along with 9 Spanish-Filipino families and an unrecorded number of Mexicans who had arrived earlier and merged with the local population.

The census of 2015 gave the island a population of 79,216. Two bridges, the Cong. Suarez Bridge and the Gov. Borja Bridge, join it to the main island of Bohol, and the Bohol–Panglao International Airport, opened in November 2018 in place of the old Tagbilaran Airport, serves the whole province. Alona Beach is the best-known spot for visitors, who come for diving, snorkelling and dolphin watching.

The surrounding waters are rich in marine life: the Panglao Marine Biodiversity Project found about 250 new species of crustaceans and 2,500 new species of molluscs around the island. In July 2018 the Panglao Island Protected Seascape was declared a national park under Republic Act No. 11038, signed by President Rodrigo Duterte.
pangu-party: The Pangu Pati, officially the Papua na Niugini Yunion Pati (Papua and New Guinea Union Party), was established on 13 June 1967 to contest the elections of 1968. Its aims set it apart from its rivals: it sought the political unification of Papua and New Guinea, stronger economic development and a larger national income, while other parties, such as the United Christian Democratic Party, favoured statehood within Australia.

Its candidates did not yet form a formal political union, but ten of them were elected to the House of Assembly in 1968. At the election of 1972, the last held under Australian authority, Pangu-endorsed candidates won eighteen seats, and candidates who supported the party reached twenty-six in all. It is the oldest party in Papua New Guinea and has held power at every level of government.

Somare led the government as head of the Pangu Party from 1972 to 1980 and again from 1982 to 1985. In 1985 Paias Wingti took a faction out of the party and won a vote of no confidence against Somare, succeeding him as prime minister. In 1988 Rabbie Namaliu replaced Somare as party leader and served as prime minister from 1988 to 1992; Somare went on to lead the National Alliance Party.

The party then shrank. Under Chris Haiveta it won 6 of 109 seats in 2002 and joined the coalition government Somare formed after that election; it won 5 seats in 2007 and stayed in his government. In 2012 it won a single seat, that of the Angoram member Ludwig Schulze, and had none after his death in March 2013.

In August 2014 the deputy opposition leader Sam Basil crossed to Pangu, revived its parliamentary wing and became its leader. A by-election won by William Samb in Goilala Open in August 2015 gave it two members, and the 2017 elections nine. At the 2022 elections it won 39 seats, its best result since 1982, after several members of the PNC, among them James Marape, had moved to Pangu; Marape continued as prime minister.
panionium: The Panionium stood on the peninsula of Mount Mycale, about 100 kilometres south of Smyrna, now İzmir in Turkey. Herodotus describes it as sacred ground on Mykale facing north, set apart for Poseidon of Helicon by the joint will of the Ionians. Strabo places it after the Samian strait, near the mountain as one sails to Ephesus, three stadia above the sea. It was in the keeping of Priene, about 15 kilometres away across the mountain, whose citizens managed the sanctuary and presided at its sacrifices and rites.

At the Panionium the Ionians held their festival and games, the Panionia. Under Persian rule activities there were curtailed. Thucydides, writing at the end of the 5th century BCE, says the Ionians were then celebrating their festival at Ephesus, and Diodorus says war in the surrounding area forced them to move it there. Under Alexander the Great the games and festival were held at the Panionium again and continued under Roman rule, without regaining their earlier importance.

The exact site was later lost. An inscription found in the area in 1673 gave a clue, and at the end of the 19th century Theodor Wiegand identified a site on a low hill called Otomatik Tepe near Güzelçamlı, 17 km south of Kuşadası, which Kleiner, Hommel and Müller-Wiener excavated in 1958. There a temenos wall encloses a long stone presumed to be the altar of Poseidon, from the end of the 6th century BCE, and below it lies a small rock-cut theatre of the 4th century BCE, presumed to be the league's council chamber. No temple has been found there.

In 2004 the German archaeologist Hans Lohmann found another site high in the mountains, a settlement with an archaic temple of the Ionic order from about the middle of the 6th century BCE, which was excavated in 2005 with the Museum of Aydın. Lohmann holds that this site should be identified as the Panionion, as it agrees better with the written sources.
panjikent: Panjakent, also written Penjikent, lies in the Sughd province of Tajikistan on the river Zeravshan. The ruins of the old town are on the outskirts of the modern city. Downstream, on the tugay-vegetated floodplain of the river, lies the Sarazm Important Bird Area. The ancient town stood about 90 km from Samarkand, to which it was a vassal state.

Ancient Panjakent, known as Panchekanth, was a small but flourishing town of the Sogdians in pre-Islamic Central Asia. The Sogdians settled in city states in the Zeravshan valley and the surrounding oases, clustered mostly around Samarkand. These states had strong rivalries, their own traditions and ruling families, and a very decentralised political system. The town grew in the 5th century, when established businessmen and landowners made their livelihoods there. In 722 Arab Muslim forces besieged and took it, and its last ruler, Divashtich, fled into the upper Zeravshan but was captured and sentenced to death.

For around fifty years the town was ruled by new administrators, and towards the end of the 8th century the town on the upper terraces was depopulated and relocated. Records of a Penjikent rulership written in Sogdian were found not far away on Mount Mug. According to Arab geographers, in the 10th century Panjakent had a formal Friday mosque, which distinguished a town from a village; it was the easternmost city of Sogd and became well known for its walnuts.

The ruins have yielded numerous murals, and many are now displayed in the Hermitage Museum and in the National Museum of Antiquities of Tajikistan in Dushanbe. They show details of dress and daily life, and a great variety of influences: Greek decorative styles meet the Iranian narratives of the Shahnameh and the epic cycle of Rostam, scenes of festivities alternate with combats, and local cults mix with Iranian and Hindu deities. One painting shows Shiva with a halo and a sacred thread, clad in a tigerskin and seated on a cushioned seat supported by two bulls, with attendants in Sogdian dress.

The production of paintings began in the 5th century and stopped in 722 with the Arab invasion, when many works were damaged or destroyed. The Russian archaeologist Boris Marshak spent more than fifty years excavating the ruins. He stayed on as director of the excavation after Tajik independence and through the civil war of 1992 to 1997, and worked with the government of Tajikistan to protect the site.
panna-national-park: With Ken Gharial Sanctuary and the adjoining forest divisions, the park forms a large part of the basin of the 406 km Ken River, which flows northeast for about 72 km through it. The park and the forests of the North and South Panna divisions are the only large wildlife habitat left in northern Madhya Pradesh. It lies where the belt of tropical and subtropical dry broadleaf forests breaks off and the moist deciduous forests of the Upper Gangetic Plains begin, at the northernmost tip of the natural teak forests.

Besides the Bengal tiger the park holds the Indian leopard, chital, chinkara, nilgai, sambar deer, sloth bear and more than 200 species of birds. The reserve had over 40 tigers six years before it was announced in June 2009 that none were left, apart from two tigresses brought in from Bandhavgarh National Park and Kanha National Park in March 2009. The Madhya Pradesh government did not determine responsibility, nor did it pass the inquiry to the Central Bureau of Investigation despite requests from the Ministry of Environment and Forests and the Prime Minister's Office.

A male, T3, brought from Pench Tiger Reserve, strayed out in November 2009 and walked towards his old home through farmland without causing conflict; forest staff tracked him for over a month and brought him back, and he then settled and mated. The tigress T1 gave birth to four cubs in April 2010, and T2 to four more some months later. The recovery has since brought the population to as many as 80 tigers.

In 2007 the Ministry of Tourism named it the best maintained national park in India. The park is the centre of the Panna Biosphere Reserve, designated by UNESCO in 2020 and covering 2,998.98 km2 with over 300 villages. A planned link of the Ken and Betwa rivers through the 283 m Daudhan Dam would flood 400 hectares of the tiger reserve.
pannonhalma-archabbey: Pannonhalma Archabbey, formally the Territorial Abbey of Saint Martin on Mount Pannonhalma, stands on a hill 282 metres high near the town of Pannonhalma and is one of the oldest historical monuments in Hungary. Saint Martin of Tours is believed to have been born at the foot of the hill, which was once called the Mount of Saint Martin. It is the second largest territorial abbey in the world, after the one at Monte Cassino. Its sights include the basilica with its crypt, the cloisters, a monumental library with 400,000 volumes and a Baroque refectory with several trompe-l'œil paintings.

Prince Géza founded it in 996 as the first Hungarian Benedictine monastery, in honour of Saint Martin of Tours, and it soon became the centre of the Benedictine order. Géza's son, King Stephen I, donated estates and privileges, and Astrik served as its first abbot. The Charter of the Tihany Benedictine Abbey, of 1055, the oldest surviving document to use the Hungarian language, is still preserved in the library. In 1096 Duke Godfrey of Bouillon, leading one of three crusader armies, spent a week there negotiating safe passage through Hungary with King Coloman. The first buildings were destroyed in 1137 and rebuilt, the present church dates from the early 13th century, and in 1486 the abbey was reconstructed in Gothic style under King Matthias.

It became an archabbey in 1541 and was fortified because of Ottoman incursions. During the occupation of Hungary by the Ottoman Empire the monks had to abandon the abbey for varying periods. A major Baroque construction was under way in the time of Archabbot Benedek Sajghó (1722–1768), and the abbey received its present form in 1832, with the library and a classicist tower. It was closed in 1786 and reopened in 1802. In 1950 the communist state confiscated the properties of the order and its schools, which were not returned until communism ended.

The abbey and its surroundings were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1996, a year after the complex was entirely reconstructed and renovated for the millennium. Its archives hold one of the richest collections of documents from the first centuries of Hungarian statehood, among them the interpolated charter of Saint Stephen of 1001–1002 and the founding charter of Tihany. A Benedictine high school, a College of Theology named after Saint Gerard of Csanád and a winery are among its present uses.
pannonia: Pannonia was a province of the Roman Empire bounded on the north and east by the Danube, on the west by Noricum and upper Italy, and on the south by Dalmatia and upper Moesia. It included western Hungary, western Slovakia, eastern Austria, northern Croatia, north-western Serbia, northern Slovenia and northern Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the Early Iron Age Transdanubia was inhabited by the Pannonians, a collection of Illyrian tribes. Celtic groups, the Scordisci, the Boii and others, later held much of the region, and the Dacian king Burebista overcame several of them between 65 and 50 BCE.

Rome's advance began with the foundation of Aquileia in 181 BCE. In 35 BCE Octavian captured Siscia after a month-long siege and occupied much of the Sava valley. In 15 BCE the future emperor Tiberius defeated the Scordisci, and his operations of 12 to 9 BCE almost certainly brought the whole of Transdanubia under Roman control. Augustus later claimed in his Res Gestae that Tiberius had brought the Pannonian peoples under Roman authority. The Bellum Batonianum, a revolt led by the Breuci under Bato the Breucian and the Daesitiates under Bato the Daesitiate, lasted three years until the last rebel laid down arms in 9 CE. Illyricum was then divided into Dalmatia and Pannonia.

Claudius finished the occupation and began building the frontier, the limes. Under Trajan, between 103 and 107, the province was divided into Pannonia Inferior and Pannonia Superior, the latter with most of the urbanised areas and three legions. Wars with the Marcomanni and Quadi under Marcus Aurelius, from 166, brought heavy destruction and loss of life to Pannonia. Diocletian and his successors divided it into four provinces, Prima, Valeria, Savia and Secunda. In 324 Constantine I annexed the plains to the east up to a new limes, the Devil's Dykes.

Rome lost the province in stages. In 433 Flavius Aetius ceded part of it to the Huns, and after the Hunnic empire collapsed in 454, Emperor Marcian settled large numbers of Ostrogoths there as foederati. Justinian I's Eastern Roman Empire held southern parts in the 6th century, the Avars invaded in the 560s, and Slavs settled over time. In the 790s the Franks invaded and used the name Pannonia for a new frontier province, the March of Pannonia.

Roman Pannonia was fairly productive, with oats and barley its chief crops, and timber an important export until the forests were cleared. Native settlements were organised in cantons, while most large towns were of Roman origin, among them Carnuntum, Vindobona, Aquincum, Savaria, Sirmium and Siscia. Christianity began to spread in the province in the 2nd century. A dialect called Pannonian Latin developed and went extinct around the 6th century. The ancient name survives in the modern term Pannonian plain.
panticapaeum: Panticapaeum, in Greek Pantikapaion, lay on the western side of the Cimmerian Bosporus, on the eastern shore of Crimea, which the Greeks called Taurica. Its name comes from the Scythian *Pantikapa, meaning fish-path. The city stood on a hill later named Mount Mithridat, and its ruins now lie within the modern city of Kerch. At its largest extent it covered about 100 hectares (250 acres). The Hermitage and the Kerch Museums hold material from the site, which is still being excavated.

In its first centuries the city relied on imported Greek goods: pottery, terracottas and metal objects, probably from workshops in Rhodes, Corinth, Samos and Athens. Athens made a special type of bowl for the city, known as Kerch ware, while local potters imitated the Gnathia style and Megarian relief bowls. The city minted silver coins from the 5th century BCE and gold and bronze coins from the 4th century BCE.

In the 5th and 4th centuries BCE it became the residence first of the Archaeanactids and then of the Spartocids, dynasties of Thracian kings of the Bosporus, and for that reason it was sometimes itself called Bosporus. Its economic decline in the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE followed the Sarmatian conquest of the steppes and growing competition from Egyptian grain.

The last Spartocid, Paerisades V, apparently left his realm to Mithridates VI Eupator, king of Pontus. His general Diophantus arranged the transfer after being sent to Taurica to help local Greek cities against Palacus of the Scythian kingdom in Crimea. Paerisades was murdered by Scythians led by Saumacus, and Diophantus escaped, returning with reinforcements to suppress the revolt around 110 BCE.

Mithridates took his own life at Panticapaeum after his defeat in the war against Rome, when his son and heir Pharnaces and the citizens of the city turned against him. Inscriptions of the 1st and 2nd centuries CE mention a local synagogue that supervised the legal freeing of slaves, and a 3rd-century Hebrew funerary inscription for a man named Isaac survives. The remains of the city lie in central Kerch.
panuco-river: The Pánuco, also called the Río de Canoas, is about 510 kilometres long and drains a basin of 98,227 km2 that takes in parts of the Mexican Plateau, the Sierra Madre Oriental and the Gulf Coastal Plain. It is formed where its two main tributaries meet. The Moctezuma rises on the plateau, where its headwaters include the Tula River, marks the border between Hidalgo and Querétaro and cuts a deep canyon through the Sierra. The Tampaón, or Tamuín, is formed by the Santa María and the Río Verde, which also cross the Sierra in canyons.

Below the confluence the Pánuco winds another 172.5 km through the coastal lowlands, joined by the Topila and the Tamesí, and its lower course forms the border between Tamaulipas and Veracruz. The basin is subtropical: the eastern slopes of the Sierra catch the rain of the easterly trade winds, strongest from late June to August, while the plateau lies in their rain shadow. The river runs highest in late summer and early autumn.

In 1519, while charting the western coast of the Gulf of Mexico, the Spanish explorer Alonso Álvarez de Pineda founded a settlement on the river, which he named Las Palmas. It was abandoned after he was killed in battle with the Indigenous people who lived nearby.

The Pánuco is the fourth-largest river of Mexico by volume of runoff, and its basin is the country's sixth-largest by area. Only its last 15 km are navigable for larger ships, and the Tampico Bridge crosses it near the mouth at Tampico–Ciudad Madero. The basin holds almost 100 species of fish, many found nowhere else, among them six Nosferatu cichlids and nine northern swordtails, and some of these are seriously threatened.
pao-people: The Pa'O are linked in their history with the Thaton region of lower Myanmar. They once wore colourful clothing, but after King Anawratha defeated Manuha, the Mon king of Thaton, the Pa'O were enslaved and made to wear indigo-dyed clothes as a sign of their status. Their origin myth holds that they descend from a shaman, or weizza, and a female dragon, and the Pa'O flag badge that men and women pin to their jackets represents the two. They are also known as the Black Karen, Pa-U and Taungthu.

The Pa'O are the second largest ethnic group of Shan State and also live in Kayin, Kayah and Mon states and the Bago Division; many have fled conflict to Mae Hong Son Province in northern Thailand. They fall into the Lowland Pa'O of Thaton and the Highland Pa'O of Taunggyi, with as many as twenty-four subgroups. Besides thanapet leaves they grow onions, garlic, chili, potatoes, rice, peanuts, beans, sesame and green tea.

Most Pa'O follow Buddhism, and some are Christian or hold animist beliefs. Boys are initiated as novice monks at Poy Sang Long, and in Buddhist Lent young people carry lanterns three times round the temple. From April to July the Fire Rocket Festival brings villages together for a week to fire rockets, once of bamboo and now of iron, to help the clouds make rain. Pa'O National Day falls on the full moon of Tabaung in March and honours ancestors and leaders such as King Suriya Janthar.

Highland men traditionally wear a turban, a white shirt, a dark jacket and long black trousers, and women a five-piece outfit with a turban and two large conical hairpins. At weddings guests tie cotton threads round the wrists of the couple. Common people are buried and monks cremated.
paolo-malatesta: Paolo Malatesta was born around 1246 in Verucchio, the third son of Malatesta da Verucchio and his first wife, Concordia dei Pandolfini. His brothers included Giovanni, known as Gianciotto, and Malatestino Malatesta. The name il Bello, the Beautiful, referred to his physical prowess, in contrast to the unattractiveness attributed to Gianciotto.

In 1269 he married Orabile Beatrice, the last heir of the counts of Ghiaggiolo, a fief in the Forlì Apennines that also took in Cusercoli, Valdoppio and Particeto. The house of Ghiaggiolo was Ghibelline and allied with the Montefeltro family, so the match was a diplomatic gain for his Guelph father, who wanted its lands. The couple had two children, Uberto II and Margherita, and Paolo founded the Malatesta di Ghiaggiolo line, which died out in 1757.

Paolo fought beside his father against the Ghibellines. In 1265 he took the field against Guido da Montefeltro and, the same year, against the Traversari together with Guido da Polenta of Ravenna. In March 1282 Pope Martin IV chose him, for his diplomatic skill, as Captain of the People in Florence, and it was probably there that Dante Alighieri met him. Tradition has portrayed him as a gentle figure given to culture and pleasure, but more recent research presents a young man closely engaged in the politics and intrigues of his day.

His marriage was unhappy. Paolo had been drawn to Francesca da Polenta, Gianciotto's wife, since their first meeting, when she believed she was to marry Paolo; he had stood in for his brother at the proxy wedding in Ravenna. After his return to Rimini, Gianciotto surprised the two together and killed them both. Tradition places the killing at the castle of Gradara.

Dante told their story in the fifth canto of the Inferno in homage to the man he had known in his youth in Florence; years later, in exile, he was called to Ravenna by Francesca's father. A tomb of a noble lady has been found at Gradara, but no trace of Paolo's grave, which his brother would have had reason to hide.
paolo-uccello: The sources for his life are few: Giorgio Vasari's biography, written 75 years after his death, and a few contemporary official documents. Born Paolo di Dono, he was probably born in Pratovecchio, near Arezzo, the hometown of his father Dono di Paolo, a barber-surgeon. His mother, Antonia, came from a high-born Florentine family. His nickname Uccello, "little bird", came from his fondness for painting birds.

From 1412 until 1416 he was apprenticed to the sculptor Lorenzo Ghiberti, creator of the doors of the Florence Baptistery, whose workshop was then the premier centre of Florentine art. It was around this time that his lifelong friendship with Donatello began. He was admitted to the painters' guild, the Compagnia di San Luca, in 1414, and joined the Arte dei Medici e degli Speziali in 1415.

By 1424 Uccello was earning his own living. That year he painted episodes of the Creation and the Fall for the Green Cloister of Santa Maria Novella in Florence, followed by scenes from the life of Noah, which brought him great fame. In 1425 he travelled to Venice to work on the mosaics for the façade of San Marco, all since lost, and he was back in Florence in 1431. In 1443 he painted the figures on the clock of the Duomo and designed stained glass windows for it.

Around the mid-1450s he painted the three panels of the Battle of San Romano for the Palazzo Medici, commemorating the Florentine victory over the Sienese in 1432. Their foreshortened forms, extending in many planes, give a controlled structure to the chaos of battle. From 1465 to 1469 he worked in Urbino with his son Donato for the Confraternity of Corpus Domini, painting the predella of its altarpiece, the Miracle of the Profaned Host.

In his Florentine tax return of August 1469 Uccello declared that he was old and ailing, his wife was ill, and he could no longer work. He made his testament on 11 November 1475 and died on 10 December at the hospital of Florence, aged 78. He was buried in his father's tomb in the church of Santo Spirito.

Vasari wrote that Uccello was obsessed with perspective and would stay up all night in his study trying to grasp the exact vanishing point. He worked in the Late Gothic tradition, emphasising colour and pageantry, and his style was idiosyncratic; he left no school of followers. His perspective influenced painters such as Piero della Francesca, Albrecht Dürer and Leonardo da Vinci.
paolo-veronese: Veronese took his usual name from Verona, where he was born in 1528, the fifth child of a stonecutter named Gabriele and his wife Caterina. He was first known as Paolo Spezapreda, after his father's trade, and later took the surname Caliari because his mother was the illegitimate daughter of a nobleman, Antonio Caliari. By 1541 he was apprenticed to Antonio Badile, later his father-in-law, and in 1544 to Giovanni Francesco Caroto, both leading painters in Verona. Trained in the Mannerism then popular in Parma, he soon developed a preference for a more radiant palette.
In 1551 the Giustiniani family commissioned an altarpiece from him for the church of San Francesco della Vigna in Venice, and in 1552 Cardinal Ercole Gonzaga commissioned one for Mantua Cathedral.

Veronese moved to Venice in 1553 after receiving his first state commission, ceiling frescoes in the Hall of the Council of Ten in the Doge's Palace. His ceilings of 1557 in the Marciana Library won a prize judged by Titian and Jacopo Sansovino.

In the late 1550s he decorated the Villa Barbaro at Maser, a new building by Andrea Palladio, with frescoes that combine portraits of the family, mythological figures and ceilings opening to blue skies. His Wedding at Cana, painted in 1562–1563 for the monastery of San Giorgio Maggiore, was to cover 66 square metres; the contract required premium pigments and as many figures as possible, and it includes portraits of Titian and Tintoretto and a self-portrait. In 1565 he married Elena Badile, the daughter of his first master. He headed a family workshop that included his brother Benedetto and his sons Carlo and Gabriele, which went on after his death in 1588, signing its works Haeredes Pauli.

In 1573 Veronese completed a Last Supper for the refectory of the Basilica of Santi Giovanni e Paolo, replacing a painting by Titian that had been burnt in a fire. At 5.55 by 12.80 metres, it showed a banquet that included German soldiers, dwarves and animals.

On 18 July 1573 the Venetian Inquisition summoned him to explain these figures, which it considered extraneous to the Last Supper. He told the tribunal that painters take the same liberties as poets and madmen. The Inquisition ordered him to repaint the scene; he opposed this remedy but was compelled to retitle the work The Feast in the House of Levi. The interrogation is described as cautionary rather than punitive. His admirers have included Rubens, Watteau, Tiepolo, Delacroix and Renoir, though his work has been felt not to permit expression of the profound.
papacy: According to Catholic tradition, the apostolic see of Rome was founded by Saint Peter and Saint Paul in the first century. The Catholic Church teaches that the bishop of Rome succeeded Saint Peter, to whom, in its reading of Matthew 16, Jesus gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the powers of binding and loosing. Cyprian of Carthage, in his Letter 55 of about 251 CE to Pope Cornelius, recognised the bishop of Rome as Peter's successor.

The word pope comes from the Greek páppas, father. In the early centuries it was applied, especially in the East, to all bishops and senior clergy. It became reserved in the West to the bishop of Rome during the reign of Leo I (440 to 461), though this was made official only in the 11th century.

In ancient times popes helped spread Christianity and intervened in doctrinal disputes. In the Middle Ages they played a role of secular importance in Western Europe, often arbitrating between Christian monarchs, and their influence eventually rivalled that of territorial rulers. From the 8th century until 1870 the pope was sovereign of the Papal States, and since the Lateran Treaty of 1929 he has headed the much smaller Vatican City State. Between 1309 and 1378 the popes lived in Avignon, France, a period often called the Babylonian captivity. The First Vatican Council defined the pope's authority on 18 July 1870, and in 1870 the dogma of papal infallibility was proclaimed for the rare occasions when the pope speaks ex cathedra on faith or morals.

The pope was originally chosen by the senior clergy in and near Rome. In 1059 the electorate was restricted to the cardinals, and in 1179 the votes of all cardinal electors were made equal. The last pope elected when not yet a bishop was Gregory XVI in 1831, and the last not a cardinal was Urban VI in 1378. Popes adopt a new name on accession.

His official seat is the Archbasilica of Saint John Lateran, and his residence the Apostolic Palace. Antipopes are claimants not canonically elected; briefly in the 15th century three separate lines of popes claimed authenticity. Eastern Orthodox churches and the Anglican Communion accept apostolic succession and a primacy of honour but reject the pope as Peter's successor in any other sense than other bishops.
papak: Pabag's homeland, Pars or Persis in the south-western Iranian plateau, had been the birthplace of the Achaemenid Empire. After Alexander the Great it was ruled by local dynasties, first under the Seleucid Empire and then as a vassal of the Parthian (Arsacid) Empire, whose Kings of Persis used the title of shah. Pabag himself ruled a small principality in the area of Khir, south of Bakhtegan Lake, as a vassal of Gochihr, the Bazrangid king of Stakhr, who was in turn a vassal of the Parthian emperor.

With Gochihr's permission, Pabag sent Ardashir to serve under Tiri, commander of the fortress of Darabgerd. Pabag reportedly served as a priest of the Temple of Anahita at Istakhr, a rallying point for local Persian soldiers who worshipped the goddess. The medieval historian Al-Tabari makes him the son of Sasan and of Rambihisht, a princess of the Bazrangid family.

The Parthian Empire under Vologases V was weakened by wars with the Romans, civil wars and regional revolts. The Roman emperor Septimius Severus invaded in 196 and again two years later, when he sacked Ctesiphon, and revolts broke out in Media and Pars. In 205 or 206 Pabag rebelled, overthrew Gochihr and took Istakhr. Al-Tabari says he acted at Ardashir's urging, but the Iranologist Touraj Daryaee considers this unlikely and holds that it was the eldest son, Shapur, who helped him, as coins bearing the portraits of both show.

Pabag then named Shapur his heir, much to the dislike of Ardashir, who had become commander of Darabgerd after the death of Tiri. In an act of defiance Ardashir left for Ardashir-Khwarrah and fortified himself there, preparing to attack his brother Shapur once their father had died.

Pabag died a natural death a few years after taking Istakhr and was succeeded by Shapur. Both brothers then minted coins with the title of king and Pabag's portrait; the reverse of Shapur's read son of His Majesty, King Pabag. Shapur died in obscure circumstances in 211 or 212, and Ardashir succeeded him, conquered the rest of Iran and established the Sasanian Empire in 224.

Ardashir's coins and his inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam call him the son of divine Pabag, the king, and his son Shapur I, in inscriptions at Naqsh-e Rajab and the Ka'ba-ye Zartosht, calls himself the grandson of Pabag. The Middle Persian Kar-Namag i Ardashir i Pabagan, the Book of the Deeds of Ardashir, son of Pabag, keeps the same link in its title.
papeete: Papeete lies on the island of Tahiti, in the Windward Islands, which are part of the Society Islands. The name Papeʻete means water from a basket. It is an effect of a naming taboo under the reign of Pōmare I, when the Tahitian word for water, vai, was replaced by pape; the older name Vaiʻete is still recognised in some areas, such as the Marquesas. The city has a tropical monsoon climate with high temperatures and humidity throughout the year. Its wet season covers most of the year, and the dry season is short, only August and September.

The town's growth in the late 19th century is recorded in its public works. A water tower at Faʻaiere, with a capacity of 150,000 litres, supplied the town with drinking water; a light railway on an inclined plane 220 metres long overcame a difference in altitude of 37 metres, with a steam-driven winch hauling three narrow-gauge trucks at a time.

In a letter of 18 June 1891 to Governor Theodore Lacascade, Paul Decauville mentioned an order for 15 kilometres of portable rail track, probably for a tramway from Papeʻete to Punaʻauia. In 1902 the post office had to be moved, and instead of being demolished it was lifted from the subsoil and moved whole on a Decauville railway.

After the outbreak of the First World War, German vessels shelled Papeʻete, causing loss of life and significant damage. The city's growth later received a boost when France moved its nuclear weapon test range from Algeria, which had become independent, to the atolls of Moruroa and Fangataufa, about 1,500 kilometres to the east of Tahiti, and built the Faʻaʻā International Airport, opened in 1962. Rioting followed French nuclear tests in 1987 and on 5 September 1995, when a riot lasted two days and damaged the airport.

Papeʻete is the capital of French Polynesia, an overseas collectivity of the French Republic, and the administrative capital of the Windward Islands. It is the main centre of government, commerce and finance of French Polynesia, and a commonly used port of call. Landmarks include the Cathedral of Notre Dame, the Territorial Assembly, the Papeʻete Market and Bougainville Park. The Territorial Assembly stands on the site of the royal residence and palace of Queen Pōmare IV, who ruled from 1827 to 1877.
papermaking: In papermaking a dilute suspension of separate cellulose fibres in water, called furnish, is drained through a sieve-like screen, so that a mat of randomly interwoven fibres is laid down. The water is then pressed out, sometimes with the help of suction or heat, and the dried sheet is flat, even and strong. By hand, the screen is a mesh stretched in a wooden mould; the frame, the deckle, leaves the slightly wavy deckle edges of handmade paper, and the wires leave laid lines and chain lines. Watermarks are made by weaving a design into the wires.

The word paper comes from papyrus, a material made from the pith of the Cyperus papyrus plant in ancient Egypt long before paper was used in China. Hemp paper served for wrapping and padding in China from the eighth century BCE, and paper with legible writing has been dated to 8 BCE. Tradition credits Cai Lun, an official of the Han dynasty court, with inventing paper about 105 CE from mulberry and other bast fibres, fishnets, old rags and hemp waste. Paper for writing was widespread by the 3rd century.

In the 8th century papermaking reached the Islamic world, where production began in Samarkand, Baghdad, Damascus, Cairo, Morocco and then Muslim Spain; in Baghdad it was supervised by the Grand Vizier Ja'far ibn Yahya. Muslim makers found a way to make a thicker sheet, water-powered pulp mills appear first at Samarkand, and Arabic geographers noted paper mills at Damascus in the 9th century.

In Europe moulds of metal wire were developed and watermarks were well established by 1300. Hemp and linen rags were the main source of pulp until cotton took over from the late 1700s. Paper at first had few advantages over papyrus and parchment, and mills multiplied only after movable type printing raised demand in the 15th century.

Modern papermaking began in the early 19th century with the Fourdrinier machine, which makes a continuous roll instead of single sheets, and John Dickinson's cylinder mould machine of 1809. In 1844 Charles Fenerty and Friedrich Gottlob Keller devised a process for using wood pulp, which ended nearly 2,000 years of pulped rags.
papiamento: Scholars dispute where Papiamento came from, and its precise history has not been established. Its parent language is West Iberian Romance, but some derive it from Portuguese and the Portuguese-based creoles, others from Spanish. Most linguists now believe it emerged from the Portuguese-based creoles of the West African coasts, since it shares many features with Cape Verdean Creole and Guinea-Bissau Creole. Bart Jacob has argued that it is a relexified offshoot of an early Upper Guinea Portuguese Creole carried to Curaçao from Senegambia in the second half of the 17th century, when the Dutch held the slave-trading island of Gorée. A local-development theory instead proposes a Portuguese-African pidgin formed in the Caribbean, with later Dutch and Spanish influences.

In 1634 the Dutch West India Company took possession of the islands, deporting most of the remaining Arawak and Spanish population and making them a hub of the Dutch slave trade between Africa and the Caribbean. After 1654 the Jewish and Portuguese-speaking population of the islands grew substantially, as Portuguese-speaking Jews and their allies fled Northeast Brazil. The Sephardic community became the main merchants, and everyday trading was conducted in Papiamento. The language itself dates from about 1650.

About 80 per cent of the vocabulary is Iberian in origin and about 20 per cent Dutch, with some words from Native American and African languages. Many Iberian words cannot be assigned to Portuguese or Spanish, such as por fabor and señora. Words of Taíno and Arawak origin, mostly for plants and animals, include maishi, corn, and kunuku, farm; African ones include pinda, peanut, from Kongo mpinda. The grammar is typical of Atlantic creoles: time and aspect markers are used instead of tenses, there is no grammatical gender, and the plural is marked by the suffix -nan on definite nouns.

There are two main dialects, Papiamento on Aruba and Papiamentu on Curaçao and Bonaire. Curaçao and Bonaire adopted the phonetic Römer-Maduro-Jonis spelling in 1976, and Aruba approved a more etymological one in 1977.

Widespread use in official documents is first seen in the early 18th century. The oldest preserved texts are letters, the earliest of 1775. In the 19th century most materials on the islands were written in Papiamento, including Roman Catholic school books and hymnals. The Catecismo Corticu of 1837, the first printed book in the language, was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2009, and the first newspaper, Civilisadó, appeared in 1871. Papiamento became an official language of Aruba in 2003 and of the Netherlands Antilles in 2007. The anthems of Aruba, Bonaire and Curaçao are in it.
papinian: Little is known about the life of Aemilius Papinianus. He was of Syrian origin and a native of Emesa, and is said to have been a kinsman of Julia Domna, the second wife of Emperor Septimius Severus, who belonged to the Emesene dynasty. One source shows him as a follower of the casuistry of Quintus Cervidius Scaevola, another as his pupil.

He was an intimate friend of Severus and accompanied him to Britain in 207, where he served in the forum of York during a rising of Scottish Highlanders. Severus made him magister libellorum, master of petitions, and attorney general (advocatus fisci). After the death of Gaius Fulvius Plautianus in 205 he became praetorian prefect. Before his death Severus commended his two sons, Caracalla and Geta, to the lawyer's charge.

Much of Papinian's output has been lost and what survives is small compared with that of Ulpian or Paul. His principal works were the Quaestiones in 37 books, written before 198, and nineteen books of Responsa, written between 204 and his death. He also wrote two books of Definitiones, a work De adulteriis and a short manual in Greek on the duties of commissioners of streets and bridges.

He was among the most revered of Roman jurists. Third-year law students bore the title Papinianistae, those worthy to study Papinian, and he was called the Asylum of Right and Treasurer of the Laws. The Law of Citations of 426 made him one of five jurists whose recorded views were decisive, with Gaius, Paulus, Modestinus and Ulpian, and his view prevailed whenever the other four disagreed.

Caracalla found sharing the government with Geta unsatisfactory and decided to usurp his brother. Papinian, trying to keep peace between them, only encouraged Caracalla's hatred. He was beheaded on Caracalla's order and his body dragged through the streets of Rome, after the killing of Geta in 212 and amid a general slaughter of Geta's friends, estimated by one source at 20,000 people. Details of his death were embellished in legend. The 16th-century French jurist Jacques Cujas wrote that there was never such a great lawyer before, nor ever would be after him. Andreas Gryphius made his death the subject of a play in 1659.
papua-new-guinea: The country covers 462,840 km2 and includes a large mainland and hundreds of islands in Melanesia, north of Australia. It lies where the north-moving Indo-Australian plate meets the west-moving Pacific plate, which gives it a highly variable geography, active volcanoes and frequent earthquakes. Mountains cover at least 72% of the country, and the highest point is Mount Wilhelm, at 4,509 metres. The Torres Strait, 152 kilometres wide, separates it from Australia's Cape York Peninsula. This terrain helps explain why the population is largely rural and divided into many small communities.

Archaeological evidence indicates that modern humans first reached what became New Guinea around 42,000 to 45,000 years ago. Agriculture was developed independently in the New Guinea highlands around 7000 BCE, making it one of the few areas where people domesticated plants without outside influence. Austronesian-speaking peoples of the Lapita culture had reached the Bismarck Archipelago by about 3,300 years ago. Communities were linked by trade, and bananas and sugarcane probably passed from New Guinea to other regions along these networks, but each community otherwise functioned largely independently.

European names for the island date from the 16th century: Jorge de Menezes called it Ilhas dos Papuas in 1526, and Yñigo Ortiz de Retez named it Nueva Guinea in 1545. In 1884 the eastern half was divided between German New Guinea in the north and British New Guinea in the south. The British territory was ceded to Australia in 1902 and became the Territory of Papua. Australia occupied German New Guinea during the First World War and then ruled it as a League of Nations mandate. The two territories were united in 1949, after fierce fighting there in World War II, and the country became independent in 1975. Europeans brought together communities that had sometimes been hostile or had no relationship at all.

Papua New Guinea is a Commonwealth realm with a governor-general representing the monarch and a unicameral National Parliament of 118 seats, in a Westminster system. Its capital and largest city is Port Moresby. There are 840 known spoken languages, the most of any country, and English and Tok Pisin serve as common languages. Most people live in customary communities, and the constitution protects traditional communities and lifestyles.
papyrus: Papyrus was first manufactured in Egypt as far back as the 3rd millennium BCE, and it is known to have been used at least as early as the First Dynasty. The earliest archaeological evidence was excavated in 2012 and 2013 at Wadi al-Jarf, an ancient Egyptian harbour on the Red Sea coast: the Diary of Merer, dated about 2560 to 2550 BCE, at the end of the reign of Khufu, describes the last years of the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza. The Egyptians also used papyrus reeds for boats, mats, rope, sandals and baskets. The Greek word biblos, from which bibliography and bible derive, referred to the inner part of the plant.

Papyrus was made from the stem of the sedge Cyperus papyrus. The outer rind was removed and the sticky inner pith cut lengthwise into strips about 40 centimetres long. The strips were laid side by side with their edges slightly overlapping, and a second layer was placed across them at right angles. While still moist, the layers were hammered into a single sheet, which was dried under pressure and polished with a rounded object. Sheets were glued together into a roll, a scroll, and texts were normally written first on the side where the fibres ran along the roll.

Pliny the Elder and Isidore of Seville described six grades sold in the Roman market. Papyrus is stable in a dry climate such as Egypt's, but humid conditions let mould destroy it, and in Europe it seems to have lasted only decades. It was cheap and easy to produce, but fragile, and it was not pliable enough to fold without cracking.

Late in its history papyrus began to be gathered into codices, which early Christian writers soon adopted. Parchment, made from animal skins, gradually overtook it in West Asia and Europe. By the beginning of the 4th century CE the most important books were being made on parchment, which was more durable in moist climates and could be written on both sides. As trade networks declined, papyrus lost its cost advantage outside Egypt. The latest certain uses in Europe are a papal decree of 1057 and an Arabic document of 1087. In Egypt it continued in use until the cheaper paper introduced from the Islamic world replaced it.

Papyri give the only surviving copy of Menander, as well as the Egyptian Book of the Dead and the Ebers, Edwin Smith, Rhind and Westcar papyri. The first modern discovery of papyrus rolls was made at Herculaneum in 1752, and the Dutch historian Caspar Reuvens began scholarly study with the Leyden papyrus, published in 1830.
paquisha-war: Peru held that the border had been settled by the Ecuadorian–Peruvian War of 1941 and the Rio de Janeiro Protocol of 1942, while Ecuador argued that the protocol could not be carried out because a 78 km section of the border was not precisely defined. At meetings in the late 1970s the military leaders of both countries had, in Peru's view, agreed a status quo line under which neither side would set up new posts in the disputed areas, which for Ecuador meant none east of the ridge of the Cordillera del Cóndor.

The conflict began on 22 January 1981, when Peru reported an attack on one of its aircraft supplying border posts on the Comaina River. President Fernando Belaúnde Terry ordered the river inspected to its source, and three Ecuadorian detachments were found holding the old observation posts Nos. 22, 3 and 4. Ecuador said they belonged to its Paquisha base; Belaúnde called the place a False Paquisha, distinct from the Paquisha recognised by the protocol, and on 2 February the Peruvian Foreign Minister, Javier Arias Stella, called the outposts fakes at the OAS.

Peru sent Mi-8TV helicopters with A-37, Su-22 and Mirage 5 aircraft in support of its jungle infantry, while the Ecuadorian air force flew 179 combat missions, and on 28 January A-37Bs of the two air forces fought a dogfight. Peruvian troops retook post PV-3 and, on 1 February, PV-4. Further Ecuadorian posts were then found, and Peru retook False Machinaza on 19 February and two more posts on 20 February; on 21 February Peruvian army aviation destroyed the last Ecuadorian installations, and the Ecuadorians were driven back to the summit of the Cordillera.

Talks between the commanders at Huaquillas and Aguas Verdes, with military delegates of Chile, Argentina, Brazil and the USA, produced the Sorrosa-Du Bois Act, which fixed where border troops could stand. Both sides built up their forces along the Cordillera and the Cenepa valley, a spiral of tension that led to the Cenepa War of 1995. In 1983 the Ecuadorian congress reaffirmed that it held the Rio Protocol void, a position Ecuador gave up in 1998 with the Act of Brasilia.
paracel-islands: The archipelago includes about 130 small coral islands and reefs, most of them grouped into the northeastern Amphitrite Group or the western Crescent Group. They are spread over a maritime area of around 15,000 square kilometres, with a land area of only about 7.75 square kilometres. The highest point, an unnamed location on Rocky Island, is 14 m above sea level. The islands lie about 350 km southeast of Hainan Island, equidistant from the coastlines of China and Vietnam. The climate is tropical, with abundant rainfall and annual typhoons, and the surrounding waters are productive fishing grounds.

The Amphitrite Group was named after the French frigate Amphitrite, which observed the islands while carrying a Jesuit mission to Canton in 1698–1700. Woody Island, the largest of the Paracels at 213 hectares, lies at its centre. The islands of the Crescent Group are named after senior figures of the British East India Company, among them James Drummond, Thomas Pattle, John William Roberts and Jonathan Duncan.

The word paracel is of Portuguese origin and probably comes from the Spanish placer, used by navigators for shallow sandy seas or submerged banks. Portuguese maps of the early 16th century marked a group of flooded islands in the area, and from the mid-1500s the group was called Ilhas do Pracel. Chinese works from the Song dynasty onward described large groups of maritime features such as Qianli Changsha and Wanli Shitang, and Xisha, meaning Western Sands, became the standard Chinese name in the 20th century. The Vietnamese name Hoàng Sa, Yellow Sands, appears in documents dating back to 1483.

The People's Republic of China, Vietnam and the Republic of China on Taiwan all claim sovereignty, and each presents its own historical case. Chinese accounts date an interest to the second century BCE; Vietnamese accounts point to the planting of a flag in 1816 and ten inscribed steles installed in 1836. Between 1881 and 1883 the German navy surveyed the islands each year without seeking permission from France or China, and published the results in 1885. China has controlled the whole archipelago since the Battle of the Paracel Islands in January 1974.
parachute: The earliest recorded attempt to slow a fall with fabric is that of Armen Firman, an Andalusian who in 852, at Córdoba, jumped from a tower wearing a large cloak. It was recorded that there was enough air in the folds of the cloak to prevent great injury. The earliest evidence of a purposely designed parachute dates from the Renaissance. The manuscript of the 1470s attributed to Francesco di Giorgio Martini shows a free-hanging man clutching a crossbar frame attached to a conical canopy, with four straps running to a waist belt. The canopy looks too small to give effective resistance, but the basic concept is apparent.

In 1691 Simon de La Loubère reported that at the court of King Narai of Ayutthaya a man would jump from a high place holding two large umbrellas, landing in trees, on rooftops and sometimes in rivers. The French physicist Louis-Sébastien Lenormand read the report a century later. He made the first recorded public jump in 1783 and in 1785 coined the word, joining the Italian para, from parare, to ward off, to the French chute, a fall.

In 1911 Grant Morton made the first parachute jump from an aeroplane, a Wright Model B flown by Phil Parmalee at Venice Beach, California, holding a throw-out parachute in his arms. In the same year Gleb Kotelnikov invented the first knapsack parachute, although Hermann Lattemann and his wife Käthe Paulus had already jumped with bagged parachutes in the last decade of the 19th century. On 4 February 1912 Franz Reichelt died jumping from the Eiffel Tower while testing a wearable parachute.

The first military users were artillery observers on tethered balloons in the First World War. A waist harness pulled the lines and canopy from a bag hung on the balloon as they jumped. The Germans adopted them on a large scale for balloon crews, then the British and the French. In fixed-wing aircraft the lines often tangled in a spinning machine, and no parachutes were issued to the crews of Allied heavier-than-air aircraft.

After the war Major Edward L. Hoffman of the United States Army led an effort to combine the best features of several designs. The resulting Airplane Parachute Type-A had a soft pack worn on the back, a ripcord and a pilot chute that draws out the main canopy. Leslie Irvin tested it by jumping from an aeroplane in 1919, and it went into production. After the Second World War parachuting became a popular sport, and nylon replaced silk.
paradiso-dante: The dates of composition are uncertain, but research by Giorgio Petrocchi suggests that Dante began planning the Paradiso while revising the Inferno and Purgatorio between 1313 and 1317, and it was probably not published until after his death. Giovanni Boccaccio claimed that the poem was at first thought unfinished until Dante's sons found its last thirteen cantos among his papers. Robert Hollander points to small contradictions absent from the first two parts and suggests that Dante may not have finished revising it. Like them it has thirty-three cantos, but it has far fewer speakers, under twenty against over fifty in each earlier part, and longer speeches with more philosophical discussion.

The journey begins in the Earthly Paradise at the top of Mount Purgatory at noon on a Wednesday in 1300, after Easter, and lasts about twenty-four hours. Beatrice leads Dante up through nine concentric spheres, as in the medieval geocentric cosmos derived from Ptolemy: the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, the Fixed Stars and the Primum Mobile, beyond which lies the non-material Empyrean. Where Hell and Purgatory were ordered by sins, Heaven is ordered by the four cardinal and three theological virtues. All the blessed live with God in the Empyrean, but they are shown to Dante in the spheres as a sign.

In the Moon he meets Piccarda Donati, in Mercury the Emperor Justinian, who recounts the history of the Roman Empire, and in the Sun Thomas Aquinas among twelve lights of the wise; Aquinas tells the life of Francis of Assisi and Bonaventure that of Dominic. In Mars his ancestor Cacciaguida, a crusader, foretells his exile. The just rulers of Jupiter form an imperial eagle, among them Trajan and Ripheus the Trojan. In the Fixed Stars Peter, James and John examine Dante on faith, hope and love, and Peter denounces Pope Boniface VIII.

In the Primum Mobile Dante sees God as a point of light ringed by nine orders of angels. In the Empyrean the saved sit as petals of a vast rose; Beatrice takes her place there, and Saint Bernard guides Dante on and prays to the Virgin Mary for him. At last Dante sees God as three circles in one space, with the human form of Christ within them, and his will is turned by the love that moves the sun and the other stars.
paraguay: Paraguay lies between latitudes 19° and 28°S in the central region of South America and is divided by the Río Paraguay into two regions. The eastern region has mostly grassy plains and wooded hills, while the western region, known as the Chaco and part of the Gran Chaco, has mostly low, marshy plains. The far eastern forest belt receives an average of 170 centimetres of rain a year, the western Chaco no more than 50 centimetres. Although landlocked, Paraguay reaches the Atlantic Ocean by the Paraná–Paraguay Waterway, a system of navigable channels shared by five countries.

The Guaraní had lived in eastern Paraguay for at least a millennium when the Spanish arrived. The Gran Chaco in the west was inhabited by nomads, of whom the Guaycuru peoples were most prominent, and the Paraguay River roughly divided the agricultural Guaraní from them. The Mbayá were known for their warrior traditions and were not fully pacified until the late 19th century. Juan de Salazar de Espinosa founded Asunción on 15 August 1537, and it became the centre of the Spanish colonial province of Paraguay.

In the eighteenth century Jesuit missions developed reductions to gather Guaraní populations and protect them from virtual slavery by Spanish settlers and Portuguese slave raiders, the bandeirantes. The reducciones flourished in eastern Paraguay for about 150 years, until the Spanish Crown expelled the Jesuits in 1767. Paraguay overthrew the local Spanish administration on 14 May 1811. José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia, nicknamed El Supremo, ruled from 1814 until his death in 1840 with very little outside contact, intending a utopian society based on Rousseau's Social Contract. The Triple Alliance War of 1864 to 1870 cost the country half its prewar population and around a quarter to a third of its territory. Paraguay then prevailed in the Chaco War with Bolivia of 1932 to 1935.

Asunción is the capital and largest city. Paraguay is a unitary presidential republic of seventeen departments and a capital district.
