The population was 6,109,944 at the 2022 census, and most people live in the east. Paraguayan culture is a fusion of European and Southern Guaraní traditions: more than 80% of Paraguayans speak both Spanish and Guaraní. The ruins of two eighteenth-century Jesuit missions, La Santísima Trinidad de Paraná and Jesús de Tavarangue, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Paraguay is a founding member of Mercosur, the United Nations and the Organization of American States.
paraguayan-war: Since independence, Brazil and the Spanish-American countries of South America had been troubled by territorial disputes, because the old Tordesillas line of 1494 did not match the actual occupation of the land. Brazil and Argentina struggled for hegemony in the Río de la Plata region. Brazil recognised Paraguay's independence in 1844, when Argentina still regarded it as a breakaway province. Brazil intervened in unstable Uruguay in 1851, 1855 and again in 1864, against Atanasio Aguirre, and this last intervention led to the war. The traditional view holds that Paraguay's president Francisco Solano López used the Uruguayan War as a pretext to gain control of the Platine basin, but the causes are also attributed to border conflicts and to Brazilian and Argentine meddling in Uruguay.

Paraguay began with over 60,000 trained men, 400 cannons and a squadron of steamboats. Paraguay took the initiative by invading the Brazilian province of Mato Grosso on 14 December 1864, followed by Rio Grande do Sul and the Argentine province of Corrientes. By the end of 1865 the Triple Alliance was on the offensive, and its armies invaded Paraguay in April of the following year.

On 10 October 1866 Brazil gave unified command to the Marquess of Caxias, who in the Pikysyry campaign took the army through the swamps of the Gran Chaco to cross behind the fortified Paraguayan line, leading to the fall of Asunción. Defeated in conventional warfare, Paraguay conducted a guerrilla resistance that further destroyed its army and civilians. The Count of Eu led the Campaign of the Hills from 1869, including the battles of Piribebuy and Acosta Ñu, where more than 5,000 Paraguayans died. López was killed by Brazilian forces at Cerro Corá on 1 March 1870.

Casualty figures are hotly disputed. Estimates of the share of its population that Paraguay lost range from 7 percent to 69 percent, and disease, hunger and exhaustion caused most of the deaths. Among the Brazilians, disease killed more than wounds did, and some historians think cholera was a leading cause. Paraguay lost about 140,000 square kilometres of disputed territory to Brazil and Argentina and was occupied until 1876, and its large war debt was forgiven in 1943 by Getúlio Vargas.

The war brought the Brazilian Empire to its peak of influence, but its public debt and the social crisis that followed are regarded as crucial factors in the fall of the Empire and the proclamation of the First Brazilian Republic.
paraiba: Paraíba is a state in the Brazilian Northeast, bordered by Rio Grande do Norte to the north, Ceará to the west, Pernambuco to the south and the Atlantic Ocean to the east. Its coast reaches Ponta do Seixas, the easternmost point of the mainland Americas, and the interior rises to the Borborema Plateau, where Pico do Jabre, at 1,208 metres, is the state's highest peak. Most of its territory has a hot semi-arid climate. It takes its name from the Paraíba river, and its area is about 56,467 square kilometres.

Before Europeans came, the Potiguara, part of the Tupi group, lived between the coast and the Borborema Plateau along the Paraíba do Norte river, and the Kiriri and Ariús lived further west. Colonisation began in 1534, when King John III of Portugal divided Brazil into fifteen captaincies. Most of what is now Paraíba fell under the Captaincy of Itamaracá, which was troubled by French piracy, especially of wood, animal skins and amber. Its sugar made the captaincy one of the most successful regions of Portuguese America.

The Dutch, who had seized Salvador in 1624, first appeared on Paraíban soil on 20 June 1625, in the Bay of Traição. Admiral Boudewijn Hendricksz allied with the Potiguara, but troops from Paraíba, Pernambuco and Rio Grande and from indigenous peoples defeated the Dutch on 1 August, at a cost to the Potiguara of 600 to a thousand dead. From 1670 colonists, led by bandeirantes such as Domingos Jorge Velho, pushed into the interior, with the enslavement and massacre of indigenous peoples. The captaincy was annexed to Pernambuco in 1756 and restored in 1799. Paraíba joined the Pernambuco Revolution of 1817, which sought Brazilian independence and spread through the Northeast, and it became a federal state in November 1889 when the republic was proclaimed.

João Pessoa is the coastal capital, and Campina Grande, in the interior, is among the fifteen largest municipalities of the Northeast. The 2022 census counted 3,974,687 people, and Portuguese is the language of the state. The economy has long drawn on sugarcane, cattle, shoes and leather goods, and tourism. A copper-bearing tourmaline of vivid blue-green colour was found in the Batalha mine in 1987. The Festa Junina, the Saint John festival brought by the Portuguese, is a major celebration.
parakoimomenos: Byzantine writers used the title anachronistically for prominent eunuch courtiers of the distant past, such as Euphratas under Constantine the Great and Chrysaphius under Theodosius II. The first secure mention comes in the chronicle of Theophanes the Confessor, who names the koubikoularios and parakoimomenos Theophanes among the courtiers dismissed under Leo IV for their iconodule sympathies. Seals of the 7th and 8th centuries show the post combined with other palace functions and with lowly dignities such as ostiarios, and seals of a Theophylact, strategos of Sicily, may make him the first known holder.

From the mid-9th century holders were raised to the dignity of patrikios, and some of them, exceptionally, were not eunuchs. The patrikios Damian served Michael III until about 865 and was replaced by Basil the Macedonian, who once emperor appointed no parakoimōmenos, judging the office too powerful. Leo VI revived it in 907 for his favourite Samonas. Basil Lekapenos, an illegitimate son of Romanos I Lekapenos, was appointed in 947, played a dominant role for the next four decades, toppling emperors, and served as virtual regent for over thirty years, until his dismissal in 985.

By the 11th century the parakoimōmenos had also taken over most of the administrative functions of the praipositos. The post survived in the Empire of Nicaea and into the Palaiologan period, when it was divided in two. The parakoimōmenos tou koitōnos supervised the imperial bedchamber and commanded its chamberlains and pages; the parakoimōmenos tēs sphendonēs kept the ring with the emperor's personal seal, used for his private letters to his family. In the absence of the prōtostratōr both carried the emperor's sword, and pseudo-Kodinos ranks them 16th and 17th in the imperial hierarchy.

In the late empire the holders were no longer palace eunuchs but noblemen and administrators. The best known was Alexios Apokaukos, a man of humble birth made parakoimōmenos in 1321, who held the post until 1341 and was the chief instigator of the civil war of 1341-1347. Among the last known holders was Theophylaktos Dermokaites, sent as an emissary to Pope Urban V in October 1367. Only one holder is known from the Empire of Trebizond, Michael Sampson, attested in 1432.
parakrama-samudra: The reservoir grew out of a group of tanks built in different periods of Sri Lanka's ancient history. Its northernmost part, the Topa wewa or Thopawewa, is the oldest and is believed to date from the 4th century, around 386. The middle section, Eramudu wewa, and the southernmost and highest section, Dumbutula wewa, were added during the reign of King Parakramabahu I (1153–1186), who linked the basins by canals as part of a wider programme to improve agriculture and manage water across his kingdom.

The work is tied to the principle that not even a drop of rainwater falling on the country should reach the sea without being made useful to man. Its size earned it the name Samudhraya, meaning the ocean. Water was brought to it from the Amban Ganga through the Angamadilla diversion system.

Parakrama Samudra is a shallow reservoir made of five basins joined by narrow channels, the northern section lying lower than the southern. Its average depth is about 5 metres and its maximum about 12.7 metres; it holds about 0.1273 cubic kilometres and drains a catchment of some 73–75 square kilometres. Its level rises and falls by about 4.4 metres over the year. The present dam is an earthfill embankment about 12.4 km long and on average about 15 metres high, and the Theppan Ala canal moves water between the basins. Remains of ancient sluices survive near Thopawewa and Bendiwewa.

After the decline of the Polonnaruwa Kingdom the system gradually fell into disrepair. It was restored in the British colonial period, with major rehabilitation between 1937 and 1944, when the Raja Bamma diversion structure at Angamadilla was rebuilt around 1939. Reconstruction in the 1950s separated some former sections, modern spillway gates were later fitted, and a dam safety project funded by the World Bank strengthened the embankment and repaired its gates.

The reservoir still irrigates more than 10,100 hectares of the Polonnaruwa District, chiefly paddy, in the Maha and Yala cultivation seasons. It also supports inland fisheries, including food and ornamental fish, home gardens, other field crops and animal husbandry, as well as wildlife habitats and nature tourism.
parakramabahu-i: Parakramabahu is generally thought to have been born around 1123, almost certainly at Punkhagama, the capital of Dakkhinadesa, the southern of the island's three kingdoms. His father, Manabharana, ruled Dakkhinadesa and his mother was Ratnavali. Through his grandmother Mitta, sister of Vijayabahu I, he belonged to what the Culavamsa calls the Arya branch of the royal house, rivals of the Kalinga branch that held Rajarata. The chronicle says a god-like figure foretold his birth in his father's dream.

As a young man he left Dakkhinadesa in secret for the court of Gajabahu II of Rajarata, having the general Sankha killed on the way when Sankha tried to report his journey. On his return he reluctantly met his uncle, Kitti Sri Megha, and on the uncle's death in 1140 he became king of Dakkhinadesa.

In Dakkhinadesa he set up a capital of his own, Parakramapura, identified with modern Panduwas Nuwara, restored shrines and the Kotabaddha causeway over the Deduru Oya, and cut canals and cleared forest for new fields. Exports of pearls, gems, cinnamon and war elephants through Kalpitiya, Chilaw and Colombo supported him. Around 1150 he seized Malaya and defeated an army of Gajabahu; he directed the war against Rajarata without leading the invasion himself, basing his strategy on the writings of Kautilya.

From 1153 he ruled from Polonnaruwa. His economic policy, also drawn from Kautilya, placed all trade, alcohol included, in the hands of the government. He set out to unite the three rival orders of the sangha and to correct monks who had married and pursued worldly gain, and he restored Anuradhapura, including the Thuparamaya, Mihintale and the Ruwanwelisaya. Revolts in Ruhuna, joined in 1156 by Queen Sugala, mother of his old rival Manabharana, and a rising of mercenaries in 1157 kept his generals Rakkha and Bhuta occupied.

He died at Polonnaruwa in 1186 and was succeeded by Vijayabahu II, described as his sister's son, whom he had summoned from Sinhapura, capital of Kalinga. Historians such as Wilhelm Geiger note that he took no steps to secure a smooth succession; the instability and renewed civil war after his reign undid many of his works. His expeditions to the mainland cost him heavily without weakening the Chola dynasty. Seven later kings took his name over the next four centuries.
paramaribo: Paramaribo lies on the banks of the Suriname River, about 15 kilometres inland from the Atlantic Ocean, in the Paramaribo District. The city is named for the Paramaribo people who lived at the mouth of the river, and the name is from the Tupi-Guarani para, large river, and maribo, inhabitants. The name is probably a corruption of the name of a native village, spelled Parmurbo in the earliest Dutch sources. It has a tropical rainforest climate with no true dry season.

The first Dutch settlement at the site was a trading post established in 1613 by Nicolaes Baliestel and Dirck Claeszoon van Sanen. English and French traders also tried to settle in Suriname, including a French post founded in 1644 near the present city. All these early settlements were abandoned before English settlers, sent by the governor of Barbados, Lord Francis Willoughby, arrived in 1650. They founded a town on the site, protected by Fort Willoughby, and in 1662 King Charles II granted Willoughby the settlement and its surrounding lands. Around 1665 the village of Paramaribo was expanded and quickly outranked the earlier settlement of Torarica.

In 1667, during the Second Anglo-Dutch War, a squadron under Abraham Crijnssen conquered Paramaribo, and the Treaty of Breda in 1667 confirmed it as the leading town of the Dutch colony of Suriname. The fort was renamed Fort Zeelandia after the Dutch province that had financed the fleet. The population has always been diverse. Many of the first British settlers were Jews, and the Neveh Shalom Synagogue, one of the oldest synagogues in the Americas, stands in the city. The population grew greatly after 1873, when formerly enslaved people, freed in 1863, were allowed to stop working for their former masters and to leave the sugar plantations.

Fires repeatedly devastated the old town, notably in January 1821, when over 400 buildings were destroyed, and in September 1832, when nearly 50 were lost. The enslaved men Kodjo, Mentor and Present were found guilty of arson and burnt alive. Paramaribo has remained the capital of Suriname through its colonial days and the independence of 1975.

Paramaribo is the capital and largest city of Suriname and holds almost half of the country's population. The Dutch colonial town of the 17th and 18th centuries along the left bank of the river became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2002, and its original architecture and street plan have largely remained intact. Landmarks include Fort Zeelandia, the Presidential Palace, the Roman Catholic cathedral of St Peter and St Paul, the Suriname Mosque and the Kwakoe memorial to the abolition of slavery. The city is the business and financial centre of the country.
parana-entre-rios: Paraná stands on the eastern shore of the Paraná River, opposite the city of Santa Fe, capital of the neighbouring Santa Fe Province. Its original name was Bajada, meaning landing. The climate is Pampean, classed as humid subtropical, with an average annual temperature of 18 °C. Winters have mild days and very cold nights, with occasional frosts, while summers are hot and bring most of the rain, about 1,069 millimetres in a year. The city and the whole province lie in an area of high tornado risk, particularly in spring and summer.

In 1730 inhabitants of Santa Fe settled on the other shore of the river and called the place Baxada del Paraná. The first settlers had been forced out of Santa Fe by raiding Payaguá and Muños peoples. They settled in what is now the Square of the first of May, where they built a fort, other defences and a series of huts. Their numbers eventually became stable enough for them to move from defence to offence, and they almost wiped out both peoples. In the middle of the 19th century the city served for some years as the capital of the Argentine Confederation, until 1861.

Paraná is the seat of the provincial government of Entre Ríos and an important river port for the transshipment of cereals, cattle, fish and lumber from the surrounding region. Its industries include the manufacture of cement, furniture and ceramics. The city centre combines colonial churches with buildings in European styles such as the 3 de Febrero Theatre and the Government House, and the Cathedral blends several architectural styles. The Hernandarias Subfluvial Tunnel, inaugurated in 1969, links the city to Santa Fe beneath the river. Its main sports clubs include the basketball team Atlético Echagüe and the football clubs Patronato and Atlético Paraná.
parana-river: The Paraná takes its name from Guarani words meaning river or sea, and eastern South America has an immense number of river names containing para- or parana-. The river forms at the confluence of the Paranaíba and Rio Grande in southern Brazil and runs southwest for about 619 kilometres to the city of Saltos del Guaira in Paraguay. For roughly the next 200 kilometres it forms the boundary between Paraguay and Brazil, up to the confluence with the Iguazu River, and after that it is the border between Paraguay and Argentina.

It turns west for some 820 kilometres and meets the Paraguay River, its largest tributary, then runs south for about 820 kilometres through Argentina and turns east near Rosario. Below the city of Diamante it splits into several arms and forms the Paraná Delta. Its final stretch, under 500 kilometres, ends at the Uruguay River, where the two form the Río de la Plata.

The first European to go up the Paraná was the Venetian explorer Sebastian Cabot, who did so in 1526 while working for Spain. Between 1973 and 1984 the Itaipu Dam was built, creating a massive, shallow reservoir. It flooded the Guaíra Falls, the Sete Quedas, a series of seven cascades once said to rival the Iguazu Falls. A second major hydroelectric project, the Yacyretá Dam, was built jointly by Paraguay and Argentina. The dams blocked ship navigation to cities further upstream, and the rising river flooded the lower parts of Encarnación.

Navigation became a matter of dispute between Paraguay and Argentina. Argentina wished to build a bridge across the river, while Paraguay would facilitate it only if the navigation issue was settled. A bilateral agreement on a bridge was signed in October 1964, and an agreement endorsing free navigation, requiring each nation to treat the other's vessels as its own, was signed in January 1973. Water-level records exist from 1904, because the river is used by oceangoing ships.

The Paraná and its tributaries drain much of south-central South America, including nearly all of Paraguay, much of southern Brazil, northern Argentina and south-eastern Bolivia. The basin contains large cities including São Paulo, Buenos Aires, Rosario, Asunción and Brasília. Much of the river is navigable as part of the Paraná–Paraguay and Tietê–Paraná waterways, linking inland cities in Argentina and Paraguay with the ocean. Fishing is a livelihood along its banks, and the delta is a well-known place for watching birds.
parantaka-i: Parantaka was the elder son of the Chola king Aditya I, born to a Chera wife; his younger half-brother, Kannara Deva, was born to a Rashtrakuta wife. When Aditya died, the Rashtrakuta king Krishna II tried to place his grandson Kannara Deva on the Chola throne. Parantaka became king instead in 907, and Krishna II invaded. At the Battle of Vallala in 911, where Parantaka and Prince Rajaditya led the Chola side against Prince Indra III, the Rashtrakutas lost many men and were driven out of Chola territory.

Parantaka took Madurai early in his reign and called himself Maturai Koṇṭāṉ, Capturer of Madurai. The Pandyan ruler Maravarman Rajasinha II sought help from Kassapa V of Anuradhapura, but the combined army was defeated at Vellur, and the Pandyan king fled to Sri Lanka with his royal insignia. When the Sinhalese kings refused to return them, a Chola army invaded the island around 946–947, sacked Anuradhapura and took the north, but Udaya IV hid the insignia in the Rohana hills; they were recovered only under Parantaka's grandson Rajendra I.

He also subdued the Bana and Vaidumba chiefs allied with the Rashtrakutas, and a Kannada inscription at Bairakur suggests a clash with the Nolamba ruler Iriva Nolamba Diliparaja around 936. In 949 the army of Krishna III defeated the Cholas at Takkolam, where Rajaditya was killed by an arrow shot by Butuga, a Ganga chief allied with the Rashtrakutas. Inscriptions from South Arcot of 952–954 acknowledge neither Chola nor Rashtrakuta rule.

For all his wars, Parantaka laid down rules for the conduct of village assemblies, dug canals across the country according to his copper-plate inscriptions, and gave spoils of war to temple charities. A devout follower of Siva, he is reported to have covered the Chidambaram temple with a golden roof, perhaps restoring an older one that Appar and Tirumangai Alvar had already described.

At least eleven of his wives appear in inscriptions, among them a Chera princess, mother of Rajaditya, whose marriage strengthened his alliance with the Cheras of Kerala. His other sons included Arikulakesari, Gandaraditya and Uttamasili. Parantaka died in 955 and was succeeded by his second son, Gandaraditya.
pararaton: The chronicle is also known as the Katuturanira Ken Angrok, the Story of Ken Angrok, after the words with which its text begins, which may have been its original title. The name Pararaton appears only in the colophons of about half the surviving manuscripts. It derives from ratu, a word for monarch that is gender-neutral in the text, and its form denotes plurality, so it may best be translated as The Monarchs or The Royals. Dates in the colophons show that the final part of the text was written between 1481 and 1600.

The text is comparatively short, 32 folio-size pages or 1126 lines. Almost half of it tells the career of Ken Arok, founder of the Singhasari kingdom, before he took the throne in 1222, and this part is mythical. In the prelude he offers himself as a sacrifice to Yamadipati, the god of death, and is promised rebirth as a king. Begotten by Brahma, he is left in a graveyard, raised by the thief Ki Lembong and declared a son by Batara Guru. Guided by the Brahmana Lohgawe, he kills Tunggul Ametung, ruler of Tumapel, to take his wife Ken Dedes and the throne.

Shorter narrative fragments follow in chronological order, many of them dated. Towards the end the episodes grow ever shorter and are mixed with genealogical information about the royal family of Majapahit.

Scholars such as C. C. Berg argued that texts of this kind are wholly supernatural and ahistorical, intended not to record the past but to determine future events. Most scholars, however, accept some historicity in the Pararaton, noting many correspondences with inscriptions and Chinese sources. In 2001 Hans Ras compared it with the Canggal inscription of 732, the Śivagŗha inscription of 856, the Calcutta Stone of 1041 and the Babad Tanah Jawi of 1836, and found clear similarities in character, structure and function, as well as similarities with texts of Malay historiography.

The first edition, with the text and a Dutch translation, was published by Jan Laurens Andries Brandes in 1896. J. Padmapuspita published the Kawi text with an Indonesian translation in 1966, and a Javanese adaptation by R.M. Mangkudimedja appeared in 1912.
parashurameshvara-temple: The temple belongs to the Parashurameshvara group, considered the oldest temples of Bhubaneswar. K. C. Panigrahi places it at 650 CE, and most scholars agree on the mid-7th century from its style and from the eight planets carved over the door of the sanctum, where later temples show nine. Some historians put it in the early 8th century, after the Satruguneswar, Bharateswar and Lakshmaneswar temples, and Fergusson thought it might have been begun around 500 CE.

It was built by the Shailodbhavas, whose family deity was Shiva and who also honoured the Shakta goddesses. Standing near the eastern coast, it suffered little in the Muslim invasions of the 12th and 13th centuries. It was repaired in 1903, when the roof of the sanctum was altered, and the Archaeological Survey of India maintains it as a ticketed monument.

The temple has two parts: the vimana, a square sanctum whose curved tower, the bada, rises to about 12.3 metres and is crowned by an amalaka, and the jagamohana, a rectangular hall for worshippers with a sloping roof in two stages and latticed windows. It is the first temple with such a hall; earlier ones had only the sanctum, and later ones added festival and offering halls. The rough join between the two parts led some scholars to think the hall was added later, though it is also put down to the building method of dragging stones up layers of earth.

Though a Shaiva shrine, its walls carry many Shakta deities. It is the first temple in Bhubaneswar with the Saptamatrikas, the seven mother goddesses, and holds the earliest known six-armed image of Durga as Mahishamardini. Other carvings show an eight-armed dancing Ardhanarishvara, Kartikeya on his peacock, Shiva subduing Ravana beneath Mount Kailasa, Shiva as Nataraja, a hunting scene and monkeys at play. The interior, as in other Odisha temples, is plain.

The name presents Shiva as lord of Parashurama, an avatar of Vishnu; according to legend, the temple takes its name from Parashurama's penance and the grace Shiva granted him. Its main festival, Parashuramashtami, falls on the eighth day of Ashadha (June–July), when the festival image of Lingaraja is brought to the temple and feasted. With the Rajarani Temple and the Vaitala Deula, it is evidence of the Devadasi tradition of the 7th and 8th centuries, in which girls were dedicated for life to the service of a deity or temple.
parcham: Babrak Karmal and Nur Muhammad Taraki founded the People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan in 1965, and by 1967 it had split into sects, the largest of which were Parcham and Khalq. The two differed in ideas and in support. The Khalqists were mainly rural Pashtuns, while the Parchamites drew on middle-class residents of the cities, most of them ethnic Tajiks. Karmal held that Afghanistan was not developed enough for a Leninist revolution and sought a patriotic, anti-imperialist united front instead, whereas Khalq wanted an immediate and violent overthrow of the government.

From 1968 to 1969 Parcham published a weekly magazine with the permission of King Mohammed Zahir Shah, while the Khalq newspaper had been closed by the government in 1966. Because Parcham at first wished to keep the constitutional monarchy, its rivals called it the Royal Communist Party.

Parchamites, especially in the Afghan Army, gave strong support to the 1973 coup, and many then held senior posts in the government and security forces of Mohammed Daoud Khan. Reports that Parchamis had taken part in the death of the former prime minister Mohammad Hashim Maiwandwal later led to their purge from his administration and to persecution by his regime.

The faction was reconciled with Khalq in 1977, and after the Saur Revolution of 1978 many Parchamis sat in the first government. They were soon purged by Taraki's hardline leadership, which accused them of revisionism, and many were jailed and executed. Parcham came to power when the Soviet Union overthrew Hafizullah Amin in Operation Storm-333 in December 1979. The government of Karmal struggled to win support after the excesses of the Khalqists, and the faction's own numbers had been reduced by the executions of 1978 and 1979.

Moscow, dissatisfied with Karmal's failure to defeat the Mujahideen, saw him replaced by Mohammad Najibullah in 1986. In June 1990 the Parcham-led party became the Watan (Homeland) Party, dropping every reference to Marxism-Leninism from its manifesto in favour of an Afghan form of Islamic socialism. The Watan Party was banned on 6 May 1992. Later attempts to revive it included Mir Afghan Bawary's Watan Party of Afghanistan and a party of the same name under General Abdul Jabar Qahraman.
parex-bank: The name Parex, a portmanteau of export parity, first belonged to a self-supporting youth enterprise created by Gints Marga on 5 August 1986 under the Riga City Committee of the Komsomol. In 1987 Valērijs Kargins, then working at VEF, bought the Parex shell for five thousand Soviet roubles, and in 1988 he went into partnership with Viktors Krasovickis, who ran a tourism agency. On 3 April 1991 Parex received the first licence issued to a private company for currency exchange in the territory of the Soviet Union, and in May it opened its first exchange office.

When the bank was founded in January 1992, Kargins and Krasovickis held equal shares. Clients from across the former Soviet Union changed money through it while the Russian rouble lost its value, and it advertised itself as closer than Switzerland. From 1993 the offshore company Europe Holdings Ltd held part of its shares, until the founders bought them back in 2002. In 2007 Petr Aven of Alfa Bank offered to buy the bank, but the owners asked €1 billion. The bank faced repeated accusations of money laundering; in 2015 Spanish prosecutors alleged that it had served Russian organised crime, among it the Tambovskaya group of Saint Petersburg.

An inspection by the Financial and Capital Market Commission from 18 August to 3 October 2008 found a shortfall of 40 million lats in provisions for bad loans. On 22 October the owners privately asked for a state deposit, which the Ministry of Finance refused, and withdrawals sped up from 27 October. On 8 November 2008 the Cabinet of Ministers decided to take a controlling interest, held through the Privatization Agency of Latvia.

On 1 August 2010 the bank was split. Citadele took over accounts, deposits and lending, while the remainder became Reverta, set up to recover the public money spent on the rescue; in 2012 it gave up its banking licence and became an asset management company. Reverta sued Kargins and Krasovickis over 14 irregular loans and deposits made between 1995 and 2008, and in October 2016 they were ordered to pay €4,284,792. Some have called the nationalisation a major cause of Latvia's crisis and of the government's €4.5 billion in bailout loans; others see it as a response to the crisis rather than its cause.
parga: Parga lies on the Ionian coast of Epirus between Preveza and Igoumenitsa, in the northwest of the regional unit of Preveza. The present municipality was formed in the 2011 local government reform by the merger of the former municipalities of Fanari and Parga. In antiquity the area was inhabited by the Thesprotians, and the ancient town of Toryne stood there in the late Hellenistic period, named for the ladle-like shape of its beach.

Parga is first mentioned in 1318, and its name is most likely of Slavic origin. In the 1390s it came under the Albanian ruler Gjin Bua Shpata of Arta. The townspeople overthrew the governor Vonko, whose rule they thought tyrannical, and asked Venice for protection. In 1401 the town passed to Venice and was administered as a mainland exclave of Corfu under a castellan. It stayed Venetian, apart from brief periods of Ottoman possession, until the fall of the Republic of Venice in 1797, and then passed to France.

The people of Parga turned against French rule and sought British protection. In 1819 the British ceded the town to Ali Pasha of Ioannina in exchange for a monetary settlement, a decision unpopular among its predominantly Greek and pro-Venetian population. The town was completely abandoned by its inhabitants, many of whom moved to Corfu, and Ali Pasha repopulated it with Albanian speakers from Chameria. Ottoman rule ended in 1913 after the Balkan Wars. In November 1924 Greece moved 1,500 Albanian-speaking Muslims from Parga to Turkey under the population exchange.

Parga is a resort town known for its natural environment, and the modern town preserves its traditional architectural features. Its castle stands on a hill above the town, first built in the 11th century. It was destroyed more than once and rebuilt by the Venetians in 1572 into a stronger fortress that stayed impregnable until 1819, when Ali Pasha added a hammam and his harem quarters at the top.
pargali-ibrahim-pasha: Little is known of Ibrahim's early years. He was born at Parga, and his ethnic origin is uncertain: older Ottoman sources call him a Frenk, later ones the son of an Italian fisherman from Genoa, and others have called him Greek, Albanian or Croatian. Evliya Çelebi stated that his family came from Razgrad. He was taken to Manisa through the devşirme system and entered the service of Prince Suleiman, remaining at his side until his death. He took part in the Belgrade campaign of 1521 and the Rhodes campaign of 1522, and rose to be chief of the imperial chamber.

On 27 June 1523 Ibrahim was appointed Grand Vizier in place of Piri Mehmed Pasha, directly from the chief of the imperial chamber, in a manner unprecedented in Ottoman law and tradition. The 17th-century writer Koçi Bey criticised the appointment as a breach of established rule. In May 1524 he married at a wedding lasting two weeks, though the identity of his wife is debated, and he was then sent to Egypt to restore order after the rebellion of Hain Ahmed Pasha.

In 1526 he commanded the campaign against Hungary that ended in victory at Mohács, and in March 1527 he was granted the rank of serasker. The number of tughs symbolising imperial power was raised from four to seven, and he was allowed to carry six.

He took part in the First Siege of Vienna in 1529 and conducted the negotiations for the Treaty of Constantinople of 1533 with Austria. From 1526 Suleiman left foreign policy largely to him, and he received ambassadors, with the help of Alvise Gritti, son of Andrea Gritti, Duke of Venice. In the Irakeyn campaign against the Safavids he captured Tabriz in August 1534. He spoke Turkish, Persian, Greek and Italian, played the violin and patronised poets. In his thirteen years as vizier he commissioned mosques, madrasas, baths and fountains, among them mosques in Constantinople, Mecca, Thessaloniki, Razgrad and Kavala.

Ibrahim had been invited to the palace for iftar, and in the night of 14 and 15 March 1536 four deaf-mute executioners strangled him in his chamber on the sultan's orders. The reason is not certain. Suggested factors include his pursuit of power and wealth, his support for Prince Mustafa, which allegedly led Hürrem Sultan to turn Suleiman against him, his harsh conduct in the Iraq campaign and his extravagance. Ottoman historians held that the empire declined after his death, and the poet Latîfî wrote that people understood his worth only once he was gone. Modern historians regard him as one of the most important Ottoman grand viziers.
parihaspora: Parihaspora, also called Parihaspur and today Paraspore, stood on a plateau above the Jhelum River about 22 kilometres northwest of Srinagar in the Kashmir Valley. The Sanskrit name Parihaspur may loosely be rendered as city of laughs: parihas means laughter and pur city. The Jhelum now meets the Sind Nallah to the northeast at the Shadpur confluence; in the past the rivers met closer to the city.

Lalitaditya Muktapida of the Karkota dynasty moved his capital here from Srinagar. Kalhana describes the founding in the fourth book of his history: the king built his residence and four temples, among them one to Vishnu as Muktakeshva, whose image he made with 84,000 tolas of gold, another with an image of Parihaskesana in as many palas of silver, and a copper Buddha that, in Kalhana's words, reached up to the sky. The main temple was larger than the one Lalitaditya built at Martand.

The city lost its rank after Lalitaditya's death, when his son moved the royal residence. Under Raja Avanti Varman (855–883 CE) Soya Pandit changed the course of the river, and the city suffered from losing its river access. According to Kalhana, Avanti Varman's son Shankar Varman took the good material of its temples and palaces for his new capital, Shankarpur (Pattan). During the war between King Harsha and Uccala (1089–1101 CE) Uccala took refuge here; Harsha set the place on fire and melted down its statues. Sultan Sikandar destroyed the temples completely in the fourteenth century.

Only large boulders, some richly carved, and carved footings remain in place, and local people call the site Kani Shahar, City of Stones. Carved figures of seated and standing atlantes have been taken to the Srinagar Museum. M. A. Stein visited the site in 1892 and placed each building from its ruins; on a later visit he found that many stones had gone, used by the Maharaja of Kashmir for the Jhelum cart road, and he persuaded the Dogra king, with the British resident's help, to stop the damage.
parikshit: Parikshit was a Kuru king of the Middle Vedic period, usually placed in the 12th to 9th centuries BCE. Michael Witzel dates the Pārikṣita dynasty to about 1200 to 1100 BCE, in the late Rig-Vedic period, while H. C. Raychaudhuri placed Parikshit in the 9th century BCE. Only one Parikshit appears in Vedic literature. The Mahabharata and the Puranas seem to name two, one before the Kurukshetra War and one after it. Raychaudhuri thought the later figure fits the Vedic king better and suggested that genealogists invented the doubling to account for anachronisms.

In the Mahabharata and the Puranas he is the son of Abhimanyu and Uttara and the grandson of Arjuna. The Bhagavata Purana says that Ashwatthama, the son of Drona, prepared a Brahmastra weapon to kill the Pandava heir in his mother's womb, and that Krishna protected the child. He was named Vişņurāta and was crowned at Hastinapura, succeeding his granduncle Yudhishthira.

A hymn of the Atharvaveda (XX.127.7-10) praises him as a great Kuru king, a Kauravya and a universal king, raja vishvajanina. In it a Kuru householder and his wife speak of the peaceful dwelling he has given them, of ripe barley bending over the path and of a dynasty that thrives in his realm. Witzel holds that Parikshit and other kings of his line were largely responsible for gathering diverse strands of material into the Rig Veda Samhita, Samveda Samhitas and Khilani collections. The Mahabharata says he married Madravati, princess of the Madra Kingdom, and ruled for 60 years. According to the Shatapatha Brahmana (XIII.5.4) he had four sons, Janamejaya, Bhimasena, Ugrasena and Śrutasena, all of whom performed the Asvamedha Yajna.

Later tradition tells of his death in several ways. In the best-known account he threw a dead snake round the neck of the meditating sage Shamika, and the sage's son Shringi cursed him to die of a snakebite within seven days. Ministers built a mansion on a single column, but Takshaka, the Naga king, reached him in the form of a worm in a fruit and killed him. His son Janamejaya succeeded him and began the Sarpasatra, a sacrifice meant to destroy all snakes, which the sage Astika stopped; the day is marked as the festival of Naga Panchami.
paris: Paris lies in northern central France, in a north-bending arc of the river Seine, whose crest includes two islands, the Île Saint-Louis and the larger Île de la Cité, which form the oldest part of the city. The Seine's mouth on the English Channel is about 375 kilometres downstream. The city is relatively flat, with its lowest point 35 metres above sea level, and the highest of its hills, Montmartre, rises to 130 metres. Excluding the outlying parks, it covers an oval of about 87 square kilometres, enclosed by the 35-kilometre ring road, the Boulevard Périphérique, and since an annexation in 1860 it has had 20 arrondissements.

The Parisii, a Gallic tribe, inhabited the Paris area from around the middle of the 3rd century BCE. A major north–south trade route crossed the Seine on the Île de la Cité, which gradually became an important trading centre, and the Parisii traded with river towns as far away as the Iberian Peninsula and minted their own coins.

Julius Caesar conquered the Paris Basin for the Roman Republic in 52 BCE, and the Roman town of Lutetia grew on the Left Bank into a prosperous city with a forum, baths, temples, theatres and an amphitheatre. By the end of the Western Roman Empire it was known as Parisius. According to legend, Saint Denis, the first Bishop of Paris, introduced Christianity in the middle of the 3rd century CE and was beheaded on the hill later called Montmartre.

For almost all of its history, except for a few brief periods, Paris was governed directly by representatives of the king, emperor or president of France. In the 17th century the Académie royale de peinture et de sculpture was established in 1648, and urbanism laws have been strictly controlled since the early 17th century. Between 1853 and 1870 Napoleon III and his Prefect of the Seine, Baron Haussmann, rebuilt the city centre, creating wide boulevards, standard facades of cream-grey Paris stone and major parks around the centre.

Paris is the capital and largest city of France, with a city population of 2.04 million and a metropolitan population of 13.3 million. The National Assembly granted it municipal autonomy in 1974, and Jacques Chirac became its first elected mayor in March 1977. Its population peaked at 2.9 million in 1921. In the 19th and early 20th centuries artists including Manet, Monet and Renoir worked there, and Impressionism, Cubism and Art Deco all evolved in the city. It hosts UNESCO, whose headquarters have been there since November 1958, and the OECD, and it has hosted the Summer Olympics in 1900, 1924 and 2024.
paris-commune: On 2 September 1870 France was defeated at the Battle of Sedan and Emperor Napoleon III was captured. Republican deputies proclaimed a Republic and formed a Government of National Defence, and the German army had surrounded Paris by 20 September. Paris workers had long demanded that the city have its own elected council, and during the siege demonstrations demanded a Commune.

After Paris faced famine and the armies were defeated, national elections on 8 February 1871 returned about 400 deputies favouring a constitutional monarchy. The National Guard in Paris had not been disarmed and had on paper 260 battalions. On 18 March two brigades climbed Montmartre to seize its 170 cannons, which had been paid for by public subscription, but National Guard members gathered there, and the Guard seized control of the city.

The Commune held its first meeting on 28 March and voted among other things to abolish the death penalty and military conscription. On 2 April it declared the separation of church and state, seized the property of religious congregations and ordered Catholic schools to become secular. The Vendôme Column honouring Napoleon I was pulled down on 16 May.

Adolphe Thiers assembled a new army at Versailles under Patrice de MacMahon, and fighting began on the outskirts of Paris in late March. Both sides shot prisoners, and on 5 April the Commune passed a Decree on Hostages. On 21 May fifty thousand soldiers entered the city through an unguarded section of the wall. Fighting went on street by street through the semaine sanglante, and the last Communards were shot at Père Lachaise cemetery on 27 May.

The army officially recorded 43,522 prisoners, and the Commune had executed the Archbishop of Paris, Georges Darboy, and about one hundred hostages in its final days. The Third Republic tried 15,895 prisoners and found 13,500 guilty. Ninety-five were sentenced to death, 251 to forced labour and 1,169 to deportation, usually to New Caledonia. All surviving prisoners and exiles were pardoned in 1880. One unconfirmed estimate from 1876 put the toll of Communards at 20,000.

Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels drew lessons from the Commune, and Engels called it the dictatorship of the proletariat. Anarchists such as Mikhail Bakunin supported it as a rebellion against the state. The wall at Père Lachaise where prisoners were shot is called the Communards' Wall and is the site of annual commemorations.
paris-lodron: Paris Lodron was born on 13 February 1586 at Castelnuovo di Noarna in Nogaredo, Trentino, the son of Count Nicolò Lodron, an imperial colonel and governor of the County of Tyrol, and Dorothea von Welsperg. At eleven he went to Trento to study theology, then to Bologna, and he completed his studies with the Jesuits at Ingolstadt in 1604. Ordained a priest in March 1614, he became provost of the cathedral chapter and president of the archbishop's exchequer at the request of Prince-Archbishop Markus Sittich von Hohenems.

After Sittich's death on 9 October 1619, Lodron was elected his successor on 13 November and received his episcopal ordination on 23 May of the next year. Sittich had refused to join the Catholic League, which allowed Lodron to keep Salzburg out of the Thirty Years' War and turn to his own lands. The master builder Santino Solari gave the town and country modern bastion fortifications: a belt of five large bastions round the Neustadt, the rocks of the Mönchsberg cut back to serve as natural walls, and an enlarged Hohensalzburg Fortress.

On 23 July 1622 he appointed the scholar Albert Keuslin first rector of the Benedictine University of Salzburg, which Emperor Ferdinand II raised from Keuslin's Akademisches Gymnasium by a resolution of 8 October. A federation of Benedictine abbeys from Salzburg, Switzerland, Bavaria and Austria maintained it, teaching theology, philosophy, law and medicine. Lodron also completed and decorated the cathedral begun under Sittich and consecrated it on 25 September 1628 with an eight-day baroque festival, and he founded collegiate houses at Laufen and Tittmoning.

Lodron died in Salzburg on 15 December 1653 and was succeeded by Guidobald von Thun und Hohenstein. Unlike some of his predecessors he kept no mistress, but he provided generously for the first and second sons of his brother Christoph, building two palaces for them in the centre of Salzburg, the Primogeniturpalast and the Sekundogeniturpalast, which still stood in the 21st century. The university is sometimes called the Paris-Lodron-Universität after him, and the Paris-Lodron-Straße near Mirabell Palace marks the border between the Altstadt and the Neustadt.
paris-peace-accords: Vietnam was divided at the 17th parallel in July 1954, and a war between the communist north and the south followed, with the United States backing the south. After the Tet Offensive of 1968 and the rise of the American anti-war movement, President Lyndon B. Johnson halted bombing of the northern part of North Vietnam on 31 March 1968, and delegations first met in Paris on 10 May. Talks stalled for five months until Johnson agreed on 31 October to end the air strikes. Disputes over recognition were settled by naming North Vietnam and the United States as the parties, and one over the shape of the table by a circular table for the two governments and square tables for the other parties.

After Richard Nixon became president in 1969, the main negotiations were secret talks between Henry Kissinger and Lê Đức Thọ, begun on 4 August 1969. On 8 May 1972 Nixon accepted a cease-fire in place before American withdrawal, and on 8 October 1972 Thọ allowed the Saigon government to remain in power. Kissinger announced that peace was at hand. President Thiệu, who had not been told of the talks, refused the draft, so Nixon ordered the Operation Linebacker II bombings in December 1972, pledged continued aid and pressed Thiệu, who had little choice but to accede. The agreement was signed at the Hotel Majestic in Paris on 27 January 1973.

The agreement provided for a cease-fire, the withdrawal of American and allied forces within sixty days, the return of prisoners and peaceful reunification, and set up an International Commission of Control and Supervision of Canada, Hungary, Indonesia and Poland. North Vietnamese troops stayed in the south. Fighting did not stop on 28 January, full-scale war had resumed by March 1973, and Thiệu declared the agreement no longer in effect on 4 January 1974. The Case-Church Amendment of June 1973 barred further American military activity in Indochina, and aid to the south was cut. North Vietnam's final offensive ended with the surrender of Dương Văn Minh on 30 April 1975. Kissinger and Thọ received the 1973 Nobel Peace Prize, though Thọ declined it.
paris-peace-conference-1919-1920: In 1917 US president Woodrow Wilson commissioned about 150 academics to research the topics likely to arise in peace talks and to develop principles for the negotiations. Their work was summarised in the Fourteen Points, which became the basis of the terms of the German surrender and of the Armistice of 11 November 1918. The conference brought together diplomats from 32 countries and nationalities. Germany, Austria-Hungary, Turkey and Bulgaria were given no voice in the deliberations, and Russia was represented, though not by its actual government.

The conference formally opened on 18 January 1919 at the Quai d'Orsay in Paris, a date chosen because it was the anniversary of the proclamation of William I as German Emperor in 1871. Delegates were assigned to 52 commissions, which held 1,646 sessions on topics ranging from prisoners of war to undersea cables. The five great powers, France, Britain, Italy, Japan and the United States, controlled it, and the Big Four leaders, Georges Clemenceau, David Lloyd George, Wilson and Vittorio Emanuele Orlando, met informally 145 times and agreed all major decisions before they were ratified.

Clemenceau's chief aim was to weaken Germany militarily, strategically and economically. Italy sought the territories promised in the secret Treaty of London. Japan proposed a racial equality clause for the League's Covenant on 13 February and claimed Germany's concessions in Shantung. The Western powers transferred those concessions to Japan, which sparked student protests in China on 4 May, later known as the May Fourth Movement; the Chinese delegation was the only one that did not sign the Treaty of Versailles.

The main result was the Treaty of Versailles with Germany, which had 15 chapters and 440 clauses. Article 231 of the treaty placed responsibility for the war on "the aggression of Germany and her allies", a provision that humiliated German leaders and citizens, and Germany stopped paying reparations after 1931, having delivered only a small portion. German and Ottoman overseas possessions passed as mandates chiefly to Britain and France, and new boundaries were drawn, sometimes after plebiscites. Delegations from Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania won recognition of their independence, while Ukraine, Ireland, Korea and Vietnam were effectively ignored.

The senior statesmen stopped working personally on the conference in June 1919, but historian Michael Neiberg notes that the formal peace process did not end until the Treaty of Lausanne of July 1923. The settlement is considered one of the great watersheds of 20th-century geopolitics, and its exclusion of the defeated powers later gave rise to political resentments that lasted decades.
parlement-of-paris: The Parlement of Paris was the oldest of the parlements of the Kingdom of France and, because of its location and history, the most significant. The parlements were judicial rather than legislative bodies, made up of magistrates. They were not representative bodies in the modern sense, but their procedures and powers could delay the otherwise unchecked power of the king. The site of its sessions in the medieval royal palace on the Île de la Cité is today occupied by the Paris Hall of Justice.

In 1589, with Paris effectively in the hands of the Catholic League, the king summoned the Parlement to meet at Tours, but only a small faction of its members obeyed. After the assassination of Henry III of France by the Dominican lay brother Jacques Clément, this Parliament of Tours went on sitting in the first years of the reign of Henry IV of France, while royalist members of the parlements of Rouen, Toulouse and Dijon withdrew to Caen, Carcassonne, Semur and Flavigny.

In the Parliamentary Fronde of 1648 to 1649 the Parlement did much to stir the nobility to resist the expansion of royal power by force of arms; in the end Louis XIV prevailed and the nobility was humiliated. At a session of 3 March 1766, known as the Séance de la Flagellation, Louis XV asserted that sovereign power resided in his person alone.

In March 1776 the Parlement addressed protests to Louis XVI against the reforms of Anne Robert Jacques Turgot, who sought to end the nobility's exemption from taxes and to abolish the guilds and corporations that restricted trade. In its remonstrance against the edict suppressing the corvée, the forced labour on roads that in practice fell only on the poorest, it feared that a new tax paid by all would replace it and introduce equality as a principle. It reminded the king that the clergy served through education, worship and alms, the nobles through their blood and counsel, and the last class of the nation through taxes, industry and physical labour.

The nobility, about 1.5% of the population, was exempt from almost all taxes, including the gabelle on salt and the taille, the land tax paid by peasants. Turgot's reforms were unpopular among commoners too, who saw the parlements as their best defence against the power of the monarchy. The quarrel over them has been called the first step toward reform that entered the political arena.
parliament-of-finland: The Parliament of Finland was preceded by the Diet of Finland, which had succeeded the Riksdag of the Estates in 1809 and was tetracameral. The Diet of Porvoo of 1809 met in several buildings in Porvoo, assembled only once and did not reconvene until 1863. When the unicameral Parliament was established by the Parliament Act in 1906, Finland was an autonomous grand duchy under the Russian tsar, who ruled as Grand Duke and not as an absolute monarch. Universal suffrage and eligibility were introduced: women could vote and run for office as equals, as could landless people, with no minority excluded. The first election was held in 1907, and the first Parliament had 19 female representatives, an unprecedented number, which grew to 21 by 1913.

The first years were difficult. Between 1908 and 1916 the power of the Parliament was almost completely neutralised by Tsar Nicholas II and the so-called sabre senate, a bureaucratic government formed by Imperial Russian Army officers during the second period of Russification. The Parliament was dissolved and new elections held almost every year. In the 1916 election the Social Democrats won a majority, the only time one party has held a parliamentary majority, and coalition governments have therefore been the rule. Until the Constitution Act of 1919 the body was known in Swedish as lantdagen, the old term for the Diet.

The Parliament has been dissolved before the end of its term fourteen times; the most recent was on 4 June 1975. It first met in a volunteer fire brigade house at Keskuskatu 7, and in 1911 moved to the Heimola House, designed by Onni Tarjanne. Both buildings were later demolished. The Parliament House now stands in central Helsinki.

The Parliament has 200 members, 199 elected every four years from 13 multi-member districts by the proportional D'Hondt method, plus one member from Åland. It passes legislation, decides the state budget, approves international treaties and supervises the government, which it can bring down. It may override presidential vetoes, and changes to the constitution need approval by two successive parliaments with an election between them. Most members work in parliamentary groups that correspond to political parties.

Its 17 committees include the Grand Committee, which deals with European Union matters, and the Constitutional Law Committee, which oversees constitutional questions because Finland has no constitutional court. The Committee for the Future assesses long-term developments. Each year the Parliament elects a speaker and two deputy speakers on the first day of the session, and members enjoy parliamentary immunity.
parliament-of-friuli: The parliament grew out of patriarchal councils of increasing size, called in the 13th century to win the money and soldiers of the Friulian barons for the patriarchs' near continual wars with their neighbours. By the end of that century it had become a regular institution, and in the early 14th century it described itself as acting in the name of the whole population of Friuli. Throughout patriarchal rule its main business was military: barons, churchmen and towns served according to duties listed in the talea militiae, which the parliament itself fixed and revised. The patriarch's chief hold over it lay in appointing the gastalds of the towns.

The parliament met up to ten times a year and mattered most during vacancies in the patriarchal office, which were frequent. Plenary sessions never lasted more than a day, and the work was done by committees. One, of sixteen men (two churchmen, two barons, eight ministeriales and four town representatives) with any appointees of the patriarch, met straight after a plenary session to apply its decisions. A second, of three members from each of the three estates and six appointees of the patriarch, sat for six months and became in effect a standing committee.

The parliament judged cases of feudal law, conspiracy and rebellion and civil suits against the patriarch, and was the court of last resort in almost all cases. In March 1355 it codified a constitution, the Constitutiones Patriae Foriiulii, amended in 1366, 1368 and 1380.

The parliament had no part in the Venetian conquest of 1420, but it went on working with a lieutenant appointed by the Venetian Senate as it had with the patriarch, and Venice confirmed the constitution in 1429; it remained the fundamental law of the Patria del Friuli until the fall of Venice in 1797. Udine and Cividale stopped taking part, the assembly divided into two for the lands east and west of the Tagliamento, and in the mid-16th century a separate body, the corpo della contadinanza, came to represent the rural districts. The antiquary Count Girolamo di Porcia wrote that Friuli under the patriarchs had had more the form of a republic than of a principality.
parliament-of-great-britain: The Parliament of Great Britain was formed in May 1707, after both the Parliament of England and the Parliament of Scotland ratified the Acts of Union, which in turn ratified the Treaty of Union of 1706. The Acts created the Kingdom of Great Britain and a new parliament housed in the former home of the English parliament in the Palace of Westminster.

All the traditions, procedures and standing orders of the English parliament were retained, though the treaty makes no provision for this, and the sitting officers and members for England made up the overwhelming majority of the new body. No new general election was thought necessary. Scots law and Scottish legislation remained separate, but new legislation was to be passed by the new parliament. England's de facto prominence has been a contentious issue.

After George I came to the throne in 1714 under the Act of Settlement of 1701, power continued to shift from the monarchy. He was a German ruler who spoke poor English and was more interested in his continental dominions, and he entrusted power to ministers, the foremost of them Sir Robert Walpole. By the end of his reign in 1727 the ministers, who had to rely on Parliament for support, were firmly established. George II did not try to regain monarchical control. The last occasion on which royal assent was withheld was in 1708, by Queen Anne, and then at her ministers' request.

The monarch kept considerable influence through patronage over a Parliament dominated by the English aristocracy. Most candidates for the Commons called themselves Whigs or Tories but formed shifting coalitions of interests. The vote was mostly restricted to property owners, in constituencies that no longer reflected the growth of manufacturing towns, so in "rotten" and "pocket" boroughs seats could be bought while major cities went unrepresented.

Defeat in the American War of Independence forced George III in March 1782 to appoint an administration of his opponents. In November 1783 he used his influence in the House of Lords to defeat a bill to reform the East India Company and appointed William Pitt the Younger. Pitt's proposals of April 1785 to redistribute seats from rotten boroughs were defeated in the Commons by 248 votes to 174.

The Acts of Union 1800 merged the British and Irish parliaments into the Parliament of the United Kingdom with effect from 1 January 1801. The House of Lords included sixteen representative peers elected by the Peerage of Scotland.
parliament-of-ireland: Like its English model, the parliament grew out of the great council summoned by the king's viceroy in the Anglo-Norman Lordship of Ireland. Counties sent elected knights of the shire from 1297 and towns from 1299. Its main task was to approve taxes for the Dublin Castle administration, and only the English of Ireland sat in it. As the crown's hold shrank to the Pale around Dublin, it became the forum of the Pale community, and fear of great families such as that of the Earl of Kildare led to Poynings' Law, which required every bill to be approved by the Irish and English privy councils.

Under surrender and regrant the Gaelic lords who accepted Henry VIII's new Kingdom of Ireland could sit as equals, and in 1537 parliament approved the Act of Supremacy. New boroughs in the planted lands of Ulster gave Protestants a majority of the Commons, and the Cromwellian Act of Settlement of 1652 barred Catholics altogether. The Catholic Patriot Parliament of 1689 sat under James II, but its acts were annulled in 1695, and the Protestant parliament then passed the Penal Laws. The Dependency of Ireland on Great Britain Act 1719 declared Westminster's right to legislate for Ireland.

Led by Henry Grattan, the parliament won the Constitution of 1782, which removed the restrictions of Poynings' Law, and in 1793 it gave Catholics back the vote. After the rebellion of 1798, William Pitt the Younger and Lord Cornwallis pressed for union. A motion against it passed 111 to 106 in January 1799, but the government then won members with offices, pensions and peerages and spent over £1,250,000 buying borough and county seats. Parliament met for the last time on 2 August 1800.

The Lord Chancellor presided over the Lords from the woolsack, and the Speaker, with no government answerable to the Commons, was the leading figure of the lower house. Sessions, opened by the Lord Lieutenant from the throne, drew the Anglo-Irish elite to Dublin for the social season. Parliament sat latterly in its own Parliament House on College Green, and its records were published from the 1750s.
parliament-of-scotland: The Parliament grew out of the king's council of bishops and earls. It is perhaps first identifiable in 1235, under Alexander II, when a colloquium already had a political and judicial role. Burgh representatives are first mentioned taking part in decisions in 1296, and Robert the Bruce began calling burgh commissioners regularly. Its consent was needed for taxation, and it had a strong influence over justice, foreign policy and war. Before about 1500 General Councils, and afterwards Conventions of Estates, could also handle taxation and legislation, but lacked the full authority of a parliament. Besides Edinburgh it met at Perth, Stirling, St Andrews and many other towns.

After the death of Alexander III the Parliament gave legitimacy to the Guardians who ran the kingdom, and John Balliol used it to resist the claims of Edward I of England. Under David II it repeatedly stopped the king from accepting an English succession to the throne, and it arguably reached the height of its power over the Crown after James I returned from English captivity in 1424. It was called less often by the early 16th century and survived in part because of the minorities and regencies that followed 1513.

In the War of the Three Kingdoms the Covenanters took power and expelled the bishops from kirk and Parliament, and after the Anglo-Scots War of 1649-1651 Scotland was joined to the English Protectorate. An independent Parliament was restored in 1661 and annulled the legislation passed since 1633; when it refused to pass the measures of King James, who succeeded in 1685, he suspended it. After the Glorious Revolution it removed the clergy in 1689 and abolished the Lords of the Articles in 1690, and from then until 1707 political parties and alliances formed within it. Older historians called it a rubber stamp for royal decisions; modern research has found that it played an active role in Scottish affairs.

The Lord Chancellor presided, and an act of 1428 creating a common speaker came to nothing. Members met in one chamber, after 1639 in Parliament House in Edinburgh, arranged in a square facing the throne; as the highest court in the kingdom it had an inner bar before the throne for the accused. Some historians identify a fourth estate of shire commissioners and a fifth of officers of state, a view that remains disputed. The term of a Parliament began and ended with the Riding of Parliament, a procession along the Royal Mile from Holyroodhouse, held for the last time on 6 May 1703.
parmehutu: Grégoire Kayibanda founded the movement in June 1957 as the Hutu Social Movement, a party of Hutu nationalists who fought on behalf of the Hutu majority, which it considered oppressed. It took the name Hutu Emancipation Movement Party on 25 September 1959 and was also known as the Republican Democratic Movement, or MDR-Parmehutu. It stressed the right of the majority ethnicity to rule and asserted the supremacy of Hutus over Tutsis, and it was the most important party of the Hutu Revolution of 1959-61.

The party dominated the local elections of 1960, winning 2,390 of 3,125 elected communal council seats and 160 of 229 burgomasters. In 1961 parliamentary elections were held together with a referendum on the monarchy of Mwami Kigeri V: MDR-Parmehutu won 35 of the 44 seats in the Legislative Assembly, and the referendum ended the monarchy. Kayibanda appointed a government of Hutus and became president at independence in July 1962. In the 1965 elections he ran unopposed for the presidency, and the party won all 47 seats in the National Assembly.

Under Parmehutu rule Tutsis were severely discriminated against, persecuted and repeatedly massacred, and hundreds of thousands of Tutsi fled the country. Bertrand Russell described the Tutsi massacres of 1963 as the worst since the Holocaust, and in 1967 another 20,000 Tutsi were killed.

In the coup of July 1973 Kayibanda was ousted by his cousin, Major-General Juvénal Habyarimana, who like other leaders from the north of Rwanda, the abakonde, felt marginalised by the southern-dominated regime. The party was suspended and was officially banned two years later, when Rwanda became a one-party state under Habyarimana's National Revolutionary Movement for Development (MRND), which was dominated by Hutu from the northern and northwestern parts of the country.
parmenides: Parmenides was born in the Greek colony of Elea in southern Italy to a wealthy and aristocratic family. Diogenes Laërtius gives his father's name as Pires. The same writer passes on two divergent accounts of his teacher. One, following Sotion, says he first studied with Xenophanes but did not follow him, and later preferred the Pythagorean Aminias. Another, following Theophrastus, makes him a disciple of Anaximander.

The date of his birth is not known. Apollodorus, as transmitted by Diogenes Laërtius, puts his prime in the years 504 to 500 BCE, which would place his birth about 40 years earlier. Plato's dialogue Parmenides shows him visiting Athens at about the age of 65, when Socrates was a young man, which would suggest a birth around 515 BCE. Most modern classicists regard that visit and meeting as fiction, and some scholars prefer other dates. He is generally thought to have been in his prime around 475 BCE.

Plutarch, Strabo and Diogenes Laërtius, following Speusippus, agree that Parmenides took part in the government of his city, organising it and giving it an admirable code of laws. In 1969 the plinth of a statue of the 1st century CE was excavated at Velia, the later Elea. It names Parmenides, son of Pires, and calls him a physicist, the word then used for philosophers who studied nature. Its third word, ouliadēs, may mean simply a native of Elea or a member of a medical school devoted to Apollo Ulius, which would make him a physician as well as a legislator. Other specialists hold that the plinth shows only his social importance in the city.

The only known work is a poem in dactylic hexameter, later titled On Nature. About 160 verses survive from an original total probably near 800, largely through long excerpts made by Sextus Empiricus and Simplicius of Cilicia. It had three parts: a proem with an allegorical narrative, the Way of Truth and the Way of Opinion, of which only small fragments and prose paraphrases remain.

In the Way of Truth, a goddess teaches that what is cannot have come from what is not, since non-Being cannot be thought or spoken of. Being is therefore eternal, indivisible, unchanging and without time, and it cannot move, because that would require space it does not already occupy. The Way of Opinion describes the world of appearances, built on the opposites of light and dark, where the senses lead mortals into false conceptions. He is credited with first defining ontology as a discipline separate from theology.

Parmenides founded the Eleatic school, continued by Zeno of Elea and Melissus of Samos. Zeno devised arguments to defend his views against critics, and Plato counted him among his main influences, alongside Socrates and the Pythagoreans.
parmigianino: Parmigianino, meaning the little one from Parma, was the eighth child of Filippo Mazzola and Donatella Abbati. His father died of the plague two years after his birth, and the children were raised by their uncles Michele and Pier Ilario, who according to Vasari were modestly talented artists. He completed a chapel decoration in San Giovanni Evangelista begun by his uncle and had finished the Bardi Altarpiece by the age of eighteen. In 1521 he was sent to Viadana to escape the wars between the French, Imperial and papal armies. There he painted two tempera panels and met Correggio, who was at work on the fresco decoration of the cupola.

In 1524 he travelled to Rome with five small paintings, among them the Circumcision of Jesus and his Self-portrait in a Convex Mirror, hoping for the patronage of Pope Clement VII. Vasari records that he was hailed there as a Raphael reborn. In January 1526 he agreed to paint the Vision of Saint Jerome for the church of San Salvatore in Lauro, but the Sack of Rome in 1527 drove him and many other artists out of the city. He lived in Bologna for nearly three years and was back in Parma by 1530.

In 1531 he was commissioned to paint two altarpieces for the unfinished church of Santa Maria della Steccata. The work was still unfinished in 1535. The Madonna with the Long Neck, which he began in 1534, was meant for the chapel of the family of Elena Baiardi. Parmigianino was a pioneer of Italian etching and designed chiaroscuro woodcuts that other artists cut. He made his etchings and chiaroscuro prints between 1527 and 1530 in Bologna, and although his output was small, it had a considerable influence on Italian printmaking. He also led a trend towards three-quarter and full-length portraits, previously mostly reserved for royalty.

Around this time he became a devotee of alchemy. Scholars now think his scientific interests may have come from a search for a new medium for his etchings. He did little work in the church, and the confraternity banned him from continuing. He was imprisoned for two months for breach of contract and was replaced by Giulio Romano, who also withdrew.

He died of a fever in Casalmaggiore on 24 August 1540, aged 37, and was buried in the church of the Servite Friars. His cousin Girolamo Bedoli and Bedoli's son Alessandro Mazzola were among those he influenced. His drawings are outstanding, and his portable works are now in major museums in Italy and elsewhere.
parni: The Parni, also called Aparni or Parnians, lived around the Ochus, the modern Tejen river, south-east of the Caspian Sea, and were one of three tribes of the Dahae confederacy. Their original homeland may have been what is now southern Russia, from where they may have moved with other Scythian tribes. They are not clearly attested in Iranian sources, and all that is known of them comes from Greek and Latin accounts, where their name is easily confused with those of other tribes such as the Sparni or Apartani. Even the name and site of a capital, if they had one, are unknown.

Their language is not directly attested but is thought to be one of the eastern substrates of the Parthian language they later adopted, with a strong east Iranian element from their nearness to the Sakas; traces survive as loanwords in Armenian. The late writer Justin described it as midway between Scythian and Median.

When Andragoras, the Seleucid satrap of Parthia, declared independence, he lost Seleucid military support and struggled to hold his borders. A man named Arsaces, of Scythian or Bactrian origin, had been chosen leader of the Parni, and under Arsaces and his brother Tiridates they invaded Parthia, took its northern region of Astabene, whose capital was Kabuchan, and soon seized the rest, killing Andragoras. A punitive expedition under Seleucus II failed, but after the Battle of Mount Labus in 209 BCE Antiochus III recovered the territory, and Arsaces II accepted vassal status. Only under Phraates I did the Arsacids again assert their independence, by which time the Parni had become indistinguishable from the Parthians.

The seizure of Astabene nominally marks the start of the Arsacid era, named after Arsaces, whose name every Parthian king adopted. The name Parni reappears in Sassanid-era documents for one of the seven Parthian feudal families allied with the Sassanid court, though that claim is probably not genuine. It has been suggested that the Parnau Hills bear their name.
parnon: Parnon, also called Malevos, is a massif on the east of the Laconian plain and the Evrotas Valley, with its western part in Laconia and its north-eastern part in Arcadia, and it forms the boundary between the two. It can be seen from Athens above the tops of the Argive mountains. From its summit the view takes in south-eastern Arcadia, South Kynouria and much of Laconia as far as the Taygetos mountains, part of central Arcadia and the southern Argolis, and the Myrtoan and Laconian Gulfs.

The range falls into three parts. The northernmost and highest runs 30 kilometres from just north of Ano Doliana in North Kynouria south-east to the Platanaki Pass, the ancient Glyppia, on the old route from Therapnes to South Kynouria between the peaks of Parnon and Psaris, 1,836 metres. Here the tree line stands at 1,750 metres, with forests of Black Pine and fir below it and grasslands above.

South of the pass, 22 kilometres of central Parnon run lower to Kounoupia, and a further 38 kilometres, lower still but mountainous, reach the sea at Epidaurus Limera, in Monemvasia; Parnon proper does not extend into the Malea Peninsula. Two forelands flank the range: Kynouria lies in the eastern one, while the western foreland runs from the northern flank to Gkoritsa in Therapnes and south into the Malea Peninsula. Villages around the massif include Kastanitsa, Agios Vasileios, Kosmas, Geraki and Vamvakou.

The range is mostly limestone and holds deep caves, among them the Peleta Sinkhole, explored by 2006 to a depth of 543 metres, and the vertical cave of Propantes, 360 metres deep. In 2025 UNESCO designated the mountain a biosphere reserve.
paropamisadae: The province largely coincided with the Achaemenid province of Parupraesanna and took in the districts of Sattagydia in the Bannu basin, Gandhara around Kabul, Peshawar and Taxila, and Oddiyana in the Swat Valley. It lay north of Arachosia, reached up to the Hindu Kush and the Pamir mountains, and was bounded on the east by the Indus River. Its peoples are recorded as the Cabolitae near Kabul, the Parsii in the northwest, the Ambautae in the east and the Par(g)yetae in the south.

The main cities were Ortospana or Carura, probably Kabul; Gauzaca, probably Ghazni; Capissa, the modern Kapisa; and Parsia, the capital of the Parsii. The name is the Latin form of the Greek Paropamisadai, taken from the Old Persian Para-uparisaina, meaning beyond the Hindu Kush. In Greek and Latin, Paropamisus came to mean the Hindu Kush itself, and editions of Ptolemy's Geography often spell the people and region Paropanisadae and Paropanisus.

Ancient Buddhist texts place the territories of Paropamisus within the mahajanapada kingdom of Kamboja. The region came under Achaemenid rule in the late 6th century BCE, under Cyrus the Great or Darius I, and is named Paruparaesanna in the Akkadian and Elamite versions of the Behistun Inscription of Darius the Great and Gandāra in the Old Persian version. Alexander the Great conquered the Achaemenid Empire in the 320s BCE.

After Alexander died in 323 BCE the area passed to the Seleucid Empire, which gave it to the Maurya dynasty in 305 BCE. Strabo wrote that Seleucus I Nicator handed these lands to Sandrocottus on terms of intermarriage and in exchange for 500 elephants. After the fall of the Mauryans in 185 BCE, King Demetrius I of the Greco-Bactrians annexed Paropamisus to his Indo-Greek Kingdom. The Eucratidians took it soon after the death of Menander I, but lost it to the Yuezhi around 125 BCE.
parshvanatha: Parshvanatha was the 23rd of 24 tirthankaras, and scholars acknowledge him as the earliest of them who was likely a historical figure. Jain tradition places him in the 9th to 8th century BCE, while historians put him between about the 8th and 7th centuries BCE, as the founder of a proto-Jain ascetic community later revived and reformed by Mahavira. Historians such as Hermann Jacobi accepted him partly because Buddhist texts mention his Four Vows. A Buddhist commentary, the Manorathapurani, names Vappa, the Buddha's uncle, as one of his followers. Paul Dundas notes that section 31 of the Isibhasiyam, which may preserve his teachings, is circumstantial evidence that he lived.

According to Jain tradition he was born in Varanasi to King Ashwasena and Queen Vamadevi of the Ikshvaku dynasty, and succeeded the 22nd tirthankara, Neminatha. He lived as a prince and soldier. At thirty, after seeing an image of Neminatha, he renounced the world, removing his clothes and hair and fasting strictly. After 84 days of meditation he is said to have attained omniscience under a dhaataki tree near Benares.

According to the Śvētāmbara tradition, Parshvanatha and his ascetic community kept a fourfold restraint, to which Mahavira added a fifth great vow, celibacy, and expanded the first four with his ideas on ahimsa. Parshvanatha did not require celibacy and allowed monks to wear simple outer garments. The Digambaras hold that there was no difference between the teachings of the two.
