The Geneva Conference of 1954 required foreign forces to withdraw and allowed the Pathet Lao to establish itself in Laos's two northern provinces, though the Viet Minh and North Vietnamese never fully left the border areas. A coalition government of monarchists and communists was formed in 1957, but in 1959 fighting resumed after two Pathet Lao battalions chosen for integration into the Royal Lao Army were surrounded and fled to North Vietnam.
North Vietnam formed Group 959 in September 1959 to secure the supply route to South Vietnam, later known as the Ho Chi Minh trail, and to train and supply the Pathet Lao.

A neutrality agreement was signed in Geneva on 23 July 1962 and the Pathet Lao joined another coalition government in June 1962, leaving it and resuming the fighting by April 1963. The armed forces took the name Lao People's Liberation Army in October 1965, with estimated strength rising from 25,000 in June 1965 to over 48,000 in 1970, and depended on the People's Army of Vietnam for weapons. China also supplied guns, grenades and bullets and trained over 700 officers. After the Paris Peace Accords the Pathet Lao and the Lao government signed the Vientiane Treaty, a cease-fire, on 21 February 1973. The movement gained control of the whole country in 1975.

The Pathet Lao's supreme headquarters lay in the Viengxay Caves near Xam Neua. Its forces were divided into regular, regional and militia or guerrilla units, with Vietnamese advisers attached, and its units had political commissars down to company level. Training stressed political indoctrination above military skill, and recruits came by appeals to patriotism or by a draft.
patiala-and-east-punjab-states-union: PEPSU was inaugurated on 15 July 1948 from six salute states, Patiala, Jind, Kapurthala, Nabha, Faridkot and Malerkotla, and two non-salute states, Kalsia and Nalagarh, which kept their native rulers; it formally became a state of India in 1950. The Maharaja of Patiala, Yadavindra Singh, was its Rajpramukh, equivalent to a governor, for its whole existence, and the Maharaja of Kapurthala, Jagatjit Singh, served as Uparajpramukh. Gian Singh Rarewala was sworn in as the first Chief Minister on 13 January 1949, and Col. Raghbir Singh succeeded him on 23 May 1951.

The state elected a 60-member legislative assembly on 6 January 1952, in which the Congress Party won 26 seats and the Akali Dal 19. On 22 April 1952 Rarewala became Chief Minister again at the head of the United Front, a coalition of the Akali Dal and independents, but his government was dismissed on 5 March 1953 and President's rule imposed. After the mid-term poll the Congress won a majority and Raghbir Singh returned on 8 March 1954; on his death Brish Bhan became Chief Minister on 12 January 1955, the last to hold the office.

PEPSU covered 26,208 km2 and in 1951 had a population of 3,493,685, of whom 19% lived in towns, spread over 64 towns and 5,708 villages. It began in 1948 with eight districts and 25 tehsils. In 1953 the districts were reduced to five: Fatehgarh Sahib and Kohistan were merged with Patiala, and Barnala was divided between Sangrur and Bhatinda. The state returned members to the Lok Sabha from four constituencies, one of them, Kapurthala-Bhatinda, a double-seat constituency.

Under the States Reorganisation Act, PEPSU was merged mostly into Punjab State on 1 November 1956. Parts of it, including the present Jind district, Pinjore, Charkhi Dadri, Bawal and Mahendragarh Narnaul, now lie in Haryana, which was separated from Punjab on 1 November 1966, and others, among them Solan and Nalagarh, in Himachal Pradesh.
patna: Ancient Patna, known as Pataliputra, was the capital of the Magadha Empire under the Haryanka, Nanda, Mauryan, Shunga, Gupta and Pala dynasties. Traditional Buddhist literature has Ajatashatru, the king of Magadha, choose a site on the bank of the Ganges and fortify it so that he could better fight the Licchavis of Vaishali, and says that Gautama Buddha passed through in the last year of his life.

The Chinese Buddhist traveller Faxian, who visited India between 399 and 414 CE, stayed in the city for many months translating Buddhist texts. Pataliputra was home to scholars including Aryabhata, Vātsyāyana and Chanakya. After the Gupta Empire broke up the city passed through uncertain times, and Bakhtiar Khilji's capture of Bihar in the 12th century ended its standing as a political and cultural centre.

Sher Shah Suri revived Patna in the middle of the 16th century, building a fort of which nothing survives and a mosque that does. Akbar reached the city in 1574 to put down the Afghan chief Daud Khan, and Abul Fazl described a flourishing trade in paper, stone and glass and in the rice later known in Europe as Patna rice. In 1704 Aurangzeb agreed to his grandson Prince Muhammad Azim's request to rename it Azimabad. Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, was born in Patna on 22 December 1666, and Patna Sahib is one of the most sacred Sikh pilgrimage sites.

In the 17th century Patna became a centre of international trade. The English East India Company set up a factory there in 1620 for calico and silk, and it grew into a trading centre for saltpetre; Portuguese traders had a factory there from at least 1580. In 1763 Nawab Mir Qasim ordered the killing of 45 mostly British employees and 200 sepoys of the Company in the Patna massacre. The Company annexed the city in 1793. In 1912, when the Bengal Presidency was partitioned, Patna became the capital of the province of Bihar and Orissa.

Patna is the capital and largest city of the Indian state of Bihar and the seat of the Patna High Court. It lies mainly on the southern bank of the Ganges, at the meeting of rivers that include the Son, Gandak and Punpun, and covers about 250 square kilometres. The pilgrimage centres of Vaishali, Rajgir, Nalanda, Bodh Gaya and Pawapuri are nearby. It remained the capital of Bihar after independence in 1947, including after Jharkhand became a separate state in 2000.
patriarch-nikon: Nikon was born Nikita Minin in 1605, the son of a Mordvin peasant farmer, in the village of Veldemanovo, about 96 kilometres from Nizhny Novgorod. He became a novice at the Makaryev Monastery at twelve, then returned home, married and served as a parish priest, later in Moscow. After his three children died by 1635 he persuaded his wife to take the veil and became a monk on Anzersky Island in the White Sea, taking the name Nikon. He became abbot of the Kozheozersky Monastery in 1643 and in 1646 impressed Tsar Alexis, who made him archimandrite of the Novospassky Monastery in Moscow.

At Novospassky he joined the Zealots of Piety, a circle around the tsar's confessor Stefan Vonifatiyev that sought a revival of Orthodox piety after the Time of Troubles. In 1649 he became metropolitan of Great Novgorod, where he quelled a riot by leading a religious procession. Elected patriarch on 1 August 1652, he accepted only after the tsar and the boyars knelt before him, and after imposing a vow of obedience in all matters of Church dogma and observance.

Nikon consulted Greek prelates and scholars of Constantinople and Kiev, who convinced him that the Muscovite service-books and many icons differed from Greek models. A synod of 1654 and a council of 1656 approved revising the books and anathematised the dissenters, among them Paul, bishop of Kolomna. He ordered the search for icons influenced by Western baroque and forbade tent-like churches. Later research, such as Meyendorff's, found that the Muscovite books followed an older recension than the Greek ones. The reforms led to the Old Believers. He founded the Valday Iversky, New Jerusalem and Kiy Island monasteries.

Between 1652 and 1658 he was a colleague of the tsar rather than a minister, and ruled as chief while Alexis campaigned in the wars with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. He held that the supreme bishop is higher than the tsar and opposed the Legal Code of 1649, which made the Church subservient to the state. In 1658, estranged from Alexis, he took off his vestments and withdrew to the New Jerusalem Monastery without resigning.

A pan-Orthodox synod presided over by the patriarchs Paisius of Alexandria and Macarius III of Antioch found him guilty of reviling the tsar and the Church, of deposing Bishop Paul contrary to the canons and of beating and torturing dependants. He was reduced to the status of a monk and sent to the Ferapontov monastery, while the same council confirmed his reforms. Allowed to return under a partial pardon in 1681, he died at Tropino on 17 August of that year, on the way to New Jerusalem.
patrice-de-macmahon: The MacMahon family is of Irish origin. After losing much of its land in the Cromwellian confiscations of 1652, a branch supported the deposed James II in 1688 and settled in France, applying for French citizenship in 1749. Patrice de MacMahon was born on 13 June 1808 at the Château de Sully near Autun in Burgundy, the sixteenth and second-youngest son of Baron Maurice-François de Mac Mahon. The family, a military one, had decidedly royalist politics. He entered the military school at Saint-Cyr on 23 October 1825 and joined the army in 1827.

MacMahon served in the French conquest of Algeria from 1830, was commended at the seizure of Algiers and was wounded at the Siege of Constantine in 1837. He became a colonel in December 1845 and a general of brigade in 1848, and in 1852 he organised in Algeria the plebiscite that approved the coup d'état of 1851. In the Crimean War he won a victory at the Battle of Malakoff in September 1855, where he is reputed to have said 'Here I am; here will I stay!' At Magenta in 1859 he advanced his troops without orders at a critical moment, which assured the French victory; Napoleon III made him a Marshal of France and Duke of Magenta.

He was Governor General of Algeria from 1864, a post in which he did not distinguish himself and which drew numerous complaints. In 1870 he led the main French army in the Franco-Prussian War, suffered defeats in Alsace and was seriously wounded at Sedan; with the Emperor he was made prisoner on 1 September. In May 1871 he led the Semaine Sanglante, the week-long campaign that defeated the Paris Commune.

In May 1873 the royalist and conservative majority of the National Assembly elected MacMahon President, with one vote against. Many hoped he would hold office until a Bourbon pretender could restore the monarchy, but he refused to meet the Count of Chambord and accepted a seven-year mandate on 9 November 1873. He remained above parties during the Constitutional Laws of 1875. After the Republican victory of 1876 he reluctantly accepted governments under Jules Dufaure and Jules Simon.

In the crisis of 16 May 1877 he dismissed Simon, had the Senate dissolve the Chamber of Deputies and campaigned across the country, but the elections of 14 October gave the Republicans a majority of 120 seats. He resigned on 30 January 1879, succeeded by Jules Grévy. He died on 17 October 1893 and was buried at the Invalides after a state funeral.
patrice-lumumba: Patrice Lumumba was born Isaïe Tasumbu Tawosa on 2 July 1925 in Onalua, in the Kasaï province of the Belgian Congo, to Julienne Wamato Lomendja and François Tolenga Otetshima, a farmer. He belonged to the Tetela ethnic group. Raised in a Catholic family, he attended a Protestant primary school, a Catholic missionary school and finally the government post office training school, where he passed the one-year course with distinction. He was known as a vocal, precocious young man who pointed out his teachers' errors in front of his classmates, and he spoke Tetela, French, Lingala, Swahili and Tshiluba.

Lumumba helped found the Mouvement National Congolais in 1958 and quickly became its leader. Unlike other Congolese parties, it did not rest on an ethnic base, and its platform of independence, gradual Africanisation of government, state-led economic development and neutrality in foreign affairs drew a large popular following. In December 1958 he represented it at the All-African Peoples' Conference in Accra, hosted by Kwame Nkrumah. Independence was set for 30 June 1960, after elections held in May in which the MNC won a plurality, and Lumumba became the first prime minister.

On 5 July 1960 troops of the Force Publique mutinied against their commander, General Émile Janssens, and the mutiny spread; this opened the Congo Crisis. Katanga and South Kasai declared independence, and Lumumba sent the army to put down the secessions. On 5 September President Joseph Kasa-Vubu announced Lumumba's dismissal, and Lumumba in turn declared the president deposed over the radio. On 14 September Mobutu Sese Seko announced a coup. Lumumba was captured while trying to reach Stanleyville, held at the barracks at Thysville from 3 December, and sent to Katanga in January 1961.

Lumumba was killed on 17 January 1961 by the separatist Katangan authorities of Moïse Tshombe, with two associates, Maurice Mpolo and Joseph Okito. Belgian officers dug up and dissolved the bodies. Katangan radio announced on 13 February that he had been killed by villagers after escaping. His killing caused protests in at least twenty countries. Letters of Belgian ministers show that they wanted his elimination and facilitated his transfer to Katanga. In 2002 Belgium formally apologised for its role, admitting moral responsibility. In 2022 a tooth of his, the only remains, was returned to his family. He is widely seen as a martyr of anti-colonial liberation and the pan-African movement.
patricio-aylwin: Patricio Aylwin Azócar was born on 26 November 1918 in Viña del Mar, the eldest of the five children of Miguel Aylwin and Laura Azócar. He studied at the Law School of the University of Chile and qualified as a lawyer, with the highest distinction, in 1943. He taught administrative law at the University of Chile from 1946 to 1967 and at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile from 1952 to 1960. He married Leonor Oyarzún Ivanovic on 29 September 1948, and they had five children. His paternal line was British: an ancestor, Richard Aylwin, emigrated from England to Chile in 1833.

Aylwin entered politics in 1945 by joining the Falange Nacional, of which he was president in 1950–51. When it became the Christian Democratic Party he served seven terms as its president between 1958 and 1989. He was elected a senator in 1965 and became president of the Senate in 1971. During the government of Salvador Allende he led the democratic opposition within and outside Congress, and he is credited, to some degree, with trying to find a peaceful solution to the political crisis.

After the 1973 coup he led his party twice, and in 1979 he spoke for the group that opposed the plebiscite approving a new constitution. He was among the first to advocate accepting that constitution as a reality in order to ease the return to democracy.

Aylwin was at the centre of the movement that defeated Augusto Pinochet in the plebiscite of 5 October 1988. Afterwards he took part in negotiations that produced 54 constitutional reforms and made a peaceful transition possible.

Aylwin was elected president on 14 December 1989 and governed from 1990 to 1994. The military under Pinochet remained powerful, and the constitution preserved its influence, so that the government could not achieve goals such as restructuring the Constitutional Court. Direct municipal elections were begun, the first in June 1992. A tax reform of 1990 raised revenue and allowed social spending to rise from 9.9 to 11.7 per cent of GDP, a new labour law widened trade union rights, and more than 100,000 homes were built. He was succeeded in 1994 by Eduardo Frei Ruiz-Tagle. Aylwin died on 19 April 2016.
patrick-henry: Patrick Henry was born on 29 May 1736 on the family farm, Studley, in Hanover County, Virginia. His father John Henry was an immigrant from Aberdeenshire, and his mother Sarah Winston Syme was a wealthy widow from a prominent local family. Henry was tutored at home by his father after about the age of ten. Because custom gave the family's land, stock and slaves to his older half-brother John Syme Jr., he had to make his own way. At sixteen he opened a store with his brother William, which failed.

While helping at Hanover Tavern he studied law on his own, and in April 1760 he passed the examination at Williamsburg, although his knowledge of procedure was scant. He soon became prominent through his victory in the Parson's Cause against the Anglican clergy.

Henry won a seat in the Virginia House of Burgesses in May 1765. In 1774 he was a delegate to the First Continental Congress. At the Second Virginia Convention in March 1775 he urged that a militia be raised independent of royal authority, and on 23 March he defended this in the speech for which he is best known. In May he led militia towards Williamsburg after the royal governor, the Earl of Dunmore, had marines seize the colony's gunpowder, and he stopped only when a member of the Governor's Council agreed to pay for it.

In May 1776 the Fifth Virginia Convention passed unanimously a resolution based largely on his, declaring Virginia independent and instructing its delegates in Congress to press for American independence. He served on the committee that drafted the Virginia Declaration of Rights and the state's first constitution, and he was elected the first governor of the new state. He served five one-year terms in all, the last two from 1784.

Henry feared a strong federal government. He declined appointment as a delegate to the 1787 Constitutional Convention, and he actively opposed ratification of the Constitution, both because he feared a powerful central government and because it had as yet no Bill of Rights. He was a slaveholder throughout his adult life and hoped to see slavery end, but he had no plan beyond ending the importation of slaves.

Henry wrote little, and only a handful of his papers and a few of his speeches survive, which has frustrated his biographers. Thomas Jefferson filled the gap with his own, often negative, recollections, and these have adversely affected Henry's historical reputation. He helped found Hampden-Sydney College, and the Red Hill Patrick Henry National Memorial preserves his final home and gravesite.
patrick-john: Patrick Roland John was born on 7 January 1938. He led the Waterfront and Allied Workers' Union and was mayor of Roseau before entering the House of Assembly for Roseau North on 1 November 1970. He became Deputy Premier and Minister of Finance in 1973 and, after the resignation of Edward Oliver LeBlanc in 1974, Premier of Dominica. His Labour Party government founded the National Commercial & Development Bank, replaced shanty dwellings in Roseau with housing at Bath Estate and River Estate, opened a deepwater harbour at Fond Cole and started the Dominica Social Security system.

Division grew after the murder of a number of tourists in the mid-1970s and the emergence of a black power movement. In 1974 his government passed the Prohibited and Undesirable Societies Act, known as the Dread Act, which made it legal to arrest any Dread without a warrant and to deny bail to anyone wearing dreadlocks. On 3 November 1978 John became the first Prime Minister of independent Dominica; he favoured a mixed economy and ties with the West, and established diplomatic relations with South Korea.

On 29 May 1979 a clash outside parliament left two people dead, among them a young man named Phillip Timothy. Public servants went on strike, the Committee for National Salvation under Charles Savarin called a general strike, and Labour ministers resigned one by one, beginning with Oliver Seraphin. President Frederick Degazon fled to Britain on 11 June, and the House of Assembly voted John out of office on 20 June 1979.

John lost his seat in the 1980 election. In 1981 he was arrested over Operation Red Dog, a plot to restore him to power with Canadian and American citizens largely affiliated with white supremacist and Ku Klux Klan groups. On 23 October 1985 he was found guilty of conspiring to overthrow the government and sentenced to 12 years. Pardoned by Mary Eugenia Charles, he was released on 29 May 1990.

He then led the Dominica Football Association, which became a FIFA affiliate in 1994, and in 2011 FIFA banned him from the sport for two years over an alleged bribery scheme. He died in Roseau on 6 July 2021, at the age of 83.
patrick-pearse: Pearse was born on 10 November 1879 at 27 Great Brunswick Street, Dublin, where his father, James Pearse, a mason and monumental sculptor, ran a stonemasonry business that gave the family a comfortable middle-class life. His mother, Margaret Brady, was from Dublin, and her father's family were native Irish speakers from County Meath. His maternal grandfather had supported the Young Ireland movement and later joined the Irish Republican Brotherhood. The influence of his grand-aunt Margaret, together with his schooling at the CBS Westland Row, gave him an early love of the Irish language and culture.
In 1896 he joined the Gaelic League, and in 1903 he became editor of its newspaper An Claidheamh Soluis. He took a degree in modern languages and was called to the bar in 1901.

Believing that the Irish school system raised young people to be good Englishmen or obedient Irishmen, Pearse founded a bilingual school for boys, St Enda's School, in 1908 and later moved it to The Hermitage in Rathfarnham. In November 1913 he was invited to the inaugural meeting of the Irish Volunteers. In December 1913 he was sworn into the Irish Republican Brotherhood, and in 1914 he became the Volunteers' Director of Military Organisation. By 1915 he sat on the IRB's Supreme Council and its secret Military Council, which planned a rising during the war. On 1 August 1915 he gave the graveside oration for the Fenian Jeremiah O'Donovan Rossa.

He also wrote stories and poems in Irish and English, plays in Irish, and essays on politics, language and education, among them The Murder Machine. He composed republican lyrics for the song Oró Sé do Bheatha 'Bhaile. The critic Louis de Paor considers him the most accomplished poet of the early Gaelic revival.

When the Easter Rising began on Easter Monday, 24 April 1916, Pearse read the Proclamation of the Irish Republic outside the General Post Office. He was chosen as President of the Republic and was the person most responsible for drafting the Proclamation. After six days of fighting he ordered the surrender. He was court-martialled and shot by firing squad, with Thomas Clarke and Thomas MacDonagh the first to be executed, on the morning of 3 May 1916, at the age of 36. His brother Willie was also executed. The British commander in Ireland, Sir John Maxwell, advised against returning the bodies to the families, fearing that the graves would become martyrs' shrines. Pearse came to be seen by many as the embodiment of the rebellion.
patrick-white: Patrick Victor Martindale White was born in Knightsbridge, London, on 28 May 1912, to Australian parents who were on an extended honeymoon. The family returned to Sydney when he was six months old. White developed asthma at the age of four, a condition that had killed his maternal grandfather, and his health was fragile throughout childhood.

From 1932 he studied French and German literature at King's College, Cambridge. After graduating in 1935 he was determined to stay in England and become a writer, supported by an allowance of £400 a year from his father. In London he met the Australian painter Roy de Maistre, who encouraged him to break from naturalistic prose and write from the inside out.

White's first published novel, Happy Valley (1939), won the Gold Medal of the Australian Literature Society. In the Second World War he served as an intelligence officer in the Royal Air Force; in Alexandria in 1941 he met Manoly Lascaris, who became his life companion. They settled in February 1948 on a small farm at Castle Hill, then semi-rural, outside Sydney. Discouraged by the reception of The Aunt's Story, White had a religious experience in late 1951 that gave him a belief in God and the inspiration to resume work on The Tree of Man (1955), which he described as an attempt to suggest every possible aspect of life through the lives of an ordinary man and woman.

That novel and Voss (1957) established his reputation in Britain and the United States, though Australian critics were divided; the poet A. D. Hope called his prose pretentious verbal sludge. Voss won the first Miles Franklin Award, and Riders in the Chariot (1961) won it again. The Eye of the Storm was published in August 1973, and in October White received the Nobel Prize in Literature, cited for an epic and psychological narrative art which had introduced a new continent into literature.

White's fiction concerns individuals, often alienated from society, who try to grasp a higher reality: pioneer settlers, explorers, artists, the simple-minded. He portrayed Australian society as materialistic and conformist, and in 1958 satirised what he called the Great Australian Emptiness. His style drew on the modernism of Joyce, Lawrence and Woolf, shifting between past and present and between the viewpoints of different characters. From the late 1960s he opposed the Vietnam War and supported Aboriginal self-determination, nuclear disarmament and environmental causes. In 1975 he founded the Patrick White Award with the prize money from his Nobel Prize.
pattadakal: Pattadakal, also called Raktapura, stands on the west bank of the Malaprabha River in Bagalkot district, about 23 kilometres from Badami and about 9.7 kilometres from Aihole, both important centres of Chalukya monuments. The river turns northwards a kilometre before it reaches the site, and in Hindu tradition a north-flowing river is called Uttarvahini Ganga. The place was considered holy for this reason. Its name means stone of coronation, and Chalukya kings held coronation ceremonies there, among them Vinayaditya in the 7th century CE. It was also known as Kisuvolal, the valley of red soil, and Ptolemy refers to it as Petirgal.

The early Chalukya rulers of the 5th and 6th centuries were followers of Vishnu who later became followers of Shiva, so the temples are generally dedicated to Shiva. There are ten major temples, nine Hindu and one Jain, with many small shrines. They are built of local sandstone, and some sculpture is of polished black granite. Four temples are in the Chalukya Dravida style of the south, four in the Nagara style of the north, and the Papanatha temple fuses the two.

The oldest of the Hindu temples is the Sangameshwara, built under Vijayaditya Satyashraya and left unfinished at his death. The Virupaksha temple, the largest and most sophisticated, was sponsored by Queen Lokmahadevi after the campaigns of King Vikramaditya II against the Pallavas. Its inscription names the chief architect, Gunda Anivaritacharya, and artists' names are inscribed beneath the panels they worked on.

The nearby Trailokeshwara temple was sponsored by Queen Trailokyamahadevi. The last temple is the Jain Narayana temple, probably of the 9th century and possibly sponsored by the Rashtrakuta king Krishna II. Inscriptions in old Kannada record grants by kings and queens, and one 8th-century column carries both the Siddhamatrika and Kannada scripts.

The friezes show scenes from the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and the Bhagavata Purana. Art historian Cathleen Cummings reads the sculpture as an expression of Hindu kingship and of the tension between the householder's life and that of the renouncing monk.

Pattadakal is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, which UNESCO has described as a harmonious blend of architectural forms from northern and southern India. It is protected under Indian law and managed by the Archaeological Survey of India. The Virupaksha temple is still an active place of Hindu worship.
patzcuaro: Pátzcuaro is a city and municipality in the state of Michoacán, on the southern edge of Lake Pátzcuaro, which still has economic and cultural importance for the town. The lake holds several islands, the best known being Janitzio, topped by a forty-metre statue of José María Morelos y Pavón. Several possible meanings of the name are given, among them "place of foundations", "place of bullrushes" and "seat of temples". The municipality covers most of the Pátzcuaro basin, within the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt, and has a total population of 79,868, including 104 other named communities besides the town.

The earliest written account of the founding is the Relación de Michoacán, written in 1539 to 1541. It says two chiefs, Páracume and Vápeani, arrived with their Chichimeca people and began building temples by placing four large rocks together. No date is given, but as the chiefs died in 1360, the founding is widely supposed to be around 1324. Tariácuri, the first chief to take the title caltzontzin, or emperor, by conquering his neighbours, began the Purépecha Empire, which was divided into three principalities, Ihuatzio, Tzintzuntzan and Pátzcuaro. Power later shifted to Tzintzuntzan, leaving Pátzcuaro as a ceremonial centre and retreat for the nobility.

When the Spanish arrived, Cristóbal de Olid forced the emperor Tanganxoan II to kneel in front of a crowd, and a chapel later built there is called El Humilladero, the Place of Humiliation. In 1526 Nuño de Guzmán came to punish the Purépecha harshly, ending in the torture and death of Tanganxoan II, and most residents fled to the mountains. Vasco de Quiroga then expelled Guzmán.

In 1538 the Diocese of Michoacán was founded with Quiroga as first bishop, and Pátzcuaro became the capital of the new province. He persuaded many Indians to return and brought Spanish families, and is considered the founder of modern Pátzcuaro. Its coat of arms came from Charles V in 1553. The cathedral was built over a temple of the goddess Cueráppari. In 1575 the viceregal authorities moved the capital to Valladolid, today Morelia, and the diocese followed.

Pátzcuaro keeps its colonial and indigenous character, with adobe or wooden houses, tiled roofs and cobblestone streets, and has been named one of the 111 Pueblos Mágicos of Mexico. The Plaza Vasco de Quiroga is the centre, and the Basilica of Nuestra Señora de la Salud, designated a basilica in 1924, holds the remains of Quiroga. The Palace of Huitziméngari belonged to the son of the last Purépecha cazonci. The town is the market hub of the lake region, whose villages make copperware, black pottery, musical instruments and baskets. The surrounding lake region is well known for its Day of the Dead celebrations.
pau-claris: Pau Claris i Casademunt was born in Barcelona on 1 January 1586. His family, from Berga, belonged to the Barcelonan bourgeoisie, and both his grandfather Francesc and his father Joan were prominent jurists. He took a doctorate in civil and canon law at the University of Barcelona, studying between 1604 and 1612. In 1612 he was sent to work in La Seu d'Urgell, the seat of the Bishop of Urgell and Andorra, and was made a canon there.

In 1626 Claris was elected a representative of the church at the Corts Catalanes, which met after Philip IV refused to ratify the Catalan constitutions. He took part in the unrest at Vic in 1634 over the seizure of church property tied to a tenth of Church revenues granted to the king, and in 1636 he secured approval of a rule that all sermons in the Principality be given in Catalan. On 22 July 1638 he was elected ecclesiastical deputy of the Diputació del General and so presided over the Generalitat.

The Count-Duke of Olivares wanted Catalonia to share the cost of the Thirty Years' War and to open a front against France. After the French took the Fort de Salses in July 1639, Catalan troops helped retake it on 6 January 1640, at a heavy cost in lives and money. In September 1640 the Generalitat's representatives signed the first Pact of Céret with an envoy of Richelieu acting for Louis XIII, and French military aid was agreed in October.

A Spanish army under the Marquis of Los Vélez invaded Catalonia on 24 November 1640, and Claris declared war on Philip IV on 23 December. As the army approached Barcelona, the Junta and the Consell de Cent accepted on 16 and 17 January 1641 a republic under French protection. On 23 January Claris proclaimed Louis XIII Count of Barcelona. The French and Catalan forces defeated the Castilians at Montjuïc three days later.

Claris fell gravely ill on 20 February 1641 and died on the night of 27 February. A theory of poisoning circulated at once, and some modern studies support it. By the Treaty of the Pyrenees of 7 November 1659 France gained Roussillon and the northern half of Cerdanya. A statue by Rafael Atché i Ferré was dedicated in Barcelona in 1917, and the city's Carrer de Pau Claris bears his name.
paul-de-chomedey-de-maisonneuve: Maisonneuve was born on 13 February 1612 and baptised two days later at Neuville-sur-Vannes in Champagne, the son of Louis de Chomedey, seigneur of Chavane and Germenoy-en-Brie, and his second wife Marie de Thomelin. He grew up in the manor-house there, near the Maisonneuve seigneury his father acquired in 1614, and began his military career at 13 in Holland, where he also learned to play the lute. Shortly before he turned 30 he was recruited by Jérome le Royer de la Dauversiere, head of the Société Notre-Dame de Montréal, to lead its colonists and keep them safe.

Ville-Marie was built on the southern shore of the Island of Montreal with a chapel and a hospital under Jeanne Mance. When a flood threatened it in 1643, Maisonneuve prayed to the Virgin Mary and, once the water fell, set up a cross on Mount Royal; a cross has stood there ever since. The settlers kept peace with the Algonquin, but the Haudenosaunee, who learned of the settlement in 1643, attacked it from the woods. On 30 March 1644 a band of 30 settlers met 250 Haudenosaunee in ambush, and Maisonneuve covered the retreat, shooting a chief who set upon him.

In 1645 he went back to France on his father's death and turned down the governorship of New France. By 1652 attacks had so reduced the colony that he returned to France to raise 100 volunteers, who arrived in the autumn of 1653 to find barely 50 people. In 1663 the colony passed to the Sulpicians, and when the governor general Augustin de Saffray de Mésy appointed him governor that October, Maisonneuve objected that only the Sulpicians could do so.

After Alexandre de Prouville de Tracy sent him home on indefinite leave, he lived quietly in Paris, where he welcomed Marguerite Bourgeoys in 1671. He died there on 9 September 1676 and was buried near the abbey of Saint-Étienne-du-Mont. Rue Saint-Paul, De Maisonneuve Boulevard, Rue Chomedey, Maisonneuve Park and the Collège de Maisonneuve are named for him, and Louis-Philippe Hébert's Maisonneuve Monument of 1895 stands on Place d'Armes, modelled on no authentic portrait.
paul-doumer: Joseph Athanase Doumer, commonly known as Paul, was born on 22 March 1857 at Aurillac in the Cantal department into a family of modest means. A former student of the Conservatoire national des arts et métiers, he became a professor of mathematics at Mende in 1877 and taught at Remiremont from 1879 to 1883, leaving on health grounds to become chief editor of a regional newspaper, the Courrier de l'Aisne. In 1878 he married Blanche Richel. They had eight children, four of whom were killed in the First World War. He was initiated into Freemasonry in 1879 and became Grand Secretary of the Grand Orient de France in 1892.

Doumer entered politics in 1885 as chef de cabinet to Charles Floquet, president of the Chamber of Deputies, and was elected Radical deputy for the Aisne in 1888. Defeated in 1889, he was returned in 1890 by the arrondissement of Auxerre. As minister of finance in 1895–1896 he tried without success to introduce an income tax.

When he arrived in Indochina the colonies were losing millions of francs a year, and his taxes were meant to put them on a paying basis. Vietnamese, Cambodians and Laotians who could not or would not pay lost their houses and land and often became day labourers. He made Indochina a market for French products and a field for French investment. In 1898 he persuaded the French government to approve the railway to Yunnan, with a view to annexing the south of that province.

Back in France he was elected deputy for Laon, refused to support the ministry of Émile Combes and led a group of dissident Radicals that eventually helped bring it down. He was president of the Chamber from 1902 to 1905, minister of finance again in 1925 and president of the Senate from 1927. On 13 May 1931 he was elected president of the Republic, defeating the better-known Aristide Briand.

On 6 May 1932, at the opening of a book fair at the Hôtel Salomon de Rothschild in Paris, Doumer was shot by Paul Gorguloff, a Russian émigré, while talking to the author Claude Farrère. He died in hospital at 04:37 on 7 May, the second French president to be assassinated and the first to be shot. Gorguloff wrote that the act was a protest on behalf of exiled White Russians and against France's relations with the Soviet Union; he was guillotined four months later. Doumer wrote L'Indo-Chine française (1904) and Le Livre de mes fils (1906).
paul-fagius: Fagius was born at Rheinzabern in 1504, the son of a teacher and council clerk. He went to the University of Heidelberg in 1515 and in 1518 was present at the Heidelberg Disputation. In 1522 he moved to Strasbourg, where he learned Hebrew and met the reformers Matthäus Zell, Martin Bucer and Wolfgang Capito. From 1527 he was a schoolmaster in the free imperial city of Isny im Allgäu, and he took part in the Bern Colloquy, where he met Huldrych Zwingli.

After further theological study at Strasbourg from 1535, Fagius returned to Isny as a priest in 1537. There he learned Hebrew from the Jewish grammarian and publisher Elia Levita, and the two founded a printing office; among its few known works is Shemot Devarim, an Old Yiddish, Hebrew, Latin and German dictionary of 1542. In 1543 he organised the church in Konstanz, and in 1544 he became professor of Old Testament studies at Strasbourg.

In 1546 Elector Frederick II charged him with reforming the University of Heidelberg, but the opposition was so strong that the reform failed and he went back to Strasbourg. After the defeat of the Schmalkaldic League in 1547 he was dismissed along with Bucer. Both were taken in by Thomas Cranmer in England, and Fagius was appointed Hebrew lecturer at the University of Cambridge.

Fagius died of plague on 13 November 1549 and was buried in St Michael's Church, Cambridge. Under Queen Mary's Catholic restoration his remains, like Bucer's, were exhumed and burned; in 1560 a memorial to him was set up again. His work included Latin translations from Hebrew of the Pirḳe Abot, Levita's Tishbi, Tobit, the Alfabeta de Ben Sira and David Ḳimḥi's commentary on the first ten psalms, an edition of the Targum Onḳelos (1546), an exegesis of the first four chapters of Genesis and an elementary Hebrew grammar.
paul-gauguin: Gauguin was born in Paris on 7 June 1848, the son of Clovis Gauguin, a liberal journalist who had to flee France when his newspaper was suppressed, and Aline Chazal, daughter of the engraver André Chazal and of the author and early socialist activist Flora Tristan. In 1850 the family settled in Peru, where he had a privileged childhood until the age of six. After schooling in France he signed on as a pilot's assistant in the merchant marine and then served two years in the French navy. In 1873 he married the Dane Mette-Sophie Gad, and they had five children.

He worked as a stockbroker and began painting in his spare time, befriending Camille Pissarro, who introduced him to other Impressionist artists. The financial crisis of 1882 damaged his brokerage career and led him to paint full time. He showed 19 paintings and a wood relief at the eighth and last Impressionist exhibition in May 1886.

Under the influence of folk art and Japanese prints, his work moved towards Cloisonnism, with flat areas of colour and heavy black outlines, as in The Yellow Christ of 1889, and later towards Synthetism. In 1887 he travelled with the painter Charles Laval to Panama, where he worked as a labourer on the French canal, and then to Martinique. Vincent van Gogh and his brother Theo, a dealer with the firm Goupil & Cie, admired his Martinique paintings, and Theo bought three of them for 900 francs.

After a successful auction at the Hôtel Drouot in February 1891, Gauguin sailed for Tahiti on 1 April, stating his aim of escaping European civilization and everything artificial and conventional. He returned to France in August 1893 and left for Tahiti again on 28 June 1895.

In the Marquesas Islands he found a society that, as in Tahiti, had lost much of its cultural identity; the population had fallen from some 80,000 in the 18th century to 4,000, largely through Western diseases. In 1903 he campaigned against the island's gendarmes and on 27 March was fined 500 francs and sentenced to three months' imprisonment for libel. Weak, in great pain and using morphine, he died suddenly on 8 May 1903.

Retrospective exhibitions at the Salon d'Automne in Paris in 1903 and 1906 strongly influenced the French avant-garde, above all Pablo Picasso, whose work of 1906 led to Les Demoiselles d'Avignon in 1907. In the 21st century critics have described his Primitivist depictions of Tahiti as colonialist and have pointed to his sexual exploitation of Tahitian girls.
paul-hasluck: Hasluck was born on 1 April 1905 in Fremantle, Western Australia, one of five children of parents who worked full-time for the Salvation Army, and he grew up in relative poverty. After Perth Modern School he joined The West Australian in 1922 as a cadet and rose to lead its press gallery staff at Parliament House. Studying part-time at the University of Western Australia, he graduated Bachelor of Arts in 1937 and became a lecturer in history there in 1939, the year he founded Freshwater Bay Press and published his first book, Into the Desert.

In 1941 Hasluck joined the Department of External Affairs and served on delegations to international conferences, among them the San Francisco Conference that founded the United Nations, where he and the minister, H. V. Evatt, conceived a lasting aversion to each other. He was Australia's first Permanent Representative to the United Nations from 1946 to 1947, wrote two volumes of the official history Australia in the War of 1939–1945, and in 1949 won the new Perth seat of Curtin for the Liberal Party.

As Minister for Territories he was also responsible for the Northern Territory, where he drafted the Welfare Ordinance 1953, which made Aboriginal people wards of the state under a policy of cultural assimilation. He allowed bauxite mining on the Gove Peninsula, and when the Yolngu of Yirrkala, who had not been consulted, sent the Yirrkala bark petitions to Parliament in August 1963, he moved for rejection of the first. As Minister for External Affairs from 24 April 1964 to 11 February 1969 he was a passionate supporter of the Vietnam War.

After Harold Holt disappeared in December 1967, Hasluck stood for the Liberal leadership mainly to offer an alternative to William McMahon, but the party chose John Gorton. As Governor-General he treated Gough Whitlam, once a bitter adversary, with complete civility, swore in Whitlam and Lance Barnard as an interim two-man government after the 1972 election, and granted a double dissolution in April 1974.

Hasluck retired to Perth, where he remained active in cultural and political affairs until his death on 9 January 1993; he was buried at Karrakatta Cemetery. Historians of the period hold that the constitutional crisis of 1975 would have ended differently had he still been Governor-General, and in a 1985 interview he argued that John Kerr had erred in taking advice from Malcolm Fraser. He was made a Knight Companion of the Garter in 1979, and the Federal Division of Hasluck is named after him and his wife, Dame Alexandra Hasluck.
paul-henri-spaak: Paul-Henri Spaak was born on 25 January 1899 in Schaerbeek into a prominent family. His mother, Marie Janson, was a socialist and the first woman to enter the Belgian Senate, and his father, Paul Spaak, was a poet and playwright. In 1914 he tried to join the Belgian army during the German invasion, was captured and spent two years as a prisoner of war in Germany. He then studied law in Brussels and played tennis for Belgium in the 1922 Davis Cup. As a lawyer he defended Communists accused of conspiracy and the Italian anarchist student Fernando de Rosa, who had tried to kill Crown Prince Umberto of Italy.

He joined the Belgian Labour Party in 1920, was elected deputy in 1932 and became Minister of Transport in 1935. From February 1936 he was Foreign Minister, keeping to Belgium's neutrality, and from May 1938 to February 1939 he was prime minister for the first time. After the German invasion of May 1940 he and Hubert Pierlot, with part of the government, reached London in October 1940. In exile he promoted a customs union with the Netherlands and Luxembourg, which became Benelux. After the war he was prime minister from 13 to 31 March 1946, the shortest government in Belgian history, and again from March 1947 to August 1949, when women received the vote.

He chaired the first session of the United Nations General Assembly and was the first President of the Council of Europe's Consultative Assembly, resigning in December 1951 after it rejected a proposal for a European political authority. In 1955 the Messina Conference made him chairman of the committee whose Spaak Report led to the Treaties of Rome, signed on 25 March 1957.

From 1957 to 1961 Spaak was Secretary General of NATO, succeeding Lord Ismay, and clashed repeatedly with Charles de Gaulle. He was Belgium's foreign minister for eighteen years between 1939 and 1966. He retired from politics in 1966, published his memoirs, Combats inachevés, in 1969 and died at Braine-l'Alleud on 31 July 1972. Nicknamed Mr. Europe, he is counted among the founding fathers of the European Union, and a building of the European Parliament in Brussels bears his name.
paul-i-of-russia: Paul was the son of Peter III and Catherine II, who was born Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst. Catherine hinted in one edition of her memoirs that her lover Sergei Saltykov was Paul's father, but later recanted and named Peter III. Empress Elizabeth took the infant almost at once, and he had limited contact with his mother. He was put in the charge of the governor Nikita Ivanovich Panin. He became crown prince in 1762, when his father took the throne, but within months Catherine deposed Peter III and Paul remained heir apparent. Mother and son kept a distant relationship. Paul criticised her expansionist wars in a dissertation on military reform, Reflections, which added to her suspicion of a conspiracy around him.

Catherine suffered a stroke on 17 November 1796 and died without regaining consciousness. Paul's first act as emperor was to look for her testament and, if possible, destroy it, since he feared it would exclude him in favour of his son Alexander. He then promulgated the Pauline Laws, establishing strict male primogeniture in the House of Romanov, rules that lasted to the end of the dynasty. He also imposed the first limits on serfdom with the Manifesto of three-day corvée. He reversed many of his mother's policies, freed Alexander Radishchev, Nikolay Novikov and Tadeusz Kościuszko, and sought to curtail the privileges of the nobility.

His army reforms, including Prussian uniforms impractical for active duty, were deeply unpopular. In foreign policy he recalled the troops Catherine had sent towards Persia. In 1799 he joined the Second Coalition against Revolutionary France with Britain and Austria, but withdrew after setbacks, and later led the Second League of Armed Neutrality against Britain. After the death of King Erekle of Kartli-Kakheti, civil war broke out over the succession, and one claimant appealed to Russia; Paul signed a decree incorporating the kingdom into the Russian Empire. He was also Grand Master of the Russian Knights Hospitaller from 1799 to 1801.

Paul's attempts to impose a code of chivalry on the nobility alienated many advisers. A conspiracy organised by Peter Ludwig von der Pahlen, Nikita Petrovich Panin and José de Ribas was delayed by de Ribas's death in December 1800. On the night of 23 March 1801 (11 March in the old style) dismissed officers entered his bedroom in the newly completed Saint Michael's Castle, tried to force him to sign an abdication, and strangled and trampled him to death after Nikolay Zubov struck him with a sword. His son Alexander I succeeded him. There is some evidence that Paul was venerated as a saint by Russian Orthodox people, though no Orthodox Church canonised him.
paul-i-subic-of-bribir: Paul was the eldest son of Stephen II of the Šubić family, the most influential noble house of the Kingdom of Croatia and Dalmatia. His father had helped King Béla IV in the war with the Mongol Empire in 1242 and received the County of Bribir as a hereditary grant in 1251, and his mother was probably related to the Árpád dynasty. Paul inherited the title of count of Bribir and first appears in 1272 as Podestà of Trogir. In 1273 he became ban of the maritime regions, was removed in 1274 over his part in the quarrels between Trogir and Split, and returned in 1275.

With his brothers Mladen I and George I, Paul brought almost all the coastal cities south of the Velebit Mountain under Šubić rule by 1278, from seats at Bribir, Skradin, Klis and Ostrovica. His campaign against the pirate Kačić family of Omiš drew him into war with the Republic of Venice, ended by treaties in 1290 and 1294, and into friendship with the House of Anjou of Naples. In the succession crisis after 1290 he was the main ally of the Angevins; in 1300 he met Charles Robert at Split and took him to Zagreb, where loyal nobles recognised him as king.

Paul took the title of lord of Bosnia in 1299, captured the region of Hum from the Serbian king Stefan Milutin in 1301, and after Mladen I was killed in 1304 led an army into Bosnia, restoring his rule by February 1305. Styling himself ban of the Croats, he ruled as a de facto independent prince, kept chancelleries at Skradin and Bribir, and issued coins of Bosnian silver modelled on the Venetian grosso.

In March 1311 an uprising in Zadar against Venice was aided by an army under his son Mladen II, who was proclaimed Count of Zadar and Prince of Dalmatia. Peace talks with Venice began in April 1312, and Paul died on 1 May while they continued. He was buried in the Franciscan church of St. Mary in Bribir, the family's funerary church, and was succeeded by Mladen II. Under his rule new dioceses were founded at Šibenik, Duvno and Omiš, and the Šubićs invoked the memory of King Demetrius Zvonimir to present their rule as continuing that of the old Croatian kings.
paul-johann-anselm-von-feuerbach: Paul Johann Anselm Ritter von Feuerbach was born on 14 November 1775 in Hainichen, near Jena, and was educated in Frankfurt am Main, where his family moved soon after his birth. At sixteen he ran away from home and went to Jena, where relations helped him to study at the university. He took a doctorate in philosophy in 1795 and married in the same year. The need to earn money turned him from philosophy and history to law, which he disliked but which offered faster advancement.

At 23 he became prominent through a vigorous criticism of Thomas Hobbes's theory of civil power. In lectures on criminal law he argued that judges should be strictly limited by the penal code, a doctrine that gave rise to a party called the Rigorists. He is the originator of the maxim nullum crimen, nulla poena sine praevia lege poenali: there is no crime, and so no punishment, if no penal law existed at the time. In 1805 King Maximilian Joseph commanded him to draft a penal code for Bavaria, and he moved to Munich with a high post in the Ministry of Justice, where he was ennobled in 1808.

Reform of Bavarian penal law began under his influence in 1806 with the abolition of torture. The code he framed was promulgated in 1813 and became the basis for new codes in Württemberg and Saxe-Weimar, was adopted in its entirety in the Grand Duchy of Oldenburg, was translated into Swedish by order of the king, and guided the reform of several Swiss cantons' codes.

His Merkwürdige Criminalfälle (1808 to 1811) and the enlarged Aktenmäßige Darstellung merkwürdiger Verbrechen (1828/29) drew on his cases in the Ministry of Justice, intended to establish a modern criminal psychology. Gerold Schmidt found that they record true events and real people, making them a source for Bavarian local and social history. In 1811 Feuerbach declared against trial by jury, though his view was later somewhat modified.

After a visit to France, Belgium and the Rhine provinces in 1821 he pleaded for publicity in all legal proceedings. In 1832 he published the first critical summary of the facts about the foundling Kaspar Hauser. He died on 29 May 1833 in Frankfurt; he and his family believed he had been poisoned because of his work on Hauser, but the cause of death remains unclear.
paul-julius-reuter: Paul Julius Reuter was born Israel Beer Josaphat on 21 July 1816 in Kassel, in the Electorate of Hesse, into a Jewish family. His father, Samuel Levi Josaphat, was a rabbi, and his mother was Betty Sanders. In Göttingen he met Carl Friedrich Gauss, who was experimenting with the transmission of electrical signals by wire. On 16 November 1845 he converted to Christianity in a ceremony at St. George's German Lutheran Chapel in London and changed his name to Paul Julius Reuter. One week later, in the same chapel, he married Ida Maria Elizabeth Clementine Magnus of Berlin, the daughter of a German banker.

After some work as a bank clerk, Reuter founded the Berlin book-publishing firm Reuter and Stargardt in 1847 with Joseph Abraham Stargardt. The firm's distribution of radical pamphlets at the beginning of the 1848 Revolution may have drawn official scrutiny to him. Later that year he left for Paris and worked in Charles-Louis Havas's news agency, Agence Havas. As electrical telegraphy developed he founded his own news agency in Aachen. Until the whole distance was connected by telegraph, messages between Brussels and Aachen were carried by homing pigeons, which gave him faster access to financial news from the Paris stock exchange than the post train.

When a telegraph line was being laid between Britain and continental Europe, Reuter moved to London and rented an office near the Stock Exchange. In 1863 he privately erected a telegraph link to Crookhaven, the farthest south-western point of Ireland, where news canisters thrown into the sea by ships from the U.S. were retrieved and telegraphed to London long before the ships reached Cork. He was naturalised as a British subject on 17 March 1857 and was granted the title of Freiherr by the Duke of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha on 7 September 1871.

On 25 July 1872 Nasir al-Din Shah of Iran signed a concession with Reuter. George Curzon described it as the most complete surrender of the industrial resources of a kingdom into foreign hands. It gave Reuter a monopoly of railways and tramways for seventy years, the working of most mines, the government forests, canals and irrigation works, the first refusal of a national bank and a farm of the customs. Businessmen, clergy and nationalists of Persia denounced it at once, and it was quickly forced into cancellation.

Reuter died in 1899 in Nice. He had three sons, and his title passed down the male line, to a fourth baron. His business became the Reuters news agency, which became part of the Thomson Reuters conglomerate in 2008. Edward G. Robinson played him in the film A Dispatch from Reuters (1941).
paul-kruger: Stephanus Johannes Paulus Kruger was born on 10 October 1825 at Bulhoek, a farm in the Steynsburg area of the Cape Colony, the third child of the farmer Casper Jan Hendrik Kruger. As a child he took part in the Great Trek. He had almost no education apart from the Bible, which he took literally and knew in large part by heart. He became a burgher at sixteen, settled near Rustenburg and married Maria du Plessis in 1842. As field cornet he took part in the Battle of Dimawe against the Tswana chief Sechele I in 1852, when the Boer commando wrecked David Livingstone's mission at Kolobeng.

A protégé of the Voortrekker leader Andries Pretorius, Kruger witnessed the signing of the Sand River Convention in 1852. In 1863 he was elected Commandant-General, a post he held for a decade. He became vice president in March 1877, shortly before Britain annexed the republic as the Transvaal, and led two deputations to London against the annexation. He was the leading figure in the movement to restore independence, which ended in the Boers' victory in the First Boer War of 1880 to 1881, and he served in an executive triumvirate until he was elected president in 1883.

In 1884 Kruger led a third deputation to London, which secured the London Convention, under which Britain recognised the South African Republic as fully independent. After gold was found on the Witwatersrand in 1886, the uitlanders, mostly British, provided almost all tax revenue but had no vote. This question dominated his presidency, which was renewed in 1888, 1893 and 1898, and led to the Jameson Raid of 1895 to 1896 and the Second Boer War.

He took no part in the fighting, directing the war from Pretoria by telegram. He left South Africa on 11 September 1900, was carried from Mozambique to Marseille on the Dutch warship Gelderland and refused to return after the British victory. He died in Switzerland in 1904, and his body was returned for a state funeral in Pretoria. Admirers see him as a tragic folk hero; critics call him a stubborn defender of an unjust cause and an oppressor of black Africans.
paul-robeson: Robeson was born in Princeton, New Jersey, in 1898, to Reverend William Drew Robeson and Maria Louisa Bustill. His mother belonged to the Bustills, a prominent Quaker family of mixed ancestry. His father was of Igbo origin and had been born into slavery; he escaped from a plantation in his teens and in 1881 became minister of Princeton's Witherspoon Street Presbyterian Church.

In late 1915 Robeson became the third African-American student ever enrolled at Rutgers, and the only one at the time. When he tried out for the football team, teammates played so roughly that his nose was broken and his shoulder dislocated, until the coach, Foster Sanford, announced that he had made the team. He was elected class valedictorian. He studied at New York University School of Law, moved to Columbia Law School in February 1920 and married Eslanda Goode in August 1921. He soon gave up law because of racism.

In December 1924 Robeson won the lead role in Eugene O'Neill's All God's Chillun Got Wings. In 1928 he played Joe in the London production of Show Boat, and the composer Jerome Kern said he had formed the melody of "Ol' Man River" after hearing the organ-like tones of Robeson's speaking voice. In 1933 he starred as Brutus in the film The Emperor Jones, the first film to feature an African American in a starring role.

Robeson saw the struggle against fascism in the Spanish Civil War as a turning point that made him a political activist. He changed the last verse of "Ol' Man River", replacing a fatalistic verse with one of defiance, and in Wales recorded a message that became his epitaph: "The artist must take sides." On 12 June 1956 he appeared before the House Un-American Activities Committee, where he invoked the Fifth Amendment. After his passport was returned in June 1958, he toured Europe, appeared in Othello at Stratford-upon-Avon in April 1959, and in October 1958 became the first black performer to sing at St Paul's Cathedral in London.

Robeson returned to the United States in December 1963 and lived mainly in seclusion. In 1965 he was hospitalised with double pneumonia and a kidney blockage. He died in Philadelphia on 23 January 1976, aged 77, after complications of a stroke, and was buried in Ferncliff Cemetery in Hartsdale, New York.

He was one of the most influential participants in the Harlem Renaissance and brought Negro spirituals into the American mainstream. He was among the first artists to refuse to perform to segregated audiences. The NAACP awarded him its Spingarn Medal in 1945.
paul-the-deacon: Paul was born Winfrid, son of Warnefrid, about 720 in the Duchy of Friuli; Paulus was his monastic name. An ancestor named Leupichis had come to Italy in 568 in the train of Alboin, King of the Lombards, and received lands at or near Cividale del Friuli. During an invasion by the Avars his five sons were carried off to Pannonia, but one of them returned and restored the family's fortunes. Paul's father Warnefrid was his grandson.

Because his family was possibly noble, Paul received an exceptionally good education, probably at the court of the Lombard king Ratchis in Pavia, where a teacher named Flavian taught him the rudiments of Greek. He was probably secretary to Ratchis's successor, Desiderius.

After Desiderius's daughter Adelperga married Arichis II, duke of Benevento, Paul wrote at her request a continuation of Eutropius's Summary of Roman History. He lived at the court of Benevento for at least several years before 774, when Charlemagne captured Pavia. He eventually entered a monastery on Lake Como, and before 782 the great Benedictine house of Monte Cassino, where he made the acquaintance of Charlemagne.

Around 776 his brother Arichis was carried off to Francia as a prisoner after a revolt in Friuli, and Paul wrote to Charlemagne on his behalf, after which Arichis was freed. Paul became an important contributor to the Carolingian Renaissance. In 787 he returned to Monte Cassino, where he died on 13 April, probably in 799.

His chief work is the Historia Langobardorum, an incomplete history in six books written after 787 and no later than 795 or 796. It covers the Lombards from their origins in the north and their migration to Italy in 568 to the death of King Liutprand in 744, and is written from a Lombard point of view. It is especially valuable for the relations between the Franks and the Lombards. Among his sources were the Origo gentis Langobardorum and the Liber pontificalis, and he drew heavily on Bede, Gregory of Tours and Isidore of Seville.

His Historia Romana continues Eutropius down to 553, with extracts from the Scriptures and ecclesiastical historians added because Adelperga complained that Eutropius said nothing of church affairs. At the request of Angilram, Bishop of Metz, he wrote a history of the bishops of Metz to 766, the first work of its kind north of the Alps. He also compiled a collection of homilies for Charlemagne, much used in the Frankish churches.
paul-von-hindenburg: Hindenburg was born on 2 October 1847 in Posen, then in the Kingdom of Prussia, into a family of minor Prussian nobility. He enlisted in the Third Regiment of Foot Guards after his cadet education. In the Austro-Prussian War of 1866 he was knocked unconscious at Königgrätz when a bullet pierced his helmet, but wrapped his head in a towel and resumed command of his detachment.

He served in the Franco-Prussian War as a battalion adjutant and attended the proclamation of the German Empire at Versailles on 18 January 1871. He entered the Kriegsakademie in Berlin in 1873, joined the General Staff, rose to lieutenant general in 1900 and retired in 1911.

Living in retirement in Hannover when the First World War began, he was selected on 22 August 1914 to command the German Eighth Army in East Prussia, with Erich Ludendorff as his chief of staff, after the previous commander Maximilian von Prittwitz had panicked. He became a field marshal on 1 November 1914. In February 1915 an attack encircled an entire Russian corps and captured more than 100,000 men in the Second Battle of the Masurian Lakes.

In 1916 he replaced Erich von Falkenhayn as Chief of the Great General Staff. He and Ludendorff used the Kaiser's extensive delegation of authority to the Supreme Army Command to establish a de facto military dictatorship. In 1917 they pressed Chancellor Bethmann Hollweg to accept unrestricted submarine warfare. After the armistice Hindenburg stepped down and retired again in 1919.

After Friedrich Ebert's death on 28 February 1925, the parties of the right chose Hindenburg as their candidate, and he won the second round with the support of the Bavarian People's Party and because the Communists refused to withdraw their candidate. He took office on 12 May 1925.

In March 1930, on the advice of Kurt von Schleicher, he appointed Heinrich Brüning chancellor of a presidential government, which the historian Eberhard Jäckel judged within the letter of the constitution but against its spirit. At 84 he was persuaded to run again in 1932, supported by parties that saw him as the only hope of defeating Hitler.

Opposed to Hitler, he nevertheless reluctantly agreed in January 1933 to appoint him chancellor in a coalition cabinet. After the Reichstag fire of February 1933 he approved the Reichstag Fire Decree, which suspended civil liberties, and he signed the Enabling Act of 1933. He died on 2 August 1934, after which Hitler combined the presidency with the chancellery.
paul-von-lettow-vorbeck: Paul Emil von Lettow-Vorbeck was born on 20 March 1870 into the Pomeranian minor nobility, the son of an army officer stationed at Saarlouis in the Prussian Rhine Province. He was educated in boarding schools in Berlin and joined the cadet corps at Potsdam and Berlin-Lichterfelde. In 1890 he was commissioned a Leutnant in the Imperial German Army and was later assigned to the Great German General Staff.

In 1900 he was posted to China with the international force against the Boxer Rebellion. From 1904, as a captain, he served in German Southwest Africa during the Herero insurrection and the subsequent genocide, fighting at the Battle of Waterberg. He also took part in the pursuit of the Nama leader Jacob Morenga, and was wounded in 1906, losing the sight of his left eye.

In August 1914 Lettow-Vorbeck commanded a garrison of 2,600 Germans and 2,472 African soldiers in fourteen askari field companies. He knew that East Africa would be a sideshow and meant to tie down as many British troops as possible, keeping them from the Western Front. Disregarding the colony's governor, Heinrich Schnee, who sought neutrality, he repelled a British amphibious assault on Tanga in the battle fought from 2 November 1914, and won a second victory at Jassin on 19 January 1915.

He then raided British East Africa, targeting forts, railways and communications, and expanded the Schutztruppe to some 14,000 soldiers, most of them askaris. For four years this force held in check a much larger one of British, Indian, Belgian and Portuguese troops. Lettow-Vorbeck returned to Germany in March 1919 to a hero's welcome. He left the Reichswehr in 1920 after the Kapp Putsch, and sat in the Reichstag for the German National People's Party from 1928 to 1930.

Under the Nazi regime Lettow-Vorbeck declined the post of head of the Reich Colonial Ministry and, in 1935, an ambassadorship in London, though in 1939 Hitler gave him the honorary rank of General of the Infantry. His two sons were killed serving in the Wehrmacht. He died in Hamburg in 1964, and two former askaris were flown in as guests to his funeral.

In the same year the West German Bundestag voted back pay for surviving askaris. Barracks of the Bundeswehr were named after him, and one, in Leer, remains. His memory is contested: in 2010 the council of Saarlouis renamed a street named for him, chiefly because of his part in the Kapp Putsch. His book Africa, as I Saw It Again defends colonial rule.
paulette-nardal: Paulette Nardal was born on 12 October 1896 in Le François, Martinique, the eldest of seven sisters. Her father, Paul Nardal, was a construction engineer trained in France, and her mother, Louise, a piano teacher; the family belonged to the island's small upper-middle-class black community. She attended the Colonial College for Girls, studied English and became a teacher before going to Paris to continue her education, enrolling at the Sorbonne to study English at the age of 24.

The salon she held with her sisters Jane and Andrée at Clamart received figures of the Harlem Renaissance and the three men later known as the founders of Négritude, Aimé Césaire, Léon Gontran Damas and Léopold Sédar Senghor. As a journalist she wrote for La Dépêche africaine, Le Cri des Nègres and other papers, publishing the short story En Exile in 1929 and a piece on the American sculptor Augusta Savage in 1930. La Revue du Monde Noir, partly funded by the Ministry of Colonies, ran to six issues before it closed in April 1932.

She then worked as secretary to Galandou Diouf, the Senegalese deputy in the French National Assembly, and in 1937 went to Senegal to rally opposition to the Italian invasion of Ethiopia. Fleeing France in 1939, she broke both knees jumping into a lifeboat when her ship was torpedoed off the English coast, and never fully recovered. In Fort-de-France she taught English to dissidents who wished to join General de Gaulle, and in 1945 founded the journal La Femme dans la Cité, which she published until 1951.

Her essay The Awakening of Race Consciousness, in the last issue of La Revue du Monde Noir, influenced both the later leaders of Négritude and the radical group Légitime Défense. It argued for African pride and a shared memory of slavery without giving up French identity. The scholars Mamadou Badiane and Shireen K. Lewis argue that her thinking on race preceded that of Césaire and Senghor by nearly a decade. A Catholic of the centre right, she favoured women's political action within existing institutions. After 18 months at the United Nations she returned to Martinique in 1948, wrote a history of its music for the centenary of abolition, and founded a choir for its African-rooted songs. She died on 16 February 1985.
paulinus-of-york: Paulinus was a monk from Rome, probably Italian by birth, sent by Pope Gregory I with Mellitus and others in the second group of the Gregorian mission, which reached Kent by 604. Little is known of his work there until he was consecrated bishop by Justus, archbishop of Canterbury, and went north with Æthelburh, sister of King Eadbald of Kent. Edwin had promised that she could remain a Christian and worship as she chose. Bede describes Paulinus as tall and slightly stooping, with black hair, a thin face and a hooked, thin nose.

According to Bede, Paulinus told Edwin that the birth of his daughter Eanflæd at Easter 626 was owed to his prayers, and the king promised to convert if he defeated the West Saxons, who had tried to assassinate him. He delayed until Paulinus revealed the details of a dream Edwin had had in exile at the court of King Rædwald of East Anglia. Historians think the willingness of the Northumbrian nobles and letters from Pope Boniface V also played a part. One story says Paulinus spent 36 days baptising converts at the royal palace of Yeavering. Among those he baptised was Hilda, later founding abbess of Whitby Abbey.

York was meant to be England's second metropolitan see, and Paulinus built a stone church there, of which no trace has been found; his church at Lincoln has been identified with the earliest phase of St Paul in the Bail. As the only Roman bishop in England, he consecrated Honorius archbishop of Canterbury after Justus died.

Edwin's death at the Battle of Hatfield Chase was followed by a sharp decline of Christianity in Northumbria, and Paulinus went south with the widowed queen, leaving James the Deacon in the north. The pallium Pope Honorius I sent him arrived too late to be of use. He died at Rochester on 10 October 644 and was buried there; Ithamar, the first Englishman consecrated to a Gregorian see, succeeded him. Revered as a saint, he is venerated by the Catholic, Anglican and Eastern Orthodox churches. Historians judge his Northumbrian mission to have been largely ineffectual: the kingdom's conversion was mainly the work of Irish missionaries brought in by Oswald.
paulo-dias-de-novais: Paulo Dias de Novais was a fidalgo of the Royal Household. In the 1550s the ruling ngola, or king, of Ndongo broke his allegiance to the Kingdom of Kongo and sought recognition from Portugal instead. Hoping for silver, slaves, converts and a colony, Lisbon sent an expedition in 1560 under Dias de Novais and the Jesuit missionary Father Gouveia. Both were captured and held in Ndongo for several years, until the ngola who had received them died and his successor proved unfriendly.

Letters sent from Ndongo by the captives drew royal attention to the country by stressing the supposed mineral wealth of the interior and the advantages of an overland route to Mozambique past the gold mines of central Africa. The young King Sebastian, eager to promote expansion overseas, granted Dias de Novais a royal charter in 1575 that made him donatário, or donee, of the territory. He landed on 11 February 1575 and, drawn by the prospect of the silver mines of Cambambe, founded the settlement of São Paulo de Luanda near the island of Luanda.

As the first Captain-Governor of Portuguese Angola he sought to take copper, ivory, cattle hides, salt, sugar and above all slaves from the land. Under orders from King Sebastian to keep peaceful relations, he made an alliance with the ngola of Ndongo, Nzinga Ngola Kilombo Kia Kasenda, who in return for military aid sold rebels, prisoners of war and subjects condemned for theft or adultery to the Portuguese as slaves, to his own great profit. Dias de Novais had paid for the Angola venture from his own purse and died bankrupt on 9 May 1589; he was buried in a simple tomb in front of the church of Massangano.
pausanias-general: Pausanias belonged to the Agiad royal house of Sparta. He was a son of the regent Cleombrotus and a nephew of the recently dead king Leonidas I, but not in the direct line of succession. After Leonidas's death, while the king's son Pleistarchus was still a minor, Pausanias served as regent. He was the father of Pleistoanax, who later became king. What is known of his life comes largely from Thucydides, Diodorus and a few other classical sources.

In 479 BCE Pausanias led the Spartan army alongside Euryanax, since Pleistarchus was too young to command, and headed the combined land forces of the Hellenic League. At Plataea the Greeks faced the Persian commander Mardonius along the Asopos River. After eleven days of stalemate the Persian cavalry fouled the river from which the Greeks drew water, and the Athenians moved in the night. Mardonius took the move for flight and sent his Persians against Pausanias, who led the Greeks to a major victory. Herodotus judged it the most glorious victory known to him.

In 478 BCE, after the capture of Cyprus and Byzantium, he was accused of releasing prisoners who were relatives of the Persian king, and of writing to Xerxes I offering to bring Sparta and Greece under Persian control in return for marriage to the king's daughter. He was said to have adopted Persian dress and customs. For want of evidence he was acquitted. According to Thucydides and Plutarch the Athenians and many allies resented his arrogance.

The Spartans recalled him again in 477 BCE, and the ephors imprisoned him but released him for lack of evidence, although some helots reported that he had offered them freedom if they joined a revolt. Later one of his messengers produced a written letter. Pursued by the ephors, Pausanias took refuge in the temple of Athena of the Brazen House. His mother Theano is said to have laid a brick at the door, and the Spartans blocked the doorway and he starved to death. The Oracle of Delphi showed displeasure at the violation of a suppliant's sanctity, and the Spartans set up two bronze statues of him at the temple.
pausanias-geographer: Nothing is known of Pausanias apart from what historians can piece together from his own writing. He was probably born about 110 into a Greek family and was probably a native of Lydia in Asia Minor. From about 150 until his death around 180 he travelled throughout the mainland of Greece, writing about monuments, sacred spaces and significant geographical sites along the way.

He grew up and lived under the rule of the Roman Empire but valued his Greek identity, history and culture. He wished to describe the glories of a Greek past that was still relevant in his lifetime, even though the country was beholden to Rome. His journey through the land of his ancestors was an attempt to establish a place in the world for this new Roman Greece, connecting the myths and stories of ancient culture to those of his own time.

In writing the Description of Greece, called Helládos Periḗgēsis in Greek, Pausanias sought to put together a lasting written account of all things Greek, panta ta hellenika. He wrote from his own observation. Unlike a modern travel guide, he tends to elaborate on a site with a discussion of an ancient ritual or a myth connected with it. He also makes natural history digressions, on the signs that herald an earthquake, the phenomena of the tides, the ice-bound seas of the north, and the fact that at the summer solstice the noonday sun casts no shadow at Syene (Aswan).

His style is straightforward and direct, and his descriptions of works of art are plain and unadorned. Some translators note that his use of prepositions and tenses can be hard to render in English; he sometimes uses a past tense where the present might be expected, which they interpret as an effort to place himself in the same time as his audience. He never doubts the existence of the gods and heroes, but he criticises some myths and legends as differing from earlier traditions that he relates. He is frank about his limits, and where he quotes second-hand information he says so.

Until twentieth-century archaeologists concluded that he was a reliable guide to the sites being excavated, classicists largely dismissed his writings as purely literary. Following Ulrich von Wilamowitz-Moellendorff, they tended to regard him as a purveyor of second-hand accounts who had not visited most of the places he described. Modern archaeological research has revealed the accuracy of much of his information, and his writing about Tartessos is aiding present research into its existence, location and culture.
pavel-bermondt-avalov: Pavel Bermondt-Avalov was born in Tbilisi, by most accounts, though both his family origins and his birth date are disputed: his own memoirs give the year 1884. One version makes his father the Georgian prince Mikhail Antonovich Avalishvili and his stepfather the staff sergeant Rafail Bermondt; another makes him the son of a converted Jewish jeweller in Vladivostok. From 1919 he called himself Prince Pavel Mikhailovich Bermondt-Avalov. Trained in music in Warsaw, he enlisted as a bandmaster with the Transbaikal Cossacks and was awarded the Order of St. George in the Russo-Japanese War.

In the First World War he served as personal adjutant to the corps commander Pavel Mishchenko in East Prussia and then in Galicia, and was wounded four times.
