In 1918 he headed the White Army's recruitment and counter-intelligence centre in Kiev, was imprisoned by the forces of Symon Petliura, and was evacuated to Germany. There he raised about 300 men from the Salzwedel prisoner-of-war camp as the Graf Keller Corps, moved to Courland in June 1919 and, at Mitau, took over the German Freikorps soldiers who hoped to gain land in Latvia.

He refused General Yudenich's order to join the Narva front, wanting instead a pro-German, anti-Bolshevik union in the Baltic. His army, the Bermontians, reached some 50,000 men, 40,000 of them German or Baltic German, and pillaged the areas it occupied in Latvia and in Samogitia. After defeats at Riga and Radviliškis the French delegate Henri Niessel ordered it back to Germany, and Avalov, declaring himself a major general, escaped through Klaipėda.

In Germany he worked for the UFA film studio, offered troops for the Kapp Putsch and in 1925 published memoirs that were supposedly written by Vladimir von Rosenberg. He welcomed the Nazi Party's coming to power in 1933 and led the Russian National Socialist Movement, but was sent to a concentration camp on suspicion of embezzling 8,000 marks of its subsidy. In 1935 he escaped to Switzerland and Italy, settled in Belgrade in 1936, and finally emigrated to New York, where he died. In Lithuania and Latvia the word Bermontiada came to mean an adventure.
pavel-kiselyov: Kiselyov was born in Moscow on 19 January 1788. In the Napoleonic Wars he served as aide-de-camp to Count Miloradovich at the Battle of Borodino and, at the close of the campaign, became aide-de-camp to Alexander I. Five years later he was made Chief of Staff of the Second Army at Tulchyn in Podolia, where his first reforms, among them limits on corporal punishment, earned him the hostility of the War Minister, Count Arakcheyev. Pavel Pestel and other Decembrists of the southern league served under him; how far his liberalism encouraged them is disputed.

During the Russo-Turkish War of 1828-1829 he commanded the Russian occupying troops in Wallachia and Moldavia, and on 19 October 1829, at Zimnicea, he was appointed president of their Divans. He remained the most powerful man in the principalities until 1834, when Sultan Mahmud II named new voivodes, Alexandru II Ghica in Wallachia and Mihail Sturdza in Moldavia. The Organic Statute stayed in force until the union of 1859, apart from a break in Wallachia during the 1848 Revolution, and in Bucharest he created Șoseaua Kiseleff, a northward continuation of Calea Victoriei.

Back in Saint Petersburg in 1835 he joined the State Council and the secret committees on the emancipation of the serfs; his reform programme of that year, believed to rest on a memorandum he had first drafted in 1816, alarmed conservative landowners. He became a count in 1839. The ascendancy of reactionary forces until the death of Nicholas I in 1855 kept him from pursuing other reforms, and Alexander II then sent him to Paris as Minister Plenipotentiary to deal with the effects of the Crimean War.

Kiselyov married Countess Sofia, daughter of Stanisław Szczęsny Potocki, but their only son died in infancy, and he spent much time with his nephews of the Milyutin family. He hoped to see Nicholas Milyutin preside over the emancipation of the serfs, a hope only partly fulfilled, while another nephew, Dmitry Milyutin, carried out sweeping reforms of the Russian army in the 1870s. Failing health made Kiselyov give up his offices in 1862; he never returned to Russia and died in Paris on 26 November 1872.
pavel-tsitsianov: Pavel Dmitriyevich Tsitsianov was born in Moscow on 19 September 1754 into the Tsitsishvili, a Georgian noble family related to the Georgian royal dynasty. His grandfather had come to Russia in the early 1700s among the émigrés accompanying the exiled King Vakhtang VI, and his father, Dmitry Pavlovich, was a writer and state official. Tsitsianov entered the Preobrazhensky Regiment in 1772, fought in the Russo-Turkish War of 1787–92 at Khotin, Ismail and Bender, served in Poland during the 1794 uprising and joined the Persian Expedition of 1796 under Count Valerian Zubov.

In 1802 Alexander I made him commander of Russian forces in Georgia, newly annexed, inspector of the Caucasian Line and military governor of Astrakhan, in effect giving him absolute authority over Russian forces in the Caucasus. He exiled the remaining members of Georgia's former ruling dynasty to Russia, upgraded the Georgian Military Road, kept Georgian as a local official language and founded a school in Tiflis for the sons of nobles. His letters to Caucasian rulers were full of threats and insults, and he held all those he called Asiatics in contempt.

His capture of Ganja in 1804, which he renamed Yelizavetpol, began the Russo-Persian War of 1804–1813. Javad Khan, his son and between 1,500 and 3,000 inhabitants were killed, among them 500 warriors sheltering in a mosque. Tsitsianov then fought the Persian army at Gyumri, Etchmiadzin and Yerevan, and in May 1805 brought the Karabakh Khanate under Russian suzerainty by the Treaty of Kurekchay with Ibrahim Khalil Khan; Shaki, Shamakhi and Shoragel followed.

In February 1806 he rode up to the walls of Baku with only his aide-de-camp Prince Eristov and a Cossack to receive the keys of the city, and was shot by the khan's men. His head and hands were cut off and, by some accounts, sent to Fath-Ali Shah in Tehran. His body lay in a ditch until Russian forces took Baku months later, and his remains were later reinterred in the Tbilisi Sioni Cathedral.

Russian writers praised him, Alexander Pushkin among them, while the Iranian chronicler Reza-Qoli Khan Hedayat called him the shedder of blood. Muriel Atkin judged him undeserving of the praise, and Walter Richmond holds that he set in motion the brutality of later Russian efforts to conquer the North Caucasus.
pavlo-skoropadsky: Pavlo Petrovych Skoropadsky was born on 15 May 1873 in Wiesbaden into a noble family that traced its origin to the Zaporozhian Cossacks; one ancestor, Ivan Skoropadsky, was Hetman of the Zaporozhian Host from 1708 to 1722. He spent his first five years in Germany, learned German first, then grew up at Trostianets under his grandfather, who kept Cossack and Ukrainian traditions. Educated at the Page Corps in Saint Petersburg, he became an officer in 1893, fought in the Russo-Japanese War, became aide-de-camp to Nicholas II in 1912 and a lieutenant general in 1916.

In July 1917 Lavr Kornilov ordered him to Ukrainise his 34th Army Corps, which he did reluctantly, and it became the 1st Ukrainian Corps. In October 1917 he was named honorary Otaman at the first Congress of the Free Cossacks. His family had thought of itself as Little Russian, and he preferred the Russian language, which set him apart from many Ukrainian political leaders.

In April 1918 German troops, present in Ukraine under the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, carried out a coup against the socialist Ukrainian People's Republic and made Skoropadsky Hetman of Ukraine. He formed a cabinet of mainly Russian speakers, Tsarists and Slavophiles and committed Ukraine to federation with a restored Russian Empire. Some Ukrainian nationalists denounced him as a German collaborator supported by wealthy landowners, and others thought him too pro-Russian. Grain requisitioned violently by German and Austrian troops fuelled rural opposition. His government nevertheless gained credit in certain circles for effective administration, diplomatic ties with many countries, a peace treaty with Soviet Russia and many schools and universities, among them the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine.

After Germany signed an armistice on 11 November 1918, his military and international support was in doubt. An uprising led by Symon Petliura nominally restored the Ukrainian People's Republic under the Directoria, a provisional government of five directors chaired by Volodymyr Vynnychenko, and Skoropadsky signed an abdication document on 14 December 1918.

Skoropadsky went into exile in Germany in 1919, settled in Berlin's Wannsee district and led the Hetmanite movement, refusing in later years all offers to collaborate with the Nazis. In the last weeks of the war in Europe he fled the Soviet advance with the retreating German army and died at Metten Abbey on 26 April 1945 after being wounded in the bombing of Plattling. His movement, which influenced a Ukrainian monarchist programme modelled on the Cossack state, continued into the early 1980s.
pavlos-kountouriotis: Pavlos Kountouriotis was born on the island of Hydra on 9 April 1855, the second of nine children of Theodoros Kountouriotis, a consul and member of the Greek Parliament, and Loukia Negreponte. His father's family was an Arvanite Hydriot family originally from the village of Kountoura in the Megarid, and he often spoke Arvanitika. His grandfather Georgios was a shipowner who took part in the Greek War of Independence. Following the family's naval tradition, he joined the Royal Hellenic Navy in 1875.

Kountouriotis served in the naval operations at Preveza in 1886 and commanded the ship Alfeios in the Greco-Turkish War of 1897. In 1900, commanding the cruiser Navarchos Miaoulis, he crossed the Atlantic to bring the flag of the Hellenic Navy to the New World for the first time, and President William McKinley invited him to the White House. In June 1911 he went to Britain to take over the newly commissioned Georgios Averof.

Appointed commander of the Aegean Fleet in September 1912, he argued that the fleet could win with its existing ships. He told Prime Minister Eleftherios Venizelos that ships without capable crews were heavy lead that sinks in water. On the Georgios Averof he led the navy to victory over the Turkish fleet at the Battle of Elli in December 1912 and the Battle of Limnos in January 1913, which brought most of the Aegean islands under Greek control. He was promoted to vice admiral and became a national hero.

In 1916 Kountouriotis, disagreeing with the pro-German feelings of King Constantine I, followed Venizelos to Thessaloniki and became minister of naval affairs in his National Defence government. After the death of King Alexander he was elected Regent of Greece on 28 October 1920 by a vote of 137 to 3, and resigned on 17 November after Venizelos lost the elections.

He served as provisional president of the Second Hellenic Republic, resigning in March 1926 in opposition to General Pangalos's dictatorship, and served again from August 1926 until December 1929. In all he was head of the Greek state four times. He died on 22 August 1935. A destroyer and a frigate were named Kountouriotis for him, and he and the Georgios Averof appeared on a gold 100 euro coin issued in 2012 for the centenary of the Balkan Wars.
pawon: Pawon stands about 1.75 km from Borobudur and 1.15 km from Mendut, and with them forms the Borobudur Temple Compounds. The detail and style of its carving suggest that it is slightly older than Borobudur. That the three temples stand on one straight line suggests a symbolic meaning linking them. Its original name is uncertain. Pawon means kitchen in Javanese, a word derived from awu, dust, and this has suggested that it was built as a mortuary temple, a per-awu-an or place of ashes, for a cremated king, though who was laid there is unknown. Local people call it Bajranalan, after the village, from the Sanskrit vajra, thunder or a Buddhist ritual tool, and anala, fire.

The temple stands on a square base and faces slightly north-west. Carved Kala-Makara figures, common in classical Javanese temples, adorn the sides of the stairs and the tops of the gates. The outer walls bear reliefs of bodhisattvas and taras, and of the kalpataru, the tree of life, flanked by kinnara and kinnari. The square chamber inside is empty, with a square basin at its centre, and small rectangular windows probably served for ventilation. Five small stupas and four small ratnas crown the roof.

For its simplicity, symmetry and harmony historians have called it the jewel of Javanese temple architecture, in contrast with the tall, slender East Javanese temples of the later Singhasari and Majapahit periods.

Yazir Marzuki and Toeti Heraty hold that the temple most probably served to purify the mind before the ascent of Borobudur. Today, at the full moon of May or June, the Buddhist community of Indonesia keeps Waisak with a procession on foot that starts at Mendut, passes through Pawon and ends at Borobudur.
pax-britannica: Pax Britannica, Latin for British Peace and modelled on the Pax Romana, refers to the relative peace between the great powers in the period roughly bounded by the Napoleonic Wars and the First World War. During it the British Empire became the world hegemon, developed an informal empire and took the role of a global policeman. Between 1815 and 1914 about 26,000,000 square kilometres of territory and roughly 400 million people were added to the empire. Victory over Napoleonic France left Britain without any serious rival, other than perhaps the Russian Empire in Central Asia.

Free trade became a central principle of British practice by the 1840s. The Royal Navy controlled most key maritime trade routes, and British merchants, shippers and bankers had such an advantage that Britain controlled trade with countries such as China, Siam and Argentina outside its formal empire. A British peace on the trade routes began in 1815 with the annexation of British Ceylon. Britain imposed the General Maritime Treaty of 1820 on the Arab rulers of the Persian Gulf, who in the Perpetual Maritime Truce of 1853 gave up the right to wage war at sea in return for British protection.

The Royal Navy suppressed piracy and blocked the slave trade, setting up the West Africa Squadron to enforce the ban of the Slave Trade Act 1807. It was superior to any other two navies combined. Sea power did not project on land, however, and the major powers fought land wars, among them the Crimean War, the Austro-Prussian War and the Franco-Prussian War. The Royal Navy also fought the First and Second Opium Wars against Qing China.

The Anglo-Egyptian War led to a British occupation of Egypt lasting seven decades. The historian A. J. P. Taylor called it a great event, the only real event in international relations between the Battle of Sedan and the defeat of Russia in the Russo-Japanese war. By 1902 the empire was linked by the telegraph network known as the All Red Line.

The Pax Britannica weakened as the continental order established by the Congress of Vienna broke down, with the decline of the Ottoman Empire, the emergence of the Kingdom of Italy and the German Empire, and the industrialisation of Germany, Japan and the United States. The start of the First World War in 1914 marked its end. Britain remained one of the leading powers until the Suez Crisis of 1956.
pax-mongolica: Pax Mongolica, Latin for "Mongol Peace" and less often called Pax Tatarica, is a historiographical term modelled on Pax Romana. It describes the stabilising effects of the Mongol conquests on the social, cultural and economic life of the Eurasian territory they ruled in the 13th and 14th centuries. It followed conquests that began with Genghis Khan in the early 13th century.

In 1203 he reorganised his army into a decimal system of arbans of ten, zuuns, myangans and tumens of 10,000, breaking down clan divisions, and by 1206 he had unified the tribes of Mongolia. The Mongols conquered the Western Xia in 1209 and the Jin Empire between 1213 and 1214, and Hulegu Khan captured Baghdad in 1258. The empire at its height stretched from Busan to Budapest.

With the Silk Road under the sole rule of the Mongol Empire, it was commonly said that a maiden bearing a nugget of gold on her head could wander safely throughout the realm. The Mongols abolished local systems of taxation and extortion, standardised weights and measures, kept garrisons along trade routes and planted trees along roads. The Yassa, the code of Mongol law, outlawed theft and animal rustling, set harsh penalties and decreed religious freedom, with religious leaders, doctors, teachers and scholars exempt from taxation. Ögedei Khan introduced the Yam, a postal system with relay stations every 25 to 30 miles, in 1234, and his brothers and nephew Batu Khan extended it.

Goods, techniques and ideas moved across the Old World. Silk, spices, gunpowder and printing and paper-making travelled west, and bills of exchange, deposit banking and insurance reached Europe. European merchants such as Marco Polo travelled to China, and John of Montecorvino, archbishop of Beijing, founded Catholic missions in India and China. A Maritime Silk Road also reached from southern China across the Indian Ocean.

The peace ended with the disintegration of the khanates and the Black Death. Historians cite incompetent and rival leaders, corruption, revolts, factional struggles and disease. William H. McNeill noted that the plague passed from ground rodents in the Himalayan foothills to Mongol soldiers who invaded the area in 1252. It was noted in China in 1331 and travelled west along the trade routes, and the Black Death is estimated to have killed one third of China's population and 25 to 50 per cent of Europe's. Weakened, the Mongols could not hold remote domains, whose revolts disrupted production and trade. Long-distance trade almost entirely stopped, and China became increasingly inward-looking over the next three centuries.
paxos: Paxos is the smallest of the seven main Ionian Islands, with an area of 25.3 square kilometres. It lies about 15 kilometres from the southern tip of Corfu and at about the same distance from the mainland town of Parga. With the nearby island of Antipaxos and adjoining islets it is also called Paxi or Paxoi. The island is about 10 kilometres long and up to 3 kilometres wide, stretching north-west to south-east. Much of its hilly landscape is covered in olive groves, running from the harbour community of Lakka in the north through Magazia to Gaios, the main town. The west coast has steep white chalky cliffs with several blue caves.

In Greek mythology Poseidon created the island by striking Corfu with his trident, so that he and his wife Amphitrite could have peace and quiet. According to tradition the Phoenicians were the first settlers, and the name is believed to come from a Phoenician word meaning trapezoidal.

The island has been inhabited since prehistoric times. In 229 BCE, during the First Illyrian War, the Battle of Paxos was fought between Greek and Illyrian fleets, as the historian Polybius records in The Histories. The Romans ruled the island in the 2nd century BCE, and later it fell prey to pirates in the Byzantine era and the Middle Ages, and to crusaders. The Venetians gained control at the end of the 14th century.

During the Napoleonic Wars the Ionian Islands were occupied by the French and by a Russo-Turkish alliance. Paxos surrendered on 13 February 1814 to the Royal Navy frigate HMS Apollo and 160 troops from the 2nd Greek Light Infantry and the 35th Regiment of the Royal Corsican Rangers. The United Kingdom established the United States of the Ionian Islands in 1815, and in 1864, after the coronation of George I of Greece, Paxos and the other Ionian Islands were ceded to Greece.

Olive oil production, soap manufacture and fishing were supplanted by tourism as the main industry in the mid-1960s, which brought a construction boom that greatly altered the coast around Gaios. The municipality has 2,466 inhabitants. Ferries link Gaios with Igoumenitsa on the mainland and with Corfu. The island belongs to the Cultural Village of Europe network and hosts the annual Paxos Festival of young performers, founded by John Gough.
payerne: Payerne is a municipality in the Swiss canton of Vaud, in the valley of the river Broye. Its German name, Peterlingen, is out of use. Traces of settlement nearby include Neolithic objects, a Bronze Age settlement, burial mounds of the Hallstatt and La Tène cultures with gold necklaces, a Celtic bridge and a Roman road. There were Roman buildings and cemeteries and a dedicatory inscription of Publius Graccius Paternus.

The village first appeared in the Early Middle Ages. In 587 Bishop Marius built the villa Paterniacum and a chapel of St Mary, which developed into the parish church. The Cluniac Payerne Priory was founded in the 10th century, and in 1033 Emperor Conrad II was crowned King of Burgundy in the priory church. The town is first mentioned in 961. Before 1302 the prior granted the citizens the right to form a council and a seal, and in 1348 the council made a town charter. Citizens and monastery were often in conflict. The town made treaties with Bern in 1344, Fribourg in 1349 and Murten in 1364.

Guillaume Farel and Pierre Viret began preaching the Protestant Reformation in Payerne in 1532–33, and the town adopted the new faith before Bern conquered Vaud in 1536. Bern then gave it a privileged legal position: its Schultheiss, who represented Bernese interests, was a citizen of Payerne and not a Bernese Vogt. A castle for the Bernese representative went up on the monastery grounds in 1640. From 1802 until 2006 Payerne was capital of the district of Payerne in Vaud, until it became part of the district of Broye-Vully. In the 1830s and 40s the city walls and three gates were demolished, leaving only four towers.

The Payerne Abbey church and former convent buildings, the Ancien Tribunal, the Swiss Reformed Church of Notre-Dame and the Fountain du Banneret are heritage sites of national significance, and the whole old city is in the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites. The present Gothic parish church was built in the 14th century over Roman foundations. The town is home to a major airbase of the Swiss Air Force and the Musée de l'aviation militaire. The Payerne sausage, a cold smoked pork sausage, has been a traditional dish since the mid-19th century.
pays-de-caux: The Pays de Caux occupies most of the département of Seine Maritime. It is an undulating plateau of Upper Cretaceous chalk, like that of the North and South Downs in England, bordered on the east by the Pays de Bray, where the older strata show through. The sea has cut its coast, the Côte d'Albâtre, into high white cliffs, and the small inland valleys end there in steep notches called valleuses, some of which hold towns such as Étretat. Dieppe lies on the same geological fault that formed the Pays de Bray, which gave it a deep harbour. Its plain farmhouses, enclosed by high earth banks and a square of sheltering trees, answer the sea winds.

Julius Caesar's Gallic War describes the Caletes, from whom the region's name derives through forms such as Cauz; the name is said to mean the hard or courageous people. Their main town stood at Lillebonne, refounded under Augustus as Juliobona, known for its Roman theatre, and their earlier oppidum may have been at Caudebec-en-Caux or Fécamp. Rescue excavation on the line of the A29 autoroute found several Gallo-Roman villas, among them one at Sainte-Marguerite-sur-Mer with mosaics and baths heated by hypocausts.

In the Merovingian period the Caux became distinct from the Talou. After the creation of the county of Rouen and the Duchy of Normandy in 911, the Vikings settled many people in the region, leaving a lasting mark on its people and its dialect. After the Hundred Years' War, with peace and prosperity restored from 1450, the gentry rebuilt their manor houses of flint and limestone, often in Renaissance style and usually with a dovecote; historians have counted 635 dovecotes in the arrondissements of Dieppe, Le Havre and Rouen.

Its chief towns are Le Havre, Dieppe, Fécamp, Yvetot and Étretat, and its population density is a little above the French average. Its traditional industries were fishing on the coast and flax growing and weaving on the plateau. Cauchois, its dialect of the Norman language, is one of the language's last strongholds outside the Cotentin. The cliffs drew painters such as Claude Monet and Gustave Courbet, and Guy de Maupassant described the region in his stories.
paysandu: The city stands on the banks of the Uruguay River, which forms the border with Argentina. It lies 378 kilometres northwest of Montevideo, at the junction of Route 3 and Route 90. A short distance to the north the General Artigas Bridge links Uruguay with Entre Ríos Province in Argentina, south of Colón.

Paysandú has a humid subtropical climate, with warm to hot summers and cool winters in which frosts and fog occur. Rainfall is spread evenly through the year, though winters are slightly drier, and averages 1,181 mm.

Paysandú was founded in October 1756 and had acquired the status of villa, or town, before the independence of Uruguay. On 8 June 1863 it was raised to the status of ciudad, or city, by Law No. 780. General Leandro Gomez led Uruguayan forces against Brazilian forces that invaded in 1864–1865, and a battle took place on 2 December 1864. The city is known as La Heroica, the Heroic City, for its resistance during the siege.

From the late nineteenth century Paysandú received a significant influx of Italian immigrants, who settled in both urban and rural areas. Many were at first engaged in river transport, trade and agriculture. By the early twentieth century the city had become one of the principal centres of Italian settlement in Uruguay, second only to Montevideo, and various associations and institutions were established to serve the community. By 1992 about 65 per cent of the population of the department was estimated to be of Italian descent. Settlers also came from Switzerland, Poland, Germany, Russia, Ukraine and Belgium.

Paysandú is the capital and most populous city of Paysandú Department, with a population of 81,550 in 2023. Its industries include the Norteña brewery, Azucarlito (sugar), Paylana (woollen fabrics) and Paycuero (leather), and it is the centre of the plantation forest industry in Uruguay, with many companies planting and harvesting eucalyptus. The Uruguay River has recreational beaches, and the city has a centre of the University of the Republic.
pazyryk-burials: The tombs lie south of the modern city of Novosibirsk, close to the borders with China, Kazakhstan and Mongolia, and comparable burials have been found in neighbouring western Mongolia. Each is a kurgan, a wooden chamber covered by a large cairn of boulders and stones; the Pazyryk finds brought the Russian word kurgan into general use. Water seeped into the chambers in antiquity and froze, and the ice, kept in the permafrost, preserved organic objects such as felt hangings, Chinese silk, wooden furniture and sacrificed horses with elaborate trappings.

M. P. Griaznov excavated barrow 1 in 1929, and Sergei Ivanovich Rudenko the next four, which he first dated to the 5th century BCE, a date since revised. Many tombs had been looted, but in barrow 2 in 1947 Rudenko found the embalmed body of a chief, 176 cm tall, who had died between 55 and 60, killed with a Scythian-type battle axe and scalped. His body was covered in animal style tattoos of a donkey, a mountain ram, deer, griffin-like monsters and a fish, and infrared photography later showed that all five bodies from the kurgans were tattooed. Barrow 5 held a man and a woman, nine horses and a disassembled four-wheeled wagon.

The Pazyryk rug, probably the oldest surviving pile carpet, measures 183 by 200 cm with about 360,000 knots per square metre; some scholars, among them Ulrich Schurmann, think it Armenian work, others Persian. Genetic study found the Pazyryk population fairly balanced between western and eastern Eurasian ancestry. The best-known undisturbed burial of the culture is the Ice Maiden found by Natalia Polosmak in 1993 at Ukok, a young woman buried with six horses in a larch coffin, wearing a tall felt headdress and tattooed.

The site is part of the Golden Mountains of Altai UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the finds of the Pazyryk barrows are exhibited at the Hermitage Museum in Saint Petersburg. The indigenous people of the region strongly disapprove of archaeological digs, which has led scientists to move their work across the border to Mongolia.
peace-and-truce-of-god: After the Carolingian Empire broke up in the ninth century, its western lands split into many small counties and lordships whose lords and knights fought each other for control. Historians explain the violence in different ways: some point to a crown unable to act and a nobility unwilling to, while André Debord linked the movement to the rapid spread of castle building in the early eleventh century, above all in Aquitaine. The eastern half of the former empire, and England, did not see the same collapse of central authority.

Church measures against violence were older. Adomnán of Iona promulgated the Cáin Adomnáin in 697, with sanctions against killing children, clerics and peasants on church land, and the Council of Trosly declared the destruction of church property a sacrilege.

At the abbey of Charroux a great crowd from Poitou, the Limousin and neighbouring regions gathered around the bodies of saints. Canons issued under Gombald, Archbishop of Bordeaux, threatened excommunication for robbing a church, for taking farm animals from peasants or the poor, and for striking or seizing an unarmed cleric; compensation could lift the sentence. Later councils added women, children, pilgrims and, in 1033, merchants and their goods. The crowds and the relics gave the Peace of God a popular character, and with the support of King Robert II of France it spread to Flanders, Burgundy, Champagne and Berry, where villagers too came to swear oaths to keep the peace.

The Truce of God grew from the custom of not fighting on Sunday. It demanded peace through Advent, Lent and the weeks around Pentecost, and a council of 1041 added Thursday, Friday and Saturday. Holy Roman Emperor Henry III proclaimed an early form at Constance in 1043, and in Normandy the nobles were made to declare a truce at Caen in October 1047, with little result.

In its own aims the movement was not very effective, but it set a precedent for later efforts to control noble violence, such as the medieval communes. Georges Duby argued that the zones where violence was forbidden helped villages grow up in the shadow of their churches. At the Council of Clermont in 1095 Pope Urban II renewed the Truce of God and turned the knights' violence outward to the crusade. Thomas Aquinas later held that war to defend the commonwealth was lawful even on holy days.
peace-of-amasya: The Peace of Amasya was agreed on 29 May 1555 at the city of Amasya between Shah Tahmasp I of Safavid Iran and Sultan Suleiman of the Ottoman Empire. It followed the Ottoman-Safavid War of 1532 to 1555, in which the two empires had fought over their frontier lands.

The treaty defined the border between Iran and the Ottoman Empire and was followed by twenty years of peace. Armenia and Georgia were divided equally between the two. Western Armenia and western Georgia, including western Samtskhe, fell to the Ottomans, while Eastern Armenia and eastern Georgia, including eastern Samtskhe, stayed in Iranian hands.

The Ottomans obtained most of Iraq, including Baghdad, which gave them access to the Persian Gulf. The Persians kept their former capital Tabriz and their other northwestern territories in the Caucasus, as before the wars, among them Dagestan and all of what is now Azerbaijan. The frontier ran across the mountains dividing eastern and western Georgia, whose princes were native vassals, through Armenia and down the western slopes of the Zagros Mountains to the Persian Gulf.

Several buffer zones were set up in Eastern Anatolia, in Erzurum, Shahrizor and Van. Kars was declared neutral and its fortress was destroyed. The Ottomans guaranteed Persian pilgrims access to Mecca and Medina and to the Shia holy sites in Ottoman Iraq. The Safavids were required to end the ritual cursing of the first three Rashidun caliphs, Aisha and other companions of Muhammad, who are held in high esteem by Sunnis. Such a condition was common in treaties between the two empires and was considered humiliating for Tahmasp.

The treaty established a frontier that held for most of a century. The decisive parting of the Caucasus and the irrevocable ceding of Mesopotamia to the Ottomans came only with the next major peace treaty, the Treaty of Zuhab in 1639.
peace-of-antalcidas: The treaty was more commonly known in antiquity as the King's Peace, a name that reflects the depth of Persian influence, as Persian gold had driven the preceding war. It was a form of Common Peace, like the Thirty Years' Peace that ended the First Peloponnesian War. By 387 BCE the central front of the Corinthian War had shifted to the Aegean, where an Athenian fleet under Thrasybulus had placed a number of cities under Athenian control and was acting with Evagoras, the king of Cyprus. Evagoras was an enemy of Persia and many of the Athenian gains threatened Persian interests, so Artaxerxes II switched his support from Athens and its allies to Sparta.

Antalcidas, commander of a Spartan fleet, was summoned to Susa along with the satrap Tiribazus, and there the Spartans and Persians worked out an agreement. To bring the Athenians to the table, Antalcidas moved 90 ships to the Hellespont, where he could threaten the grain route from the Black Sea. The Athenians remembered their defeat in 404 BCE, when the Spartans had controlled the Hellespont, and agreed to negotiate. Thebes, Corinth and Argos, unwilling to fight on without Athens, were also forced to negotiate, and at a conference in Sparta all the belligerents accepted the terms laid down by Artaxerxes.

As Xenophon records the decree, Artaxerxes held it just that the cities in Asia should belong to him, as well as Clazomenae and Cyprus among the islands, and that the other Greek cities should be autonomous, except Lemnos, Imbros and Scyros, which should belong to the Athenians. Ionia and Cyprus were abandoned to the Persians, and the Athenians had to give up their gains in the Aegean. The insistence on autonomy ended the union of Argos and Corinth, which had merged politically in a sympoliteia with joint citizenship, and the Thebans had to disband their Boeotian league. Sparta's Peloponnesian League was overlooked.

Persia regained firm control of Ionia and parts of the Aegean, and the treaty placed Greece under Persian suzerainty. Will Durant called it the most disgraceful event in Greek history. Sparta, charged with enforcing the peace, forced Mantinea to disband into villages and in 382 BCE campaigned against the Chalcidian League. In 383 its commander Phoebidas seized the Theban Kadmeia. Pelopidas and his companions liberated Thebes in 379 BCE, and general fighting resumed in the Boeotian War of 378 to 371 BCE. The idea of a Common Peace endured, but later attempts had little more success.
peace-of-augsburg: Charles V had issued the Augsburg Interim in 1548, a ruling on the two religious creeds in the empire that he hoped a general council of the Catholic Church would resolve. Its 26 articles largely reflected Catholic practice, though they allowed the clergy to marry and the laity to receive both bread and wine. The Protestant territories resisted and proclaimed their own Interim at Leipzig the following year. In 1552 the Protestant elector Maurice of Saxony and his allies overthrew the Interim by revolt, and the Peace of Passau that summer gave the Lutherans religious freedom, but only until the next imperial Diet, which was called for early 1555.

The treaty was signed at Augsburg on 25 September 1555 and negotiated on the emperor's behalf by his brother Ferdinand. It rested on three principles. The first, cuius regio, eius religio (whose realm, his religion), let a prince choose Lutheranism or Catholicism for his domain. Subjects who would not conform had a period in which to emigrate and sell their estates, a new idea in the 16th century, though serfs were in effect excluded from the right.

The second, the reservatum ecclesiasticum, held that if the prelate of an ecclesiastical state changed his religion, its inhabitants did not have to follow; he was expected to resign. The third, the Declaratio Ferdinandei, exempted knights and some cities where the reformed religion had been practised since the mid-1520s. Ferdinand inserted it at the last minute on his own authority, and it was kept secret for almost two decades. Article 17 excluded all who belonged to neither confession, so that Zwinglians and Anabaptists were left without legal recognition, and Calvinism was not recognised either.

The settlement ended the first wave of organised military action between Protestants and Catholics, but it left problems unresolved. The ecclesiastical reservation was tested in the Cologne War of 1583 to 1588, after the prince-archbishop Gebhard Truchsess von Waldburg converted to Protestantism. The Catholic revocation of the Declaratio Ferdinandei in the Edict of Restitution of 1629 helped fuel the Thirty Years' War, and the Peace of Westphalia later forbade rulers to convert their subjects by force and gave serfs the right to emigrate. The Peace has been described as the first step on the road toward a European system of sovereign states. Charles V, meanwhile, abdicated and divided the Habsburg lands between his brother Ferdinand and his son Philip II.
peace-of-bautzen: After the death of Emperor Otto III, Bolesław I had backed Eckard I, Margrave of Meissen, for the succession against Duke Henry IV of Bavaria. When Eckard was murdered at Pöhlde on 30 April 1002, Bolesław took Meissen and the march of Lusatia. At a Hoftag in Merseburg on 25 July 1002 Henry, now King Henry II of Germany, gave him Lusatia and Upper Lusatia as a fief in return for allegiance and the return of Meissen. Bolesław was ambushed as he left the meeting, and Henry neither protected him nor punished the attackers.

In 1003 Bolesław conquered the Duchy of Bohemia and allied with German nobles opposed to Henry, who in turn allied with the pagan Lutici. A peace near Poznań in 1005, mediated by Tagino, Archbishop of Magdeburg, cost Poland Lusatia and Meissen. Fighting resumed in 1007, and a second peace at Merseburg in 1013 restored Lusatia to Bolesław as a fief, sealed by the marriage of his son Mieszko II to Richeza, a niece of Otto III.

Bolesław did not help Henry's Italian campaign and instead supported the antipope Gregory VI. In July 1015 Henry renewed the war with his Lutician allies, but Bolesław kept the imperial armies from joining, and Margrave Gero and two hundred German knights were killed by Polish bowmen. In 1017 Henry found Głogów too strongly fortified and besieged Niemcza without success; the chronicler Thietmar of Merseburg, generally ill-disposed towards Poles, praised the defenders' bravery. Henry declared Bolesław a public enemy, and at the end of 1017 Polish troops invaded the land between the Mulde and Elbe rivers.

Thietmar gave no precise conditions for Bolesław's hold on the Lusatian lands. The German historian Schneidmüller held that they were an imperial fief, the Polish historian Paweł Jasienica that they carried no obligation, and the Cambridge Medieval History describes purely nominal terms of vassalage. Thietmar summed up the peace as not as it should have been but as was possible. Hostages were exchanged, Henry did not attend, and the peace was confirmed by Bolesław's fourth marriage, to Oda of Meissen, daughter of Eckard I. Henry promised three hundred knights for the Kiev expedition, and he never renewed the war.
peace-of-cambrai: The peace ended French involvement in the War of the League of Cognac, which had lasted since 1526. It was negotiated and signed at Cambrai, the centre of a principality-bishopric in the Netherlands, in what is now the French department of Nord. It is known as the Ladies' Peace because women prepared it: Louise of Savoy, mother of Francis I, represented the king, and Margaret of Austria, aunt of Charles V, represented the emperor, helping both monarchs not to lose face. Marguerite of Navarre was also instrumental. The treaty renewed the Treaty of Madrid of 1526 and added clauses meant to settle long-standing disputes, mainly over the Burgundian inheritance.

Francis renounced his claims to Italian lands, including the Kingdom of Naples and the Duchy of Milan. France accepted that the former Burgundian domains within the Holy Roman Empire, including the Free County of Burgundy, would stay with the emperor, and gave up its suzerainty over the counties of Artois and Flanders, which the emperor already held. Charles in turn accepted that the other Burgundian domains within the Kingdom of France, including the Duchy of Burgundy and the Picardian counties, would remain French.

The treaty provided for the return to France of the Dauphin François and Prince Henry, the future Henry II, in exchange for a ransom of 2 million écus. Francis I confirmed his consent to marry Charles V's sister Eleanor, and he married her on 7 July 1530.

The treaty confirmed effective Habsburg hegemony in the Duchy of Milan and the Kingdom of Naples. Together with the Treaty of Barcelona between the emperor and the pope, concluded in June 1529, it brought about the disintegration of the Cognac League. Only the Florentine Republic went on fighting Charles V, which led to the siege and surrender of Florence in 1530. The terms did not satisfy Francis I, and in 1536 a new conflict began between France and the Holy Roman Empire.
peace-of-cateau-cambresis: The Italian Wars between the House of Valois and the House of Habsburg began in 1494 and lasted over sixty years. Charles V abdicated in January 1556 and divided his possessions: the Habsburg lands went to his brother Ferdinand, later Holy Roman Emperor, and his son Philip II of Spain ruled the Spanish Netherlands and Milan, with Spain, Naples, Sicily and Sardinia added. Philip's victories at St Quentin in 1557 and Gravelines in 1558 let him negotiate from strength, but he could no longer pay his troops. Henry II of France was also ready for peace, having occupied the Three Bishoprics in 1552 and retaken Calais in January 1558, and divisions caused by the rise of Protestantism weakened his nobility.

The settlement consisted of two treaties: one between England and France on 2 April 1559 and one between France and Spain on 3 April, both approved by Emperor Ferdinand I. Henry II gave up his claims in Italy, recognised Philip II as ruler of Milan and of the kingdoms of Naples, Sicily and Sardinia, returned Corsica to Genoa and ceded the Presidi to Spain. Spain gave back Saint Quentin, Ham and Le Catelet in northern France.

France withdrew from Piedmont and restored the Duchy of Savoy to Emmanuel Philibert, who married Henry's sister Margaret. France kept five fortresses there, among them Pinerolo and Chivasso. Henry also kept the Three Bishoprics of Toul, Metz and Verdun. England granted France the Pale of Calais for eight years, a mechanism to save face, and Elizabeth I, who had succeeded Mary I in November 1558, was formally recognised as queen. Calais stayed French afterwards. Philip II married Henry's daughter Elisabeth of Valois.

Henry II was injured in a jousting accident during the tournament held to celebrate the peace and died on 10 July 1559. His son Francis II died in December 1560 and was succeeded by the 10-year-old Charles. Political instability and the demobilisation of thousands of unpaid troops led to the outbreak of the French Wars of Religion in 1562.

Italy was left divided between Spanish viceroyalties in the south and imperial fiefs in the north, among them Tuscany under the Medici, Milan under the Spanish Habsburgs and Piedmont under Savoy. Spain's control of Milan, Naples, Sicily and Sardinia was confirmed, and the division lasted until the wars of succession of the 18th century. England's loss of Calais, its last stronghold on the Continent, damaged its reputation.
peace-of-constance: The peace was issued on 25 June 1183 by Frederick I and his son and co-ruler Henry VI, King of the Romans, to end the rebellion of the Lombard League that had begun in 1167. It replaced the six-year truce imposed by the Treaty of Venice of 22 July 1177. As the truce neared its end, talks began early in 1183, with proposals and counter-proposals, a separate settlement of the disputed status of Alessandria and a preliminary agreement at Piacenza, which became the basis of the final text. Because an emperor could not formally make a treaty with his own subjects, it took the form of an imperial privilege.

The cities of the Kingdom of Italy kept the regalia they had long exercised, among them rights over woods, pastures, bridges, water and mills, armies, the defence of the cities and criminal and civil jurisdiction. They could elect their own councils, make their own laws, build fortifications and keep and renew the League. In return their consuls swore fealty to the emperor and received investiture from him or his envoy every five years, and citizens aged fifteen to seventy swore allegiance.

Appeals above a set sum went to an imperial representative in the city, who had to give judgment within two months, so that no one had to travel to Germany. Privileges granted against the League during the war were annulled, and the cities owed the emperor an annual payment, the customary supplies and repairs of roads and bridges when he came into Lombardy. Pavia, Cremona, Como, Tortona, Asti, Alessandria, Genoa and Alba, of the imperial party, swore to the peace as well.

The jurist Baldo degli Ubaldi later argued in his Commentaria in usus feudorum that the emperor could break parts of it, since his oath was temporary, but the Hohenstaufen made no attempt to do so. The cities stopped meeting their obligations during the struggle for the crown after the death of Henry VI in 1197, and the peace stood at the centre of the war between the second Lombard League and Emperor Frederick II from 1226 to 1250. For the rest of the Middle Ages it was remembered as the only imperial recognition of the autonomy of a large group of Italian cities.
peace-of-munster: Negotiations began in 1641 in the town of Münster, in the Holy Roman Empire. Spain did not recognise the Dutch Republic, but it agreed that the Lords States General of the United Netherlands were sovereign and could take part in the talks. On the Dutch side this followed strong political pressure from the Bicker-De Graeff clan, whose leaders Andries and Cornelis Bicker, Cornelis and Andries de Graeff and Jacob de Witt pressed for peace. Once talks began, Dutch trade with the Levant and the Iberian Peninsula flourished, and Dutch merchants came to dominate markets that English traders had held.

Eight Dutch representatives arrived in Münster in January 1646, and Spain sent Gaspar de Bracamonte, Count of Peñaranda, and Antoine Brun, with wide authority from Philip IV. On 30 January 1646 Adriaan Pauw and Johan de Knuyt reached an armistice of twenty years and recognition of sovereignty. A provisional agreement of 8 January 1647 recognised the status quo in the East and West Indies and the patents of the Dutch East India Company and the West India Company.

The negotiators reached agreement relatively quickly, because the text of the Twelve Years' Truce of 1609 served as the foundation and many of its articles could be copied with few changes. Spain formally recognised the States General as a sovereign entity, the first point of the treaty, and stopped regarding the inhabitants of the Republic as rebellious Spanish subjects, as it had done for nearly a century. France, with which the Republic had agreed to a joint treaty, hindered progress by repeatedly making new demands, so the States decided to conclude a separate peace with Spain.

The parties agreed on 30 January 1648. Philip IV ratified the treaty in Madrid on 1 March and the States General in The Hague on 18 April. It was published in the town hall of Münster on 15 May, when the envoys swore an oath before a large crowd. The delegate of Zeeland refused to attend, and the States General approved the treaty only narrowly, on 5 June 1648. There was considerable opposition because the treaty let Spain keep the Southern Provinces and allowed religious toleration for Catholics. The support of Holland carried it, but these differences led to political conflict. The text was adopted in four copies, two in French and two in Dutch.
peace-of-nicias: In 425 BCE the Spartans lost the battles of Pylos and Sphacteria, and the Athenians held 292 prisoners, at least 120 of them Spartiates. In 424 BCE the Spartan general Brasidas captured Amphipolis, but the Athenians suffered a major defeat at Delium in Boeotia. In 422 BCE they were beaten again at Amphipolis, where both Brasidas and the Athenian politician Cleon were killed. Both sides were by then exhausted. Athens feared that its allies might revolt, and Sparta was shaken by its losses and by the failure of its yearly invasions.

Sparta also faced a problem with Argos. Its thirty-year peace with Argos was about to expire, and the Argives would not renew it unless the border region of Cynuria was returned to them. The Spartans judged it hard to fight Athens and Argos at the same time.

The negotiations were started by Pleistoanax, king of Sparta, and the Athenian general Nicias. Most places were to return to their prewar state, except that Athens kept Nisaea and Thebes kept Plataea. Pylos was to go back to Sparta, Amphipolis to Athens, and the prisoners were to be exchanged. Temples were to be open to worshippers from all cities, and the oracle at Delphi was to regain its autonomy. Athens would go on collecting tribute from the states that had paid it since the time of Aristides but could not force them to become allies, and it agreed to help Sparta if the helots revolted. Six cities, Argilus, Stagirus, Acanthus, Stolus, Olynthus and Spartolus, were listed as neutral.

Seventeen representatives from each side swore an oath to keep the treaty for fifty years. The Spartans included the kings Pleistoanax and Agis II, and the Athenians included Nicias, Laches, Lamachus and Demosthenes. Athens's chief goal, the return of Amphipolis, was blocked when Clearidas obtained a clause in the treaty cancelling the transfer.

Few of Sparta's allies agreed to the peace; Boeotia, Corinth, Elis, Megara and Amphipolis opposed it. Boeotia refused to return Athenian captives and the fortress of Panactum, while Corinth's quarrels over Potidaea, Corcyra and its lost territory in the north-west were unresolved. Megara had lost its port of Nisaea, and Elis resented Sparta's conduct. Most of the terms were ignored or only partly carried out. According to Thucydides the treaty lasted about six years and ten months, during which the two sides attacked each other's territory, and many historians blame militant factions that gained power in both cities.
peace-of-nisibis-299: The treaty, also called the First Peace of Nisibis, ended the Roman–Sasanian War of 296–299. Despite earlier successes in Mesopotamia, Shah Narseh was defeated twice in Armenia by the Roman Caesar Galerius. After the second battle, at Satala in 298, Roman forces seized Narseh's camp, treasury, harem and wife, and Galerius marched south to take the Sasanian capital, Ctesiphon, before returning to Roman territory.

In 298 Narseh sent his ambassador Apharban to plead for the return of his family; Apharban was dismissed and told to await an envoy. Diocletian and Galerius met at Nisibis in the spring of 299. Galerius allegedly proposed conquering the Sasanian Empire, but Diocletian's more moderate terms were adopted, and the magister memoriae Sicorius Probus carried them to Narseh in Media.

The terms are known from a 6th-century summary by Peter the Patrician, written in the reign of Justinian I. Persia was to cede five satrapies east of the Tigris, though writers disagree on which: some name Ingilene, Sophene, Arzanene, Corduene and Zabdicene, others Arzanene, Moxoene, Zabdicene, Rehimene and Corduene. The Tigris was to be the border, Armenia's frontier was extended to the fortress of Zintha in Media Atropatene, and the Roman Empire took suzerainty over Iberia and the right to appoint its kings. Nisibis was to be the only legal place of trade between the empires. George Rawlinson held that Narseh accepted all but this last condition, which Probus withdrew; Timothy Barnes wrote that Probus refused to revise anything and Narseh submitted.

Diocletian then built and strengthened the fortifications of the Limes Arabicus and the Strata Diocletiana along the eastern frontier and stationed more soldiers there. The treaty kept the two empires at peace for forty years, until Shapur II invaded Roman Mesopotamia in the late 330s, and its border held until the Second Peace of Nisibis.
peace-of-phoenice: The war between Rome and Carthage upset the Greek political balance between Macedon under Philip V and the Aetolian League. Seeking to strengthen his position, Philip raised a fleet and sent envoys to Hannibal, who was then occupying part of Italy. Rome, fearing that Philip might give Carthage open military help, hoped to confine the Macedonians to the east of its province of Illyria. Between 214 and 212 BCE Philip made two unsuccessful attempts to invade Illyria by sea and made slow progress by land, until he captured the port of Lissus and the province capitulated.

Rome then drew the Aetolians into an alliance against him, beginning the First Macedonian War. For two years the allies won minor victories and gained more allies among the Greek city-states, but when the Romans withdrew from the field Philip's forces advanced against the Aetolians and turned the fortunes of the war. The Macedonians largely regained their original position, and both the Romans and the Aetolians were ready to make peace.

The treaty, drawn up at Phoenice in 205 BCE, formally recognised the favourable position of Macedon, including its gains in Illyria, while Philip in effect gave up his alliance with Hannibal. Rome was to control the Parthinians, Dimallum, Bargulum and Eugenium, and Macedon, pending the approval of the Roman Senate, was to control Atintania.

Other states were parties to the treaty on each side. With Philip stood Prusias of Bithynia, the Achaeans, the Boeotians, the Thessalians, the Acarnanians and the Epirots; with Rome stood the Ilians, Attalus, Pleuratus, Nabis of the Lacedaemonians, the Eleans, the Messenians and the Athenians.
peace-of-prague-1635: The Thirty Years' War began in 1618 when Frederick V of the Palatinate accepted the crown of Bohemia. Emperor Ferdinand II suppressed the Bohemian Revolt with Bavarian support, and in 1622 Maximilian I, Elector of Bavaria, invaded the Palatinate and sent Frederick into exile. Christian IV of Denmark invaded northern Germany for the Protestant cause until he withdrew in 1629.

Ferdinand then issued the Edict of Restitution, which required property transferred since 1552 to be restored to its original owner, nearly always the Catholic Church. By effectively undoing the Peace of Augsburg of 1555, it pushed moderate Protestants such as John George of Saxony and George William of Brandenburg into opposition.

Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden invaded Pomerania in 1630. After his death at Lützen in 1632, Sweden formed the Heilbronn League, which lost at Nördlingen in 1634. From February 1633 Ferdinand had accepted that Catholicism could not be imposed by force and opened talks on amending the Edict. Mediators from Denmark-Norway and Hesse-Darmstadt helped agree a draft in November 1634.

The treaty was a bilateral agreement between Ferdinand and John George, and other states joined later. Eight days of negotiation took place in Prague Castle, where the Defenestrations of Prague had begun the war in 1618. The Edict of Restitution was effectively revoked, with 12 November 1627 set as the date for returning properties, though Protestant administrators of former Catholic prince-bishoprics and imperial abbeys were excluded from the Imperial Diet.

Alliances between states of the Empire, or with outside powers, were prohibited, which dissolved the Catholic and Heilbronn Leagues. The armies of the states were in principle unified as the Army of the Holy Roman Empire, but this proved almost impossible to enforce. A general amnesty covered those who had fought the Imperial troops, apart from the descendants of Frederick V.

Many states acceded, among them Brandenburg, Mainz, Hesse-Darmstadt, Saxe-Weimar, Hamburg, Bremen and Nuremberg. Württemberg was excluded and Strasbourg did not accede. William V of Hesse-Kassel acceded but in 1636 allied with France and was put under an imperial ban. Saxony, which had occupied Lower and Upper Lusatia in 1623, received both in perpetuity under the Traditionsrezess of 1636.

It is generally agreed that the peace ended the war as primarily one of religion. Fighting continued, however. France declared war on Spain on 19 May 1635 and entered the war as an active belligerent, and in 1642 Sweden won at Breitenfeld and overran Saxony. Peace came only with the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.
peace-of-pressburg-1805: The treaty followed the French victory over the Russians and Austrians at the Battle of Austerlitz on 2 December 1805. A truce was agreed on 4 December and negotiations began. Johann I Joseph, Prince of Liechtenstein, and the Hungarian Count Ignác Gyulay signed for the Austrian Empire, and Charles Maurice de Talleyrand for France, on 26 December 1805 at Pressburg, today Bratislava. The Holy Roman Emperor Francis II and Napoleon Bonaparte were the principals.

Beyond clauses of peace and amity, the treaty took Austria out of the Third Coalition and required substantial concessions. It repeated the French gains of the earlier treaties of Campo Formio and Lunéville. Recent Austrian acquisitions in Italy and southern Germany were ceded to France and Bavaria. Venetia, Istria and Dalmatia were incorporated into the Kingdom of Italy, of which Napoleon had become king earlier that year, and the Principality of Lucca and Piombino was recognised as independent of the Holy Empire.

Austrian holdings in Swabia passed to the King of Württemberg and the Elector of Baden, while Bavaria received Tyrol and Vorarlberg and the former Free Imperial City of Augsburg. Austrian claims on those German states were renounced without exception. As a minor compensation Austria annexed the Electorate of Salzburg, under Habsburg rule since 1803, and its elector, the emperor's brother, received the Duchy of Würzburg, created from lands of the former prince-bishopric. The treaty also provided for an indemnity of 40 million francs to France.

Francis II recognised the kingly titles assumed by the Electors of Bavaria and Württemberg, which foreshadowed the end of the Holy Roman Empire. Within months, after Napoleon had created the Confederation of the Rhine, Francis II renounced his title as Holy Roman Emperor. Remaining territorial questions, including the establishment of the new border along the Isonzo river, were settled by the Treaty of Fontainebleau on 10 October 1807.
peace-of-riga: The First World War removed state borders across Europe, and the Treaty of Versailles re-established Poland's independence after a century and a half of partition. The Russian Civil War gave Poland, under Józef Piłsudski, a chance to regain parts of the former Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. In 1920 Piłsudski's offensive into Ukraine, meant to establish an independent Ukraine allied to Poland, was met by a Soviet counter-offensive into central Poland, which the Soviets saw as a land bridge to Western Europe. The war culminated in the Battle of Warsaw, won by the Poles, and further setbacks persuaded Soviet Russia to negotiate.

Talks began in Minsk on 17 August 1920 and moved to Riga, where they resumed on 21 September. The chief negotiators were Jan Dąbski for Poland and Adolph Joffe for the Soviet side, and an armistice signed on 12 October took effect on 18 October. Soviet delegates offered substantial territorial concessions, but the Polish delegation, dominated by the National Democrats, preferred a border further west to keep non-Polish minorities below one third of the population. A parliamentary delegation rejected an offer that would have left Minsk on the Polish side.

The treaty has 26 articles. Poland recognised Soviet Ukraine and Belarus and withdrew recognition of the Ukrainian People's Republic, its only ally in the war, which meant giving up Piłsudski's federal programme. The border lay about 250 kilometres east of the Curzon Line and brought large numbers of Ukrainians and Belarusians into the Second Polish Republic. Russia and Soviet Ukraine abandoned claims to lands west of the line. Poland was to receive 30 million gold rubles and railway materials worth 29 million gold rubles, and Russia was to return works of art taken from Polish lands after 1772. Both sides renounced war compensation, and article 7 guaranteed minorities the use of their language and religion.

The Allied Powers, who had backed the Curzon Line, were at first reluctant to recognise a treaty made without them. France, the United Kingdom, Italy and Japan recognised it in March 1923, and the United States in April. In Poland it was criticised from the start; Piłsudski, who took part only as an observer, called it an act of cowardice, and on 15 May 1921 he apologised to Ukrainian soldiers at the internment camp at Kalisz. The treaty contributed to the failure of his plan for a Polish-led federation of Eastern Europe. It lasted until the Soviet invasion of Poland in 1939, and a 1945 agreement redefined the borders.
peace-of-szatmar: During the Great Turkish War the forces of the Habsburg monarchy conquered large parts of Ottoman Hungary, but the new rulers soon met resistance from Hungarian magnates led by Francis II Rákóczi. From 1703 his rebellion spread through Upper Hungary, today mostly Slovakia, as well as Transylvania and Carpathian Ruthenia. In the 1708 Battle of Trencsén a Habsburg army under Field Marshal Sigbert Heister, backed by Rascian forces, decisively defeated the rebels, yet the conflict dragged on.

Prince Eugene of Savoy, president of the Hofkriegsrat, appointed the loyal Hungarian Field Marshal János Pálffy as chief negotiator. In November 1710 Pálffy contacted the Kuruc commander Sándor Károlyi, and a truce followed on 13 January 1711.

Pálffy and Rákóczi met at Vaja on 31 January, but Rákóczi refused the conditions offered. On 21 February he left for Poland to seek help from the envoys of Tsar Peter the Great, who was occupied with the Great Northern War. He named Károlyi commander-in-chief of the remaining Kuruc strongholds and forbade further talks. Károlyi ignored the order and called an assembly of the insurgents at Szatmár, which on 4 April agreed preliminary conditions and ordered a ceasefire.

On 17 April Emperor Joseph I died. His brother and successor, Charles VI, needed an end to the fighting in order to secure the Hungarian crown, and his envoys soon reached agreement at Szatmár, the present-day Satu Mare in Romania. Rákóczi appeared there and refused all concessions, but he could no longer prevail and returned to Poland. The treaty was concluded on 29 April, and Pálffy, Károlyi and numerous Imperial, Hungarian, Kuruc and Transylvanian envoys held a signing ceremony on 1 May 1711.

The accord granted a full royal pardon to the leaders and rank and file of the insurrection alike. The nobility kept their ancestral privileges on condition of an oath of fealty to the House of Habsburg, and the peasantry kept their existing liberties. The Crown promised free exercise of religion, the constitutional integrity of both the Kingdom of Hungary and the Principality of Transylvania, and the regular summoning of parliament, and it suppressed new foreign institutions judged harmful to the Hungarian estates. On 1 May 1711 some 12,000 former followers of Rákóczi swore allegiance to the House of Habsburg in the fields outside Majtény.
peace-of-szeged: The settlement followed the first campaign of the Crusade of Varna, which began officially on 1 January 1443 with a crusading bull of Pope Eugene IV. In mid-October 1443 King Vladislaus of Hungary, John Hunyadi and Despot George Branković invaded Ottoman lands and won the first encounters, but they were defeated in the snow at Zlatitsa Pass just before Christmas. On the retreat they won the Battle of Kunovica, capturing Mahmud Bey, brother-in-law of Sultan Murad II, and returned home claiming victory.

Murad is believed to have wanted an end to the war, pressed by his sister and by his wife Mara, the daughter of Branković. Peace talks began in March 1444, yet on 24 April Vladislaus also swore before Cardinal Julian Cesarini to lead a new expedition against the Ottomans that summer.

The treaty was made in two halves. At Edirne, Vladislaus's ambassador Stojka Gisdanić and the envoys of Hunyadi and Branković completed the text on 12 June 1444, in haste because İbrahim II of Karaman had invaded Murad's lands in Anatolia. Murad was to return 24 Serbian cities, including Golubac and Smederevo, to Branković as an Ottoman vassal and to release his two blinded sons, Grgur and Stefan, and a ten-year truce was set with Hungary.

The Ottoman envoys Baltaoğlu Süleyman and Vranas brought the treaty to Szeged in August. On 4 August Vladislaus, following a solution devised by Cesarini, solemnly agreed to abjure any treaties he had made or would make with the sultan. After ten more days of talks the final terms also bound the Ottomans to an indemnity of 100,000 gold florins, while Hungary agreed not to attack Bulgaria or cross the Danube. Hunyadi and Branković swore to the treaty at Várad on 15 August 1444.

Branković retook Serbia on 22 August. Hunyadi, who had received the lordship of Világosvár and other estates from Branković, became the largest landowner in the kingdom. Believing his borders secure, Murad abdicated in favour of his twelve-year-old son Mehmed II. On 20 September 1444 the Hungarian army began marching south from Szeged, and the Ottomans recalled Murad.

At the Battle of Varna on 10 November 1444 the Ottomans fought under Murad's standard with the broken treaty nailed to it. The crusaders were decisively defeated and Vladislaus disappeared. Hungary relapsed into civil war, and with the threat to their Balkan front removed the Ottomans could concentrate their forces on the conquest of Constantinople in 1453.
peace-of-vervins: Henry IV had declared war on Spain in 1595. After his victory at the Siege of Amiens in 1597 he promulgated the Edict of Nantes on 13 April 1598, which brought the Wars of Religion in France, including the Brittany Campaign, to an end. The conflict had by then spread into a war across Europe. Vervins lies in Picardy, close to the territory of the Habsburg Netherlands, and the surrounding Thiérache region had suffered heavily in the recent fighting; its many fortified churches of the 16th century still survive.

The representatives of the two kings were hosted by Guillemette de Coucy, co-seigneur of Vervins, in her Châteauneuf de Vervins. The terms were worked out under the auspices of the papal legate of Clement VIII, Alessandro de' Medici, whom the historian Bernard Barbiche called the architect of the treaty. Philip II recognised the formerly Protestant Henry as King of France and withdrew his forces from French soil, leaving what remained of the Catholic League without support. Calais and the coastal fortress of Risban, both taken by the Spaniards in 1596, were returned to France.

Philip II died on 13 September 1598, and his heir Philip III kept to the treaty. Charles Emmanuel I, Duke of Savoy, who had stayed out of the peace, was defeated by Henry IV in 1599 and made a separate Treaty of Lyon with him in 1601. Some historians see Vervins as the final defeat of Philip II, who had pursued dynastic aims by championing ultra-Catholic principles, and as a sign of the long decline of Habsburg Spain and the gradual rise of France to dominance in Europe during the Grand Siècle that followed.
peace-of-westphalia: Europe had been battered by the Thirty Years' War and by the overlapping Eighty Years' War, begun about 1568, in which the Dutch Republic struggled for independence from Spain. The Thirty Years' War, centred on the Holy Roman Empire, killed between 4.5 and 8 million people. The Peace of Prague of 1635 ended most of its religious aspects. Negotiations between France and the Emperor began in Cologne in 1636 but were blocked by Cardinal Richelieu, who insisted on including all his allies. In December 1641 Sweden, France and the Empire agreed a preliminary peace at Hamburg.

The main talks were held in the neighbouring Westphalian cities of Münster and Osnabrück, both kept neutral and demilitarised. The Empire and France negotiated in Catholic Münster, and the Empire and Sweden in Osnabrück, which was held by Protestant forces. A total of 109 delegations took part, but they never met in plenary session; they arrived between 1643 and 1646 and left between 1647 and 1649. The papal nuncio Fabio Chigi and the Venetian envoy Alvise Contarini acted as mediators. Portugal did not take part, because Spain threatened to withdraw.

Two treaties were signed in October 1648: the Treaty of Münster, between the Emperor and France with their allies, and the Treaty of Osnabrück, between the Emperor and Sweden with theirs. The Dutch Republic and Spain signed their own treaty on 30 January 1648.

The settlement recognised Catholicism, Lutheranism and Calvinism, Calvinism receiving legal recognition for the first time. It replaced the principle by which subjects followed their ruler's religion: rulers could no longer dictate the religion of their subjects, and 1 January 1624 was fixed as the normal year for deciding a state's official religion. France kept the bishoprics of Metz, Toul and Verdun and received the cities of the Décapole in Alsace, except Strasbourg, and Pignerol. Sweden received an indemnity of five million thalers, Western Pomerania, Wismar and the Prince-Bishoprics of Bremen and Verden, which gave it a seat in the Imperial Diet. France and Sweden became guarantors of the imperial constitution.

Pope Innocent X condemned the settlement in the brief Zelo Domus Dei as null, void and unjust. Some terms were ambiguous: The Swedish-Brandenburg border in Pomerania was settled only in 1653. Many scholars of international relations see the Peace as the origin of Westphalian sovereignty, but some historians argue that this view emerged in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Older accounts say the Emperor was stripped of power, but modern research holds that he kept significant influence, for example in the Imperial Diet.
peace-of-zsitvatorok: The Peace of Zsitvatorok, also called the Treaty of Sitvatorok, ended the thirteen-year Long Turkish War between the Ottoman Empire and the Habsburg monarchy. It belonged to a system of peace treaties that also ended the anti-Habsburg uprising of Stephen Bocskai, which lasted from 1604 to 1606. It was negotiated between 24 October and 11 November 1606 at the former mouth of the Žitava River, called Zsitva in Hungarian, where it flows into the Danube in Royal Hungary, now part of Slovakia. The place later became the small settlement of Žitavská Tôňa. Sultan Ahmed I and Archduke Matthias of Austria signed on behalf of the Holy Roman Empire, and Matthias's brother, the Emperor Rudolf II, ratified the treaty on 9 December.

The peace was signed for twenty years. Diplomatic historians have interpreted it in different ways, partly because the Ottoman Turkish and Hungarian texts differ. The Hungarian text had a payment of 200,000 florins as a once-and-for-all tribute in place of the annual tribute of 30,000 guldens paid before the war, whereas the Ottoman text foresaw that the payment would be repeated after three years. The treaty prohibited Ottoman looting campaigns into Royal Hungary and allowed Hungarian settlements under Ottoman rule to collect taxes themselves through village judges. The Ottomans also acknowledged the tax-free privilege of nobles, though they never really complied with these terms. The Crimean Khanate was explicitly included as a vassal of the Ottoman Empire.

The Ottomans' inability to penetrate further into Royal Hungary during the war was one of their first geopolitical defeats. Even so, the treaty stabilised the Habsburg-Ottoman frontier for half a century to the benefit of both sides: the Habsburgs faced serious domestic opposition in the following years, while the Ottomans, apart from internal rebellion, had open conflicts on other frontiers, in Poland and Iran.

The treaty also mattered for protocol. The sultan, who had borne the title Kayser-i Rûm, Caesar of the Roman Empire, since the fall of Constantinople, titled the Holy Roman Emperor Padishah, one of his own titles, for the first time. Until then Ottoman diplomacy had regarded the emperor as merely the kral, king, of Vienna. Christian Europe read this as an acceptance of a divisio imperii between West and East. The next European ruler granted such respect was Catherine the Great of Russia, in the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca of 1774.
peacock-throne: Shah Jahan ruled from the newly built capital of Shahjahanabad, and his court was meant to be a mirror of paradise on earth. A ruler at its centre would be worthy of a Throne of Solomon, covered in gold and jewels and approached by steps, so that he seemed to float above the ground. Said Gilani and workers of the imperial goldsmiths' department built it in seven years, at twice the cost of the Taj Mahal. It stood in the Diwan-i-Khas in the Red Fort of Delhi.

It was first called the Jeweled Throne, Takht-Murassa, and later historians named it from the peacock figures on its canopy. Its inauguration in March 1635 was set by astrologers for a day that coincided with Eid al-Fitr and Nowruz.

No painting matching the early descriptions is known. The Mughal historians Abdul Hamid Lahori and Inayat Khan describe a throne with a canopy on twelve pillars, set with rubies, garnets, diamonds, pearls and emeralds, with peacocks on the pillars, reached by three jewelled steps. Lahori names the Koh-i-Noor and the Timur Ruby among its stones.

François Bernier saw the emperor seated on it and put its value at four crores of rupees. Jean-Baptiste Tavernier inspected it in 1665 and counted 108 large balas rubies and 116 large emeralds, but named none of the great historic stones, which may have been with Shah Jahan, then confined at Agra. Tavernier is considered among the least reliable sources from a conventional historical perspective.

Nader Shah took the original in 1739 after his invasion of India, with the Koh-i Noor and Darya-i Noor diamonds, and his plunder was so great that he stopped taxation for three years. Another throne was made for the Mughal emperor, shown in 19th-century Indian paintings, which disappeared during or soon after the Indian Rebellion of 1857. Part of the original may have been converted into the Sun Throne of the Persian crown jewels. Later Shahs of Persia were sometimes said to hold the Peacock Throne, symbolically. In the 1860s King Ludwig II of Bavaria had a romanticised version built in the Moorish Kiosk at Linderhof Palace.
peada: Peada was a son of Penda of Mercia, who made him king of the Middle Angles. Bede calls him an excellent youth, most worthy of the title and person of a king. When Peada sought to marry the daughter of King Oswiu of Northumbria, still a pagan like his father, Oswiu made the marriage conditional on his conversion and that of the Middle Angles. Bede says Peada declared he would become a Christian even if refused the bride, persuaded above all by a son of Oswiu, his friend and kinsman, who had married Peada's sister Cyneburga.

Peada was baptised by Bishop Finan of Lindisfarne, with all his earls, soldiers and servants, at a royal village called At the Wall, and returned home with four priests to teach and baptise his people: Cedd, Adda, Betti and Diuma, the last a Scot. Bede reports that they were willingly heard, and that many nobles and commoners were baptised daily. On 15 November 655 Oswiu defeated and killed Penda at the Battle of the Winwaed and took power in Mercia. He allowed Peada to rule the southern part, which Bede reckons at 5,000 families, against 7,000 in the north, the two divided by the River Trent.

According to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, Peada and Oswiu together founded the minster of Medeshamstede at Peterborough in honour of St Peter, naming it after a spring called Medeswael, and entrusted it to a monk named Seaxwulf. The Chronicle adds that Peada ruled no length of time, because he was betrayed by his own queen at Eastertide. Bede likewise reports that he was killed through his wife's treachery during the celebration of Easter in 656.
peanut: The genus Arachis is native to South America, east of the Andes, around Peru, Bolivia, Argentina and Brazil. The cultivated peanut, Arachis hypogaea, arose from a hybrid between two wild species, thought to be Arachis duranensis and Arachis ipaensis. The first hybrid would have been sterile, but spontaneous chromosome doubling restored its fertility. Genetic analysis suggests the hybridisation happened only once, giving rise to a wild form found in a few places in north-western Argentina, and by artificial selection to the cultivated plant.

Domestication made the plant bushier and more compact, with a different pod structure and larger seeds. Cultivation spread from its centre of origin and formed further centres of diversity in Peru, Ecuador, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay. The oldest known remains of pods, about 7,600 years old, were found in Peru, where dry conditions preserve organic material; cultivation almost certainly began earlier in the moister centre of origin.

The peanut is a legume grown mainly for its seeds, which are held in pods that develop underground, a trait called geocarpy and unusual among legumes. After fertilisation a short stalk grows into the soil, and the fruit ripens there. Botanically the pods are not nuts. Like other legumes, peanuts harbour nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules, which improve soil fertility and make them valuable in crop rotation.

The seeds yield oil and are eaten roasted, boiled or ground into peanut butter and sauces. Peanut sauces are used in Latin America, West Africa and Southeast Asia, and in the Indian subcontinent peanuts are made into chikki, a sweet brittle. The plant tops are used for silage and the oilcake left after pressing is fed to livestock. Between 1.4 and 2 per cent of people in Europe and the United States experience allergic reactions to peanuts, which can be fatal.

Many pre-Columbian cultures, such as the Moche, depicted peanuts in their art, and cultivation was well established in Mesoamerica before the Spanish arrived. The conquistadors found the plant, called tlālcacahuatl in Nahuatl, on sale in the marketplace of Tenochtitlan. European traders later spread it across the tropics and subtropics. In West Africa it substantially replaced the Bambara groundnut, another legume whose pods ripen underground.

In the United States peanuts were introduced in the colonial period and grown as a garden crop; from 1870 they served as animal feed until human consumption grew in the 1930s. George Washington Carver promoted the peanut in the American South, where repeated cotton planting had depleted the soil.
