The allied forces appeared before Jerusalem and demanded its surrender, and the prophet Isaiah supported Ahaz. The allies had proposed to put a son of Tabeel on the throne of Judah. Ahaz instead appealed to Tiglath-Pileser for help, and Judah became a tributary of Assyria.

After Ahaz paid tribute, the Assyrians sacked Damascus and annexed Aram. According to 2 Kings 16:9 the population of Aram was deported and Rezin executed. According to 2 Kings 15:29 Tiglath-Pileser also attacked Israel and took Ijon, Abel Beth Maacah, Janoah, Kedesh and Hazor, and Gilead and Galilee, including all the land of Naphtali, and deported the people to Assyria. Tiglath-Pileser records this in one of his inscriptions.

Pekah was assassinated by Hoshea ben Elah, a captain in his own army, who took the throne. An inscription of Tiglath-Pileser mentions that the Israelites killed Pekah, and it has been inferred that the people, seeing the inevitable outcome of the contest with Assyria, removed their fighting king and submitted. His end can be established fairly firmly as 732 or 731 BCE.

The biblical data for his reign use two conflicting reckonings. One gives him a long reign of twenty years, the other a shorter reign starting in the 52nd year of Uzziah. Carl Lederer proposed in 1887 and H. J. Cook argued in 1954 that Pekah ruled a rival kingdom in Gilead beside Menahem's kingdom in Samaria, and that the two systems reflect this rivalry. E. R. Thiele accepted the view, which is consistent with the Assyrian chronicles. Others reject all or part of the biblical sources on Pekah, and William F. Albright dated his reign differently.
pekan: Local lore holds that the town is named after the Bunga Pekan, a white flower like jasmine that once grew wild along the banks of the Pahang River and is said to be extinct; other sources derive the name from Pekan Sehari, a Sunday market that still exists. Pekan is also the name of the district around the town and of a parliamentary constituency. The town lies about fifteen minutes from the sandy beaches of the coast, and Lake Chini, one of the largest freshwater lakes in Malaysia, is an hour's drive away.

Pekan is thought to have existed since the Old Pahang Kingdom, when the town was called Inderapura, or Pura for short. The old capital lay on both banks of the Pahang and the Pahang Tua rivers as far as Tanjung Langgar, and Arab and Chinese writers mentioned it.

The town was divided into Pekan Lama, Old Pekan, where the first shops were built and some original wooden shophouses still stand, and Pekan Baharu, once known as Kampung Cina. In the late 19th century the sultan and the villagers were close: when a gong was struck in the palace, villagers gathered for his service, for example to join him hunting. The people of Kampong Mengkasar nearby are said to descend from Tok Tuan of Makassar in Sulawesi.

Under British rule a residence for the British Resident was built in 1929, and the Chiefs' Rest House, a wooden guest house for the chiefs of Pahang attending the palace, was completed in 1926. The sultan acquired the Resident's house in 1948 as Kota Beram Palace, moving in 1965 to the new Abu Bakar Palace. From the early 1970s, under Tun Abdul Razak Hussein, the second Prime Minister of Malaysia, who was born in Pekan, the town became a base for vehicle assembly.

Pekan is the royal capital of Pahang and the home of its royal family. Its landmarks include the Royal Palace, the Royal Mausoleum, the Masjid Abdullah of the 1920s, the Abu Bakar Royal Mosque and the Sultan Abu Bakar Museum, opened in October 1976 in the former Resident's house. A campus of Universiti Malaysia Pahang Al-Sultan Abdullah stands there.
peking-university: After China's defeat in the Sino-Japanese War, intellectuals including Kang Youwei, Liang Qichao and Yan Fu called for reform of the education system. On 11 June 1898 the Guangxu Emperor authorised the Imperial University of Peking, called in Chinese Jingshi Daxuetang, as part of the Hundred Days' Reform. It was formally established on 3 July 1898, when the emperor approved the charter written by Liang. William Alexander Parsons Martin was its first president. Most of the reforms were abolished when the Empress Dowager Cixi seized power on 21 September, but the university survived with reduced scope. It opened on 31 December with 160 students instead of the 500 planned, teaching mathematics, astronomy, physics, botany and zoology.

After the Xinhai Revolution the Imperial University was renamed the Government University of Peking in 1912 and the National University of Peking in 1919. Cai Yuanpei was appointed president on 26 December 1917. Inspired by the German model of academic freedom, he introduced faculty governance and democratic management. The university became the country's largest institution of higher learning, with 14 departments and more than 2,000 students. He recruited figures of the New Culture Movement, among them Hu Shih, Li Dazhao, Chen Duxiu and Lu Xun, while conservatives such as Gu Hongming also taught there.

On 1 May 1919 students learned that the Treaty of Versailles would allow Japan to take over Germany's rights in Shandong province. On 4 May students from thirteen universities marched to Tiananmen, demanding that the Beiyang government refuse to sign and that three officials who they believed cooperated with Japan be dismissed. Strikes and boycotts of Japanese goods spread to China's major cities, and the government released arrested students, dismissed the three officials and did not sign the treaty. During the Second World War, from 1938 to 1946, its staff joined those of Tsinghua and Nankai universities in the National Southwestern Associated University at Kunming.

In 1952, after the founding of the People's Republic, the university merged with Yenching University in a nationwide restructuring of universities, and in April 2000 Beijing Medical University was merged into it. It now has eight faculties and six affiliated hospitals, and a Shenzhen Graduate School opened in 2001. The main campus in Haidian stands on the former site of Qing dynasty imperial gardens and keeps traditional Chinese landscaping, including pagodas and Weiming Lake. The American architect Talbot Hamlin designed some of the buildings put up between 1919 and 1922. Tu Youyou, an alumna, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2015.
pelagius-of-asturias: Pelagius was born around 685, but the details of his early life are largely unknown. He was traditionally depicted with Visigothic origin, though recent scholarship increasingly supports the idea that he was a nobleman of Hispano-Roman descent, linked to the local Asturian elite. He is believed to be the son of Favila. The Chronica Albeldense, written three centuries after his death, says Favila was a dux of Gallaecia killed by the Visigothic king Wittiza, while the Chronicle of Alfonso III calls Pelagius a grandson of Chindasuinth and says his father was blinded in Córdoba at Wittiza's instigation. Both agree that Wittiza exiled him from Toledo.

A later tradition tells of Munuza, the Berber governor of Iegione, who was attracted to Pelagius's sister and sent word to Tariq ibn Ziyad, who ordered Pelagius captured and sent to Córdoba. If Munuza's seat was Gijón, the Arabs had already established their rule in Asturias, and Pelagius may not have led a local resistance.

At some point Pelagius is said to have rebelled, for reasons that are unknown; such rebellions by local authorities were a common theme in Visigothic Spain. A Muslim army under the command of Alkama and the Christian bishop of Seville, Oppa, was sent against him. In a battle near Covadonga Alkama was killed and Oppa captured. Moorish chronicles describe Pelagius and his small force as thirty wild donkeys. Dates for the battle vary between sources.

Pelagius was elected princeps of the Asturians by the local magnates in the Visigothic manner and made his capital at Cangas de Onís. His kingdom, at first centred on the eastern Asturias, soon grew. He married his daughter Ermesinda to the future king Alfonso I, son of his eastern neighbour, Duke Peter of Cantabria.

Pelagius reigned for eighteen or nineteen years until his death in 737 and was succeeded by his son Fafila. He was buried in the church of Santa Eulalia de Abamia, near Cangas de Onís. King Alfonso X of Castile later moved his remains, with those of his wife Gaudiosa and his sister, to the Holy Cave of Covadonga.

He is credited with initiating the Reconquista, the Christian reconquest of the Iberian Peninsula, and with establishing the Asturian monarchy. The chief sources for his life are two Latin chronicles written in the late ninth century in the kingdom he founded, the Chronica Albeldensia of about 881 and the Chronicle of Alfonso III.
pelagonia: Pelagonia is a plain shared between North Macedonia and Greece. It includes the cities of Bitola and Prilep, in the Pelagonia Statistical Region of North Macedonia, and the city of Florina, in Western Macedonia in Greece. The border crossing at Medžitlija-Niki lies on it. In antiquity it was bounded by Paeonia to the north and east, Lynkestis and Almopia to the south and Illyria to the west, and corresponded roughly to the present municipalities of Prilep, Bitola, Mogila, Novaci, Kruševo and Krivogaštani. A tract of 137,000 hectares of the plain is a designated Important Bird Area.

The region took its name from the Pelagones, an ancient tribe of Upper Macedonia centred on the plain. Greek mythology made their eponym Pelagon a son of the river-god Axios and the father of Asteropaeus, a Paeonian leader in Homer's Iliad. Mycenaean objects have been found in the area and are shown in the Museum of Bitola. Menelaus of Pelagonia, around 360 BCE, is said to have fled to Athens when Philip II annexed his kingdom to Macedon. Strabo called the region Tripolitis.

In medieval times Pelagonia took on a broader meaning and was contested for centuries between the Byzantine and Bulgarian empires, before the Serbian Empire annexed it in the 14th century. After that empire fragmented it belonged to the Lordship of Prilep until the Ottoman conquest at the end of the century. The Battle of Pelagonia in 1259, between the Byzantines of Nicaea and the Latins, was fought during the Struggle for Constantinople. Its site is disputed: the sources name only Boril's Wood, which scholars have placed near Prilep, Kastoria or Bitola, and two modern scholars suggest the plain north of Kastoria near Vevi.

Florina was taken by the Greek Army from the Ottomans in November 1912, but the army turned east towards Thessaloniki on news of the Bulgarian advance, and most of the plain was annexed by Serbia. The Monastir Gap, the open stretch of the Greek border here, was strategically important in World War I, during the Monastir Offensive, and in April 1941, when German forces came through it and took Florina on 10 April before the Battle of Vevi on 11 and 12 April.
peleliu: Peleliu, also spelled Beliliou, is an island of the nation of Palau. With two small islands to its north-east it forms one of the sixteen states of Palau. It lies about 10 kilometres north-east of Angaur and 40 kilometres south-west of Koror, at the southern tip of the lagoon that encircles the main group of islands. The island is a raised platform of coral limestone of about 17 square kilometres, ringed by mangrove forest. On its west side a steep spine rises to 75 metres, a tangled maze of jagged limestone spires, later named Bloody Nose Ridge.

Westerners first recorded the sighting of Peleliu, Babeldaob and Koror when the Spanish expedition of Ruy López de Villalobos passed at the end of January 1543, charting them as Los Arrecifes, the Reefs. After its defeat in the Spanish–American War, Spain sold Palau, Peleliu included, to Germany in 1899, and control passed to Japan in 1914.

Expecting an American invasion, the Japanese turned Peleliu into a fortress. Palauans were evacuated to Babeldaob in 1943, and as many as 10,000 Japanese dug into the natural caves and fissures of the limestone, reinforcing them with concrete bunkers. They withstood a naval bombardment and met the American invasion force at nearly full strength on 5 September 1944. Their defence in depth in the caves and rock formations of the Umurbrogol Mountains maximised casualties among the attackers. More than 2,000 Americans and 10,000 Japanese were killed; no local civilians were, having been moved to other islands. Koror stayed in Japanese hands to the end of the war.

The ruins of many military installations, such as the airstrip, are still intact, shipwrecks from the battle lie visible just off the coast, and war memorials stand to both the American and the Japanese dead. The whole island is listed in the United States as the Peleliu Battlefield and designated a National Historic Landmark. In 1947 more than 30 Japanese were still hiding in caves, and they surrendered when the Americans sent a senior Japanese officer to persuade them. Peleliu was placed under United States control in 1947 as part of the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, and when Palau became independent in 1978 it became a state of the new republic, with its own constitution adopted in 1982.
pelias: In Greek myth Pelias was the son of Tyro and the god Poseidon. Tyro was married to King Cretheus of Iolcus, with whom she had three sons, Aeson, Pherês and Amythaon, but she loved the river god Enipeus. Poseidon disguised himself as Enipeus and lay with her, and the twins Pelias and Neleus were born. Tyro exposed them on a mountain, where a herdsman raised them, or in another account a maid. As adults they found their mother and killed her stepmother Sidero for mistreating her, which earned Pelias Hera's undying hatred.

Pelias wished to rule all Thessaly. He banished Neleus and Pherês and locked Aeson in the dungeons of Iolcus, near the modern city of Volos. There Aeson married and had several children, of whom Jason was the best known. Aeson sent Jason away for fear that Pelias would kill him as a possible heir.

Pelias ruled Iolcus and had many children, among them Acastus and the daughters known together as the Peliades. An oracle warned him to beware a man wearing one sandal. Jason, raised by the centaur Chiron on Mount Pelion, came to Iolcus when Pelias was offering a sacrifice to Poseidon by the sea, having lost one sandal in the flooded river Anaurus. Pelias asked what Jason would do if he met the man destined to be his downfall, and Jason answered that he would send him after the Golden Fleece.

Pelias sent Jason to Colchis for the fleece, which hung on an oak in a grove sacred to Ares and was guarded by a dragon. Jason had the shipwright Argus build the Argo, and with the Argonauts he won the fleece with the help of Medea, daughter of King Aeëtes. In his absence Pelias, thinking the Argo had sunk, told Aeson and Promachus so, and they killed themselves by poison. It is unknown, but possible, that Pelias killed them himself.

On Jason's return Pelias still refused to give up the throne. Medea showed his daughters how she could turn an old ram into a young one by cutting it up and boiling it, and a live young ram leapt from the pot. The Peliades cut their father into pieces and threw him in a pot, expecting him to emerge rejuvenated, and he did not survive. Jason, now an accessory to the crime, was not made king, and Pelias's son Acastus banished Jason and Medea to Corinth and reclaimed the kingdom. At the funeral games for Pelias, Atalanta defeated Peleus at wrestling, a match that became a popular subject in Greek art.
peljesac: Pelješac is the second largest peninsula in Croatia and lies in southern Dalmatia, in Dubrovnik-Neretva County. It is 65 km long from the isthmus at Ston to Cape Lovišta. The Bay of Mali Ston separates it from the Klek peninsula of Bosnia and Herzegovina and from the Croatian mainland, and the Strait of Pelješac divides it from the island of Korčula. Its highest peak, Sveti Ilija, reaches 961 m. The name most likely comes from Pelisac, a hill above the port town of Orebić, and is a relatively new one: earlier names include Stonski Rat, Puncta Stagni and Ponta di Stagno.

The site of Nakovana preserves artefacts showing continuous human settlement over several millennia. After the Illyrian Wars the area became part of the Roman province of Dalmatia, and it came under Byzantine rule in the 6th century. After the Slavs arrived, Ston and Rat, the then name of the peninsula, lay in the principality of Zahumlje, which passed through several rulers, among them Stefan Nemanja in 1168 and Stjepan II Kotromanić from 1325.

The Republic of Ragusa, or Dubrovnik, bought the peninsula in several purchases, first in 1333 and again on 15 January 1399. After an earthquake in 1252 destroyed old Ston, the people of Dubrovnik settled a new town in 1326 to defend the peninsula and protect the salt works from which they earned large revenue. Dubrovnik worked to spread Catholicism and expelled the Orthodox clergy in 1335. The Walls of Ston, built by the Republic, are the second longest walls in Europe. France occupied the region in 1806, and it passed to Austria in 1815, to Yugoslavia in 1918 and to the Republic of Croatia in 1991.

The peninsula is divided into the municipalities of Orebić, Trpanj, Janjina and Ston. Car ferries link Trpanj to Ploče, Orebić to Korčula and Prapratno to Mljet. The Pelješac Bridge near Brijesta joins the peninsula to the mainland near Komarna and bypasses the strip of coast at Neum that gives Bosnia and Herzegovina access to the sea. Forests of Aleppo pine, kermes oak and holm oak cover much of it.
pellegrino-rossi: Rossi was born in Carrara, then in the Duchy of Massa and Carrara, and studied at the universities of Pisa and Bologna, becoming professor of law at Bologna in 1812. In 1815 he backed Joachim Murat's Neapolitan anti-Austrian expedition, and the Rimini Proclamation, an early call for Italian unification, is widely attributed to him. When Murat fell he fled to France and then to Geneva, where his course on Roman law won him the rare honour of citizenship of Geneva.

Elected to the cantonal council of Geneva in 1820 and a member of the diet of 1832, Rossi drafted a revised constitution, the Pacte Rossi. Its rejection by a majority of the people affected him deeply, and he accepted François Guizot's invitation to settle in France. In 1833 he took the chair of political economy at the Collège de France left by the death of Jean-Baptiste Say; he became a French citizen and professor of constitutional law in Paris in 1834, a peer in 1839 and dean of the law faculty in 1843.

In 1845 Guizot sent him to Rome as ambassador, with the question of the Jesuits as his task. The Revolution of 1848 brought down Guizot's government and cut Rossi's tie with France, and he stayed in Rome as a minister of Pope Pius IX. His moderate liberal programme, with the vote limited to the well-off, had narrow appeal: the clerical party blocked it and the revolutionaries dismissed it as paltry. On 15 November 1848 he was stabbed in the neck at the Palazzo della Cancelleria, on his way to open parliament.

That night crowds outside his widow's house praised the hand that had killed him. In 1854 a man named Gabriele Constantini was convicted and executed for the murder, though the killer is said to have been Luigi Brunetti, son of Ciceruacchio, acting at the urging of Pietro Sterbini. Rossi's chief work, the Cours d'économie politique, follows Smith, Say, Malthus and Ricardo in favouring free trade and labour while valuing associations. His use of statistics earned him the name geometrician of economy, and he wrote an essay on the principle of non-intervention. Carrara raised a statue to him.
pelopidas: Pelopidas came from a distinguished family and had great wealth, which he spent on his friends and on public service while he lived the rough life of an athlete. According to Plutarch he took care of the deserving poor of Thebes and was ashamed to spend more on himself than the poorest Thebans did. When friends urged him to look after his money for the sake of his wife and children, he pointed to a blind, crippled pauper named Nicodemus and said that money was necessary for Nicodemus.

In 384 BCE he served in a Theban contingent sent to support the Spartans at the Siege of Mantinea, where the Arcadians wounded him seven times in front. Epaminondas defended his body and arms single-handed until the Spartan king Agesipolis came to their aid. Plutarch says the incident cemented their friendship, and Pelopidas was Epaminondas's partner in politics for the next twenty years.

After the Spartans seized the Theban citadel in 382 BCE, Pelopidas fled to Athens and led a conspiracy to free the city. Sparta installed oligarchic governments in the cities it conquered. In 379 BCE his democratic faction rose in a surprise revolt, killed many of the aristocrats who supported Spartan rule, and the Spartan garrison surrendered to the army he gathered.

He was elected boeotarch, or war leader, in that year and in twelve later ones. Around 375 BCE he routed a much larger Spartan force at Tegyra, a victory owed mainly to the Sacred Band, an elite corps of 300 soldiers. At Leuctra in 371 BCE he made the Sacred Band close with the Spartans so quickly that Epaminondas's new oblique order succeeded, and Thebes began to replace Sparta as the leading city of Greece. In 370 BCE both generals entered the Peloponnese and refounded Messene as an independent city, which permanently deprived Sparta of its hegemonic power. In 367 BCE Pelopidas went as envoy to the Persian king Artaxerxes II and obtained a settlement of Greece to Theban wishes, including the independence of Messene.

In 369 BCE he marched against Alexander of Pherae at the request of the Thessalians and then arbitrated in Macedon between two claimants to the throne, bringing hostages home to Thebes, among them the king's younger brother Philip, later king himself. Alexander of Pherae later seized him, and two expeditions from Thebes were needed to free him.

In 364 BCE the Thessalian towns appealed again against Alexander of Pherae. An eclipse of the sun limited the troops Pelopidas could bring, yet he defeated the tyrant's larger force on the ridge of Cynoscephalae. Wishing to kill Alexander himself, he rushed forward and was cut down by the tyrant's guards. Plutarch considered him a leader who threw away his life through recklessness and anger.
peloponnese: The Peloponnese is a peninsula at the southern tip of mainland Greece, covering 21,549.6 square kilometres. It is joined to the rest of the country by the Isthmus of Corinth, which separates the Gulf of Corinth from the Saronic Gulf; the Corinth Canal was cut across the isthmus in 1893. The interior is mountainous, with extensive lowlands in the west, in the Evrotas Valley in the south and on the Argolid Peninsula in the north-east. The climate is mostly Mediterranean, with more rain on the west coast than in the east.

The peninsula has been inhabited since prehistoric times, and its name means the island of Pelops, after a hero said in myth to have conquered the region. In the Bronze Age the Mycenaean civilization dominated it from palaces such as Mycenae, Pylos and Tiryns, and collapsed suddenly at the end of the 2nd millennium BCE. In classical antiquity the cities of Argos, Corinth and Sparta lay here, and Olympia, in Elis, was the site of the Olympic Games, first held in 776 BCE. In the 6th century BCE Sparta established its hegemony by founding the Peloponnesian League, which defeated Athens in the Peloponnesian War of 431–404 BCE. Rome razed Corinth in 146 BCE and made the Peloponnese part of the province of Achaea.

After 395 the peninsula belonged to the Byzantine Empire, and the Hexamilion wall was built across the isthmus after Alaric's raid of 396–397. The scale of Slavic settlement in the 7th and 8th centuries is disputed, and is now thought to have been much smaller than once believed. Under Ottoman rule the Morea became a province, and later a separate eyalet with Patras as its capital. The Greeks of the Peloponnese rose with Russian aid in the Orlov Revolt of 1770, which was crushed by Albanian mercenaries, and the Greek War of Independence began there, when rebels took Kalamata on 23 March 1821.

The Peloponnese is divided among three administrative regions, most of it belonging to the Peloponnese region. Its largest city is Patras, followed by Kalamata and Corinth. Its archaeological sites, from the Bronze Age to the Middle Ages, include Mycenae, Tiryns, Olympia, Epidaurus, Bassae and the Byzantine town of Mystras, all of which are World Heritage Sites, with the medieval fortress towns of Monemvasia and Methoni. The Nemea region is known for red wine and the Kalamata olive for its produce.
peloponnesian-league: The Peloponnesian League is the modern name for the Spartan system of alliances, which lasted from about 550 to 366 BCE. The name is inaccurate, since some members lay outside the Peloponnese and it was not really a league; its ancient name was the Lacedemonians and their allies. Sparta had expanded by conquering Laconia and Messenia and reducing their populations to slavery as helots, but its attempt to subjugate Tegea failed at the battle of the Fetters.

Sparta then turned to diplomacy, the so-called bones policy of appropriating the relics of mythical heroes, beginning with the bones of Orestes, brought from Tegea. Tegea then signed an alliance treaty with Sparta, the starting point of the League. Fear of Argos drove its other neighbours, among them Mantinea, Phlius, Corinth and Epidaurus, to conclude treaties on the same model, and by the 540s Sparta had alliances with all the Peloponnesian cities except Argos and those of the Achaean north.

There was no collective treaty. Sparta, as hegemon, concluded a separate treaty with each member, who swore to have the same friends and enemies as the Spartans and to follow them wherever they led. Members were bound only to Sparta and could even wage war on each other. The treaties were permanent and forbade secession, and many members stayed because Sparta supported the oligarchs who ruled most of them.

After a failed Spartan attempt to impose Isagoras on Athens, about 506 BCE, in which the Corinthians turned back, Sparta had to concede a congress of the League where members voted on war and peace. Spartan citizens first debated in their assembly, and if the vote was positive the allies then voted in the congress. Allies rejected Spartan proposals on occasion, with Corinth most influential. In war Sparta held exclusive command. In 378 BCE the League was reorganised into ten military districts, each owing 3,000 to 4,000 hoplites.

Tensions between the Peloponnesian League and the Delian League led by Athens were key to the outbreak of the First Peloponnesian War in 460 BCE, after Megara, a member, defected to Athens. The two leagues came into conflict again in the Peloponnesian War, in which the League defeated Athens and its allies in 404 BCE, and Athens was forced to join it. Sparta later grew more interventionist, forcing Elis back into the League about 400 BCE and disbanding Mantinea into villages in 385 BCE.

The defeat of Sparta by Thebes at Leuctra in 371 BCE shook its control. The Arcadians founded their own federal Arcadian League and left, and the Theban liberation of Messenia in 369 BCE reduced the League further. Corinth's departure in 366 BCE effectively ended it.
peloponnesian-war: After defeating the second Persian invasion of Greece in 480 BCE, Athens led the Delian League, named from the island of Delos where it kept its treasury, in attacks on Persian territory in the Aegean and Ionia. Some formerly independent allies became tribute-paying subjects, which caused resentment. Thucydides wrote that the growth of Athenian power and the alarm it caused in Lacedaemon made war inevitable.

The Thirty Years' Peace was tested in 440 BCE, when Samos rebelled from Athens, but a congress of Sparta's allies, with Corinth opposed, voted against war. The more immediate cause was a quarrel between Corinth and its colony Corcyra. Athens made a defensive alliance with Corcyra, and its ships took part in the Battle of Sybota.

The first phase, the Archidamian War, began on 4 April 431 BCE with a Theban attack on the Athenian outpost at Plataea. Spartan forces invaded Attica for about three weeks at a time, since soldiers were expected home for the harvest; the longest invasion, in 430 BCE, lasted 40 days. Athens gained the upper hand at Sphacteria in 425 BCE but lost to Thebes at Delium in 424, and the Peace of Nicias was signed in 421 BCE. A Spartan victory at Mantinea in 418 BCE then restored its control of the Peloponnese.

In 415 BCE Athens sent the Sicilian Expedition against Syracuse. Alcibiades, charged with religious crimes after the mutilation of the hermai, defected to Sparta. By 413 BCE the entire Athenian fleet had been destroyed and virtually the whole army sold into slavery. On Alcibiades's advice Sparta fortified Decelea, and as many as 20,000 Athenian slaves were freed there. Persia, whose king Darius II resented Athenian power, backed Sparta with money and ships. Lysander destroyed 168 Athenian ships at Aegospotami in 405 BCE, and only 12 escaped.

Athens fell in 404 BCE and the Delian League was dissolved. Athens was ruled for a short time by the Thirty Tyrants, a regime set up by Sparta, until Thrasybulus overthrew them and restored democracy in 403 BCE. Sparta was defeated by Thebes at Leuctra in 371 BCE, and Macedon later became the strongest power in Greece.

Athens never regained its pre-war prosperity. The conflict between a democratic and an oligarchic alliance turned limited, formalised warfare into total war between rival ideologies, and civil war between those factions became common. The main source is Thucydides, an Athenian exiled in 423 BCE, whose account breaks off in 411 BCE and was continued by Xenophon.
pelusium: Pelusium lay at the eastern extreme of the Nile Delta, about 30 kilometres south-east of modern Port Said, between the seaboard and the marshes and about two and a half miles from the sea. Its port was choked by sand as early as the first century BCE, and by the third century CE the city was at least four miles from the Mediterranean.

Flax of very fine quality grew in the neighbouring lands, and the city was known as an early producer of beer, called the Pelusian drink. It stood as a border fortress on the frontier, protecting Egypt on the side of Syria and the sea, and so was directly exposed to any invader. It was often besieged, and several important battles were fought around its walls.

The battle of 525 BCE, fought near Pelusium, transferred the throne of the pharaohs to Cambyses II of Persia; Herodotus wrote that the fields were still strewn with bones when he visited. In 373 BCE the Persian satrap Pharnabazus and the Athenian commander Iphicrates withdrew without attacking, because Nectanebo I had flooded the neighbouring lands and blocked the channels of the Nile. About 340 BCE the Persians took the city, whose garrison held 5,000 Greek mercenaries, after Nectanebo II was defeated in a pitched battle. In 333 BCE it opened its gates to Alexander the Great.

Antiochus Epiphanes defeated the troops of Ptolemy Philometor under its walls in 173 BCE. In 55 BCE Mark Antony took it as cavalry commander of the Roman proconsul Gabinius. Pompey was murdered near it in 48 BCE, and Augustus was admitted in 30 BCE. The Plague of Justinian first emerged at Pelusium in 541. In 639 it offered protracted but ineffectual resistance to Amr ibn al-As, and in 1118 Baldwin I of Jerusalem razed it. Under the later sultans the harbours were neglected, and the city, long in decline, almost disappeared from history.

Pelusium became a Roman provincial capital, that of Augustamnica Prima, and a metropolitan see; its bishop Dorotheus took part in the First Council of Nicaea in 325. It remains a titular see of the Catholic Church and the seat of a metropolitan bishopric of the Eastern Orthodox Church. The first excavations began in 1910 under the French Egyptologist Jean Cledat, and salvage work started in 1991, when the planned Peace Canal threatened the site.

Egyptian teams explored the Roman theatre and the Byzantine basilica, and a Polish expedition worked in the Great Theater, of the 2nd or 3rd century, from 2003 to 2009. In 2019 an Egyptian mission revealed a Graeco-Roman building of 2,500 square metres, and in 2022 archaeologists found the remains of a temple of Zeus-Kasios.
pemba-island: Pemba covers 988 square kilometres and lies about 50 kilometres north of Unguja, the largest island of the Zanzibar Archipelago, and about 50 kilometres east of mainland Tanzania across the Pemba Channel. Surrounded by relatively deep water, it is thought to have split from the mainland along the Pemba rift some 10 million years ago. It is hillier and more fertile than Unguja, with a tropical climate somewhat milder than that of the mainland. A group of small islets, including Fundo, Kojani, Misali and Makoongwe, lies off its coasts, and its coral reefs and fishing grounds attract divers and anglers.

Archaeological research shows that Pemba was central to the trading system of the Swahili coast as early as 600 CE. Urban settlements at Chwaka on the northern coast later flourished from the eleventh century to about 1500. On the peninsula of Ras Mkumbuu, west of Chake-Chake, stand some of the oldest and best preserved early ruins on the islands, the Ndagoni ruins, probably of the 14th century. At Pujini, east of Chake-Chake, the Mkama Ndume ruins form the only known early fortification on the whole Swahili coast, dated to the fifteenth century.

The Arab geographer Yaqut al-Hamawi records that in the mid-13th century two independent sultans ruled over parts of the island. Pemba later became known for its cloves, and it holds the largest concentration of clove trees in Zanzibar, about 3.5 million, since growing conditions are better than on Unguja. In 1964 Zanzibar was united with the former colony of Tanganyika to form Tanzania.

Pemba is administered by the Revolutionary Government of Zanzibar and divided into North Pemba, with its capital at Wete, and South Pemba, with its capital at Mkoani. Chake-Chake, near the airport, is regarded as the island's capital. The population is a mix of Arab and Swahili inhabitants, including a large Arab community that immigrated from Oman, and a significant part identifies as Shirazi; the great majority are Muslim. Besides cloves, the island grows rice, coconuts, bananas, cassava and red beans. BirdLife International has designated it an Important Bird Area.
pemba-mozambique: Pemba lies on a peninsula in Pemba Bay, the third largest bay in Africa, northeast of Maputo. A coral reef surrounds the city, and whales, sunfish and sea turtles frequent its coast, which makes it a destination for divers and water sports. The municipality covers 100 square kilometres and recorded 201,846 people in the 2017 census, though the actual settlement is mostly just the tip that faces the bay, and most of the land is undeveloped. It has a tropical savanna climate with two seasons: a wet season from December to April, with March typically the wettest month at an average of 202.2 mm of rain, and a dry season from May to November.

The site was mainly a fishing ground for visiting Malagasy and Swahili fishermen. The first Portuguese attempt at settlement was a temporary fort in the late 19th century, dismantled after a few years. The town was founded by the newly formed, land-controlling Niassa Company as a small trading port and was soon renamed Porto Amélia, after the last Queen of Portugal, Amélie of Orléans. When the Niassa Company ended in 1929, the town passed to direct Portuguese control and became the capital of the newly created district of Cabo Delgado. It took that role from the nearby village of Ibo, in part because Pemba had access for large ships. It was renamed Pemba at the end of Portuguese rule, in 1975.

Pemba is the capital and largest city of Cabo Delgado province. Its inhabitants are primarily Swahili, Makondes, Macuas and Mwanis. Kimwani and Makhuwa are spoken locally, and Portuguese is widespread. The N1 Highway links it directly to Montepuez to the west, and a highway also connects it to Mecúfi. Its port is the main logistics hub of the province, and Pemba Airport has flights to Johannesburg and Nairobi. The city is twinned with Aveiro in Portugal and Reggio Emilia in Italy.
pembroke-castle: Pembroke Castle stands on a rocky promontory beside the Pembroke River and the Milford Haven Waterway in Pembrokeshire. It was the original seat of the Earldom of Pembroke. The first fortification was a Norman motte-and-bailey with earthen ramparts and a timber palisade, at the heart of the Norman-controlled lands of south-west Wales. Arnulf de Montgomery held it and appointed Gerald de Windsor as his castellan. After Arnulf joined a failed rebellion against Henry I he forfeited his lands, and Henry reappointed Gerald in 1102. King Stephen gave the castle to Gilbert de Clare by 1138, and de Clare used it as a base for the Norman invasion of Ireland.

In August 1189 Richard I arranged the marriage of Isabel, de Clare's granddaughter, to William Marshal, who received the castle and the earldom. Marshal had it rebuilt in stone, creating most of the structure that remains. The inner ward holds the huge round keep with its domed roof, 23 metres tall with walls up to 6 metres thick at the base. Its first-floor entrance was reached by an external stair, and a spiral staircase connected its four storeys. The outer ward was later defended by a twin-towered gatehouse, a barbican and round towers. Marshal's third son Gilbert enlarged the castle between 1234 and 1241.

Beneath the castle lies Wogan Cavern, a natural limestone cave reached by a 55-step spiral staircase made in the 13th century. Excavations that began in 2021 found intact sediment layers and evidence of prehistoric occupation, including bones of reindeer and woolly mammoth.

In 1247 the castle passed to William de Valence, who became Earl of Pembroke through his marriage, and it was his base in Edward I's conquest of North Wales. The Hastings family held it later, and in 1452 Henry VI gave it and the earldom to his half-brother Jasper Tudor. In 1457 Jasper's sister-in-law Margaret Beaufort gave birth there to the future Henry VII.

In the English Civil War Pembroke declared for Parliament. In 1648 its commander, Colonel John Poyer, led a Royalist uprising, and Oliver Cromwell took the castle on his arrival on 24 May 1648 after a siege of seven weeks. Its three leaders were found guilty of treason, and Cromwell ordered the castle destroyed. It decayed until a restoration in 1880, and from 1928 Major-General Sir Ivor Philipps carried out an extensive restoration. It is a Grade I listed building and open to the public.
pembroke-pembrokeshire: Pembroke, in Welsh Penfro, stands on the South Pembrokeshire limestone peninsula beside the estuary of the River Cleddau, with woodland and arable farmland on all sides. It lies 8 miles south of Haverfordwest, the county town. The names of the town and the county both come from the Cantref of Penfro, from pen, head or end, and bro, region or land, which has been taken to mean either Land's End or headland.

The town is centred on Main Street, the only street inside the original town walls. Pembroke Dock, the ferry port established in 1814, lies 3 miles to the north-west, and the village of Monkton to the west is part of the community of Pembroke.

Pembroke Castle, the substantial remains of a stone fortress founded by the Normans in 1093, stands at the western tip of a peninsula surrounded by water on three sides. It was the seat of the powerful Earls of Pembroke and the birthplace of Henry Tudor, later Henry VII of England. Gerald de Windsor was the first recorded Constable of Pembroke. After the final extension of the castle about 1254 the town was extended and walls were built round its edge; they survive on their medieval foundations. Many of the original burgage plots also survive.

Monkton Priory, on a hill across the river, was founded in 1098 by Arnulf de Montgomery and granted by him to the Benedictine order. Monkton Hall beside it is regarded as the oldest domestic building in Pembrokeshire and possibly in Wales. The first stone building in the town was a defensive tower on a cliff edge, now called the Medieval Chapel. During the English Civil War the county was largely in the hands of Parliament, which aimed to prevent communication with Ireland.

Pembroke was an ancient borough, with evidence of charters back to at least 1168, and became a municipal borough in 1836. Pembroke Dock grew from the early nineteenth century and came to rival the old town. The borough council was abolished under the Local Government Act 1972, and in 1974 the area joined the new district of South Pembrokeshire in Dyfed. In 1986 the community was divided into Pembroke Dock and a smaller Pembroke.

Pembroke has historic buildings, town walls and the castle. The millpond is held by the town's main bridge over the River Pembroke, which also acts as a dam. The town is twinned with Bergen in Lower Saxony and with Pembroke in Malta.
pembrokeshire: Pembrokeshire is bordered by Ceredigion to the north-east, Carmarthenshire to the east and otherwise by the sea. Its coast, formed by the complex geology of the area, includes high sea cliffs, wide sandy beaches, the ria of Milford Haven and offshore islands such as Ramsey, Skomer and Caldey, which are home to seabird colonies. The interior is relatively flat and gently undulating, except for the Preseli Mountains in the north. Most of the coast is protected by the Pembrokeshire Coast National Park, the only park in the United Kingdom established primarily because of its coastline, and it can be walked on the Pembrokeshire Coast Path.

Human habitation dates back between 125,000 and 70,000 years, and there are many prehistoric sites, particularly in the Preseli Mountains, including Pentre Ifan and other Neolithic remains. Roman influence was limited, with a few forts, coins and roads, and much of the area stayed beyond sustained Roman control. In the sub-Roman period the Irish Déisi settled and merged with local populations to form the Kingdom of Dyfed, which became part of Deheubarth in the 10th century. The region saw Viking raids and limited settlement.

In the Middle Ages the Normans built several castles, such as Pembroke and Cilgerran, and St David's Cathedral became an important pilgrimage site. Until the 12th century a great extent of the county was virgin woodland, and clearance in the lowland south began under Anglo-Flemish colonisation. Because of immigration, including the influx of Flemish people, the south has fewer Welsh speakers than the north. The rough boundary between the two regions is the Landsker Line, and the south has been called Little England beyond Wales; George Owen of Henllys remarked on the distinction as early as 1603.

During the Industrial Revolution the county stayed relatively rural, except for Milford Haven, which was developed as a port and Royal Navy dockyard. Slate quarrying was a significant industry in the 19th and early 20th centuries, and coal was mined between the 14th and 20th centuries, the last mine closing at Kilgetty in 1950. Since the 1950s petrochemical and liquefied natural gas industries have developed along the Milford Haven Waterway. The county town is Haverfordwest, and St Davids is the smallest city in the United Kingdom. Under the Local Government (Wales) Act 1994 Pembrokeshire became a unitary authority in 1996, after the abolition of Dyfed. It has more than 1,600 listed buildings.
pemex: Asphalt and pitch had been worked in Mexico since the time of the Aztecs, and small quantities of oil were first refined into kerosene around 1876 near Tampico. By the early 20th century subsidiaries of the British Pearson and American Doheny companies were extracting and refining oil in commercial quantities, which drew the attention of the Mexican government, which claimed all mineral rights for the state under its constitution.

In 1938 President Lázaro Cárdenas sided with oil workers who were striking against the foreign-owned companies for higher pay and social services. On 18 March 1938, citing Article 27 of the Constitution of 1917, he expropriated the resources and facilities of the United States and Anglo-Dutch companies. He asked the nation for the moral and material support needed to face the consequences of a decision that, he said, the government would neither have sought nor desired. Pemex was established by his decree of 7 June 1938. Expropriation was not outright confiscation, since the government promised compensation, but many foreign governments retaliated by closing their markets to Mexican oil until demand for petroleum in the Second World War ended the boycott.

Pemex became a lasting symbol of Mexican nationalism. In 1979 its Ixtoc 1 exploratory well in the Bay of Campeche suffered a blowout that caused one of the largest oil spills in history; the company spent 100 million dollars on the clean-up and avoided most compensation claims by asserting sovereign immunity. On 19 November 1984 a series of explosions at a Pemex liquefied petroleum gas storage facility at San Juan Ixhuatepec, near Mexico City, killed about 500 to 600 residents and injured up to 7,000 more, and it is counted among the deadliest industrial accidents in history.

Annual production fell each year between 2004 and 2007. Presidents Vicente Fox and Felipe Calderón proposed opening the sector to private investment, and the proposals met opposition in Congress. In 2008 the Mexican Congress created the National Hydrocarbons Commission to increase oversight of the company. Later events included a pipeline explosion at Tlauhuelilpan, Hidalgo, on 18 January 2019, in which at least 137 people died while gathering fuel from an illegal tap. In 2021 Pemex took over the operation of the Zama oil field, which Talos Energy had discovered in 2017, and Talos disputed the decision. The Dos Bocas refinery opened in 2024.
penal-transportation: Banishment had been a punishment since at least the 5th century BCE in ancient Greece. In England transportation arose under the Bloody Code of the 17th to early 19th centuries, when many offences carried death and judges had few other sentences. Offenders thought too minor to hang were pardoned, and transportation was legally a condition of the pardon rather than a sentence in itself, presented as a public show of the king's mercy. In 1615, under James I, a council committee gained the power to choose prisoners fit for service beyond the seas, and by 1670 transportation could be imposed for life or for a set term.

From the early 1600s until 1776 convicts went to the West Indies and the mainland colonies, Maryland receiving more than any other province. In the 17th century the convicts or the shipowners bore the cost of the voyage. The Transportation Act 1717 allowed seven-year sentences to America, made returning early a capital offence, and from 1720 the Crown paid merchants to carry the convicts. Prisoners of war from Ireland and Scotland were sold into indentured servitude.

When the American Revolution ended this, the prisons filled and old ships moored in ports served as hulks. After trials at Cape Coast Castle and Gorée in West Africa the government turned to New South Wales, and the First Fleet sailed in 1787. A convict there who had served part of a term could apply for a ticket of leave, which allowed some to marry and raise a family. Few could afford to return home once released.

As the policy grew unpopular in Australia the Cape Colony was considered instead, but the Convict Crisis of 1849 kept southern Africa from becoming a penal colony. France sent convicts to Devil's Island in Guiana from 1852 to 1953 and about 22,000 criminals and political prisoners, many of them Communards, to New Caledonia until 1897; Alfred Dreyfus was held on Devil's Island. The Soviet Union deported up to 1.9 million people from its western republics during the Second World War, among them Volga Germans and Chechens.
penang: Penang is divided into two parts by the Penang Strait, which is only 3 kilometres wide at its narrowest point. Penang Island to the west holds the capital, George Town, and Seberang Perai lies on the mainland to the east, where the state borders Kedah and Perak. Penang Island covers 295 square kilometres and has a hilly, mostly forested interior, with Penang Hill, 833 metres high, as the state's highest point. George Town began as a small settlement at the island's northeastern tip. The name comes from the Malay Pulau Pinang, meaning areca palm island.

Remains found in Seberang Perai show that around 5,000 to 6,000 years ago nomadic Melanesians lived there in the Neolithic era. Pali inscriptions on the Cherok Tok Kun megalith suggest that the Bujang Valley civilisation, based in what is now Kedah, held authority over parts of Seberang Perai by the 6th century. The whole of Penang later formed part of Kedah, which came under Siamese suzerainty by the late 18th century. Penang's modern history began in 1786, when Francis Light of the British East India Company obtained the island from Sultan Abdullah Mukarram Shah of Kedah in exchange for military aid.

Light founded the Port of Penang as a free port alongside George Town, and Penang later joined Malacca and Singapore in the Straits Settlements. A Royal Charter of 1807 led to the founding of a Supreme Court at Fort Cornwallis. During the Second World War the Japanese army took Penang without a struggle on 19 December 1941, and the British regained control in 1945. The state merged with the Federation of Malaya, which became independent in 1957.

Penang is a state of Malaysia, linked across the strait by the Penang Bridge and the Second Penang Bridge. It is one of four Malaysian states without a hereditary monarchy, and its head of state is a Governor appointed by the King of Malaysia. The unicameral State Legislative Assembly has 40 seats and meets in George Town. Its people include Chinese, Malays, Indians, Eurasians and Siamese. After the free port status was withdrawn in 1969, Chief Minister Lim Chong Eu set up the Bayan Lepas Free Industrial Zone in 1972, and the economy shifted from entrepôt trade to electronics manufacturing.
penataran: The complex lies in the village of Penataran in Blitar Regency, roughly 12 km northeast of Blitar, on the lower southwestern slopes of the Kelud volcano. Construction began in 1197, in the Kediri era, and continued into the 15th century. The temple is mentioned in the Nagarakretagama, which identifies it as the Palah temple and records that King Hayam Wuruk visited it during his royal tour across East Java; he is said to have considered it his favourite sanctuary.

The complex is laid out in three courtyards, one behind the other, an arrangement that resembles the Balinese puras, with the most sacred structures in the rear courtyard nearest the mountain. The first courtyard holds two rectangular platforms that once carried thatched roofs on wooden pillars and gave space for rituals and ceremonies; the smaller is richly decorated with nagas, mythical snakes. Beside the entrance to the second courtyard stands a small stone shrine known as the Dated Temple, after a lintel inscribed with a date equivalent to 1323 found nearby. The second courtyard contains the Naga Temple, devoted to the nagas.

The main temple in the rear courtyard is dedicated to Shiva. Its reliefs form one of the largest Indonesian collections showing the stories of Vishnu's avatars: the Rama story of the Javanese Ramayana and the Krishna story as told in Triguna's Krishnayana. No stones that could have formed a stone roof have been found, so some scholars believe the main temple carried a tiered roof of wood and palm fibre or thatch, like the Pura Yeh Gangga near Perean on Bali, dated 1334. According to the Indonesian scholar R. Soekmono the central shrine held no divine image, marking a transition from the classical stone-roofed temple to the type now common in Bali.

Only the stone remains survive; the wooden and other perishable buildings and objects are lost, though reliefs at Borobudur and the Shiva temple near Prambanan show that such structures existed. The site was added to the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List on 19 October 1995 in the cultural category, but in 2015 it was withdrawn from the list together with 11 other sites.
pencil: The word pencil comes from the Old French pincel and the late Latin penicillus, a little tail, and first meant an artist's fine brush of camel hair, which was also used for writing. The Romans used a stylus, a thin metal stick for scratching papyrus or wax tablets. The graphite from Cumbria was called plumbago, Latin for lead ore, and the mistake lives on in the name lead for a pencil core. The German Bleistift and the Irish peann luaidhe both mean lead pen. Because graphite could line the moulds for cannonballs, the Crown took over the mines and guarded them, and flooded them when enough had been stored. The graphite for pencils had at first to be smuggled out.

A pencil leaves marks by abrasion, a trail of solid core material that clings to the paper, which sets it apart from pens that dispense liquid ink. Most cores are graphite mixed with a clay binder, and the ratio of graphite to clay decides how hard the core is. The commonest casing is thin wood, usually hexagonal in section. Other cores include charcoal and carbon for fuller blacks, wax-based coloured cores and greasy cores that write on glass or porcelain. Copying pencils, invented in the late 19th century, held a dye that dissolved into coloured ink when moistened, so that the writing could be pressed onto another sheet.

England kept a monopoly on pencils until a method of reconstituting graphite powder was found in Germany in 1662, and square English pencils were still cut from natural graphite into the 1860s. Keswick still has a pencil factory and the Derwent Pencil Museum. Under the naval blockade of the Napoleonic Wars France could import neither English graphite nor the poorer German substitute, which led Nicolas-Jacques Conté to his clay method.

American colonists imported their pencils from Europe. Benjamin Franklin advertised them in 1729, and George Washington used a three-inch pencil when surveying the Ohio Country in 1762. William Munroe of Concord, Massachusetts, made the first American wood pencils in 1812, and Ebenezer Wood of Acton automated the work, building the first hexagonal casings. Eberhard Faber built a factory in New York. By the end of the 19th century more than 240,000 pencils were used each day in the United States. Hymen Lipman received the first patent for an attached eraser on 30 March 1858.
penda-of-mercia: Penda was a son of Pybba of Mercia and is said to have been an Icling, with a lineage traced back to Wōden in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. The Historia Brittonum says Pybba had twelve sons, of whom Penda and Eowa of Mercia were best known to its author. The time at which Penda became king is uncertain. Bede mentions an earlier Mercian king, Cearl, as a contemporary of the Northumbrian king Æthelfrith, and it is unclear whether the two were related or rivals. The origin of the name Penda is unknown, with suggestions divided between Celtic and Germanic origins.

Penda took the Severn Valley in 628 after the Battle of Cirencester. In October 633 he joined the Welsh king Cadwallon ap Cadfan of Gwynedd in defeating Edwin of Northumbria at the Battle of Hatfield Chase, where Edwin was killed. He was probably the lesser partner. On 5 August 642 he defeated Oswald of Northumbria at the Battle of Maserfield, probably in alliance with men of Powys. According to Bede, Oswald's body was dismembered, and Oswald came to be revered as a saint. After this Penda was probably the most powerful Anglo-Saxon ruler of his time.

He fought the East Angles repeatedly, killing their king Egric and the former king Sigebert, and in 654 killed King Anna. When Cenwalh of Wessex repudiated Penda's sister, Penda drove him into exile in East Anglia in 645, where he stayed three years. Penda placed his son Peada as ruler in Middle Anglia. Peada married Oswiu's daughter Alhflaed after agreeing to be baptised, and Bede says Penda tolerated Christian preaching among his Mercians. In 655 he invaded Bernicia with a large army reported as thirty warbands, including Cadafael ap Cynfeddw of Gwynedd. He was killed at the Battle of the Winwaed by Oswiu, on 15 November 655.

After the Winwaed, Oswiu briefly dominated Mercia, allowing Peada to rule its southern part. Penda's sons Wulfhere and Æthelred later ruled Mercia in succession after Northumbrian control was overthrown in the late 650s. Descendants of Penda held the kingship until the death of his grandson Ceolred in 716. His reign marked Mercia's emergence from obscurity, and it has been said that the hostility of Bede obscured his importance as an overking whose hegemony included lesser rulers of Anglo-Saxon and British origin, Christian and non-Christian alike.
pendulum-clock: Galileo Galilei investigated pendulums around 1602 and discovered that they are isochronous, swinging with a period independent of the size of the swing. In 1637 he described to his son Vincenzo a mechanism to keep a pendulum swinging, which Vincenzo partly built in 1649. Christiaan Huygens had the first clock built by Salomon Coster and described it in his manuscript Horologium of 1658. By 1659 pendulum clocks were made by the French clockmaker Nicolaus Hanet and by Ahasuerus Fromanteel in England.

A mechanical pendulum clock has a power source, a gear train, an escapement that gives the pendulum timed impulses, the pendulum itself and a dial. The early clocks had verge escapements and swings of 80 to 100 degrees. In 1673 Huygens showed that wide swings made the clock inaccurate. Robert Hooke's anchor escapement of around 1658 reduced the swing to 4 to 6 degrees and became standard, and the seconds pendulum, about 0.994 m long, came into wide use. William Clement made the first long narrow cases around 1680, called grandfather clocks, and minute hands appeared from around 1690.

The deadbeat escapement, invented by Richard Towneley in 1675 and popularised by George Graham around 1715, gradually replaced the anchor. Heat made rods expand and clocks slow in summer, which Graham's mercury pendulum of 1721 and John Harrison's gridiron pendulum of 1726 compensated. By the mid-18th century precision clocks kept time to a few seconds a week.

Until the 19th century clocks were handmade and expensive, and their ornament made them status symbols of the wealthy. Factory production of parts gradually brought them within reach of middle-class families. During the Industrial Revolution, work shifts and train services depended on pendulum clocks, and regulators in businesses and railway stations were used to set other clocks. Astronomical regulators in naval observatories were used to set marine chronometers for finding longitude.

From 1909 the US National Bureau of Standards based its time standard on Riefler pendulum clocks, and in 1929 it changed to the Shortt-Synchronome clock, accurate to better than one second a year. In the 1930s and 1940s synchronous electric clocks began to replace them in homes. Behind the Iron Curtain, where quartz technology was unavailable, Feodosii Fedchenko's AChF-3 clock of 1955 reached the accuracy of quartz clocks.
penedes: Penedès is a natural and historical region in the south of Catalonia, lying between the pre-coastal mountain range, the Serralada Pre-litoral, and the Mediterranean Sea. Its wine country is framed by the coastal hills of the Serra del Garraf and by the higher inland mountains that skirt the Catalan Central Depression.

From the start of the ninth century Penedès was a border region within the county of Barcelona. Its centre was the former military town of Olèrdola, fortified again in 929 because of the Christian advance. In the second half of the twelfth century Olèrdola lost its defensive significance and its place as capital to Vilafranca del Penedès. During the thirteenth century the Vegueria of Vilafranca was formed, covering all of Penedès and most of Anoia, the latter as the sots-vegueria of Igualada.

The provincial division of 1833 split the region between the province of Barcelona, which took Alt Penedès and Garraf, and the province of Tarragona, which took Baix Penedès. The comarcal divisions of the Generalitat de Catalunya in 1936 and 1987 then created the three comarques, with their capitals at Vilafranca del Penedès, el Vendrell and Vilanova i la Geltrú.

Penedès is one of the most ancient viticultural areas in Europe and has long been considered one of Spain's best wine regions after the Rioja. Its Denominación de Origen Protegida covers the whole region and municipalities of four other comarques: Anoia, Alt Camp, Baix Llobregat and Tarragonès. White grape varieties predominate, though the region also produces oak-aged reds, and Cava, a sparkling wine, has had its own Denominació d'Origen since 1986.
peng-dehuai: Peng Dehuai was born on 24 October 1898 in the village of Shixiang, Xiangtan County, Hunan, into a poor peasant family. His grand-uncle had fought in the Taiping Rebellion and told him of its ideals, that everyone should have enough food, women should not bind their feet and land should be redistributed equally. Poverty forced him to stop his education at ten, and he worked as a manual labourer. In March 1916 he joined a Hunan warlord army as a private, and over ten years rose to major in the armies of several warlords. One of his commanding officers, a Nationalist veteran of the 1911 revolution, led him to sympathise with the Kuomintang's aims of social reform and national reunification.

In 1926 his forces joined the Kuomintang, and he took part in the Northern Expedition. After the Wuhan government's defeat he joined the Chinese Communist Party, allying himself with Mao Zedong and Zhu De. He helped defend the Jiangxi Soviet and joined the Long March: of the 18,000 men under his command at its start in October 1934, only about 3,000 reached Shaanxi in October 1935. In the war against Japan he argued that the Red Army should genuinely fight the Japanese, against Mao's wish for token resistance. After 1945 he commanded the Northwest Field Army, and defeated the Kuomintang in Northwest China.

North Korea invaded South Korea on 25 June 1950, and Peng was among the few senior leaders who backed Mao's proposal to intervene. He directly commanded the Chinese People's Volunteer Army for the first half of the war. Convinced that the army had to be more professional and better equipped, he became Minister of National Defense in 1954 and began to reform it on the Soviet model. In January 1955 he attacked and occupied a chain of islands held by the Kuomintang off Zhejiang. He resisted Mao's personality cult during the 1950s.

The Great Leap Forward, begun in 1958, caused a man-made famine in which tens of millions starved by 1959. At the Lushan Conference of July 1959 Mao invited criticism and promised not to attack anyone personally, and Peng, critical of Mao's leadership, spoke. Mao won the confrontation, labelled Peng the leader of an anti-Party clique and in September replaced him with Lin Biao, who reversed his reforms.

Peng lived under constant surveillance near Beijing. In 1966 Jiang Qing directed Red Guards in Sichuan to arrest him, and they abducted him in chains on 25 December 1966. He died on 29 November 1974. The party leadership concealed his death for years, and his wife, Pu Anxiu, learned of it only on returning to Beijing in 1978, when the news was first publicly disclosed.
penghu: Penghu is an archipelago of 90 islands and islets in the Taiwan Strait, about 50 kilometres west of the main island of Taiwan across the Penghu Channel, covering 141 square kilometres. It is the remnant of a Miocene shield volcano, and its layers of basalt are interbedded with sandstone and mudstone. The largest city, Magong, stands on the largest island. Finds of red cord-marked pottery show that Austronesians from south-western Taiwan visited about 5,000 years ago, though they did not settle permanently.

The islands first appear in the written record in the Tang dynasty. Han Chinese from southern Fujian began to establish fishing communities in the 9th and 10th centuries, and by 1171 settlers were cultivating land there, when raiders landed and plundered their fields and the Song government began regular patrols. In November 1281 the Yuan dynasty set up the Penghu Patrol and Inspection Agency under Tong'an County. Wang Dayuan described thirty-six islands in his Daoyi Zhilüe of 1349, with grass but no trees, flocks of goats and a salt tax. In the 15th century the Ming ordered the islands evacuated under a maritime ban, and fishing communities returned in the late 16th century. The Ming established a permanent military presence from 1597.

After the Dutch were defeated by the Portuguese at the Battle of Macau in 1622, they seized Penghu and built a fort, demanding trade with China. They raided the Fujian coast until 1624, when the governor of Fujian sent 40 to 50 warships with 5,000 troops and the Dutch withdrew to Fort Zeelandia on Taiwan. The Qing overthrew the Kingdom of Tungning of the Zheng family in 1683 after the Battle of Penghu and made the islands a sub-prefecture of Taiwan Prefecture. French forces captured Penghu in March 1885 and left four months later, Admiral Amédée Courbet dying of cholera there on 11 June 1885.

Japan occupied Makung in March 1895, and Penghu was ceded with Taiwan in the Treaty of Shimonoseki that April. Under Japanese rule Makō was a major naval base. The administration passed to the Republic of China on 25 October 1945.

Penghu County is divided into one city and five rural townships, with its seat at Magong, and its people are mostly descendants of settlers from Tong'an in Fujian who speak Taiwanese Hokkien. The islands depend on sea and air transport and have long relied on fishing. Penghu National Scenic Area covers most of the archipelago, known for its columnar basalt, and tourism is a main source of income.
peninsular-war: The Treaties of Tilsit of July 1807 ended the War of the Fourth Coalition. Napoleon was irritated that Portugal, Britain's oldest ally in Europe, remained open to trade with Britain, and Prince John of Braganza, regent for his mother Queen Maria I, had declined to join the Continental System. French troops under Junot, with Spanish cooperation, set out for Lisbon on 19 November 1807 and occupied it on 30 November. The prince regent fled to Brazil with his family, court and treasure aboard an Anglo-Portuguese fleet. In February 1808 French divisions crossed the Pyrenees and occupied Navarre and Catalonia, and Napoleon then forced the abdications of Ferdinand VII and Charles IV and installed his brother Joseph Bonaparte on the Spanish throne.

On 2 May 1808 the citizens of Madrid rose against the French, and the next day the French army shot hundreds of them, as Francisco Goya's painting The Third of May 1808 shows. Spaniards rose across the country, and guerrilla warfare, from which English took the word, spread. In July 1808 the Spanish army in Andalusia defeated the French at the Battle of Bailén. Arthur Wellesley, later the Duke of Wellington, landed in Portugal in August and beat Junot at Vimeiro. Napoleon himself invaded in November 1808, but the Spanish armies, though often beaten, regrouped and kept French troops tied down.

The Cortes, besieged by 70,000 French troops, took refuge at Cádiz in 1810, while Wellington built the Lines of Torres Vedras to protect Lisbon. In 1812, as Napoleon invaded Russia, an allied army defeated the French at Salamanca on 22 July, and Joseph abandoned Madrid. The Coalition defeated Joseph's army at Vitoria in 1813, and Marshal Soult led a fighting withdrawal across the Pyrenees in the winter of 1813 to 1814. Wellington attacked Soult at Orthez on 27 February 1814.

The war drained France: its communications and supplies were strained, and its units were repeatedly isolated or harassed by Spanish partisans. Napoleon called it the Spanish ulcer. It allowed the rest of Europe to challenge him again. The Cortes of Cádiz promulgated the Spanish Constitution of 1812, later a cornerstone of European liberalism. Yet the war destroyed the social and economic fabric of both Spain and Portugal, and the civil wars between liberals and absolutists that followed ushered in revolts in Spanish America that led to the independence of all of Spain's colonies on the American mainland. The siege of Zaragoza alone left an estimated 64,000 corpses, 10,000 of them French.
penkovka-culture: The core of the culture seems to lie in Left-bank Ukraine, along the Sula, Seim, Psel, Donets and Oril rivers, and its western edge is usually placed at the middle Prut and Dniester, where it meets the Korchak culture. Its hand-made pottery, with a biconical profile and out-turned rims, is also found in eastern and southern Romania, where archaeologists call it the Ipotești–Cândești culture, and even in Byzantine forts of the north-eastern Balkans. Michel Kazanski and others trace it, like the closely similar Kolochin culture, to the Kyiv culture; some see the Chernyakhov culture among its ancestors.

Settlements stood on river terraces, usually in a line. Most buildings were square post-hole houses dug into the ground with an oven in a corner, but there were also rounded ones, not found elsewhere among the Slavs, which have been linked to nomadic influence. Settlements were often abandoned and reoccupied years later, reflecting shifting agriculture. Two fortified sites are known, Seliste and Pastyrske; the latter, an Iron Age fort of 25 ha reused in early medieval times, shows specialised industry, and Bartlomiej Szmoniewski suggests it may have been the seat of a ruler.

The dead of the forest-steppe were cremated with few goods, while richer inhumations lay in the open steppe. Florin Curta argues that these inhumations, whose pottery and metalwork match those of the settlements, marked chiefs and big men rather than Turkic nomads.

Hoards of silver and gold ornaments of the 7th century, called Antian antiquities or the Martynivka culture, are linked with the Penkovka and Kolochin cultures. Their style mixes steppe, Byzantine, Sassanian, Caucasian, eastern Germanic and forest-zone elements. Curta doubts the link with the Antes, since such features last into the 8th century, long after the Avars defeated the Antes in 602; Kazanski replies that the culture's uniform appearance argues for a single people.

The culture's end, around the second half of the 7th century, is thought to be tied to invasions by the Bulgars and Khazars, probably at Byzantine bidding. Wheel-made Saltovo ware then appears on its sites, and Slavs of the Prague-Korchak tradition later moved east into the region.
penn-museum: The museum was founded after a successful expedition to the ancient site of Nippur, then part of the Ottoman Empire, when Provost William Pepper persuaded the trustees of the University of Pennsylvania to erect a fireproof building for its finds. Like other museums of the time, it shared the ownership of excavated objects with the host countries, so most of its holdings have a known archaeological context. Its building, in the Arts and Crafts and Eclectic style, was designed by Wilson Eyre, Cope & Stewardson and Frank Miles Day, and is only about a third of the original plan. The first phase was completed in 1899, the rotunda in 1915 and the Sharpe Wing in 1929.

The collections fall into three divisions: archaeology, ethnology and physical anthropology. Among the most important are the finds from the Royal Tombs of Ur, co-excavated with the British Museum, including crowns, figures and the Bull-headed lyre, and almost 30,000 clay tablets in Sumerian and Akkadian cuneiform, among them the largest number of Sumerian school tablets of any museum. A museum expedition to Egypt in 1915 brought a 13-ton granite Sphinx of Ramesses II from the palace of Merenptah, and the museum excavated the Maya city of Tikal in Guatemala from 1956 to 1970. Its scientists have conducted more than 300 expeditions, and it has published Expedition magazine since 1958.

The Museum Library began in 1900 with the personal library of Daniel Garrison Brinton, professor of American archaeology and linguistics. Under Cynthia Griffin, its first full-time librarian from 1942, it was opened to students and grew from nearly 20,000 volumes in 1945 to over 46,000 in 1965.

In November 2008 the administration cut 18 research specialist posts and closed the Museum Applied Science Center for Archaeology, a step scholars criticised as a departure from its mission and which administrators attributed to the 2008 financial crisis.

The museum holds about 196 objects taken in the Benin Expedition of 1897, including Benin Bronzes, and has said it is open to returning them. It also holds about 1,300 skulls gathered by the physician Samuel George Morton, long criticised for using science to uphold racism; in 2018 students found that 55 were of enslaved people, and in July 2020 the museum moved the collection into storage. In April 2021 the museum and the university apologised for allowing remains of victims of the 1985 MOVE bombing to be used in research and teaching.
penne-abruzzo: Penne stands on several hills on the Adriatic side of Abruzzo, between the valleys of the Tavo and Fino rivers, about 20 km from the sea. It lies 31 km from Pescara, 35 km from Chieti and 67 km from Teramo, and opens the way to the Gran Sasso and Monti della Laga national park through the regional natural reserve of the Lake of Penne. The old town is built almost entirely of brick, which gave it the name Città del mattone, the Town of Bricks, and in the past earned it the title of the small Siena.

The site has been occupied since at least the mid-Neolithic period. It was a seat of government of the Vestini people by 300 BCE at the latest. The Vestini and other Italic tribes were defeated by the Romans in the Social War and became Roman citizens; the town was known as Pinna Vestinorum under the Roman Republic.

In the Middle Ages Penne was held by the Lombards as part of the Duchy of Spoleto, and from around 1130 it belonged to the Kingdom of Sicily. In 1538 Emperor Charles V gave it to his daughter Margaret of Parma as a gift for her wedding to Ottavio Farnese. Under Margaret, Penne became a centre of power in Abruzzo and many palaces and civic buildings were erected. In 2006 the town received the Silver Medal of Civic Merit for what it suffered in the Second World War.

The Duomo, the church of San Massimo, was built on a 10th-century crypt that may stand on an ancient temple of Vesta; it was badly damaged by bombing in 1944 and restored in 1955. It now houses the Diocese Museum, with a crypt dating from the 8th century. Other buildings include the 12th-century church of Santa Maria in Colleromano and the Cistercian convent founded there in 1197, and Renaissance and Baroque palaces such as the Palazzo Scorpio, once the home of Margaret. Four old gates survive, among them the Porta San Francesco, rebuilt in 1780. Penne is listed among the most beautiful villages of Italy and had 12,451 inhabitants at the census of 2014.
pennine-alps: The Pennine Alps, called the Valais Alps when the term is applied to the northern Swiss part, lie in the canton of Valais in south-western Switzerland and in the Aosta Valley and Piedmont of Italy. Their names are Alpes Pennines in French, Walliser Alpen in German, Alpi Pennine in Italian and Alpes Poeninae in Latin. Together with the Bernese Alps and the Graian Alps, which include the Mont Blanc massif, the Pennines are among the three highest major subranges of the Alps.

The range straddles the border between Switzerland and Italy. The Italian side is drained by the Dora Baltea, Sesia and Toce rivers, all tributaries of the Po, and the Swiss side by the Rhône. The Great St Bernard Tunnel runs under the Great St Bernard Pass from Martigny in Switzerland to Aosta in Italy.

The main watershed between the Mediterranean Sea and the Adriatic Sea runs from west to east along the border. East of Mont Vélan, the first high summit beyond the St Bernard Pass, the chain contains many four-thousanders, among them the Matterhorn and Monte Rosa. The valleys on both sides are similar, generally running perpendicular to the main chain and descending into the Rhône Valley to the north and the Aosta Valley to the south. Unlike many ranges, the higher peaks, such as Grand Combin, Weisshorn, Mischabel and Weissmies, often lie outside the main chain, between the northern valleys. There are 126 peaks over 2,106 metres.

The main glaciers include the Gorner, Corbassière, Findel, Zmutt, Zinal, Otemma, Allalin and Ferpècle glaciers. Regional nature parks lie on both sides of the main water divide: the Parco Naturale Alta Valsesia, the Mont Mars Nature Reserve and the Regional park of Binn valley.
pennines: From the Tyne Gap in the north the range extends south through the North Pennines, the Yorkshire Dales, the South Pennines and the Peak District, and ends near the valley of the River Trent. It is divided in two by the Aire Gap, a wide pass formed by the valleys of the Aire and Ribble, and it has western spurs such as the Rossendale Fells and the Forest of Bowland. Most of it is high moorland cut by more fertile river valleys, and the highest point is Cross Fell in eastern Cumbria at 893 metres. For much of its length it is the main watershed of northern England, dividing rivers that flow west to the Irish Sea from those that reach the North Sea.

The range is a broad anticline of Carboniferous limestone overlain with Millstone Grit, and the limestone has formed large cave systems, such as Gaping Gill, and the pavements of Malham Cove. The Pennine Way, 268 miles long, is Britain's oldest long-distance footpath.

The Pennines contained Bronze Age settlements, and evidence remains of Neolithic settlement, including stone circles and henges such as Long Meg and Her Daughters. The uplands were controlled by the Brigantes, a federation of small tribes that cooperated on defence and external affairs and evolved an early form of kingdom. The Romans dominated them and exploited the Pennines for natural resources. The range was an obstacle to Anglo-Saxon expansion westwards, though the Anglo-Saxons travelled through the valleys.

In Norse times Viking Danes settled in the east and Norwegian Vikings in the west, and they influenced place names, culture and genetics. When England was unified the Pennines were incorporated. They were never a distinct political polity but were divided between neighbouring counties, a major part lying in the West Riding of Yorkshire.

The Pennines are sparsely populated by English standards, with the larger towns and cities in the foothills and lowlands around them, among them Manchester, Leeds, Sheffield and Bradford. Gaps such as the Tyne Gap, the Stainmore Gap and the Aire Gap allow communication across the range.
