Three trans-Pennine canals were built during the Industrial Revolution, the Huddersfield Narrow Canal with its Standedge Tunnel, the Rochdale Canal and the Leeds and Liverpool Canal, and the first Woodhead Tunnel was completed in 1845. The range is protected by national parks and national landscapes, including the Yorkshire Dales and the Peak District.
pennsylvania: Pennsylvania is officially the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. It lies in the Mid-Atlantic, Northeastern, Appalachian and Great Lakes regions, and is bordered by Delaware, Maryland, West Virginia, Ohio, New York, New Jersey and, across Lake Erie, the Canadian province of Ontario. The Mason-Dixon line forms its southern boundary. The Appalachian Mountains run through its centre, and about 59 per cent of the state is forested. Of the original Thirteen Colonies, it is the only one that does not border the Atlantic Ocean, though it has waterfront on Lake Erie and the tidal Delaware River.

Humans lived in what is now Pennsylvania for thousands of years before the colony was founded. The Meadowcroft Rockshelter in Jefferson Township holds the earliest known signs of human activity in the state and perhaps in all of North America, and may pre-date the Clovis culture. By 1000 CE the native population had developed agricultural techniques and a mixed food economy. Between 1638 and 1655 a south-eastern portion of the state was part of New Sweden, a Swedish colony.

In 1681 a royal land grant gave the territory to William Penn, son of the man after whom it is named. The colonial Province of Pennsylvania was known for relatively peaceful relations with native peoples, an innovative system of government and religious pluralism. Philadelphia hosted the First and Second Continental Congress; the latter formed the Continental Army under George Washington in 1775 and unanimously adopted the Declaration of Independence the following year. On 12 December 1787 Pennsylvania was the second state to ratify the United States Constitution, after Delaware. It has been known as the Keystone State since 1802, for its central place among the original colonies.

The capital is Harrisburg, and the largest cities are Philadelphia and Pittsburgh. The 2020 census counted 13,011,844 residents. The state has had five constitutions, in 1776, 1790, 1838, 1874 and 1968. Its industrial past gave it the lesser nicknames of the Coal State, the Oil State and the Steel State, and its five manufacturing centres were Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, Erie, Scranton-Wilkes-Barre and the Lehigh Valley.
pennsylvania-dutch: The immigrants sought land, safety and tolerance. Many, the Amish and Mennonites among them, had faced religious persecution, and war, famine and scarce land had hit the German lands in the 17th and 18th centuries. Pennsylvania, founded by William Penn as a haven for religious minorities, offered freedom of worship and fertile farmland to people who were mostly farmers and craftsmen. About three quarters of the Germans in Pennsylvania worked off their passage as indentured servants, known as redemptioners; the German Society of Pennsylvania was founded in 1764 to protect them.

The historian Marianne Wokeck estimates that just under 81,000 German speakers entered the port of Philadelphia between 1683 and 1775, about 35,000 of them between 1749 and 1754. In 1790 ethnic Germans made up 38% of the population of Pennsylvania, some 165,000 people. Not all were welcome: in 1751 Benjamin Franklin complained that the Palatine newcomers would Germanize the colony.

In the American Revolution the nonsectarian Fancy Dutch generally supported the Patriot cause, while the nonviolent Plain Dutch did not fight. Frederick Muhlenberg, a Lutheran pastor, became Speaker of the United States House of Representatives. In the American Civil War nearly every Pennsylvania regiment had Pennsylvania Dutch members, and the 153rd Pennsylvania Volunteer Infantry was made up of them entirely.

Some settled in Canada. A group founded the Township of Monckton in Nova Scotia in 1766, and from 1800 Mennonites from Pennsylvania moved to what became Waterloo County, Ontario, often by Conestoga wagon.

After the Civil War English-only schools replaced Pennsylvania German ones, and literary German faded from schools, churches and newspapers, leaving Pennsylvania Dutch mainly a spoken language. Anti-German feeling during the two world wars brought discrimination and pushed the language out of the streets of Allentown, Reading, Lancaster and York into the countryside. Most descendants assimilated, while the Amish and Mennonite plain groups stayed apart, which has fed the mistaken belief that Pennsylvania Dutch means Amish. The Pennsylvania Dutch Country today stretches in an arc from Bethlehem and Allentown through Reading, Lebanon and Lancaster to York and Chambersburg.
penobscot: The Penobscot call themselves Pαnawάhpskewi, the people of where the white rocks extend out, a name first given to their territory on the Penobscot River between present-day Old Town and Verona Island, which European colonists heard as Penobscot. Indigenous peoples are thought to have lived in Maine for at least 11,000 years. The Penobscot and other Wabanaki hunted beaver, moose, caribou and fish, gathered eggs, berries, nuts and roots, practised some agriculture and moved with the seasons; food grew scarce only in February and March.

Contact came in the 16th century through the fur trade, which brought metal tools, guns and alcohol but reduced the game. Measles, smallpox and other diseases, dams that cut off the fish runs, clear-cutting for logging and massacres by settlers cut a population of probably about 10,000 at the start of the 17th century to below 500 by the early 19th. The sachem Madockawando led his people against the English in King William's War. In the French and Indian War the Penobscot sided with the French, and in 1755 the Massachusetts governor Spencer Phips put a scalp bounty on them; in the American Revolution, urged by the sachem Joseph Orono, they sided with the Patriots.

Between 1794 and 1833 they ceded most of their lands to Massachusetts and then Maine in treaties the US Senate never ratified, contrary to the Nonintercourse Act of 1790. From about 1800 they lived on Indian Island under a state-appointed Tribal Agent, as wards whose funds the state controlled. Their suit of the 1970s, over land covering 60% of Maine, ended in the Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act of 1980 and an $81.5-million settlement for buying land.

The Penobscot Nation, a federally recognised tribe, sends a nonvoting representative to the Maine House of Representatives. Its people spoke a dialect of Eastern Abenaki; the last known speaker, Madeline Tower Shay, died in the 1990s, Frank Siebert compiled a dictionary, and the language is taught again to children on Indian Island. Women traditionally make baskets of sweet grass, brown ash and birch bark, and birch-bark canoes were once a main means of travel. Their cosmology centres on Klose-kur-beh, or Gluskbe; today some practise traditional spirituality, others are Catholic or Protestant.
pensacola: Pensacola stands on the north side of Pensacola Bay in the Florida Panhandle, a seaport protected by the barrier island of Santa Rosa, which connects to the Gulf of Mexico. It lies 59 miles (95 km) east of Mobile, Alabama, and 196 miles (315 km) west of Tallahassee. In the Age of Sail it was the busiest port on the Gulf Coast, having the deepest harbour. The area was first inhabited by Muskogean-speaking peoples. The Pensacola people lived there at the time of European contact and probably gave the bay and then the city its name, while Creek people came regularly from present-day southern Alabama to trade.

Spanish expeditions reached the bay early: Pánfilo de Narváez in 1528 and Hernando de Soto in 1539, who recorded the name Bay of Ochuse. Tristán de Luna founded a short-lived settlement in 1559, six years before St. Augustine, but it was abandoned after a severe hurricane and not resettled until 1698, when the Spanish established a presidio from which the modern city gradually developed. Control then changed several times: Spain until 1719, France from 1719 to 1722, and Spain again until 1763.

Spain ceded Florida to Britain in 1763 after the French and Indian War, and nearly all the Spanish population left by ship for Veracruz and Cuba. The British made Pensacola the capital of West Florida, strengthened the defences around Fort San Carlos de Barrancas with the Royal Navy Redoubt, and in 1764 set up a colonial assembly under the first governor, George Johnstone. West Florida declined the invitation to send delegates to the First Continental Congress, and during the American War of Independence its colonists remained overwhelmingly loyal to the Crown. Britain held Pensacola until 1781, and Spain ruled it again from 1781 to 1821.

In the final stages of the War of 1812 American troops attacked the Spanish and British garrisons, which surrendered after two days; the United States took the city again in 1818. In 1819 the Adams–Onís Treaty recognised American control of Florida in exchange for American recognition of Spanish control of Texas. A Spanish census of 1820 counted 181 households. The Confederate States held it from 1861 to 1862, and in 1860 it was Florida's largest city, with 2,876 people.

Pensacola is the county seat and only city of Escambia County and is nicknamed the City of Five Flags, for the five governments that have ruled it: Spain, France, Great Britain, the United States and the Confederate States. Naval Air Station Pensacola, commissioned in 1914 as the first naval air station of the United States Navy, trained naval aviators including John H. Glenn and Neil Armstrong, and the city is called the Cradle of Naval Aviation. The University of West Florida lies north of the centre.
penukonda: Penukonda, also called Penugonda, lies in the Sri Sathya Sai district of Andhra Pradesh, 70 km from the town of Anantapur. Under British rule it was the headquarters of a subdivision and taluk of Anantapur district in the Madras province, which held 96 villages over 677 square miles, bounded by the Penner River on the west and the Chitravati on the east. The taluk had 92,482 people in 1901, against 81,104 in 1891, and the town itself 6,806.

The town and fort were established by early Hoysala kings, who practised Jainism, and the region was held at different times by the Chalukyas, Vijayanagara, the Nawabs, the Maratha chieftain Murari Rao, Tipu Sultan and the Nizam of Hyderabad, who ceded it to the British. After Vijayanagara's defeat at the Battle of Talikota in 1565, Tirumala moved the empire's capital to Penukonda, where it stayed until 1592. Raya Dalavayi Koneti Naidu later governed Penukonda with the forts of Rayadurgam and Kundurpi for about 17 years, from 1635 to 1652, and his descendants ruled after him.

Penukonda is one of the most revered places for Jains. The Tamil Jain tradition counts it among the four Jain centres of learning, with Delhi, Kolhapur and Jina Kanchi, and it was the seat of a Jain Bhattaraka established in 1359, which later became extinct as the local Jain population declined. The green stone image of the Pache Parsvanath Swamy Temple was consecrated in 1359, according to its inscription. The Vijayanagara royal teacher Shri Vyasarajaru is said to have installed half of his 732 idols of Hanuma, Bhima and Madhwa within 10 km of the town.

The Pache Parsvanath temple is well preserved, and the Ajitnath temple of the same period was renovated by the Dharmasthala institution after years in poor condition. A garden of 5 acres holds a statue of the sleeping Kumbhakarna of the Ramayana, 142 feet long and 32 feet high, into whose belly visitors can walk. The town also has the tomb of the Sufi saint Baba Fakruddin, who settled there.
people-power-revolution: Ferdinand Marcos was elected president in 1965 and re-elected in 1969, and on 23 September 1972 he declared martial law under Proclamation No. 1081. He dissolved Congress, shut down critical media and ordered the arrest of opponents, among them Senator Ninoy Aquino. His spending relied heavily on debt, and after the recession of 1981 the economy declined, contracting by 6.8% in 1983 and by 7.3% in each of 1984 and 1985. On 21 August 1983 Aquino was assassinated as he disembarked at Manila International Airport after three years in exile. The killing outraged many Filipinos and led to non-cooperation and civil disobedience.

The election of 7 February 1986 pitted Marcos against Aquino's widow, Corazon Aquino. The Commission on Elections gave Marcos 10,807,197 votes to her 9,291,761, whereas the poll watcher NAMFREL's returns from 70% of precincts had her ahead by 7,835,070 to 7,053,068. On 16 February Aquino held a rally at Luneta Park, attended by about two million people, and announced a nonviolent civil disobedience campaign and a boycott of businesses linked to Marcos.

Officers of the Reform the Armed Forces Movement had planned a coup, and the revolt began on 22 February around Camp Crame and Camp Aguinaldo. Crowds filled Epifanio de los Santos Avenue, or EDSA. On 24 February helicopters of the 15th Strike Wing under Colonel Antonio Sotelo, sent to attack Camp Crame, landed there instead, a turning point against Marcos. On 25 February some 20,000 people blocked the Bamban Bridge and stopped loyalist reinforcements. Marcos held a rival inauguration while preparing to flee, and he and his family were flown by helicopter to Clark Air Base and then to exile in Hawaii.

Aquino issued Proclamation No. 3, a provisional constitution, and abolished the Batasang Pambansa pending a plebiscite on a new constitution. Officers of the movement that had launched the failed coup were dissatisfied with her rise to power and attempted further coups during her term. The revolution inspired later nonviolent changes of government, including those in East Germany and other former Soviet Bloc countries. In 2001 a similar EDSA uprising led to the resignation of President Joseph Estrada, and the radio broadcast of the revolution was inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2003.
peoples-action-party: Lee Kuan Yew, Toh Chin Chye and Goh Keng Swee took part in the Malayan Forum, a London-based student group opposed to colonial rule in Malaya in the 1940s and early 1950s. After returning to Singapore they met regularly to discuss independence and looked for like-minded people, among them the journalist S. Rajaratnam, English-educated left-wing students and Chinese-educated union and student leaders. The party was registered on 21 November 1954. Its first Central Executive Committee brought together trade unionists, lawyers and journalists, with Lee as secretary-general and Toh as founding chairman.

The party won the 1959 general election, the first to produce a fully elected parliament and a cabinet with full internal self-government. Lee became the first Prime Minister, a post he held for 31 years. Lee sought to reposition the party towards the centre and in 1961 expelled its leftist faction, which reorganised as Barisan Sosialis. Singapore joined Malaysia in 1963, and the party acted as an opposition at the federal level. Relations with the United Malays National Organisation worsened when each contested seats in the other's sphere, and Tunku Abdul Rahman forced Singapore to leave Malaysia on 9 August 1965.

Barisan Sosialis resigned from Parliament in 1966, after several of its leaders had been arrested in Operation Coldstore as alleged communists. Most opposition parties boycotted the 1968 election, so the party won every seat, and from 1965 to 1981 it was the only party in Parliament. It lost its first seat in a 1981 by-election in Anson to the Workers' Party. Lee stepped down as Prime Minister in 1990 in favour of Goh Chok Tong, and Lee Hsien Loong became Prime Minister in 2004.

Early on the party followed a Leninist form of organisation. Power lies in the Central Executive Committee under the secretary-general, who by convention has been the Prime Minister since 1959. The party recruits candidates by invitation, through talent spotting among the civil service, armed forces, academia, the professions and business, and says this prevents nepotism and primary elections. Members vote along the party line once a decision is made. Its youth wing was formed in 1986 as the Youth Committee and renamed the Young PAP in 1993.

The party describes its aims as pragmatism, meritocracy, multiracialism and Asian values, in analysts' account, and it supports free-market policies together with state-owned enterprises. Its symbol, a red flash and blue circle on white, was inspired, Lee Kuan Yew acknowledged, by that of the British Union of Fascists, though the colours were changed. At rallies members wear white shirts and trousers to signify incorruptibility.
peoples-army-of-vietnam: The People's Army of Vietnam was first conceived in September 1944 as the Information, Communication and Education Unit of the Liberation Army, meant to educate, recruit and mobilise the Vietnamese to drive out the French colonial and Japanese occupiers. Under the guidelines of Hồ Chí Minh, Võ Nguyên Giáp was given the task of establishing the brigades, and the Propaganda Unit of the Liberation Army came into existence on 22 December 1944. Its first formation had thirty-one men and three women, armed with two revolvers, seventeen rifles, one light machine gun and fourteen breech-loading flintlocks, and it fought its first engagements at Khai Phat and Na Ngan against French soldiers in late 1944.

In 1954 Hồ Chí Minh's administration formally named the Viet Minh's main armed wing Quân đội nhân dân Việt Nam, the Military of the people of Vietnam. In Ho's words the name stressed an army from the People, fighting for the People and serving the People.

During the French Indochina War the army was often called the Việt Minh. Its first regiment, the 102nd Capital Regiment, was created on 7 January 1947 for operations around Hanoi, and its first division, the 308th, followed. In late 1951 five new divisions were created, and the 351st Division became its first artillery division. Before the Battle of Dien Bien Phu it received 24 captured US 105 mm howitzers supplied by the Chinese People's Liberation Army. In 1954 four of its divisions, supported by this artillery, defeated the French Union forces at Dien Bien Phu, ending 83 years of French rule in Indochina.

In the Vietnam War its opponents called it the North Vietnamese Army, to tell it from the southern Viet Cong, though both worked under the same command structure. In 1976, after reunification, the Liberation Army of South Vietnam was disbanded and merged with it. It had forces in Laos to secure the Ho Chi Minh trail and support the Pathet Lao, aided the Khmer Rouge in toppling Lon Nol's government in 1975, and in 1978 helped topple Pol Pot's Democratic Kampuchea. It also fought in border wars with China.

The People's Army of Vietnam is the armed wing of the Communist Party of Vietnam and the core component of the Vietnam People's Armed Forces. It includes the Ground Force, the Navy, Air Defence and Air Force, the Border Guard and the Coast Guard. It is administered by the Ministry of National Defence under the party's Central Military Commission, which holds most power over the military, although the President of Vietnam is commander-in-chief on paper. Conscription applies in principle to every male aged 18 to 27.
peoples-commissar: Each people's commissar, or narkom, headed a People's Commissariat (narkomat), the central body managing one field of state activity or one sector of the economy. The first were created by the decree establishing the Council of People's Commissars, adopted by the 2nd Congress of Soviets on 9 November 1917. It entrusted the branches of state life to commissions working with the mass organisations of workers, sailors, soldiers and peasants, and vested government power in the collegium of their chairmen. The Congress and its All-Russian Central Executive Committee could oversee and dismiss the commissars.

The first council had thirteen commissariats, among them internal affairs, agriculture, labour, military and naval affairs, education, finance, foreign affairs, justice, food, posts and telegraphs, national affairs and railways. On 15 December 1917 the Supreme Council of National Economy was added with the status of a commissariat. A decree of 1 December 1917, proposed by Lenin, set a commissar's pay at 500 rubles plus 100 for each family member unable to work, roughly a worker's average wage.

The same pattern spread to the other Soviet republics. Article 43 of the 1918 Constitution of the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic listed much the same commissariats, and autonomous republics formed their own councils, as the Kirghiz Autonomous Socialist Soviet Republic did in its constitution of 1929. The Ukrainian constitution of 1919 provided for commissariats without listing them.

With the Treaty on the Creation of the Soviet Union the work was divided. Union commissariats took foreign affairs, military and naval affairs, foreign trade, communications and posts, while others, such as justice, education, health and agriculture, stayed with the republics. Some fields, among them labour, food and finance, were run at both levels.

The number of commissariats grew as the economy did, through the splitting of old ones and the founding of new. In 1932 the Supreme Council of National Economy of the Soviet Union became three commissariats, for heavy industry, light industry and the forest industry, and between 1936 and 1939 the total rose to 24, as when fish and meat and dairy were divided from the food industry in 1939. In 1946 the commissariats at every level became ministries of the same names.
peoples-consultative-assembly: On 18 August 1945, the day after Sukarno proclaimed Indonesia's independence, the Preparatory Committee for Indonesian Independence approved a constitution providing for the assembly as the supreme legislative authority; the day is still marked as its official birthday. Until it could be formed, the Central Indonesian National Committee (KNIP), with 135 appointed deputies, took its place, and an edict of Vice President Hatta of 16 October 1945 gave the KNIP full legislative powers. After the federal United States of Indonesia and the provisional constitution of 1950, Sukarno reimposed the 1945 Constitution by decree on 5 July 1959, restoring the assembly's role.

In 1960 Sukarno set up a Provisional People's Consultative Assembly (MPRS) of appointed members, which in 1963 named him President for Life, in violation of Article 7 of the Constitution. In 1966, purged of 180 members either loyal to Sukarno or linked to organisations implicated in the alleged coup attempt of 30 September 1965, it revoked the life presidency, banned communism and gave legal form to the transfer of power to Suharto; its Special Session of March 1967 ended Sukarno's presidency, and in 1968 it appointed Suharto president.

The first elected assembly met in March 1973 with 920 members, later 1,000. It elected Suharto to every term down to his seventh in 1998, approved the integration of East Timor as a province in 1978 and gave him the title Father of Development in 1983. After his fall in May 1998 a Special Session limited presidential terms. In 1999 it rejected B.J. Habibie's accountability speech, recognised the East Timor referendum and elected Abdurrahman Wahid, whom it removed in July 2001 in favour of Megawati Sukarnoputri.

From 1999 to 2002 the assembly amended the Constitution, creating the Regional Representative Council, abolishing the Supreme Advisory Council and requiring that 20 percent of the national budget go to education. Since 2004 it has stood on equal terms with the House of Representatives, the Audit Board, the Supreme Court and the Constitutional Court. It amends the Constitution by a two-thirds vote, inaugurates and may impeach the president and vice-president, and elects them only when both offices are vacant. It lost the power to issue binding resolutions in 2003. For the 2024–2029 term it had 580 House members and 152 senators.
peoples-court-germany: The People's Court (Volksgerichtshof) was established on 24 April 1934 by decree of Reich Chancellor Adolf Hitler. The immediate cause was the Reichstag fire trial before the Reich Court of Justice, in which all but one of the defendants were acquitted, though Hitler had already called in Mein Kampf for a "national tribunal" to execute "tens of thousands" of people he regarded as traitors. The law that created it moved treason, high treason, major sabotage and assassination of members of the government from the Reich Court of Justice and made the penalties substantially more severe. H. W. Koch names three features of German history behind it: the stab-in-the-back myth, the Enabling Act and the Führerprinzip.

A decree of 18 April 1936 made the court, described as a temporary expedient, a full court. Otto Georg Thierack, formerly vice-president of the Reich Court of Justice, became president on 1 May 1936. Its judges gained the red robes of the supreme court, and its jurisdiction grew to include misprision of treason, economic sabotage, Wehrkraftzersetzung, evading military service, sedition and espionage. In August 1942 Thierack became Reich Minister of Justice and Roland Freisler, a Nazi Party member since 1923, took the presidency and kept the most important cases for himself. Joseph Goebbels told the court that it was to start not from the law but from the decision that the man must be got rid of.

Each senate had five judges, two trained and three lay judges, about two thirds of whom came from Nazi organisations and one third from the armed forces. The court rejected judicial independence, due process, appeal and the right to counsel, and punished "criminal mentality" regardless of written law. Before the war it sentenced on average two per cent of defendants to death, but it treated members of the KPD and SPD more harshly. Between 1941 and 1943 death sentences by the People's and Special Courts rose from 1,292 to 5,336. Freisler died in an air raid in early 1945, and no trials are documented after April 1945.

Estimates of the court's work differ: Müller counts at least 14,319 defendants and at least 5,191 executions, and Wachsmann and Hoffmann 5,179 executions. Victims included the White Rose members Sophie Scholl, Hans Scholl, Alexander Schmorell, Willi Graf, Christoph Probst and Kurt Huber, and the seventeen-year-old Helmuth Hübener. After the war Ernst Lautz, chief prosecutor, was sentenced to ten years and the judge Oswald Rothaug to life in 1947. At least 29 of its judges and 69 prosecutors later worked in the West German court system. On 25 January 1985 the Bundestag declared it an instrument of judicial murder and state terrorism, and in 1998 all its judgments were annulled by federal law.
peoples-democratic-party-of-afghanistan: The party was formed at a unity congress of factions of the Socialist Party of Afghanistan on 1 January 1965. Twenty-seven men met at Nur Muhammad Taraki's house in Kabul and elected him Secretary General, with Babrak Karmal as Deputy Secretary General. Its secret constitution described its ideology as the practical experience of Marxism–Leninism, but in public it used labels such as national democratic and socialist. Four members won seats in the 1965 parliamentary election, and the party was known for its ties to the Soviet Union.

In 1967 the party split into the Khalq faction of Taraki, drawing mostly on rural Pashtuns, and the Parcham faction of Karmal, drawing on urban supporters. Soviet mediation reunited them in 1977. The party helped Mohammad Daoud Khan overthrow King Mohammad Zahir Shah in 1973, but relations with him worsened, and in the Saur Revolution of 1978 the party seized power, with Taraki as prime minister.

The government pursued rapid reform: separating mosque and state, a literacy campaign, land reform and the emancipation of women. It also launched a repression that killed thousands, mostly at Pul-e-Charkhi prison, where estimates of those executed between April 1978 and December 1979 run as high as 27,000. Olivier Roy estimated that between 50,000 and 100,000 people disappeared in the Taraki–Amin period. In December 1979 Soviet special forces killed Hafizullah Amin at the Tajbeg Palace, and Karmal became leader as the Soviet–Afghan War began. Mohammad Najibullah replaced Karmal as general secretary in May 1986. After the Soviet withdrawal in 1989, Najibullah renamed the party the Homeland Party in June 1990 and dropped Marxism–Leninism. Mujahideen took Kabul in 1992 and banned the party.

The party was organised on the model of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, with a Politburo, usually of seven to nine members, as its main executive body between sessions of the congress and the Central Committee. From 1982 it spread into the countryside, though it was organised in only about 2,000 of an estimated 25,000 villages. Its successors included the Watan Party, formed in 1997, and the National United Party of Afghanistan, registered in 2003.
peoples-front-for-democracy-and-justice: The historical region of Eritrea joined Ethiopia as an autonomous unit in 1952. The Eritrean Liberation Movement was founded in 1958 and succeeded by the Eritrean Liberation Front (ELF) in 1961, which grew after Emperor Haile Selassie abolished Eritrea's autonomy and annexed it as a province in 1962. Through the 1960s and 1970s the ELF waged a guerrilla war against the Ethiopian government, and in 1970 a faction broke away to form the Marxist-Leninist Eritrean People's Liberation Front (EPLF).

The EPLF won control of much of the countryside and built administrations in the areas it held. Fighting among the EPLF, the ELF and other rebel groups from 1981 checked its advance, but it emerged as the principal Eritrean guerrilla group. As Soviet support for Ethiopia's socialist government collapsed in the late 1980s, it allied with guerrillas in Tigray and elsewhere in Ethiopia. After a referendum supervised by the United Nations in April 1993, it declared Eritrea independent the following month.

At the EPLF's third congress delegates voted to turn the 95,000-member organisation into a mass political movement, with a transitional mandate to draw the population into politics and prepare the country for constitutional democracy. The new party set up a transitional National Assembly of 150 members, which chose its secretary-general, the former EPLF leader Isaias Afwerki, as president. In 1997 the assembly adopted a constitution for a multi-party system. After independence a committee of former senior fighters reviewed the laws inherited from Ethiopia to adapt them to the new state and to the EPLF's values.

An early attempt to shape the country's values failed because the former fighters were a minority, but the border war of 1998 to 2000 with Ethiopia gave the party a second chance to impose its ideology. On 12 November 2021 the Office of Foreign Assets Control of the U.S. Department of the Treasury placed the party on its sanctions list for activities contributing to the crisis in northern Ethiopia; the sanctions were lifted on 19 September 2026.

The party describes itself as left-wing and nationalist but holds itself open to nationalists of any political affiliation. Observers debate whether it is a true party or a broad governing association in transition, and some see it as an amorphous nationalist umbrella.
peoples-liberation-army: The People's Liberation Army (PLA) traces its origins to the left-wing units of the National Revolutionary Army of the Kuomintang, which broke away in 1927 in an uprising against the nationalist government as the Chinese Red Army. In 1925 the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) had renamed its Central Military Department the Central Military Commission; it was first led by Zhang Guotao and from 1926 by Zhou Enlai. During the First United Front it was less a unified command than an administrative liaison with other armed communist groups.

During the Second Sino-Japanese War the communist units were reintegrated into the National Revolutionary Army as the New Fourth Army and the Eighth Route Army. The two were reconstituted as the PLA in 1947.

After the People's Republic was established in 1949, the army was reorganised. An Air Force leadership structure was set up in November 1949 and a Navy structure the following April. The early PLA consisted overwhelmingly of peasants and treated soldiers and officers in an egalitarian way; formal ranks were not adopted until 1955. The sociologist Alessandro Russo describes this as a break with traditional Chinese hierarchies. The first Military Service Law of 1955 created compulsory service.

Its engagements include the Chinese Civil War, the Second Sino-Japanese War, the incorporation of Xinjiang in 1949 and of Tibet in 1950, the Korean War under the banner of the Chinese People's Volunteer Army (1950–1953), the Taiwan Strait crises of 1954–1955 and 1958, the Sino-Indian War of 1962, the Sino-Soviet border conflict of 1969 and the Sino-Vietnamese War of 1979. It has also sent units, often engineers and logistics troops, on United Nations peacekeeping missions in Lebanon, the Republic of the Congo, Sudan, Ivory Coast and Haiti.

The PLA is the armed wing of the CCP, which holds that the party commands the gun. It is governed by the Central Military Commission, which exists as a party body and a state body with identical membership. Regiments, brigades and larger units have party committees and political commissars, who are officially equal to commanders in status. Operational control is divided between the service headquarters and theatre commands, grouped by geography.

The PLA now has four services, the Ground Force, Navy, Air Force and Rocket Force, and four arms established on 19 April 2024. Women took part extensively in combat during the revolutionary period and the civil war; after 1949 their role shrank mostly to support, medical and logistics duties.
peoples-national-movement: Eric Williams began building a political base after his return to Trinidad in 1948, giving lectures between 1948 and 1955 under the Political Education Movement, a branch of the Teachers Education and Cultural Association. He launched the party on 15 January 1956, taking inspiration from Norman Manley's People's National Party in Jamaica. In that year's elections the PNM won 13 of the 24 elected seats in the Legislative Council with 38.7% of the vote; the Secretary of State for the Colonies let Williams name the five appointed members, against the governor's wishes, and he became Chief Minister.

The party won 20 of 30 seats in 1961 and, after the West Indies Federation collapsed, led the country to independence on 31 August 1962. Discontent grew and came to a head in the Black Power Revolution of April 1970, when the deputy leader A. N. R. Robinson resigned and Williams declared a state of emergency during an army revolt. In 1971 the main opposition parties boycotted the election and the PNM won all 36 seats. In 1973 Williams announced that he would step down, then returned as leader in December, and Karl Hudson-Phillips, whom most nominating party groups had backed, was forced out.

After Williams died on 29 March 1981, President Ellis Clarke chose George Chambers as prime minister, and Chambers won that year's election. In 1986 the National Alliance for Reconstruction under Robinson reduced the party to three of 36 seats. Patrick Manning, promising a new PNM, returned it to power in 1991, lost in 1995 and 2000, and was appointed prime minister after an 18–18 tie in 2001 before winning in 2002 and 2007 and losing in 2010. Keith Rowley led the party back in 2015 and won again in 2020; under his successor, Stuart Young, it lost the 2025 election to the United National Congress.

The party's symbol is the balisier flower, and its headquarters, Balisier House, is in Port of Spain. It has drawn most of its support from Afro-Trinidadians and Tobagonians, the Creole-Mulatto population and the towns, as well as from minorities such as the Chinese, Christian Indians other than Presbyterian Indians, and Muslims. Tobago has a semi-autonomous branch, the Tobago Council of the People's National Movement, with its own members, executive and leader. From 1957 to 1962 the PNM sat with the West Indies Federal Labour Party in the federal parliament.
peoples-national-party: Norman Washington Manley led the party from its founding in 1938 until his death in 1969. It is the second-oldest party in Jamaica, after Marcus Garvey's People's Political Party of 1929. It won only four of 32 seats at the first universal election in 1944, and in 1949 took more votes than the Jamaica Labour Party but fewer seats, 13 to 17. In 1954 it expelled the Marxist Richard Hart and three others, known as the four Hs, which parted it from the Trade Union Congress.

The party first won in 1955, with 18 of 32 seats. Manley became chief minister and in 1959 Jamaica's first premier, and his governments opened secondary education to many poorer Jamaicans through state scholarships. After Jamaica voted in 1961 to leave the West Indies Federation, Manley called an election for April 1962, which the JLP won by 26 seats to 19.

Under Norman Manley's son Michael Manley the party returned in 1972 committed to democratic socialism and closer ties with the Global South, and won a landslide in 1976. After years of inflation and rising unemployment it was routed in 1980 by Edward Seaga's JLP in a campaign marked by violence, boycotted the snap election of 1983 and returned in 1989. P. J. Patterson, leader from 1992, became the first Jamaican leader to win three successive general elections, in 1993, 1997 and 2002.

Portia Simpson-Miller succeeded him in 2006 as the party's first female president and Jamaica's first female prime minister. The PNP lost in 2007, ending 18 years in power, won 42 of 63 seats in 2011 and lost by one seat in 2016. After a heavy defeat in September 2020, Mark Golding was elected its sixth president in November 2020.

The party describes itself as social democratic, and its constitution calls it democratic socialist; it also adheres to republicanism. It is a full member of the Socialist International and a member of COPPPAL, and from 1957 to 1962 it belonged to the West Indies Federal Labour Party in the parliament of the West Indies Federation.
peoples-progressive-party-guyana: The party was founded on 1 January 1950 as a merger of the British Guiana Labour Party, led by Forbes Burnham, and the Political Affairs Committee, led by Cheddi Jagan. It was the first mass party in the colony, at first multi-ethnic and backed by workers and intellectuals, and held its first congress on 1 April 1951. In 1953 Burnham tried and failed to become party leader, and the party went on to win 18 of the 24 elected seats in the House of Assembly, making Jagan Chief Minister. The British sent in troops, citing the threat of a Marxist revolution, and replaced the assembly with an unelected Interim Legislative Council.

The party split into factions under Jagan and Burnham, which ran against each other in 1957, winning nine and three seats; Burnham's followers founded the People's National Congress (PNC), dominated by Afro-Guyanese, leaving the PPP to represent Indo-Guyanese voters. The PPP won the 1961 elections by a 1.6% margin but took almost twice the PNC's seats, and serious inter-racial violence followed. Convinced that Jagan was likely a Communist, the Kennedy administration used the Central Intelligence Agency and pressed a reluctant United Kingdom to help a campaign against his government. After the 1964 elections the PNC and the United Force formed a government, and Governor Richard Luyt removed Jagan from office.

Elections through the 1970s and 1980s were rigged by the PNC. Free elections in 1992 brought Jagan the presidency, and the party moved from socialism towards a market economy under a structural adjustment programme of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund. After Jagan's death in March 1997 his widow, Janet Jagan, won that year's election; ill health made her resign in 1999, and Bharrat Jagdeo succeeded her. In 2004 Ronald Gajraj, minister for home affairs, resigned over allegations of phantom death squads; a commission later exonerated him while noting an unhealthy relationship with organised crime.

The party lost power in 2015 to a combined opposition list under David A. Granger and returned in 2020, when Irfaan Ali was sworn in as president five months after the March election, which Granger had refused to accept. On 5 May 2024 its 32nd Congress removed Marxism-Leninism and socialism from its constitution while keeping democratic centralism.
peoples-radical-party: The party grew out of a circle of young Serbian followers of Svetozar Marković and Nikola Pašić in Zurich, whose programme called for a new constitution, freedom of the press, judicial independence, reform of education and stronger local self-government. Its first main assembly met in Kragujevac in July 1882, adopted a programme inspired by French Radicalism and elected Pašić president of the central committee. Over its history the party moved from socialism and radicalism towards conservatism in the early 20th century.

The Radicals published their own daily newspaper, Samouprava (Self-Government), which criticised the monarchy and demanded democracy, public liberties and reform of the bureaucracy. Its leaders, among them Pera Todorovic, Sima Lozanić, Lazar Paču, Raša Milošević and Stojan Protić, were the first to mobilise the Serbian peasantry and the provincial middle classes, including teachers, peasant leaders and priests, and the party also drew intellectuals and diplomats such as Milovan Milovanović and Milenko Vesnić. It supported uniting all Serb-inhabited lands under the slogan Balkans to the Balkan nations, and in foreign policy it was anti-Austrian, mostly Russophile and Francophile.

In September 1883 King Milan Obrenović ordered the army to confiscate the peasants' arms, and the Timok Rebellion broke out in eastern Serbia. The king blamed an article in Samouprava; the rising was put down in ten days, most of the party's leaders were captured and many sentenced to death, while Pašić escaped to the Principality of Bulgaria. An amnesty followed for Radicals who entered the government in 1887, and the party was instrumental in the parliamentary Constitution of 1888, after which it held almost 80 percent of the vote.

A dissident faction formed in 1901 and became the Independent Radical Party in 1905. After the return of the Karađorđević dynasty in 1903, Radical governments led Serbia through its Golden Age and the First World War, and in 1917 Pašić signed the Corfu Declaration with the Yugoslav Committee. In the new kingdom the party held the premiership for eight of the years from 1918 to 1928, helped by electoral rules that favoured Serbia. After Pašić died in 1926, Aca Stanojević led the party and later called for an end to the royal dictatorship.
peoples-rally-for-progress: The party, known in French as the Rassemblement populaire pour le Progrès (RPP), was founded at Dikhil on 4 March 1979 and has been dominant in the politics of Djibouti since then. It tends to have more influence among the Issa population. It was declared the sole legal party in October 1981 and kept that status until the referendum of September 1992 introduced multiparty politics.

At its congress of 19–20 March 1997 Hassan Gouled Aptidon was re-elected party president and a Central Committee of 125 members was chosen. In the parliamentary election of December 1997 the RPP stood in alliance with the moderate faction of the Front for the Restoration of Unity and Democracy (FRUD), which had signed a peace agreement with the government in December 1994; the alliance won 79% of the vote and all 65 seats in the National Assembly.

On 4 February 1999 Gouled Aptidon announced that he would retire at the next election, and an extraordinary congress chose Ismaïl Omar Guelleh as the party's candidate. Standing for the RPP and the moderate FRUD, Guelleh won the presidential election of 9 April 1999 with 74% of the vote against the independent Moussa Ahmed Idriss. In the election of 10 January 2003 the party belonged to the Union for a Presidential Majority (UMP), which won 63% of the vote and all 65 seats, and the UMP again took every seat in February 2008, when the opposition boycotted the vote.

The Eighth Ordinary Congress opened on 4 March 2004, the party's 25th anniversary; Guelleh was re-elected party president by acclamation for a three-year term and the Central Committee grew from 180 to 250 members. At the Ninth Ordinary Congress on 4 March 2007 he was re-elected again, and three women were added to the Political Bureau, which then had 17 members.
peoples-revolutionary-government-grenada: Grenada, a Caribbean island state of 350 km2 in the Lesser Antilles, became an associated state in 1967 and gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1974 under Sir Eric Gairy of the Grenada United Labor Party, whose government drifted towards authoritarian rule. A new generation of middle-class intellectuals, many trained at British and American universities, returned as the Black Power movement spread through the Caribbean. The New JEWEL Movement built a following with its weekly paper, and after Bernard Coard, Bishop's childhood friend, returned in September 1976 the party moved towards Marxism. Early in 1979 Gairy planned to arrest its leaders, who went into hiding before taking power.

Fifteen days after taking power the government declared the constitution suspended and Parliament dissolved, taking executive and legislative powers for itself and postponing the elections it had announced. People's Law No. 8 allowed the internment of anyone suspected of threatening public security, and by April 1979 there were 80 political prisoners. After a plot in November 1979 and a bomb in June 1980 that killed three young girls at a meeting Bishop addressed, the government turned against its enemies. It nationalised much of trade, infrastructure and non-agricultural business while farming stayed private. Per capita growth continued in 1981, according to the World Bank, and unemployment fell from 49% in 1979 to 14% in 1983.

The government quickly formed secret links with Cuba, which supplied weapons, and through Cuba made agreements with the USSR, Vietnam and Czechoslovakia. Relations with the United States worsened after Bishop backed the Soviet intervention in Afghanistan early in 1980, and the airport built with Cuban help alarmed the administration of Ronald Reagan. Within the party a power struggle grew between the popular Bishop and Coard, who favoured democratic centralism.

On returning from Czechoslovakia, Hungary and Cuba on 8 October 1983, Bishop was accused of spreading rumours of a plot against him and placed under house arrest with Jacqueline Creft, his companion and Minister of Education. After his killing on 19 October, Hudson Austin headed a Revolutionary Military Council until the invasion of 25 October. The airport, completed after the fall of the government, was renamed Maurice Bishop International Airport in 2009, and the last of the Grenada 17 convicted for the putsch and Bishop's death were released in 2009.
peoples-united-party: In the 1940s politics in British Honduras was led by trade unionists of the Workers and Tradesmen's Union, later the General Workers Union. A group of college-educated men, among them John Smith, George Price, Herbert Fuller and Herman Jex, won seats on the Belize Town Board and later the Legislative Council. On 31 December 1949 the governor devalued the British Honduras dollar after saying he would not, and in January 1950 they formed the People's Committee to speak out against the devaluation and colonial rule.

On 12 February 1950 a crowd of 10,000 marched to Government House in Belize City; police used tear gas on a meeting at Battlefield Park, and a state of emergency lasted until July. In September the committee concluded that its work needed a political party, and on 29 September 1950 it dissolved itself and the People's United Party was born. In 1951 the colonial government dissolved the PUP-dominated Belize City Council and jailed the leaders Leigh Richardson and Phillip Goldson for an article justifying revolution.

Price became head of the General Workers Union in 1952, the year of a 49-day strike that greatly raised support for the union and the party. At the first general elections, on 28 April 1954, the PUP won eight of nine seats. In 1956 Richardson, Goldson and other central committee members left, and Price led the party unchallenged for nearly four decades; in 1961 it took all eighteen seats. After Hurricane Hattie struck Belize City in October 1961 it called for a capital on higher ground, which led to the building of Belmopan.

In 1981 Price brought back the Heads of Agreement, proposals meant to end Guatemala's claim to the country; protests forced a state of emergency, under which Belize became independent on 21 September 1981. The PUP lost the December 1984 election to the United Democratic Party by 21 seats to 7, returned under Price in 1989 and lost again in 1993.

Price resigned as leader in 1996, and under Said Musa the party won a landslide in 1998 and 22 of 29 seats in 2003. It lost heavily in February 2008, winning six of 31 seats, stayed in opposition after the elections of 2012 and 2015, and won in 2020, holding 26 seats in 2025.
peoples-volunteer-army: Every unit of the army was in fact transferred from the People's Liberation Army on the orders of Chairman Mao Zedong, but it was constituted separately as volunteers so that China would avoid an official war with the United States. Preparations began soon after the war broke out: on 13 July 1950 the military command ordered the Thirteenth Army Group of the Fourth Field Army to become the Northeastern Border Defense Army, with Deng Hua coordinating. Chen Geng and Deng Hua acted as commander and commissar after Peng Dehuai fell ill in April 1952. About 3 million Chinese civilian and military personnel served in Korea during the war.

The army crossed the Yalu River in secret on 19 October 1950, the day Pyongyang fell to United Nations forces, and attacked on 25 October before withdrawing into the mountains. Its second offensive from 25 November overran several UN divisions at the Battle of the Ch'ongch'on River, destroyed Task Force Faith at the Chosin Reservoir and retook Pyongyang in December. Its forces and the North Koreans captured Seoul on 4 January 1951, but the exhausted army was driven out of the city again on 16 March.

A spring offensive of about 700,000 men from 22 April 1951 was halted north of Seoul and in the east by 22 May. The front then settled roughly along the 38th parallel while talks went on from 10 July 1951 at Kaesong, prolonged by the dispute over whether prisoners should be repatriated by force. The army relied on attacks on flanks and rear, infiltration and local superiority in numbers, and was armed mainly with captured Japanese and Nationalist weapons.

Its dead are commemorated in North Korea at the Cemetery of the Fallen Soldiers of the Chinese People's Volunteers Army in Hoechang County. In China the soldiers became known as the most beloved people, after an essay of 1951 by Wei Wei, and the war is widely regarded as an honourable struggle, the first in a century in which a Chinese army withstood a Western one. After the armistice 14,235 prisoners held by the UN were taken to Taiwan, where they began arriving on 23 January 1954; that day became World Freedom Day in their honour.
pepi-i: Pepi I Meryre, also written Pepy I, was the third king of the Sixth Dynasty and ruled for over 40 years, possibly 49 or 50, toward the end of the Old Kingdom. He was the son of Teti, the founder of the dynasty, and of Iput, who may have been a daughter of Unas, the last ruler of the Fifth Dynasty. He came to the throne after the brief reign of Userkare. The later historian Manetho claims that Teti was assassinated by his bodyguards, and the Egyptologist Naguib Kanawati supports the claim, noting the growing number of guards at court and the deliberate erasure of the names of several officials, among them the vizier Hezi.

Egypt's government had been decentralising since the Fifth Dynasty, with provincial families marrying into the royal house and holding high office. Pepi answered with a vast building programme, raising temples to local gods and many chapels for his own cult throughout Egypt, and he became the most prolific builder of the Old Kingdom. He recruited officials of non-noble origin and extended a network of warehouses from which taxes and labour could be collected. Probably after his twentieth year he faced a conspiracy in the harem, and he strengthened his position by marrying two daughters of Khui, the nomarch of Abydos, Ankhesenpepi I and Ankhesenpepi II, and making Khui's wife Nebet and her son Djau viziers.

He sent military campaigns against Nubia, Sinai and the southern Levant, landing troops on the Levantine coast from Egyptian transport boats. Trade with Byblos, Ebla and the oases of the Western Desert flourished, and he launched mining and quarrying expeditions to Sinai and beyond. He had at least six consorts and at least four sons. Ankhesenpepi I probably bore Merenre Nemtyemsaf I, who succeeded him, and Ankhesenpepi II was the mother of Pepi II Neferkare.

Pepi built his pyramid complex at Saqqara, originally 52.5 metres tall, with at least six further pyramids for his consorts. Its walls carry the most extensive corpus of Pyramid Texts from the Old Kingdom, appearing for the first time in some consorts' pyramids as well. The complex was called Pepi Mennefer and gave its name to the nearby capital, Memphis. His cult continued into the Middle Kingdom and stopped early in the Second Intermediate Period; in the New Kingdom his monuments began to be quarried for stone, and in the Mamluk era they were almost entirely dismantled.
pepi-ii: Pepi II Neferkare, whose second name means beautiful is the Ka of Re, came to the throne at the age of six after the death of Merenre Nemtyemsaf I. He was long thought to be the son of Pepi I, but many Egyptologists now hold that his father was Merenre, who married Pepi II's mother Ankhesenpepi II after Pepi I's death; stone blocks found at Saqqara in the 1999 to 2000 season support this. His mother most likely ruled as regent in his early years, perhaps helped by her brother Djau, who had been a vizier. A statuette in the Brooklyn Museum shows him as a child in full regalia on her lap.

The king sent expeditions into Nubia for ivory, ebony and other goods. A letter he wrote as a child to Harkhuf, the governor of Aswan, is preserved on Harkhuf's tomb: the king promised a great reward if a captured pygmy were brought back alive, and the inscription has been called the first travelogue. Copper and turquoise were mined in Sinai, alabaster quarried at Hatnub, and his name appears in inscriptions at Byblos. He had several wives, and three of them, Neith, Iput II and Udjebten, had minor pyramids in his own complex at Saqqara.

Later tradition remembered the length of his reign. The Turin King List gives 90 or more years and Manetho a still longer figure, but the latest contemporary evidence dates from about his 62nd year, and some Egyptologists suggest no more than 64 years. Others point out that missing later dates do not exclude a longer reign. His pyramid, 78.5 metres at the base, followed the standard format and was no larger than those of his predecessors.

The Old Kingdom declined sharply in his time. Nomarchs, the regional representatives of the king, had been gaining power since before him, and during his reign wealth and authority passed to high officials, who built large tombs in the provinces; the nomarchs were free from taxation and their positions became hereditary. Late in his reign he divided the office of vizier between Upper and Lower Egypt, a further decentralisation away from Memphis. Some scholars suggest that an aging ruler, not replaced because of his divine status, led to a succession crisis and stagnation. With no dominant central power, local nobles raided each other's territories, and the Old Kingdom ended within a couple of years of his reign, leading to the First Intermediate Period.
pepin-i-of-aquitaine: Pepin was the second son of Emperor Louis the Pious and his first wife, Ermengarde of Hesbaye. In August 817 his father assigned each of his sons a kingdom within the Empire, and Pepin received Aquitaine, which had been Louis's own subkingdom under Charlemagne. The only coin issue bearing Pepin's name was struck around this time, probably at Louis's wish. In 822 he married Ingeltrude, daughter of Theodobert, count of Madrie.

The court poet Ermoldus Nigellus accompanied Pepin on a campaign into Brittany in 824. Around 827-8 Louis sent him to support Bernard of Septimania against an incursion into the Iberian March, but his army arrived too late, and its co-leaders, Hugh of Tours and Matfrid of Orléans, were deposed.

Pepin rebelled in 830 with his elder brother Lothar I, perhaps in reaction to that deposition. He marched with Gascons to Paris with Neustrian support and captured his father at Compiègne, but the rebellion broke up when Louis agreed to remove Bernard from power. In 832 Pepin escaped from his father's prison in Trier and fled to Aquitaine, and took Limoges. In 833 Lothair joined, and with the help of Ebbo, archbishop of Reims, the sons deposed their father. Lothair's conduct alienated Pepin, who stood beside his father when Louis was restored on 1 March 834 and was himself restored.

Pepin died scarcely four years after that settlement and was buried in the Church of St. Radegonde in Poitiers. His sons, Pepin II and Charles, later Archbishop of Mainz, were minors, and Louis the Pious awarded Aquitaine to his youngest son Charles the Bald, but the Aquitainians elected the younger Pepin as Pepin II. His brother Charles also briefly claimed the kingdom. Both died childless.
pepin-ii-of-aquitaine: Pepin II, called the Younger, was the eldest son of Pepin I of Aquitaine and Ingeltrude, daughter of Theodobert, count of Madrie, and a grandson of the Emperor Louis the Pious. In 832 Louis had appointed his own son Charles the Bald, Pepin's uncle and about the same age, as king of Aquitaine, nominally dispossessing the elder Pepin. When Pepin I died in 838, the nobles of Aquitaine, keen to establish their independence from the empire, elected the young Pepin king. Charles contested the kingship, and Louis disinherited his grandson fully at Crémieu and again at Worms in two later divisions of the empire.

Louis demanded that the Aquitainians send Pepin to Aachen to learn the ways of good governance, but they refused. Pepin held Aquitaine in complete control until 841, when he went to the aid of his uncle Lothair I at the Battle of Fontenoy. There he defeated Charles the Bald, but Lothair was routed by Louis the German, another son of the emperor. Pepin returned to Aquitaine and continued the war against Charles.

In 844 Pepin asked for help from Jarl Oscar, a Viking adventurer, and guided his forces up the Garonne to Toulouse, which gave them the chance to scout the land for plunder. In 845 he welcomed Seguin of Bordeaux, who had defected from the emperor's side, and made him dux Wasconum to help in the fight against Sans II Sancion of Gascony. Oscar seized Bordeaux, then held by Charles, in 847 with the aid of disaffected citizens. The loss of the city to a heathen pirate, together with Pepin's heavy drinking and loose living, eroded his support among the nobles until by 848 he had none.

Sans II captured Pepin in 851 or 852 and handed him over to Charles, who held him in the monastery of Saint Médard in Soissons. In 854 Pepin escaped with the help of some of the aristocracy and recovered part of his old authority and lands, while Vikings established in the Loire valley ravaged Poitiers, Angoulême, Périgueux, Limoges, Clermont and Bourges as Charles was busy with him. In 864 Pepin joined the Vikings, rumoured to have turned from Christianity to the worship of Woden, and took part in an attack on Toulouse. He was captured again later that year, deposed by the Edict of Pîtres and imprisoned in Senlis.
pepin-of-herstal: Pepin II, known as Pepin of Herstal, was the son of the Frankish statesman Ansegisel and the grandson and namesake of Pepin I the Elder, through the marriage of Pepin I's daughter Begga to Ansegisel. That marriage united the houses of the Pippinids and the Arnulfings, which created what would be called the Carolingian dynasty. He was probably born at Herstal in modern Belgium, where his centre of power lay, which gave him his byname. He was the grandfather of Pepin the Short and the great-grandfather of Charlemagne.

Pepin became Mayor of the Palace in Austrasia in 680. With Martin, duke of Laon, he fought the Neustrian mayor Ebroin, who had designs on all Francia and defeated the Austrasians at the Battle of Lucofao but was assassinated in 681. Pepin made peace with his successor Waratton. Waratton's successor Berchar and the Neustrian king Theuderic III then made war on Austrasia, and were decisively defeated at the Battle of Tertry in 687. Pepin followed them to Paris and forced a peace, with the condition that Berchar leave office. He became mayor in all three Frankish kingdoms, Austrasia, Neustria and Burgundy, and began calling himself Duke and Prince of the Franks.

The Neustrians barely tolerated an Austrasian overlord, but Pepin turned to Germany. Over the next years he subdued the Alemanni, the Frisians and the Franconians, and between 690 and 692 Utrecht fell, giving the Franks control of trade routes on the Rhine to the North Sea. He supported the missionary work of Willibrord. In 695 he placed his son Drogo in the Burgundian mayorship and his other son Grimoald in the Neustrian one.

Around 670 Pepin had married Plectrude, mother of Drogo and Grimoald II, both of whom died before their father. His mistress or second wife Alpaida bore him Charles Martel and Childebrand. Just before his death Plectrude convinced him to disinherit Alpaida's sons in favour of his grandson Theudoald, a young child. Pepin died suddenly on 16 December 714, at the age of 79, at Jupille. Charles had gained favour among the Austrasians through his military prowess and the booty he brought, and despite Plectrude's imprisoning of him he became sole mayor of the palace, and de facto ruler of Francia, after a civil war of more than three years. Pepin's statesmanship further decreased Merovingian royal authority and secured acceptance of his family's right to rule.
pepin-of-italy: Pepin was born Carloman in 777, the second son of Charlemagne and his wife Hildegard, and had an older brother, Charles the Younger, and a half-brother, Pepin the Hunchback. In 781 Charlemagne and Hildegard took him to Rome at the request of Pope Adrian I, with his younger brother Louis the Pious and his sisters Rotrude and Bertha. His parents had delayed his baptism so that the pope could perform it. Adrian baptised him, renamed him Pepin, and crowned him king of the Lombards, later styled king of Italy, while Louis was crowned king of Aquitaine. The name was probably chosen to recall his grandfather Pepin the Short, remembered as a firm ally of the papacy.

Although only four years old, Pepin was brought to Lombardy to live under advisers provided by Charlemagne, the most important of whom were Adalard of Corbie, Waldo of Reichenau, the Lombard duke Rotchild and Angilbert. His court was based chiefly at Verona, with palaces also at Mantua and at Pavia, the traditional Lombard capital. He was king in his own name, but Charlemagne took a strong hand in Italy into Pepin's adulthood and sometimes issued laws directly.

Pepin took part in his father's campaign against Tassilo III of Bavaria in 786. In 796 he led a campaign against the Avar Khaganate, took its stronghold and precipitated the collapse of the Avar state, which allowed the Frankish realm to expand eastward; the Latin poem De Pippini regis Victoria Avarica commemorates the victory. He also led several raids against the Duchy of Benevento and, in 810, a campaign against the Republic of Venice. In 806 Charlemagne's Divisio Regnorum confirmed Pepin in Italy and gave him most of Bavaria and Alamannia.

Pepin died on 8 July 810. Over 810 and 811 his sister Rotrude, his aunt Gisela, his half-brother Pepin and his brother Charles also died, possibly victims of an epidemic that had spread from cattle. Charlemagne then declared Pepin's son Bernard ruler of Italy and Louis the heir to the rest of the empire. Pepin had married Theodrada, a cousin of his father, and Louis later used the closeness of the relation to portray the marriage as illegitimate in order to sideline Bernard. Bernard's male-line descendants ruled as counts of Vermandois into the eleventh century, the longest-surviving direct male line of Charlemagne. Pepin also had five daughters and was an ancestor of Hugh Capet.
pepin-the-short: Pepin was the son of the Frankish prince Charles Martel and his wife Rotrude, and was educated by the monks of the Abbey Church of St Denis near Paris. When Charles Martel died in 741 he divided rule between Pepin, who became Mayor of the Palace of Neustria, and his elder brother Carloman, who took Austrasia. Their half-brother Grifo demanded a share; the brothers besieged him at Laon and imprisoned him in a monastery. In 743 Carloman raised Childeric III, the last Merovingian, to the throne as a figurehead.

Carloman entered a monastery in 747, leaving Pepin sole mayor of the palace. Grifo escaped and fled to Duke Odilo of Bavaria, married to Pepin's sister Hiltrude, and Pepin put down his revolt. Holding the power of a king while Childeric had only the title, Pepin asked Pope Zachary whether it was proper that kings of the Franks no longer had royal power. The pope, hard pressed by the Lombards, replied that the one who wields power should be called king. Childeric was confined to a monastery and Pepin was elected by an assembly of nobles and anointed in 751.

In 754 Pope Stephen II anointed him again at the Basilica of St Denis, together with his sons Charles and Carloman, and gave him the title Patricius Romanorum, the first recorded crowning of a civil ruler by a pope. Pepin made war on the Lombard king Aistulf and confirmed the papacy in possession of Ravenna and the Pentapolis, the Donation of Pepin, which formed the legal basis of the Papal States.

Around 752 Pepin turned to Septimania, received the submission of Nîmes, Maguelone, Béziers and Agde, and took Narbonne in 759. In Aquitaine he fought Duke Waiofar from 760, capturing strongholds, deporting Gascon garrisons with their families and burning villas and vineyards. By 767 he held Toulouse and Bordeaux, the nobles accepted peace, and Waiofar was killed by his own followers in 768.

Pepin died in 768 and was buried at the Basilica of Saint Denis. The realm was divided under Salic law between Charlemagne and Carloman I. He was among the most powerful rulers of his time, but his reign is largely overshadowed by that of Charlemagne.
pequot-war: In the 1630s the Connecticut River Valley was in turmoil. Epidemics had cut the American Indian population over three decades, and the Pequot extended their power at their neighbours' expense while the nations competed for the fur trade with the Dutch and the English. The Mohegans, once one people with the Pequot, sided with the English, and the Pequot with the Dutch. In 1634 Western Niantics, tributaries of the Pequot, killed the trader John Stone and seven of his crew; the Pequot said it was revenge for the Dutch killing of their sachem Tatobem. On 20 July 1636 the trader John Oldham was killed off Block Island, and his killers found refuge with the Pequot.

In August 1636 John Endecott led about 90 men from Massachusetts Bay to burn Niantic villages on Block Island and then a Pequot village. Through the winter the Pequot besieged Fort Saybrook, and on 23 April 1637 the Wangunk chief Sequin, with Pequot help, killed nine settlers at Wethersfield; in all the towns lost about 30 settlers. Captain John Mason, with John Underhill, 70 Mohegans under Uncas and about 200 Narragansetts, then marched on Mistick Fort.

At the fort on 26 May 1637 the soldiers set the village ablaze, and of an estimated 500 Pequots inside, seven were taken prisoner and seven escaped. The allied warriors were horrified at the manner of the English fight. The Pequot fled west; at the Fairfield Swamp Fight several hundred, mostly women and children, surrendered, and the Mohawk killed the sachem Sassacus and sent his head and hands to Hartford.

About 200 Pequots survived to come under the Mohegan and Narragansett sachems, who received them by the treaty signed on 21 September 1638. Others were enslaved in English households or shipped to Bermuda and the West Indies. No large battles followed in southern New England for about 38 years, until King Philip's War in 1675. The historian Andrew Lipman links the war to the taking of body parts as battle trophies, and Alden T. Vaughan holds that the Bay colony's escalation of violence made all-out war unavoidable.
perak-river: The river begins at the confluence of the Machang and Merah rivers, deep in the Royal Belum State Park near the tripoint of Perak, Kelantan and Thailand in the Titiwangsa Mountains. The Machang rises along the Perak–Kelantan border, the Merah near Bang Lang National Park in the Sankalakhiri Range of Yala province on the Thai side. The Perak passes Gerik and Lenggong in the district of Hulu Perak, meets the Kangsar River at Kuala Kangsar, then winds through Parit, Pasir Salak and Kampung Gajah in Perak Tengah before emptying into the Straits of Malacca near Bagan Datuk.

Its basin covers almost every district of Perak except Kerian and Larut, Matang and Selama, since the Bintang Mountains divide it from the basin of the Kerian River to the west. Its tributaries include the Bidor River and the Kinta River, and Sungai Siput, Manong and Teluk Intan are among the other towns of its basin.

Most settlements of what is now Perak lay near the river until the 19th century, when tin deposits were discovered elsewhere, most notably at Ipoh. At Kuala Kangsar the British Resident, adviser to the Sultan, lived on a hill above the bank, Bukit Residen, and held council meetings there with the Sultan and the district chieftains. The chieftains came by sailing boat, while royalty and palace officials rode on elephants. The meetings usually lasted more than three days, and the people who camped below made them a riverside festival. Local usage derives the name Kangsar from the word council, while kuala means a confluence.

Rudyard Kipling mentioned the river in The Crab That Played with the Sea, one of the Just So Stories. There the man complains to the eldest magician that once a day and once a night the sea runs up the Perak, driving the fresh water back into the forest and wetting his house, and then runs down again, leaving only mud and upsetting his canoe.
percheron: The Percheron comes from the valley of the Huisne in western France, part of the former province of Perche, which gave the breed its name. Its exact origins are unknown. Foundation stock may have included mares captured by Clovis I from the Bretons, or Barb stallions brought from Spain by the Moors in the 8th century. Barb stallions were certainly crossed with local mares in the 8th century, and more Oriental blood came with the Comte du Perche on his return from the Crusades. Breed historians agree that the terrain and climate of Perche shaped it most.

After the age of the armoured knight, breeders sought horses able to pull heavy stagecoaches at a fast trot, the Diligence Horse, gray being preferred for its visibility at night. When railways replaced the coaches a heavier type arose for farm work and hauling goods. The breed nearly became extinct when horse breeding was suppressed during the French Revolution. Jean le Blanc, foaled in 1823, is the stallion to which all Percherons trace their ancestry, and the breed grew to a draft horse averaging about 910 kilograms. The French stud book was created in 1893.

Edward Harris II of Moorestown, New Jersey, first imported Percherons to the United States in 1839. After the American Civil War demand for large draft horses grew, and about 7,500 were exported in the 1880s. In the 1930s Percherons made up over 70 per cent of purebred draft horses in the United States, but mechanisation after World War II caused a steep decline, and only 85 were registered there in 1954.

The Percheron is the best known and most numerous French draft breed. It was used to improve the Ardennes and Vladimir Heavy Draft horses and to create the Spanish-Norman. By the end of the 19th century Percherons made up most of the driving horses of Paris. They are still used for draft work and forestry, and for parades, sleigh rides and carriage work.
percy-cox: Percy Zachariah Cox was born on 20 November 1864 at Harwood Hall, Herongate, in Essex, one of seven children of the cricketer Arthur Zachariah Cox and Julienne Emily Cox. After Harrow School, as a third son with little inheritance, he entered the Royal Military College, Sandhurst, in February 1884 and was commissioned into the Cameronians in India. In 1889 he moved to the Bengal Staff Corps and on 14 November married Louisa Belle, daughter of the surgeon-general John Butler Hamilton.

After minor posts in India he served in British Somaliland at Zeila and Berbera, and in 1895 defeated the Rer Hared clan, which had been raiding the coast, in six weeks with 52 regulars and 1,500 untrained irregulars. In October 1899 Lord Curzon made him Political Agent and consul at Muscat, where the French had leased a coaling station and protected the slave trade. In June 1904 he became Acting Political Resident in the Persian Gulf, at Bushehr, and from 1906 urged India to change its policy towards Ibn Saud of Nejd.

In the war with the Ottoman Empire he served in Mesopotamia as Chief Political Officer and on 9 December 1914 took the formal surrender of Subhi Bey, governor of Basra, ending the Battle of Qurna. He signed a treaty guaranteeing Ibn Saud £5,000 a month, was made honorary major-general in May 1917, and from November 1918 represented Britain at Tehran, where the Anglo-Persian Agreement was concluded on 9 August 1919.

After the Iraqi Revolt of 1920 he became the first High Commissioner under the mandate, set up a largely Arab Council of State under the Naqib of Baghdad, Abd Al-Rahman Al-Gillani, and at the Cairo Conference of 1921 backed Faisal, whom he proclaimed king on 23 August 1921. When Faisal fell ill with appendicitis in August 1922, Cox took direct control, jailing opponents, silencing parties and newspapers and ordering the bombing of tribal insurgents. John Townsend wrote that it demonstrated British infallibility, illusory though it might have been; Ahmad Shikara called the measures severe and unpopular.

Cox worked closely with Gertrude Bell in Iraq, and each wrote of the other with admiration. His only son, Derek, was killed in action in 1917. After leaving Baghdad he held no further government post and was president of the Royal Geographical Society from 1933 to 1936. He collapsed and died while hunting at Melchbourne, Bedfordshire, on 20 February 1937; the coroner recorded heart failure. He is considered one of the main architects of the Middle East's present borders.
percy-family: The house descends from William de Percy (d. 1096), a Norman who crossed to England after William the Conqueror in December 1067, took his name from the manor of Percy-en-Auge in Normandy and became the first feudal baron of Topcliffe in Yorkshire. By the reign of Henry II the line was represented only by an heiress, Agnes de Percy. Adeliza of Louvain, widow of Henry I, married her to her own young half-brother Joscelin of Louvain, a nobleman from Brabant, whose descendants took the name Percy.

In 1309 Henry de Percy, 1st Baron Percy, bought Alnwick Castle from Antony Bek, Bishop of Durham, and from then on the family's fortunes were tied to Alnwick. The 2nd Baron received Warkworth in 1328 and commanded the right wing of the English army at the Battle of Neville's Cross in 1346. As nearly every Percy was a Warden of the Marches, Scottish affairs often concerned them more than English ones.

After the 1st Earl's rebellion his estates were forfeited, but Henry V restored Hotspur's son as 2nd Earl. The long Percy-Neville feud with the House of Neville fed into the Wars of the Roses, in which the Percys were staunch Lancastrians and the 3rd Earl and three of his brothers lost their lives. The 4th Earl's slowness at the Battle of Bosworth Field, through indecision or treachery, helped bring down Richard III, and in 1489 his own tenants pulled him from his horse and murdered him.

The 6th Earl was the accepted suitor of Anne Boleyn before Henry VIII married her. Later the Rising of the North, the plots to free Mary, Queen of Scots, and the Gunpowder Plot each drew in a Percy, and the 8th and 9th Earls spent years in the Tower of London, while the 10th Earl, Algernon, fought against King Charles in the Civil War. The male line ended with Joceline Percy, 11th Earl, who died in 1670.

His daughter Elizabeth married Charles Seymour, 6th Duke of Somerset. Their son Algernon Seymour was created Earl of Northumberland in 1749, with the title to pass to Sir Hugh Smithson, the Yorkshire baronet who had married Algernon's daughter Elizabeth. Smithson took the name Percy and in 1766 was made the first Duke of Northumberland. His descendants hold the dukedom, with Alnwick Castle as their seat, and the dukes are buried in the Northumberland Vault of Westminster Abbey, the last family to keep that privilege.
perdiccas: According to the 2nd-century historian Arrian, Perdiccas was the son of the Macedonian nobleman Orontes, a descendant of the independent princes of the province of Orestis. His date of birth is unknown, but he seems to have been of an age with Alexander. In 336 BCE, when Pausanias assassinated King Philip II of Macedon, Perdiccas was among those who chased the assassin down and killed him. He was a somatophylax, or bodyguard, and a hetairos, an elite cavalry commander, of Alexander, and he distinguished himself at the conquest of Thebes in 335 BCE, where he was heavily wounded, and at Gaugamela, before following Alexander into India.

After Alexander died on 11 June 323 BCE at Babylon, Perdiccas was very influential, as his second-in-command and the holder of the signet ring Alexander had given him. The army divided, with the aristocratic cavalry officers on one side and the infantry on the other. Perdiccas proposed waiting for Alexander's wife Roxana, who was pregnant, to give birth, and when Aristonous proclaimed him king he hesitated and the moment was lost. In the Partition of Babylon a compromise made him regent of the empire for the disabled Philip III and the infant Alexander IV, and supreme commander of the army. To secure power he had thirty infantry leaders trampled by war elephants and then executed Meleager.
