His authority was never secure. He distributed satrapies, sent away officers who threatened him and attached Cleomenes of Naucratis to Ptolemy in Egypt, probably to limit Ptolemy's power. Agreeing to marry Nicaea, daughter of Antipater, he later considered Cleopatra of Macedon, Alexander's sister, a match that would have given him a claim to the throne. Ptolemy diverted Alexander's body to Egypt, and Perdiccas, regarding it as an act of war, invaded Egypt while Antipater, Craterus and Antigonus moved against him.

When the invasion foundered, his soldiers mutinied, and his officers Peithon, Antigenes and Seleucus murdered him in his tent, probably about three years after he took the regency. The army went over to Ptolemy. News of Eumenes' victory over Craterus at the Hellespont, which would have restored his authority, arrived the next day.

Ancient accounts are largely negative, calling him arrogant and imperious, and Diodorus Siculus called him a man of slaughter; this may owe much to the rivalry with Ptolemy, whose lost account lies behind Arrian. Waldemar Heckel sees a tale of lofty ideals combined with excessive ambition, and calls him a great but flawed man. His death has been seen as the end of the empire as Alexander envisioned it.
perdiccas-ii-of-macedon: Perdiccas II was the oldest son of King Alexander I of Macedon and had four brothers: Alcetas, Amyntas, Menelaus and Philip. Menelaus became the father of the later king Amyntas II, and the grandson of Amyntas became king Amyntas III. Perdiccas married at least two women during his reign, Simache and Cleopatra. Simache was the mother of Archelaus and Aeropus II. Plato, through speakers in the Gorgias, accuses her of having been a slave of Alcetas, but this is doubtful, since Archelaus was treated as legitimate.

Cleopatra, who was possibly a Lyncestian or even an Argead, bore Perdiccas a son. According to Plato, Archelaus drowned this boy in a well when he was seven, because he was regarded as the legitimate heir. There is strong evidence that Cleopatra later married her stepson Archelaus, though historians such as Nicholas Hammond dispute this.

The unexpected death of Alexander I caused a dynastic crisis. Perdiccas took the throne as the oldest son, but Philip and Alcetas each obtained a local realm. He annexed the territory of Alcetas at an unknown date. Philip's hold on the Axios Valley was harder to overcome: Philip allied himself with King Derdas I of Elimiotis and with Athens, and Perdiccas answered by stirring up revolt in Athenian tribute cities, including Potidaea. Athens sent troops and ships, took Therma and besieged Pydna. It then allied with Perdiccas, who broke the treaty at once and marched to Potidaea. That fighting, together with the Battle of Sybota, led directly to the Peloponnesian War.

In 429 the Thracian king Sitalces invaded Macedonia with Philip's son Amyntas, supposedly with 150,000 men, and ravaged Mygdonia, Crestonia and Anthemus. The invasion faltered for want of supplies and because the Athenian fleet never came. Sitalces' nephew Seuthes persuaded him to leave after Perdiccas secretly promised a large dowry and the hand of his sister Stratonice.

In 424 Perdiccas helped the Spartan general Brasidas take Amphipolis from Athens, a blow to the Athenians, who relied on Macedonian timber. The Illyrians then changed sides in the Battle of Lyncestis, the Macedonians fled, and the angry Spartans plundered the Macedonian baggage train. Perdiccas allied with Athens in 423, joined the Spartan-Argive alliance by 417, and a few years later broke with the Peloponnese and aided Athens against Amphipolis. He died about 413 BCE, leaving his son Archelaus as heir.
perdido-river: The Perdido, known in the past as the Rio Perdido and by its native name of Cassaba, is 65.4 miles (105.3 km) long; perdido is Spanish for lost. It rises in Escambia County in south-western Alabama, about 8 miles (13 km) north-west of Atmore, and flows south about 5 miles (8 km) to latitude 31° N, below which it forms the border between Alabama and Florida. It then winds generally east-south-east and enters the north end of Perdido Bay on the Gulf of Mexico, about 10 miles (16 km) west of Pensacola. It is a designated Outstanding Florida Waters river.

From 1682 to 1763 the Perdido divided the French colony of Louisiana from the Spanish colony of Florida. After the French and Indian War, Great Britain received the French lands between the Mississippi River and the Perdido as well as Spanish Florida, and split its gains into West Florida and East Florida at the Apalachicola River. Twenty years later the Treaty of Paris returned all of Florida to Spain, which kept the British division. In 1800, by the Treaty of San Ildefonso, Spain returned Louisiana to France, keeping the lands east of the Mississippi except New Orleans, and in 1803 France sold Louisiana to the United States.

Against the claim of the United States, Spain held that only the lands west of the Mississippi had been returned to France, so the Gulf coast south of the 31st parallel between the Mississippi and the Perdido remained in dispute. In 1810 the Republic of West Florida declared its independence, and ninety days later United States forces entered its capital, St. Francisville, though this did not reach as far as the Perdido. During the War of 1812 United States forces took the surrender of the Spanish officials at Mobile, and the land west of the river was joined to the Mississippi Territory, from which the Alabama Territory was carved in 1817.

The dispute ended with the Adams-Onís Treaty of 1819, by which Spain ceded all of Florida to the United States; the Spanish government ratified it a couple of years later. In 1822 the Florida Territory was established, with the Perdido as its coastal boundary with the new state of Alabama.
pereiaslav: Pereiaslav lies near the confluence of the Alta and Trubizh rivers, some 95 km south-east of Kyiv, in Boryspil Raion of Kyiv Oblast. It was one of the key regional centres of power in the Middle Ages and the capital of a principality.

Pereiaslav is first mentioned in a 911 treaty with the Byzantine Empire. Vladimir I, grand prince of Kiev, built a large fortress there in 992 to protect the southern limits of Kievan Rus' from raids by steppe nomads. The city was the capital of the Principality of Pereyaslavl from the mid-11th century until the Tatars demolished it in 1239 during the Mongol invasions.

In the 14th century it was annexed by the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and later formed part of the Kiev Voivodeship, which became part of the Crown of the Kingdom of Poland in 1569. In the later 16th century it became a regimental city of the Zaporozhian Host. In 1654 Bohdan Khmelnytskyi held the Pereiaslav council, where the Zaporozhian Cossacks voted for a military alliance with the Tsardom of Russia and accepted the Pereiaslav Agreement, which brought their lands under Russian rule. It established the Cossack Hetmanate in left-bank Ukraine, subject to the Tsardom. By the Truce of Andrusovo in 1667 Pereiaslav became part of Russia.

A Jewish community is first recorded in 1620. Its members were among the first killed in the Khmelnytskyi uprising, and the chronicler Nathan Hannover lists Pereiaslav among the communities that died as martyrs. Sholem Aleichem was born in the town in 1859 and studied at its Russian gymnasium until 1876. A pogrom took place there from 30 June to 2 July 1881, and another in June 1919 killed 20 people. In autumn 1941 about 800 Jewish residents were shot on the outskirts.

In October 1943 the Soviet government renamed the town Pereiaslav-Khmelnytskyi to stress Khmelnytskyi's role in the Pereiaslav Agreement, and made it a museum and tourism centre. The Ukrainian parliament restored the historic name Pereiaslav in 2019. It has more than 20 museums, including the Museum of Folk Architecture and Household Traditions, and landmarks such as St Michael's Church dating from the 17th century and the Ascension Monastery, with a cathedral built between 1695 and 1700.
perekop: Perekop is a village on the Perekop Isthmus, which connects the Crimean peninsula to the Ukrainian mainland. It is known for the Or Qapı fortress, which served as the gateway to Crimea. The original name was that of the Greek settlement of Taphros, meaning a dug-out locality, whose people were called Taphrians. The Crimean Tatar name Or Qapı means trench gate. In the Middle Ages the place was known as Tuzla. The Slavic name Perekop means an over-dug locality.

Because of its key position Perekop endured many sieges. During the Russo-Turkish War of 1735 to 1739 the Russian field marshal Burkhard Christoph von Münnich stormed the fortifications on 17 June 1736 and left the Tatar fortress in ruins, a serious blow to the independence of the Crimean Khanate. The town was virtually wiped out in the Siege of Perekop by the Red Army in 1920, a key episode of the Russian Civil War, whose success allowed the Bolsheviks to drive Pyotr Wrangel's White Army from Crimea. Twelve years later the Soviets founded the new town of Krasnoperekopsk, 32 kilometres to the south.

In World War II German forces occupied Perekop from 27 September 1941 to 1 November 1943. Its capture, by the Wehrmacht in 1941 and by the Red Army in 1943, was used to cut Crimea off from Ukraine. The village lies within Armiansk Municipality, and the Ukrainian census of 2001 counted 894 inhabitants.
pereshchepina-treasure: The hoard came to light in 1912 in the village of Mala Pereshchepyna, about 20 km from Poltava, when a shepherd boy stumbled over a golden vessel and fell into what is sometimes believed to be a grave. The find was first described by Makarenko, and its extraction was supervised by the archaeologist Count Aleksey Bobrinsky, who published a description of it in 1914. The objects are kept in the Hermitage Museum in Saint Petersburg.

The deposit holds 19 silver vessels and 16 gold vessels, among them a rhyton and the remains of a second one. The museum also lists a staff with gold facing, an iron sword with a ring-shaped end and gold facing on the hilt and scabbard, a torque, an earring, seven bracelets and seven rings set with amethysts, sapphires, tiger-eyes, garnets, rock crystal and emeralds, and square gold plaques that once faced a wooden funeral structure. In all the gold weighs more than 21 kilograms and the silver more than 50 kilograms.

Among the finds is a necklace of Byzantine gold coins running from the reign of Emperor Maurice (582-602) to that of Constans II, down to 646, which has often been taken to fix the earliest possible date of the deposit. A Sassanian dish shows Shapur the Great, and a Byzantine dish carries an inscription of an early 6th-century bishop of Tomis. Other pieces probably date as late as the 670s. The most valued items are a sword held to be a gift from Emperor Heraclius and a ring with the ruler's monogram as a patrician. On 24 May 2019 the sword left Russia for the first time, for a display in Sofia.

The owner of the hoard has been disputed. The Great Soviet Encyclopaedia ascribed it to a Slavic chieftain said to have taken the objects in a raid on Byzantium, and some more recent scholars attribute it to the Khazars. Many agree that, at least in its earlier phase, it was the treasure of Kubrat, the first attested khan of the Bulgars and father of Asparuh, founder of the First Bulgarian Empire. On that view the treasure later passed to the Khazars as the Bulgars left the region. It is counted among the richest witnesses to the material culture of Old Great Bulgaria.
pereslavl-zalessky: Pereslavl-Zalessky lies in southern Yaroslavl Oblast, near the border with Moscow Oblast, on the main Moscow–Yaroslavl road. It stands on the south-eastern shore of Lake Pleshcheyevo, at the mouth of the Trubezh River, 140 kilometres north-east of Moscow and 123 kilometres south-west of Yaroslavl. The climate is humid continental, with long, cold and snowy winters and short, warm and rainy summers.

George I of Vladimir founded the town in 1152 as a projected capital of Zalesye, a name that means beyond the woods. The inhabitants of the nearby town of Kleshchin were relocated to it. Between 1175 and 1302 Pereslavl was the seat of a principality. In 1302 it was inherited by the prince of Moscow after the childless death of Ivan, son of Dmitry of Pereslavl. The Mongols devastated it many times between the mid-13th century and the early 15th century, and it suffered again in the Polish invasion of 1611–1612.

Between 1688 and 1693 Peter the Great built his fun flotilla on Lake Pleshcheyevo for his own amusement, among it the small boat that could be considered the forerunner of the Russian fleet. A scale model of it is now in the Central Naval Museum. In 1708 the town became part of the Moscow Governorate. Among those associated with the town are the saint Nicetas Stylites, who founded the Monastery of St Nicetas in the 12th century, and Alexander Nevsky, prince and saint, born in 1221.

The town is part of the Golden Ring of Russia and had a population of 41,925 at the 2010 census. Its monuments include the white stone Savior's Cathedral of 1152–1157, the Church of Metropolitan Peter of 1585, and the Troitse-Danilov, Nikitsky, Feodorovsky and Goritsky monasteries, built between the 16th and 19th centuries. The Museum-Preserve of Pereslavl-Zalessky is in the Goritsky Monastery. About two kilometres from the town the Kleshchin earthworks, the remains of an old defensive wall, can still be walked along.
pergamon: Pergamon lies on the north edge of the Caicus plain in Mysia, in north-west Turkey, 26 kilometres from the Aegean coast. The city was centred on a mesa of andesite 335 metres high that formed its acropolis. Three natural terraces on its south side give a route to the top. The Selinus River flows to the west of the acropolis and the Cetius to the east. In Hellenistic times the town of Elaia at the mouth of the Caicus served as its port.

Settlement can be detected from the late 8th century BCE, through pottery imported from the west. The earliest mention in literature is in Xenophon's Anabasis, since the march of the Ten Thousand ended at Pergamon in 400 to 399 BCE, when the city belonged to the family of Gongylos of Eretria, a Greek favourable to the Achaemenid Empire. Lysimachus, King of Thrace, took possession in 301 BCE, and his lieutenant Philetaerus enlarged the town. When the kingdom of Thrace collapsed in 281 BCE, Philetaerus became an independent ruler and founded the Attalid dynasty, which ruled until 133 BCE.

Eumenes I gained territory down to the coast after the Battle of Sardis in 261 BCE against Antiochus I. In 238 BCE his successor Attalus I defeated the Galatians, to whom Pergamon had paid tribute, and declared himself leader of an independent kingdom. Under Eumenes II and Attalus II the city expanded, with a new street network, wall and marketplace.

In 88 BCE Mithridates VI Eupator made Pergamon his headquarters in his first war against Rome. The Romans deprived it of its status as a free city and made it pay tribute, but it remained a prominent city, and Augustus granted it a neocorate, the first centre of the imperial cult in the province of Asia. The Arabs captured it in 663/4 CE, after which settlement shrank to the acropolis, and attacks in 1109 and 1113 after the Seljuk invasion largely destroyed it. Manuel I Komnenos rebuilt it around 1170, and it fell to the Karasids shortly after 1300 and then to the Ottomans.

The ruins stand north-west of the modern city of Bergama. They include the foundations of the Pergamon Altar, probably dedicated to Zeus and Athena, whose frieze is displayed in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin. Three kilometres south of the acropolis lies the Asclepieion, where patients bathed in a sacred spring and hoped that Asclepius would appear in their dreams, and where the physician Galen worked for many years. Pergamon was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2014, and it was the northernmost of the seven churches of Asia cited in the Book of Revelation.
pergamon-altar: The Pergamene kingdom, founded by Philetaerus at the start of the 3rd century BCE, was first part of the Seleucid Empire. Attalus I won full independence and proclaimed himself king after defeating the Celtic Galatians in 228 BCE. His son Eumenes II secured the Treaty of Apamea in 188 BCE as an ally of Rome, and the Attalids wished to show their importance through imposing buildings. Until the later 20th century some scholars thought the altar was endowed in 184 BCE after a victory over the Tolistoagian tribe, but study of its construction and friezes showed that it was not conceived as a monument to a particular victory.

The structure measured 35.74 metres wide and 33.4 metres deep, and its front stairway was almost 20 metres wide. A high-relief frieze on the base shows the battle of the Olympian gods against the Giants, children of Gaia, the Gigantomachy. A smaller frieze in the inner court told the life of Telephus, founder of Pergamon and son of Heracles and Auge. It is probably the altar of a temple, perhaps that of Athena on the terrace above, and not a temple itself, but no theory is generally accepted. Wolfgang Radt concluded that no research is undisputed concerning its builder, date, occasion or purpose.

The altar is mentioned in antiquity only by the Roman Lucius Ampelius, who called it a great marble altar 40 feet high, and by Pausanias. In the 7th century the acropolis was fortified against the Arabs and the altar partly destroyed for building material. In 1625 William Petty took two relief panels to England for the Earl of Arundel; forgotten, they were rediscovered in the 1960s, so they are missing from the Berlin reconstruction. The German engineer Carl Humann began official excavations in 1878 and they lasted until 1886, and the relief panels were transferred to Berlin. Many scholars have also identified the altar with the Seat of Satan in the Book of Revelation.
periander: Periander was the second tyrant of the Cypselid dynasty of Corinth and the son of Cypselus, the founder of the dynasty, and of Cratea. He married Lyside, whom he often called Melissa, a daughter of Procles and Eristenea of Epidaurus, and they had two sons, Cypselus, said to have been weak-minded, and Lycophron, a man of intelligence. Diogenes Laertius reports that Periander killed his wife in a fit of rage, and Herodotus alludes to suggestions that he defiled her corpse.

Periander made Corinth one of the major trading centres of ancient Greece and one of its wealthiest city states. He founded colonies at Potidaea in Chalcidice and at Apollonia in Illyria, conquered Epidaurus, formed good relations with Miletus and Lydia, and annexed Corcyra. He is also credited with the Diolkos, a transport route across the Isthmus of Corinth. Tolls on goods entering the port made up nearly all government revenue, and he spent it on temples and public works and on literature and the arts, bringing the poet Arion from Lesbos to an arts festival.

Several accounts describe Periander as cruel and harsh, while others claim he was fair and worked to keep the distribution of wealth in Corinth fairly even. According to Herodotus, he asked Thrasybulus, the tyrant of Miletus, for advice on governing; Thrasybulus silently cut down the tallest ears of wheat in a field, and Periander took this as advice to remove the most prominent citizens. He was also said to have written a didactic poem of 2,000 lines, and Diogenes Laertius lists him among the Seven Sages, though some ancient writers held that the tyrant and the sage were two men of the same name.

Grief at the death of Lycophron, whom the people of Corcyra killed rather than let him leave to join his father, is said to have driven Periander into a despondency that led to his death. Diogenes Laertius also tells a legend that Periander arranged to be killed and buried at night so that no one would know his grave. His nephew Psammetichus succeeded him and ruled for three years as the last of the Cypselid tyrants.
peribsen: Seth-Peribsen, also written Ash-Peribsen, Peribsen or Perabsen, is the serekh name of a king of the Second Dynasty of Egypt. His place within the dynasty is unknown, who ruled before and after him is disputed, and the length of his reign is unknown. His serekh was found pressed into clay jar seals and inscribed on vessels of alabaster, sandstone, porphyry and black schist, excavated from his tomb and at Elephantine. A clay seal with his name was found in the mastaba K1 at Beit Khallaf. A cylinder seal of unknown origin gives his name in a cartouche with the epithet beloved of the gods; because royal cartouches came into use long after his reign, Egyptologists conclude it was made later, in his memory.

His name is unusual because Seth, not the falcon god Horus, was his patron deity. He is the only known pharaoh to have the Seth animal alone above his serekh, although the 13th Dynasty king Seth Meribre and the Ramesside rulers Seti I and Seti II also linked themselves with Seth. Until the mid-20th century Egyptologists including Percy Newberry, Jaroslav Černý and Walter Bryan Emery held that Peribsen was a heretic who introduced a monotheistic cult of Seth, or that rival priests of Horus and Seth fought a civil war.

Later evidence points the other way: seal impressions show several deities worshipped under him, and officials' mastaba tombs show that mortuary cults ran successfully throughout the dynasty. Egyptologists such as Michael Rice, Francesco Tiradritti and Wolfgang Helck hold that if the realm was divided, the division was peaceful. Seal impressions also show changes in officials' titles that suggest reduced power, and the earliest seal impressions with complete sentences date from his reign.

His tomb was found in 1898 at Abydos, well preserved and showing traces of restoration in later dynastic periods. Two rough granite stelae found there look unfinished, perhaps deliberately, for reasons unknown. Peribsen's name is missing from the Ramesside king lists, among them the Abydos King List and the Turin canon, compiled about 1,500 years after his death, and some have doubted his existence. Tombs of Fourth Dynasty priests who served his funerary cult name him correctly, which shows he was regarded as a legitimate pharaoh. Some Egyptologists identify him with Sekhemib-Perenmaat, another Second Dynasty ruler, on the evidence of clay seals at his tomb's entrance, but others argue that Sekhemib succeeded Peribsen and buried him.
pericles: Pericles was born around 495 BCE in Athens, the son of the politician Xanthippus, who commanded the Athenian contingent in the Greek victory at Mycale. His mother, Agariste, belonged to the powerful Alcmaeonid family, and her connections helped to start his political career. His early years were quiet, and he preferred study to public appearances. In the spring of 472 BCE he presented The Persians of Aeschylus at the Greater Dionysia as a liturgy, which shows that he was one of the wealthier men of Athens.

In 463 BCE Pericles was the leading prosecutor of Cimon, the leader of the conservative faction, who was acquitted. Around 461 BCE his mentor Ephialtes proposed reducing the powers of the Areopagus, a council controlled by the aristocracy, and the Assembly adopted the reform, signalling an era of radical democracy. In the same year Cimon was ostracised on the charge of aiding Sparta, and Ephialtes was murdered, which left Pericles the unchallenged leader of the democratic party.

Pericles began a project that produced most of the surviving structures on the Acropolis, including the Parthenon. He proposed the Megarian decree, which excluded Megarian merchants from the market of Athens and its empire and strained the peace with Sparta. In 431 BCE, when the Spartan king Archidamus II invaded Attica, Pericles had already arranged for the whole rural population to move within the walls of Athens, and he refused to meet the Spartan army in battle, relying on the navy.

In summer 430 BCE an epidemic broke out in Athens, whose identity is uncertain. Public anger led Pericles to defend himself in a final speech, which Thucydides records, and his opponents managed to deprive him of the generalship and fine him. His sister and both his legitimate sons, Xanthippus and Paralus, died in the plague, and he died in 429 BCE. Scholars differ over his leadership, with some calling him a populist and a hawk and others admiring him.
perigueux: Périgueux lies on the Isle river in the Dordogne department, in the region of Nouvelle-Aquitaine in south-western France. It is the prefecture of Dordogne, was the capital of the historic region of Périgord, and is the seat of a Roman Catholic diocese. The oceanic climate is mild for its latitude and inland position, because maritime air from the Bay of Biscay, warmed by the Gulf Stream, softens the winters, while the distance from the coast keeps the summers relatively warm.

The name comes from Petrocorii, from Celtic words meaning the four tribes, the Gallic people who held the area before the Roman conquest. Périgueux was their capital. In 200 BCE the Petrocorii came from the north and settled there, establishing an encampment at La Boissière. After the Roman invasion they left that post and settled on the plain of the Isle, where the town of Vesunna was created. The Roman city was eventually given temples, baths, amphitheatres and a forum. At the end of the third century CE it was surrounded by ramparts, and the town took the name Civitas Petrocoriorum.

In the 10th century Le Puy-Saint-Front was built around an abbey next to the old Gallo-Roman city, and it was organised as a municipality around 1182. In 1940 many Jews from Alsace and many other Alsatians were evacuated to Périgueux.

The town had 29,876 inhabitants in 2022, and its metropolitan area 114,349. Among its sights are the remains of the Roman amphitheatre, known locally as the arènes romaines, and the remains of a temple of the Gallic goddess Vesunna. The Domus of Vesunna, a Roman villa built around a garden courtyard with a colonnaded peristyle, is housed in the Vesunna Gallo-Roman Museum.

The cathedral of St Front was built after 1120 and restored in the 19th century. Scholars have long argued over its models: one saw a copy of St Mark's Basilica in Venice, another of the church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople, while M. Brutails thought it a local work of about 1120 to 1173 imitating a foreign monument. The architect Paul Abadie made radical changes to it in the 19th century. The cathedral is part of the World Heritage Sites of the Routes of Santiago de Compostela in France.
periodic-table: In 1817 the German physicist Johann Wolfgang Döbereiner began one of the earliest attempts to classify the elements. In 1829 he found that he could form some of them into groups of three with related properties, which he termed triads. Chlorine, bromine and iodine formed a triad, as did calcium, strontium and barium. Later chemists found more relationships between small groups of elements but could not build one scheme that took in all of them.

In 1864 John Newlands published an article in Chemical News showing that if the elements are arranged by atomic weight, every eighth element repeats the properties of the first, like the eighth note of an octave in music, which he called the Law of Octaves. The same year a book by the German chemist Lothar Meyer contained an early table of 28 elements, grouped into six families by valence, the first grouping of elements in that way.

The periodic table arranges the chemical elements in rows called periods and columns called groups, and elements in the same group tend to show similar chemical characteristics. Each element has a unique atomic number, the number of protons in its nucleus, and the elements are listed in order of increasing atomic number. A new row starts when a new electron shell has its first electron, and the columns are determined by the electron configuration of the atom. The table depicts the periodic law, which states that when elements are arranged by atomic number an approximate recurrence of their properties is evident.

Metallic character increases going down a group and from right to left across a period. The first generally accepted table was that of the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869, who formulated the law as a dependence of chemical properties on atomic mass. Because not all elements were then known, his table had gaps, and he used the law to predict properties of some missing elements. The law was explained early in the 20th century by the discovery of atomic numbers and by work in quantum mechanics, and a recognisably modern form was reached in 1945 with Glenn T. Seaborg's discovery that the actinides are f-block rather than d-block elements.

The periodic law was recognised as a fundamental discovery in the late 19th century, and the table is an icon of chemistry, also widely used in physics and other sciences. In nature only elements up to atomic number 94 exist; later ones are synthetic. By 2010 the first 118 elements were known, completing the first seven rows. Within 100 years of Mendeleev's table, Edward G. Mazurs had collected an estimated 700 different published versions and there is no consensus on whether an optimal form exists.
perioeci: The name perioeci derives from the Greek peri, "around", and oikos, "dwelling", and roughly means those dwelling around or nearby. The polis of Sparta was formed during the Greek Dark Ages and controlled the plains around the Eurotas river. Communities already living there that could not be assimilated into the Spartan state or subjugated as helots became the perioeci. It is unknown whether they were Dorians like the Spartans or descended from earlier populations of the Peloponnese. Perioeci and Spartans together were called the Lakedaimonians.

The perioeci were free, unlike the helots, but not full citizens. They lived in their own cities, which ancient authors described as poleis, and which governed their own domestic affairs under Spartan control. They had political rights only in their own city. They supplied men to the army and, like the full Spartan citizens, the hómoioi, fought as hoplites, probably in the same units.

They could own land, which the army service required. Because Spartans were not permitted economically productive work in the Classical period, the perioeci made weapons and armour and conducted trade, and the masks and figurines found at the Sanctuary of Artemis Orthia were probably made by perioecic craftsmen.

Like the Spartans they owned helots, so that the main division in Spartan society lay between Spartans and perioeci on one side and helots on the other. During the Peloponnesian War, in 413, Athens raided the perioecic city of Epidaurus Limera hoping to trigger a helot revolt against the perioeci. Some helots could rise to perioecic status as neodamodes after military service, but Spartan citizens could not be demoted to it.

Graham Shipley has identified at least 33 perioecic cities, 23 in Laconia and 10 in Messenia. Aithaia and Thouria were the only two to join the helot revolt of 464. Sparta lost the Messenian cities after Epaminondas founded Messene in 369 and after Philip II's campaign in the Peloponnese in 338. Other cities, such as Elis and Argos, also controlled perioecic cities.

Aristotle's Politics uses the word more generally. In his ideal state, those who perform trades should be slaves or perioeci, because such work does not produce virtue, according to him. In that sense the perioeci are free men who do not own property and cannot vote or hold office, a middle class below the citizens and above slavery. He sometimes calls them barbarian, implying non-Hellenic foreigners. Ancient authors such as Thucydides, Xenophon and Diodorus Siculus name individual perioeci, among them the spy Phrynis, the fleet commander Diniades and the cavalryman Eudicus.
periplus-of-the-erythraean-sea: A periplus, literally a sailing-around, is a logbook of sailing itineraries with commercial, political and ethnological details of the ports visited. In an era before maps were in general use it served as a combination of atlas and traveller's handbook. The Erythraean Sea meant the Red Sea in the Greek sense, which included the Gulf of Aden and, in this work, the Persian Gulf and the Indian Ocean as one maritime area. The text was written in Koine Greek and has been ascribed to dates between the first and third centuries, but a mid-first-century date is now the most commonly accepted. John Hill and L. Casson place it between 40 and 70 CE, and Wilfred Harvey Schoff around 60 CE.

The author is unknown. Schoff concluded that he was a Greek in Egypt and a Roman subject, not a highly educated man, and probably resident at Berenice rather than Alexandria. The tenth-century Byzantine manuscript attributes the work to Arrian, apparently only because it stands beside Arrian's Periplus of the Euxine Sea.

The work has 66 sections, most about the length of a long paragraph, and describes ports and goods from Roman Egyptian harbours such as Berenice Troglodytica along the Red Sea, the Horn of Africa, the Persian Gulf, the Arabian Sea and the Indian coast. At Malao, near Berbera, it lists imports such as tunics, cups and iron and exports such as myrrh, frankincense and cinnamon. It names Opone as a centre for cinnamon, and Rhapta as the last port of trade on the coast of Azania, whose site is disputed, with candidates on the Rufiji River in Tanzania and near Quelimane in Mozambique.

It records that Aksum was a market for ivory, whose ruler Zoscales also held Adulis and Avalites and was acquainted with Greek literature. In Arabia it names Charibael as king of the Homerites and Sabaites and a friend of the emperors, and Eleazus, king of the Frankincense Country. In India it describes Barygaza, with its imports of wine and its exports of cotton and spikenard, and Muziris and Nelcynda on the Malabar Coast, which traded pepper with Greek ships. It says a direct sea route across the open ocean to India had been discovered by Hippalus. Its note on China describes a great inland city, Thina, as a source of raw silk.

The Periplus survived through a single manuscript of the fourteenth or fifteenth century in the British Library, a corrupt copy of a tenth-century Byzantine manuscript now in Heidelberg. Sigmund Gelen's edition, published by Hieronymus Froben in 1533, served as the basis of other editions for three centuries. Schoff made the first English translation in 1912. Some names of trade goods occur nowhere else in ancient literature, and the identification of many places remains debated.
periyar-river: The Periyar is the longest river of Kerala and has its largest discharge potential. It is one of the few perennial rivers in the region and gives drinking water to several major towns. It is about 244 kilometres long, with a catchment of 5,398 square kilometres, of which 5,284 are in Kerala and 114 in Tamil Nadu. Its source is on Chokkampatti Mala in the remote forests of the Periyar Tiger Reserve in the Western Ghats. After some 48 kilometres it is joined by the Mullayar at Mullakudy. Near Aluva the river divides into two distributaries, one reaching the sea at Munambam and the other draining into the Vembanad backwaters at Varapuzha.

The Periyar has been called the Lifeline of Kerala. It supplies irrigation, domestic water and a fishery, and about a quarter of the state's industries lie on its banks, mostly in the Eloor-Edayar region north of Kochi. The Mullaperiyar dam was one of the earliest inter-basin transfers in peninsular India. It met a demand for water but led to salt intrusion and pollution in the lower reaches. The Idukki Dam, commissioned in 1976, is the largest hydroelectric project in Kerala, a concrete double-curvature arch dam with generators of 780 MW at an underground station at Moolamattom, built by an India-Canada joint venture. Diversions have left the Periyar with 22 per cent less of its average flow.

The control and safety of the Mullaperiyar dam and the fairness of its lease have been disputed between Kerala and Tamil Nadu. Kerala holds that the Periyar is an intrastate river, since it originates, flows and meets the sea entirely in Kerala. Tamil Nadu admits those facts but argues that it is inter-state because part of its catchment lies in Tamil Nadu.

South of the Mullaperiyar reservoir an unbroken stretch of about 350 square kilometres of unmodified rainforest lies within the Periyar Tiger Reserve. Of an estimated 3,800 species of flowering plants in Kerala, 1,966 have been reported from the reserve. The Aluva Sivarathri festival is held every year on the sand bank at Aluva, and the town of Kalady is the birthplace of the philosopher Adi Shankara, with a temple consecrated to him in 1910.
perkonkrusts: Celmiņš had founded the fascist group Ugunskrusts (Fire Cross) in 1932, and when the government outlawed it the organisation reappeared at once under the name Pērkonkrusts. Thunder Cross is one of the Latvian names for the swastika, which served as its symbol; members wore a grey shirt and black beret and greeted one another with a variant of the Roman salute and the words Cīņai sveiks. By 1934 it is estimated to have had between 5,000 and 6,000 members, drawn mostly from towns such as Riga, Cēsis, Valmiera and Jelgava and from students at the University of Latvia.

Its slogan, Latvia for Latvians! Work and bread for Latvians!, summed up its aim of placing all political and economic control in the hands of ethnic Latvians. It rejected the laws that gave national minorities cultural autonomy, directed its propaganda against Baltic Germans and Jews, whom it accused of taking over the economy, and attacked parliamentary politicians as corrupt. It rejected Christianity as foreign and proposed Dievturība, an attempted revival of pre-Christian Latvian religion. The historian Roger Griffin called it a small but genuine fascist opposition, while Uldis Krēsliņš has argued that it was neither affiliated with nor a copy of German Nazism.

After Kārlis Ulmanis's coup of May 1934, which banned all parties and the Saeima, Celmiņš was imprisoned for three years and then banished, setting up a liaison office in Helsinki. Under the Soviet occupation of 1940 to 1941 more members were arrested and some deported to Siberia. When the Germans invaded in June 1941 the group was briefly allowed to operate, and former members were recruited for the Arajs Commando; historians Rudīte Vīksne and Andrievs Ezergailis hold that only a handful took part in the killing of Jews, their role lying more in antisemitic propaganda. The Germans banned it in August 1941.

From February 1942 Celmiņš headed the committee recruiting Latvian men for the auxiliary police battalions, which took part in massacres of rural Jews and other civilians. His underground anti-German paper Brīvā Latvija led to his arrest and imprisonment in Flossenbürg concentration camp. A new group took the name in 1995; two of its members were killed on 5 June 1997 while trying to bomb a Soviet war monument in Riga.
perkunas: Most information about Perkūnas comes from folklore songs, legends and fairy tales, which were mostly collected late in the 19th century and so preserve only fragments of the mythology. The earliest attestation seems to be in the Ruthenian translation of the Chronicle of John Malalas in 1261, and the Livonian Rhymed Chronicle of about 1290 mentions the idol Perkūnė.

The Constitutiones Synodales of 1530 list him among the gods and identify him with the Roman Jove. In Christian compositions he appears as a malicious spirit or demon. The etymology of the name is unclear. Some Indo-Europeanists reconstruct a Proto-Indo-European thunder god from Perkūnas and the Slavic Perun, but linguists such as Michał Łuczyński and Martin L. West reject the reconstruction.

In Lithuanian and Latvian mythology Perkūnas is documented as the god of sky, thunder, lightning, storms, rain, fire, war, law, order, fertility, mountains and oak trees, and the Latvian Pērkons is closely associated with Dievs. He is pictured as a middle-aged man armed with an axe and arrows, riding a two-wheeled chariot harnessed to goats, or driving a fiery chariot or riding a fiery horse. In most myths his wife is Žemyna, the Earth. Thursday is his day, a day of thunderstorms, rain and weddings.

An important role of Perkūnas is to fight Velnias, the god of the underworld and death. Velnias has stolen fertility and cattle, and hides in trees, under stones or in the shape of animals such as a black cat or a pig. The hunt ends in a thunderstorm, which clears the ground of evil spirits and returns the stolen cattle or weapons.

About 1520 Simon Grunau described a Prussian banner showing Perkūns as an angry middle-aged man with a twisted black beard, standing between Patrimpas and Patulas. At the Romowe sanctuary the sacred oak stood at the centre of his worship, and before it an eternal fire, his symbol, was burned. Special priests served there and the Old Prussians appealed to the god in prayers.

Latvians sacrificed black calves, goats and roosters to Pērkons, especially during droughts. Surrounding peoples came to eat and drink together, after pouring beer on the ground or into the fire for him. Cooked food was offered before meals to prevent thunderstorms, and during storms honeycombs were placed in fires to disperse the clouds. Ancient Latvians wore tiny axes on their clothing in his honour.
peronism: Peronism gained popularity after earlier governments, such as that of Hipólito Yrigoyen, failed to answer workers' pleas for better wages and conditions or to oppose the Argentine oligarchy. Juan Perón became labour secretary after taking part in the 1943 military coup and was elected president in 1946. He introduced social programmes that benefited the working class, supported trade unions and called for greater state involvement in the economy. His wife Eva championed the rights of migrant workers, the poor and women, and played a crucial role in securing women's suffrage until her death from cancer in 1952.

Because of economic problems and political repression, the military overthrew Perón in 1955 and banned the Justicialist Party. Open elections were held again only in 1973, when Perón was re-elected with 62 per cent of the vote. He died the following year, and his widow and vice president, Isabel, succeeded him.

Peronism is defined by three flags: social justice, economic independence and political sovereignty. In the Cold War it took a third position, expressed in the phrase: we are neither Yankees nor Marxists. Perón grouped the sectors of society into organisations, among them the CGT for workers, and the trade unions remained a key part of the movement. Its measures included the expansion of workers' rights, women's suffrage, free tuition at public universities and a constitutional right to housing.

Scholars often classify it as left-wing populism. Perón himself wrote in 1973 that Peronism was a left-wing movement, though a Justicialist left and not a communist or anarchist one, and he named Christian socialism, Franklin D. Roosevelt and Harold Laski among his inspirations. Historians also stress the influence of Catholic social teaching.

Peronism has spanned much of the ideological spectrum. Vandorism, or neo-Peronism, was the trade unionism that sought Peronism without Perón during the resistance after 1955. The orthodox sector demanded total attachment to Perón's presidencies, while the Revolutionary Tendency, mainly young, linked Peronism to socialist revolution. After the electoral defeat of 1983 the Peronist Renovation was formally constituted in 1985 by Antonio Cafiero, Carlos Grosso and Carlos Menem, joining Peronist values to liberal democracy. Menem, president from 1989 to 1999, broke with protectionist orthodoxy in favour of neoliberal policies, and Kirchnerism later formed around the governments of Néstor Kirchner and Cristina Fernández de Kirchner.
peroz-i: Peroz I was a son of Yazdegerd II. When Yazdegerd died in 457 he had reportedly named no successor, and, according to the medieval historian al-Tha'alibi, left the task to the elite and the leading marzbans. His eldest son Hormizd III declared himself king at Ray, while Peroz fled to the north-east of the empire and raised an army. Their mother, Queen Denag, ruled temporarily as regent from Ctesiphon. Armenian historians say that the House of Mihran supported Peroz, while later Persian sources report that he fled to the Hephthalites and enlisted their help. After a two-year struggle he took the throne.

During the dynastic struggle Vache II, the Arsacid king of Caucasian Albania, declared independence and let the Huns into Derbent. Peroz allowed Huns to pass through the Darial Gorge to ravage Albania, and Vache abdicated in 462. A severe drought in 461 caused a famine that lasted until 467. In the mid-460s Byzantine authorities found that their general Ardaburius had been urging Peroz to attack them, and Emperor Leo I removed him from office. Around 464 the Kidarites declared war on Peroz; he lacked the men, and the Byzantines refused him financial aid. Peroz eventually put an end to the Kidarites and briefly extended Sasanian rule into Tokharistan.

The Hephthalites then spread over all of Tokharistan. Peroz attacked them in 474, but was ambushed and captured near the border of Gurgan, and was ransomed by Zeno. According to Procopius, the Hephthalite king demanded that Peroz prostrate himself, and on his priests' advice he did so at dawn, before the rising sun. Many historians hold that he fought the Hephthalites three times. In 482 revolts broke out in Armenia and Iberia, led by Vahan Mamikonian and Vakhtang I.

Against the advice of the aristocracy and the clergy, Peroz prepared a third campaign in Gurgan, leaving his brother Balash in charge. He was defeated and killed in 484. Nishapur, Herat and Marw came under Hephthalite rule, his daughter Perozdukht was captured and married to the Hephthalite king, and the Nezak Huns seized Zabulistan. His wars were called foolhardy by contemporaries and modern historians. The shahanshah became a client of the Hephthalites and paid tribute, and the nobility and clergy acted as king-makers. Order was restored under Peroz's son Kavad I. Though a devout Zoroastrian, Peroz supported Nestorianism, declared the doctrine of the Iranian church just before his death. He founded cities including Perozapat and Ram Peroz near Ray.
perpignan: Perpignan lies in the middle of the Roussillon plain at the foot of the Pyrenees, 13 kilometres from the Mediterranean coast, and is the southernmost city of metropolitan France. The Têt, the largest river of Roussillon, and its tributary the Basse cross it. It is the prefecture of the Pyrénées-Orientales department, with 119,656 inhabitants in 2021. Its name appears in 927 as Perpinianum and probably derives from the Roman name Perpennius.

Settlement in the area goes back to Roman times, but the medieval town seems to have been founded around the beginning of the tenth century, and it soon became the capital of the counts of Roussillon. In 1172 Count Girard II bequeathed his lands to the counts of Barcelona. The town gained the institutions of a partly self-governing commune in 1197. When James I the Conqueror founded the Kingdom of Majorca in 1276, Perpignan became the capital of its mainland territories. The decades that followed are regarded as the city's golden age, with cloth, leatherwork and goldsmithery. King Philippe III of France died there in 1285 on his return from a failed crusade against the Crown of Aragon.

Peter IV of Aragon annexed the kingdom in 1344, and a few years later the Black Death took about half the population. Louis XI of France occupied the city in 1463, and a rising against French rule in 1473 was put down after a long siege. Charles VIII restored it to Ferdinand II of Aragon in 1493. The French besieged and captured it again in September 1642, during the Thirty Years' War, and Spain ceded it formally 17 years later in the Treaty of the Pyrenees.

The Palace of the Kings of Majorca, of the thirteenth century, stands on the citadel behind ramparts that Louis XIV's engineer Vauban updated in the seventeenth century. The town walls were razed in 1904, but the Castillet, the main gate, a fourteenth-century fortress later used as a prison, survives. Work on the cathedral began in 1324 and finished in 1509. In 1963 the painter Salvador Dalí declared the railway station the centre of the universe. The city hosts the Visa pour l'Image festival of photojournalism each September, and many street signs are in both French and Catalan.
persaeus: Persaeus was the son of Demetrius and a favourite student of Zeno of Citium. Later writers claimed he had been Zeno's slave, perhaps a secretary sent to him by Antigonus II Gonatas, but the story seems to go back to a jibe by Bion of Borysthenes, who saw a statue inscribed Persaeus the pupil of Zeno and said it should read Persaeus the servant of Zeno.

Around 276 BCE Antigonus invited Zeno to his court at Pella; Zeno declined on account of his age and sent Persaeus and Philonides of Thebes instead. A story tells that the king, to test him, had false news brought that his estate had been ravaged by the enemy, and when his face fell remarked that wealth was evidently not a matter of indifference. Persaeus became an important figure at the Macedonian court, and after Antigonus took Corinth around 244 BCE he was placed in charge of the city.

Only a few fragments of his writings survive. Diogenes Laërtius lists among them an Ethical School, On Kingship, a Constitution of the Lacedaemonians, On Marriage, On Impiety, a Thyestes, On Love, Exhortations, Conversations, Apophthegms, Reminiscences and a work on Plato's Laws.

Cicero reports his view of the gods: that men who had discovered some great aid to civilisation came to be regarded as gods, and that the names of divinities were also given to useful material things, so that Persaeus held these to be divine themselves rather than merely the creations of God.
persephone: The origins of Persephone's cult are uncertain, but it was based on ancient agrarian cults of farming communities. The many forms of the name, among them Persephassa, Persophatta and Phersephona, suggest that it may have a pre-Greek origin. In cult she was often called Kore, the Girl, and the Romans knew her as Proserpina and identified her with Libera, an Italic goddess. Myths similar to her descent and return also appear in the cults of male gods such as Attis, Adonis and Osiris, and in Minoan Crete.

In Greek mythology Persephone is the daughter of Zeus and Demeter and became queen of the underworld after her abduction by her uncle Hades, who later married her. The abduction is mentioned briefly in Hesiod's Theogony and told in detail in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter. According to the Hymn she was gathering flowers with the Oceanids, Athena and Artemis when Hades burst through a cleft in the earth. Her cyclical return to the surface represents the growth of vegetation, especially grain, which disappears into the earth when sown and is harvested when grown.

When Ascalaphus told the gods that she had eaten pomegranate seeds in the underworld, she was obliged to return there each year, for four months, or in later versions six. In Homer she always appears with Hades in the underworld, and Odysseus meets dread Persephone there. A tradition forbade speaking her name, which came from her conflation with an old chthonic divinity, Despoina, the Mistress. In the Orphic tradition she was the mother, by Zeus, of Dionysus, also called Iacchus or Zagreus, and of Melinoe.

With Demeter, Persephone was the central figure of the Eleusinian Mysteries, which promised the initiated a happy afterlife. Her return from the underworld each spring symbolised immortality, and she is frequently shown on sarcophagi. In Athens the mysteries of the month of Anthesterion were dedicated to her. In Epizephyrian Locris, in modern Calabria, she is a goddess of marriage and childbirth.

In Classical Greek art she is always robed, often carrying a sheaf of grain, and she appears most often being carried off by Hades. Plutarch identified her with the spring season, and Cicero called her the seed of the fruits of the fields.
persepolis: Persepolis stands in the plains of Marvdasht, encircled by the southern Zagros Mountains in Fars province, near the small river Pulvar, which flows into the Kur River. The site includes a terrace of 125,000 square metres, partly artificial and partly cut from a mountain, with its east side resting against Rahmat Mountain. Its exact function remains unclear.

It was not one of the largest cities of ancient Iran but appears to have been a grand ceremonial complex occupied only seasonally, raised on a walled platform with five palaces or halls of varying size. Until recently most archaeologists held that it was used chiefly to celebrate Nowruz, the Persian New Year, when the Iranian nobility and tributary peoples brought gifts to the king, as the stairway reliefs show.

The earliest remains date to 515 BCE. The French archaeologist André Godard, who excavated the site in the early 1930s, believed that Cyrus the Great chose it but that Darius I built the terrace and the palaces, which inscriptions on the buildings support. The country's true capitals were Susa, Babylon and Ecbatana, which may be why the Greeks did not know the city until Alexander the Great took and plundered it. Darius built the Apadana, the largest palace, for official audiences; its foundation tablets of gold and silver bear his Old Persian inscription.

After invading Achaemenid Persia in 330 BCE, Alexander sent the main force of his army to Persepolis by the Royal Road and allowed his troops to loot the city. Soon afterwards the wooden parts of the complex were destroyed by fire. According to one theory Alexander set the fire deliberately to avenge the Persian destruction of Athens; according to another, he did so at the urging of the courtesan Thaïs during a feast, while drunk. In 316 BCE Persepolis was still the capital of Persia as a province of the Macedonian Empire, but it gradually declined.

Persepolis is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the key cultural heritage sites of Iran. The ruins of colossal buildings of dark-grey marble stand on the terrace, with fifteen pillars intact and three more re-erected since 1970; the Tachara Palace is the most intact building, having escaped the burning. García de Silva Figueroa in 1618 was the first Western traveller to identify the site known in Iran as Chehel Minar with the Persepolis of the classical authors. Study of the trilingual royal inscriptions found there led to the initial decipherment of cuneiform in the early 19th century.
perseus-of-macedon: Perseus was the son of King Philip V of Macedonia and a concubine, probably Polycratia of Argos. His father spent most of his reign trying to maintain Macedonian hegemony over Greece and, later, against an expanding Roman Republic. After defeat in the Second Macedonian War Philip had to accept Roman power in Greece, and he later helped Rome in the war against Nabis in 195 BCE and the Aetolian War of 191–189 BCE. Perseus is recorded as having commanded Macedonian troops in both the Second Macedonian War and the Aetolian War.

Because he was a concubine's son, he feared the throne might pass to his legitimate younger brother Demetrius, who had been sent to Rome as a hostage and led a pro-Roman faction at court. In 180 BCE Perseus forged a letter, supposedly from the Roman general Titus Quinctius Flamininus, suggesting that Demetrius was planning to overthrow Philip, and it persuaded Philip to execute Demetrius.

Philip died the next year, and Perseus succeeded him on 22 June 179 BCE. In 178 BCE he married Laodice V, daughter of Seleucus IV of Syria. In 172 BCE Eumenes II of Pergamon, fearing Macedonian expansion, accused Perseus before the Roman Senate of threatening the stability of the Greek world, and soon Rome and Perseus went to war in the Third Macedonian War of 171–168 BCE. Perseus had some initial success, but the war ended with his decisive defeat by the Roman general Lucius Aemilius Paullus at the Battle of Pydna and his surrender. The Antigonid kingdom was dissolved and replaced with four republics.

Perseus was led captive in the triumph of Paullus in 167 BCE and imprisoned in Rome with his half-brother Philippus and his son Alexander. According to Plutarch, the Romans decided after two years to kill him by keeping him from sleeping until he died of exhaustion in 166 BCE, while Livy writes that he was shown clemency and kept in good conditions at Alba Fucens for the rest of his life.

His son Alexander, still a child at Pydna, was held at Alba Fucens, became a skilled metalworker, learned Latin and worked as a public notary. In 149 BCE Andriscus, claiming to be a son of Perseus, announced he would retake Macedonia, but the Romans defeated him in 148 BCE. In 146 BCE the four republics were dissolved and Macedon became a Roman province.
persian-carpet: A Persian carpet is a heavy textile made for a wide variety of utilitarian and symbolic purposes and produced in Iran, historically known as Persia, for home use, local sale and export. The beginning of carpet weaving is unknown, since carpets are subject to wear and to destruction by insects and rodents. Woven rugs probably developed from earlier floor coverings of felt or from flat weaving. The Pazyryk carpet, excavated in 1949 from the grave of a Scythian nobleman in the Pazyryk Valley of the Altai Mountains, was woven in the 5th century BCE according to radiocarbon testing. It measures 183 by 200 centimetres and has 36 symmetrical knots per square centimetre, and it is considered the oldest known carpet in the world.

Persian rugs were woven in parallel by nomadic tribes, in village and town workshops, and in royal court manufactories. They represent several simultaneous lines of tradition. Town workshops at Tabriz, Kerman, Kashan, Isfahan, Nain and Qom are marked by specific techniques and high-quality materials. Rugs woven by villagers and tribes are distinguished by fine wool, bright colours and traditional patterns, and the bolder, coarser designs of nomads are considered the most authentic. Gabbeh rugs are the best-known type of this line.

In most Persian rugs the pile is sheep's wool. Cotton forms the foundation of the warps and wefts of most modern rugs, since it can be spun more tightly than wool and tolerates more tension. Silk is expensive and has been used for representative carpets, notably in Kashan, Qum, Nain and Isfahan. Hand-woven pile rugs are made by knotting threads individually into the warps and cutting the thread after each knot, a process that may take from a few months to several years.

Xenophon, around 400 BCE, mentions Persian carpets in the Anabasis. The Safavid dynasty arose in 1501, and its rulers Shah Ismail I, Shah Tahmasp I and Shah Abbas I became patrons of the arts. Court manufactories were probably set up by Tahmasp at Tabriz and certainly by Abbas at Isfahan, after he moved the capital there following the Ottoman–Safavid War of 1603–18. Their carpets are noted for elaborate colours and design and are treasured in museums and private collections. Carpet weaving suffered periods of decline, notably after synthetic dyes arrived in the second half of the nineteenth century, and no records of it survive from the Afsharid and Zand eras.

The weavers of Tabriz founded the modern industry around 1885. In 1935 Rezā Shāh founded the Iran Carpet Company and brought weaving under government control. In 2010 the traditional skills of carpet weaving in Fars province and Kashan were inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage Lists.
persian-cossack-brigade: Naser al-Din Shah had admired the Cossacks who escorted him across Russian Armenia on his journey to Europe in 1878–1879, and in Tiflis he asked Grand Duke Mikhail for Russian help in raising such a unit; Emperor Alexander II approved. Unlike true Cossacks, who served in return for grants of land, the brigade was recruited from volunteers and conscripts. Lieutenant-Colonel Aleksey Domantovich formed it with 400 Caucasian muhajirs, descendants of Circassians and Transcaucasian Muslims who had fled Russian rule. He enforced discipline and paid the men on time, but the Russian minister in Tehran saw him as a rival and had him removed in 1881.

Under his successors the brigade shrank through budget cuts, desertion and cholera to just 150 men. Colonel Kosagovskij revived it, ending the muhajirs' privileges after their mutiny of 1895. When Naser al-Din was assassinated on 1 May 1896 the brigade held Tehran, and on 7 June 1896 it escorted the heir, Mozaffar ad-Din Shah, into the capital. By 1903 it had about 1,500 men and was seen by British observers as under the direct control of the Russian legation.

Under Colonel Liakhov it shelled the parliament for Mohammad Ali Shah, but forces led by Sattar Khan and Yeprem Khan retook Tehran and the shah abdicated. In 1916 the Russians enlarged it to a division of about 8,000 men, which fought Ottoman troops. After the Russian Revolution Britain paid its wages from December 1917 and most of the Russian officers left.

On 14 January 1921 the British general Ironside gave Reza Khan, who had joined the brigade at sixteen, command of the whole force. Reza Khan's men from Qazvin and Hamadan, 3,000 to 4,000 strong, then seized Tehran in a largely bloodless coup. Merged with the gendarmerie into a new army of 40,000, the brigade became its core, and its former officers held key posts as Reza Khan made himself shah and founded the Pahlavi dynasty. Soviet historians long portrayed it simply as a tool of Russian imperialism, which the historians Uzi Rabi and Nugzar Ter-Oganov say left much about it unstudied.
persian-gulf: The Persian Gulf, sometimes called the Arabian Gulf, is a mediterranean sea in West Asia of some 251,000 square kilometres. It is 989 kilometres long and about 56 kilometres wide at its narrowest, in the Strait of Hormuz, which joins it to the Gulf of Oman. The water is shallow, averaging 50 metres in depth. At its north-western end the Shatt al-Arab delta carries the waters of the Euphrates and the Tigris. Eight states have coasts on it: Bahrain, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

During most of the Last Glacial Period much of the Gulf was dry land, a floodplain where several rivers met. The modern sea formed as sea levels rose between about 12,000 and 6,000 years ago. Seagoing vessels from the mid-sixth millennium BCE have been found at H3 in Kuwait, when the Gulf belonged to a trade network linking Ubaid settlements in Mesopotamia with communities along its coast. At the end of the fourth millennium BCE the Dilmun civilization dominated its southern part. Between 625 BCE and 226 CE a succession of Persian empires held the northern side, and the Achaemenid navy kept bases on the Shatt al-Arab and in Bahrain, Oman and Yemen.

In 1521 a Portuguese force under Antonio Correia invaded Bahrain for its pearl industry, after Afonso de Albuquerque had captured the kingdom of Hormuz. On 29 April 1602 Shah Abbas of the Safavid Empire expelled the Portuguese from Bahrain, and in 1622, with British naval support, he took the island of Hormuz; trade moved to Bandar Abbas. Piracy was prevalent until the nineteenth century, and the British mounted the Persian Gulf campaign of 1819, which led to the General Maritime Treaty of 1820 with the sheikhs of the Pirate Coast. From 1763 until 1971 Britain held varying degrees of political control over several Gulf states.

The name Persian Gulf is the historical and internationally established one, though Arab governments use Arabian Gulf or the Gulf. The Gulf and its coastlands hold very large reserves of petroleum and natural gas, and Qatar and Iran share the largest gas field across the median line.
persian-language: Modern Persian is a continuation of Middle Persian, an official language of the Sasanian Empire (224–651 CE), which was itself a continuation of Old Persian, used in the Achaemenid Empire (550–330 BCE). It originated in the region of Fars in southwestern Iran. Old Persian is attested in cuneiform inscriptions from the 6th to the 4th century BCE, the oldest being the Behistun Inscription from the time of King Darius I (reigned 522–486 BCE). Middle Persian is attested in Pahlavi and Manichaean scripts, and New Persian literature was first recorded in the ninth century, after the Muslim conquest of Persia. Gernot Windfuhr treats New Persian as an evolution of both earlier stages, but states that none of the known Middle Persian dialects is its direct predecessor.

Persian belongs to the Western Iranian group of the Iranian languages. It has three standard varieties: Iranian Persian, Dari in Afghanistan and Tajiki in Tajikistan, all based on classic Persian literature and mutually intelligible to a relatively high degree. Iranian Persian and Dari are written in the Persian alphabet, a modified form of the Arabic alphabet; after the Arab conquest it took about 200 years before Persians adopted the Arabic script in place of Pahlavi. Tajiki is written in a Cyrillic alphabet.

Modern Persian has no grammatical gender and its usual word order is subject–object–verb. Its core vocabulary is of Middle Persian origin, but it also contains a considerable number of Arabic loanwords. John R. Perry estimates that about 20 percent of everyday vocabulary, and around 25 percent of that of classical and modern literature, is of Arabic origin.

Persian was the first language to break the monopoly of Arabic on writing in the Muslim world, and Persian poetry became a tradition in many eastern courts. It served as a language of bureaucracy even for non-native speakers, among them the Ottomans in Anatolia, the Delhi Sultanates and Mughals in the Indian subcontinent, and the Pashtuns in Afghanistan. It influenced Turkic, Armenian, Georgian, Greek and Indo-Aryan languages, as well as other Iranian ones. Works written in it include the Shahnameh by Ferdowsi, the works of Rumi, the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, the Divân of Hafez and the Gulistan and Bustan by Saadi Shirazi. Approximately 130 million people speak it worldwide.
persian-miniature: A Persian miniature is a small painting on paper, either an illustration in a book or a separate work meant for an album called a muraqqa. Persian art under Islam never completely forbade the human figure, and in miniatures figures, often in large numbers, are central. The miniature was a private form, kept in a book or album and shown only to chosen people, so it allowed more freedom than wall painting.

Its bright, pure colours are a striking feature, and the pigments are normally mineral-based. Faces are youthful and seen in three-quarter view, lighting is even and without shadow, and costumes and architecture are always those of the painter's own time. Artists were men grouped in workshops, of which the royal workshop was the most prestigious. Shah Tahmasp I, who reigned from 1524 to 1576, was an amateur artist and a leading patron.

The earliest known illustrated manuscript in Persian is a copy of the epic Varka and Golshah, made around 1250, probably at Konya under the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum. After the Mongol invasion of 1219 onwards, the Ilkhanid court imported Chinese works and probably artists and sponsored a revival of book painting. Chinese influence shows in cloud bands, stylised rocks, knotted tree trunks and dragons. The tradition passed through the Jalayirids, who introduced Chinese-inspired landscapes, to the Timurids. Herat was a leading centre, especially when the Timurid prince Baysonqor governed it in the 1420s and commissioned the Baysonghor Shahnameh. Painting reached its highest point in the 15th and 16th centuries.

The Persian miniature became the dominant influence on the Ottoman miniature in Turkey and the Mughal miniature in the Indian subcontinent, and Persian artists were sought after by their courts. In 2020 UNESCO inscribed the art of miniature on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity on the nomination of Azerbaijan, Iran, Turkey and Uzbekistan. Henri Matisse said that the Persian miniatures he saw at the Munich exhibition of 1910 showed him how to suggest a greater, plastic space.
persis: Persis, also called Persia proper, is a historical region in south-western Iran that roughly corresponds to the modern province of Fars. Iranian-speaking peoples are thought to have migrated from Central Asia and to have reached Persis in the early first millennium BCE, giving rise to the Persians. They were present in the region from about the 10th century BCE. The ruins of Persepolis and Pasargadae, two of the four capitals of the Achaemenid Empire, lie in Fars.

Under the Achaemenid dynasty, founded in the late 6th century BCE, the Persians ruled the largest empire the world had yet seen. Alexander the Great defeated the Achaemenid dynasty in 330 BCE. Several satraps of Persis are known, among them Phrasaortes, who ruled from 330 to 324 BCE, and the Macedonian general Peucestas, who learned the Persian language and followed local customs. Seleucus took possession of the region in 312 BCE.

Under the Seleucid Empire Persis emerged as a state with some independence that minted its own coins. A line of rulers called the Frataraka acted as Seleucid representatives from the end of the 3rd century BCE, and Vahbarz, or Vādfradād I, obtained independence around 150 BCE. When the Parthian king Mithridates I took control of Persis he left the Persian dynasts in office as the Kings of Persis, and they kept minting coins with the title of king.

Babak, ruler of the small town of Kheir, and his eldest son Shapur expanded their power over all of Persis. After Babak's death around 220 his son Ardashir, governor of Darabgird, defeated the last Parthian king, Artabanus, in 224 and was crowned at Ctesiphon, founding the Sasanian Empire. He built a capital at Ardashir-Khwarrah, modern Firouzabad, in the south of Persis.

Arab invaders ended Zoroastrian rule in the 7th century, after which Islam became dominant, and Persis passed through numerous dynasties. The ruins of Bishapur, Persepolis and Firouzabad remain as reminders of its ancient history.
persius: According to the Life preserved in the manuscripts, Persius was born into an equestrian family of good stock on both sides at Volterra, a small Etruscan city. He lost his father when he was six, and his stepfather died a few years later. At twelve he came to Rome, where he was taught by Remmius Palaemon and the rhetor Verginius Flavus. Over the next four years he made friends with the Stoic Lucius Annaeus Cornutus, the lyric poet Caesius Bassus and the poet Lucan. He also became close to Thrasea Paetus, with whom he shared many journeys over ten years, and met Seneca, whose genius did not impress him.

As a boy Persius wrote a tragedy on an episode of Roman history and another work, probably on travel. Reading the satires of Lucilius made him want to write in that manner, and he began a book of satires, but he wrote seldom and slowly, and an early death prevented him from finishing it. After his death Cornutus suppressed everything but the satires, altered them slightly and handed them to Bassus for editing. They were an immediate success and became very popular in the Middle Ages. They are written in hexameters, apart from a short prologue in scazons, and run to fewer than seven hundred lines.

The first satire censures the literary tastes of the day as a reflection of moral decadence. The others deal with what may justly be asked of the gods, the importance of having a definite aim in life, the need for self-knowledge among public men, the Stoic doctrine of liberty, introduced with generous allusions to Cornutus, and the proper use of money. Persius describes the seamy side of life, especially the link between excess of consumption and moral failure, and shows little of Horace's easy acceptance of human weakness.

Persius died young, leaving his considerable fortune to his mother and sister. He was said to have a gentle disposition and to have lived a life of devotion to his mother Fulvia Sisennia, his sister and his aunt. His style is obscure, and its straining of expression and excess of detail compare poorly with the clear prose of Seneca's letters, yet some judge that in earnestness and moral purpose he reaches the highest note of Roman satire. Montaigne mentions him several times. Isaac Casaubon, Otto Jahn and John Conington produced important editions.
personal-computer: Early experimental machines could be operated by a single attendant: ENIAC, operational in 1946, could be run by one highly trained person. Computers for laboratory, instrumentation or engineering work, such as the Bendix G15 and LGP-30 of 1956, were operated interactively, but they were far too expensive to be owned by an individual. The personal computer depended on advances in semiconductor technology: the silicon integrated circuit chip, developed by Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor in 1959, the MOS transistor, developed by Mohamed Atalla and Dawon Kahng at Bell Labs, and the first single-chip microprocessor, the Intel 4004 of 1971, developed by Federico Faggin.

A personal computer is designed to be operated directly by an end user, rather than by a computer expert, administrator or technician, and it does not rely on time-sharing by many people at once. In 1968 the SRI researcher Douglas Engelbart gave a preview of features that later became staples, among them e-mail, hypertext, word processing, video conferencing and the mouse, though the demonstration needed technical staff and a costly mainframe.

By the mid-1970s some microprocessor-based machines were sold in kit form, mainly to hobbyists, programmed with toggle switches and displaying results on front panel lamps. The Micral N, built from 1972 around the Intel 8008, was the earliest commercial, non-kit microcomputer based on a microprocessor, and a few hundred were sold.

Early personal computers were very expensive, but falling production costs and the commercial availability of microprocessors from the mid-1970s made them affordable to small businesses and individuals. In the early 1980s home computers were developed for household use and typically used a television as the display. The Sinclair ZX Spectrum, introduced in 1982, sold 8 million units and the Commodore 64 17 million.

The IBM Personal Computer was released in 1981, and IBM PC compatibles soon followed, so that the term PC came to refer to them. By 1984 mass-market systems with graphical user interfaces were available. In 1991 the World Wide Web was made available for public use, and powerful personal computers together with the Internet became the foundation for a significant part of modern life.
pertamina: In 1957 the assets in Indonesia of Royal Dutch Shell, trading as Bataafse Petroleum Maatschappij, were nationalised, and from them Permina was founded as a state oil monopoly headed by Lieutenant-General Ibnu Sutowo. His position as second deputy of Abdul Haris Nasution began the armed forces' involvement in the oil industry. Permina distributed oil for the whole archipelago and in 1962 set up an Oil Academy in Bandung, whose graduates became its main source of labour. Pertamin, established in 1961, was made responsible for exploration and production under a policy that oil and gas extraction be carried out only by a state company.

Permina and Pertamin merged in August 1968 as PN Pertamina. It did little drilling itself and made production-sharing agreements with foreign companies. By the end of 1973 it produced 28.2 per cent of Indonesia's oil, with Caltex and Stanvac the rest, and its assets included seven refineries, 116 tankers and an airline. The oil price rises of 1974 brought revenues of 4.2 billion dollars, about one sixth of Indonesia's gross domestic product, and Sutowo spent much of it widening the company's interests into steel, construction and tankers. It built the Bina Graha, the presidential executive office in Jakarta.

In February 1975 Pertamina could no longer pay its American and Canadian creditors. An investigation found debts of over 10 billion dollars, about thirty per cent of Indonesia's gross national product, though others give 15 billion, together with mismanagement and corruption. Charges against Sutowo were dismissed. The government took over the company's operation, and a large bail-out nearly doubled Indonesia's foreign debt. Under the Oil and Natural Gas Act of 2001 it became PT Pertamina (Persero) in 2003.

Pertamina is a state-owned company headquartered in Jakarta, under the State Minister of State-owned Enterprises, and has 27 subsidiaries. They include Pertamina EP for exploration, Pertamina Gas and Pertamina Geothermal Energy, which was listed publicly in 2023. It has the largest network of fuel stations in Indonesia. In June 2024 the Jakarta Corruption Court sentenced Karen Agustiawan, its president director from 2009 to 2014, to nine years in prison for graft over a gas purchase, and the conviction was upheld in August.
perth: Perth lies mostly on the sandy, relatively flat Swan Coastal Plain, between the Darling Scarp and the Indian Ocean. The Swan River, also known as Derbarl Yerrigan, runs through it; the Dutch captain Willem de Vlamingh named it for the black swans he found there when exploring in 1697. The central business district and the port of Fremantle both stand on the river. Summers are hot, sunny and dry and winters mild and wet, a hot-summer Mediterranean climate. The nearest city of more than 100,000 people is Adelaide, over 2,100 km away, which makes Perth one of the most isolated major cities in the world.

People have lived in the Perth area for at least 48,000 years. Noongar country covers the south-west corner of Western Australia, and the wetlands of the Swan Coastal Plain hold spiritual importance and were a source of food. The Whadjuk Noongar are the traditional owners of the land, and the Noongar name for the place is Boorloo. In 1619 the Dutch explorer Frederick de Houtman sighted the coast near present-day Perth, which he and Jacob Dedel called Dedelsland.

Perth was founded as the administrative centre of the Swan River Colony in 1829, the first comprehensive European settlement in the west of the continent, after New South Wales had set up a convict-supported outpost at King George's Sound in 1826 in response to rumours of French annexation. Stirling's proclamation of the colony was read at Fremantle on 18 June 1829. The name honours Sir George Murray, Secretary of State for War and the Colonies, who sat in the House of Commons for Perthshire. The colony was officially designated Western Australia in 1832.

In 1850, at the request of farmers and businesspeople short of labour, Western Australia accepted convicts, and over eighteen years 9,721 arrived on 43 ships, outnumbering the roughly 7,300 free settlers. Queen Victoria announced Perth's designation as a city in 1856, but it remained a tranquil town. After a referendum in 1900 Western Australia joined the Federation of Australia in 1901, the last colony to agree, and only after concessions that included a transcontinental railway from Port Augusta to Kalgoorlie.
