From 1927 to 1954 Indigenous people were prohibited from entering large parts of Perth.

Perth is the capital and largest city of Western Australia and the fourth most populous city in Australia, a position it has held since 1984. Mining booms in the late 20th century made it the headquarters of significant mining operations in the state. Kings Park and Botanic Garden is one of the world's largest inner-city parks, and Fremantle Prison is a World Heritage Site.
perth-amboy: Perth Amboy lies in northeastern Middlesex County, New Jersey, within the New York metropolitan area, and borders the Arthur Kill. The Lenape called the point on which it stands Ompoge, meaning level ground or standing upright. The name Amboy descends from that word, and the colonists later joined it to the name of their settlement. Perth Amboy and South Amboy, across the Raritan River, are together called the Amboys, and the city is linked to Staten Island by the Outerbridge Crossing.

Scottish colonists settled the place around 1683, recruited to occupy the share of the East Jersey colony owned by Robert Barclay, a Quaker who later became the province's absentee governor. They called it New Perth in honour of James Drummond, 4th Earl of Perth, one of the twelve associates of the company of Scottish proprietors. In 1686 it was designated capital of East Jersey, while Burlington was capital of West Jersey; after the two were united as a royal colony in 1702, the two cities alternated as capital of the province. A royal charter followed on 4 August 1718, and the New Jersey Legislature confirmed the city's status on 21 December 1784.

By the middle of the 19th century immigration and industry had transformed the city. Factories such as A. Hall and Sons Terra Cotta, Guggenheim and Sons and the Copper Works Smelting Company employed many residents, and the city became the tidewater terminal of the Lehigh Valley Railroad and a coal shipping point. Immigrants from Denmark, Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Italy, Russia and Austria dominated the factory jobs and formed close ethnic neighbourhoods such as Budapest, Dublin and Chickentown. The Perth Amboy Public Library, one of the first Carnegie libraries in the state, opened in 1903.

The waterfront keeps the Perth Amboy Ferry Slip, once an important crossing on the route south from New York City and listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1978, as well as the Proprietary House, the former governor's mansion, which now holds a museum. St. Peter's Episcopal Church and the Raritan Yacht Club, one of the oldest yacht clubs in the United States, also stand there. The 2020 census counted 55,436 people, and most residents are Hispanic, with Puerto Rican and Dominican communities among them.
perth-scotland: Perth stands on the banks of the River Tay, on a natural mound raised slightly above the flood plain. The area has been occupied since the arrival of Mesolithic hunter-gatherers, and nearby standing stones and circles date from about 4000 BCE. Close to the city is Scone Abbey, which formerly housed the Stone of Scone, on which the kings of Scots were traditionally crowned. The name comes from a Pictish word for a wood or copse, related to the Welsh perth, meaning hedge or thicket. In the later medieval period its inhabitants called it St John's Toun, after the church of St John the Baptist.

The frequent residence of the royal court gave Perth the reputation of a capital of Scotland. King William the Lion granted royal burgh status in the early 12th century. The city became one of the richest burghs in the country, trading with France, the Low Countries and the Baltic and importing Spanish silk and French wine. It grew from a plan of two parallel streets, High Street and South Street, linked by vennels. In 1437 King James I was assassinated in Perth by followers of Walter Stewart, Earl of Atholl, at Blackfriars church.

In 1559 a sermon by John Knox in St John's Kirk was followed by the sacking of the Greyfriars and Blackfriars houses, two of the city's four monastic institutions. Jacobite supporters occupied the city in 1689, 1715 and 1745. Perth Academy was founded in 1760, and linen, leather, bleach and whisky became major industries. The first railway station opened in 1848. In 1829 Sir George Murray, born in Perth, asked that the new Swan River Colony in Western Australia be named Perth.

Perth is the administrative centre of Perth and Kinross and the historic county town of Perthshire. It has been known as the Fair City since Sir Walter Scott published The Fair Maid of Perth in 1828. St John's Kirk, much altered, keeps a 15th-century brass candelabrum imported from the Low Countries, a rare survival in Scotland. Its arms, recorded on a seal of 1378, show a paschal lamb holding a saltire, and the North Inch and South Inch were given to the city in 1377 by King Robert III.
perthshire: Perthshire, or the County of Perth, is a historic county in central Scotland. It extends from Strathmore in the east to the Pass of Drumochter in the north, Rannoch Moor and Ben Lui in the west and Aberfoyle in the south. It is known as the big county, or the Shire, for its roundness and its rank as the fourth largest historic county in Scotland.

The landscape runs from rich agricultural straths in the east to the high mountains of the southern Highlands, with the Grampian Mountains, many lochs and glens, the Ochil and Sidlaw Hills, and the Carse of Gowrie, a flat farming area on the north shore of the Firth of Tay. The highest point is Ben Lawers at 1,214 m. The county town is Perth, and other towns include Auchterarder, Blairgowrie, Crieff, Dunblane and Scone.

The origins of Perthshire as a shire, an area administered by a sheriff, are obscure, but it seems to have been created in the reign of David I (1124-1153). The Sheriff of Perth had authority over several provinces, including Atholl, Breadalbane, Gowrie, Menteith and Strathearn.

Commissioners of Supply were established in 1667, and elected county councils followed under the Local Government (Scotland) Act 1889, with the first meeting of Perthshire County Council on 22 May 1890. In 1930 Perthshire and Kinross-shire were joined under one county council, and the administrative counties were abolished in 1975.

The county coat of arms seems to have been granted for the colours of volunteer and militia units raised in the late eighteenth century. The Earl of Kinnoull presented the arms in 1800. The shield resembles the Scottish royal arms, because Perthshire was the home county of the House of Dunkeld and contained the former royal capital, Scone, and the crest, a Highland soldier, refers to the Black Watch, which was formed in the county.

Perthshire historically straddled the Highland line between the Gaelic-speaking and English-speaking parts of Scotland. Around 45 percent of its people have been estimated to have spoken Gaelic in 1698. In 1881 Gaelic was recorded as spoken habitually by 12.1 percent, and by 1971 by 1.7 percent.

Much of historic Perthshire, together with Kinross-shire, forms the Perth and Kinross council area, while the south-west lies in the Stirling council area and a few parishes in Clackmannanshire. The boundaries of the historic county are still used for some official purposes connected with land registration. Notable places include Scone Palace, Blair Castle, Drummond Castle and Dunkeld Cathedral. Birnam Wood and Dunsinane Hill are known from Shakespeare's Macbeth. The Highland Main Line railway connects Perth to Inverness.
peru: Peru covers 1,285,216 km2 on the Pacific coast of South America, the third-largest country on the continent. The Andes run parallel to the ocean and define three traditional regions: the costa, a narrow and largely arid coastal plain; the sierra, the highlands, which include the Altiplano and the highest peak, Huascarán at 6,768 metres; and the selva, the Amazon rainforest, which covers almost 60 percent of the country.

The Amazon basin covers 75% of Peruvian territory, and Lake Titicaca, shared with Bolivia, is the largest lake in South America. The name may derive from Birú, a local ruler near the Bay of San Miguel in Panama, and the Capitulation of Toledo of 1529 gave it legal status as the name of the province that was the Inca Empire.

The earliest evidence of people in Peruvian territory, about 12,500 BCE, comes from Huaca Prieta. The Caral-Supe civilization flourished on the coast, and the Chavín culture, from 1500 to 300 BCE, was probably more a religious than a political phenomenon. Later coastal cultures included the Paracas, Nazca, Moche and Chimu. The Chimu flourished from about 1140 to 1450 as a loose confederation of walled cities with its capital at Chan Chan, and in the highlands the Tiahuanaco and Wari cultures developed large urban settlements between 500 and 1000 CE.

The Spanish Empire conquered the region in the 16th century, and Charles V established a viceroyalty, the Kingdom of Peru, with its capital at Lima. According to the historian Noble David Cook, the Amerindian population fell from nearly 5–9 million in the 1520s to around 600,000 in 1620, mainly from infectious disease. The National University of San Marcos was founded in Lima in 1551. Peru proclaimed independence in 1821 and completed it in 1824, with the battle of Ayacucho. Guano exploitation brought relative stability until the War of the Pacific, 1879–1884.

Peru is a unitary semi-presidential republic under its 1993 constitution, with a president elected for five years without immediate re-election. The population was 33,396,698 in estimates to 2022, about 80 percent of them urban, and the Lima metropolitan area has over 9.8 million people. Spanish is the main language, but many Peruvians speak Quechuan languages, Aymara or other Indigenous languages.
perugino: Pietro Vannucci was born in Città della Pieve, Umbria, the son of Cristoforo Maria Vannucci. His nickname marks him as from Perugia, the chief city of Umbria. Scholars dispute the standing of his family: some hold that he worked his way out of poverty, others that the family was among the wealthiest in the town. He most likely began studying painting in local workshops in Perugia, such as those of Bartolomeo Caporali or Fiorenzo di Lorenzo.

According to Vasari he was apprenticed in the Florentine workshop of Andrea del Verrocchio alongside Leonardo da Vinci, Domenico Ghirlandaio and Filippino Lippi, and Piero della Francesca is thought to have taught him perspective. In 1472 he was enrolled as a master in the Confraternity of St Luke. He was one of the earliest central Italian painters to work in oil.

Around 1480 Pope Sixtus IV called him to Rome to paint fresco panels on the walls of the Sistine Chapel. These included the Baptism of Christ and the Delivery of the Keys; Pinturicchio went with him and became his partner. The frescoes on the altar wall were later destroyed to make room for Michelangelo's Last Judgement. Between 1486 and 1499 he worked mainly between Florence and Perugia, keeping a studio in each. In 1496 the bankers' guild of Perugia asked him to decorate the audience hall of the Collegio del Cambio, with planets and zodiac signs on the vault and sacred scenes on the walls; he placed his own portrait bust on the central pilaster.

He became one of the priors of Perugia in 1501. Michelangelo is said to have called him a bungler in art, and Perugino brought an unsuccessful action for defamation. His Annunziata Altarpiece in Florence, painted in 1504 to 1507, was accused of lack of innovation, and he lost his students. Pope Julius II summoned him to paint a ceiling in the Vatican, but soon preferred Raphael, who had been trained by Perugino, and from 1512 Perugino retired to Perugia.

His last frescoes were painted in 1521 and 1522 in churches and monasteries around Umbria. He died of the plague in 1523 at Fontignano and, like other victims, was hastily buried in an unconsecrated field, the spot now unknown. He left considerable property and three sons. Vasari states that he had very little religion and doubted the immortality of the soul. His likely pupils included Raphael, whose early work shows his influence most, and Perugino's Marriage of the Virgin, now in Caen, served as the model for Raphael's Sposalizio of 1504. Perugia dedicated a monument to him in 1923.
perusine-war: Lucius Antonius was the younger brother of Mark Antony, and he fought in Antony's name against Octavian, the future Emperor Augustus. Antony's wife Fulvia held that her husband should rule Rome alone rather than share power in the Second Triumvirate, above all with Octavian. Her prominent part in the conflict was unusual in Roman society, which kept women out of power and seldom recorded what they did in politics.

Lucius raised eight legions in Italy and held Rome for a short time, but was then forced to fall back on Perusia in Umbria. The Umbrians were sympathetic to his cause, since some of their towns and lands had been taken by Octavian to settle his veterans after the defeat of Brutus and Cassius at Philippi in 42 BCE. Octavian's army besieged the city through the winter of 41–40 BCE, and the defenders gave in once they saw that no relief would come from Italy or the East.

Octavian spared Fulvia and Lucius and, as a gesture to his brother, sent Lucius to govern a Spanish province. He pardoned the soldiers and most of the townspeople, but many others were marked for death. Suetonius wrote that 300 senators and knights were slaughtered as sacrificial victims before an altar to Caesar on the Ides of March, and Cassius Dio gives a similar account, naming Tiberius Cannutius among them.

Antony exiled Fulvia to Sicyon, where she died of an unknown illness in 40 BCE, and she was afterwards blamed as the sole cause of the quarrel between the two men. Their alliance was restored and sealed by Antony's marriage to Octavian's sister Octavia. The settlement collapsed eight years later, when the civil war between Antony and Octavian began again.
peruvian-war-of-independence: Peru had seen uprisings throughout the colonial period, the most significant the rebellion of Túpac Amaru II in 1780-1781, which broke out against the Bourbon Reforms and was violently repressed; historians debate whether such movements aimed at independence. When Napoleon Bonaparte's invasion of Spain in 1808 left the empire without central authority, Viceroy José Fernando de Abascal y Sousa made Peru a base for royalist armies against the juntas of the Río de la Plata and annexed Upper Peru. Rebellions in Tacna in 1811, Huánuco in 1812 and Cuzco in 1814-1815, where the aged curaca Mateo Pumacahua joined the criollo leaders, were all put down, and Pumacahua was executed.

After freeing Chile, the patriots prepared an amphibious invasion, paid for mostly by Bernardo O'Higgins's Chilean government. On 21 August 1820 the Liberating Expedition of 4,118 soldiers sailed from Valparaíso under José de San Martín, with Admiral Thomas Alexander Cochrane commanding the fleet, and landed at Pisco on 7 September. General Juan Antonio Álvarez de Arenales campaigned in the highlands, Cochrane captured the royalist frigate Esmeralda, and a royalist battalion changed sides. Viceroy Pezuela was replaced by General José de la Serna, who left Lima for the highlands and later moved his headquarters to Cuzco, and San Martín proclaimed independence in the Plaza Mayor.

Royalists still held most of the country. After the Guayaquil Conference, where San Martín favoured a constitutional monarchy and Simón Bolívar a republic, San Martín left for Valparaíso on 22 September 1822. Royalist victories at Ica, Torata and Moquegua followed, and General José de Canterac reoccupied Lima without a fight on 18 June 1823. Congress appealed to Bolívar, who reached Lima on 10 December 1823, and in 1824 the battles of Junín and Ayacucho, the latter won by Antonio José de Sucre, ended royalist power.

Peru won full sovereignty only after the end of Bolívar's influence: the last Gran Colombian garrison handed the Real Felipe Fortress to the Peruvians on 16 February 1827. Spain renounced its continental American territories in 1836. Political dependence on Spain had ended, but Peru remained economically dependent on Europe, and the seizure of indigenous lands grew worse under the republic. The rivalries of criollo factions and caudillos made the country hard to organise, and only three civilians reached the presidency in its first seventy-five years.
peruzzi-family: According to the family's genealogist Luigi Passerini, the modest beginnings of the Peruzzi reached back to the mid-11th century. Their standing in Florence was confirmed by patronage: in his will of 1299 Donato di Arnoldo Peruzzi left money for a memorial chapel in a transept of the Basilica of Santa Croce. Probably his grandson Giovanni di Rinieri Peruzzi engaged Giotto, who from 1313 painted its walls with murals honouring John the Evangelist and John the Baptist.

The company that bore the family name was run by about half a dozen Peruzzi, while many other members followed careers of their own. Its capital came from the textile trade, the main source of Florence's wealth: English wool finished as cloth in Bruges was bought by Peruzzi agents and sold to the courts of Paris and Avignon or sent back to London.

Links with the Knights Hospitaller gave the firm a foothold in Rhodes, a transit port for silks, spices and drugs from the East. By the 1330s the Peruzzi bank was the second largest in Europe, with fifteen branches from the Middle East to London, capital of more than 100,000 gold florins and about 100 agents. Its courier system also served to gather news and was often drawn into diplomacy.

Economic historians now regard loans to Edward III of England as only part of the reason for the collapse of 1343. Florence's war with Castruccio Castracani of Lucca drained coin to pay mercenaries, France and England went to war over Aquitaine, and a peasant revolt in Flanders was put down with mercenaries paid in Peruzzi florins. The Bardi, their partners in risk, fell with them.

The surviving Peruzzi account books of 1335-1343 are a primary source for the economic history of late medieval Florence, alongside the chronicle of Giovanni Villani. Not all of the family's wealth was lost, and the Peruzzi remained among the patrician families of the city: in 1849 Ubaldino Peruzzi was gonfaloniere of Florence. The tower of the fortified Villa Peruzzi at Antella, south of Florence, commands the main road into the Chianti district.
pervez-musharraf: Pervez Musharraf was born on 11 August 1943 in Delhi, British India, to an Urdu-speaking family of Sayyids. His father, Syed Musharrafuddin, worked in the foreign office of the British Indian government and became an accounting director, and his mother, Zarin, took a degree in English literature at Delhi University. In 1961, aged 18, he entered the Pakistan Military Academy at Kakul.

Musharraf first saw battle with an artillery regiment during the Second Kashmir War of 1965 and received the Imtiazi Sanad medal for gallantry. In 1987 he commanded a new brigade of the Special Services Group near the Siachen Glacier. Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif promoted him to four-star general and Chief of the Army Staff in October 1998. From March to May 1999 he ordered the secret infiltration of forces into the Kargil district, and a fierce Indian offensive nearly led to a full-scale war. Sharif withdrew support in July under international pressure, which antagonised the army, and Sharif's attempt to dismiss Musharraf was followed by the coup of October 1999.

Musharraf governed as Chief Executive, appointed himself president on 20 June 2001, and in August 2002 issued the Legal Framework Order, which made many amendments to the Constitution. After the attacks of 11 September 2001 he allied Pakistan with the United States against the Taliban. His government liberalised the media and presided over rapid economic growth, while his rule also saw curbs on the judiciary and a growing insurgency in the North-West Frontier Province.

His dismissal of Chief Justice Iftikhar Chaudhry in March 2007 and the state of emergency of November cost him support, and he announced his resignation on 18 August 2008. He founded the All Pakistan Muslim League in 2010. On 17 December 2019 a special court sentenced him in absentia to death for suspending the constitution in November 2007. He died on 5 February 2023, aged 79, of amyloidosis, and was buried with military honours in Karachi. Judgements of his rule are sharply divided between those who credit him with economic stabilisation and those who point to the erosion of democratic institutions.
pescennius-niger: Gaius Pescennius Niger was born around 135 into an old Italian equestrian family and was the first of it to become a Roman senator. According to the Historia Augusta his parents were Annius Fuscus and Lampridia. Little is known of his early career; he may have held an administrative post in Egypt and served in a campaign in Dacia early in the reign of Commodus. He was elected suffect consul in the late 180s, and Commodus made him imperial legate of Syria in 191.

News of the murder of Pertinax and the auctioning of the imperial title to Didius Julianus reached him in Syria. Niger was well regarded in Rome, and a popular demonstration there called on him to come and claim the throne. Julianus is alleged to have sent a centurion east to assassinate him at Antioch. The eastern legions proclaimed Niger emperor by the end of April 193, and he took the additional name Justus, the Just. Septimius Severus had claimed the title on 14 April and later propaganda made Niger the first rebel, but Niger's envoys to Rome were intercepted by Severus, who entered the city in early June 193.

Niger won the support of the governors of the Asiatic provinces, among them Asellius Aemilianus, who occupied Byzantium for him, and took control of Egypt. His resources were weaker, however: six legions against the sixteen Danubian legions of Severus. His force defeated part of Severus' army under Lucius Fabius Cilo at Perinthus, but in the autumn of 193 Severus' general Tiberius Claudius Candidus defeated Aemilianus at Cyzicus, and Niger had to abandon Byzantium for Nicaea, where he was beaten again in December. He held the passes of the Taurus Mountains for some months while support fell away: Laodicea and Tyre changed sides, and Egypt and the legate of Arabia declared for Severus by February 194.

In May 194 Niger met Severus' general Publius Cornelius Anullinus at Issus and was decisively defeated after a long struggle. He was captured while trying to flee from Antioch to Parthia and beheaded, and his head was taken to Byzantium, which refused to surrender, and later to Rome, where it was displayed. Severus stormed and destroyed Byzantium and then rebuilt it. The Historia Augusta says he put Niger's wife and children to death, but the work is unreliable, and one scholar judges it more likely that they were allowed to live in retirement. His name means black Pescennius, a nickname that contemporaries linked to his dark-skinned neck.
peshawar: Peshawar lies in the broad Peshawar Valley, which mountain ranges surround on three sides, with the fourth side opening to the Punjab plains. The city stands on the level floor of the valley, known as the Gandhara Plains. Its economic importance has long rested on its position at the entrance to the Khyber Pass, the ancient route by which most trade between Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent passed. Its name derives from the reconstructed Sanskrit Puruṣapura, meaning City of Men; the Chinese monks Faxian in the 5th century and Xuanzang in the 7th recorded it under Chinese equivalents of that name.

Its recorded history reaches back to at least the 6th century BCE. The city likely first existed as a small village in the 5th century BCE, near the Gandharan capital of Puṣkalāvatī, close to present-day Charsadda. In the winter of 327–326 BCE Alexander the Great subdued Gandhara, and the valley afterwards came under Seleucus I Nicator. Puruṣapura served as capital of the Kushan Empire under Kanishka the Great in the 2nd century CE. The Ghaznavids conquered it from the Hindu Shahis in 1001, after Sabuktigin first fought the Hindu Shahis under their king Anandpal in 986–87.

Emperor Babur captured Peshawar in July 1526, called it Begram and rebuilt its fort. It remained an important centre on the trade routes between India and Central Asia under Mughal rule; over one thousand camel-loads of merchandise were destroyed by an accidental fire at the Bala Hissar fort in 1586. Sher Shah Suri began building the Grand Trunk Road in the 16th century. Nader Shah's Afsharid Empire held it from 1738, and the Durrani Empire later made it a winter capital. The East India Company annexed it in 1849. In 1901 it became capital of the North-West Frontier Province.

Peshawar has been part of Pakistan since 1947 and is the capital and largest city of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Until the mid-1950s it was enclosed within a city wall with sixteen gates. The University of Peshawar was established there in 1950. Hindko was long its common language, but Pashto has since become the main one, and Pashtuns now form most of the population, while the Peshoris, its original urban population, remain in the old Walled City. The city has a hot semi-arid climate and a population of about 1.9 million.
peshwa: The word comes from Persian pēshwā, meaning foremost or leader, and was inherited from earlier Persianate states in the Deccan. As early as 1397 the Bahmani Sultanate called its prime minister the peshwa, and the Ahmednagar Sultanate and the Bijapur Sultanate continued the practice. After Shivaji's coronation in 1674 he appointed Moropant Trimbak Pingle as his first Peshwa, as head of the Ashta Pradhan, the council of eight ministers. Pingle's son Nilopant Moreshvar Pingale succeeded him under Sambhaji after 1683. All Peshwas under Shivaji, Sambhaji and Rajaram belonged to the Marathi Deshastha Brahmin community.

After the war of succession between Tara Bai and Shahu, Shahu became Chhatrapati and appointed Balaji Vishwanath of the Bhat family as Peshwa in 1713. His appointment of Balaji's son Baji Rao I in 1720 made the post hereditary in the Bhat family. Baji Rao defeated the commander in chief Trimbak Rao Dabhade, who rebelled over the revenue collection of Gujarat, at the Battle of Dabhoi on 1 April 1731. Shahu then gave the Peshwas more responsibility and authority to command the armies, and from the time of Balaji Rao the Peshwas were the supreme authority while the Chhatrapati's position became nominal.

The office was most powerful under Baji Rao I. He and his son Balaji Baji Rao oversaw the period of the widest Maratha expansion, which ended with defeat by an Afghan army at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761. Chiefs such as the Scindias, Holkars, Gaekwads and Bhonsles gained autonomy while often holding allegiance to the Peshwa. Decline began when Raghunath Rao and his wife Anandibai had Narayanrao, his 18-year-old nephew, assassinated.

The last Peshwa, Baji Rao II, was defeated by the British East India Company at the Battle of Khadki, part of the Third Anglo-Maratha War of 1817–1818. The Peshwa's land was annexed to the Company's Bombay province and Baji Rao II was pensioned off. Tradition holds that Baji Rao I lived as his troops did, sharing their food and sometimes going without for two or three days when they did.
pest-hungary: Pest lies on the eastern bank of the Danube and makes up about two thirds of the area of Budapest. It is flatter and much more heavily urbanised than Buda across the river. According to Ptolemy the settlement was called Pession in antiquity, and its official Roman name was Contra-Aquincum, after the Roman town of Aquincum on the opposite bank, in what became Óbuda. The name Pest may instead come from a Slavic word meaning furnace or oven, probably referring to a local cave where fire burned. The spelling Pesth was used in English as late as the early 20th century.

Pest began as a Celtic settlement and then became a fortified Roman camp, Contra-Aquincum, facing the military border camp at Aquincum. Remains of the Roman camp can still be seen at Március 15. tér. In the Middle Ages Pest was an independent city, separate from Buda, which became an important economic centre between the 11th and 13th centuries. Its first written mention dates from 1148.

The Mongol invasion of Hungary destroyed Pest in 1241, but it was rebuilt soon afterwards. In the 15th century Pest was mostly Hungarian, while Buda had a German-majority population. In 1838 the Danube flooded the city, with parts under as much as eight feet of water, and the flood destroyed or badly damaged three quarters of its buildings. The first permanent bridge between Pest and Buda, the Széchenyi Chain Bridge, was built in 1849, and in 1873 the two cities were unified with Óbuda as Budapest.

Many of the best-known sites of Budapest lie in Pest: the Inner City, the Parliament, the Opera, the Great Market Hall, Heroes' Square and Andrássy Avenue. In colloquial Hungarian the name Pest is sometimes used for the whole of Budapest. Pest was the birthplace of the writer and statesman László Teleki, the painter Henrik Weber, Theodor Herzl, founder of the political Zionist movement, and the illusionist Harry Houdini.
petar-i-petrovic-njegos: Petar was the son of Marko and Anđelija, née Martinović, and like others of his family became a monk and a deacon. He spent four years in Imperial Russia, finishing the Military School he entered in 1765. After the death of Metropolitan Sava Petrović in 1781, Sava's chosen successor Arsenije Plamenac held the office with little power, while the guvernadur family of Radonjić, with Venetian and then Austrian support, sought to push the Petrović metropolitans aside. The chieftains proposed Petar for the bishop's seat, and he was ordained by Mojsije Putnik at Sremski Karlovci on 13 October 1784.

Petar shared the leadership with guvernadur Jovan Radonjić, who wanted secular power for himself and leaned on Austria, while the metropolitan held to Russia. In 1785, while Petar was abroad, Kara Mahmud Pasha of Scutari invaded and burnt Njeguši. In 1796 Petar and Radonjić each led half of the Montenegrin army, and after the battle at Martinići they defeated the pasha's larger army at Krusi on 22 September, where he was killed; the Bjelopavlići and Piperi tribes then joined the state. In 1797 Petar ended a 32-year blood feud between the Njeguši and the Ceklin, and in 1798 he introduced Montenegro's first laws.

During the First Serbian Uprising he worked with the rebel leader Karađorđe, and in 1807 he proposed to the Russian court a revived Serbian empire uniting Montenegro with Bosnia, Herzegovina, the Bay of Kotor and Dalmatia under the Russian emperor. In 1806 his army, with Russian troops and Admiral Dmitry Senyavin's fleet, drove the French from the Bay of Kotor back to Dubrovnik, but the Treaty of Tilsit gave the bay to France. He later refused a French offer to make him patriarch of the Serbs in exchange for a French protectorate, and waged a successful campaign against the Bosnia Eyalet in 1819.

Petar died on 31 October 1830. His long rule had united quarrelling tribes and prepared the way for taxes, schools and larger commercial enterprises; the state came to be called Montenegro and the Hills. His successor Petar II Petrović-Njegoš canonised him as Saint Peter of Cetinje, and the Serbian Orthodox Church celebrates him on 31 October. He also wrote verse and a Short History of Montenegro.
petar-ii-petrovic-njegos: He was born Radivoje Petrović in the mountain village of Njeguši, near Cetinje, to a family of the Petrović clan, and became the spiritual and political leader of Montenegro after the death of his uncle Petar I. In 1833 he travelled to Saint Petersburg, where he was consecrated despite being under the canonical age of thirty, and Emperor Nicholas I granted him 36,000 rubles. Russia also pressed for a Governing Senate in 1832 to regulate the powers of the vladika.

His taxation policies were unpopular with the tribes and caused several revolts. To strengthen the Petrović name he arranged the canonization of Petar I in October 1834. He enlarged the Perjanici and the Gvardija, built roads, artesian wells and two gunpowder factories at Rijeka Crnojevića, and introduced the Obilić Medal for Valour. A defeat at Podgorica in 1832 and the Ottoman invasion of 1843 under Osman Pasha showed how hard it was to resist the Ottoman Empire.

Njegoš began writing poetry at seventeen, drawing on Serb folklore, lyric poetry and biblical stories. His works include The Voice of a Stone-Cutter (1833), The Ray of the Microcosm (1845), The Mountain Wreath (1847) and The False Tsar Stephen the Little (1851), which are all epic poems. The Mountain Wreath was seen after his death as the Montenegrin national epic and, for Serbs, evoked the Kosovo epics. Gavrilo Princip knew it by heart.

He met the language reformer Vuk Stefanović Karadžić in Vienna, and his travels brought him into contact with ideas of South Slav unity. In 1848 he corresponded with Prince Aleksandar of Serbia and Ilija Garašanin; they agreed that, in a unified Serbian state, Aleksandar would be hereditary secular leader and Njegoš Patriarch of a unified Serbian Orthodox Church.

By 1849 Njegoš had tuberculosis. He travelled to Italy in 1850 and again in January 1851, visiting Venice, Milan, Genoa, Rome and Pompeii, and died in October 1851. He was first buried at the Cetinje Monastery, and in 1855 his remains were moved to the chapel on Mount Lovćen that he had designed and had built in 1845. In 1916 the Austro-Hungarian occupiers had them returned to Cetinje; the chapel was reconstructed and he was reburied there in September 1925.
petar-kresimir-iv: Peter Krešimir was one of two children of King Stephen I of Croatia and his wife Hicela, daughter of the Venetian Doge Pietro II Orseolo. He succeeded his father in 1058 and was crowned the next year, at an unknown place; some historians suggest Biograd. He was the last ruler of the Krešimirović branch of the Trpimirović dynasty.

Pope Nicholas II wrote to him in 1059 and again in 1060, asking him to reform the Croatian church according to the Roman rite, which mattered to the papacy after the Great Schism of 1054. At a church sabor in Split in 1061 Krešimir and the upper nobility backed the pope. The reforms struck the Glagolitic priesthood, who used Slavonic rather than Latin, and a revolt led by Cededa, bishop of Krk, and a priest named Vuk was declared heretical in 1064. Krešimir supported its excommunication and harshly quelled the opposition.

He relied on the income of the cities and fostered Biograd, Nin, Šibenik, Karin and Skradin, which is first mentioned in 1066. He built Benedictine monasteries at Biograd and in 1066 granted a charter to the new monastery of St Mary in Zadar, founded by his cousin, the abbess Čika. In 1067 Ulric I, Margrave of Carniola, occupied part of Kvarner and the east coast of Istria, and his ban Demetrius Zvonimir later liberated them. In 1069 the Byzantine Empire recognised him as supreme ruler of the Theme of Dalmatia, and he held the lands together as the regnum Dalmatiae et Chroatia.

In 1074 the Normans of southern Italy, invited by the Dalmatian coastal cities and by Byzantium, invaded Dalmatia and held Split, Trogir, Biograd and Zadar from 19 March for almost a year. Count Amico of Giovinazzo besieged Rab for almost a month without success, took Cres on 9 May, and captured the Croatian king. A church sabor at Split in November 1074 is the last to mention him, and he seems to have died in a Norman prison. He had named Demetrius Zvonimir as heir. Venice expelled the Normans in February 1075. Krešimir was buried in the church of St Stephen at Salona, which the Ottoman Turks later destroyed.
petar-snacic: Almost nothing certain is known of Petar's life before he claimed the throne. The only reliable mention of him comes from the 13th-century Hungarian chronicle Gesta Hunnorum et Hungarorum by Simon of Kéza, and it is unknown whether he was ever crowned. It is assumed that he had served as a ban under King Demetrius Zvonimir of Croatia. A 14th-century note in the Supetar Cartulary names a ban of Zvonimir's time called Petar of the Snačić family, but it is not reliable enough to identify the king with him; the name Svačić or Snačić became accepted largely through a misreading by the historian Franjo Rački.

Ferdo Šišić's identification of Petar with Petar Slaven, another ban, is also judged unsuccessful. The Croatian historian Mladen Ančić holds that all these men named Petar were probably one person, while Neven Budak calls him possibly a former ban of the Snačić kindred.

The crisis began when King Stephen II, the last of the Trpimirović dynasty, died without an heir. Jelena, the widow of Zvonimir, backed her brother, King Ladislaus I of Hungary, who invaded Croatia in 1091 and met resistance only at the mountain Gvozd, fighting the local nobility as far as northern Dalmatia. Part of the Croatian nobility and clergy rejected his claim and turned to rivals of their own: first the dux Simeon, then King Slavac and finally Petar, who probably ruled only central Croatia from his seat at Knin.

Ladislaus died in 1095, leaving his nephew Coloman to continue the campaign. In 1097 Petar marched from Knin to meet him and was killed in the battle. According to the Pacta conventa, whose authenticity is debated, the Croats then recognised Coloman as king, and he promised self-government under a ban and respect for the kingdom's rights, laws and privileges. The personal union with the Kingdom of Hungary that followed lasted until 1918.
pete-seeger: Peter Seeger was born on 3 May 1919 in Manhattan. His father, Charles Louis Seeger Jr., a composer and musicologist, established the first musicology curriculum in the United States at the University of California, Berkeley, and helped found the discipline of ethnomusicology. His mother, Constance de Clyver Seeger, was a concert violinist who later taught at the Juilliard School.

His parents did not press him to play an instrument, and he took up the ukulele on his own. In the summer of 1935 he heard the five-string banjo for the first time at a folk festival near Asheville, North Carolina. In 1936 he joined the Young Communist League, and in 1942 he joined the Communist Party USA, which he left in 1949.

In 1941 Seeger co-founded the Almanac Singers with Millard Lampell and Lee Hays, a topical group that was meant to act as a singing newspaper for industrial unionisation and other progressive causes. He later co-founded the Weavers, and in 1943 he recorded the album Songs of the Lincoln Battalion in support of the republican side in the Spanish Civil War. In 1948 he wrote How to Play the Five-String Banjo, which sold over 100,000 copies in its 1962 edition, and he devised the long-neck Seeger banjo.

During the blacklist years of the late 1950s and early 1960s he earned money teaching music in schools and summer camps and touring colleges, and he recorded as many as five albums a year for Folkways Records. His songs against war, including Where Have All the Flowers Gone?, written with Joe Hickerson, and Turn! Turn! Turn!, adapted from Ecclesiastes, won wide currency. In 1963 he helped organise a Carnegie Hall concert for the Highlander Folk School, and he sang We Shall Overcome on the walk from Selma to Montgomery. In 1966 he and his wife Toshi founded the Hudson River Sloop Clearwater, which works to protect the Hudson River.

Seeger died on 27 January 2014. He said that it was he who changed the words of We Shall Overcome from the traditional we will overcome to the more singable we shall. He coined the phrase Woody's children for the new generation of politically committed folk singers, and the Byrds had a number one hit with Turn! Turn! Turn! in 1965. His championing of the five-string banjo helped make it known across the United States as an American folk instrument, where it had once been largely limited to Appalachia.
peter-behrens: Peter Behrens studied painting in his native Hamburg, in Düsseldorf and in Karlsruhe from 1886 to 1889. In 1890 he married Lilly Kramer and moved to Munich, where he worked at first as a painter, illustrator and bookbinder in an artisanal manner. He moved in bohemian circles interested in the reform of lifestyles, and the Munich Secession, in which young artists called for art that reflected modern German life, formed part of his background. In 1899 Grand Duke Ernst Ludwig of Hesse invited him to the recently founded Darmstadt Artists' Colony.

At Darmstadt he designed everything in his Jugendstil house of 1901, from furniture to towels and pottery, and the project is regarded as the turning point of his life, since it showed him a talented architect in his first building. In 1903 he became director of the Kunstgewerbeschule in Düsseldorf, where he reformed the teaching of design. In 1907 he was one of the founders of the German Werkbund, which aimed to raise the level of taste in Germany by improving everyday objects and products.

In 1907 the electrical firm AEG retained him as artistic consultant. He designed its logotype, products and publicity, which is why he is considered the first industrial designer, and a series of factories in Berlin, above all the Turbine Factory of 1909. His growing office trained assistants who became leading modernists: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, Le Corbusier, Adolf Meyer, Jean Kramer and Walter Gropius. He also designed the German Embassy in St Petersburg in 1912 and the administration building for Continental AG in Hannover, built in 1912 to 1914.

After the First World War he turned to Brick Expressionism in the Technical Administration Building of Hoechst AG outside Frankfurt, built between 1920 and 1924. From 1922 to 1936 he headed the architecture school at the Academy of Fine Arts Vienna. His house New Ways in Northampton, designed in 1926 for Wenman Joseph Bassett-Lowke, is often regarded as probably the first modernist house in Britain, and he later worked in the style of New Objectivity, as in the tobacco factory at Linz, completed in 1935.

In 1936 Behrens left Vienna to teach at the Prussian Academy of Arts in Berlin, reportedly with Hitler's approval, and took part in plans for the rebuilding of Berlin, receiving the commission for the new AEG headquarters on Albert Speer's planned axis. He died at the Hotel Bristol in Berlin on 27 February 1940, where he had sought refuge from his country estate. He also designed three typefaces for the Klingspor Type Foundry.
peter-canisius: Peter Canisius, in Dutch Pieter Kanis, was born in 1521 at Nijmegen in the Duchy of Guelders, the son of a wealthy burgomaster, Jacob Kanis. His mother, Ægidia van Houweningen, died shortly after his birth. He studied at the University of Cologne and took a master's degree in 1540, at the age of 19. There he met Peter Faber, one of the founders of the Society of Jesus, and in 1543 he became the first Dutchman to join the Jesuits. He was ordained in 1546.

Canisius attended several sessions of the Council of Trent in 1547 and became an influential preacher and teacher in the German-speaking lands. He supervised the founding and upkeep of the first German-speaking Jesuit colleges, often with few resources. In 1554 he was offered the see of Vienna but declined, serving only as administrator of the diocese for a year. He was one of the main Catholic theologians at the Colloquy of Worms in 1557 and main preacher in the Cathedral of Augsburg from 1559 to 1568. In 1562 he founded what became the University of Innsbruck.

His lasting contribution is three catechisms, published in Latin and German, which defined the basic principles of Catholicism in the German language and spread widely in Catholic regions. He urged Rome to be more flexible with German Protestants, arguing that an honest explanation of the faith would be more effective than a polemical attack, and he rejected attacks on John Calvin and Philip Melanchthon. He also wrote on the Virgin Mary, in a book of 1577 ordered by Pope Pius V.

For the last twenty years of his life Canisius lived in Fribourg, where he founded the Jesuit Collège Saint-Michel. In 1591, at the age of 70, he suffered a stroke that left him partly paralysed, but he went on preaching and writing with the help of a secretary until his death in Fribourg on 21 December 1597.

He was beatified by Pope Pius IX in 1864 and canonised and declared a Doctor of the Church by Pope Pius XI on 21 May 1925. From the mid-19th century German churchmen, among them Michael Cardinal von Faulhaber, regarded him as a new Apostle of Germany, a successor of Saint Boniface. Schools and colleges in Vienna, Nijmegen, Buffalo, Berlin and Jakarta are named after him.
peter-claver: Claver was born on 26 June 1580 in Verdú in Urgell, into a devoutly Catholic and prosperous farming family. As a student at the University of Barcelona he was noted for intelligence and piety, and after two years he wrote in his notebook that he must dedicate himself to the service of God until death, on the understanding that he was like a slave. He entered the Society of Jesus at Tarragona at the age of 20 and studied philosophy at Palma on Mallorca, where the college porter Alphonsus Rodriguez urged him to serve in the colonies.

Claver arrived at Cartagena in 1615 to work under the missionary Alonso de Sandoval, and spent six years studying theology at Tunja and Bogotá before ordination. Cartagena was a slave-trading hub, and some 10,000 enslaved people reached the port each year; an estimated one third died on the crossing from West Africa. When he was solemnly professed in 1622 he signed himself in Latin as the servant of the Ethiopians, meaning Africans, forever.

Claver met the slave ships as they arrived, bringing fruit, water and tobacco, and nursed the sick and injured. With African translators he taught the catechism in Spanish and in the captives' own languages together, used memory aids so that the enslaved could recall the sacraments, and learned the language of Angola himself.

He urged the enslaved to marry in the Church and condemned their ritual dances as superstition. In seasons when fewer ships called he visited plantations and lived in the slaves' quarters. He also ministered to merchants, to Muslims and English Protestants in the city, and to condemned criminals. He is estimated to have baptised about 300,000 people.

In his last years Claver was too ill to leave his room and was neglected, and by one account mistreated by an ex-slave hired to care for him. He died on 8 September 1654 and was given a large public funeral. Pope Leo XIII canonised him in 1888, together with Rodriguez, and in 1896 named him patron of missionary work among all African peoples. His body lies in the Jesuit church at Cartagena that bears his name, and Colombia's Congress declared 9 September a national day of human rights in his honour.

His canonisation drew unease, since he himself held slaves; the sources describe his treatment of them as uncommonly mild, though the scholar Katie Grimes argues that honouring him as the saint of the slave trade upholds anti-blackness.
peter-constable-of-portugal: Peter was the eldest son of Infante Peter, Duke of Coimbra, and Isabella of Urgell. His father governed Portugal as regent for Afonso V from 1439 to 1448. Through his maternal grandfather James II, Count of Urgell, the last male descendant of the House of Barcelona, Peter inherited a claim to the throne of Aragon.

In 1443, after the death of his cousin Infante Diogo and at his father's urging, he was made Constable of Portugal, angering Afonso, Marquis of Valença, son of the 1st Duke of Braganza, who believed the title was his. The same year he received the mastership of the Order of Aviz on the death of his uncle Ferdinand.

When Afonso V came of age in 1448, the Duke of Braganza's influence led the king to void the laws of the regency, and Peter lost both the constableship and the mastership. The quarrel ended at the Battle of Alfarrobeira, where his father died. His siblings went to their aunt Isabella in Burgundy, but Peter fled to Castile. Exile was his main period as a writer: a disciple of Rodríguez de Padrón, he completed the Satira de Infelice e Felice Vida and the Tragédia de la insigne reina doña Isabel, among the earliest examples of sentimental fiction. Reconciled with the king and the Duke of Braganza in 1456 or 1457, he recovered his family's possessions and joined Afonso's expeditions to northern Africa.

The Catalan institutions at war with John II of Aragon offered him their crown in 1463, and the Consell de Cent crowned him King of Aragon, Count of Barcelona and King of Valencia. He ruled in fact over Barcelona, most of Catalonia and parts of Aragon, but Valencia, held by John II, only in name; his status as king is disputed. With the support of his aunt Isabella, Duchess of Burgundy, he became engaged to Margaret of York, who later married Charles the Bold. After an ineffectual reign he died of natural causes on 30 June 1466 and was buried in the Church of Santa Maria del Mar in Barcelona. The Catalans then offered the crown to René of Anjou.
peter-fraser: Fraser was born at Hill of Fearn, near Tain in Easter Ross, and left school early because his family was poor. Apprenticed to a carpenter, he gave up the trade because of very poor eyesight, and later in life he asked for spoken rather than written reports. He read socialists such as Keir Hardie and Robert Blatchford, became secretary of the local Liberal Association at 16 and joined the Independent Labour Party in London in 1908. Unable to find work there, he emigrated to New Zealand in 1910.

In Auckland he worked on the wharves, joined the New Zealand Socialist Party and managed the campaign of Michael Joseph Savage. After an arrest for breaches of the peace in 1913 he turned from direct action to the parliamentary road. He helped found the Labour Party in 1916 and later that year was jailed for a year for sedition after opposing conscription, a verdict he always rejected. Elected for Wellington Central in 1918, he came to reject the Bolshevik leaders and pressed for communists to be kept out of the party. In 1923 he lost the Wellington mayoralty by only 273 votes.

In Savage's cabinet from 1935 he held external affairs, health, education and other portfolios, often working seventeen hours a day, and named C. E. Beeby to the Education Department. As prime minister he introduced conscription, which he had opposed in the First World War, and some called his style authoritarian. In 1943 he brought 6,000 battle-weary soldiers home on furlough, and many refused to return. He signed the Australian-New Zealand Agreement of 1944 with H. V. Evatt.

Wartime reforms ended flogging in 1941, gave all workers two weeks of annual leave in 1944, raised the school leaving age to 15 and set a minimum wage in 1945. At the San Francisco conference of 1945 he opposed the veto of the permanent members of the Security Council and often spoke for smaller states. His government adopted the Statute of Westminster in 1947, but slow removal of rationing and peacetime compulsory military training cost it support. He died in Wellington on 12 December 1950 and is buried in Karori Cemetery.
peter-i-duke-of-brittany: Peter was the second son of Robert II, Count of Dreux, and Yolande de Coucy, and through his grandfather Robert I of Dreux, a younger brother of Louis VII, a second cousin of Louis VIII of France. As a younger son of a cadet branch he could expect only a few scattered fiefs in the Île-de-France and Champagne. He was destined for a career in the clergy but gave it up, which is the origin of the name Mauclerc, the bad cleric.

In 1212 King Philip II wanted a weak and loyal ruler for Brittany, which lay across the sea lanes between England and Gascony and bordered Anjou and Normandy. He broke off the betrothal of the heiress Alix to the Breton lord Henry of Penthièvre and gave her to Peter, who did homage for Brittany on 27 January 1213. The king and the Pope called him count; in his own charters he called himself duke.

In 1214 Peter drove King John of England away from Nantes, though he did not harass John's march up the Loire, perhaps by some agreement between them. A constant aim of his was the English Earldom of Richmond, and after the peace of 1218 the regent William Marshal recognised him as earl, with the estates outside Yorkshire. At home he imposed new rules on his barons by decree, crushed a baronial revolt at the Battle of Châteaubriant in 1222, and was excommunicated in 1219–1221 for seizing the revenues and holdings of the six Breton bishops.

Alix died on 21 October 1221, and Peter ruled on as regent for their son John. He served Louis VIII at Niort and La Rochelle in 1224 and on the Albigensian Crusade, then joined Theobald IV of Champagne and Hugh X of La Marche in the risings against Blanche of Castile from 1227 to 1234. In 1235 he renounced his allegiance to Henry III and lost Richmond.

After John came of age in 1237, Peter went on the Barons' Crusade of 1239, defeating Mamluk horsemen near Jaffa and, with Ralph of Soissons, raiding a Muslim caravan on its way to Damascus. Back in France he won some success against the English at sea in 1242 and 1243. He joined the Seventh Crusade to Egypt in 1249 and died at sea on the way home on 26 May 1250. He was buried at Braine.
peter-ii-count-of-savoy: Peter was born around 1203, possibly at Susa in Piedmont, probably the seventh child of Thomas I, Count of Savoy, and Margaret of Geneva. As a younger son he began in the church, serving from 1226 to 1233 as a canon at Lausanne, where he was briefly acting bishop, before he left church life in 1234. After his father died he demanded a substantial share of the county from his eldest brother Amadeus, and at Chillon in 1234 they agreed a settlement that recognised Amadeus as head of the house and gave Peter the castles of Cornillon and Angeville. His marriage to Agnes of Faucigny in 1236 brought him territory and influence in Faucigny and the Free County of Burgundy.

Peter's conflict with his uncle William II of Geneva ended in 1237 with a treaty obliging Geneva to pay 20,000 marks and give up the castle of Arlod. In 1244 Rudolph III, Count of Gruyère, surrendered Gruyères Castle to him. He gained key towns and trade routes in the Pays de Vaud, rebuilt much of the Château de Chillon, and by 1253 was protector of Bern. One scholar suggests that his conquests partly explain why French is the language of western Switzerland.

In January 1236 his niece Eleanor of Provence married Henry III of England, and Peter went to England with other Savoyards. Henry gave him the Honour of Richmond in 1240 and knighted him on 5 January 1241; he was popularly called Earl of Richmond but never took the title. He also held the Honour of Eu and the wardship of John de Warenne, 6th Earl of Surrey, with much land in Sussex, and was granted land on the Strand by the Thames, where he built the Savoy Palace, destroyed in the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. In 1258 he joined the barons who swore to support reform, but broke with them in 1260 when Simon de Montfort had him removed from the ruling council.

When his nephew Boniface, Count of Savoy, died without heirs in 1263, Peter returned and was recognised as count over Thomas III of Piedmont, a dispute that outlasted both men. He built rounder castles, divided the county into bailis and castellanies, set up an office of accounts at Chambéry and was the first count to issue laws for the whole county. Peter died without a male heir on 15 May 1268 at Pierre-Châtel and was buried at Hautecombe Abbey. His brother Philip succeeded him, and his will left his English lands to Eleanor of Provence.
peter-ii-duke-of-bourbon: Peter was born on 1 December 1438, a son of Charles I, Duke of Bourbon, and Agnes of Burgundy. He was first betrothed to Marie d'Orleans, sister of Louis, Duke of Orleans, the future Louis XII, but King Louis XI broke the engagement to prevent an alliance between two great feudal houses of France. Instead Peter married the king's elder daughter, Anne, on 3 November 1473. As a mark of favour Louis XI made Peter's older brother John II, Duke of Bourbon, grant him the fief of Beaujeu, and gave him a seat on the royal council.

Peter was one of the few royal servants who kept Louis XI's favour throughout his reign, and on his deathbed in 1483 the king gave him guardianship of the new king, Charles VIII. Peter and Anne took up their duties at once, and the young king, though he ruled in name, was in practice guided by the couple. In 1488 the death of John II and the enforced renunciation of the next brother, Charles II, gave Peter the Bourbon inheritance: the Duchies of Bourbon and Auvergne and the Counties of Forez and l'Isle-en-Jordain.

The couple added Bourbon-Lancy in December 1488 and in June 1489 traded l'Isle-en-Jordain with the Armagnacs for Murat and the viscountcy of Carlat, holding these lands in absolute right. By 1491 their influence was waning. Charles VIII renounced his marriage to Margaret of Austria to marry Anne, Duchess of Brittany, against their advice, and they could not prevent his Italian expeditions, though both were left in control of France during several of his absences.

Their daughter Suzanne was born on 10 May 1491, and with no surviving son Peter's last years turned on her marriage. He broke with the heir Louis of Bourbon-Montpensier, who had condemned letters patent confirming Suzanne's rights, and on 21 March 1501 at Moulins betrothed her, then nine, to Charles IV, Duke of Alençon, a favourite of Louis XII. Peter died of a fever at Moulins on 10 October 1503 before the marriage took place. Anne then married Suzanne to Charles of Bourbon-Montpensier, the next heir in the male line, averting a dispute over the inheritance.
peter-ii-of-aragon: Peter was born in Huesca in July 1178, the son of Alfonso II of Aragon and Sancha of Castile. In 1205 he acknowledged the feudal supremacy of the papacy and was crowned in Rome by Pope Innocent III, swearing to defend the Catholic faith, which gave him his epithet, the Catholic. He was the first king of Aragon to be crowned by the pope. In the first decade of the thirteenth century he commissioned the Liber feudorum Ceritaniae, an illustrated codex cartulary for the counties of Cerdagne, Conflent and Roussillon.

On 15 June 1204 Peter married Marie of Montpellier, daughter and heiress of William VIII of Montpellier, as her third husband. She gave him a son, James, but Peter soon repudiated her. Marie was popularly venerated as a saint for her piety and marital suffering, though she was never canonised, and she died in Rome in 1213.

Peter took part in the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212, which marked the turning point of Muslim domination in the Iberian peninsula. The Crown of Aragon was widespread in the area that is now south-western France, then under the control of vassal princes such as the counts of Toulouse. Pope Innocent III had called on Philip II of France to suppress the Cathars, who rejected the authority and teachings of the Catholic Church, and the Albigensian Crusade under Simon de Montfort began in 1209. It killed about 20,000 men, women and children, Cathar and Catholic alike.

Returning from Las Navas in autumn 1212, Peter found that Montfort had conquered Toulouse and exiled Count Raymond VI, his brother-in-law and vassal. He crossed the Pyrenees and reached Muret in September 1213. Raymond urged him to avoid battle and starve out Montfort's forces, but the suggestion was rejected. The Battle of Muret began on 12 September 1213. The Aragonese forces were disorganised and gave way under Montfort's assault, and Peter, caught in the thick of the fighting, was thrown to the ground and killed. His army broke in panic.

The conflict ended with the Treaty of Meaux-Paris in 1229, which agreed the integration of the Occitan territory into the French crown. Peter's kingdom passed to his only son by Marie of Montpellier, the future James the Conqueror.
peter-ii-of-cyprus: Peter, called the Fat, was the son of Peter I of Cyprus and Eleanor of Aragon, and the eleventh king of Cyprus of the House of Lusignan. He was declared king on 17 January 1369, but as he was still a minor his uncle John of Lusignan, Prince of Antioch, ruled as regent. Eleanor believed John had been involved in her husband's murder and secretly asked European powers for military help to punish the killers. The Genoese answered, seeing a chance to gain power in Cyprus.

Peter was crowned king of Cyprus in the Cathedral of St Sophia in Nicosia on 6 January 1372 and king of Jerusalem in the Cathedral of St Nicholas in Famagusta on 10 October. The quarrel over which community should hold the right rein of the royal horse spread from the feast into the streets, and the Genoese were blamed and arrested. Genoa sent an expedition under Peter di Campofregoso, brother of the doge. To gather his forces, Peter gave up Antalya, taken by his father, to Emir Teke. He left the resistance to his uncles John and James; Famagusta let the Genoese in, supposedly for negotiations, and the king and his mother were taken prisoner.

The Genoese attacked Limassol and Paphos and entered Nicosia, while John and James held out at Saint Hilarion Castle and Kyrenia. The settlement Peter was forced to accept also required James to leave Cyprus, and the Genoese arrested him on his way. Before leaving they executed those accused of the murder of Peter I, and in 1375 Eleanor had Prince John killed. After her conflicts with Peter's wife, Valentina Visconti, daughter of Bernabò Visconti of Milan, whom he had married by proxy in 1376, the king sent Eleanor back to Castile in 1378.

Peter made peace with the Sultan of Egypt, improved the fortifications of Nicosia and built a royal villa at Potamia. His reign saw the decline of the kingdom: the loss of its possessions in Asia Minor and of Famagusta, its chief harbour, which then declined. He died on 13 October 1382 at the Palace of La Cava in Nicosia and was buried at St Dominic's. His only daughter had died in infancy, and his uncle succeeded him as James I.
peter-ii-of-yugoslavia: Peter was born on 6 September 1923 in Belgrade, the eldest son of Alexander I of Yugoslavia and Maria of Romania. His godparents included King George V of the United Kingdom, for whom the Duke of York stood proxy. He was tutored at the Royal Palace and then attended Sandroyd School in Surrey. On 9 October 1934, at the age of eleven, he succeeded to the throne after his father was assassinated in Marseille during a state visit to France, and a regency was set up under his father's cousin Prince Paul.

Paul held that he must hand the kingdom to Peter unaltered when he turned eighteen, and he resisted attempts to revise the 1931 constitution. On 20 August 1939 he did allow an agreement between the prime minister Dragiša Cvetković and Vladko Maček of the Croatian Peasant Party, which created a Banovina of Croatia with substantial autonomy. It was very unpopular with the Serbs.

Prince Paul declared on 25 March 1941 that Yugoslavia would join the Tripartite Pact. Two days later General Dušan Simović led a pro-British coup in the name of the seventeen-year-old Peter, who climbed down a drain-pipe to greet the rebels. Simović saluted him as king, and the crowds in Belgrade cheered him. Germany attacked on 6 April 1941; the Luftwaffe bombed Belgrade, killing between 3,000 and 4,000 people, and the government surrendered on 17 April. Italy, Bulgaria, Hungary and Germany annexed parts of the country, and the rest was governed by two German-controlled puppet governments.

Peter reached London in June 1941, where a government-in-exile was set up. His engagement to Princess Alexandra of Greece and Denmark, announced in July 1943, caused controversy at home, since Serbian tradition held that a leader must not marry during a national emergency. He dismissed the prime minister Slobodan Jovanović, who opposed the announcement. The couple married in March 1944.

In November 1944 the prime minister Šubašić agreed with Stalin that Peter would not return until a plebiscite was held, and that a three-man regency council would govern meanwhile; Peter objected that he was twenty-one and needed no regent. The Constituent Assembly, elected on 11 November 1945 amid reported fraud and intimidation, deposed him on 29 November 1945 and proclaimed a republic. Peter settled in the United States and lived much of his exile in the Chicago area.

He suffered from depression and alcoholism, and developed cirrhosis of the liver. He died in Denver on 3 November 1970 after a failed liver transplant and was buried at the Saint Sava Monastery Church in Libertyville, Illinois. His remains were returned to Belgrade on 22 January 2013 and buried at Oplenac on 26 May 2013.
peter-iii-of-aragon: Peter was the eldest son of James I of Aragon and his second wife Violant of Hungary. On 13 June 1262 he married Constance II of Sicily, daughter and heiress of Manfred of Sicily, and he gained military experience in his father's wars against the Moors. When James died in 1276 the Crown's lands were divided: Peter received the Kingdom of Aragon, the Kingdom of Valencia and the Principality of Catalonia, while his younger brother became James II of Majorca. Peter and Constance were crowned at Zaragoza in November 1276.

Peter's early years as king brought revolt in Catalonia, led by the viscount of Cardona and backed by several counts, who resented his severity under his father and his failure to summon the General Court of Catalonia. In 1280 he besieged the rebels at Balaguer for a month and defeated them. Abroad, he prepared a fleet of 140 ships with 15,000 men to invade Tunisia. After the Sicilian Vespers, the uprising against Charles I of Anjou on 30 March 1282, a Sicilian embassy asked him to take the throne, which he claimed through Constance. He landed at Trapani on 30 August 1282 and was proclaimed king in Palermo on 4 September. Pope Martin IV excommunicated him.

His admiral Roger of Lauria defeated the French at the Battle of Malta and in the Gulf of Naples in 1284, where Charles of Salerno was taken prisoner. Peter and Charles agreed to settle their quarrel by a duel at Bordeaux, which never took place. At home he faced the Union of Aragon and was forced to grant the Privilegio General, and he took Albarracín from the noble Juan Núñez de Lara. In 1284 Pope Martin IV granted Aragon to Charles of Valois and sanctioned a crusade, and a large French army entered Roussillon, took Girona in 1285, but then lost its fleet to Roger of Lauria at Les Formigues on 4 September and was struck by dysentery. Philip III of France died in October.

Peter died at Vilafranca del Penedès in November 1285, one month after Philip III, and was buried at the Monastery of Santes Creus. In his will of 2 November 1285 he told his successor to return Sicily to the pope and release Angevin prisoners, but his successors ignored it: Alfonso III inherited Aragon, James II received Sicily and Frederick later succeeded James there. The kingdom was to remain a tenaciously pursued inheritance of the Aragonese royal house for five centuries. Peter was a patron of troubadours and wrote two sirventesos himself, and Dante placed him in Purgatory singing in accord with his former rival Charles I of Anjou.
peter-iii-of-russia: Peter was born on 21 February 1728 at Kiel in the duchy of Holstein-Gottorp, the son of Duke Charles Frederick and Grand Duchess Anna Petrovna, a daughter of Peter the Great. His mother died a few weeks after his birth and his father in 1739, and he became Duke of Holstein-Gottorp at eleven. His maternal aunt Elizabeth, Empress of Russia, proclaimed him her heir presumptive in 1742. He converted to Orthodoxy that November, which disqualified him from the Swedish throne. Elizabeth arranged his marriage to Sophia of Anhalt-Zerbst, who took the name Catherine, on 21 August 1745. Their son was the future Paul I.

Peter became emperor on 5 January 1762 and in 186 days of government passed 220 new laws. He exempted nobles from compulsory service in peacetime, forbade landowners from murdering peasants on pain of lifelong exile, ended the persecution of the Old Believers and abolished the Secret Chancellery. He issued a manifesto on secularising church lands, which Catherine later began to carry out, and founded Russia's first state bank.

He withdrew Russia from the Seven Years' War, signed a peace with Prussia on 5 May 1762 and gave up Russian conquests in Prussia. He also planned a war against Denmark-Norway to recover parts of Schleswig for Holstein. Many in the army and at court feared further concessions to Prussia, and in spring 1762 Catherine, with Grigory Orlov and others, began plotting against him.

On 28 June 1762 [O.S.] Catherine marched to the Winter Palace and was proclaimed ruler. Peter tried to reach Kronstadt by boat but was turned back, and he was arrested and forced to abdicate. He was taken to Ropsha, where he died. The official cause was a severe attack of colic and an apoplectic stroke, while others say he was assassinated.

Catherine's memoirs describe him as an idiot, a view repeated in older histories, while the historian Elena Palmer portrays him as an open-minded reformer. Several pretenders claimed to be Peter, the best known being Yemelyan Pugachev, who led a rebellion in 1774. In December 1796 Paul I had his remains reburied in the Peter and Paul Cathedral.
peter-iv-of-aragon: Peter IV (Catalan: Pere IV d'Aragó) was born on 5 September 1319 at Balaguer, the eldest son of Alfons IV, then Count of Urgell, and his first wife, Teresa d'Entença. He inherited all his father's titles except Urgell, which went to his younger brother James. On succeeding he called a corts at Zaragoza for his coronation and crowned himself, disappointing the Archbishop of Zaragoza and rejecting the surrender Peter II had made to the papacy. He then stopped at Lleida to affirm the Usatges and Constitutions of Catalonia, which offended Barcelona, where the ceremony had usually been performed. In 1338 he married Maria, daughter of Philip III and Joan II of Navarre.

Peter was from 1336 king of Aragon, Sardinia-Corsica and Valencia and count of Barcelona. His reign was occupied with strengthening the crown against the Union of Aragon and other devices of the nobility, and with wars in Sardinia, Sicily, the Mezzogiorno, Greece and the Balearics. He took Majorca from his brother-in-law James III after declaring him a contumacious vassal in February 1343. His fleet landed in May, James's army was defeated at the Battle of Santa Ponça, and Peter had himself crowned king of Majorca in 1344.

His quarrels with the Union were violent. In Valencia he was held under guard by the Union, and he and his queen were forced to dance with the common folk to show his subservience. The Black Death struck Valencia in May 1348 and enabled him to escape. At the Battle of Epila on 21 July 1348 he defeated the unionist forces, executed thirteen Union leaders at Zaragoza, and had the bell that summoned the Valencian Union melted and poured down the throats of its leaders. In 1356 he began the War of the Two Peters with Peter I of Castile, which ended in 1375 with the Treaty of Almazan and no winner.

Peter's wars in Greece made him Duke of Athens and Neopatria. At the Catalan Courts of 1358–1359 he instituted the Deputation of the General, or Generalitat, whose first president was Berenguer de Cruïlles, Bishop of Girona. Around 1370 he ordered the compilation of the Chronicle of Sant Joan de la Penya to record the historical basis of the crown's authority. In 1350, in response to the plague, he ordered the mayor of Lleida to build a new Jewish cemetery. He had frequent conflicts with the inquisitor general of Aragon, Nicolas Eymerich. Peter died in Barcelona, aged 67, on 6 January 1387, leaving sons by his third marriage, among them John I and Martin I.
peter-kenilorea: Kenilorea was born on 23 May 1943 in Takataka village on Malaita, of ꞌAreꞌare ethnicity. After school in Malaita and Honiara he won a scholarship to New Zealand, where he attended Wesley College, Whanganui Collegiate School and Ardmore College, training as a teacher at Ardmore. He then taught in Malaita and co-founded the Solomon Islands Christian Association. A founding member of the Solomon Islands United Party, he lost the ꞌAreꞌare seat to David Kausimae in 1973 but won East ꞌAreꞌare in 1976, when the six other potential candidates withdrew for him.

As chief minister he was a leading figure of the independence movement, criticising British rule for failing to advance the country economically and for building only one school, and he took part in the negotiations in London. Prime minister at 35 in a society that associated leadership with elders, he held that traditional leadership could live on among the people while national leadership should rest with the well educated. After the 1980 election the United Party's 16 seats and the 15 of the Independent Group kept him in office, but a motion of no confidence in October 1981 brought in Solomon Mamaloni.

Returning after the 1984 election with 21 members of parliament behind him against 13 for Mamaloni, Kenilorea organised the country's provincial system of government and passed tribal land rights into law. He resigned in 1986 after being implicated in a financial scandal and was succeeded by his deputy, Ezekiel Alebua. He later served as Minister of Foreign Affairs in 1988-1989 and 1990-1993.

During the conflict between the Malaita Eagle Force and the Isatabu Freedom Movement he co-chaired the peace talks of 2000 with Paul Tovua, respected by both groups, and then chaired the Peace Monitoring Council. He was Speaker of Parliament from 2001 to 2010. He died on 24 February 2016 after a period of illness; his body lay in state in the parliament, and his funeral in Honiara on 1 March was a national day of mourning. He is recognised as the founding father of Solomon Islands.
peter-kropotkin: Pyotr Alexeyevich Kropotkin was born in Moscow on 9 December 1842, the youngest of four children. His father, Alexey, was a royal officer who owned serfs in three provinces. His mother died of tuberculosis when he was three, and he and his brother Alexander were raised mostly by their German nurse. In 1862 he chose to serve with the Amur Cossacks in east Siberia, a post that allowed him to travel and become financially independent of his father. There the exiled poet Mikhail Mikhailov introduced him to anarchism by recommending an essay by Pierre-Joseph Proudhon.

In 1872 Kropotkin travelled to Switzerland, where he met the Jura Federation of followers of Mikhail Bakunin and was converted to anarchism. In 1879 he started the fortnightly Le Révolté in Geneva, which published his articulation of anarchist communism, the idea of distributing the product of work by need. In France he was imprisoned for almost four years. He then lived in England until 1917 and co-founded the monthly Freedom in London in late 1886.

In The Conquest of Bread (1892) he proposed an economy of voluntary cooperation in which everyone could take what they needed from the social product. In Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution (1902) he answered the social thinkers who stressed competition by arguing that cooperation made for the success of species. He returned to Russia in June 1917 and refused the Provisional Government's offer of a cabinet seat. He argued with Lenin against the Bolsheviks' hostage policy and centralisation.

Kropotkin died of pneumonia on 8 February 1921. His family refused an offer of a state funeral, and the Bolsheviks permitted a restrained official memorial in Moscow, the last major anarchist demonstration of the period in Russia, since the movement and his writings were suppressed later that year. He had little influence on the Russian Revolution, but his books and pamphlets were the most widely read of anarchist literature and influenced revolutionaries such as Nestor Makhno and Emiliano Zapata.
peter-losha: Pjetër Losha's genealogy and date of birth are unknown. He belonged to the Losha fis, or clan, which according to Aristidh Kola was a branch of the Bua tribe, and he was presumably born in Epirus, where his tribe came from. He led a combined force of his own clan and the Mazaraki and Malakasi fis, and had a son named Gjin. The Chronicle of the Tocco is an important primary source for his life and for the Albanians of medieval Epirus.

Losha took part in the Albanian attacks on what remained of Byzantine Epirus. In 1358–59 the Albanian clans overran the regional feudal rulers and established themselves under Gjin Bua Shpata and Losha, who led the Albanian force against Nikephoros II Orsini at the Battle of Achelous. With the help of the Mazaraki and Malakasi he founded his domain around Arta, which also took in Rogoi, the modern Filippiada, and Amphilochia, as the Chronicle of Ioannina records. In 1360 Simeon Uroš, the titular Serbian emperor, left Arta and Aetolia to Shpata and Losha, seeking to avoid conflict and acknowledging their military strength.

When Toma Preljubović succeeded Simeon as ruler of Epirus in 1366, hostilities resumed. From 1367 to 1370 Ioannina, Preljubović's capital, was under constant siege and blockaded by the Mazaraki and Malakasi under Losha. A truce followed when Losha's son Gjin was betrothed to Preljubović's daughter Irina.
Losha died in 1374 and was succeeded by his close ally Gjin Bua Shpata. Irina died in the plague that struck the region in 1375, and fighting with Ioannina broke out again.
peter-minuit: Peter Minuit was born in Wesel, in what is now northwestern Germany, between 1580 and 1585. His Calvinist family had moved there from Tournai in the Southern Netherlands, then controlled by Spain, to avoid the Catholic authorities. His surname means midnight in French. After his father Johann died in 1609, Peter took over the household and the family business. He married Gertrude Raedts of Cleve on 20 August 1613, and a will drawn up in Utrecht in 1615 names him as a diamond cutter. By 1624 Wesel was in economic decline, and in 1625 he left for Holland.

Minuit joined the Dutch West India Company, probably in the mid-1620s, and went to New Netherland in 1625 to look for tradable goods other than furs. In 1626 he was appointed director, succeeding Willem Verhulst, and reached the colony on 4 May. The sum of 60 guilders for Manhattan comes from a letter of November 1626 by Pieter Janszoon Schagen. The Lenape did not share European ideas of owning land, so the two sides probably understood the agreement differently.

Minuit was the colony's highest judge, assisted by a council of five colonists. During his administration several mills were built, trade grew and the population rose to almost 300. The Company suspended him for reasons that are unclear, probably because he had abetted the landowning patroons in an illegal fur trade. He returned to Europe to explain himself, was dismissed, and was succeeded by Wouter van Twiller.

In 1637 Minuit arranged with Samuel Blommaert and the Swedish government to found the first Swedish colony in the New World, New Sweden, on the lower Delaware River in territory earlier claimed by the Dutch.
