His ships, the Fogel Grip and the Kalmar Nyckel, reached present-day Wilmington, Delaware, on 29 March 1638. He sailed on 20 May to St. Christopher to barter salt and wine for tobacco, and drowned while visiting the Flying Deer, which was lost with all hands in a hurricane near St. Kitts. Swedish colonization was damaged by the loss, and nine expeditions reached the colony before the Dutch captured it in 1655.
peter-ochs: Ochs was born on 20 August 1752 in Nantes, France, into a family that claimed roots in the Basel aristocracy, and settled in Basel in 1769. In 1776 he obtained a doctorate of laws, became a magistrate and entered politics, gaining many useful contacts through his marriage. Switzerland was then a confederacy of self-governing cantons held together by a loose military alliance, with no central government, and the privileges of its wealthiest families bred resentment and uprisings, such as that of Major Abraham Davel against Bern's rule over Vaud.

When the French Revolution broke out in 1789, Ochs joined the partisans of reform. With Frédéric-César de La Harpe he called on the French to send troops into Switzerland, overthrow what he called the decayed Confederation and found a unified nation. In 1798 French troops entered the country and took it over against little resistance. The constitution Ochs drew up abolished the Confederacy and set up a central government on the French model, with a two-chamber legislature.

Ochs served as the first president of the Helvetic Senate and later as president of the Directory, the state executive. He fell out with La Harpe and was forced out of government on 25 June 1799. The Helvetic Republic itself lasted only until the Act of Mediation of 1803, which made Switzerland a confederacy once more.

Back in Basel, Ochs gained local standing for his part in drawing up new codes of government and of criminal law and in reorganising the city's university. He died in Basel on 19 June 1821. Peter-Ochs-Strasse in the city bears his name.
peter-of-cantabria: Peter, Petrus in Latin and Pedro in Spanish, was an eighth-century Duke of Cantabria. Various writers have tried to name his parentage, making him a son or brother of King Erwig, but the early sources say nothing more specific than the chronicle of Pseudo-Alfonso, which calls him descended from the bloodline of Liuvigild and Reccared I. Even this has been challenged as a possible politically motivated fiction, created to support his descendants' later claim to exclusive kingship.

According to the Muslim chroniclers, Musa ibn Nusair sacked Amaya, the capital of Cantabria, in 714, a year after Tariq had done so. Peter, the provincial dux, led his people to refuge in the mountains. When the local noble Pelayo of Asturias rebelled against the Berber garrison set over the mountain passes of neighbouring Asturias, Peter and other western Galician nobles gave their support against the common enemy. Some scholars have suggested that Pelayo may have been a Cantabrian relative, defending the western access to the duchy from his own county seat.

After the Battle of Covadonga, in which Pelayo avoided defeat by a larger invading force and drove its governor Munuza out of Asturias, Peter seems likely to have sent his son to Pelayo's court at Cangas de Onís. Sending noble children to the royal court was a Visigothic practice, so the act amounted to a tacit admission of Pelayo's regality.

The Crónica Albeldense records the marriage that joined the two leaders' lands, and Cantabria and the rest of what would be called Asturias merged into one realm. Peter's son Alfonso later succeeded to the Asturian throne and was the first to use the title of king. His other son, Fruela of Cantabria, was the father of the kings Aurelius and Bermudo I. Iberian Muslim scholars called the line the Beni Alfons; it is more commonly known as the Astur-Leonese dynasty.
peter-of-castile: Peter was born on 30 August 1334 in Burgos, the son of Alfonso XI of Castile and Maria of Portugal. He was to marry Joan, daughter of Edward III of England, but she died of the plague in 1348 on her way to Castile. He began his reign when almost sixteen, at first under the control of his mother and encouraged by the Portuguese minister Count Alburquerque. He was the last ruler of the main branch of the House of Ivrea.

In the summer of 1353 Peter married Blanche of Bourbon and two days later abandoned her for María de Padilla. In 1355 he married Juana de Castro, persuading her that his marriage to Blanche was void, and deserted her after two nights. Blanche died in 1361, and accounts of her death differ: French historians say Peter had her murdered, others that she was poisoned or shot with a crossbow, though plague is possible. Peter was excommunicated by Pope Urban V for his persecutions of the clergy. From 1356 to 1366 he fought the War of the Two Peters with Aragon, whose king supported Peter's bastard brothers. In this period he carried out the series of murders that made him notorious.

In 1366 his half-brother Henry of Trastámara invaded with soldiers of fortune including Bertrand du Guesclin and Hugh Calveley. Peter retreated from Burgos, Toledo and Seville without giving battle and fled to Portugal and then to Galicia. He took refuge with Edward, the Black Prince, who restored him the following year after the Battle of Nájera. The Black Prince left the peninsula with two of Peter's daughters, Constance and Isabella, as hostages for payment, and married them to his brothers John of Gaunt and Edmund of Langley. Henry returned in September 1368 and the cortes of Burgos recognised him as king. On 14 March 1369 the two armies met at Montiel, where Henry prevailed with du Guesclin's help.

Peter took refuge in the fortress of Montiel and negotiated with du Guesclin, offering him 200,000 gold coins and several towns to betray Henry. Du Guesclin told Henry and bargained for more. On the night of 23 March 1369 he led Peter to his tent, where Henry was waiting and killed him with a knife. The body was left unburied for three days.

Peter's reputation is divided. He was called the Cruel by his enemies and the Just by his admirers, and the chronicler Pero López de Ayala admitted that many regretted his fall, among them peasants, burghers and merchants. Geoffrey Chaucer lamented his death in The Monk's Tale. His death ended the old alliance of Castile with England for a time, and his daughter Constance's marriage to John of Gaunt gave England a claim to the Castilian throne.
peter-of-moscow: Peter was born in Volhynia, part of the Kingdom of Galicia–Volhynia, around 1260, to parents named Theodore and Eupraxia. At twelve he entered a monastery, where he learned icon painting, and its igumen had him ordained a hieromonk. After years of ascetic life he left, with the igumen's blessing, to seek solitude and built a cell by the Rata River, where a monastery later grew up. As igumen of the Ratsk monastery he painted the icon of the Theotokos later called Of St Peter, which he gave to Maximus, Metropolitan of Kiev and all Rus', when Maximus visited.

In 1308 King Yuri I of Galicia nominated Peter to the vacant see, and in Constantinople Patriarch Athanasius consecrated him and gave him the vestments, staff and icon of his office. Mikhail Yaroslavich, Grand Prince of Vladimir and Tver, had wanted a candidate of his own, and the long hostility between the two eventually led Peter to seek the protection of the Prince of Moscow. Under Tatar rule Rus' was in turmoil, and Peter often had to change his residence. Arriving at Kiev a year after his return, he moved his duties from depopulated Kiev to Vladimir.

In 1325, at the request of Grand Prince Ivan Kalita, he transferred the metropolitan see from Vladimir to Moscow. The move strengthened Moscow's political position and made it the spiritual capital of a divided Rus'. The founding of the Vysokopetrovsky Monastery in Moscow is ascribed to him, and he wrote a few sermons and epistles.

After his canonisation his veneration spread widely, and many churches in Moscow and other Russian cities were dedicated to him; he came to be regarded as a patron saint of Moscow. His feasts fall on 24 August, the translation of his relics to the Dormition Cathedral, on 5 October, shared with the metropolitans Jonah and Alexis, and on 21 December. Although the see was now in Moscow, the office kept the title Metropolitan of Kiev and all Rus' until the election of Jonah in 1448.
peter-parler: Peter was born around 1333 in Schwäbisch Gmünd, where his father Heinrich Parler the Elder, a stonemason from Cologne Cathedral, had been invited to take over the building of the parish church of the Holy Cross. Peter worked alongside his father when the cornerstone of the choir was laid in 1351. He then travelled as a journeyman to Cologne, perhaps to Paris, and certainly to Strasbourg, whose cathedral he knew precisely. In Cologne he met Gertrud, daughter of the architect Bartholomäus von Hamm, and they married. Sometime after 1352 he joined the building of the Frauenkirche in Nuremberg, where the first sculptures can be directly ascribed to him.

By 1355 his style had come to the attention of Charles IV, who meant to make Prague the showcase capital of Central Europe. Research usually places Peter's appointment in 1356. He took over the building of St. Vitus Cathedral, which had languished since the death of Matthias of Arras in 1352, and gradually changed the earlier plan. In 1357 Charles commissioned him to build a new bridge over the Vltava. The first foundation stone was laid on 9 July 1357 at 5:31 am, a time chosen by the royal astrologers and fixed by the palindromic number 135797531 carved into the tower, and construction lasted until 1402.

He also built the Old Town Bridge Tower, whose arch holds the first net vault in Bohemia, and was the main designer of Prague's New Town. His other works include the All Saints' Chapel in Prague Castle and the chancel of St. Bartholomew's church in Kolín. He was granted citizenship in Prague in 1379 and was still named as cathedral master on a panel at St. Vitus in 1396.

Peter's first wife Gertrude died in the late 1360s, and in 1380 he married Elisabeth Agnes von Bur. His son Johann Parler the Younger took over as master builder of St. Vitus in 1398, and Wenzel became master stonemason at St. Stephen's Cathedral in Vienna. Peter died in Prague on 13 July 1399 and was buried in St. Vitus Cathedral. The designs of his father and himself became known as the Parler style and spread across Central Europe, with examples at St. Martin's Church in Landshut. In the Hussite wars of 1419–1434 much of his sculpture was destroyed, though his buildings stand.
peter-paul-rubens: Rubens was born on 28 June 1577 to Jan Rubens and Maria Pypelincks, whose family came from Antwerp. His father, a lawyer, converted to Calvinism, and in 1568 the family fled to Cologne, fearing persecution under the Duke of Alba. After Jan Rubens died in 1587 the family moved to Antwerp, where Peter Paul studied Latin and classical literature. In 1590 he had to start working, and after serving as a page to a countess he began an apprenticeship with the landscape painter Tobias Verhaecht in 1592.

In 1600 Rubens travelled to Italy, where in Venice he saw paintings by Titian, Veronese and Tintoretto. He entered the service of Duke Vincenzo I Gonzaga of Mantua, painting portraits of the ducal family and copying works in his collection, and in 1601 went on to Rome, where he studied classical sculpture and the art of Michelangelo, Raphael and Leonardo. He returned to Antwerp in 1608, and in September 1609 was appointed court painter by Archduke Albert and the Infanta Isabella Clara Eugenia, with permission to keep his studio in Antwerp. He married Isabella Brant on 3 October 1609, and from 1610 he lived and worked in a villa he designed, now the Rubenshuis Museum. His pupils and collaborators included Anthony van Dyck.

In 1621 Marie de' Medici commissioned him to paint two cycles for the Luxembourg Palace in Paris, and the one on her own life was installed in 1625. After the Twelve Years' Truce ended in 1621 the Spanish Habsburg rulers entrusted him with diplomatic missions, and between 1627 and 1630 he travelled between the courts of Spain and England to seek peace between the Spanish Netherlands and the Dutch Republic. Philip IV of Spain raised him to the nobility in 1624, Cambridge gave him an honorary degree in 1629, and Charles I of England knighted him in 1630. His output was large: Michael Jaffé's catalogue lists 1,403 works, not counting the many copies made in his workshop.

In 1630 Rubens, whose first wife Isabella had died four years earlier, married the 16-year-old Helena Fourment, who became the model for the full-figured women of many of his paintings of the 1630s. In 1635 he bought the Steen, an estate outside Antwerp, and painted landscapes there. He died on 30 May 1640 of heart failure resulting from chronic gout and was buried in Saint James' Church in Antwerp, where a family chapel was completed in 1650 with an altarpiece he painted himself. He is considered the most influential artist of the Flemish Baroque, and the terms Rubensian and Rubenesque are derived from his name.
peter-stuyvesant: Peter Stuyvesant was born around 1610, probably at Peperga in Friesland, the son of Balthasar Stuyvesant, a Reformed Calvinist minister, and Margaretha Hardenstein. He went at 20 to the University of Franeker, where he studied languages and philosophy, but was expelled after seducing his landlord's daughter. His father sent him to Amsterdam, where he joined the Dutch West India Company.

In 1630 the company made him a commercial agent on Fernando de Noronha, and in 1638 he was moved to Curaçao, where he became acting governor of the colony, and also of Aruba and Bonaire, until 1644. That April he led an attack on Saint Martin, where he was wounded in the leg, which was amputated; he later wore a wooden peg studded with silver nails.

In 1645 the company chose him to replace Willem Kieft as director-general of New Netherland, and after a delay for confirmation he arrived at New Amsterdam by May 1647. The colony was in terrible condition, with only 250 to 300 men able to bear arms. Telling its people that he would govern them as a father his children, he appointed an advisory council, the Nine Men, in September 1647. His administration issued building codes and built a protective wall on Wall Street, the canal that became Broad Street, and Broadway. He created a system of fire wardens and a volunteer fire watch, the first volunteer fire department in America.

His most notable success came against New Sweden, which he invaded and annexed in 1655. The Treaty of Hartford of 1650 was a victory for the English, as he gave up claims to the Connecticut Valley. He was strongly committed to the Dutch Reformed Church. He refused Lutherans a church, tried to bar Jewish refugees, and ordered the public torture of the Quaker preacher Robert Hodgson in 1657; company directors reversed some of these measures.

In 1664 Charles II ceded New Netherland to his brother, the Duke of York, and four English ships with 450 men under Richard Nicolls seized the colony. The settlers refused to fight, forcing Stuyvesant to surrender. The Articles of Capitulation were signed on 6 September 1664 and the city was renamed New York; they secured civil rights and freedom of religion. He spent his last years on his farm, the Great Bouwerie, which gave its name to the Bowery, and died in August 1672. The historian Eleanor Bruchey called him a difficult man thrust into a difficult position, whose religious intolerance worsened relations with colonists. His name is now attached to places in Manhattan and beyond, including Stuyvesant Square and Bedford-Stuyvesant.
peter-the-great: Peter was born on 9 June 1672 and grew up at the Izmaylovo Estate. When his father, Tsar Alexei, died in 1676 the throne passed to Peter's half-brother Feodor III. When Feodor died in 1682 without children, the Miloslavsky and Naryshkin families, the families of Alexei's first and second wives, disputed the succession. Ivan V was next in line but was weak-minded and blind, and the Boyar Duma, the council of nobles, chose the ten-year-old Peter, with his mother Natalya Naryshkina as regent. A hole was cut in the back of the throne so that she could whisper to the two boys, who ruled jointly until Ivan's death in 1696.

In March 1697 Peter travelled to Western Europe on an 18-month journey with a large delegation, the Grand Embassy, hoping to find allies against the Ottoman Empire; he failed to enlarge the anti-Ottoman alliance. In 1699 he moved the new year from 1 September to 1 January and had years counted from the birth of Christ. In 1700 he refused to allow a new patriarch to be elected, and the church later came under a Holy Synod controlled by a procurator.

He declared war on Sweden in the Great Northern War. The Russian army was defeated at Narva in 1700, but the Swedish king Charles XII then turned against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which gave Peter time to reorganise his army. Russia captured Nöteborg, renamed Shlisselburg, and founded Saint Petersburg on the Neva, and in 1712 Peter moved the capital there from Moscow. After his victory Russia annexed much of the eastern Baltic coast and became an empire. He created a Governing Senate in 1711 and a Table of Ranks in 1722, and brutally suppressed rebellions by the Streltsy, the Bashkirs, Astrakhan and the Bulavin Rebellion.

Peter's health was never robust. He began to suffer from problems of the bladder in the winter of 1723 and died early on 8 February 1725 at the age of 52; an autopsy found his bladder infected with gangrene. He is buried in the Saints Peter and Paul Cathedral. A story that he caught his fatal illness rescuing drowning soldiers rests on a single source and is viewed with scepticism by some historians. For Old Believers he was the Antichrist, because of the calendar changes and the poll tax, and mid-19th-century Slavophiles deplored the westernisation of Russia. The so-called Will of Peter the Great was a forgery made in Paris on Napoleon's order in 1812.
peter-tordenskjold: Peter Jansen Wessel was the tenth child of the Trondheim alderman Jan Wessel. An unruly boy, he stowed away on a ship to Copenhagen in 1704 and tried without success to become a naval cadet. The king's chaplain, Peder Jespersen, sent him on a voyage to the West Indies and at last found him a cadetship. After voyages to the East Indies he was made second lieutenant on 7 July 1711. The Norwegian admiral Waldemar Løvendal gave him the four-gun sloop Ormen and in June 1712 the 18-gun Løvendals Galej, against the advice of the Danish admiralty, which thought him unreliable.

He took part in the destruction of Swedish transports at Rügen on 29 September 1712. On 26 and 27 July 1714, off Lindesnes, he fought the 28-gun Swedish privateer Olbing Galley until both ships were badly damaged, then sent to thank her crew and to ask for more ammunition so as to go on. King Frederick IV had him court-martialled for disclosing his lack of ammunition and for risking his ship against a stronger one; he was acquitted on 15 December and made captain on 28 December.

At Kolberg on 24 April 1715 he captured the Swedish Rear-Admiral Hans Wachtmeister and the frigate Hvita Örn, which became his flagship. At Dynekilen on 8 July 1716, with two frigates and five smaller ships, he took or destroyed around 30 Swedish vessels. A failure against the Gothenburg squadron in 1717 brought a second court-martial in 1718, which was quashed after Ulrik Christian Gyldenløve intervened. He became rear-admiral in December 1718 and vice-admiral after partly destroying and partly capturing the Gothenburg squadron on 26 September 1719.

On 12 November 1720, aged 30, he was killed by the sword of the Livonian colonel Jakob Axel Staël von Holstein in a duel at Gleidingen near Hildesheim. The quarrel arose at a dinner where Tordenskiold spoke of a friend cheated at gambling. As duelling was against Danish law, his body was brought to Holmen Church without much ceremony. He is named in the Danish anthem Kong Christian stod ved højen mast of 1778 and the Norwegian anthem Ja, vi elsker dette landet of 1864. A story that at Marstrand his men moved from post to post to seem more numerous gave Danish and Norwegian the phrase Tordenskjold's soldiers.
peter-von-biron: Peter was born on 15 February 1724 in Jelgava (Mitau), the eldest son of Ernst Johann von Biron and Benigna von Trotha. From 1730 to 1740 the family lived in Moscow and St. Petersburg, where his father was the lover and favourite of Anna of Russia. At sixteen he followed his family into exile, first to Tobolsk Governorate in Siberia and then, from 1742 to 1762, to Yaroslavl. In 1765 he married Princess Caroline of Waldeck and Pyrmont; their only son was stillborn in 1766.

His father gave him the duchy in 1769, though Peter had already acted as duke in practice for several years, and in 1770 he took an oath to the Courland Knighthood. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1771. In 1775 he founded the Academia Petrina at Jelgava, hoping it would grow into a university, but Immanuel Kant and Johann Gottfried Herder both refused his invitations to become professors there.

He bought the Palais Kurland on Berlin's Unter den Linden in 1782, the park and palace of Friedrichsfelde in 1785 and, in April 1786, the Duchy of Sagan from the Bohemian Lobkovic family. When Russia and its allies began the third partition of Poland in 1795, he gave up his rights to Russia in return for a high appanage, and with the final document signed on 28 March 1795 the Duchy of Courland ceased to exist.

He married Yevdokiya Yusupova in 1774 and divorced her in 1778, and in 1779 married Dorothea von Medem, of the old Courland nobility. He is known to have been abusive to at least two of his wives. Of his six children with Dorothea four daughters survived: Wilhelmine inherited Sagan, Pauline married Prince Friedrich Hermann of Hohenzollern-Hechingen, and Dorothea married Edmond de Talleyrand-Périgord. Peter died at Gellenau on 13 January 1800 after several months of illness, and in 1847 was reburied in a Lutheran church in Żagań.
peter-von-scholten: Peter Carl Frederik von Scholten was born on 17 May 1784 in Vestervig, Thy, the son of Captain Casimir Wilhelm von Scholten and Catharina Elisabeth de Moldrup. He joined the Danish army and in 1803 became an ensign in a unit stationed in the West Indies, but was taken to Great Britain when the British occupied the Danish West Indies in 1807. Serving in Copenhagen, he rose to staff captain by 1813 and became adjutant to Frants Cristopher Bülow, general adjutant of Frederick VI of Denmark. In 1810 he married Anne Elisabeth Thortsen, with whom he had three daughters.

When the British occupation ended in 1814, von Scholten took his first post on St Thomas as a customs officer, which brought him wealth during the trade boom of the wars between the nearby Spanish islands and the South American insurgents. He kept rising in the army, becoming major general in 1829. From 1835 his authority as governor-general covered all three islands, St Thomas, St Croix and St John. He ruled as a patriarchal administrator, seeking to lighten the burden of the enslaved and to restrain racial tensions, founding schools for the black population and allowing them to own property.

On St Croix he lived with Anna Heegaard, a woman of colour, and modern scholars broadly agree that she influenced his more humane policy. Yet he opposed the ruling of Christian VIII of Denmark that every child born to an unfree woman should be free from birth, fearing it would cause dangerous discontent, and he saw the rebellion of 1848 as proof that he had been right.

In Denmark he faced a humiliating trial for treason, accused of harming colonial interests by abolishing slavery, and was at first denied his pension. He was the last governor-general of the islands, as the Danish state and its colonial administration began to be democratised. He died in Altona, Holstein, on 26 January 1854, leaving little to his heirs, and was buried in Assistens Cemetery, Copenhagen. Ole Ernst played him in the Danish film Peter von Scholten of 1987.
peterborough: Peterborough lies 74 miles (119 km) north of London on the River Nene, on the western edge of the Fens. The land is flat and in places below sea level; Holme Fen, just south of the city, is said to be the lowest point on land in Britain. The city has been called the Gateway to the Fens. Settlement began here because the Nene creates permanently drained land at this point. The Oxford Clay, dug in brick pits, has yielded fossils of Jurassic marine reptiles and, in 1898, a sauropod skeleton later named Cetiosauriscus.

The Flag Fen site east of the city centre shows Iron Age settlement and what is thought to be religious activity. The Romans founded a fortified garrison town at Durobrivae, now Water Newton, around the middle of the 1st century CE, and a large fort at Longthorpe, perhaps as early as 44 to 48 CE, built for about 3,000 soldiers. The area produced Nene Valley Ware, traded as far as Cornwall and the Antonine Wall.

The original town was the monastery of Medeshamstede, founded in 655. From the late tenth century the name became Burgh, possibly after Abbot Kenulf built a defensive wall around the abbey, which was dedicated to Saint Peter; this became Peterborough. The present cathedral was rebuilt between 1118 and 1238. When the abbey church became a cathedral in 1541 the last abbot became the first bishop and the town was deemed a city. Catherine of Aragon and Mary, Queen of Scots were buried there, though Mary's remains were later moved to Westminster Abbey by her son James I.

The Great Northern Railway's line from London to York, opened in 1850, turned a market town into an industrial centre known for brickworks and engineering. The Great Fire of Peterborough destroyed much of the old centre on 22 August 1956, and the city was designated a new town in the 1960s.

The 2021 census counted 192,178 people in the urban area, and the city is a unitary authority within Cambridgeshire. Peterborough Cathedral, one of the most intact large Norman buildings in England, is known for its early English Gothic west front with three great arches. The Nene Viaduct of 1847, by Sir William and Joseph Cubitt, is the oldest surviving cast-iron railway bridge in the country.
peterborough-abbey: The first church, Medeshamstede, was founded in the reign of the Anglo-Saxon king Peada of the Middle Angles, in about 655, as one of the first centres of Christianity in central England. The monastic settlement lasted at least until 870, when it was supposedly destroyed by Vikings. In the mid-10th-century monastic revival a Benedictine abbey was created and endowed in 966, principally by Athelwold, Bishop of Winchester. It was dedicated to Saint Peter and surrounded by a palisade called a burgh, which is why the town was eventually named Peterborough. Dunstan, Archbishop of Canterbury, further revived the community in 972.

The abbey was damaged in the struggle between the Norman invaders and Hereward the Wake, but it was repaired until an accidental fire destroyed it in 1116. Abbot John de Sais began a new Norman church on 8 March 1118, and the painted wooden ceiling of the nave, finished between 1230 and 1250, still survives. The Great West Front was added in 1237, and the building was consecrated in 1238 by Robert Grosseteste, Bishop of Lincoln.

After Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries the relics were lost, but the church survived as the cathedral of a new Anglican diocese, with the last abbot, John Chambers, as its first bishop. Catherine of Aragon was buried there in 1536. Parliamentarian troops vandalised the church in 1643, destroying almost all the stained glass, the choir stalls and the cloisters.

The monks, as in all Benedictine abbeys, vowed to remain in the abbey until death and lived by the Rule of St Benedict, centred on the daily Conventual Mass and the Liturgy of the Hours. They also pursued scholarship, education and pastoral care, and welcoming guests and pilgrims was probably the main focus of activity. Pilgrims came for the relics, which the monk Hugh Candidus listed in the mid-12th century. Shortly before the Reformation the abbey had the sixth-largest monastic income in the country and about 120 monks.
peteris-stucka: Pēteris Stučka was born in the Governorate of Livonia, then part of the Russian Empire, the son of a prosperous farmer and a teacher. He went to a German lyceum in Riga and studied law at St Petersburg University, where he shared a room with the poet Rainis, whose sister Dora Pliekšāne he married. After graduating in 1888 he practised law in Latvia, led the New Current movement, wrote and translated widely and edited Latvian newspapers. Arrested in 1897, he was sentenced to five years of exile in Vyatka province.

When the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party split, Stučka sided with Vladimir Lenin's Bolsheviks, and in 1904 he helped organise the Latvian Social Democratic Workers' Party. After the February Revolution he backed Lenin's April Theses and organised the detachment of Latvian riflemen who played a crucial role in the October Revolution. As People's Commissar for Justice from 7 November 1917 he abolished the existing courts, replacing them with local courts of a judge and two assessors, and decreed that old laws held only where they did not contradict the revolutionary conscience; he later wrote that from November 1917 to 1922 law was formally lacking.

He headed the government of the Latvian Socialist Soviet Republic until its collapse in August 1919 under a counter-offensive by the Latvian Army and allied troops. The writer Victor Serge described a strictly egalitarian regime in which the Party Committee was also the government and vodka was banned. Stučka returned to Russia for good, worked in the Comintern from 1920 and chaired its International Control Commission for four years from 1924. In 1923 he became the first Chief Justice of the Russian SFSR, a post he held until he died.

Stučka died on 25 January 1932, and his ashes were placed in the Kremlin Wall Necropolis near Lenin's Mausoleum. From 1958 to 1990 the University of Latvia bore his name, and the town of Aizkraukle was called Stučka from its founding in the 1960s until 1991.
peterloo-massacre: After the end of the Napoleonic Wars in 1815, a brief boom in textile manufacture gave way to chronic depression among cotton weavers and spinners. Weavers who could have expected 15 shillings for a six-day week in 1803 saw their wages cut to 5 shillings, or even 4s 6d, by 1818. The Corn Laws, the first of which was passed in 1815, kept the price of food high. Only around 11 percent of adult males could vote, and Lancashire had 17,000 voters in a county of nearly a million people. Reform petitions were rejected by the House of Commons in the winter of 1816–17, the largest, from Manchester, bearing over 30,000 signatures.

The Manchester Patriotic Union, formed by radicals from the Manchester Observer, asked Henry Hunt to chair a great assembly, held on Monday 16 August 1819, a hot, cloudless day. Hunt had urged everyone to come armed with no weapon but a self-approving conscience, and the contingents arrived in order and in their Sunday best, the largest, of 10,000, from Oldham Green. Contemporaries put the crowd at 30,000 to 150,000; modern estimates are lower.

William Hulton, chairman of the magistrates, watched from a house at the edge of the field. He issued a warrant for the arrest of Hunt, Joseph Johnson, John Knight and James Moorhouse, and wrote to Major Thomas Trafford of the Manchester and Salford Yeomanry Cavalry, saying the civil power was wholly inadequate. The Yeomanry charged, knocking down a woman and killing a child, and took Hunt. Hulton then summoned the 15th Hussars, who charged with sabres drawn.

No official count or inquiry followed. The Manchester Relief Committee gave the number injured as 420, while radical sources listed 500. John Lees, an Oldham cloth-worker who had fought at Waterloo and died of his wounds on 9 September, was reported to have said: "At Waterloo there was man to man but there it was downright murder." The Manchester Observer was prosecuted and closed in February 1820.

Hunt and eight others were tried for sedition at York in March 1820; five were convicted, and Hunt received 30 months in Ilchester Gaol. In 1822 a civil case against four Yeomanry members ended with all found not liable. The historian Robert Poole has called Peterloo the bloodiest political event of the 19th century on English soil. A memorial by Jeremy Deller was inaugurated on 16 August 2019.
petersberg-citadel: The hill takes its name from the Benedictine Monastery of St Peter and Paul, first recorded in 1060; its church, the Peterskirche, rebuilt from 1103 to 1147, is the oldest surviving building of the citadel. In November 1181 Emperor Frederick I held an Imperial Diet there at which Henry the Lion submitted to him. The city wall was carried around the hill about 1168, and about 1625 the council strengthened it with a hornwork and the bastions Gabriel and Michael. King Gustav II Adolf of Sweden, whose troops held Erfurt from 1631, planned a fortress there but died in 1632.

The foundation stone was laid on 1 June 1665 on the orders of Johann Philipp von Schönborn, Archbishop-Elector of Mainz, who wanted to show his power to the townspeople and discourage rebellion. The first phase, to 1707, used a plan by the Erfurt architect Caspar Vogel and was shaped by the court architect Antonio Petrini; it built the walls and bastions, the Peterstor gate, three barracks and the Horchgänge, passages in the walls where soldiers listened for enemies tunnelling in. A second phase, from 1707 to 1728 under Maximilian von Welsch, strengthened the defences.

In April 1813 Napoleon ordered the citadel equipped to hold 2,000 men under siege for six months, and over 3,000 civilians dug its ditches. Prussian, Austrian and Russian forces opened fire on 6 November 1813, setting buildings and parts of St Peter's Church alight, but General Alexandre d'Alton handed it over only on 5 May 1814. The Prussians then rebuilt it until 1868, adding the Defence Barracks, the fortress bakery and caponiers. From 1935 the Nazis held communists, trade unionists and other political opponents there, many sent on to concentration camps and some murdered at the citadel, and ran a military court that could pass death sentences.

The East German Army used the citadel from 1956 until 1963, after which it served mainly for storage, and the Stasi kept workshops there until 1990. After German reunification a large restoration began, funded by the city, the Thuringian state and the federal government: most buildings added since 1868 were removed, older ones restored, ditches cleared and the 1832 bakery brought back into use. The walls run for 2,180 metres in a star of eight bastions and now three ravelins. The Lower Barracks house archives of the Stasi Records Agency, and St Peter's Church has shown concrete art since 1993.
petra: Petra lies in a basin surrounded by mountains on the eastern flank of the Arabah valley, which runs from the Dead Sea to the Gulf of Aqaba. Flash floods visit the area, but excavations show that the Nabataeans controlled them with dams, cisterns and water conduits, which stored water through long droughts and created an artificial oasis. Enclosed by rocks and watered by a perennial stream, the city had the advantages of a fortress and controlled the commercial routes to Gaza, to Bosra and Damascus, to the Red Sea, and across the desert to the Persian Gulf.

By 7000 BCE some of the earliest recorded farmers had settled at Beidha, just north of Petra. In the Iron Age the area was held by the Edomites. The Nabataeans, a northern Arabian people who had roamed the desert with their herds, settled there in the fourth century BCE, and their name for the city appears to have been Raqēmō. Petra flourished in the first century CE, when its population peaked at an estimated 20,000 and Al-Khazneh, possibly the mausoleum of the king Aretas IV, was built.

In 106 the Romans annexed the Nabataean realm as the province of Arabia Petraea. The native dynasty ended, but the city continued to flourish under Roman rule. Its importance declined as sea-based trade routes grew, and an earthquake in 363 destroyed many buildings and crippled the water system. Petra became the capital of the Byzantine province of Palaestina III, and papyri found in the Byzantine Church show that it still thrived in the sixth century. The site was lost to the outside world until the Swiss traveller Johann Ludwig Burckhardt reached it in 1812.

Petra is a World Heritage Site, called the Rose City for its sandstone. Visitors enter through the Siq, a narrow gorge ending at Al-Khazneh, the Treasury. Other monuments include the Royal Tombs, among them the Urn Tomb, which was made into a church in 446, and the High Place of Sacrifice on Jebel Madbah. The Monastery, Ad Deir, the largest monument, dates from the first century BCE and is thought to have been dedicated to the deified king Obodas I.
petrarch: Petrarch was born on 20 July 1304, the son of Ser Petracco and his wife Eletta Canigiani. His birth name was Francesco di Petracco, which he Latinized to Franciscus Petrarcha. His family followed Pope Clement V to Avignon, where the papacy had moved in 1309. His father, a notary, insisted that he and his brother Gherardo study law, at Montpellier from 1316 to 1320 and at Bologna from 1320 to 1326. Petrarch preferred Latin literature and thought the seven years wasted. His father once threw his books into a fire.

After their parents died, Petrarch and his brother returned to Avignon in 1326, where he held clerical offices that left time for writing. His Latin epic Africa, about the Roman general Scipio Africanus, made him a European celebrity. On 8 April 1341 he was crowned on the Capitoline Hill in Rome by the senators Giordano Orsini and Orso dell'Anguillara, the second poet laureate since classical antiquity. He travelled widely and served as an ambassador.

He collected crumbling Latin manuscripts, and in 1345 he found in the Chapter Library of Verona Cathedral a collection of Cicero's letters not known to have survived, the Epistulae ad Atticum. About 1368 he moved with his daughter Francesca and her family to Arquà in the Euganean Hills near Padua, where he spent his remaining years in religious contemplation. The da Carrara lords of Padua seized his library, and its manuscripts are now scattered across Europe.

Petrarch is best known for the Rerum vulgarium fragmenta, or Canzoniere, a collection of 366 poems, 317 of them sonnets. The poems centre on Laura, whom he said he first saw in the church of Sainte-Claire d'Avignon on 6 April 1327. She may have been Laura de Noves, though he always denied that she was an invented figure. The Petrarchan sonnet still bears his name, and in the 16th century Pietro Bembo made his verse a model for the Italian language.

Most of his writing was in Latin, including the Secretum, an imagined dialogue with a figure inspired by Augustine of Hippo, and a large body of letters. He valued the study of ancient history and literature as the study of human thought and action, and is often called the father of humanism. He is credited with creating the idea of a historical "Dark Ages", a notion most modern scholars find inaccurate and misleading.
petro-shelest: Shelest was born on 14 February 1908 into a peasant family in the village of Andriivka in the Kharkiv Governorate, the seventh child of the household. As a boy he herded livestock on a state farm, worked as a hired labourer, a postman and a railway loader, and later as a locksmith at the Kharkiv Locomotive Repair Factory. He joined the Komsomol in October 1923 and the Communist Party of the Soviet Union in 1928, and graduated from the Mariupol Metallurgical Institute in 1935.

After a year in the Red Army he moved to party work in 1937, as thousands of members were swept away in the Great Purge. From 1943 to 1954 he managed large factories in Leningrad and Kyiv, and from 1954 he rose through the Kyiv city and regional party committees, becoming First Secretary of the Kyiv regional committee.

As First Secretary from 1963 Shelest tried to run Ukraine with some independence from Moscow, pressing for economic management at the republic's level, and construction of the four nuclear plants at Chernobyl began in his time. He became a full member of the Presidium when Nikita Khrushchev fell in November 1964. Historians disagree on how far he personally backed the Sixtiers, and he was criticised by Viacheslav Chornovil for the arrests of 1965–1966. Party membership in Ukraine reached 2.5 million by 1971.

In 1968 he took a leading part in the Soviet response to the Prague Spring, attending every meeting with the Czechoslovak leaders alongside Leonid Brezhnev. He insulted František Kriegel as a Galician Jew, and on 3 August received from Vasiľ Biľak the letter inviting Soviet troops that served as a pretext for the Warsaw Pact invasion on 20 August.

Removed in May 1972, Shelest spent eleven months as a Deputy Premier in Moscow before being demoted again; officially his health was blamed. In April 1973 a Ukrainian press article condemned his book O Ukraine, Our Soviet Land of 1970 for ideological errors likely to encourage nationalism. He managed an aircraft design bureau near Moscow from 1973 to 1985, blamed his fall on intrigues by Brezhnev and Volodymyr Shcherbytsky, and returned to lecture in Ukraine after the Soviet collapse. He died in Moscow on 22 January 1996.
petrobey-mavromichalis: Petros was born on 6 August 1765, the son of Pierros Mavromichalis Pierrakos and Katerina Koutsogrigorakos, a doctor's daughter. His family had a long record of risings against the Ottoman Empire: his grandfather Georgakis and his father were among the leaders of the Orlov Revolt. In the feuding among the leaders of Mani that followed, the young Petros won a reputation for settling disputes and reconciling the warring families.

After failed uprisings he helped many klephts and other rebels escape to the French-controlled Heptanese, which gave him useful contacts, and he may have reached an understanding with Napoleon Bonaparte, then fighting in Egypt, for a Greek revolt timed with a French blow against the Ottomans. Napoleon's failure in Egypt ended the plan.

By 1814 the Maniots were again a threat, and the Sultan made concessions that included naming him Bey of Mani, formalising the autonomy the region already had. Under Petrobey, as he was now called, the Maniots kept the southern Peloponnese against Albanian raiders on the Sultan's behalf, while he took part in the plans of the Moreot captains for a rising. He joined the Filiki Eteria in 1818 and in 1819 brokered a pact among the leading captains' families.

On 17 March 1821 he raised his war flag at Areopolis, and his men took Kalamata on 23 March. After the summer of 1822 he left the fighting to his sons, two of whom were killed, and went on mediating quarrels among the captains and writing to leaders and philhellenes in Europe and the United States for support.

Petrobey sat in the first Greek Senate under Ioannis Kapodistrias, but the two clashed over Kapodistrias's plan for a centralised administration of appointed officials in place of the old loyalties of family. When his brother Ioannis rose against the appointed governor of Lakonia, both brothers were arrested on coming to negotiate. After the assassination by his brother Konstantinos and his son Georgios, which he publicly disapproved of, he served under King Otto as vice-president of the Council of State and later as a senator, and received the Grand Cross of the Order of the Redeemer. He died in Athens on 17 January 1848 and was buried with the highest honours.
petrobras: Petrobras was created in 1953 under President Getúlio Vargas with the slogan The Oil is Ours, and was given a legal monopoly in Brazil. Brazil then produced only 2,700 barrels of oil a day. The REDUC refinery near Rio de Janeiro began operating in 1961, and the Cenpes research centre opened in Rio in 1963. In 1961 the company's geologist Walter K. Link published a memorandum implying that exploring offshore was more promising than onshore. In 1963 Petrobras found the Recôncavo Baiano and Carmópolis oil fields, and in 1968 it set up the subsidiary Petroquisa for petrochemicals.

The oil crisis of 1973 halted the company's growth and ended the Brazilian miracle, a period of annual growth above 10%; Petrobras came close to bankruptcy. A discovery in the Campos Basin in 1974 restored its finances, and in 1975 the government temporarily allowed foreign operators into Brazil. Production reached 1 million barrels a day in 1997 and passed 2 million barrels of oil equivalent a day in 2003.

Law 9.478 of 1997 ended the monopoly and created the National Petroleum Agency, and in 1999 the agency signed agreements with other companies. In 2000 Petrobras set a world record for deep-water exploration at 1,877 metres. In 2006 the P-50 platform in the Campos Basin made Brazil self-sufficient in oil. In 2007 and 2008 discoveries in the Santos Basin, among them the Tupi field, about 300 km off the coast of Rio de Janeiro, opened the pre-salt reserves. In 2010 the company completed a share offering of US$70 billion to develop the new fields.

The company is headquartered in Rio de Janeiro and operates in refining, exploration and production, distribution, gas and power, biofuels and international business. Brazil's government directly holds 54% of its voting common shares. Its shares are traded on B3 in Brazil and on the New York and Madrid stock exchanges. Brazil accounted for 92% of its production in 2014, and the company has also held assets in Bolivia, Colombia, Argentina and elsewhere.

Operation Car Wash, a federal police investigation begun in Curitiba, expanded from a money-laundering inquiry to allegations that Petrobras executives took bribes for awarding inflated contracts to construction firms. Petrobras agreed in 2018 to pay settlements to US and Brazilian authorities and shareholders.
petrocaribe: Petrocaribe was founded on 29 June 2005 at Puerto La Cruz in Venezuela, at the first of its summits, where 14 countries joined. It developed from the Caracas Accord, built on the payment terms of the San José Agreement and the Caracas Energy Accord, and formed part of the pink tide in Latin America seeking post-neoliberal development. Rafael Ramírez, Venezuela's Energy and Petroleum Minister and president of PDVSA, said it sought to cut out the middleman: it offered not discounts but financial facilities, direct deliveries of products and infrastructure.

Members bought oil at market value, paying 5 to 50% up front with a grace period of one to two years; the rest could be paid over 17 to 25 years at 1% interest when oil was above US$40 a barrel. Petrocaribe had 18 members in all, 12 of them from the Caribbean Community. Haiti, not at first invited because Venezuela did not recognise its government after Jean-Bertrand Aristide, joined after Hugo Chávez courted President René Préval, and it received its first shipment on 8 March 2008. Honduras joined in December 2007, left after the 2009 coup and rejoined in May 2012; Guatemala joined in July 2008 and left in November 2013, saying the promised low rates had not come.

In 2013 Petrocaribe established links with the Bolivarian Alliance for the Americas (ALBA), aiming to go beyond the oil trade. The deal had fallen apart by 2019. Venezuela's output fell from nearly 3 million barrels a day in 2014 to less than a million, and corruption, price swings and United States sanctions, which made bank payments to Venezuela almost impossible, took their toll. Critics said Petrocaribe had held back renewable energy and burdened small nations with billions of dollars of debt. In November 2022 Saint Vincent and the Grenadines became the first country to receive oil on its terms again, and in 2023 Venezuela announced its intention to revive the programme.
petroleos-de-venezuela: Venezuela nationalised its oil industry on 1 January 1976 under President Carlos Andrés Pérez, whose economic plan, La Gran Venezuela, called for it. The ceremony took place at the site of the Zumaque oilwell 1 at Mene Grande. The foreign concessionaires were replaced by Venezuelan companies such as Lagoven (formerly Standard Oil), Maraven (Shell) and Llanoven (Mobil). Each kept the structures and functions of its multinational predecessor, and all became affiliates of PDVSA, under both the company and the Ministry of Energy. PDVSA thus inherited engineers with full technical training from the old firms.

In the 1990s the company opened to outside partners in the policy known as Apertura. From 1993 to 1998 it shared extraction rights with several multinationals in arrangements called strategic associations, which were controversial because of their lenient taxation and the loss of control over domestic resources. PDVSA had bought half of the American fuel brand Citgo in 1986 and the other half in 1990. In 1998 it produced 3.4 million barrels a day and had 40,000 employees.

After Hugo Chávez was elected in 1998 he directed the company, which had run autonomously, to serve as a source of funds for state social programmes, the Bolivarian Missions. In December 2002 many managers and employees, together with the trade union federation CTV, struck to press Chávez to call early elections, and oil production nearly stopped for two months. Many thousands of employees, most of them experienced professionals, were dismissed and production resumed with workers loyal to the government. In 2007 PDVSA took majority control of projects of foreign firms; ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips refused to restructure and their assets were expropriated, while Total, Chevron, Statoil and BP agreed and kept minority shares.

Production fell from 3.5 million barrels a day in the 1990s to about 800,000 in the 2020s. The United States imposed sanctions on the company in August 2017, and in 2017 Nicolás Maduro put Major General Manuel Quevedo at its head. A gas leak at the Paraguaná refinery complex in August 2012 caused an explosion that killed 48 people.

PDVSA is directed by a board appointed by presidential decree and explores, produces, refines and exports oil, and also explores for and produces natural gas. Venezuela's reserves include conventional oil and extra-heavy crude from the Orinoco Belt, from which the fuel Orimulsion was refined. Its overseas holdings have included Citgo in the United States and a half share of Nynäs Petroleum in Sweden. The company also runs the radio network Circuito Radial PDVSA and the internet channel PDVSA TV.
petronas: Oil exploration in the region began before Malaysia existed. Royal Dutch Shell started in Miri, Sarawak, after Charles Brooke signed the first Oil Mining Lease in 1909, and the first well was drilled there in 1910. Shell was still the only oil company in the area in 1963, when the Federation of Malaya united with Sarawak and Sabah to become Malaysia, and it brought the country's first offshore oilfield into production in 1968.

Several factors in the early 1970s led the government to found a state-owned company. The oil price rose from US$1.50 a barrel in 1972 to US$12.00 after war in the Middle East and an oil embargo by OPEC. Other countries had adopted production sharing agreements in place of concessions. The government also believed that foreign companies did not inform it properly of discoveries in their concessions, and the New Economic Policy of the early 1970s encouraged Malaysians, and bumiputeras in particular, to take control of modern industries.

Production-sharing contracts between Petronas and foreign oil companies were signed in 1976. Of the oil produced, 20 per cent went to the companies to recover costs and 10 per cent was paid as royalty, shared equally between the federal and state governments. The remaining 70 per cent, the profit oil, was divided 70:30 between Petronas and the companies, and Petronas did not take over the companies' equity.

Early in the 21st century the company expanded abroad. In March 2000 it finalised an oil production deal in Chad, and in July 2000 it found oil in the Samarang-Asam Paya contract area in Sabah. In 2001 it began construction on the Chad-Cameroon Integrated Oil Development and Pipeline Project. It also sponsored the Sauber Formula One team from 1995 to 2009, and then the Mercedes team.

Petronas is a legal entity incorporated under the Malaysian Companies Act 1965, and the federal government is its sole shareholder. Its logo, designed in 1974 by Dato' Johan Ariff, combines an oil drop with the letter P, in emerald green for the sea from which oil and gas are drawn. It is vertically integrated, with exploration, refining, distribution, power generation and trading. Petronas Carigali is its principal exploration and production subsidiary, and the Malaysia Petroleum Management division has overseen the country's upstream assets since the company was established. It also runs a research university, Universiti Teknologi Petronas, built in 1997 at Seri Iskandar in Perak.
petronas-twin-towers: Planning of the Petronas Towers began on 1 January 1992 and included rigorous tests and simulations of wind and structural loads. César Pelli chose a distinctive postmodern style intended to create a 21st-century icon for Kuala Lumpur. Seven years of construction followed on the site of the former Selangor Turf Club, starting on 1 March 1993 with excavation, which meant moving 500 truckloads of earth every night to dig 30 metres down. The superstructure began on 1 April 1994.

Test boreholes showed that the site sat on the edge of a cliff, with decayed limestone under one half and soft rock under the other, so the whole site was moved 61 metres to rest on the soft rock. Because the bedrock lay so deep, the towers stand on very deep foundations of 104 concrete piles, 60 to 114 metres long. Each tower's concrete raft, 4.6 metres thick, was poured continuously over 54 hours.

The structural system is a tube in tube design, invented by the Bangladeshi-American architect Fazlur Rahman Khan. The towers are built largely of reinforced concrete, with a steel and glass facade whose motifs resemble Islamic art, and their cross section is based on the Rub el Hizb, with circular sectors added to provide office space. Because importing steel was costly, the builders used super high-strength concrete, which is familiar to Asian contractors and twice as effective as steel in reducing sway, though it makes the building twice as heavy on its foundation.

The government required completion within six years, so two consortia worked at once. A Japanese group led by the Hazama Corporation built Tower 1 and a South Korean group led by Samsung C&T built Tower 2. A batch of concrete once failed a strength test and halted construction, at a cost of US$700,000 a day, and one floor was demolished. A double-decker skybridge joins the towers on the 41st and 42nd floors, 170 metres above the ground, and also lets people move between the towers in high winds.

The towers stand at 451.9 metres and were the tallest buildings in the world from 1998 to 2004, when Taipei 101 surpassed them. They remain the tallest twin skyscrapers, ahead of the original World Trade Center towers in New York. Below them are the Suria KLCC shopping centre, the Petronas Philharmonic Hall, home of the Malaysian Philharmonic Orchestra, and the 6.9-hectare KLCC Park. The towers are a major landmark of Kuala Lumpur.
petronilla-of-aragon: Petronilla was the daughter of Ramiro II of Aragon and Agnes of Aquitaine. Her father was bishop of Barbastro-Roda when his brother Alfonso I died childless in 1134. Alfonso had left the kingdom to the Knights Templar, the Hospitallers and the Knights of the Holy Sepulchre, but his decision was not respected: the aristocracy of Navarre elected a king of their own, restoring their independence, and the Aragonese nobility raised Ramiro to the throne. Pope Innocent II rejected the election, and Ramiro married Agnes in 1135 without papal approval.

Petronilla's marriage was a very important matter of state. The nobility rejected a proposal by Alfonso VII of Castile to marry her to his son Sancho and have her educated at his court. Instead, when she was a little over a year old, she was betrothed at Barbastro on 11 August 1137 to Raymond Berengar IV, Count of Barcelona, who was twenty-three years her senior.

At El Castellar on 13 November 1137 Ramiro abdicated, transferred authority to Ramon Berenguer and returned to monastic life. Ramon Berenguer ruled the kingdom under the title Prince of the Aragonese. The betrothal was ratified at a wedding in Lleida in August 1150, when Petronilla was fourteen, and the marriage was consummated early in 1151. It produced five children, among them Alfonso II of Aragon, born in 1157, and Sancho, born in 1161.

In April 1152, pregnant with her first child, she wrote a will leaving her kingdom to her husband should she die in childbirth, and in it she already styled herself Queen of Aragon. While her husband was in Provence in 1156–57, she presided over the court from Barcelona. After his death in 1162 she received the County of Besalú and the Vall de Ribes for life and was the only ruler of Aragon for the next two years.

On 18 June 1164 Petronilla abdicated in favour of her seven-year-old son, who took the name Alfonso out of deference to the Aragonese. The historian Jerónimo Zurita described her as regent during his minority. She died in Barcelona in October 1173 and was buried in Barcelona Cathedral; her tomb has been lost.

Historians have long debated whether she was the true ruler of Aragon, since some hold that Ramiro gave the kingdom to his son-in-law and that her role was secondary. Zurita reported a clause in the pact with Ramon Berenguer that Aragon would pass to the children of a later marriage if she died. Her case served as a precedent after the death of King Martin, when Ferdinand I was enthroned under the Compromise of Caspe, his claim resting on descent through a woman.
petrozavodsk: Petrozavodsk stretches for some 27 kilometres along the western shore of Lake Onega. Its name means Peter's factory, combining the name of Peter the Great with the Russian zavod, factory. Archaeological finds show a settlement on the site as long as seven thousand years ago, and during the Middle Ages several lakeside villages marked it. A map by the Flemish cartographer Abraham Ortelius at the end of the 16th century places a settlement called Onegaborg there, and Finnish forces later used a translation of that name, Äänislinna, during their occupation in the Continuation War.

On 11 September 1703 Prince Menshikov founded the settlement of Petrovskaya Sloboda at the behest of Peter the Great, who needed a new iron foundry to make cannon and anchors for the Baltic Fleet during the Great Northern War. The foundry was first called Shuysky zavod and later Petrovsky zavod, after the reigning monarch. By 1717 the settlement was the largest in Karelia, with about 3,500 inhabitants, a timber fort, a covered market and miniature palaces of the Tsar and Menshikov. After Peter's death it was depopulated, and the factory closed in 1734.

Catherine the Great revived the industry in 1773 with a new iron foundry, named Alexandrovsky after Alexander Nevsky, to supply cannon for the Russo-Turkish Wars; Charles Gascoigne supervised its expansion in 1787–96. In her municipal reform of 1777 the settlement became a town named Petrozavodsk, and a Neoclassical centre was built around the Round Square.

In 1784 it replaced Olonets as the administrative centre of the region, and Olonets Governorate, abolished by Emperor Paul, was revived in 1801 with Petrozavodsk as its centre. From 14 October 1941, during the Finnish occupation of 1941–1944, Finnish authorities opened concentration camps, eleven by the time the city was recaptured. A commemorative site was created in 1992 for several hundred people shot during the Great Terror.

Petrozavodsk is the capital and largest city of the Republic of Karelia. It is distinguished among towns of northern Russia by its Neoclassical heritage, including the Round Square of 1775 and the Alexander Nevsky Cathedral, consecrated in 1832. Its institutions include the National Museum of the Republic of Karelia, founded in 1871, and Petrozavodsk State University. The suburb of Martsialnye Vody, founded by Peter the Great in 1714, is the oldest spa in Russia, and boats from the harbour reach Kizhi, a World Heritage Site with an outdoor museum of ancient wooden architecture.
petru-aron: Petru Aron, an illegitimate son of Alexandru cel Bun, ruled Moldavia from October 1451 to February 1452, from August 1454 to February 1455, and from May 1455 to April 1457; the first two reigns fell during a civil war with Alexăndrel. He came to the throne by assassinating Bogdan II while Bogdan was at a wedding in Rauseni, and he later forced Alexăndrel to take refuge in the fortress of Cetatea Albă.

He confirmed the commercial privileges his father had granted to Polish traders in Moldavia and took an oath of vassalage to King Casimir IV of Poland. In 1456, to secure his southern borders, he agreed to pay the Ottomans a tribute of 2,000 gold ducats. He also issued new billon and copper coins on the grosh design but struck in better silver, probably as part of a reform of monetary standards.

The real challenge came from Bogdan II's son, Ștefan cel Mare, who had been protected by John Hunyadi, captain-general of the Kingdom of Hungary, and, after Hunyadi's death, by Vlad the Impaler, the new Prince of Wallachia; on one reading of the Chronicle of Putna, Vlad offered Ștefan his full support. In April 1457, after two battles, Petru Aron was deposed and fled, first to Poland and then to the Székely Land, where he helped to raise tensions between Ștefan and King Matthias Corvinus of Hungary. He was later captured and executed.
petru-rares: Petru Rareș was probably born at Hârlău, the illegitimate child of Stephen the Great. His mother was Maria Răreșoaia of Hârlău, whose existence is not historically documented; she is said to have been the wife of a wealthy boyar fish-merchant nicknamed Rareș, so that Rareș was the husband's nickname and not Petru's own name. In his youth Petru was a fish merchant. Prince Ștefăniță, a grandson of Stephen the Great, recommended him on his deathbed as a suitable contender for the throne. He is said to have shared his father's ambition, daring and piety, but also to have been inconstant and lacking in political instinct.

Petru was voivode of Moldavia from 20 January 1527 to 18 September 1538 and again from 19 February 1541 to 3 September 1546. In the Hungarian contest between Ferdinand Habsburg and John Zápolya he first sided with Ferdinand, then switched to Zápolya when the Ottomans recognised him. He crushed Ferdinand's forces at Feldioara on 22 June 1529 but could not take Bistrița or Brașov. In 1530 he occupied Pokuttya, and Jan Tarnowski defeated him at Obertyn on 22 August 1531. In 1534 his vassal Huru delivered the Ottoman agent Lodovico Gritti to his enemies, who killed him.

In 1538 Petru was deserted by his boyars, his capital Iași was ablaze, and a Turkish, Tatar and Polish army under Suleiman the Magnificent brought Ștefan Lăcustă to the throne. Petru fled to his Transylvanian fortress of Ciceu. After more than two years he won the sultan's forgiveness and regained the throne in early 1541. He could no longer retake the Budjak, which Suleiman had occupied. In 1541 he seized the Transylvanian voivode István Majláth on the sultan's orders.

Petru lent 200,000 florins to Joachim II of Brandenburg for a proposed crusade against the Ottomans, which was abandoned when Buda was besieged in 1542. He died, still a Turkish vassal, on 3 September 1546 and is buried at Probota Monastery, which he endowed. Continuing the tradition of Stephen the Great and aided by his wife Jelena, he built and repaired churches at Baia, Botoșani, Hârlău, Târgu Frumos and Roman. Probota is considered his finest achievement. His sons Ilie II Rareș and Ștefan VI Rareș both became princes of Moldavia.
petun: The Petun emerged in the Late Ceramic period of Ontario archaeology, which began around 1,100 years ago, and belong with the Wendat and Neutral peoples to the Ontario Iroquois tradition. In that period farming grew in importance, settlements of longhouses were often enclosed by palisades, and burial customs came to include secondary burials and ossuaries. Shortly before contact with Europeans the northern groups had formed a Huron-Petun cultural grouping, distinct from the Neutrals and the Erie to the south.

Their name, Tionontati, is rendered as the people of the place where the mountain stands. The French name comes from pétun, a word of Tupi origin for tobacco. Champlain first used it for one village he visited in 1616, but no contemporary French account mentions tobacco growing among the Petun, and the claim first appears in notes to a map of 1632.

Like the Wendat, the Petun formed a tribal confederacy, made up of two groups the Jesuits called the Nation of the Wolves and the Nation of the Deer. Champlain counted about eight villages in 1616 and the Jesuits nine in 1639. One modern estimate puts their number at about 8,000, falling to about 3,000 by 1640 after epidemics. The Jesuit missionaries noted that the Wendat and Petun were close allies who had once fought bitter wars with each other. The Petun were also allied with the Neutrals and the Odawa, and in 1652 the Jesuit Relations described tattooing as almost universal among them.

The French traded chiefly with the Wendat, which kept the Petun from direct access to European goods. During the Beaver Wars the Haudenosaunee, supplied with Dutch firearms, destroyed the Wendat villages in 1648 and 1649, and Wendat refugees fled to the Petun. By the end of 1649 the Haudenosaunee had turned on the Petun as well. Many survivors were absorbed into Haudenosaunee society, while a large group of Petun and Wendat took refuge with the Odawa and Potawatomi in the upper Great Lakes. Moving by stages to the Detroit area and Lake Erie, they became one people known as the Wyandot. The federally recognised Wyandotte Nation of Oklahoma regards itself as descended chiefly from the Petun.
peugeot: The Peugeot family of Valentigney, near Montbéliard in Franche-Comté, began manufacturing in 1810 with a steel foundry, which soon made saws and other hand tools. Around 1840 to 1842 it added coffee grinders. In the 1850s it introduced waist corsets made with light steel blades, in 1874 pepper grinders, and about 1880 bicycles. On 20 November 1858 Émile Peugeot applied for the lion trademark, and in 1882 Armand Peugeot introduced the penny-farthing called Le Grand Bi, with a range of other bicycles.

Armand Peugeot became interested in the automobile early, after meeting Gottlieb Daimler and others. The first Peugeot car, a three-wheeled steam car designed by Léon Serpollet, appeared in 1889, and only four were made, since steam power was heavy and slow to warm up. In 1890, after meeting Daimler and Émile Levassor, Peugeot abandoned steam for a four-wheeled car with a petrol engine built by Panhard under Daimler licence. One was sold to the young Alberto Santos-Dumont, who exported it to Brazil. Automobiles Peugeot was created in 1896. The company had a long record in racing, including victories at the Indianapolis 500 in 1913, 1916 and 1919.

During the Second World War Peugeot made armoured vehicles for the German war effort, while its management was generally sympathetic to the French Resistance. Workers sabotaged production, and Rudolphe and Jean-Pierre Peugeot lent one hundred thousand francs to the Special Operations Executive agent Harry Rée. After a bombing raid in July 1943 that left 110 dead, management agreed with Rée to continue sabotage at the Sochaux plant to avoid further bombing. Car production restarted in 1946 with the 202, and the 203 of 1947 remained in production until 1960. The 403 of 1955 sold a million copies, and the 404 of 1960 won the East African Safari Rally four times.

In 1974 Peugeot bought 30% of Citroën and took it over completely in 1975, forming the PSA Peugeot Citroën group. The Peugeot 205, launched in 1983, is largely credited with turning the company's fortunes around, and the 206 became the best-selling Peugeot model of all time, with 8,358,217 cars sold by 2012.

Peugeot's Sochaux plant is still a large manufacturing site and houses the Peugeot Museum. Peugeot cars have won six European Car of the Year awards, the first for the 504 in 1969 and the second for the 405 in 1988.
pevensey-castle: The fort stands on a spur of sand and clay about 10 metres above sea level, which in Roman times was a peninsula projecting into a tidal lagoon and marshes. Silting and reclamation of the Pevensey Levels have since pushed the coast out by about 1.5 kilometres, leaving the castle inland. It covers about 3.67 hectares in an oval of 290 by 170 metres, the largest of the nine Saxon Shore forts, with walls up to 8.2 metres high and 4.2 metres thick at the base. Ten D-shaped towers survive on the north-eastern and western sides, where the site was most exposed.

Wooden piles found under the walls in 1994 date the fort, named Anderitum in the Notitia Dignitatum, to around 290, and it seems to have been the base of a fleet, the Classis Anderidaensis. It was long linked to defence against Saxon and Jute pirates, but coins of Carausius and Allectus in its foundations have led to the suggestion that these usurpers built it to keep out Rome. Civilians appear to have moved inside after the Roman army left in 410, and finds show they imported wares from as far as Macedonia and Syria.

William the Conqueror's army sheltered there on the night of 28 September 1066 before marching on Hastings. The Normans divided the interior into an inner and an outer bailey; the stone keep may date from the 1190s, though a Tower of Pevensey is mentioned in 1130. Its garrison was twice starved into surrender, but it was never stormed. King John had it slighted around 1216 during the First Barons' War, when he could not hold it against Prince Louis of France, and in 1587 guns were placed in the outer bailey against the Spanish threat.

In 1925 the 9th Duke of Devonshire gave the castle to the state, and it is now a scheduled monument in the care of English Heritage, open to visitors. One of the two Elizabethan iron demi-culverins, marked with a Tudor rose and the initials E.R., is mounted in the inner bailey. Machine-gun posts built into the walls between 1940 and 1945, when the castle was garrisoned against a German invasion, can still be seen.
pfalzgrafenstein-castle: The castle stands on Falkenau island. Its central tower is pentagonal, 36 metres high with six storeys, shaped to break waves and ice since it first stood alone. The outer wall, 2.60 metres thick, gives the castle a footprint of 51 by 21 metres. To force payment, chain booms were raised across the narrow river passage; a ship that refused was seized and its crew held in the dungeon, a wooden raft at the bottom of a well, until a ransom was paid. The wider channel could not be used because of dangerous water downstream, and the tolls themselves were paid at a customs house in Kaub.

The tower threatened the tolls that the bishops of Mainz, Trier and Cologne collected at the Mouse Tower at Bingen and at Stolzenfels Castle, and Pope John XXII urged them to excommunicate King Ludwig IV the Bavarian and act against the toll at Kaub, though nothing was done. The dispute probably led Ludwig to add the six-sided wall around the tower in about 1340. In 1339 he gave the castle to his nephew Rudolph II, the Elector Palatine. In 1504, during the War of the Succession of Landshut, it withstood a 39-day siege by Landgrave William II of Hesse unscathed.

Elector Friedrich IV added a gun bastion in 1607, making it the first Middle Rhine castle adapted to modern guns. Spanish forces under General Spinola took it without a fight in 1620 and held it until Hessian forces forced their surrender in January 1632. The baroque tower cap was added in 1714. In 1803 the castle passed to the House of Nassau, and on 1 January 1814 Russian engineers built a pontoon bridge by the island for Field-Marshal von Blücher's army of 60,000 men to cross in pursuit of Napoleon. After Prussia annexed Nassau in 1866, toll collection ended in 1867.

The castle has belonged to the state of Rhineland-Palatinate since 1946 and was restored between 1967 and 1975. It is a public museum, reached by ferry from Kaub, and lies in the Rhine Gorge, added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in June 2002. Victor Hugo described it as a stone ship, eternally floating on the Rhine.
pforzheim: Pforzheim lies at the northern rim of the eastern Black Forest and the edge of the hilly Kraichgau, in an open valley where the rivers Enz, Nagold and Würm meet. Because of this it is called the three-valleys town and the Gateway to the Black Forest. It stands about halfway between Stuttgart and Karlsruhe, on the border of Baden and Württemberg, on the Baden side. Romans settled the site earlier than the present centres of Stuttgart and Karlsruhe, and built a ford just past the confluence of the three rivers for their military highway.

Its position later made Pforzheim a centre of the timber-rafting trade, which carried logs from the Black Forest down the Enz, Nagold and Würm, the Neckar and the Rhine, to markets that included the Netherlands, where the timber was used in shipbuilding and for the foundations of Amsterdam. Guilds of tailors, bakers, weavers, wine-growers, skippers and timber raftsmen were founded between 1410 and 1512. In 1501 Margrave Christoph I of Baden-Baden issued an ordinance on the rafting profession. Margrave Karl II installed the Protestant Reformation in the Margraviate of Baden in 1556, when Pforzheim was its capital, and the town stayed Protestant for centuries.

In 1618 Pforzheim had an estimated 2,500 to 3,000 inhabitants and was the largest town in Baden. In 1645, near the end of the Thirty Years' War, Bavarian troops burned the old town. In 1718 an institution for orphans, the sick and the poor opened in the former Dominican convent by the Enz; some fifty years later it became the starting point of the town's jewellery and watchmaking industries. In 1836 Ferdinand Öchsle invented a device for measuring the sugar content of grape juice, still used in winemaking. Watchmaking revived from 1900 and thrived in the 1920s.

Pforzheim is a city of more than 135,000 inhabitants in Baden-Württemberg, known as the Goldstadt for its jewellery and watchmaking. On the evening of 23 February 1945 the Royal Air Force carried out the largest of its air raids on the city, one of the most devastating area bombardments of the Second World War. About 17,600 people, nearly a third of the population, were killed, and about 83 per cent of the buildings were destroyed. The Allies believed that precision instruments were made there and that the town was a transport centre.

After French occupation it was administered by the United States from 1945 to 1948, and was rebuilt over the following twenty years. The rubble was heaped on the Wallberg hill, where a monument stands.
pha-that-luang: Pha That Luang, meaning Great Stupa, stands about 4 km from the centre of Vientiane at the end of Pha That Luang Road. According to tradition, Buddhist missionaries from the Mauryan Empire were sent by Emperor Ashoka, among them Bury Chan, also called Praya Chanthabury Pasithisak, and five Arahanta monks, who brought a relic believed to be the Buddha's breastbone and enshrined it in the stupa.

In the 16th century King Setthathirat moved his capital from Luang Prabang to Vientiane and ordered the construction of the temple in 1566. Its bases were each 69 metres long, and the stupa stood 45 metres high, surrounded by 30 smaller stupas.

In 1641 Gerrit van Wuysthoff, an envoy of the Dutch East India Company, visited Vientiane and was received ceremonially at the temple by King Sourigna Vongsa. He wrote that he was particularly impressed by the enormous pyramid, whose top was covered with gold leaf weighing about a thousand pounds. The stupa was repeatedly plundered by the Burmese, Siamese and Chinese.

It was destroyed in the Thai invasion of 1828. Not until 1900 did the French restore it to its original design, working from detailed drawings made in 1867 by the French architect and explorer Louis Delaporte. That first attempt was unsuccessful, and the stupa had to be redesigned and rebuilt in the 1930s.

The monument rises in three levels. The first measures 223 by 226 feet (68 by 69 metres), the second 157 feet (48 metres) along each side, and the third 98 feet (30 metres) along each side. From ground to pinnacle it is 147.6 feet (45.0 metres) high.

The area around the stupa is gated to keep out traffic, though visitors could once drive around the whole complex. The encircling walls are roughly 279 feet (85 metres) long on each side and contain Lao and Khmer sculptures, including one of Jayavarman VII.
phags-pa-script: The ʼPhags-pa script, also written Phagspa, is an alphabet designed by the Tibetan monk Drogön Chögyal Phagpa (1235-1280) for Kublai Khan (r. 1264-1294), the founder of the Yuan dynasty, as a unified script for the written languages within the Yuan. The Mongol rulers wanted a universal script for the languages of the peoples they had subjugated. The Uyghur-based Mongolian alphabet did not fit Middle Mongol perfectly, and it would have been impractical to extend it to a language with a very different phonology such as Chinese.

Around 1269 Kublai Khan therefore asked Phagpa to design a new alphabet for the whole empire. He extended his native Tibetan alphabet to cover Mongol and Chinese, and the result was 38 letters, later counted as 41 basic letters, known by names such as square script.

The script descends from the Tibetan script and belongs to the Brahmic family, but it is unusual in being written from top to bottom. Although it is an alphabet, it is written like a syllabary or abugida, with the letters of a syllable linked into syllabic blocks.

Unlike Tibetan, all its letters are written in the order in which they are spoken and in line, and vowels are not diacritics. Short /a/ is not written except at the start of a word, which makes the script transitional between an abugida, a syllabary and a full alphabet. Letters 1-30 follow the traditional order of the thirty basic Tibetan letters. It was written in a standard blocky form, a still blockier Tibetan form and an elaborate seal form used on imperial seals.

It was used to write and transcribe varieties of Chinese, Tibetic languages, Mongolian, Uyghur, Sanskrit and probably Persian. It never gained wide acceptance, even among the Mongol elite, but it remained an official script of the Yuan dynasty until the early 1350s, when the Red Turban Rebellion began. It then served mainly as a phonetic gloss for Mongols learning Chinese characters, and its actual use lasted about a hundred years before it fell out of use with the Ming dynasty.
