The islands lie on the western fringes of the Pacific Ring of Fire, with 23 active volcanoes and about five recorded earthquakes a day, most too weak to be felt. On an expedition of the 16th century Ruy López de Villalobos named Leyte and Samar Felipinas after the Prince of Asturias, later Philip II of Castile, and the name Las Islas Filipinas was later used for the Spanish possessions. The title Republic of the Philippines appeared in the 1935 constitution.

Evidence of early hominins dates to as early as 709,000 years ago, and bones from Callao Cave may represent an unknown species, Homo luzonensis, who lived 50,000 to 67,000 years ago. The first Austronesians reached the islands from Taiwan around 2200 BCE and settled the Batanes Islands and northern Luzon. The earliest known surviving written record is the Laguna Copperplate Inscription of 900 CE, in Old Malay. By the 14th century large coastal settlements had become trading centres, trade with China had begun under the late Tang dynasty and widened under the Song, and Islam was established in the Sulu Archipelago by the 15th century.

Ferdinand Magellan's arrival marked the beginning of Spanish colonization. Catholicism became the dominant religion, and Manila became the western hub of trans-Pacific trade. The Philippine Revolution began in 1896 and became entwined with the Spanish–American War of 1898, after which Spain ceded the territory to the United States and revolutionaries declared the First Philippine Republic. The ensuing Philippine–American War left the United States in control until the Japanese invasion in the Second World War, and the Philippines became independent in 1946.

Ferdinand Marcos ruled under martial law from 1972 to 1981, and the People Power Revolution overthrew him in 1986. The Philippines is a constitutional republic with a presidential system, in which the president serves a six-year term, and its population was 112,729,484 in July 2024. The largest ethnic group in the 2020 census was the Tagalog, at 26.0 percent, and indigenous peoples comprise 110 ethnolinguistic groups. Spanish and American rule left lasting marks, among them the dominance of Catholicism, the use of English and Spanish surnames resulting from an 1849 edict.
philips: Philips & Co. was founded in Eindhoven in 1891 by Gerard Philips and his father Frederik Philips to make incandescent electric lamps. Gerard's younger brother Anton Philips joined in 1895 and helped expand the commercial side. The business became N.V. Philips' Gloeilampenfabrieken on 11 September 1912, and in 1914 it opened a physics laboratory, later called the NatLab, whose research fed its later work in lighting, radio and medical X-ray equipment. Queen Wilhelmina gave it the Dutch Royal designation in 1916, though Koninklijke entered its legal name only in 1998. In 1924 it joined Osram and other lamp makers in the Phoebus cartel. The Philips Sports Association, which includes the football club PSV Eindhoven, was founded in 1913 for its employees.

In March 1927 experimental shortwave transmissions from the Philips laboratories, using the PCJJ transmitter, were received in the Dutch East Indies, and Eddie Startz began presenting the Happy Station through it in 1928. In 1939 the company introduced the Philishave rotary shaver, invented by its engineer Alexandre Horowitz. Its laboratory also helped revive the Stirling engine, first as a possible power source for portable radios; by the late 1940s it had built a generator set known as the MP1002CA, or Bungalow set.

After the German invasion of the Netherlands in May 1940, several senior executives left the country, while Frits Philips, son of Anton Philips, stayed in Eindhoven. On 6 December 1942 the Royal Air Force carried out Operation Oyster, a low-level raid on Philips sites that produced components for the German war economy. It severely damaged the works and caused substantial civilian casualties in surrounding parts of Eindhoven.

After the war Philips grew into a major maker of televisions, audio equipment and other consumer electronics. In August 1963 it introduced its first Compact Cassette recorder at the Funkausstellung in Berlin, and in the early 1970s the N1500 videocassette recorder, described by the Science Museum Group as the first practical domestic video recorder. In 1984 it and ASM International founded ASM Lithography, later ASML, and in 1987 it joined in founding TSMC. After heavy losses it announced in 1990, under Jan Timmer, plans to cut about 10,000 jobs. In the 2010s it moved towards health technology, transferring most of its television business to TP Vision in 2012 and separating its lighting business in 2016, later renamed Signify.

Philips introduced the compact cassette format, which became a widely adopted standard for tape recording, and later worked with Sony to develop the compact disc standard. It also held a controlling interest in PolyGram, sold to Seagram in 1998. Its headquarters moved from Eindhoven to Amsterdam from 1998, after a decision in October 1997.
philistines: The Philistines lived along the southern coast of Canaan during the Iron Age, in a confederation of city-states called Philistia. Their identity seems to have begun with the arrival in Canaan of a migrant group from the Aegean, thought to have settled around 1175 BCE amid the Late Bronze Age collapse and to have mixed with the indigenous Canaanite societies. Egyptian sources name one of the Sea Peoples as the Peleset, and Ramesses III is said to have settled some of them in southern Canaan after his victory at the Battle of the Delta, around 1175 BCE. Excavation has not confirmed such a settlement.

The Hebrew Bible says the Philistines came from Caphtor, possibly Crete. Most scholars agree on an Aegean origin, because the figurines, pottery and fire-stands of the Philistine strata resemble Aegean ones. A minority holds that the similarities result from later contact. A study of skeletons at Ashkelon in 2019 found that most of their ancestry came from the local Levantine population, with a Southern-European-related share that suggests an influx in the 12th century BCE.

Philistia was a pentapolis of five city-states, Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Ekron and Gath, from Wadi Gaza in the south to the Yarqon River in the north. The Philistines are known chiefly from the Hebrew Bible, which tells of their wars with the Israelites. In it they dominate the Israelites in the time of Samson, capture the Ark of the Covenant at Aphek and keep it for several months, forbid Israelite blacksmiths so that weapons had to be sharpened by the Philistines, and kill King Saul and his sons at Mount Gilboa. The same books tell that David defeated Goliath near the Valley of Elah.

The Philistines came under the rule of the Neo-Assyrian Empire and were vassals of the Assyrians, the Egyptians and then the Babylonians. In 604 BCE Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon defeated them, and the sources suggest that his armies destroyed Ashkelon and Ekron after a revolt and exiled much of the population. By the late 5th century BCE the Philistines no longer appear as a distinct group, though how far they were assimilated is debated.

Excavated Philistine cities show careful town planning with industrial zones. Ekron alone had about 200 olive oil installations, and breweries, wineries and shops selling beer and wine are attested, while complex objects of gold, bronze and iron show skilled metalworking. The Philistines worshipped deities already known in Canaan, among them Baal, Astarte, Asherah and Dagon. Their language is poorly attested. Most Philistine names are Semitic, but Goliath, Achish and Phicol seem non-Semitic, and some scholars suggest that the Philistines first spoke an Indo-European language.
philitas-of-cos: Little is known of the life of Philitas, whom ancient sources call a Coan, a native or long-time inhabitant of Cos. His student Theocritus gave his father's name as Telephos. The Suda yields an estimated birth about 340 BCE. Ptolemy had captured Cos in 310 BCE during the Wars of the Diadochi, and his son Ptolemy II Philadelphus was born there in 308 BCE. Philitas was appointed Philadelphus' tutor, which suggests he moved to Alexandria about 297/6 BCE and returned to Cos in the later 290s BCE. He also taught the poets Hermesianax and Theocritus and the grammarian Zenodotus, and after his return he seems to have led for at least ten years a brotherhood of intellectuals and poets that included Aratus.

Philitas wrote a vocabulary of rare literary words, local dialect words and technical terms, probably a lexicon, called Disorderly Words. Only a few fragments survive. About thirty fragments of his poetry are known, with four definite titles. Demeter, his best-regarded work, was in elegiac couplets and seems to have told of Demeter's search for Persephone and her welcome on Cos by its royal family of Meropids. Hermes was a short mythological narrative in hexameter, telling of Odysseus' visit to Aeolus, keeper of the winds, and his secret affair with the king's daughter Polymele. Playthings held shorter poems in the form of epigrams. At most fifty verses survive.

Philitas seems to have died on Cos in the 280s BCE. He was the first person known to be called both poet and scholar, and as tutor to Philadelphus he is assumed to have influenced the Mouseion at Alexandria. Theocritus and Callimachus acknowledged his work as a classic, and he directly influenced Callimachus and Apollonius of Rhodes. Propertius linked him with Callimachus, and Quintilian ranked him second only to Callimachus among elegiac poets. Almost all his writing seems to have vanished within two centuries. A marble bust found at Crest in 1770, a Roman copy of a lost bronze, is thought to be his only portrait, and is in the Louvre.
philo-of-alexandria: Philo's dates of birth and death are unknown. He called himself old when he joined the delegation to the emperor Gaius Caligula, and a reference to an event under Claudius suggests that he died between 45 and 50 CE. His family was noble and wealthy. Either his father or his paternal grandfather was granted Roman citizenship by Julius Caesar, and Jerome wrote that he came from a priestly family. His brother Alexander Lysimachus was the tax administrator of customs in Alexandria, a friend of the emperor Claudius and, it was said, the richest man in the city.

Philo was educated in the Hellenistic culture of Alexandria, in the traditions of Judaism and in Greek philosophy. Plato was his largest philosophical influence, above all the Timaeus and the Phaedrus, and he also drew on the Stoics, Homer, Euripides and Demosthenes. He read the Jewish scriptures chiefly in the Greek Septuagint, and how much Hebrew he knew is debated.

He lived in an era of ethnic tension in Alexandria. Some Greeks condemned the Jews for a supposed alliance with Rome, while Rome sought to suppress Jewish identity in Judaea. According to Josephus, the Alexandrian Jewish community chose Philo as their chief representative before Caligula after civil disorder between Jews and Greeks. Josephus says that he and the community refused to treat the emperor as a god or to build statues, altars and temples for him. This is the only event of his life that can be dated with certainty. Philo also recounts that he visited the Second Temple in Jerusalem at least once.

Philo wrote in Greek on philosophy, politics and religion. He used allegory to harmonise the Hebrew Bible, mainly the Torah, with Greek philosophy, following the practice of both Jewish exegesis and Stoicism, though he also often favoured a literal reading. He held the Bible to be the source of all truth and Moses its true medium of revelation. His God is transcendent, without physical features or human emotions, unchangeable and beyond time and space. His Logos has a special relation to humans, as an interpreter of God's designs and a pattern for the shaping of the mind.

About fifty of his works survive and twenty to twenty-five are lost. Most are commentaries on the Torah, among them the Quaestiones on Genesis and Exodus, which survive in Armenian, an Allegorical Commentary on Genesis and an Exposition of the Law. Others include On the Life of Moses and the historical works Ad Flaccum and De legatione ad Gaium.

Early Church Fathers such as Clement of Alexandria and Origen used his work to connect the Bible with philosophy, and Eusebius, Jerome and Ambrose cited him extensively. Rabbinic Judaism gave him little attention.
philo-of-byblos: Philo was born in the 1st century in Byblos, in what is now Lebanon. He lived into the reign of Hadrian, of which he wrote a history that is now lost. His Roman name, Herennius, suggests that he was a client of the consul suffectus Herennius Severus, through whom he may have gained the status of a Roman citizen. He is known as an antiquarian who wrote grammatical, lexical and historical works in Greek.

Philo wrote a dictionary of synonyms, a collection of scientific writers and their works arranged by category, a catalogue of cities with their notable citizens, and a Life of the Emperor Hadrian. Some of his writings are known by title only, and others survive in fragmentary quotations in Christian authors. The catalogue of cities was epitomized by the grammarian Aelius Serenus and was one of the chief authorities of Hesychius and Stephanus of Byzantium. An epitome of On Synonyms by Ammonius Grammaticus survives.

He is chiefly known for the Phoenician History, called the Phoenicica, which he presented as a translation of the work of Sanchuniathon, said to have lived before the Trojan War. Considerable fragments were preserved by Eusebius in the Praeparatio evangelica. They give a euhemeristic reworking of Phoenician theology and mythology. According to Eusebius, Philo found secret mythological writings that Sanchuniathon had transcribed from pillars in the temples of Byblos. Porphyry added that Sanchuniathon wrote a history of the Jews, using information from a priest named Hierombalus, and dedicated it to Abelbal, king of Berytus.

Eusebius often quoted the Phoenician History to disparage Phoenician religion, so his purpose differed from Philo's. The fragments mix Phoenician lore with Greek mythology, Zoroastrian beliefs and Egyptian ideas about the ibis-headed god Thoth, whom Philo calls Taautos or Tauthos and describes as everlasting, unbegotten and undivided. The order of the gods and their genealogy long seemed to support the scheme of Hesiod's Theogony.

Some scholars thought Sanchuniathon an imaginary figure whose name was formed from that of the god Sanchon. P. B. R. Forbes of Edinburgh argued that documents from Ugarit of the 14th century BCE, published since 1929, showed Sanchuniathon to be real, because of the many correspondences with them.
philo-of-byzantium: Philo was a Greek engineer, physicist and writer on mechanics of the latter half of the 3rd century BCE, also called Philo Mechanicus, Latin for Philo the Engineer. Though he came from Byzantium he spent most of his life in Alexandria in Egypt. He was probably younger than Ctesibius, although some place him a century earlier.

His large work, the Syntaxis, or System of mechanics, had nine parts: an introduction on general mathematics, and treatises on leverage, harbour construction, siege engine construction, pneumatics, the construction of automatons, preparations for sieges, siegecraft, and correspondence, including coding and hidden letters for military use. The military sections, on missiles and the construction of fortresses, provisioning, attack and defence, survive in Greek, as do fragments of the introduction and of the automatons. The pneumatic section survives in a Latin translation of an Arabic translation, and further portions probably survive in derivative form in Vitruvius and Arabic authors.

Recent research suggests that a section of the Pneumatics once regarded as a later Arabic addition contains the first description of a water mill, placing its invention by the Greeks in the mid-3rd century BCE. His works also contain the oldest known chain drive, in a repeating crossbow whose two flat-linked chains were wound back and forth on a windlass to fire arrows until the magazine was empty. He is said to be the first to describe a gimbal, in an eight-sided ink pot, and the earliest known escapement, in a washstand, remarking that it resembles the construction of clocks. He is also credited with an early thermoscope.

In mathematics he took up the doubling of the cube, which arises from needing a second catapult that fires a projectile twice as heavy. He solved it by finding the intersection of a rectangular hyperbola and a circle, and the Philo line is attributed to him. A treatise on the Seven Wonders of the World sometimes attributed to him more probably belongs to a different Philo of Byzantium, perhaps of the 4th or 5th century CE.
philopoemen: Philopoemen was born at Megalopolis, the son of Craugis, whose death left him to be adopted by an important citizen of the city, Cleander. His teachers were the academic philosophers Ecdemus and Demophanes, Megapolitans who had helped to depose tyrants, and he absorbed ideas of freedom and democracy.

He strove to emulate the Theban general Epaminondas and held that a public servant must be personally virtuous, so he wore humble clothes all his life and spurned expensive adornment. He first came to notice in 223 BCE when he helped defend Megalopolis against the Spartan king Cleomenes III, losing his horse and being wounded but fighting on until the citizens had time to evacuate.

At the Battle of Sellasia, Philopoemen led a cavalry force that attacked when the Illyrian infantry were surrounded, and he fought on behind enemy lines after a javelin wound. The Spartans were massacred and Cleomenes fled to Egypt. From 221 BCE he spent ten years in Crete as a mercenary captain. Returning in 210 BCE, he became cavalry commander of the Achaean League and killed Damophantus, who led Aetolians and Eleans, with a lance thrust.

Appointed strategos in 209 BCE, he modernised and enlarged the Achaean army, updating its equipment and tactics. At the Battle of Mantinea in 207 BCE the Achaeans defeated the Spartans, and Philopoemen killed their ruler Machanidas in single combat. The Achaeans set up a bronze statue of the fight at Delphi.

He later drove the successor Nabis from Messene, and after a second spell as a mercenary leader in Crete, of six years, was again strategos from 193 BCE to fight Nabis. When Aetolians murdered Nabis and briefly held Sparta, Philopoemen entered the city with his army and forced Sparta into the League. In 188 BCE his army demolished Nabis's wall, he restored the exiles, abolished Spartan law and education and introduced Achaean institutions.

These measures provoked opposition even among his supporters in Sparta, whose opponents appealed to the Roman Senate. Philopoemen and his supporters rejected every Roman proposal, arguing that Rome had recognised the League's independence by treaty, and Achaean politics split. When Messene revolted under Dinocrates, Philopoemen marched against them, was thrown from his horse behind enemy lines, captured and invited to drink poison. The League's members then joined forces and took Messene. His body was cremated and the historian Polybius carried the urn at the public funeral, later writing his biography. Pausanias wrote that after his death Greece ceased to bear good men.
phitsanulok: Phitsanulok lies in the geographic centre of its province, on the fertile plains along the Nan River, which flows south to join the Chao Phraya. It grew from an older settlement called Song Khwae, meaning two rivers, because it stood between the Nan and the Khwae Noi, which now drains into the Nan ten kilometres to the north. The name Phitsanulok comes from Sanskrit Vishnu and loka, world, and may loosely be translated as Vishnu's heaven.

The area is one of the oldest in Thailand. A moated Dvaravati settlement, Muang Yommarat, lay eight kilometres north-west of the present centre. The Northern Chronicles credit King Thammaracha I of Sukhothai with founding Song Khwae, building Wat Phra Si Rattana Mahathat and casting the Buddha images Phra Buddha Chinnarat and Phra Buddha Chinnasri. Song Khwae became the royal seat of the Sukhothai Kingdom in 1378. After the last king of Sukhothai died there in 1438, Prince Ramesuan of Ayutthaya ruled it, and in 1448, when he was crowned King Trailokanat, it was incorporated into Ayutthaya.

During the war between Ayutthaya and Lanna, Trailokanat moved his residence to Song Khwae, renamed it Phitsanulok and expanded it to the west bank of the Nan. In the sixteenth century it was the seat of the heir to the Ayutthaya throne. Its ruler submitted to Burma's King Bayinnaung in 1563, and in 1584 Prince Naresuan ordered the evacuation of the cities of the Sukhothai region before a Burmese invasion; Phitsanulok was abandoned until 1593.

After Ayutthaya fell in 1767 a monk, Chao Phra Fang, ruled the town as a local lord until King Taksin of Thonburi took it in 1768. A Burmese siege destroyed it in 1775, and it lay in ruins and depopulated through the nineteenth century; the Phuan people were deported from Laos in 1834 to resettle the region. It became the seat of a monthon in 1894 and of Phitsanulok Province in 1932.

Wat Phra Si Rattana Mahathat, known as Wat Yai, built in 1357, houses Phra Buddha Chinnarat, one of the most revered and most copied Buddha images in Thailand. Chan Palace was the birthplace of King Naresuan, and a shrine to him stands there. The city lies on the Northern Line between Bangkok and Chiang Mai, and Naresuan University, named after the king, is the main university of the lower north.
phnom-kulen: Phnom Kulen, whose name means the mountain of the lychees, is less a range of hills than an isolated chain of small plateaux south of the Dângrêk Mountains. It runs for about 40 kilometres from west-north-west to east-south-east, and its flat top lies at about 400 metres, rising to some 500 metres at its highest point. The rock is sandstone, quarried in Angkorian times mainly in the south-eastern corner of the massif; the Samré people, who once lived at the mountain's edge, cut the stone and carried it to the royal sites.

Phnom Kulen is honoured in Cambodia as the birthplace of the Khmer Empire, and Jayavarman II is held to have begun there the Devaraja, a royal cult of the linga. Scholars debate whether the Java from which he declared independence was the island or Champa, which the Khmer word chvea could also mean. Under Udayadityavarman II the mountain became the capital, with many temples and residences and the thousand lingas of Kbal Spean, and at its height the settlement on Kulen was among the largest cities of the 11th-century world. Angkor later eclipsed it, but its waters still irrigated the whole region. In 1979 the Khmer Rouge made it one of their last strongholds during the Cambodian–Vietnamese War.

The mountain is a holy place for Hindu and Buddhist pilgrims and lies within Phnom Kulen National Park, set up to preserve its scenery and waterfalls. At Kbal Spean the riverbed carvings include Vishnu lying on the serpent Ananta with Lakshmi at his feet and Brahma rising on a lotus from his navel. The 16th-century monastery of Preah Ang Thom holds a reclining Buddha 8 metres high, the largest in the country, and other rock sites such as Peung Tbal and the elephant sculpture of Srah Damrei date from the 8th or 9th century. The site was placed on Cambodia's Tentative List for World Heritage on 27 March 2020.
phnom-penh: Phnom Penh lies in the south-central region of Cambodia, on the banks of the Tonlé Sap, the Mekong and the Bassac rivers, and is fully surrounded by Kandal province. It is a typical flood plain, and flooding in the monsoon season is a problem when the river sometimes overflows its banks. The city takes its name from Wat Phnom, the hill temple, and from Lady Penh, its founder.

Excavations at Choeung Ek, in the south of the city, uncovered one of the largest kiln pottery centres in Cambodia, which produced ceremonial vessels from the 5th to the 13th century, and suggest settlement from the 5th century. According to a tale first recorded a century after it is said to have taken place, a woman named Penh found a floating koki tree in the river in 1372. Inside it were four Buddha statues and one of Vishnu, and she raised a hill with a shrine to house them, later known as Wat Phnom.

King Ponhea Yat moved the capital here from Angkor Thom after Siam captured and destroyed it. Later kings abandoned Phnom Penh because of fighting between royal pretenders and set up their capitals at places such as Pursat, Longvek and Oudong. Japanese immigrants settled on the outskirts of the city in the 17th century, and a Portuguese community carried on commercial and religious activity there. It became the capital again in 1865 and was the national capital under French colonial rule. After independence it was modernized, and earned the nickname the Pearl of Asia for its French colonial, New Khmer and Art Deco architecture.

During the Vietnam War thousands of refugees fled to the city from the fighting, and by 1975 its population was two to three million. The Khmer Rouge cut off supplies for more than a year before the city fell on 17 April 1975, and then forcibly evacuated all its residents. The city faced persecution, forced labour and genocide, and remained largely uninhabited until Vietnam-backed forces took it in 1979, when people began to return. Reconstruction followed with foreign investment and aid.

Phnom Penh is the capital and most populous city of Cambodia and the seat of its monarchy at the Royal Palace. It is an autonomous municipality with a status equal to that of the provinces. The official language is Khmer, and English and French are also used. Its census population was 2,129,371 in 2019. Its Water Festival marks the reversing of the flow of the Tonlé Sap River, and the city holds buildings of the New Khmer Architecture of the 1950s and 1960s, associated with the architect Vann Molyvann.
phocaea: Phocaea was the northernmost of the Ionian cities, on the boundary with Aeolis, near the mouth of the river Hermus, now the Gediz. It stood on the peninsula that separates the Gulf of Cyme from the Gulf of Smyrna, now İzmir, and had two natural harbours, each with small islands, which allowed a seafaring economy and a strong navy. Surveys show a city that was large for the archaic period, and Herodotus describes its walls as several stadia long.

According to Pausanias, Phocians under Athenian leadership founded Phocaea on land given by the Aeolian people of Cyme, and the city entered the Ionian League after accepting the line of Codrus as kings. Herodotus calls the Phocaeans the first Greeks to make long sea voyages, to the coasts of the Adriatic, Tyrrhenia and Spain. He says that Arganthonios, king of Tartessos, invited them to settle in Spain and, when they declined, gave them money to build a wall around their city.

Their main colonies lay in the west: Massalia (Marseille), founded about 600 BCE, Emporion in Catalonia, dated to 575 BCE, Alalia on Corsica and Rhoda in Spain. They probably also helped to settle Amisos and Lampsacus and traded with Naucratis in Egypt. The Phocaeans were among the earliest users of coined money, which they first made in electrum.

The city stayed independent until the Lydian king Croesus, and then passed with the rest of mainland Ionia to the Persian king Cyrus the Great. Rather than submit, the Phocaeans abandoned it. Some may have fled to Chios or to the western colonies, and many founded Elea around 540 BCE. Phocaea joined the Ionian Revolt in 500 BCE, and a Phocaean named Dionysius commanded the Ionian fleet at Lade in 494 BCE, though the city supplied only three ships. It later paid two talents in tribute to the Delian League and rebelled with the rest of Ionia in 412 BCE.

Under Seleucid and then Attalid rule, and in the Roman period, Phocaea made the pottery known as Phocaean red slip. The Genoese ambassador Benedetto Zaccaria received the town as a hereditary lordship, and his family grew rich on its alum mines. It remained a Genoese colony until the Turks took it in 1455.
phocas: Phocas was most likely born in 547, since he was said to be 55 when he became emperor, and he was probably of Thraco-Roman or Cappadocian origin. His life before the usurpation is obscure, but he is said to have served as a centurion in the army in Thrace under Emperor Maurice. Late in Maurice's reign the army sent him to Constantinople as spokesman to complain about the conduct of the general Comentiolus; he argued with the emperor and had his beard pulled by an outraged patrician.

In autumn 602 the Thracian army rebelled, largely from exhaustion and outrage at orders to keep campaigning north of the Danube in winter, and at earlier wage cuts. The troops made Phocas their leader and marched on Constantinople. When riots broke out, Maurice and his family fled on a warship on the night of 22 November 602. Phocas was crowned by the patriarch Cyriacus on 23 November and entered the city on 25 November. Maurice and his sons were soon captured and executed, and Maurice's wife Constantina and their daughters were put to death around 605.

Phocas distrusted the elite of Constantinople, to whom he was a usurper and a provincial boor, and filled senior posts with relatives, among them his brother Domentziolus as magister officiorum in 603. The Sasanian Empire invaded the eastern provinces, and Phocas, dealing with conspiracies at home, could not stop them. When the general Narses defected to the Persians, Phocas invited him to Constantinople under a promise of safe conduct and had him burnt alive. The Balkan frontier stayed stable, and he made a treaty with the Avars in 604.

In 608 the general Priscus appealed to Heraclius the Elder, the exarch of Africa, to rebel. Heraclius cut off the grain supply to Constantinople and began his invasion in 609. His son Heraclius reached the capital on 3 October 610 and seized it on 5 October, when he was declared emperor and had Phocas executed. According to the sources, when Heraclius asked, "Is this how you have ruled, wretch?", Phocas replied, "And will you rule better?"

The surviving sources are universally hostile to Phocas, describing an incompetent tyrant who purged opposition and left the empire open to invaders. Some of the earliest were written under Heraclius, whose dynasty had an interest in blackening his reputation, so how far they can be trusted is hard to judge. Phocas was shown with a beard on coins, which became the convention until the end of the Byzantine Empire.
phocion: Phocion, nicknamed The Good, was the subject of one of Plutarch's Parallel Lives. In his youth he was a pupil of Plato and a friend of Xenocrates, but he first came to notice as a soldier. He served in the campaigns of the general Chabrias, who esteemed him, and in 376 BCE commanded the leading left wing in the Athenian naval victory at Naxos, the first clear Athenian victory since the Peloponnesian War.

In the Athenian Assembly he usually stood against the political class. When an oracle from Delphi said that one man would oppose all the others, he rose and said that he was that person. He was appointed strategos a record 45 times without canvassing for it. Sent to the Aegean to collect contributions for the Second Athenian League, he took only his own trireme and negotiated each payment so diplomatically that he returned with a large allied fleet.

Between 351 and 349 BCE he helped the Persian king Artaxerxes III subdue a Cypriot rebellion, and in 349 BCE he went to Euboea against Philip II of Macedon, whose bribes had corrupted local politicians. Later he was sent to the Dardanelles region, where Byzantium welcomed him on the guarantee of his friend Leon, and he liberated several cities from Macedonian garrisons.

Phocion held that Macedon was a rising power and opposed a foreign policy too hostile to it, against orators such as Demosthenes, Lycurgus and Hypereides. When Alexander was about to attack Thebes he urged caution, and after Thebes was destroyed he argued that the wrath of the conqueror must be reduced rather than opposed. In 323 BCE, when rumours of Alexander's death reached Athens, he warned against hasty celebration and opposed the Lamian War, though he shared the generalship with Leosthenes.

In the late 320s Macedon under Antipater gained complete control of Athens, and Phocion defended the city and its citizens and refused some dishonourable requests. In 319 BCE Antipater chose Polyperchon as his successor, and Cassander plotted against him. Nicanor took the Piraeus, and Phocion was accused of delaying action against him. Polyperchon sent him back to Athens, where the restored popular assembly sentenced him to death for treason.

He was known for incorruptibility; ancient sources report that he could have been very wealthy but was not. George Grote judged him severely, holding that during his fifty years of influence the Greeks fell from freedom into servitude and that Phocion helped Philip by sneering down Demosthenes's efforts.
phoenice: The city stood high on an almost impregnable hill commanding a fertile valley. It was the wealthiest city in Epirus and had the strongest walls until the Roman conquest. Its earliest walls were of massive blocks up to 3.6 metres thick, built against Corcyraeans and Illyrian raiders, and they were extended at the end of the 4th century BCE as part of the defences of Pyrrhus. Public buildings rose on the acropolis from the second half of the 5th century BCE, a large theatre was built in the 3rd century BCE, and the patron god was probably Athena Polias. The name, shared with at least 16 places of the Greek world, is of non-Indo-European origin.

After the assassination of Queen Deidamia II, last of the Aeacid dynasty, in about 233 BCE, the monarchy of Epirus was abolished and Phoenice became the centre of the federal government of the Epirote League. Teuta's Illyrians took the town when its garrison of 800 Gaulish mercenaries surrendered it, and defeated a relieving army of the league at the Battle of Phoenice. Their murder of Roman merchants there led in time to the First Illyrian War. In the Third Macedonian War the Chaonians and Thesprotians sided with Rome from Phoenice under Charops, and the city was spared the devastation that followed the Roman conquest of 167 BCE.

The Romans later renovated the city; its great cistern dates from the 2nd century CE. In the 5th and 6th centuries it was the see of a bishop, with a baptistery and a basilica, and Emperor Justinian I fortified a neighbouring hill. The city vanished after the 6th century, when the centre of the area moved to nearby Mesopotamon.

Excavations began in 1924 with an Italian mission under Luigi Ugolini, whose work served the ambitions of Fascist Italy, and resumed in 1958 with a joint Albanian-USSR team. Work in 1980 to 1981 uncovered the theatre, and excavations have continued since 2000. The city is now part of an archaeological park.
phoenicia: The Phoenicians were a Semitic-speaking people who inhabited city-states in Canaan along the Levantine coast, primarily in present-day Lebanon, with a cultural core stretching from Arwad to Mount Carmel. They emerged directly from the Bronze Age Canaanites and continued their cultural traditions into the Iron Age.

Phoenicia is a Greek name, from phoinix, that corresponded to no unified native identity: the independent city-states, notably Byblos, Sidon and Tyre, each kept their political autonomy, and a person was named by their city, as a Sidonian or a Tyrian. The inscriptions suggest that Phoenician speakers identified themselves by their native cities and families, though they may have called themselves Canaanites. Little Phoenician literature survives, so much of what is known comes from other civilizations and from excavation.

The first known account of the Phoenicians tells of the conquests of the pharaoh Thutmose III (1479–1425 BCE), who subjugated those the Egyptians called Fenekhu. The coastal cities gave Egypt access to Mesopotamian trade and to cedarwood, which had no equivalent in Egypt. The Late Bronze Age collapse between 1200 and 1150 BCE weakened or destroyed most civilizations in the region, but the Phoenician cities survived and filled the power vacuum, building a vast mercantile network.

By the end of the 11th century BCE an alliance between Tyre and Israel had created a new geopolitical order, and commerce now involved colonization. Carthage was founded from Tyre, with 814 BCE the date generally accepted by modern historians, and grew into an empire until Rome destroyed it in the Punic Wars (264–146 BCE).

Lacking the size and population to support a large military, the cities increasingly fell under the sway of neighbouring empires from the Assyrians onward. After Cyrus the Great took Babylon in 539 BCE, the Phoenicians submitted to the Persians. The area was divided into four vassal kingdoms, Sidon, Tyre, Arwad and Byblos, whose kings kept their offices and could mint coinage.

Alexander the Great conquered Phoenicia: Tyre capitulated after a siege of about seven months, and, after its refusal to let him visit the temple of Melqart led to the killing of his envoys, 2,000 of its leading citizens were crucified. Sidon surrendered peacefully. The Phoenicians' most enduring legacy is the earliest verified alphabet, which gave rise to the Greek alphabet and so to the Latin and Cyrillic scripts.
phoenician-alphabet: The earliest known proto-alphabetic inscriptions are in the Proto-Sinaitic script, sporadically attested in the Sinai Peninsula and in Canaan in the late Middle and Late Bronze Age. Its signs were inspired by Egyptian hieroglyphs. The Phoenician script continues the Proto-Canaanite script of the Bronze Age collapse period, and arrowheads found at al-Khader near Bethlehem, dated to about 1100 BCE, offer the missing link between the two. The Ahiram epitaph on a sarcophagus at Byblos, whose dating is controversial, shows an essentially fully developed script. The conventional date of 1050 BCE reflects a gap in the record: no Phoenician inscription is securely dated to the 11th century, and the oldest belong to the 10th.

The script is an abjad of 22 consonant letters that leaves vowels implicit, though late varieties sometimes used matres lectionis to mark some of them. It was the first script with a fixed writing direction, horizontally from right to left, whereas earlier systems ran in several directions. Letters were originally incised with a stylus and are mostly angular, with cursive forms growing more common over time and ending in the Neo-Punic alphabet of Roman North Africa. Each letter was named by acrophony: the second letter was based on the Egyptian sign for house, the Semitic word bet, and so took the sound b.

The numerals had separate signs for 1, 10, 20 and 100, and no zero. The script wrote Canaanite languages: Phoenician, Hebrew, Moabite, Ammonite and Edomite. It was used at Carthage until the 2nd century BCE, to write Punic.

From the 9th century BCE the alphabet was adapted into Greek, Old Italic and Anatolian scripts. Its strength was that one symbol stood for one sound, so only a few dozen signs had to be learned, while cuneiform and hieroglyphs needed long training and kept literacy to a small elite. Phoenician merchants carried it across the Mediterranean. Herodotus credits the prince Cadmus with bringing the letters to the Greeks. The Greeks added vowels, and from the Greek alphabet come the Latin, Cyrillic, Armenian and Georgian scripts. Aramaic, also descended from Phoenician, gave rise to the Hebrew and Syriac alphabets and, through Nabataean, to Arabic. The Samaritan alphabet is a direct continuation.

Jean-Jacques Barthélemy deciphered the script in 1758, though its link with the Phoenicians was not recognised until the 19th century. In 2005 UNESCO accepted the Phoenician alphabet on its Memory of the World register.
phoenix-islands: The Phoenix Islands, also called Rawaki, are eight atolls and two submerged coral reefs east of the Gilbert Islands and west of the Line Islands in the central Pacific, north of Samoa. Their combined land area is 28 square kilometres. Besides Canton, also called Kanton or Abariringa, the group includes Enderbury, Rawaki, Manra, Birnie, McKean, Nikumaroro and Orona. The name Phoenix came into use around the 1840s, generalised from one island named Phoenix earlier in the century, probably after the whaling ships of that name.

The islands had no permanent inhabitants until European colonisation, but archaeological sites on Manra and Orona show earlier settlement, probably from around 1000 BCE, and an ethnologist, K. P. Emory, estimated that two groups lived on Manra, one from eastern Polynesia and one from Micronesia. Basalt tools from Samoa, the Marquesas and the Cook Islands reached the Phoenix and Line Islands in the 12th to 14th centuries CE. The hard life on such isolated islands probably led to the extinction or emigration of these communities. Whalers charted the islands between 1821 and 1825, and the United States Exploring Expedition under Charles Wilkes surveyed them in the 1840s. Several were worked for guano, McKean until 1870 and Manra from 1884.

Most of the islands were annexed by Great Britain in the late 19th century. In 1937 Britain incorporated them into the Gilbert and Ellice Islands colony, except Howland and Baker, which the United States had claimed in 1935. In 1939 Britain and the United States agreed to govern Canton and Enderbury jointly, an arrangement that lasted until 1979. Canton was developed as a seaplane base and then as a refuelling station for trans-Pacific flights until 1958. Between 1938 and 1940 Orona, Manra and Nikumaroro were settled under the Phoenix Islands Settlement Scheme, the last colonial expansion attempted by the British Empire, to relieve overcrowding in the Gilbert Islands. The settlements were judged unworkable by 1963, and the population was moved to the Solomon Islands.

The islands became part of Kiribati when it gained independence in 1979, after the United States released its claims in the Treaty of Tarawa. They are uninhabited except for a few families on Canton. The Phoenix Islands Protected Area, established in 2008, is one of the largest protected marine areas in the world and is home to about 120 species of coral and more than 500 species of fish. McKean holds the world's largest nesting population of lesser frigatebirds, and Nikumaroro has drawn expeditions searching for traces of Amelia Earhart, who disappeared in 1937, though none has found conclusive proof.
phonograph: Sound recording began before the phonograph. Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville invented the phonautograph in 1857, a device that traced sound waves in graphic form on paper for visual study. On 30 April 1877 the French poet and inventor Charles Cros deposited a sealed envelope with the French Academy of Sciences describing how a traced line might be used to reproduce sound.

Thomas Edison conceived the principle of recording and reproducing sound between May and July 1877, as a by-product of efforts to play back recorded telegraph messages and to automate speech for transmission by telephone. He announced the invention on 21 November 1877, demonstrated it on 29 November, and patented it on 19 February 1878 as US Patent 200,521. His first machines recorded on tinfoil wrapped around a grooved cylinder, with the stylus indenting the foil in hill-and-dale variations. The first demonstrations astonished onlookers, one of them at the office of Scientific American in December 1877.

A phonograph records sound vibrations as corresponding deviations in a spiral or helical groove on a rotating cylinder or disc. To play it back, the surface is rotated while a stylus traces the groove and is vibrated by it. In early acoustic machines the stylus drove a diaphragm that sent sound through a flaring horn, or through stethoscope-type earphones. Terms differ by region: in American English, phonograph was properly the name for Edison's machines, and Emile Berliner's disc machine was the gramophone.

Edison's tinfoil machine was too hard to use well; the foil tore easily, reproduction was distorted and good for only a few playbacks, and he did not at once improve it. Alexander Graham Bell and two associates began work at the Volta Laboratory in Washington, D.C., in 1879 and were granted basic patents for recording in wax in 1886. The Volta Graphophone Company was created in January 1886, and American Graphophone, formed in March 1887, later evolved into Columbia Records.

From 1890 makers began to mass-produce cylinders by duplication, and a pantograph process could make 90 to 150 copies at once. In 1892 Berliner began commercial production of disc records and gramophones, five inches across at first. Discs were not inherently better than cylinders; their advantage was that they could be stamped and their matrices shipped to other plants, while cylinders could not be stamped until Edison's gold moulding process of 1901–1902. In the 1930s vinyl came into use for radio transcription discs, and the disc record was the dominant commercial audio format throughout most of the 20th century. Phonographs were the first home audio equipment that people owned in their residences.
phormio: Phormio was the son of Asopius. He first appears in 440 BCE, when he shared with Thucydides, Hagnon and others the command of the Athenian fleet in the later part of the Samian War. In 432 BCE he led 1,600 hoplites to the siege of Potidaea, approached slowly from the side the Athenians had not yet surrounded, and built a counter-wall that completed the city's investment. He then campaigned against Athens' enemies in the Chalcidice, and the next year attacked the Chalcidians again alongside Perdiccas II, king of Macedon.

Sent to the Corinthian Gulf with 20 triremes, he based himself at Naupactus and blockaded Corinthian shipping. Sparta prepared a fleet and army to overrun Acarnania, take Zacynthus and Cephallenia and perhaps Naupactus itself. When the Peloponnesian fleet of 47 ships, many loaded with heavy infantry, tried to cross from the south shore to the north in open water, it formed a defensive circle with prows outward. Phormio's ships circled it, driving it tighter at the risk of being rammed in the flank, until a wind made the inexperienced crews foul their oars; the Athenians then routed them and seized 12 ships.

Shortly afterwards he faced 77 Peloponnesian ships in the narrow waters of the gulf. Drawn in to protect Naupactus, the Athenians were at first routed and divided, but 11 ships pursued into Naupactus turned on their pursuers and won. The victory preserved Athenian naval supremacy in the gulf and ended Peloponnesian attempts to challenge it in that period of the war.

After a land campaign in Acarnania in 428 BCE he is not recorded in command again. A defeat in the gulf would have struck hard at Athenian influence in the north-east and at the city's name for naval invincibility. After his death Athens erected a statue of him on the acropolis and buried him in the state cemetery, and he is counted with Themistocles and Cimon among its great admirals. His son, also named Asopius, commanded a naval expedition during the war.
photisarath: Photisarath was the son of King Visoun of Lan Xang, who reigned from 1500 to 1520; his mother's name is not known. He is considered the most devout of the Lao kings. In 1533 he married Queen Yot Kam Tip, also called Nang Nhot-Kham, a daughter of Mueangketklao, king of Lan Na at Chiang Mai, and he took several other consorts, among them a princess of Ayutthaya. His sons included Setthathirath, Phra Lancharng, Phra Vorawong and Vorawongse I, who reigned in Lan Xang from 1575 to 1579.

His 1527 decree called the worship of spirits groundless superstition and ordered their shrines destroyed and their altars thrown into the river, and he built temples on the sites of spirit shrines. He worked to undermine Brahmanic practices as well as animism. He lived much of the time not in the capital, Luang Prabang, but in Vientiane, farther south, which had better communications with the main states of the region.

His reign drew Lan Xang into the wars of mainland Southeast Asia. Allied with Burma, he sent campaigns against the Ayutthaya Kingdom, to Phitsanulok in 1535 and to Vieng Prangarm in 1539. In 1540 King Chairachathirat of Ayutthaya invaded with a large army, took Muang Khouk and crossed the Mekong, but was routed at the Battle of Sala Kham, his army leaving enormous casualties behind. When Mueangketklao died in 1546 without a male heir, Photisarath's son Setthathirath was placed on the throne of Chiang Mai.

After Photisarath's death, his sons divided the kingdom. Phra Vorawong seized Luang Prabang and the lands north of Chiengkarn, and Phra Lancharng took those to the south. Setthathirath returned from Chiang Mai, expelled Phra Vorawong and joined the two kingdoms under his rule. Phra Lancharng was defeated and taken prisoner, then pardoned and made governor of Saenmuong. The union was soon caught up in the Burmese–Siamese wars that devastated much of the region over the next half-century.
phra-bang: The Phra Bang stands 83 centimetres tall, its palms facing forward in the mudra of dispelling fear, from which its name, Royal Buddha Image in the Dispelling Fear mudra, is taken. It was cast in thong, an alloy of bronze, gold and silver. According to local lore it was made in Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, sometime between the 1st and 9th centuries, but the features of the image suggest a much later Khmer origin.

The image came to Lan Xang from Angkor during the reign of Fa Ngum, the first monarch of Lan Xang, who ruled from 1353 to 1373. In 1359 the Khmer king gave it to Fa Ngum, his son-in-law, to lend Buddhist legitimacy to his rule and so to the sovereignty of Laos, and it was used to spread Theravada Buddhism in the new kingdom. It was kept in Luang Prabang, the former royal capital, which is named after it.

Devout Buddhists have long seen the image as a symbol of the right to rule Laos, holding that only a virtuous government deserves to be the caretaker of so sacred an object. It was taken to Vientiane in 1705. In 1778 the Siamese invaded Vientiane and carried it off to Bangkok, but political upheaval and misfortune there were blamed on the statue, and it was returned to the Lao in 1782. The Siamese captured it again in 1828 and, after a similar period of upheaval, gave it back in 1867.

In 2013 the image was moved from the Lao National Museum to the Haw Pha Bang, on the grounds of the Royal Palace. Each year, on the third day of Pi Mai, the Lao New Year, it is carried in procession to Wat Mai and set in a shrine, where devout laypeople ritually bathe it during the festivities.
phraates-ii: Phraates II was born around 147 BCE, the son of Mithridates I, the fifth Parthian king, and a noblewoman named Rinnu, daughter of a Median magnate. His name is the Greek form of the Parthian Frahāt, from an Old Iranian word meaning gained or earned. He succeeded his father in 132 BCE while still a minor, and his mother ruled with him for a few months.

In this period he gave Darayan I the kingship of Persis in southern Iran. He also defeated and captured Tigraios, ruler of Elymais, and set Kamnaskires the Younger on the throne there as a Parthian vassal.

Continuing his father's plan to conquer Syria, Phraates meant to use his captive, the former Seleucid king Demetrius II Nicator, against Demetrius's brother, the new Seleucid king Antiochus VII Sidetes. According to the Roman historian Justin, Demetrius twice tried to escape and was twice brought back. Antiochus, aware of the scheme, invaded Parthia in 130 BCE, was reportedly well received by many magnates and, after three battles, reclaimed Babylonia.

Antiochus demanded the release of Demetrius, the return of all lost lands and renewal of tribute, and Phraates broke off negotiations. Antiochus's army wintered in Babylonia or Media, where it alienated the local people by making them pay for its upkeep. When Phraates attacked the winter quarters in the spring of 129 BCE, the local population supported him. Antiochus was defeated and died, in battle or by suicide. Phraates held a royal funeral and sent the body to Syria in a silver coffin, together with Seleucus, one of Antiochus's captured children, and he later married Laodice, another. He also released Demetrius, who became king of the Seleucid realm a second time.

On the eastern frontier nomadic tribes, including the Saka and Tokhari, had destroyed the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom and by 129 BCE threatened the Parthian realm. Phraates marched east, appointing Himeros as governor of Babylon, who became a tyrant. His army included many captured Seleucid soldiers, who refused to fight for him, and he was defeated and killed in battle. His uncle Artabanus I succeeded him.

On his coins he used the title great king rather than King of Kings, and, like his father, the honorific Arsaces and the title Philhellene, friend of the Greeks. Babylonian tablets also record him as King of the Lands. His victory left Syria all that remained of the Seleucid empire.
phrae: Phrae stands at an elevation of 159 metres, mostly on the east bank of the Yom, 555 km north of Bangkok by road. Hills rise on both sides: the Phlueng Range to the east reaches about 800 metres and the Phi Pan Nam Range to the west about 500 metres. A few kilometres north, at Phae Muang Phi, erosion has carved a landscape of mushroom rocks and pillars. The town combines Isan and Lan Na culture and cuisine.

The town's founding is dated to 828 CE. Wat Phra That Cho Hae, on a hill nine km from the centre, was among its earliest temples, built around 1336–1338 in the Sukhothai period. In the 19th century the teak forests around Phrae brought foreign firms such as the Bombay Burmah Trading Corporation, which received a logging concession in 1889, and the East Asiatic Company, which logged from 1897 to 1936, with residents from the United Kingdom, the United States and Denmark and an American Presbyterian mission.

Phiriya Theppawong became the last chao luang, or king, of Phrae on 5 April 1889, and in 1897, under King Chulalongkorn's centralising reforms, Bangkok appointed a governor. On 25 July 1902 Shan miners led by Sala Po Chai and Phaka Mong seized the town in the Ngiao rebellion, forced the chao luang to aid them and killed Central Thai residents, among them the governor. Siamese authority returned on 16 August 1902. The chao luang went into exile in Luang Prabang, and the Kingdom of Phrae came to an end.

Phrae is the capital of Phrae Province and of Mueang Phrae district, with 15,316 people in the town itself in 2019. Its temples include Wat Pongsunan and Wat Chorm Sawan, and the royal residence of Khum Chao Luang, built in 1892, still stands. The Wichai Racha Residence of 1891 sheltered members of the Free Thai movement during World War II.
phraortes: Phraortes, son of Deioces, was the second king of the Median kingdom. All ancient information about him comes from Herodotus. According to Herodotus, Phraortes united all the Median tribes into a single state. He also subjugated the Persians, the Parthians and other nations of ancient Iran before declaring war on the Assyrians. He ruled for twenty-two years, c. 675 to c. 653 BCE, until his death in battle with Assyria.

Like his father, Phraortes started wars against Assyria, but he was defeated and killed by the Assyrian king, widely agreed to have been Ashurbanipal. Herodotus says the Assyrians were at that time left without support, their allies having revolted from them. Media was then ruled by Scythians, allies of Assyria, for 28 years before Phraortes's son Cyaxeres overthrew Scythian domination and became king in 625.

Although the identification has sceptics, Phraortes is commonly identified with Kashtariti, a powerful Median chieftain who had invaded Assyria with the help of a confederacy of Median tribes and other allies. Esarhaddon called Kashtariti king of the Medes around 678 BCE, shortly after the death of Deioces.

Various scholars have identified Phraortes with Arphaxad, king of the Medes, in the Book of Judith. Fulcran Vigouroux held that the battle between Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, and Arphaxad corresponds to the battle between Ashurbanipal and Phraortes in the seventeenth year of Ashurbanipal's reign, and he read the two battles of the Septuagint version as the clash of the two empires in 658–657 BCE and Phraortes's death in 653 BCE. Jean-Baptiste Glaire took Arphaxad to be a name altered by copyists from Phraortes, and Nebuchadnezzar to be Ashurbanipal.
phraya-phahon-phonphayuhasena: Phot Phahonyothin was born in Phra Nakhon Province, present-day Bangkok, to a Teochew Thai Chinese father, Colonel Kim, and a Thai Mon mother, Chap. His family took the surname Phahonyothin in 1913 by royal decree. After attending the Chulachomklao Royal Military Academy, he was sent in 1903 on a royal scholarship to the Prussian Military Academy in Lichterfelde, near Berlin, where he was allegedly a classmate of Hermann Göring.

He then went to the Engineering College of Copenhagen, but completed only one year before his scholarship funds ran out, and he returned to Siam in 1912. In 1931 King Prajadhipok raised him to the title Phraya Phahonphonphayuhasena with the rank of colonel, and in 1932 he became Commander of the Royal Siamese Army.

Phraya Phahon belonged to the conspirators known as the Four Musketeers, part of the Khana Ratsadon, or People's Party, which carried out the revolution of 1932. Afterwards three factions formed: the senior military faction under Phraya Phahon, a junior army and navy faction under Luang Phibunsongkhram, and a civilian faction under Pridi Banomyong. As the most senior member he was seen as the de facto leader of the party, and he read the Declaration of the New Siamese State in the Royal Plaza, announcing the end of absolute monarchy.

In March 1933 the Yellow Cover Dossier incident, which arose from Pridi's draft economic plan with socialist elements, led Prime Minister Phraya Manopakorn Nititada to expel Pridi from the cabinet and suspend the constitution. Phraya Phahon resigned on 15 June, citing health, and on 20 June led a bloodless coup. The next day he made himself the second prime minister of Siam, and the king reluctantly endorsed him. Phraya Manopakorn was exiled to British Malaya.

His five years as prime minister were a struggle to keep power. The royalist Boworadet Rebellion broke out in October 1933, and government troops won after weeks of fighting. The cabinet was divided, and Luang Phibunsongkhram, as minister of defence, gained influence. A scandal over the sale of crown land to senior officials below market prices began in 1937, and the first direct elections to the People's Assembly took place on 7 November 1937. The cabinet resigned in September 1938 after budget problems, and elections in December made Phibunsongkhram prime minister. Phraya Phahon later served as Inspector General of the Royal Thai Armed Forces during the Second World War and died of a cerebral haemorrhage in February 1947.
phrygia: Phrygia lay on the western end of the high Anatolian plateau, an arid region quite unlike the forested lands to its north and west, centred on the Sangarios, or Sakarya, River. The climate is harsh, with hot summers and cold winters, and the land is used mostly for livestock grazing and barley. In the north-west lay Dorylaeum and the capital Gordion; to the south stood Midas City (Yazılıkaya), Akroinon with its marble quarries at Docimium, and Synnada, and at the western end Aizanoi and Acmonia.

Greek tradition held that the Phrygians had migrated from the Balkans, where Herodotus says they were called Bryges. Their language, which survived until the 6th century CE, was Indo-European and had some vocabulary like Greek, and was not an Anatolian language like Hittite. Some scholars treat the migration as legend and place the Phrygians' arrival around the collapse of the Hittite Empire at the start of the 12th century BCE, while others seek their origins among peoples already subject to the Hittites.

In the 8th century BCE the kingdom, with its capital at Gordium in the upper Sakarya valley, grew into an empire dominating most of central and western Anatolia and bordering Neo-Assyria and Urartu. Its last independent king was a Midas; Cimmerians sacked Gordium around 695 BCE. Lydia expelled the Cimmerians by about 620 BCE and absorbed much of Phrygia, and in the 540s BCE it passed to the Achaemenid Empire when Cyrus the Great conquered Lydia. Darius the Great made the Persian satrapy of Phrygia in the west with its capital at Dascylium, and during the 5th century the region was split into Hellespontine Phrygia and Greater Phrygia.

Alexander the Great cut the Gordian Knot at Gordium in 333 BCE. After his death Celts overran northern Phrygia, which became part of Galatia, and destroyed Gordium. In 188 BCE the southern remnant came under the Attalids of Pergamon, and in 133 BCE it passed to Rome. Diocletian divided it into Phrygia Salutaris, with Synnada as capital, and Pacatiana, with Laodicea on the Lycus. The Turks overran it after the Battle of Manzikert in 1071, and the name remained in use until the Ottoman conquest of 1453.

Greek myth told of Phrygian kings: Gordias, whose knot Alexander cut, Midas, who turned what he touched to gold, and Mygdon, who warred with the Amazons. In the Iliad the Phrygians are close allies of Troy. Phrygian religion was headed by a goddess, Matar Kubeleya, the Mother of the Mountain Peaks. Over the centuries the Phrygians became Christian and Greek-speaking and assimilated into the Byzantine state.
phrygians: The Phrygians spoke the Phrygian language, a member of the Indo-European family, and lived in central-western Anatolia. Ancient Greek authors used the name for a vast ethno-cultural complex in central Anatolia, not for a single tribe. According to Herodotus the Phrygians first lived in the southern Balkans under the name Bryges and became Phryges after their final migration to Anatolia by way of the Hellespont. Many historians support a migration from Europe, but Anatolian archaeologists have generally abandoned the idea for lack of European pottery. After the collapse of the Hittite Empire, Indo-European migrants and Sea Peoples filled the political vacuum, and it is not known whether the Phrygians helped bring down Hattusa or simply moved in afterwards.

The state of Phrygia arose in the 8th century BCE from tribal and village beginnings, with its capital at Gordium. Assyrian sources speak of a king Mita of the Mushki, identified with Midas of Phrygia, an ally of Sargon of Assyria in 709 BCE. Under kings alternately named Gordias and Midas, the kingdom kept close trade contacts with its eastern neighbours and the Greeks. The invasion of the Cimmerians proved fatal to it, and according to legend its last king, Midas, killed himself. Gordium was sacked and burnt.

Phrygia was then subsumed into the Lydian empire, and after Cyrus conquered Croesus in 546 BCE it passed to Persia. It later passed to the empire of Alexander and his successors, then to the Attalids of Pergamon and finally to the Roman Empire. The last mention of the Phrygian language in literature dates to the 5th century CE, and it was probably extinct by the 7th century.

Modern consensus regards Greek as the closest relative of Phrygian. The Phrygians worshipped the goddess Cybele, called Matar, Mother, in their language, and venerated Sabazios, a sky and father god shown on horseback. The earliest traditions of Greek music are in part connected to Phrygian music, and the aulos, a reed instrument with two pipes, came from Phrygia. The Phrygian cap, which marked Paris as non-Greek in Greek art, survived as the liberty cap of the American and French revolutionaries.
phrynichus-tragic-poet: Phrynichus was the son of Polyphradmon and a pupil of Thespis, and counts among the earliest Greek tragedians. Some ancient writers regarded him as the real founder of tragedy. He won his first victory in a drama contest in 511 BCE. Tradition has him dying in Sicily, and his son Polyphrasmon also wrote plays. The titles of his other known plays, among them Actaeon, Alcestis, Antaeus, Daughters of Danaus, Egyptians, Pleuroniai and Tantalus, show that he treated myth as well as contemporary events.

Phrynichus wrote two of the three known Greek tragedies that took their subject from contemporary history, both drawn from the Persian Wars and neither surviving. The Capture of Miletus was probably composed soon after the Persians took that city during the Ionian Revolt. Miletus was a colony of Athens and held especially dear by it. The audience was moved to tears, and the poet was fined for reminding the Athenians of familiar misfortunes; the play was banned from further performance.

In 476 BCE he succeeded with the Phoenissae, named for the Phoenician women who formed its chorus, which marked the defeat of Xerxes I at the Battle of Salamis four years earlier. Themistocles paid for it as choregos, and one aim of the play was to remind the Athenians of his deeds. The Persians of Aeschylus, produced in 472 BCE, was modelled on it.

Phrynichus is credited with introducing a separate actor, distinct from the leader of the chorus, and so laying the foundation for theatrical dialogue. In his plays, as in early tragedy generally, the chorus and the dance carried more weight than the drama. According to the Suda, he was the first to bring female characters on stage, played by men in masks, and he made special use of the trochaic tetrameter. Aelian, in his Varia Historia, says that his martial verses so stirred the Athenians that they made him a general. Fragments of his work were collected by Johann August Nauck in 1887.
phthia: In the Catalogue of Ships of the Iliad, Achilles leads fifty ships from those who dwelt in Pelasgic Argos, in Alos, Alope and Trachis, and who held Phthia and Hellas, called Myrmidons, Hellenes and Achaians. These names are generally believed to refer to places in the Spercheios valley in what is now Phthiotis in central Greece. The river was linked with Achilles: in the Iliad he says that his father Peleus vowed he would dedicate a lock of his hair to the Spercheios on returning safely home. Some scholars suggest that Pelasgic Argos was a general name for all of northern Greece.

Other ancient sources, among them Euripides' Andromache, placed Phthia further north, around Pharsalus. Strabo records a shrine to Thetis, the Thetideion, near the cities of Pharsalus and Palaepharsalus, and Mycenean remains have been found at Pharsalus and nearby sites, but according to Denys Page whether Homer's Phthia is Pharsalus remains as doubtful as ever.

In myth Phthia was founded by Aeacus, the grandfather of Achilles, and was the home of his father Peleus, his mother, the sea nymph Thetis, and his son Neoptolemus, who reigned there after the Trojan War. Euripides set his Andromache there, after the war, when Neoptolemus has taken Hector's widow Andromache as a slave.

In Plato's Crito, Socrates in prison awaiting execution tells of a dream in which a woman in white said he would arrive at fertile Phthia on the third day. The words echo the Iliad, where Achilles, his honour insulted by Agamemnon, rejects his gifts and says that with good weather he might reach fertile Phthia, his home, on the third day. The scholar Mackie (2002) notes the link between the name and the Greek word phthisis, wasting away, and suggests a possible wordplay in Homer tying Achilles' home to a withering death.
phu-tho-province: Phú Thọ lies in northern Vietnam at the head of the triangle of the Red River Delta, between the delta and the northern mountains, and is called the West Gate of Hanoi. Its capital, Việt Trì, is 80 kilometres from Hanoi. The province lies at the confluence of the Red and Da rivers, and three rivers, the Red, Lô and Da, flow through it. It links the delta with the mountainous provinces and with the Chinese provinces of Guangxi and Yunnan, and it borders Tuyên Quang and Lào Cai to the north and Sơn La to the west. The climate is subtropical monsoon, with most rain falling between April and September.

Tea was the main industrial crop. In the 19th century the tea industry was established in Vietnam, particularly in Phú Thọ, and three research stations were set up to promote plantations. The tea gardens were deserted until 1945, and the industry restarted after the war with help from other tea-producing countries. In December 1999 Nguyễn Thị Thủy, the leader of an unregistered Protestant house church in the province, was sentenced to one year in prison, which caused some religious controversy. In 2025 the National Assembly merged Hòa Bình Province and Vĩnh Phúc Province into Phú Thọ.

Ethnic Vietnamese (Kinh), Mường, Dao and Sán Chay are the main groups living in the province. The Dao build houses on stilts, level with the ground or half on stilts and half earth, and Du village, within the Xuân Sơn National Park, is a tourist attraction. The park, established in February 2002, covers 15,048 hectares and shelters 168 species of birds and 61 of mammals, among them Tibetan bears and gibbons. The province is also known for grapefruit, rice and cassava, and freshwater fish from the Red River. Việt Trì is a river port at the meeting of three rivers, and National Highway 2 and a railway line from Yunnan to Hanoi pass through it. Hung Vuong University is among its educational institutions.
phuket: Phuket lies in the Andaman Sea off the west coast of mainland Thailand and is joined to Phang Nga province in the north by the Sarasin Bridge. The province consists of Phuket Island and 32 smaller islands, and covers 547 square kilometres. A mountain range runs along the western side of the island, part of a larger range that stretches about 440 kilometres from the Kra Isthmus. The name comes from the Malay word bukit, meaning hill, which is how the island looks from a distance. It was formerly called Thalang, from the Malay telong, meaning cape, and Western charts knew it as Junk Ceylon.

Phuket was historically inhabited by Austronesian Malays before the Thai settled it through the southward expansion of Siamese kingdoms. It lay on a major trade route between India and China, and ships from Portugal, France, the Netherlands and England mention it in their logs, though no European nation colonised it. The Portuguese Fernão Mendes Pinto, who arrived in Siam in 1545, calls it Junk Ceylon and describes it as a port of call for supplies, though he notes that pirates and difficult seas were reducing its importance by the mid-16th century.

Tin mining was central to the economy from the 16th century until its decline in the 20th, and rubber also became important. In 1785 Burmese forces invaded, and the Two Heroines Monument in Thalang District commemorates Thao Thep Kasattri and Thao Sri Sunthon, who rallied the people against them. The Thalang National Museum was established in 1985 for the 200th anniversary of the Thalang War.

Under King Chulalongkorn, who reigned from 1868 to 1910, Phuket became the administrative centre for the tin-producing southern provinces of Siam. In 1876 Chinese laborers in the tin mines of Phuket and neighbouring provinces rose in unrest, which was linked to falling tin prices and the government's fiscal policies. Monthon Phuket was dissolved in 1933, making Phuket a separate province.

Phuket is a province of Thailand divided into three districts. Buddhism is the predominant religion, and about a fifth of the population follows Islam, mainly descendants of the island's original Austronesian inhabitants. Many others are of Chinese ancestry, descended from tin miners who came in the 19th century, among them the Peranakan community known locally as Phuket Babas. Tourism developed from the 1980s around the beaches of Patong, Karon and Kata, and a 45-metre Big Buddha overlooks Chalong Bay. The tsunami of 26 December 2004 devastated the island's west coast.
phuntsog-namgyal: Phuntsog was a fifth-generation descendant of Khye Bumsa, a 13th-century prince of the Mi-nyak House in Kham in eastern Tibet. According to legend, Guru Rinpoche, a 9th-century Buddhist saint, had foretold that a Phuntsog from the east would be the next Chogyal of Sikkim. In 1642 three lamas, coming from the north, the west and the south, went in search of the chosen person. Near present-day Gangtok they found a man churning milk, who offered them refreshment and shelter, and so impressed were they by his deeds that they recognised him as the one foretold.

Phuntsog was crowned at the age of 38 at Norbughang near Yuksom, on a stone slab on a pine-covered hill, and anointed with water sprinkled from a sacred urn. With the lamas he converted the local Lepcha people to Buddhism, and he extended his kingdom to the Chumbi Valley in Tibet, parts of present-day Darjeeling and parts of eastern Nepal. He moved his capital from Yatung to Yuksom and instituted the first centralised administration, dividing the kingdom into twelve Dzongs, or districts, under a Lepcha Dzongpon (governor) who headed a council of twelve ministers. During his reign Buddhism was consolidated as the established religion of Sikkim.

Phuntsog is credited with creating Lho-Mon-Tsong-Sum, the idea of unity between the Bhutias, Lepchas and Limbus that forms the core of Sikkimese national identity. In 1663 representatives of the three communities met the Chogyal to formalise this unity in a written treaty and to create a council, the Lo-Men-Chong, to represent their interests at the national level; the same document established autonomy for the Limbu subbas. He was succeeded by his son, Tensung Namgyal, in 1670.
pi-ramesses: The name means House of Ramesses. The city stood on the banks of the Pelusiac branch of the Nile, the easternmost branch of the Delta in the reign of Ramesses II. It had served as a summer palace under Seti I and may have been founded by Ramesses I. Ramesses II was born and raised in the area, but geopolitical reasons may have mattered more: the city lay much closer to the Egyptian vassal states in Asia and to the border with the hostile Hittite empire, and the main corps of the army was encamped there, ready to meet incursions of Hittites or Shasu nomads.

With a population of over 300,000, Pi-Ramesses was one of the largest cities of ancient Egypt, and it flourished for more than a century after Ramesses' death. Ground-penetrating radar shows a huge central temple, a precinct of mansions on the river set in a grid of streets, and an irregular collection of houses and workshops in the east. Manfred Bietak's team found many canals and lakes and called it the Venice of Egypt.

The Pelusiac branch began to silt up around 1060 BCE, leaving the city without water as the river settled in a new course to the west. The pharaohs of the Twenty-first Dynasty established Tanis on the new branch, 100 km to the north-west, as the capital of Lower Egypt. They carried the Ramesside temples, obelisks, statues and sphinxes there, moving obelisks and statues weighing over 200 tons in one piece and dismantling major buildings to reassemble them. The old city became largely a quarry.

Flinders Petrie dug at Tanis in 1884 and Pierre Montet explored it in the 1930s, and the masses of Ramesside stonework there led archaeologists to identify Tanis as Pi-Ramesses. It later became clear that none of these monuments originated at the site. In the 1960s Bietak mapped the branches of the ancient Delta and showed that the Pelusiac was the easternmost in Ramesses' reign, and excavations at Tell el-Dab'a and Qantir followed. Qantir was recognised as the site of Pi-Ramesses, about 30 km south of Tanis. The name is generally linked with the Raamses of Exodus 1:11, one of the cities the Israelites were forced to build.
piast-dynasty: The early dukes and kings of Poland are said to have regarded themselves as descendants of the Piast the Wheelwright, a figure known from tradition, first mentioned in the Deeds of the Princes of the Poles, written c. 1113 by Gallus Anonymus. The term Piast dynasty is not documented in contemporary sources; the Polish historian Adam Naruszewicz introduced it in a historical work.

The first Piasts, probably of Polan descent, appeared around 940 at the stronghold of Giecz in Greater Poland. Shortly afterwards they moved their residence to Gniezno, where Mieszko I ruled the Civitas Schinesghe from about 960. At various times the dynasty also ruled Pomerania, Bohemia and the Lusatias, as well as part of Ruthenia and the Hungarian Spiš region.

The Polish monarchy had to deal with the expansionist policies of the Holy Roman Empire. Piast rulers such as Mieszko I, Casimir I the Restorer and Władysław I Herman tried to protect the state by treaties, oaths of allegiance and marriage alliances with the Ottonian and Salian dynasties. Other powerful neighbours were the Bohemian Přemyslid dynasty, the Árpáds and their Anjou successors in Hungary, Kievan Rus', the State of the Teutonic Order and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.

The dynasty was decisively weakened by the fragmentation that followed the Testament of Bolesław III Wrymouth in 1138. For nearly 150 years the Polish state was divided into several duchies, and Piast dukes fought for the throne at Kraków; Mieszko III the Old, Władysław III Spindleshanks and Leszek I the White were each crowned, only to be overthrown. The senior Silesian branch went its own way and from the 14th century was vassal to the Bohemian Crown.

After the Polish royal line died out in 1370, the crown passed to Louis I of Hungary, son of Casimir the Great's sister Elizabeth Piast. The Masovian branch became extinct with the death of Duke Janusz III in 1526, and the last ruling duke of the Silesian Piasts, George William of Legnica, died in 1675.

About 1295 Przemysł II used a coat of arms with a white eagle, later called the Piast Eagle. In the 14th century the Silesian Piasts used an eagle modified by a crescent, which became the coat of arms of the Duchy of Silesia. The Piasts intermarried with several noble lines of Europe and held numerous titles, some within the Holy Roman Empire, and Piast daughters became queens consort in Hungary, Bohemia, Denmark and elsewhere. The Jagiellonian kings who ruled after the death of Casimir IV were also descended in the female line from a daughter of Casimir the Great.
piaui: Piauí has the shortest coastline of any coastal Brazilian state, 66 kilometres, and was colonised from the interior towards the ocean, unlike the rest of the region. It is bounded by Maranhão, Ceará, Pernambuco, Bahia and Tocantins. The Parnaíba River forms the boundary with Maranhão along its whole length, and the state lies almost entirely in the basin of the Parnaíba and its tributaries. The coast and lower Parnaíba are low, swampy and historically malarial; to the south the land rises to a plateau of open campos, with flat-topped plateaus called chapadas between the river valleys. The east is dry caatinga shrubland, and cerrado savanna covers the south-west.

The state holds many archaeological sites, among them Serra da Capivara National Park and Sete Cidades National Park, rich in remains of prehistoric Paleo-Indian and settled Indigenous cultures.
