Among the early settlers was Francisco Dias d'Ávila from Bahia, who brought the first herds of cattle, and Domingos Afonso Mafrense, from Portugal, who founded what is now Oeiras. The first settlement dates from 1674, when Domingos Afonso Mafrense established a number of cattle ranges.

In the 17th century impoverished noblemen and Jesuit priests settled there, together with enslaved Black and Amerindian people. Large estate owners looking for new pasture came from neighbouring states such as Bahia and Maranhão. At the start of the 20th century stock raising remained the principal industry. Goats were a secondary one, and cotton, sugar and tobacco, rubber, carnauba wax and dyewoods were also produced. Hides, skins, rubber, wax, tobacco and cotton were exported.

Teresina was the first planned city in Brazil. An architect designed it in 1852, taking a chessboard as his inspiration. It stands where the Parnaíba and Poti rivers meet and is known as the Green City for the mango trees that line its streets. A battle of Brazil's war of independence was fought at Jenipapo on 13 March 1823, and the date was added to the state flag in 2005.

Piauí is divided into 224 municipalities, and Teresina is its capital and the only capital in the north-east that lies inland. The 2022 census counted 3,271,199 people. Portuguese is the language of schooling. The Serra da Capivara National Park, in the south-east, has more than 400 archaeological sites and a very large concentration of rock paintings, and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
picardy: Picardy is a historical and cultural territory of northern France, never a duchy, county or principality, and its boundaries shifted over the centuries. The historical province stretched from Senlis to Calais, through most of the Oise and Aisne departments, the whole of the Somme and the west of the Pas-de-Calais, with the province of Artois separating it from French Flanders. The geographer Albert Demangeon described a Picard plain, a vast chalk plain stretching from Beauvais to Arras. Picardy runs from the sand beaches of the Somme estuary in the west to the forests and pastures of the Thiérache in the east.

From the 5th century the area formed part of the Frankish Empire, and in the feudal period it held the six countships of Boulogne, Montreuil, Ponthieu, Amiénois, Vermandois and Laonnois. By the Treaty of Verdun in 843 it became part of West Francia. The name was first used in the early 13th century for all lands where the Picard language was spoken, and it is said to come from the Old French pic, meaning pike. A Picard Nation of students existed at the University of Paris. In 1358 the region was the centre of the Jacquerie peasant revolt.
From 1419 the Burgundian duke Philip the Good acquired the Picard counties, which Charles VII confirmed at the Congress of Arras in 1435, and in 1477 Louis XI occupied key towns there.

In 1557 Habsburg forces under Emmanuel Philibert, Duke of Savoy, invaded, ransacked St Quentin after a siege of seventeen days and burned Noyon. Napoleon I introduced sugar beet, and the sugar industry has remained prominent. Between September 1914 and August 1918 four major battles were fought along the Somme in northern Picardy, among them the Battle of the Somme.

Since 1 January 2016 Picardy has formed part of the Hauts-de-France region, and its various definitions fall largely within it. Amiens was the regional capital, and the main towns include Beauvais, Saint-Quentin, Laon, Soissons, Compiègne and Abbeville. The Picard language, one of the languages of France, is still spoken by a minority, and also in Artois and in parts of the Belgian province of Hainaut. The region holds some of the great Gothic cathedrals, among them Amiens Cathedral, the largest cathedral in Europe, and Saint-Pierre in Beauvais, which has the tallest transept of the Gothic period.
picenum: Picenum lay between the Apennines and the Adriatic Sea. Strabo places it from the mouth of the Aesis River south to Castrum at the mouth of the Truentinus River, about 800 stadia or 148 km. His coastal cities, from north to south, include Ancona, Auxumum, Firmum Picenum with its port at Castellum, Cupra Maritima and Truentum, and in the interior he names Adria and Asculum Picenum. The inland width of the region varies irregularly. The Piceni or Picentes were its native population, though not of uniform ethnicity, and they kept a sanctuary of the Sabine goddess Cupra at Cupra Marittima.

Picenum was first settled at the beginning of the Iron Age, around 1200 BCE. Excavated tombs at the Novilara necropolis show that the Piceni buried their dead wrapped in the garments they wore in life. Warriors were buried with a helmet, weapons and vessels for food and drink, and imported swords seem to come from the Balkans. Beads, amber and fibulae point to active trade on the Adriatic coast in the ninth and perhaps tenth centuries BCE. The Liburnians had colonies on this coast until the 6th century BCE.

In 390 BCE the Senones, a Gaul people, occupied Picenum north of the Esino River, and groups of them settled further south. The Romans expelled them in 283 BCE and annexed the land down to Ancona as the Ager Gallicus. In 268 BCE they defeated the Picentes after a rebellion, deporting part of the population and giving others citizenship without the vote, though Asculum stayed an allied city, and in 264 BCE they founded the colony of Firmum nearby. Picenum sided with Rome against Hannibal. In the Social War some Picentes stayed loyal while others fought for citizenship, which all received after the war.

Picenum is now in the Marche and the northern part of Abruzzo. South Picene, a Sabellic language that is neither Oscan nor Umbrian, was written in an unusual version of the Italic alphabet, while North Picene is undeciphered and generally thought not to be Italic. Pliny the Elder listed 24 cities in Regio V, and the Edict of Diocletian counted Picenum's wine among the dearest, with that of Falerno.
picquigny: Picquigny is a commune in the Somme department in Hauts-de-France, on the banks of the river Somme about 13 kilometres north-west of Amiens, downstream. It lies at the junction of the N235, D141 and D3 roads, and its station has rail connections to Amiens and Abbeville. It was already a Gallic settlement before the Romans arrived, and a Gallo-Roman cemetery was found in 1895 in the area called Les Vignes.

On 17 December 942 Arnulf I, Count of Flanders, and William I, Duke of Normandy, came to Picquigny to sign a peace treaty. Having both left their armies behind, they met on a small island in the river Somme. William left after the meeting and was then assassinated by Arnulf's supporters.

By the 14th century the town had commune status and a county judge. In 1307 several Templars were arrested and imprisoned in the dungeons of the château by order of Philip IV of France. In 1475 Edward IV of England invaded France to claim the French throne, and Louis XI bought him off at the Treaty of Picquigny with an annual payment of fifty thousand crowns and a promise not to support his domestic enemies. Edward then withdrew his army. In 1547 Henry II of France established a market there, to be held on every second Monday of the month.

The Château de Picquigny was built around the beginning of the 11th century and rebuilt over the following centuries. It was severely damaged in World War I, but its remains are still imposing. Outside the ramparts stand other medieval buildings, among them a prison, a kitchen, two cellars and the Pavillon Sévigné. The church, originally the château's chapel, stands inside the ramparts behind the ruins. Its roof was destroyed in a fire early in the 20th century. Warmund of Jerusalem, a Crusader who became Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem in the early 12th century, is the town's notable native.
picts: The Latin word Picti first occurs in a panegyric of 297 and is most commonly explained as meaning painted, a reference to tattooing or body paint. Claudian, writing around 404, speaks of designs on the bodies of dying Picts. In Old Irish the Picts were called Cruithni and in Old Welsh Prydyn. Roman sources used the term of unromanised people in northern Britain, probably as a pejorative. James Fraser argues that it became an endonym only in the late seventh century, after the Battle of Dun Nechtain in 685.

Bede's account makes the Picts settlers from Scythia who reached northern Ireland by chance. It is recognised as a pseudohistorical literary invention, probably of Pictish origin and composed around 700, and its purpose seems to have been to legitimise the annexation of Pictish territories by Fortriu. A study published in 2023 sequenced eight genomes from the Pictish period and found broad affinities with Iron Age Britons and with present-day people of western Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland and Northumbria, supporting a local origin.

For much of the seventh century Northumbria was the most powerful kingdom in Britain, and the Picts were probably tributary to it until King Bridei mac Beli defeated the Angles at Dun Nechtain in 685. Under King Óengus mac Fergusa (reigned 729 to 761) Dál Riata was subject to the Picts, and Caustantín mac Fergusa (793 to 820) placed his son Domnall on its throne. Attempts at similar dominance over the Britons of Alt Clut were not successful.

In a major battle in 839 the Vikings killed Eógan mac Óengusa, king of Fortriu, and Áed mac Boanta, king of Dál Riata. In the 840s Kenneth MacAlpin became king of the Picts. In the reign of his grandson Caustantín mac Áeda (900 to 943) outsiders began to speak of the Kingdom of Alba rather than the Kingdom of the Picts, as Gaelicisation advanced. Probably during the 11th century all the inhabitants of northern Alba became fully Gaelicised Scots and Pictish identity was forgotten.

Pictland was not united. Later sources point to seven kingdoms, among them Fortriu, centred on Moray, Fib (Fife) and Cait in the north, though that number may owe more to the seven sons of the founder Cruithne than to fact. The Picts were farmers in small communities, keeping cattle, sheep and pigs. No towns are known in Scotland until the 12th century. They left carved stones bearing symbols such as the Pictish Beast, as well as silver chains and the St Ninian's Isle Treasure; the symbols have defied attempts at translation. Their language, known from names and inscriptions, was an Insular Celtic language probably related to Brittonic.
pide: The force grew out of a long line of police reorganisations under the First Republic and the Ditadura Nacional. With Salazar as prime minister, the Political and Social Surveillance Section became an autonomous police in January 1933 and in August merged with the Portuguese International Police as the PVDE, by Decree-Law 22992. Its founder and head, Captain Agostinho Lourenço, kept close ties with MI6 and became president of Interpol in 1956. In 1936 the Tarrafal prison camp was opened under its control in Cape Verde; 32 people died there over the years of the regime.

From the Spanish Civil War and an anarchist attempt on Salazar's life in 1937 the PVDE turned chiefly against the underground Portuguese Communist Party, with Italian and German advisers helping it to adopt a model like the Gestapo's. During World War II neutral Lisbon became a centre of espionage, but the PVDE stayed neutral toward foreign spies as long as they kept out of Portuguese politics. Renamed PIDE in 1945, it was presented by the regime as following the Scotland Yard model and was given full powers to investigate, detain and arrest.

Many authors count it among the most effective secret services in history. It placed agents in almost every underground movement, including the independence movements of Angola and Mozambique, and rewarded informers, called bufos. It vetted candidates for public employment and could keep activists in prison after their sentences ended; the law student Aurora Rodrigues was kept awake for weeks and subjected to simulated drowning. In the Colonial War it formed the paramilitary Flechas. Under Marcelo Caetano its violence lessened, and with it its effectiveness.

On 25 April 1974 agents firing from the headquarters on António Maria Cardoso Street in Lisbon killed four demonstrators, and one agent was killed while fleeing: the only deaths of the revolution. Most records were destroyed, and many agents escaped to Spain, though the director-general Silva Pais was among those captured; 89 broke out of Alcoentre penitentiary in June 1975. In the colonies the service lived on as the Military Information Police until 1975. Only the killers of Humberto Delgado were tried, in absentia, and none served time. Its surviving papers have been in the Torre do Tombo National Archive since 1990, and Portugal set up a new intelligence system, SIRP, only in 1984.
piedmont: Piedmont is one of the 20 regions of Italy, in the northwest, and the second largest in area after Sicily. It borders Liguria, Lombardy, Emilia-Romagna and the Aosta Valley, as well as Switzerland and France. The Alps surround it on three sides, among them Monviso, where the Po rises, and Monte Rosa. The region is 43.3 per cent mountainous, 30.3 per cent hills and 26.4 per cent plain, from the rice paddies of Vercelli and Novara to the hillsides of the Langhe, Roero and Montferrat. The name comes from the medieval Latin Pedemontium, at the foot of the mountains, attested from the end of the 12th century.

Celtic-Ligurian tribes such as the Taurini and the Salassi lived there until the Romans subdued them about 220 BCE and founded colonies including Augusta Taurinorum (Turin) and Eporedia (Ivrea). After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the region was invaded by Burgundians, Ostrogoths, East Romans, Lombards and, in 773, the Franks. In 1046 Otto of Savoy added Piedmont to the County of Savoy, whose capital was Chambéry, though Asti, Alessandria, Saluzzo and Montferrat stayed independent. Duke Emanuele Filiberto moved the seat to Turin in 1563, and in 1720 the Duke of Savoy became King of Sardinia.

France created client republics in Piedmont from 1796 and annexed it in September 1802; the Congress of Vienna restored the Kingdom of Sardinia and gave it the Republic of Genoa as a barrier against France. Piedmont was the springboard of Italian unification in 1859 to 1861, after unsuccessful wars with Austria in 1820 to 1821 and 1848 to 1849. Turin was the first capital of the Kingdom of Italy, from 1861 to 1865; when the capital moved the region lost administrative importance, though the Italian crown prince was still styled Prince of Piedmont, and it was one of the most important regions of early Italian industrialisation.

Piedmont has 4,255,006 inhabitants and Turin as its capital. It is a great winegrowing region, producing Barolo and Barbaresco from the Langhe and sparkling Asti, and the Montferrat wine district was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014. The Residences of the Royal House of Savoy have been World Heritage Sites since 1997. Besides Italian, Piedmontese, Occitan, Franco-Provençal and Walser are spoken.
pieds-noirs: The pieds-noirs are people of French and other European descent who were born in Algeria during French rule from 1830 to 1962. European settlement began in the 1830s, after the French seized Algiers in 1830 and began the conquest. The Dey of Algiers had struck the French consul with a fly-swatter in 1827, though economic reasons are also cited. The French met long resistance from Emir Abd al-Kader and forced his surrender in 1847. In 1848 Algeria was divided into three departments, Alger, Oran and Constantine, and became part of France. The settlers often took land forcibly taken from the local population. Nearly half of the settlers of the 1880s came from Spain, southern Italy or Malta, and the rest were mostly poor French.

The term pied-noir came into common use shortly before the end of the Algerian War in 1962. Its origin is disputed: one theory points to sailors working barefoot in ships' coal rooms, another to the black boots of French soldiers.

The pieds-noirs were about 10 percent of Algeria's population from the later nineteenth century to independence, peaking at 15.2 percent in 1926. In 1959 they numbered 1,025,000, and in the Oran metropolitan area they were 49.3 percent of the population. They included peasants and large landowners, the latter called grands colons. The settlers had full political representation in France, but Muslim Algerians had none in the National Assembly until 1945, and to obtain citizenship they had to renounce their Muslim identity, so that only about 2,500 did so before 1930. The Jews of Algeria received French citizenship through the Crémieux Decree of 1870, which the Vichy regime abolished and the Free French restored in 1943, and came to be counted as part of the community.

Many pieds-noirs felt alienated from both Algeria and mainland France: 28 percent had never visited France. During the Algerian War, which began in 1954, a vast majority supported French rule and opposed the National Liberation Front.

After independence in 1962 about 800,000 pieds-noirs of French nationality evacuated to mainland France, and about 200,000 remained in Algeria, of whom there were about 100,000 in 1965 and 30,000 in 1993. In France they met ostracism from some left-wing movements for their perceived exploitation of Muslims, and others blamed them for the war and the collapse of the Fourth Republic. Their history is marked by a double alienation, from the land of their birth and from their adopted homeland. Some express a feeling of nostalgia for French Algeria, called nostalgérie. The community adopted as an unofficial anthem Captain Félix Boyer's 1943 version of Le Chant des Africains, which was banned as official military music from 1962 until August 1969.
pier-luigi-farnese: Pier Luigi Farnese was born on 19 November 1503, the illegitimate son of Cardinal Alessandro Farnese, later Pope Paul III, and Silvia Ruffini. Pope Julius II legitimised him in 1505 so that he could inherit the Farnese estates, and Leo X did so again in 1513, but his birth troubled him all his life. His father arranged his marriage to Gerolama Orsini, which took place in 1519. He became a mercenary soldier in the pay of Venice from 1520 and then under Charles V until 1527, and was present at the Sack of Rome that year.

During the sack he quartered his men in the family palace, which saved it. After it he taxed the Roman countryside heavily, and Pope Clement VII threatened him with excommunication. In 1528 he fought for the emperor in Apulia. When his father became pope in 1534, Paul III made Pier Luigi's son Alessandro a cardinal and on 31 January 1537 named Pier Luigi Captain General of the Church. The pope then created the Duchy of Castro for him, formed from the family lands around Castro and Ronciglione, and he commissioned Antonio da Sangallo the Younger to plan a new capital there. The duchy remained under the direct control of the Holy See.

In 1538 his son Ottavio married Margaret of Parma, an illegitimate daughter of Charles V, and in 1543 his son Orazio married Diane de France, an illegitimate daughter of Henry II of France. In 1545 Paul III made Pier Luigi Duke of Parma and Piacenza, which had been part of the Papal States, in exchange for the duchies of Camerino and Nepi and a yearly payment of 9,000 ducats to the Holy See. Pier Luigi took possession on 23 September 1546.

His tyrannical rule and his taxes made him enemies in the cities, and Charles V encouraged the discontent, partly in order to annex Parma and Piacenza to the Duchy of Milan. Ferrante Gonzaga, the governor of Milan, organised a plot with Louis Gonzaga and Count Giovanni Anguissola, who was joined by other noblemen. Pier Luigi was stabbed to death at Piacenza on 10 September 1547 and his body hung from a window of his palace. Gonzaga then took the duchy, and Paul III accused him of the murder. The duchy returned to Pier Luigi's son Ottavio in 1551. Pier Luigi's body was buried at Piacenza and later taken to the family tomb on the island of Bisentina on Lake Bolsena.
piero-di-lorenzo-de-medici: Piero was born on 15 February 1472, the eldest son of Lorenzo de' Medici and Clarice Orsini. He was raised with his younger brother Giovanni, the future Pope Leo X, and his cousin Giulio, the future Pope Clement VII, and was educated to succeed his father by tutors such as Angelo Poliziano and Marsilio Ficino. His character, described as feeble, arrogant and undisciplined, proved unsuited to the role. Poliziano died of poisoning on 24 September 1494, very possibly at Piero's hand. In 1486 his uncle Bernardo Rucellai arranged his marriage to Alfonsina Orsini, daughter of Roberto Orsini, Count of Tagliacozzo, and they met in 1488. Their children included Clarice, who married Filippo Strozzi the Younger, and Lorenzo, later Duke of Urbino.

Piero took over as leader of Florence in 1492 on his father's death. The balance among the Italian states that Lorenzo had built collapsed in 1494 when Charles VIII of France crossed the Alps to assert hereditary claims to Naples, lured, according to the account, by Ludovico Sforza. Charles asked Piero to support his claim and let his army pass through Tuscany. Piero waited five days and replied that Florence would stay neutral, which was unacceptable to Charles, who sacked and massacred the fortress of Fivizzano.

Piero received little support from a Florentine elite under the influence of the Dominican Girolamo Savonarola, and even his cousins Lorenzo and Giovanni allied themselves with Charles. By the end of October, without consulting the Signoria, he went to Charles's camp and acceded to all the king's demands, surrendering the fortresses of Sarzana, Pietrasanta, Sarzanello and Librafratta and the towns of Pisa and Livorno. When he reported to the Signoria he met public outrage, and he and his family fled to Venice. The family palazzo was looted and the Medici were formally exiled.

In exile Piero and his family lived by selling Medici jewels collected by Lorenzo, with help from the French diplomat Philippe de Commines. He tried several times to return, once appearing at the Porta Romana with a band of men who left for Siena when the Florentines did not welcome them. In 1503 he drowned in the Garigliano River while fleeing after the Battle of Garigliano, lost by the French with whom he was allied, and he was buried at the Abbey of Monte Cassino in a tomb designed by Antonio and Battista da Sangallo. No Medici ruled Florence again until 1512, when Giovanni de' Medici forced the city to surrender, and in 1513 he was elected Pope Leo X.
piero-soderini: Piero di Tommaso Soderini was born in Florence, the son of Tommaso di Lorenzo Soderini, a member of an established family associated with medicine, and his second wife Dianora Tornabuoni, who came from a prominent Florentine family and was an in-law of Piero di Cosimo de' Medici. His brother Paolo Antonio Soderini was a statesman and supporter of Girolamo Savonarola, and another brother, Francesco, was a cardinal and bishop of Volterra. In 1481 Piero was Prior of the city, and he later formed political ties with Piero di Lorenzo de' Medici, who in 1493 made him ambassador to the Kingdom of France.

In 1502 the Florentines elected Soderini gonfaloniere for life, wishing to give greater stability to the republican institutions restored after the expulsion of Piero de' Medici and the execution of Savonarola. His administration followed relatively moderate policies. He replaced foreign mercenaries with a national militia. The long war with Pisa ended during his government with the Florentine capture of that city in 1509. Niccolò Machiavelli, author of The Prince and the Discourses on Livy, served under him as second chancellor and as ambassador to Cesare Borgia, Rome and France. Machiavelli's assessment of Soderini's character changed after the events that removed Soderini from power. Soderini kept a pro-France alliance in Italian politics.

In 1512 the Medici returned to Florence with the help of a Spanish army, deposed Soderini and drove him into exile. He took refuge at Orašac, near Dubrovnik, until the election of Pope Leo X, who summoned him to Rome and extended his patronage to him. Soderini lived in Rome for the rest of his life and continued to advocate for the welfare of Florence, to which he was never allowed to return. He died in Rome in 1522 and was buried in the church of S. Maria del Popolo.
piero-strozzi: Piero, or Pietro, Strozzi was born in Florence, the son of Filippo Strozzi the Younger and Clarice de' Medici. In 1539 he married another Medici, Laudomia di Pierfrancesco, a sister of Lorenzino de' Medici, yet he was a fierce opponent of the main line of that family. He fought in the army of Florentine exiles led by his father to drive the Medici from Florence, and after their defeat at the Battle of Montemurlo he fled to France, to the court of Catherine de' Medici.

In French service during the Italian War of 1542, he raised an army of Italian mercenaries but was defeated by the Imperial and Spanish forces at the Battle of Serravalle. An encoded letter of 1547 from Charles V to his ambassador in France, examined by cryptographers and historians in 2022, shows a fear that Strozzi would send an assassin. In 1548, during the war of the Rough Wooing, he was in Scotland supporting Mary of Guise on behalf of Henry II of France, designing fortifications against the English at Leith and Haddington and works at Dunbar Castle.

Shot in the thigh by an arquebus at Haddington, he supervised the works at Leith from a chair carried by four workmen. In 1551 he defended Mirandola against papal troops in the War of Parma. Leading a French army for the Republic of Siena against Cosimo de' Medici, he won a costly victory at Pontedera on 11 June 1554, but could not be supplied by the ships of his brother Leone, who had been killed near Castiglione della Pescaia, and he fell back on Pistoia before the defeat of 2 August.

In 1556 he was made superintendent of the papal army and lord of Épernay. Two years later he served under Francis, Duke of Guise, at the siege of Thionville, near Metz in Lorraine, and died there of his wounds on 21 June 1558. He is generally credited with inventing the dragoon, the mounted arquebusier. His son Filippo Strozzi also became a military commander, and his daughter Clarice married Onorato I of Savoia in 1558.
pierre-buyoya: Pierre Buyoya was born in Rutovu, Bururi Province, on 24 November 1949, in Belgian-administered Ruanda-Urundi. His father, Rurikumunwa, was a Tutsi-Hima of the Batyaba clan. Buyoya was not a family surname but a descriptive name that can be translated as baby: his parents had lost several other children and feared he too might die young, and the name was never changed.

He was educated at a Catholic mission in Rutovu and then at the Ecole moyenne pédagogique, before enlisting as an officer and studying at the Royal Military Academy in Brussels, at the General Staff College in France and at the Bundeswehr Command and Staff College in West Germany. He joined the single party, the Union for National Progress (UPRONA), and sat on its Central Committee from 1979.

In September 1987 Buyoya led a coup against Jean-Baptiste Bagaza and chaired a 31-person military committee. In August 1988 a Hutu uprising in the communes of Ntega and Marangara killed about 300 Tutsi, and the army retaliated by killing approximately 20,000 Hutu. Buyoya then appointed a Commission of National Reconciliation, named the Hutu Adrien Sibomana as prime minister and allowed public debate on policy.

A Charter of Unity was approved by referendum in 1991, and a new constitution of 1992 provided for a multi-party system. The researcher Nigel Watt judged the unity measures cosmetic. Buyoya lost the June 1993 election to Melchior Ndadaye, who was assassinated in an attempted army coup in October 1993. Some human rights groups suspected Buyoya of supporting the plotters, and the civil war that followed killed 300,000 people.

On 25 July 1996 Buyoya returned to power in a coup that ousted interim President Sylvestre Ntibantunganya. International economic sanctions were eased as he formed an ethnically inclusive government and, in June 1998, a partnership with the National Assembly, dominated by the Hutu-backed FRODEBU. This led to the Arusha Accords of 2000, which introduced ethnic power-sharing. He chose a Hutu, Domitien Ndayizeye, as vice-president and handed power to him on 30 April 2003.

After the war Buyoya became a senator for life under the 2004 constitution and led African Union peace missions in Chad, from 2008, and in Mali. In his 2007 book the former ambassador Robert Krueger accused him of orchestrating the 1993 putsch. On 19 October 2020 the Supreme Court of Burundi sentenced him in absentia to life imprisonment for the murder of Ndadaye. He contracted COVID-19 in Mali and died on 17 December 2020 near Paris, and was buried in Bamako. In July 2024 his remains were returned to Burundi and buried in Rutovu.
pierre-chanel: Peter Louis Marie Chanel was born on 12 July 1803 in the hamlet of La Potière near Montrevel-en-Bresse, in the département of Ain, France, the fifth of eight children. From about the age of seven to twelve he worked as a shepherd, until the local parish priest persuaded his parents to let him attend a small school. His interest in foreign missions began when he read letters from missionaries in America. He studied at the minor seminary at Meximieux, at the Belley diocesan college and at the major seminary at Brou, and was ordained on 15 July 1827. His request to go to the missions was refused, and he served for three years as parish priest of Crozet.

In 1831 Chanel joined the new Society of Mary, the Marists. It appointed him spiritual director at the seminary of Belley, where he stayed five years. When the Marists were asked in 1836 to send missionaries to the south-west Pacific, Chanel became superior of the seven who left Le Havre on 24 December aboard the Delphine, with the new Bishop of Maronea, Jean-Baptiste Pompallier. After stops in Valparaíso, the Gambier Islands and Tahiti, Chanel went on to Futuna with the lay brother Marie-Nizier Delorme, arriving on 8 November 1837.

King Niuliki of Alo received them well at first. After a cyclone on 2 February 1839 destroyed almost all the houses and plantations, Chanel tended the sick and baptised the dying, winning the name the man with the kind heart.

Niuliki believed Christianity would undermine his authority as high priest and king. When his son Meitala asked to be baptised, the king sent his son-in-law Musumusu to do whatever was necessary. Musumusu feigned the need of medical attention and, while Chanel treated him, others ransacked the house; Musumusu clubbed the priest to death with an axe on 28 April 1841. Most islanders later became Catholic, and Musumusu himself converted. Chanel was beatified on 17 November 1889 and canonised on 12 June 1954 by Pope Pius XII, and is recognised as the protomartyr and patron saint of Oceania. His relics were returned to Futuna in 1977.
pierre-corneille: Corneille was born in Rouen on 6 June 1606, the son of a distinguished lawyer. He received a Jesuit education at the Collège de Bourbon, where acting was part of the training, and began to study law at 18, though his practical legal work was largely unsuccessful. His father secured him two magisterial posts with the Rouen department of Forests and Rivers.

He wrote his first play, the comedy Mélite, which he brought to a group of traveling actors in 1629; it succeeded in Paris, and he moved there that year. His early comedies depart from the farce tradition by reflecting the language and manners of fashionable Parisian society. His first true tragedy, Médée, was produced in 1635.

In 1634 Corneille wrote verses for Cardinal Richelieu's visit to Rouen and was chosen as one of Les Cinq Auteurs, who were to give dramatic form to Richelieu's ideas for a drama of virtue. The Cardinal's demands proved too restrictive, and Corneille left and returned to Rouen. Le Cid, based on Guillem de Castro's Mocedades del Cid, was first printed in 1637 as a tragicomedy.

It was an enormous popular success but provoked the Querelle du Cid, a pamphlet war in which Georges de Scudéry attacked it harshly. Richelieu had the Académie française analyse it, and Jean Chapelain's Sentiments of 1638 held that it broke too many of the classical unities of time, place and action.

After the quarrel Corneille returned to the theatre in 1640 with Horace, followed by Cinna and Polyeucte; with Le Cid these are known as his Classical Tetralogy. He later revised Le Cid, labelling it a tragedy in editions from 1648. He married Marie de Lampérière in 1641, and they had seven children.

After the poor reception of Pertharite in 1652 he left the stage and finished a verse translation of The Imitation of Christ in 1656. He returned in 1659, and in 1660 he published Trois discours sur le poème dramatique, defending his departures from the rules. His Tite et Bérénice of 1671 was generally thought inferior to Jean Racine's Bérénice, written on the same subject, and his last play, Suréna of 1674, failed completely.

Corneille retired from the stage after Suréna and died at his home in Paris on 1 October 1684. His grave in the Église Saint-Roch had no monument until 1821. Voltaire produced a twelve-volume annotated edition, the Commentaires sur Corneille, first published in 1764; in the second edition he added five hundred critical notes, which polarised opinion further. In the 19th century opinion turned against Voltaire, and Napoleon's stated preference for Corneille revived his reputation as a dramatist.
pierre-daubusson: Pierre d'Aubusson was born in the castle of Le Monteil, in what is now the French department of Creuse, the fifth son of Jean d'Aubusson. His elder brother Antoine served Charles VII and Louis XI, and his three other brothers became bishops. The story of his youth up to 1444 that has circulated since the 17th century is unreliable: it goes back to a biography of 1677 by the Jesuit Dominique Bouhours. He probably joined the Knights of Saint John in 1444 or 1445 and then went to Rhodes.

A close associate of Grand Master Piero Raimondo Zacosta, he was put in charge of repairing and modernising the fortifications of Rhodes, the Order's castles in the Dodecanese and the Château Saint Pierre at what is now Bodrum. Early in 1476 he was elected Grand Prior of the Langue d'Auvergne, and in June of that year Grand Master.

In May 1480 an Ottoman fleet of Sultan Mehmed II arrived carrying some 100,000 men under Mesih Pasha, a Palaiologos who had converted to Islam. Reinforced by 500 knights and 2,000 soldiers brought from France by his brother Antoine, the defenders held out until August; after three failed assaults the Turkish force withdrew, leaving 9,000 dead. D'Aubusson was wounded three times, and the siege made his name across Europe.

When Mehmed's sons Bayezid and Cem fought over the throne, the defeated Cem sought refuge at Rhodes under a safe-conduct and was then sent, with his consent, to Bourganeuf in France under the guard of d'Aubusson's nephew Guy de Blanchefort. D'Aubusson accepted 45,000 ducats a year from Bayezid II to keep Cem from appealing to the Christian powers.

Besides the cardinal's hat he received the right to confer the Order's benefices without papal sanction, and the Order absorbed the Order of the Holy Sepulchre and some Italian houses of the Knights of St. Lazarus. His plans for a crusade found no support with Rodrigo Borgia on the throne of St. Peter, and an expedition against Mytilene in 1501 failed through dissension. He expelled all adult Jews from Rhodes and had their children forcibly baptised. He died on 3 July 1503.
pierre-de-la-baume: Pierre de La Baume was born at the château de Montrevel in Bresse, Savoy, the second son of Gui de La Baume, later count of Montrevel and a knight of the Order of the Golden Fleece, and of Jeanne de Longuy. He received a doctorate in theology at the University of Dole in 1502. A worldly and well-connected courtier abbot, he held several abbeys in commendam, drawing their revenues without living in them; his favourite, Saint-Oyend at Condat, was given to him in 1511 by Margaret of Austria, whom his father served.

La Baume was a councillor of Charles III, Duke of Savoy, and represented him at the Fifth Lateran Council. Chosen bishop of Geneva on 10 October 1522, he disappointed those who hoped he would defend the city's liberties against the duke, leaving local affairs to his vicar, Amé Lévrier, during his frequent absences. The duke had Lévrier arrested on 12 March 1524 and put to death. After Charles forced the Genevans to accept his sovereignty at the Conseil des hallebardes on 15 December 1525, they rose in revolt and allied themselves with Bern, Fribourg and the Swiss cantons.

Returning after two years away, La Baume could raise no support for Savoyard claims. In 1527 he handed the administration of justice to a tribunal of citizens and withdrew to Condat. Charles then seized his benefices of Saint-Claude de Pignerol and Suze, and the bishop submitted completely to regain his revenues. The dominant Protestant party in Geneva twice expelled him, and after the second time he withdrew to Annecy.

He was made a cardinal on 19 December 1539 and received the see of Besançon on 29 December 1541, and Emperor Charles V made him a Prince of the Empire. He died on 5 May 1544. The predella panels of the great retable he commissioned for the abbey of Saint-Oyend at Saint-Claude, now the cathedral of Saint-Pierre, Saint-Paul et Saint-André, survive, and his nephew Claude de La Baume became a cardinal in 1578.
pierre-de-rigaud-marquis-de-vaudreuil-ca: Pierre de Rigaud de Vaudreuil de Cavagnial was born in Quebec on 22 November 1698, the son of Philippe de Rigaud Vaudreuil, Governor-General of New France, and his wife Louise-Élisabeth, daughter of Pierre de Joybert de Soulanges et de Marson. Commissioned into the French Royal Army while still a youth, he was awarded the Cross of St. Louis in 1730 and was appointed governor of Trois-Rivières in 1733.

Appointed governor of French Louisiana in 1742, he served there from 10 May 1743 to 9 February 1753 and proved a skilled officer and capable administrator. In Louisiana he married Jeanne-Charlotte de Fleury Deschambault, a widow about 15 years older than he. He moved to France in 1753, and in 1755 King Louis XV appointed him governor of New France. He was one of three governors-general of Canada known to have owned enslaved people: during his tenure he owned 16, of whom 13 were Africans.

Vaudreuil held supreme civil authority in Canada and was in principle commander-in-chief of all French forces, but he clashed often with Montcalm, the commander in the field, who resented his oversight. The two men came to detest each other, to the harm of the French war effort. After Montcalm's defeat by Major-general James Wolfe in the Battle of the Plains of Abraham, Vaudreuil tried in vain to rally resistance and surrendered Montreal to Major-general Jeffrey Amherst.

He was one of several men blamed for France's losses in the New World. Imprisoned in the Bastille on 30 March 1762 and released on 18 May, he was among those tried with Bigot and others; of the 21 brought to trial, 10 were condemned and six acquitted. A military tribunal exonerated him in December 1763 and awarded him a pension and a decoration.

He sold his Canadian seigneuries of Vaudreuil and Rigaud to his cousin Michel Chartier de Lotbinière and retired to his family estate near Rouen, his fortune ruined by the affair. He died in Paris on 4 August 1778. Kenneth Roberts made him a menacing offstage presence in his novels Arundel and Rabble in Arms.
pierre-dugua-de-mons: Pierre Dugua de Mons was born about 1558 at the Château de Mons in Royan, Saintonge, to Guy and Claire Goumard Dugua. A Calvinist, he fought for Henri IV in the French wars of religion, and the king rewarded him with an annual pension of 1,200 crowns and the governorship of the town of Pons. He first travelled to north-eastern North America in 1599 with Pierre de Chauvin de Tonnetuit, and in 1600 went with him to Tadoussac.

In 1603 King Henry granted him the sole right to colonise North America between 40° and 60° North, a monopoly of its fur trade and the title of Lieutenant General for Acadia and New France; in return he promised to bring 60 new colonists each year. His expedition of 1604, backed by merchants of Rouen, Saint-Malo and La Rochelle, sailed with 79 settlers, among them François Gravé Du Pont, Samuel de Champlain, the Baron de Poutrincourt, the priest Nicolas Aubry and the interpreter Mathieu de Costa, the first recorded black man in North America.

On St Croix Island many settlers died of the harsh winter and scurvy. Searching the coast for a better site, with the Native guide Panounias and his wife, the French met peoples who farmed in ways new to them. In 1606 the Dutch captain Hendrick Lonck boarded two of his ships and took their furs and munitions. Port-Royal survived and prospered somewhat until 1607, when rival merchants protested against the monopoly and the king revoked it.

Dugua ceded Port-Royal to Poutrincourt and turned to the St Lawrence valley. He never returned to the New World, but he sent Champlain to found Quebec, so playing a major part in founding the first permanent French colony in North America. He was Lieutenant General of New France until 1610. From 1610 to 1617 he governed the Protestant city of Pons, where he oversaw a grand staircase of six levels joining the upper and lower towns. He died in 1628 at the Château d'Ardenne in Fléac-sur-Seugne.
pierre-esprit-radisson: Radisson was probably born in the lower Rhône region near Avignon, and by his own account he emigrated to Canada on 24 May 1651, perhaps with his sisters Élisabeth and Françoise and his half-sister Marguerite Hayet, who later married Médard Chouart des Groseilliers. After his time with the Mohawk he went with them to Fort Orange, the Dutch post at present-day Albany, and escaped there on 29 October 1653. The Jesuit Joseph Antoine Poncet helped him reach Holland in 1654, and he returned to Trois-Rivières that year. In 1657 he joined a Franco-Iroquois expedition to Simon Le Moyne's mission in Onondaga territory, which the French abandoned in 1658.

In the winter of 1659–1660 Radisson and Des Groseilliers lived south of Lake Superior, in present-day Wisconsin, among the Huron, Ottawa, Ojibwa and Dakota. They came back to Québec on 24 August 1660 with many furs, but Governor Pierre de Voyer d'Argenson taxed them heavily, and after failing in the courts they sought English backing in Boston. Hearing of a salt sea rich in furs, they aimed for Hudson Bay by sea. In 1665 they met King Charles II in England, and in September 1668 the Nonsuch reached the Rupert River on James Bay, where about 300 Cree came to trade in 1669.

With Prince Rupert of the Rhine as patron, Radisson received the royal charter of 2 May 1670 that founded the Hudson's Bay Company, and in 1672 he married Mary Kirke, daughter of the investor Sir John Kirke. As anti-French feeling grew in England, the two partners returned to French service in 1675. Radisson helped fund Jean II d'Estrées's expedition against Tobago in 1677 and in 1681 founded a fort on the Nelson River under the French flag. Recruited back by the English ambassador Lord Preston, he sailed to the Hayes River in 1684 and was made superintendent of trade at Port Nelson in 1685.

Removed after making charges against the superintendent of York Factory in 1687, Radisson lived in England on an irregularly paid company pension and died in 1710. Many French Canadians long accepted his French contemporaries' verdict that he was a traitor to France. Towns in Quebec, Saskatchewan and Wisconsin, a Montreal Metro station and HMCS Radisson bear his name, Paul Muni played him in the 1941 film Hudson's Bay, and Martin Fournier wrote his academic biography in 2001.
pierre-gaultier-de-varennes-sieur-de-la-: La Vérendrye was born on 17 November 1685 in Trois-Rivières, New France, the eldest son of René Gaultier de Varennes, a soldier who had come to Canada in 1665, and of Marie, daughter of Pierre Boucher, the first governor of Trois-Rivières. His father died when he was three, and he was educated at the Jesuit seminary in Quebec.

As a young cadet he took part in the raids of Queen Anne's War, including the Raid on Deerfield in Massachusetts, and in a failed attack on St. John's, Newfoundland. He then fought in Flanders in the War of the Spanish Succession and was badly wounded at the Battle of Malplaquet. Back in Canada he married Marie-Anne Dandonneau in 1712 and lived by farming and the fur trade.

In 1728 he became commandant of the poste du Nord on the north shore of Lake Superior. Britain had held Hudson Bay since the Treaty of Utrecht of 1713, and the French hoped to find a River of the West leading to the Pacific. A Cree guide, Auchagah, drew him a map of the canoe routes to Lake Winnipeg, and in 1730 he agreed a plan with Governor Beauharnois, paid for by Quebec merchants who expected a share of the fur trade. Whether exploration was his real aim or a pretext for trade is not clear.

His son Jean-Baptiste built Fort St. Pierre on Rainy Lake, Fort St. Charles followed on Lake of the Woods, and Fort Maurepas was raised near the mouth of the Red River. In 1736 Jean-Baptiste, the Jesuit priest Jean-Pierre Aulneau and about twenty others were killed by the Sioux on Massacre Island.

In October 1738 he built Fort La Reine at Portage la Prairie and crossed the prairie with a band of Assiniboines to a Mandan village, probably near present-day New Town, North Dakota, returning in January 1739. His son Louis-Joseph later went west, probably as far as the Big Horn Mountains of Wyoming in 1742-1743.

The French minister Maurepas suspected him of trading in furs when he should have been exploring, and La Vérendrye resigned in 1743. Reappointed in 1746, he was planning an expedition up the Saskatchewan River when he died on 5 December 1749, shortly after receiving the Order of Saint Louis. His sons were then pushed out of the western command. A statue by Joseph-Émile Brunette stands in Saint Boniface, Manitoba, and parks, streets and a mountain in British Columbia bear his name.
pierre-joseph-proudhon: Proudhon was born in Besançon on 15 January 1809, the son of a brewer and cooper. In 1827 he began an apprenticeship at a printing press, and later worked at a press in Besançon that mostly published ecclesiastical works. Reading this Christian literature for hours every day made him question his religious beliefs and eventually reject Christianity.

He qualified as a journeyman compositor in September 1830, but unemployment and poverty followed. A friend, Fallot, offered financial help if he came to Paris to study philosophy, and Proudhon walked there from Besançon. Fallot's death in 1836 ended the support, but the friendship led him to leave printing for philosophy.

In 1839 the Academy of Besançon set an essay prize on the utility of celebrating Sunday. Proudhon used the subject to discuss a range of political and philosophical ideas; his ideas on authority, morality and property disturbed the judges, and he received only the bronze medal, which he took as a sign that his writing unsettled elite academics. His first major work, What Is Property?, published in 1840, contains his best-known assertion, that property is theft, and drew the attention of the French authorities and of Karl Marx, who began a correspondence with him.

After the Revolution of 1848 Proudhon sat in the French Parliament and called himself a federalist. He unsuccessfully tried to create a national bank offering interest-free loans, to be funded by an income tax on capitalists and shareholders that came to nothing. Marx answered Proudhon's The System of Economic Contradictions with The Poverty of Philosophy, a dispute that became one source of the split between anarchist and Marxist wings of the International Working Men's Association.

Proudhon was the first person known to call himself an anarchist. He sought a third form of society, the synthesis of communism and property, which he called liberty, and described mutualism as the synthesis of private property and collective ownership. Under mutualism, self-employed artisans, peasants and cooperatives would trade their products on the market, and large workplaces would be run by democratic labour associations.

The state would be replaced by a federation of free communes. In 1863 he wrote that all his economic ideas could be summed up as agricultural-industrial federation. He opposed dictatorship, militarism, nationalism and war, and considered a social revolution achievable peacefully. He died in Passy on 19 January 1865 and was buried at Montparnasse cemetery.
pierre-laval: Pierre Jean Marie Laval was born on 28 June 1883 in Châteldon, near Vichy in Auvergne, the son of Gilbert Laval and Claudine Tournaire. His father worked as a café proprietor and postman, and the family was comfortably off compared with the rest of the village. Laval abandoned natural science studies for law and in 1909 became a lawyer who defended strikers, trade unionists and left-wing agitators against government prosecution. In 1914 he was elected to the Chamber of Deputies as a Socialist for the Seine, at nearly 31 the youngest member of the Chamber, and during the First World War he held to pacifist convictions.

After losing his seat in 1919 Laval left the Socialist party, was elected mayor of Aubervilliers in 1923, and returned to the Chamber as an independent in 1924. He was Minister of Public Works in 1925, held other posts under Aristide Briand, and later served as Minister of Labour. Between 1927 and 1930 he accumulated a sizeable personal fortune, which after the war led to charges that he had used his political position to enrich himself.

He formed his first government on 27 January 1931. During the Austrian banking crisis of that year he blocked a proposed international loan for nationalist reasons and demanded diplomatic concessions from Austria, and the Creditanstalt declared bankruptcy on 11 May 1931. He joined Gaston Doumergue's government in 1934, became Foreign Minister after Louis Barthou was assassinated in October, and returned as prime minister in 1935. His handling of the Abyssinia Crisis was widely denounced as appeasement of Benito Mussolini and prompted his resignation in 1936.

In Philippe Pétain's Vichy government Laval was vice-president of the Council of Ministers from July to December 1940. He openly sympathised with National Socialism, was convinced that Germany would win the war, and worked to dismantle the Third Republic. Pétain dismissed him on 13 December 1940, citing an incompatibility of working styles, and had him arrested and driven to his home. Laval returned to power in April 1942. In a radio speech on 22 June 1942 he said he wished for a German victory, since otherwise Bolshevism would establish itself everywhere, and the speech made plain to many that the Vichy government was subservient to Germany.

After the Liberation of France in 1944 the Germans arrested him and moved him with the Vichy remnant to Sigmaringen. He fled to Spain in April 1945, was expelled and arrested by the Free French, and was imprisoned at Fresnes. His trial, which scholars such as Robert Paxton and Geoffrey Warner say showed the poisonous atmosphere of the purge trials, ended in a death sentence for plotting against the security of the state and collaboration. Laval was executed by firing squad on 15 October 1945.
pierre-le-moyne-diberville: Iberville was born at Fort Ville-Marie, now Montreal, the third son of Charles le Moyne de Longueuil et de Châteauguay, a Norman who had become lord of Longueuil, and Catherine Thierry Messier of Rouen. Most of his eleven brothers became soldiers; Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville later founded New Orleans. Raised a Catholic and educated in a Sulpician seminary, he was meant for the priesthood but chose a military life. At 12 he was a cabin boy on his uncle's ship trading to Port Royal in Acadia, and he later worked in the fur trade at Sault Ste. Marie.

In 1686 he joined the expedition of Pierre de Troyes against the Hudson's Bay Company, which took the three English posts on James Bay; at Fort Rupert he captured the sloop Craven. He returned in 1688 and took three company ships, captured Fort Severn in 1690 and York Factory in 1694, and after the English retook it he won it again in 1697, when it stayed French until 1713. In King William's War he was second in command in the raid of 1690 that ended in the Schenectady massacre, and in 1696 he took Pemaquid on 14 August before the Newfoundland campaign, in which 36 settlements were destroyed and St. John's taken.

Sent by Pontchartrain, the minister for the navy, to find the mouth of the Mississippi, he sailed from Brest in October 1698 and entered the delta in March 1699. He left a garrison of 81 men at Fort Maurepas, and on a third voyage in February 1701 built a fort at Mobile, where Henri de Tonti helped him win good relations with the Indians. He left Louisiana for the last time in April 1702.

Weakened by malaria, he led twelve vessels from France early in 1706, and with Henri-Louis de Chavagnac devastated Nevis from 1 to 22 April. He died suddenly in Havana in July 1706, perhaps of yellow fever, and was buried in the Church of San Cristóbal. An inquiry into his fortune and accusations of embezzlement lasted more than thirty years, and his widow, Marie Thérèse Pollet, had to repay much of her inheritance. He won all his battles but could never hold what he had won.
pierre-mendes-france: Pierre Isaac Isidore Mendès France was born on 11 January 1907 in Paris, the son of a textile merchant from Limoges and a descendant of Portuguese Jews who settled in France in the 16th century. He joined the Radical Party in 1924, took a doctorate in law and in 1926, at nineteen, became the youngest member of the Paris bar. In 1932 he was elected to the Chamber of Deputies for the Eure, the youngest member of the Assembly, and in 1938 the government of Léon Blum appointed him Under Secretary of State for Finance.

In October 1940 the Vichy regime tried him for desertion after he boarded the liner SS Massilia for Casablanca to continue the fight, and imprisoned him. He escaped to Britain and joined the Free French forces under Charles de Gaulle, flying in a dozen bombing raids. After the liberation of Paris in August 1944 de Gaulle appointed him Minister for National Economy, but he resigned when de Gaulle sided with the Finance Minister, René Pleven, against his support for state regulation of wages and prices.

Mendès France failed to form a government in June 1953. After the French defeat at Dien Bien Phu in May 1954, the government of Joseph Laniel resigned on 12 June, and he formed a government with support from the centre-right. He negotiated at once with Ho Chi Minh, saying there was no choice but total withdrawal from Indochina, and the Assembly backed him by 471 votes to 14. Nationalist opinion was shocked, and he was the target of abuse, much of it anti-Semitic.

On Algeria, after the outbreak of the war in 1954, he declared that its departments were an integral part of the French Republic and that the idea of secession was unthinkable. He agreed with Habib Bourguiba on the independence of Tunisia by 1956 and began discussions with nationalist leaders in Morocco. He also helped bring about the Western European Union, but the National Assembly rejected the proposed European Defence Community. His cabinet fell in February 1955.

In 1956 he served as Minister of State under Guy Mollet but resigned over Mollet's handling of the Algerian War, and he resigned as Radical Party leader in 1957. He opposed de Gaulle's return to power in 1958, lost his seat that November, and later joined the Unified Socialist Party. He sat again in the Assembly in 1967 to 1968 and expressed sympathy for the student protesters of May 1968. In 1971 he supported François Mitterrand's new Socialist Party, and he died on 18 October 1982, having lived to see Mitterrand elected president.
pierre-montet: Jean Pierre Marie Montet was born on 27 June 1885 in Villefranche-sur-Saône in the Rhône and began his studies under Victor Loret at the University of Lyon. In 1911 he worked in Cairo with Jules Barthoux, and in 1912 they published the hieroglyphic and hieratic inscriptions of the Ouâdi Hammâmât. For his service in the First World War he was awarded the Croix de Guerre and made a Commander of the Legion of Honor.

Montet taught Egyptology at the University of Strasbourg from 1919 to 1948 and at the Collège de France in Paris from 1948 to 1956. He excavated at Byblos from 1920 to 1924 and published Byblos et l'Egypte in 1928. At Tanis the season of 1939–1940 brought the intact tombs of three pharaohs, Psusennes I, Amenemope and Shoshenq II, and the partly plundered tomb of Takelot I, which held a gold bracelet of his father Osorkon I and a heart scarab. He also found the plundered tomb of Osorkon II and the partly plundered tomb of that king's son, Prince Hornakht.

The start of the Second World War in Western Europe in May 1940 stopped all work at Tanis. After the war Montet returned and in 1946 uncovered the intact tomb of General Wendjebauendjed, commander-in-chief of the army under Psusennes I, as well as two wells within the Amoun temple. He described the work in Tanis, douze années de fouilles dans une capitale oubliée du delta Égyptien (1942) and La Necropole Royale de Tanis (1958).

Montet died in Paris on 19 June 1966. He believed that Tanis was Pi-Ramesses, but the Austrian Egyptologist Manfred Bietak later showed that, although stonework from Pi-Ramesses had been found at Tanis, the city itself lay some 30 km to the south. Montet is therefore credited as the discoverer of the transplanted city. He also wrote for a wider public, in Everyday Life in the Days of Ramesses the Great (1958) and Eternal Egypt (1964).
pierre-nkurunziza: Pierre Nkurunziza was born on 18 December 1964 in Bujumbura, shortly after Burundi's independence from Belgian rule, one of six children of a family from Buye in Ngozi Province. His father, Eustache Ngabisha, a Hutu and Catholic, was a politician of UPRONA and a provincial governor who was killed in the genocidal violence of 1972. His mother, Domitille Minani, was a Tutsi and Protestant nurse's assistant. Nkurunziza was considered Hutu. He took a degree in physical education at the University of Burundi in 1990, taught at a school in Muramvya, became an assistant lecturer in 1992, and coached football; he also taught at the Higher Institute for Military Cadres, where he met officers who later became leading figures in the rebel groups.

After President Melchior Ndadaye was assassinated in an attempted coup in October 1993, ethnic violence between Hutu and Tutsi began the Burundian Civil War. Nkurunziza fled the university in 1995 after hundreds of Hutu students were killed and spent several years in hiding. A government-backed court sentenced him to death in absentia in 1998. He joined the CNDD–FDD, a rebel group largely supported by Hutus, rising to General Secretary by 1998, and became its president on 28 August 2000. All five of his siblings were killed in the war, three of them fighting for the CNDD–FDD.

Agreements in 2003 brought the movement into national politics, and Nkurunziza became a minister in the transitional government of Domitien Ndayizeye. The CNDD–FDD won the elections and Parliament elected him president, and his term began on 26 August 2005.

In his first term he oversaw the rebuilding of the state on the inter-ethnic compromise of the Arusha Accords, which divided state positions between Tutsi, Hutu and the minority Twa. The last Hutu rebel faction, PALIPEHUTU–FNL, was demobilised in 2008, and Burundi's public debt was cancelled in 2009. He won a second term in July 2010 in polls boycotted by the opposition.

On 25 April 2015 he announced that he would seek a third term. The announcement set off protests, and on 13 May soldiers loyal to Godefroid Niyombare attempted a military uprising that collapsed. He was re-elected in July 2015.

Nkurunziza died on 8 June 2020, before the planned transfer of power; government sources gave a heart attack as the cause, while others said COVID-19. Ndayishimiye was sworn in on 18 June. He is recorded as the longest-serving president in Burundian history, at nearly fifteen years.
pierre-pigneau-de-behaine: Pierre Joseph Georges Pigneau was born on 2 November 1741 at Origny-en-Thiérache. His father's family owned a small estate called Béhaine, but he was not of noble birth, and the particle seems to have appeared first in the 1787 Treaty of Versailles. Sent out by the Paris Foreign Missions Society, he reached Hà Tiên in March 1767 and headed the Seminary of the Holy Angels, moved there from Ayutthaya after the Burmese invasion.

In 1768 he was jailed for three months in a cangue after Siamese complaints that the school had sheltered a fugitive Siamese prince, and in 1769 pirates massacred some of the students and burned the school. At Virampatnam near Pondicherry he compiled the Dictionarium Anamitico-Latinum, a Vietnamese-Latin dictionary published in 1838. Named bishop of Adran and Apostolic Vicar of Cochinchina in 1771, he was ordained in 1774.

In 1777, when the Tây Sơn brothers took Saigon and wiped out almost the entire Nguyễn dynasty, the fifteen-year-old Nguyễn Ánh sheltered at Pigneau's seminary, and from then on Pigneau acted more as a politician than a missionary. He procured Portuguese weapons and shared Nguyễn Ánh's flights to Phú Quốc and Siam. Asked to seek French help, he took the young Prince Cảnh to Versailles, arriving in February 1787, after the French administration at Pondicherry had refused to act.

The treaty of 21 November 1787 promised four frigates, 1650 French soldiers and 250 Indian sepoys in return for Pulo Condore and access to Tourane, but on 2 December the foreign minister left its execution to Thomas Conway, Governor of Pondicherry, who held back. "I shall make the revolution in Cochinchina alone," Pigneau wrote. With money from French merchants, and volunteers and deserters such as Jean-Baptiste Chaigneau and Jean-Marie Dayot, he equipped ships that reached Vũng Tàu on 24 July 1789.

The French contingent modernised Nguyễn Ánh's army, navy and fortifications; Olivier de Puymanel built the citadels of Saigon in 1790 and Diên Khánh in 1793 on the principles of Vauban. From 1794 Pigneau took part in every campaign with Prince Cảnh. He died of dysentery at Qui Nhơn on 9 October 1799 and was buried in Saigon on 16 December before 40,000 mourners. He had hoped for a Catholic ruler of Vietnam, but Cảnh was never converted. In 1983 his tomb was dismantled and his remains were sent to the Paris Foreign Missions Society.
pierre-poivre: Poivre was born in Lyon on 23 August 1719 into the family of a wealthy silk merchant. He joined a Jansenist mission at sixteen and the Society of Foreign Missions four years later, which sent him to East Asia in 1740, to Macau and Canton. On 25 January 1745 his ship, the Dauphin, was attacked by the English in the Straits of Banca, and a cannonball wound cost him part of his right arm. After time in Java, Pondicherry and Ile de France he reached France in June 1748 and gave up missionary life.

Sent as an envoy to Cochinchina, he obtained the right to set up a trading post from King Vo Vuong in 1749 and then raided Dutch territories for plants; five of his nutmeg plants reached Mauritius in December 1753. A voyage of 1754–1755 in search of cloves took him towards Manila and Timor, and he brought back cacao and breadfruit. After capture by the English he retired to Lyon in 1757 and wrote Voyages d'un Philosophe, published in 1769 and read by Thomas Jefferson.

The Duc de Praslin offered him the post of intendant of Ile de France and Bourbon in 1766, and he sailed in 1767 with his wife, Françoise Robin. He made the islands self-sufficient in food, improved the harbour of Port Louis, protected forests against erosion and employed Philibert Commerson to lay out the garden of Pamplemousses. He limited slaves' working hours but also brought in measures against runaways and inter-racial marriages, and the number of slaves rose from 15,000 in 1767 to 49,000 in 1797.

Poivre resigned in 1772 and returned to France, where a royal pension was decided in 1775; he died at his home in Lyon. His widow later married Pierre Samuel du Pont de Nemours, who wrote his biography. The Pamplemousses garden, developed further by Jean-Nicolas Céré, is now the Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam Botanical Garden, and the Poivre Islands atoll of the Amirante Islands in the Seychelles is named after him. Some authors see his name, which means pepper, behind the Peter Piper rhyme.
pierre-savorgnan-de-brazza: Born Pietro Paolo Savorgnan di Brazzà in Rome on 26 January 1852, he was the seventh of thirteen children of the nobleman and artist Ascanio Savorgnan di Brazzà. Interested from an early age in exploration, he won entry to the French naval school at Brest. In 1870 he sailed to Algeria, where he witnessed the bloody suppression of the Mokrani Revolt, which committed him to a philosophy of non-violence. He first reached Africa in 1872 on an anti-slavery mission near Gabon, and he took French citizenship in 1874 and adopted the French spelling of his name.

His first expedition, from 1875 to 1878, explored the Ogooué with partial government funding and the rest from his own pocket. He carried only cotton textiles and tools for barter, and his peaceful manner won the trust of river peoples whose resistance had kept every other European out. The French government authorised a second mission from 1879 to 1882, to prevent Henry M. Stanley, in the service of Leopold II of Belgium, from occupying the whole Congo Basin. Following the Ogooué upstream and then going overland to the Lefini, Brazza reached the Congo River in 1880.

There Makoko Iloo I of the Téké Kingdom, aware of Stanley's advance and interested in trade, signed a treaty accepting French protection. Makoko also arranged a French settlement at Mfoa on Malebo Pool, later Brazzaville, left in the care of the Senegalese Sergeant Malamine Camara. The French press called Brazza the peaceful conqueror. He was later in charge of the French Congo until his dismissal in 1897 over poor revenue and reports that the treatment of Africans was too good. He himself had become disillusioned with the concession companies' exploitative and repressive practices.

In 1905 Brazza was sent to investigate reports of forced labour and brutality under the concession companies. His report was revealing and damning, but it was suppressed. He fell sick near the end of the mission and died in Dakar on 14 September 1905, aged 53. His widow Thérèse maintained that he had been poisoned by the colonial authorities. He was reburied in Algiers, and in 2006 his remains were moved to a mausoleum in Brazzaville. That decision drew protests from some Congolese, who regarded him as a coloniser and not a humanist.
pierre-trudeau: Joseph Philippe Pierre Yves Elliott Trudeau was born on 18 October 1919 and raised in Outremont, Quebec. He was fluently bilingual from his earliest years. He studied law at the Université de Montréal from 1940 until 1943 and in late 1944 began a master's degree in political economy at Harvard.

On returning to Montreal in 1949 he became a leading opponent of Premier Maurice Duplessis and supported the workers in the Asbestos strike. He co-founded and edited the dissident journal Cité Libre, which helped to provide the intellectual basis for the Quiet Revolution. Duplessis blacklisted him from teaching law, and from 1949 to 1951 he worked in the Privy Council Office in Ottawa. In 1965 he joined the Liberal Party with Gérard Pelletier and Jean Marchand, and he won the Montreal seat of Mount Royal, which he held until 1984.

As minister of justice from 1967 to 1968 he introduced the Criminal Law Amendment Act, which decriminalised homosexual acts between consenting adults and legalised contraception, abortion and lotteries. His energetic campaign, called Trudeaumania, helped him win the Liberal leadership in 1968, and he succeeded Lester B. Pearson as prime minister. He led the Liberals to victory in 1968, 1972, 1974 and 1980, losing narrowly in 1979, and served as leader of the Official Opposition from 1979 to 1980.

His government pioneered official bilingualism and multiculturalism. It established Petro-Canada and launched the National Energy Program, which generated significant controversy in oil-rich Western Canada. He invoked the War Measures Act in response to the October Crisis of 1970 and led the federalist campaign in the 1980 Quebec referendum. In foreign policy he established diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China and oversaw Canada's entry into the G7 forum. In 1982 he enacted the Constitution Act, which patriated the Constitution and established the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Trudeau retired from politics shortly before the 1984 federal election and practised law at the Montreal firm of Heenan Blaikie. He spoke against the Meech Lake and Charlottetown accords, arguing that they would strengthen Quebec nationalism. He died on 28 September 2000, aged 80. Critics have accused him of arrogance, economic mismanagement and unduly centralising decisions to the detriment of Quebec's culture and the economy of the Prairies, while admirers have praised his intellect and political skill, which they say helped maintain national unity during the Quebec sovereignty movement.
pierre-werner: Pierre Werner was born on 29 December 1913 at Saint-André-lez-Lille in northern France to Luxembourgish parents. He studied at the Cours Supérieurs de Luxembourg in 1933 and 1934, then at the Law Faculty of the University of Paris and the École libre des sciences politiques until 1937, and completed a doctorate in law in Luxembourg in 1938.

He chaired the Association of Catholic Students from 1935 to 1937. After a short time as a lawyer in Luxembourg City he became a banker. During the Nazi occupation of 1940 to 1945 he gave clandestine support to the resistance. After the war he became Controller of the banking system and attended the Bretton Woods Conference, which set up the International Monetary Fund.

Werner became Finance Minister in 1953 and was the 19th and 21st prime minister, titled President of the Government, from 1959 to 1974 and from 1979 to 1984. He governed in coalition with the Democratic Party from 1959 to 1964, with the Luxembourg Socialist Workers' Party from 1964 to 1969, and again with the Democratic Party from 1969 to 1974.

The Christian Social People's Party went into opposition from 1974 to 1979, during which time he led it in parliament. His last government was another coalition with the Democratic Party. In 1965 he helped end the empty chair crisis by persuading France, whose president Charles de Gaulle had suspended its participation in European meetings, to resume its seat.

In 1970 the heads of state or government gave Werner the mandate to draft, with a group of experts, a blueprint for an economic and monetary union within the EEC. His report advocated gradual reforms, the irreversible fixing of exchange rates and a single currency within a decade. It was not implemented at the time, owing to internal political disagreements and the oil crisis, but Jacques Delors later revived it, and its principles were enshrined in the Treaty of Maastricht, which paved the way for the euro.

At home Werner worked to diversify an economy hit by a Europe-wide crisis in the steel industry, attracting new industrial investment and financial services. He is remembered for using tripartite mediation between industry, labour and government to overcome the steel crisis of 1979 to 1984.

He negotiated the relocation of several European institutions to Luxembourg and, after leaving politics in 1984, chaired the Société Européenne des Satellites from 1989 to 1996, having laid the ground for the company. He sponsored culture, especially music, and promoted the restoration of Vianden Castle. He died in Luxembourg City on 24 June 2002. The Pierre Werner Institute was created in Luxembourg in 2003, and the country's main cricket ground at Walferdange is named after him.
piet-cronje: Cronjé was born on 4 October 1836 in the Cape Colony and raised in the South African Republic. Short, black-bearded and reputed to have considerable personal courage, he made his name in the First Boer War of 1880–1881 by besieging the British garrison at Potchefstroom. He could not force its surrender until after the general armistice had been concluded, and was accused of keeping news of the armistice from the garrison.

His force rounded up Leander Jameson at Doornkop at the end of the Jameson Raid on 2 January 1896. In the Second Boer War he commanded in the western theatre and began the sieges of Kimberley and Mafeking, where a force of between 2,000 and 6,000 men faced 1,200 regulars and militia under Colonel Robert Baden-Powell. When Lord Methuen tried to relieve Kimberley, Cronjé fought him at the Battle of Modder River on 28 November 1899, a Pyrrhic victory for the British.

His tactics there, infantry placed at the foot of the hills rather than on the tops to make the most of their rifles' flat trajectory, earned Cronjé a place in military history, although they had been urged on him by General Koos de la Rey and President Martinus Theunis Steyn. The repulse of Methuen at the Battle of Magersfontein on 11 December was likewise due to De la Rey's planning, while Cronjé stayed in camp. An attritionist who saw little value in manoeuvre, he was enveloped by Lord Roberts' forces at Paardeberg.

Cronjé had been accompanied on campaign by his wife, Hester, and the two were sent to a prisoner-of-war camp on Saint Helena, where he stayed until the peace of 1902. His defeat lowered Boer morale, and Bloemfontein, capital of the Orange Free State, fell without a shot. Shunned by the other Boer generals, ridiculed in the press and left out of the peace talks at Vereeniging, he took part in re-enactments of the war at the World Fair in St. Louis in 1904 and then in a show on Coney Island. He later returned to South Africa and died at Klerksdorp on 4 February 1911.
piet-mondrian: Pieter Cornelis Mondriaan was born on 7 March 1872 in Amersfoort, the second of his parents' children. His father was a qualified drawing teacher. With his uncle Frits Mondriaan, a pupil of Willem Maris of the Hague School, the young Piet often painted and drew along the river Gein. After a strict Protestant upbringing he entered the Academy for Fine Art in Amsterdam in 1892, already qualified as a teacher.

His early work is naturalistic or Impressionistic, mostly landscapes of windmills, fields and rivers, and it shows the influence of pointillism and the vivid colours of Fauvism. The painting Evening (Avond) of 1908 uses a palette of almost entirely red, yellow and blue and is the earliest of his paintings to emphasise primary colours.

Mondrian moved to Paris in 1912 and dropped an a from his surname to mark his break with the Netherlands. The Cubism of Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque appeared at once in his work, but he saw it as a port of call rather than a destination. Staying in the Netherlands when the First World War began in 1914, he met Bart van der Leck and Theo van Doesburg at the Laren artists' colony, and van der Leck's use of only primary colours influenced him. With Van Doesburg he founded the journal De Stijl, in which he published essays defining his theory of neoplasticism.

He returned to France in 1918 and began grid-based paintings in late 1919. The lines in the early works are thin and grey, and in late 1920 and 1921 thick black lines separate larger and fewer forms, with more of them left white. In September 1938 he left Paris for London in the face of advancing fascism, and in 1940, after the Netherlands was invaded and Paris fell, he moved to Manhattan. His late New York canvases have more lines than any of his work since the 1920s, in an overlapping arrangement that looks almost like a map.

Mondrian's art was utopian and sought universal values. He proclaimed in 1914 that art is higher than reality and has no direct relation to it. In 1913 he began to fuse his art with his theosophical studies, which marked his final break from representational painting. He limited his vocabulary to the three primary colours, red, blue and yellow, the three primary values of black, white and grey, and the two primary directions, horizontal and vertical. He died on 1 February 1944.
piet-retief: Pieter Retief was born on 12 November 1780 in the Wagenmakersvallei, now the town of Wellington, to Jacobus and Debora Retief, Boers descended from the Huguenot refugee François Retif, who came from Mer near Blois in 1689. He worked on the family vineyard Welvanpas until he was 27. Settling on the frontier near Grahamstown in 1814, he grew wealthy in livestock but lost repeatedly to Xhosa raids, and is reported to have gone bankrupt at least twice, mainly through land speculation. He commanded punitive expeditions in the sixth Xhosa War.

As spokesman of the discontented frontier farmers, Retief wrote their manifesto, dated 22 January 1837 and published in the Grahamstown Journal on 2 February. It complained that the British government gave them no protection against raids and had ruined them through the Slavery Abolition Act 1833, whose compensation hardly reached a quarter of the slaves' market value. His household left the Winterberg District in early February 1837, and where parties of trekkers met at the Vet River he was elected governor of the United Laagers, a coalition that soon broke up.

From a camp at Kerkenberg near the Drakensberg he rode to Port Natal in October 1837 with Jan Gerritze Bantjes and fourteen men, and in November opened talks with Dingane kaSenzangakhona. Gerrit Maritz and Andries Hendrik Potgieter joined him in January 1838. Dingane agreed to Boer settlement if the trekkers recovered cattle taken by the Tlokwa, and they brought back some 700 head.

Dingane signed the deed of cession of the Tugela-Umzimvubu region on 6 February 1838, then invited the party to watch his soldiers perform and had them seized. About 100 people, among them Retief's son Pieter Cornelis and their servants, were killed by clubbing on the ridge of kwaMatiwane, Retief last. Attacks on the laagers followed in which 534 men, women and children were killed. After Blood River, Andries Pretorius's commando buried the remains on 21 December 1838 and recovered the deed from Retief's purse. The town of Piet Retief and, in part, Pietermaritzburg bear his name.
pieter-bruegel-the-elder: Bruegel's birth date is not documented. It is inferred from his entry into the Antwerp painters' guild in 1551, which usually happened between the ages of twenty and twenty-five, giving a range of 1525 to 1530. Lodovico Guicciardini recorded that he was born in Breda, while Karel van Mander named a village near Breda called Brueghel, which fits no known place. Nothing is known of his family background.
