The development of the East from the Assyrians to the Parthians is covered extensively, while early Roman history and the history of the Iberian Peninsula are briefly treated in the last two books.

The work drew on earlier Greek historians such as Theopompus, whose Philippica may have suggested the title, Ephorus, Timaeus and Polybius. Because such a work was thought beyond the ability of a Gallo-Roman, it is generally assumed that he used a Greek compilation such as the Universal History of Timagenes of Alexandria. Trogus criticised Sallust and Livy for putting elaborate speeches into the mouths of their characters.

The Philippic Histories is lost and survives in excerpts by other authors, including Jerome and Augustine, and in a loose epitome by Justin, who preserved the parts he found most important or interesting. The last event Justin records is the recovery of Roman standards from the Parthians in 20 BCE. Separate summaries of the books, the prologi, are preserved in the manuscripts of Justin. Even in this mutilated state the work is an important authority for the ancient history of the East. Trogus's books on animals and plants were quoted extensively by Pliny the Elder. His account of the Jews, set in the history of the Seleucid Empire, is, with the passages in Tacitus, the most extensive description of the Jews in classical Latin literature.
pompey: Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus was born in Picenum, the eldest son of Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo, who was the first of his family branch to reach senatorial status and became consul in 89 BCE. Pompey began his career serving with his father in the Social War. After Strabo died in 87 BCE, Pompey stood trial for his father's alleged embezzlement and was acquitted. In 83 BCE he raised a legion from his father's clients and veterans and joined Sulla, who greeted him with the title imperator.

In Sulla's civil war Pompey defeated the Marian forces in Sicily and Africa. His opponents nicknamed him adulescentulus carnifex, the young butcher, for the execution of Carbo, while his troops called him Magnus, after Alexander the Great. He later commanded in Spain against Quintus Sertorius and arrived in Italy in time to massacre 6,000 fugitives from the army of Spartacus. He was consul with Marcus Licinius Crassus in 70 BCE, when the tribunes recovered powers Sulla had removed.

Under the Lex Gabinia he was given wide powers to suppress the pirates of the Mediterranean, and under the lex Manilia he took over the war against Mithridates VI of Pontus. He then reorganised the East and intervened in Judea, backing Hyrcanus II against his brother Aristobulus II. Back in Rome he held a third triumph in 61 BCE, but the Senate refused to ratify his eastern settlement. In 60 BCE he joined Crassus and Julius Caesar in the First Triumvirate and married Caesar's daughter Julia.

Julia died in 54 BCE and Crassus at Carrhae in 53 BCE, removing the ties that held the alliance. Pompey aligned himself with the optimates, was elected sole consul in 52 BCE, and in 49 BCE war broke out with Caesar. Defeated at the Battle of Pharsalus in 48 BCE, he fled to Egypt and was killed on 28 September 48 BCE at Pelusium by Lucius Septimius, a Roman officer serving the Egyptian army.

Ancient and later writers treated his fall as a great subject. Lucan retold the civil war in his epic De Bello Civili, now known as the Pharsalia, and Renaissance English and French dramatists returned to the story, among them George Chapman and Pierre Corneille. Pompey's money also built the Theatre of Pompey, one of the best known structures of ancient Rome.
pomponius-mela: Little is known of Pomponius Mela beyond his name and birthplace, the small town of Tingentera or Cingentera on Algeciras Bay in southern Spain, identified as Iulia Traducta. The text naming it is corrupt. He wrote under the emperor Claudius: his allusion to a proposed British expedition by the reigning emperor is almost certainly to that of Claudius in 43 CE, and several references to events of the reign of Augustus, especially new names given to Spanish towns, show it cannot refer to Julius Caesar. Mela belonged to the Italic communities settled in Spain, like the two Senecas, Lucan, Martial and Quintilian. It has been conjectured that he was related to Marcus Annaeus Mela, son of Seneca the Elder and father of Lucan.

His short work, De situ orbis in three books, fills less than a hundred pages of ordinary print. Apart from the geographical parts of Pliny's Historia naturalis, which cites Mela as an important authority, it is the only formal treatise on the subject in Classical Latin. It mainly agrees with Greek writers from Eratosthenes to Strabo. Mela describes the coasts in the manner of a periplus, probably because his material came from navigators. He begins at the Straits of Gibraltar, follows the south coast of the Mediterranean, goes round Syria, Asia Minor and the Black Sea and returns to Spain, then follows the ocean coast from Spain and Gaul round to India and back.

He divides the Earth into five zones, of which only two are habitable, and uniquely among ancient geographers asserts that antichthones live in the southern temperate zone, cut off by the torrid zone. Like most classical geographers he regards the Caspian Sea as an inlet of the Northern Ocean. His knowledge of western Europe was ahead of the Greek writers: he defines the coasts of Spain and Gaul and the Bay of Biscay more accurately than Eratosthenes or Strabo, and he is the first to name the Orcades, or Orkney Islands. He also speaks of a great northern bay, the Codanus sinus, with a large island called Codanovia.

The work remained in use nearly to the year 1500. The first printed edition appeared at Milan in 1471, and the first critical edition was by Joachim Vadian in 1518. Johann Friedrich Gronovius edited it in 1685 and 1696, Arthur Golding's English translation appeared in 1585, and F. E. Romer published a recent English translation in 1998.
ponary-massacre: Ponary, now Paneriai, is a suburb of Vilnius. After the Soviet invasion of Poland in September 1939 the region was occupied and, on 10 October, transferred to Lithuania under the Soviet-Lithuanian Mutual Assistance Treaty. Following the Soviet annexation of Lithuania in June 1940, work began near Ponary on an oil storage facility for a future military airfield. It was never completed, and the Wehrmacht took the area in June 1941 during Operation Barbarossa. The killing squads used the six large pits dug for the storage tanks to hide the bodies of those they killed.

The killings began as soon as SS Einsatzkommando 9 reached Vilna on 2 July 1941. Most were carried out by the Ypatingasis burys, a Lithuanian volunteer unit eighty men strong. The Vilna Ghetto was established in September, and that month 3,700 Jews were shot in one operation and 6,000 in another, after being rounded up in the city and walked to Paneriai. Most victims were stripped before being shot. By the end of 1941 about 50,000 to 60,000 Vilna Jews had been killed, though estimates for this period differ widely. The pace slowed in 1942, when the Wehrmacht took on the ghettoised Jewish workers as slave labour.

As Soviet troops advanced in 1943, the Nazi units tried to hide the crime under the directive known as Aktion 1005. Eighty prisoners from the Stutthof concentration camp were forced to dig up the bodies and burn them. On 19 April 1944 the prisoners escaped through a tunnel dug with spoons, and the eleven who survived the war helped reveal the massacre.

The total number of victims is put at up to 100,000, of whom about 70,000 were Jews. Among the others were Polish intellectuals, including the professor Kazimierz Pelczar and the priest Romuald Świrkowski, members of the Armia Krajowa resistance, Soviet prisoners of war and Romani people. Under Soviet rule the official line was that the site held only Soviet citizens. The Polish journalist Kazimierz Sakowicz recorded the killings in a diary kept in hiding, which Rahel Margolis found and published in 1999. The site has monuments to Holocaust victims, erected in 1991, and to Polish victims, erected in 1990 and rebuilt in 2000, and a small museum.
ponce-puerto-rico: Ponce lies on the southern coastal plain of Puerto Rico, on the shore of the Caribbean Sea, south of Adjuntas, Utuado and Jayuya and between Peñuelas and Juana Díaz. The municipality has 31 barrios, 12 of them in the urban area, and is the second largest on the island by land area. It includes Cerro de Punta, the island's highest peak at 1,340 metres, and part of the Toro Negro Forest. Its historic district, Ponce Pueblo, lies about 4.8 kilometres inland from the coast.

The region belonged to the Taíno territory of Guaynia. Agüeybaná, a cacique who led it, was among those who greeted Juan Ponce de León when he came to the island in 1508. Four archaeological sites in the municipality are significant: Canas, Tibes, Caracoles and El Bronce. The city was founded on 12 August 1692 and is named after Juan Ponce de León y Loayza, great-grandson of the conquistador. Its first mayor was Pedro Sánchez de Matos. In the early 19th century Ponce was still one of dozens of hamlets on the island, whose people lived on subsistence agriculture, cattle raising and maritime contraband with foreigners.

During the 19th century a new architectural style, later called Ponce Creole, was born in the city, and architects mixed Art Nouveau and neoclassical styles. The Teatro La Perla was built in 1864. Ponce was the first city in Puerto Rico where Protestant churches were built, and the Ponce Cathedral dates from 1839. When the United States invaded Puerto Rico in 1898, Ponce was the largest city on the island, with a population of 22,000, and it had the best road to San Juan and underwater telegraph cables to Jamaica and the West Indies.

The taking of the port by American troops was a turning point in the campaign, since it let them bring in men and war material. Bomba and Plena music grew up mainly in the south of the island, and Ponce, especially Barrio San Antón, is known as a birthplace of these rhythms.

Ponce became the first municipality in Puerto Rico to obtain autonomy, on 27 October 1992, under the Autonomous Municipalities Act. Its historic centre has been revitalised under the Ponce en Marcha project, and it has many museums. The economy was long based on sugarcane and now rests on manufacturing, retail and tourism, and the Port of Ponce is the island's chief Caribbean port. Ponce has 166,327 inhabitants according to the 2010 census, and March 21 is observed each year in memory of the Ponce massacre.
pondicherry: Pondicherry stands on the south-east coast of India, with the Bay of Bengal to the east and the state of Tamil Nadu around it. Its name comes from the Tamil putu-cēri, new village, and the French first spelt it Poudichéry. The u was later misread as n, and the spelling Pondichéry stuck. It was also known as Vedapuri, as the settlement was once the home of scholars versed in the Vedas. A marketplace called Poduke, mentioned in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea as a port for Roman trade, has been identified with Arikamedu, about 3 kilometres from the modern city.

Before the Europeans came, the area was ruled in turn by the Pallavas, the Cholas, the Pandya dynasty, the Nayaks of Gingee under the Vijayanagara Empire, and from 1614 to 1638 by the Sultan of Bijapur. Portuguese traders came in 1521, followed by the Dutch and the Danes in the 17th century. In 1674 the French East India Company set up a trading centre, and François Martin turned it into the chief French settlement in India. He dealt with the sultans of Golconda, traded in jewellery and precious stones, and faced strong opposition from the Dutch and the English. A canal divided the city into a French Quarter and an Indian Quarter.

The Dutch captured Pondicherry on 21 August 1693, during the Nine Years' War, after a fleet of seventeen ships under Laurens Pit the Younger bombarded it for two weeks until Martin surrendered. It was handed back to the French in 1699 under the Peace of Ryswick. The British took it on 16 January 1761 and returned it by the Treaty of Paris of 1763, took it again in 1793 and returned it in 1814. France added Mahé in 1720, Yanam in 1731 and Karaikal in 1738.

In March 1954 the municipalities of Pondicherry and Karaikal, representing roughly 90 per cent of the people of the French possessions, called for a merger with India. A vote of 178 councillors on 18 October 1954 gave 170 votes in favour. The de facto transfer took place on 1 November 1954, and the treaty for the de jure transfer, signed in 1956, was ratified by the French National Assembly only on 16 August 1962.

Pondicherry, officially Puducherry, is the capital of the Union Territory of Puducherry, and most of its people speak Tamil. Its old districts keep colonial buildings, churches and French-style avenues. The Sri Aurobindo Ashram on Rue de la Marine is one of the most important ashrams in India, and the township of Auroville lies about 8 kilometres to the north-west. The French Institute of Pondicherry and a French consulate are among the French institutions in the city.
ponhea-yat: Ponhea Yat, also known as Borom Reachea I, was the third son of King Thommasaok Reachea and succeeded his father on the throne. Early in his reign he looked to Ming China for support against the neighbouring kingdom of Champa: in 1408 and 1414 he complained to the Yongle Emperor of raids by the Cham king Indravarman VI, and he sent an envoy, Kun Si-li Ren-nong-la, to China. Close ties with the Ming, carried largely by trade along the Mekong River, remained the core of his foreign policy.

In 1431 the king left Yasodharapura, the capital at Angkor, because it could not be defended against the Siamese. He settled first at Basan, in present-day Srey Santhor, but when floods struck the site he moved again to Chaktomuk, the meeting of the rivers that is now part of Phnom Penh. Khmer tradition adds a story in which he sent twelve spies, disguised as palace servants, to kill the Siamese king Intharachathirat at Angkor, and then retook the city with an army of about 70,000 before judging the damaged capital too exposed to keep.

At Chaktomuk the king had the ground built up against flooding and a palace raised. He also ordered six Buddhist monasteries to be built around the city; those named in tradition include Wat Botum, Wat Koh, Wat Langka, Wat Ounalom and Wat Phnom. Such monasteries served as schools, libraries and refuges for orphans, the elderly and the children of the poor. Khmer accounts remember his reign as a time of peace, with few outbreaks of war.

Ponhea Yat died in 1463, and his remains are kept in a stupa behind Wat Phnom. He had sons by three concubines, Buppha Devi, Sisangam and Potumkesar; Sisangam had earlier been the consort of the Siamese king Intharachathirat. His eldest son, Noreay Reachea, succeeded him and reigned until 1469, followed by a second son, Srey Reachea. In time his sons divided the Khmer lands into three parts, each ruling his own, and wars broke out among them.
pont-du-gard: Nemausus was awkwardly placed for a water supply. Plains to its south and east lay too low for water to flow to the city, and the hills to the west were too difficult for engineers, so the only real alternative was the springs of the Fontaine d'Eure near Ucetia (Uzès). The straight-line distance is only about 20 km, but the aqueduct winds for around 50 km to get round the Garrigues de Nîmes, since a tunnel through them would have been 8 to 10 kilometres long.

The spring lies only 17 m above the distribution basin in Nîmes, giving an average gradient of about 1 in 3,000. Newer excavations suggest construction took place between 40 and 60 CE: coins found in the outflow at Nîmes are no older than the reign of Claudius (41–54 CE). It is believed to have taken about fifteen years and 800 to 1,000 workers.

The bridge is 274 m long, with three recessed levels of arches whose main piers stand in line one above another. Its width varies from 9 m at the bottom to 3 m at the top. It was built largely without mortar or clamps, from an estimated 50,400 tons of local shelly limestone; some blocks weigh up to 6 tons. Many blocks carry numbers and inscriptions such as fronte dextra, guiding the builders to their places.

The water conduit runs along the top. Its walls are dressed masonry and its floor concrete, covered with a stucco containing shards of pottery and tile and sealed with maltha, a mixture of slaked lime, pork grease and the juice of unripe figs. The aqueduct is estimated to have supplied about 40,000 cubic metres of water a day, which took nearly 27 hours to reach the city. Constant cleaning by workers called circitores was needed to remove mineral deposits and roots.

Maintenance was neglected from the 4th century, and the aqueduct had probably gone out of use by about the 6th century. The bridge survived largely because it served as a toll bridge: in the 13th century the French king granted the seigneurs of Uzès the right to levy tolls, which later passed to the Bishops of Uzès, who were responsible for its upkeep. In the 1620s the Duke of Rohan had one side of the second row of arches cut back to move his artillery across, weakening it severely.

A road bridge by the engineer Henri Pitot was added in 1743–47, and Napoleon III backed repairs carried out between 1855 and 1858. Jean-Jacques Rousseau, visiting in 1738, wrote that it was the only time in his life that an object surpassed his expectation. UNESCO listed the site in 1985, and from 1996 a four-year project removed traffic and built a visitor centre.
pontic-caspian-steppe: The steppe stretches from the northern shores of the Black Sea, the Pontus Euxinus of antiquity, to the northern area around the Caspian Sea, where it ends at the Ural-Caspian narrowing and joins the Kazakh Steppe of Central Asia as part of the larger Eurasian Steppe. It covers about 994,000 km2 across north-eastern Bulgaria, south-eastern Romania, Moldova, southern and eastern Ukraine, the North Caucasus and the Lower Volga region. The East European forest steppe bounds it on the north, and the drier Caspian lowland desert lies between it and the Caspian Sea. Its flora and fauna are distinctive, and the Ponto-Caspian seas are the remains of the Turgai Sea, an extension of the Paratethys.

The area corresponds to the Cimmeria, Scythia and Sarmatia of classical antiquity. Across several millennia numerous tribes of nomadic horsemen used the steppe, and many went on to conquer lands in the settled regions of Central and Eastern Europe, West Asia and South Asia. Genetic research has identified the region as the most probable place where horses were first domesticated. The Kurgan hypothesis, the most prevalent theory in Indo-European studies, places the homeland of the speakers of Proto-Indo-European on the steppe.

A sequence of prehistoric cultures is listed for the region, among them the Khvalynsk culture (5000-3500 BCE), the Sredny Stog culture (4500-3500 BCE), the Yamnaya or Kurgan cultures (3500-2300 BCE), the Catacomb culture (3000-2200 BCE) and the Srubna culture (1600-1200 BCE). Peoples and states with origins on the steppe include the Cimmerians, Scythians and Sarmatians, then the Ostrogoths, Alans, Huns, Avars, Khazars and Pechenegs, the Kipchaks and Cumans of the 11th to 13th centuries and the Golden Horde of the 13th to 15th. Kievan Rus', the Cossacks, Kalmyks, Nogais, the Crimean Khanate and the Russian Empire belong to its later history.
pontifical-swiss-guard: The Guard has its origins in the 15th century. Pope Sixtus IV allied with the Swiss Confederacy and built barracks in Via Pellegrino, foreseeing the recruiting of Swiss mercenaries. Innocent VIII renewed the pact to use Swiss troops against the Duke of Milan, and Alexander VI used them in his alliance with the King of France. During the Italian Wars the Swiss were a fixture on the front lines among the warring factions. Cardinal Giuliano della Rovere, who had been Bishop of Lausanne and knew the Swiss well, became Pope Julius II in 1503 and asked the Swiss Diet for a constant corps of 200 mercenaries, financed by the Augsburg merchants Ulrich and Jacob Fugger.
The first contingent of 150 soldiers left on foot in September 1505 under Kaspar von Silenen and entered Rome on 22 January 1506, now regarded as the official date of the Guard's foundation.

Its most significant hostile engagement came on 6 May 1527 during the Sack of Rome. As the troops of Emperor Charles V advanced, 147 of the 189 Guards, including their commander Caspar Röist, died fighting so that Clement VII could escape through the Passetto di Borgo, escorted by the other 42. Clement replaced the depleted Guard with 200 German mercenaries, and in 1537 Paul III ordered it reinstated; anti-papal sentiment in Switzerland hindered recruitment.

After the Italian Wars the Guard ceased to serve as a combat unit and became mostly a protection and honour guard, though twelve members served at the Battle of Lepanto in 1571. It was disbanded and reinstated in 1800, 1814 and 1849, and in the later 19th century it declined into a ceremonial body with low standards. The modern Guard is the product of reforms by its commander Jules Repond from 1910 to 1921, who recruited only native Swiss, introduced rigorous exercises and designed the Renaissance-style uniform, completed in May 1914. His strictness led to a week of open mutiny in July 1913.

The Guard protects the Pope and the Apostolic Palace in Vatican City and accompanies the Pope on journeys abroad. Overall security in the city-state is the work of a separate body, the Corps of Gendarmerie of Vatican City. After the attempt on the life of Pope John Paul II on 13 May 1981 the Guard placed greater emphasis on its non-ceremonial roles and equipped itself with modern small arms, though its dress uniform of striped red, dark blue and yellow, high plumed helmet and halberd remain. Recruits must be unmarried Swiss Catholic men between 19 and 30 who have completed basic training with the Swiss Armed Forces.
poona-pact: Seats in legislative bodies were first allocated by identity under the Indian Councils Act of 1909, and the depressed classes received some seats in 1919, increased in 1925. During the Second Round Table Conference the British government proposed separate electorates for the depressed classes, Muslims, Sikhs, Indian Christians and others, and the Communal Award of Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald followed in August 1932. Gandhi accepted separate electorates for the other groups but not for the depressed classes, writing that they would vivisect and disrupt Hinduism. B. R. Ambedkar argued that upper-caste reformers could not represent the depressed classes, who needed leaders of their own.

The pact was signed at 5 pm on 24 September 1932 at Yerwada Central Jail, with Madan Mohan Malaviya signing on behalf of the Hindus and Gandhi's son Devdas Gandhi among the signatories. The reserved seats were divided among the provinces: 30 each in Madras and Bengal, 25 in Bombay with Sindh, 20 each in the Central Provinces and the United Provinces, 18 in Bihar and Orissa, 8 in Punjab and 7 in Assam. In each constituency the depressed-class voters on the general roll would first choose a panel of four candidates, from whom the joint electorate would elect the member.

The same system applied to the Central Legislature, where 18 per cent of the general seats for British India were reserved. Ambedkar had proposed that the primary elections end automatically after ten years, Gandhi a referendum after five; the compromise ended the primaries after ten years unless the communities agreed otherwise. The pact also barred any disability in local elections or public appointments on account of membership of the depressed classes, and earmarked part of each province's education grant for them.

8 January 1933 was observed as Temple Entry Day. The pact set Gandhi's view of caste reform as a social and spiritual task against Ambedkar's insistence that caste was a political question. Writers such as Perry Anderson and Arundhati Roy have asked whether Gandhi coerced Ambedkar, while the historian Gitanjali Surendran holds that Ambedkar was content with the outcome.
popayan: Popayán lies in the Pubenza Valley in southwestern Colombia, between two mountain ranges, at 1,760 metres above sea level, with an average temperature of 18 °C. The city is known as the white city for the colour of its colonial buildings and as the University City, since the University of Cauca, founded in 1827 by decree of General Francisco de Paula Santander, is based there. The origin of the name is uncertain: one theory reads it as two villages with reed roofs, another derives it from a cacique named Payán, and a third from the Quechua for the valley of the river.

Nothing is recorded of the pre-Hispanic village of Popayán. El Morro del Tulcán, a truncated pyramid built between 500 and 1600 CE, was already abandoned when the Spanish arrived, and analysis of dental samples suggests that those buried there probably belonged to the upper class. The conquistador Sebastián de Belalcázar arrived on 13 January 1537. In the 16th and 17th centuries Popayán was governed by an appointed governor under the Royal Audience of Quito, part of the Viceroyalty of Peru.

Its position between Lima, Quito and Cartagena made it important, and even after the Pacific was reached it remained a transfer point for gold and other riches going to Cartagena on their way to Spain. It also served as a colonial mint, producing gold escudo coins and silver reales from 1760 through 1819, and it continued to strike coins for the Republic of Colombia after 1826. A battle for independence was fought at the country house of Calibio on 15 January 1814. During that struggle Antonio Nariño had the lead weights of the cathedral clock tower's English clock, installed in 1737, changed to supply metal for ammunition. In 1873 the Humilladero Bridge was built over a fault, and it has stayed intact through many earthquakes.

Popayán is the capital of the department of Cauca, with a municipal population of 318,059 and an area of 483 square kilometres. It has been the home of seventeen Colombian presidents. An earthquake of 31 March 1983, lasting eighteen seconds, toppled many of the city's buildings; reconstruction took more than ten years, and the quake led to Colombia's first seismic design code. The historic centre keeps its baroque architecture and its churches, among them San Francisco, Santo Domingo and the cathedral. In 2005 UNESCO named Popayán its first city of gastronomy, and in 2009 it declared the Easter Week processions of Semana Santa a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Patrimony of Humanity.
pope: Spanish rule over the Pueblo peoples of the Rio Grande valley began in 1598. The Pueblo then numbered 40,000 to 80,000, but their many independent towns, often speaking different languages and hostile to one another, could not unite. Violence, forced labour and European diseases brought their number down to about 15,000 by the later 17th century, and the Spanish suppressed their religious ceremonies.

Po'pay, whose Tewa name means ripe squash, first appears in the record in 1675 as one of 47 religious leaders of the northern Pueblo arrested for witchcraft by the government of Juan Francisco Trevino. Three were executed and one took his own life; the rest were whipped and imprisoned in Santa Fe. Seventy Pueblo warriors then came to the governor and pressed for their release, which he granted, probably because Apache and Navajo raids left the colony unable to risk a Pueblo rising.

From Taos Pueblo, Po'pay held secret talks with the leaders of the other pueblos. His message was to destroy the Spanish and their influence and return to the old ways, and he promised that the ancient gods would then reward the Pueblo with health and prosperity. He killed his own son-in-law, Nicolás Búa, fearing he would betray the plot. Only the Tiguex area near Santa Fe declined to join. When the rising came in August 1680, about 1,000 Spaniards were besieged in the Governor's palace at Santa Fe before they broke out and withdrew to El Paso; 21 of the 33 priests in New Mexico were among the dead.

Later accounts, possibly prejudiced, say Po'pay then set himself up as sole ruler of the Pueblos and tried to erase every trace of the Spanish. His army repelled a Spanish force of 300 men in 1681, and another attempt failed in 1687. Drought, renewed raids and old rivalries divided the villages, and many Pueblos came to regard him as a tyrant.

Po'pay died, probably in 1688, with the Pueblo state he had sought divided and weak. In 1692 Governor Diego de Vargas began the reconquest, offering pardon rather than punishment. Afterwards the encomienda system of forced labour was prohibited in New Mexico, and Franciscan priests no longer interfered with Pueblo ceremonies so long as the outward forms of Catholicism were kept. What is known of him comes through Spanish chroniclers and their informants, most of them his opponents. A statue of him by Cliff Fragua, holding a knotted cord, was unveiled in the National Statuary Hall of the United States Capitol on 22 September 2005.
pope-adrian-i: Adrian came from a family of the Roman military aristocracy known as the domini de via Lata. His father, Theodore, died while Adrian was very young, and he was taken in by his paternal uncle Theodotus, a consul, dux and primicerius. He was bishop of Rome from 1 February 772 until his death on 25 December 795. The popes then had to contend with repeated Lombard attempts to expand in Italy at the expense of the papacy. Receiving no support from Constantinople, they looked to the Franks.

When Carloman I died in December 771 and Charlemagne took his lands, Carloman's widow Gerberga and her sons fled to the Lombard court at Pavia. King Desiderius asked Adrian to crown the boys Kings of the Franks. The pope refused, and Desiderius invaded the Duchy of the Pentapolis, which Charlemagne's father had given to the papacy in 756.

Charlemagne crossed the Alps in 773 and besieged Pavia. The Lombards surrendered in exchange for their lives, Desiderius was sent to the abbey of Corbie, and Charlemagne took the title King of the Lombards. The pope received additions to the Duchy of Rome, the Exarchate of Ravenna and the Pentapolis. Adrian struck the earliest papal coin, gave Charlemagne the title Patrician of Rome and from 781 dated papal documents by Charlemagne's reign instead of the Byzantine emperor's.

Adrian approved the Second Council of Nicaea of 787, which confirmed the veneration of icons. Charlemagne, who had received its decisions in a poor Latin translation, answered with the Capitulare contra synodum of 792, and his theologians wrote the Libri Carolini; a synod at Frankfurt in 794 refused to receive them. In 787 Adrian raised the diocese of Lichfield to an archdiocese at the request of King Offa of Mercia. He restored Roman aqueducts and rebuilt the churches of Santa Maria in Cosmedin and San Marco.

His pontificate was the longest since Saint Peter until that of Pius VI in the late 18th century. Charlemagne commissioned Adrian's epitaph in 796 and held a competition for its text, which Alcuin won. Carved in Roman square capitals on black limestone, it is now in the portico of St Peter's, a notable example of Carolingian monumental script.
pope-adrian-iv: Nicholas Breakspear was the son of Richard Breakspear, from a relatively humble family, and was probably born in or near St Albans in Hertfordshire. The year of his birth is unknown; he was probably about 55 when elected. Much of what is told of his youth comes from writers working more than thirty years after his death. He studied canon law at Arles, then became a canon regular at the Abbey of Saint-Ruf at Avignon, where he rose to abbot; the monks complained that he was overly strict. Pope Eugene III made him Cardinal-Bishop of Albano, and he met his lasting friend John of Salisbury.

In 1152 Breakspear went as legate to Scandinavia. Norway was in civil war and King Inge I's authority was weak; he reconciled the warring factions, if only for a time, and reorganised the church there before moving to Sweden, where he was acclaimed and chroniclers later called him a saint. He was elected pope on 4 December 1154. He was the only pope born in England until the election of a pope from the United States in 2025.

Rome was unsettled by the republican commune and by Arnold, who was captured by imperial troops in summer 1155 and hanged. Frederick Barbarossa was crowned emperor on 18 June 1155, secretly, to mislead the Romans. Adrian then allied with the Byzantine emperor Manuel I and southern Italian rebels against William I of Sicily, whom he had excommunicated, but William won decisive victories in 1156, and at the Concordat of Benevento the pope had to invest him with his lands, receiving homage and an annual tribute.

The pact with William angered Frederick. In 1157 a letter used the Latin word beneficium of the imperial crown, which some of Frederick's councillors translated as fief, implying that the emperor held it from the pope; Adrian explained it meant a good deed. In 1159 Frederick claimed extensive lands in northern Italy, and Adrian gave him forty days to withdraw on pain of excommunication. He died at Anagni on 1 September 1159.

The cardinals then split, electing Alexander III and the antipope Victor IV, which began a long schism. Adrian is said to have granted Henry II the bull Laudabiliter authorising the invasion of Ireland, but scholars are uncertain whether it ever existed. His decretal Dignum est allowed serfs to marry without their lord's consent.
pope-alexander-iii: Rolando was born in Siena. From the 14th century he was said to belong to the aristocratic family of Bandinelli, though this has not been proven. He is not the canonist Master Roland of Bologna, as was once thought. He probably studied at Bologna, where he taught theology.

In October 1150 Pope Eugene III made him Cardinal-Deacon of Santi Cosma e Damiano, and he later became Cardinal-Priest of St Mark. In 1153 he became papal chancellor and led the cardinals opposed to Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa. In 1156 he negotiated the Treaty of Benevento, which restored peaceful relations between Rome and the Kingdom of Sicily.

After Adrian IV died on 1 September 1159, Rolando was elected on 7 September and took the name Alexander III. A minority of cardinals chose Octavian instead, who became Victor IV and Frederick's antipope. Alexander refused to attend Frederick's council at Pavia, stating that a pope can be judged only by God, and the council recognised Victor in February 1160. Alexander excommunicated Victor and Frederick, and monarchs such as Géza II of Hungary, the king of France and Henry II of England came to recognise him. Because of imperial strength in Italy he spent much of his pontificate outside Rome, leaving it between 1162 and 1165 and again in 1167.

The dispute continued with Victor's successors Paschal III and Calixtus III until Frederick's defeat at Legnano in 1176, and Frederick recognised Alexander in the Peace of Venice of 1177. Alexander returned to Rome on 12 March 1178. At the Third Council of the Lateran in March 1179 he secured a law that no one could be elected pope without two-thirds of the cardinals' votes. Soon afterwards the Roman Republic forced him to leave the city, which he never re-entered.

Alexander rejected the proposals of the Byzantine emperor Manuel I Komnenos to end the schism of the eastern and western churches in 1166 and 1168. He created the Archbishopric of Uppsala in 1164 and sanctioned the crusades against pagans in northern Europe in the bull Non parum animus noster. He canonised Edward the Confessor in 1161 and Thomas Becket in 1173, and in 1179 the bull Manifestis Probatum recognised Afonso Henriques as king of Portugal.

He died at Civita Castellana on 30 August 1181, one week short of twenty-two years after his election, the longest papacy since that of Adrian I in the 8th century. The city of Alessandria in Piedmont is named after him.
pope-alexander-vi: Roderic de Borja y Llançol was born around 1431 at Xàtiva, in the Kingdom of Valencia under the Crown of Aragon, into the prominent Borja family. His career in the Church began in 1445 at the age of 14, when his uncle Alfons, a cardinal, had him appointed sacristan of the Cathedral of Valencia.

In 1448 he became a canon of three cathedrals, drawing the income without residing there so that he could go to Rome. He then studied law at Bologna. After his uncle's election as Pope Callixtus III in 1455 the family name was Italianized from Borja to Borgia. Rodrigo was made a cardinal and, a year later, vice-chancellor of the Church.

He was elected on 11 August 1492 and took the name Alexander VI, in a period when nepotism and simony were widespread among the clergy. At first he kept to strict justice and orderly government, but before long he began endowing his relatives. His son Cesare, then seventeen and a student at Pisa, was made Archbishop of Valencia; another son, Giovanni, inherited the Spanish Dukedom of Gandia.

For Giovanni and a third son, Gioffre, he proposed fiefs carved from the Papal States and Naples, which brought him into conflict with Ferdinand I of Naples. He later created twelve new cardinals, among them the eighteen-year-old Cesare and Alessandro Farnese, brother of his mistress Giulia Farnese, who became Pope Paul III. His bulls of 1493 confirmed the rights of the Spanish crown in the New World after the finds of Christopher Columbus.

On 31 March 1495 the Holy League of the pope, the emperor, Venice, Ludovico il Moro and Ferdinand of Spain was formed, in fact to expel the French from Italy. Charles VIII was crowned King of Naples on 12 May but then retreated northward. The Florentine friar Girolamo Savonarola denounced the corruption of the Curia, and Alexander ordered the friar investigated. For the Jubilee of 1500 he formalized the rite of the holy door, opened at St. Peter's on Christmas Eve 1499 and sealed on the Epiphany in 1501.

Alexander VI died on 18 August 1503. He is one of the most controversial Renaissance popes, partly because he acknowledged fathering several children by his mistresses, and his Italianized surname, Borgia, became a byword for libertinism and nepotism. The historian Mallett asserts that there is no evidence that the Borgias resorted to poisoning, judicial murder or extortion. The only contemporary accusations of poisoning came from servants whose statements were extracted under torture by Alexander's bitter enemy della Rovere, who succeeded him as Pope Julius II.
pope-benedict-ix: Theophylact was the youngest son of Count Alberic III of Tusculum and his wife Ermelina. He was closely related to several popes: a nephew of Benedict VIII and John XIX, a grandnephew of John XII and a great-grandnephew of John XI. His father obtained the papal chair for him in October 1032 by bribing the Romans. He is generally said to have been about twenty, though Rodulfus Glaber, a monk of St. Germanus at Auxerre, whose testimony is unsubstantiated, put his age at 11 or 12.

His first pontificate was marked by factional strife and by accusations of a scandalous life. Later writers, among them Peter Damian, Pope Victor III and Bishop Benno of Piacenza, made serious charges of vice and violence. The historian Reginald Lane Poole cautions that such accusations were believed in a time of political hostility, and that the picture comes from a period when Benedict's opponents were in the ascendant; he thought him a negligent pope and very likely a profligate man. Benedict was briefly forced out of Rome in 1036 and returned with the help of Emperor Conrad II. In September 1044 opposition forced him out again, and Sylvester III was elected in his place.

His forces returned in April 1045 and expelled his rival. Doubting his hold on the see and wishing to marry his cousin, Benedict resigned in May 1045, handing the papacy to his godfather, the priest John Gratian, who paid him for his election expenses and became Gregory VI. Benedict soon regretted this and returned to Rome. A number of clergy and laity appealed to King Henry III, who crossed the Alps and held the Council of Sutri in December 1046; Benedict IX and Sylvester III were declared deposed and Gregory VI was encouraged to resign, since his arrangement with Benedict was simoniacal. A German was elected as Clement II.

When Clement II died in October 1047, Benedict seized the Lateran Palace in November and again became pope, until German troops drove him away in July 1048. Damasus II was then elected and universally recognised. Benedict refused to appear on charges of simony in 1049 and was excommunicated. His later fate is obscure; Leo IX may have lifted the ban. He was buried at the Abbey of Grottaferrata about 1056, and its abbot, Saint Bartholomew of Grottaferrata, said he had been penitent. He remains the only person to have been pope more than once and the only one accused of selling the papacy.
pope-benedict-viii: Benedict VIII was born around 980 as Theophylact, a son of Count Gregory I of Tusculum. His family had already produced three popes: John XI, who reigned from 931 to 935, John XII, from 955 to 964, and Benedict VII, from 973 to 974. He became pope on 18 May 1012. Unusually for a medieval pope, he held strong authority both in Rome and abroad.

An antipope, Gregory VI, forced him to flee Rome, and King Henry II of Germany restored him and was crowned emperor by him on 14 February 1014. The two stayed on good terms throughout his pontificate. When Saracens renewed their attacks on southern Italy, made a settlement in Sardinia and sacked Pisa, the pope allied himself with the Normans, who were beginning to settle in Italy, and brought about the defeat of the Saracens in Sardinia. He also subjugated the Crescentii.

In 1020 he travelled to Germany to confer with Henry about the renewed Byzantine threat in the south of Italy. He reached Bamberg at Eastertide, consecrated its new cathedral and obtained a charter from Henry confirming the donations of Charlemagne and Otto the Great. In 1022 he received Archbishop Æthelnoth of Canterbury, who had come to Rome for the pallium. That year he held a synod at Pavia with the emperor to restrain simony and the incontinence of the clergy.

He backed the reform sponsored by Cluny Abbey, was a friend of its abbot Odilo, and encouraged the Truce of God. Horace Mann judged him one of the few popes of the Middle Ages who was at once powerful at home and great abroad. He died on 9 April 1024 and his brother succeeded him as John XIX.
pope-boniface-viii: Benedetto Caetani was born in Anagni, about 50 kilometres southeast of Rome, a younger son of Roffredo Caetani, a member of a baronial family of the Papal States. His mother, Emilia Patrasso di Guarcino, was a niece of Pope Alexander IV, which kept him not far from the seat of ecclesiastical power and patronage. In 1252 he followed his uncle Pietro Caetani, the new Bishop of Todi, to Todi and began legal studies there.

Pope Celestine V abdicated on 13 December 1294 at Naples, where he had set up his court and lived like a monk. Accounts differ on whether Benedetto pressured Celestine to abdicate or merely showed that Church law allowed it. Benedetto was elected in his place and took the name Boniface VIII.

In 1298 Boniface ordered published the Liber Sextus, a sixth book of canon law that collected papal decisions, some 88 of them his own, with a set of legal principles known as the Regulae Juris. In 1297 he removed Cardinal Jacopo Colonna and his nephew Pietro from the College of Cardinals and excommunicated them. The Colonna declared that his election had been illegal because of Celestine's abdication, and the dispute became open warfare. By the end of 1298 his army had captured Palestrina and razed it, and a new Città Papale later replaced it.

He proclaimed 1300 a jubilee year, and the first of many held in Rome was a success, with an estimate by Giovanni Villani of some 200,000 pilgrims. In his bull Clericis laicos of February 1296 he forbade lay taxation of the clergy without papal approval, which began his conflict with Philip IV of France. In his bull Unam sanctam of 1302 he stated that every human creature must be subject to the Roman pontiff for salvation.

In September 1303 Philip IV's troops attacked the pope's residence at Anagni on 7 September and captured him. Boniface was held for three days and died about a month afterwards, on 11 October 1303. Philip later pressured Pope Clement V into staging a posthumous trial of Boniface for heresy, but no verdict was delivered.

His claims of temporal as well as spiritual power led to bitter quarrels with Albert I of Germany, Philip IV and Dante Alighieri, who wrote his treatise Monarchia to dispute Boniface's claims, and who expected him in the Divine Comedy to arrive among the simoniacs in the eighth circle of Hell. The Liber Sextus remains important to canon lawyers.
pope-callixtus-ii: Guy of Burgundy was born in Besançon, the son of Count William I of Burgundy. At the age of eight he became a member of the cathedral chapter of St. John of Besançon. His brothers Rainald, Stephen and Hugh all died on crusade. Guy first appears in contemporary records when he became archbishop of Vienne in 1088. He held strong pro-papal views on the Investiture Controversy and was appointed papal legate to France by Pope Paschal II.

In 1111 Paschal, under pressure from Emperor Henry V, issued the Privilegium, yielding much of the papal prerogative that Gregory VII had claimed. The concessions met violent opposition, above all in France, where Guy led it. After attending the Lateran Synod of 1112 he convened an assembly of French and Burgundian bishops at Vienne, which denounced lay investiture as heretical and excommunicated Henry V; Paschal confirmed its decrees on 20 October 1112.

After Gelasius II died at Cluny on 29 January 1119, Guy was elected there on 2 February by nine cardinals and crowned at Vienne on 9 February as Calixtus II. At first he seemed willing to negotiate with Henry V, but at a meeting planned near Reims Henry arrived with an army of over thirty thousand men, and Calixtus stayed at Reims, where on 30 October 1119 the emperor and his antipope were excommunicated. Returning to Italy, Calixtus gained the upper hand over the antipope Gregory VIII, who fled to Sutri and was taken prisoner with Norman help.

In 1120 he issued the bull Sicut Judaeis, forbidding Christians on pain of excommunication to force Jews to convert, harm them, take their property, disturb their festivals or interfere with their cemeteries; later popes reaffirmed it. Negotiations with Henry began at Würzburg in October 1121, and the Concordat of Worms was concluded on 23 September 1122. The emperor gave up investiture with ring and crosier and granted free election to sees, while bishops received investiture with the sceptre, with elections held in the emperor's presence in Germany.
To confirm the settlement Calixtus convened the First Lateran Council on 18 March 1123. It also passed decrees against simony, concubinage among clergy and violators of the Truce of God.

In his last years Calixtus worked to restore papal control over the Roman Campagna and rebuilt the church of Santa Maria in Cosmedin. He died on 13 December 1124. The Codex Calixtinus, a twelfth-century collection of tales, liturgy and a guide to the pilgrimage to Santiago, takes its name from a letter attributed to him.
pope-callixtus-iii: Borgia was born in 1378 at La Torreta in the Kingdom of Valencia, then part of the Crown of Aragon, the eldest child of Juan Domingo de Borja y Doncel and Francina Llançol. His sister Isabel became the mother of Pope Alexander VI. He studied grammar, logic and the arts in Valencia and in 1392 went to the University of Lleida, where he obtained a doctorate in both canon law and civil law and began his career as a professor of law. Around 1411 he attended a sermon by Vincent Ferrer, whom he later canonised on 3 June 1455.

Borgia was chosen in 1416 as delegate of the Diocese of Lerida to the Council of Constance, but King Alfonso V of Aragon opposed the council and he did not take part. From 1424 he served the Aragonese king, who wished to see him a cardinal; Pope Martin V refused. During the Great Western Schism he supported Antipope Benedict XIII and was the driving force behind Antipope Clement VIII's submission to Martin V in 1429. Martin V then made him Bishop of Valencia. He acted as a diplomat for the kings of Aragon, tutored Alfonso's illegitimate son Ferrante, and was made a cardinal by Pope Eugene IV on 2 May 1444 after reconciling the pope and Alfonso.

He was elected pope at an advanced age as a compromise candidate in the conclave of 8 April 1455. Less than two years after the fall of Constantinople in 1453, he was chiefly concerned with organising Europe against the Ottoman Empire. A building programme in Rome was cancelled and its money turned to a crusade, and nuncios and preachers were sent across Europe, though the princes were slow to respond because of national rivalries. John Hunyadi defeated the Turks at Belgrade on 22 July 1456. On 29 June 1456 the pope had ordered church bells rung at noon to call the faithful to pray for the defenders, and he fixed the Feast of the Transfiguration on 6 August to mark the victory.

Callixtus ordered a new trial for Joan of Arc, at which she was vindicated after her death. He canonised four saints and appointed nine cardinals in two consistories in 1456, among them his nephew Rodrigo de Borgia, later Pope Alexander VI. A story first found in a biography of 1475 holds that he excommunicated Halley's Comet; no known primary source supports it, and his bull of 29 June 1456 does not mention the comet. He died on 6 August 1458 and in his will left 5000 ducats to found a hospital. The Catholic historian Ludwig von Pastor judged that, except for his nepotism, he deserved high praise for his energy in defending Europe against Turkish power.
pope-clement-ii: Suidger was born in Hornburg in the Duchy of Saxony, the son of Count Konrad von Morsleben-Horneburg and his wife Amulrad von Meyendorf. In 1040 he became Bishop of Bamberg. In 1046 he accompanied King Henry III of Germany to Italy, where Henry went at the request of the laity and clergy of Rome to restore order and receive the imperial crown.

In the autumn of 1046 three rivals claimed the papacy: Benedict IX and Sylvester III, backed by rival noble factions, and Gregory VI, who had paid Benedict to resign in order to free the city from the House of Tusculum. The transaction looked like simony, and doubts about any of them could undermine Henry's coronation. The Council of Sutri deposed Benedict and Sylvester and accepted Gregory's resignation. Henry then proposed Suidger, who was elected as Clement II and became the first pope placed on the throne by the power of the German emperors.

He kept the see of Bamberg and governed both it and Rome. His election was criticised by the reform party in the curia because of the royal involvement and because he already held a diocese. His first act was to crown Henry and Agnes of Poitou, and he gave Henry the title and diadem of a Roman patrician, understood to carry the right to indicate who should be pope. His Roman synod of 1047 passed decrees against simony, and a dispute among Ravenna, Milan and Aquileia over precedence was settled for Ravenna.

Clement went with Henry through southern Italy and laid Benevento under an interdict for refusing to open its gates. He canonised Wiborada, a nun of St Gall martyred by the Hungarians in 925. He died near Pesaro on 9 October 1047, and his body was taken to Bamberg Cathedral, where it lies in the western choir; it is the only tomb of a pope north of the Alps. A toxicological examination in the mid-20th century found lead sugar in his remains, which confirmed old rumours of poisoning, though it is not clear whether he was murdered or whether the substance was used as medicine.
pope-clement-iii: Paolo Scolari was born in Rome, in the rione of the Pigna, into a family of high social standing but not noble. He was the son of Giovanni and Maria, and according to some scholars was related to the mother of Pope Innocent III. Pope Alexander III made him archpriest of the Liberian Basilica and cardinal-deacon of Sergio e Bacco, and in December 1180 cardinal bishop of Palestrina.

He was elected on 19 December 1187, two days after the death of Gregory VIII. The cardinals' first choice, Theobald of Ostia, had refused, and Scolari had been passed over two months earlier because of poor health. Only eight cardinals voted, three of them Romans, and the electors may have hoped that a Roman pope would bring the curia back to the city.

That is what happened. He ended a conflict of half a century between the popes and the citizens of Rome by an agreement allowing the citizens to elect their magistrates while the pope kept the nomination of the governor. A treaty of 31 May 1188 settled the old grievances, and the papacy returned to Rome after an exile of six years. He found a depleted College of cardinals, no more than twenty, and created thirty-one cardinals in three promotions, most of them Romans.

He sent Josias, Archbishop of Tyre, to persuade King Henry II of England and King Philip II of France to undertake the Third Crusade. He urged the Christian kings of Spain to unite against the Muslims, comparing the Reconquista to the crusades in the Holy Land, and called for a full trade embargo with the Islamic world. In March 1188 he made the Scottish church independent of the Archbishop of York, subject only to Rome.

In April 1189 Clement ended the conflict with Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa. He agreed to crown Henry VI as emperor but angered him by giving Sicily to Tancred, a son of Roger III, Duke of Apulia, and the dispute was acute when the pope died in 1191. The cardinals unanimously elected the 85-year-old Celestine III the same day, a man who belonged to neither the imperial nor the Sicilian faction.
pope-clement-iv: Gui Foucois, also called Guy le Gros, was born in Saint-Gilles-du-Gard in the County of Toulouse, the son of a lawyer, Pierre Foucois. At nineteen he enlisted as a soldier to fight the Moors in Spain, then studied law in Toulouse, Bourges and Orleans and became a noted advocate in Paris, where he acted as secretary to King Louis IX. He married and had two daughters, and after his wife's death entered the Church.

His rise was rapid. He became pastor of Saint-Gilles in 1255, Bishop of Le Puy in 1257 and Archbishop of Narbonne in 1259. In December 1261 he became the first cardinal created by Pope Urban IV, for the see of Sabina, and from 1262 to 1264 he was papal legate in England.

His election followed a four-month conclave at Perugia, during which the cardinals argued over whether to call in Charles I of Anjou, the youngest brother of Louis IX, to carry on the papal war against the Hohenstaufen. Clement was in France when elected and had to enter Italy in disguise. He settled at Viterbo, since the Ghibelline party controlled Rome. Charles recognised him as feudal overlord, and with papal money and supplies marched on Naples, defeating and killing Manfred at the Battle of Benevento. At the Battle of Tagliacozzo Conradin, the last of the Hohenstaufen, was taken prisoner and later beheaded at Naples. Clement is said to have disapproved of Charles's cruelties, though Gregorovius's charge that he was an accomplice is contested.

In 1264 he renewed the prohibition of the Talmud, ordering that the Jews of the Crown of Aragon submit their books to Dominican censors, without condemning those who kept copies to death. In February 1265 he summoned Thomas Aquinas to Rome as papal theologian. In 1267 and 1268 he corresponded with the Mongol Ilkhanate ruler Abaqa, who proposed a Franco-Mongol alliance, and answered non-committally.

Clement died on 29 November 1268 and was buried at the Dominican convent of Santa Maria in Gradi outside Viterbo; in 1885 his remains were moved to the church of San Francesco alla Rocca there. Divisions among the cardinals left the papal throne vacant for nearly three years. Contemporaries praised his asceticism and his refusal to enrich his relatives. He ordered the Franciscan scholar Roger Bacon to write the Opus Majus, which is addressed to him and includes treatises on optics and the scientific method.
pope-clement-vi: Pierre Roger was born in the château of Maumont in Limousin, the son of the lord of Maumont-Rosiers-d'Égletons. He entered the Benedictine order as a boy in 1301, at the Abbey of La Chaise-Dieu, and in 1307 went to Paris to study theology and canon law. In 1323 Pope John XXII ordered the Chancellor of Paris to confer on him the doctorate in theology. He lectured on Peter Lombard's Sententiae, promoted the works of Thomas Aquinas, and in 1325 wrote a treatise condemning the Defensor Pacis of Marsilius of Padua.

Church office followed quickly. He became Abbot of Fécamp in 1326, Bishop of Arras in 1328, Archbishop of Sens in 1329 and Archbishop of Rouen in 1330, serving King Philip VI of France as a councillor. Pope Benedict XII made him a cardinal priest on 18 December 1338.

The cardinals, fourteen of the nineteen of them French, elected him on 7 May 1342, and he was crowned on 19 May. He chose to stay in Avignon, refusing invitations to return to Rome from its people and from the poet Petrarch. To placate the Romans he issued the bull Unigenitus in 1343, reducing the interval between one Great Jubilee and the next from a hundred years to fifty. He enlarged the papal palace, kept composers of the Ars Nova style at court, and filled the College of Cardinals with Frenchmen, among them several nephews.

During the Black Death he stayed in Avignon, supervised the care of the sick and the burial of the dead, and granted remission of sins to all who died of the plague. In two bulls of 1348 he condemned the violence against Jews and rejected the claim that they caused the plague, noting that it afflicted Jews too.

He excommunicated the emperor Louis IV on 13 April 1346 and directed the election of Charles IV. He also removed Cola di Rienzo from Rome by a legate in December 1347 and made Prague an archbishopric in 1344.

Clement had suffered from kidney stones for years, and a tumour caused an abscess and fever in his last week. He died on 6 December 1352. His body was taken in procession to the abbey of La Chaise-Dieu, where a tomb begun in 1346 and completed in 1351 stands in the choir. Huguenots attacked it in 1562 and destroyed its forty-four statues of his relatives.

He left the reputation of a fine gentleman, a prince munificent to profusion and a patron of the arts and learning, but no saint. He is said to have remarked that he had lived as a sinner among sinners.
pope-clement-vii: Giulio de' Medici was born illegitimately in Florence on 26 May 1478, one month after his father, Giuliano de' Medici, brother of Lorenzo de' Medici, was murdered in Florence Cathedral in the Pazzi conspiracy. He spent his first seven years with his godfather, the architect Antonio da Sangallo the Elder, and was then raised by Lorenzo alongside the future Pope Leo X. When Leo was elected in March 1513, Giulio became Archbishop of Florence within three months, and a papal dispensation recognised his birth as legitimate. Leo made him a cardinal on 23 September 1513. He governed Florence from 1519 to 1523.

After Adrian VI's death Giulio was elected on 19 November 1523 as Clement VII, with a reputation as a statesman, though contemporaries thought him worldly and indifferent to the Reformation. Charles V and Francis I each demanded that he take a side. After Francis conquered Milan in 1524 Clement joined France and Venice in a treaty of January 1525, but Francis was crushed and imprisoned at Pavia and Clement turned back to Charles.

His wavering led to the Sack of Rome in 1527, during which he was imprisoned. In 1527 Henry VIII asked him to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, the emperor's aunt; Clement refused, possibly under pressure from Charles, whose effective prisoner he was. In 1533 he married his cousin's granddaughter, Catherine de' Medici, to the future Henry II of France at Marseille.

Clement was a patron in the Medici tradition. He commissioned or supervised Michelangelo's Last Judgment in the Sistine Chapel, the Medici Chapel and the Laurentian Library, and Raphael's Villa Madama, and he appointed Benvenuto Cellini head of the Papal Mint. In 1533 he approved Copernicus's heliocentric theory.

He died on 25 September 1534 after months of illness, having reigned ten years, and was buried in St Peter's. Contemporaries blamed poison, but his symptoms do not support that. He has been called the most unfortunate of the popes. The historian Paul Strathern writes that without his guidance the Medici could not have reached the heights they later did.
pope-clement-viii: Ippolito Aldobrandini was born in Fano in the Papal States on 24 February 1536, the son of Silvestro Aldobrandini and Lesa Deti, from a Florentine family. Like his father he became a canon lawyer and an Auditor of the Roman Rota, the highest ecclesiastical court of the Holy See. He was ordained a priest only on 31 December 1580, at forty-five. Sixtus V made him Cardinal-Priest of S. Pancrazio in 1585 and in 1588 sent him as legate to Poland, where he won the gratitude of the Habsburgs by securing the release of Archduke Maximilian. His confessor for thirty years was Saint Philip Neri.

Elected on 30 January 1592 after a stormy conclave in which a minority of Italian cardinals refused to be dictated to by Philip II of Spain, he took the name Clement VIII and aimed to free the papacy from dependence on Spain. In November 1592 he published the Clementine Vulgate, which remained the official Bible of the Catholic Church until the Nova Vulgata replaced it in 1979.

Henry IV of France embraced Catholicism on 25 July 1593, and in the autumn of 1595 Clement solemnly absolved him despite Spanish displeasure, ending the thirty years of religious war in France. When Alfonso II d'Este, Duke of Ferrara, died childless on 27 October 1597, Clement resolved to attach Ferrara to the Papal States; Henry IV's threats deterred Spain and the emperor from helping Cesare d'Este, and a papal army entered Ferrara almost unopposed. In 1594 he began an alliance of Christian powers for the Long War against the Ottoman Empire.

Clement was severe in matters of order and belief. He had several noble troublemakers put to death, including Beatrice Cenci, who had murdered her father, probably after his repeated abuses, and he rejected many pleas for clemency. In 1599 the miller Menocchio was burned after trial by the Inquisition, and in 1600 Giordano Bruno was burned at the stake, Clement taking part in the final phase of the trial. The bull Caeca et Obdurata of 1593 banned Jews from living in the Papal States outside Rome, Ancona and Avignon.

The jubilee of 1600 brought three million pilgrims. Crippled by gout in his last years, Clement died on 3 March 1605 and was buried in St Peter's; his remains were moved in 1646 to Santa Maria Maggiore. He left a reputation for prudence, munificence, ruthlessness and capacity for business.
pope-clement-xiii: Carlo della Torre di Rezzonico was born on 7 March 1693 into a recently ennobled patrician family of Venice. His father bought and finished the palace on the Grand Canal now called Ca' Rezzonico. He received a Jesuit education in Bologna, took a doctorate in canon and civil law at the University of Padua, and attended the Pontifical Academy of Ecclesiastical Nobles in Rome. He became Governor of Fano in 1721, was ordained priest on 23 December 1731, and was made a cardinal by Pope Clement XII in 1737. As Bishop of Padua from 1743 he visited his diocese often and reformed its running.

After Pope Benedict XIV died in 1758, negotiations between rival factions led to Rezzonico's election on 6 July 1758 with 31 votes of 44. He was crowned on 16 July. Modest in character and generous with his private fortune, he permitted vernacular translations of the Bible in Catholic countries and placed the Encyclopédie of D'Alembert and Diderot on the Index. He favoured dialogue with Protestants without compromise on doctrine, and recognised the Hanoverians as kings of Great Britain, refusing to recognise Charles Edward Stuart as Charles III after the death of James Francis Edward Stuart in 1766.

His pontificate was dominated by pressure to suppress the Society of Jesus. In 1758 the Marquis of Pombal expelled the Jesuits from Portugal. The Parlement of Paris suppressed them in France by the arrêt of 2 August 1762, which Clement annulled, and Louis XV expelled them in November 1764. The bull Apostolicum pascendi of 7 January 1765 praised the order but was largely ignored. On the night of 2–3 April 1767 Charles III of Spain had every Jesuit house in Spain surrounded and the Jesuits shipped to Civitavecchia.

In 1768 Clement issued a monitorium against the government of Philip, Duke of Parma, and the question of Parma's investiture, technically a papal fief, worsened the dispute. The Bourbon kings seized Avignon, Benevento and Pontecorvo and in January 1769 demanded the total suppression of the Jesuits. Clement agreed to call a consistory, but died on the eve of its meeting. Poison was suspected, but there appears to be no conclusive evidence.

He collapsed on the night of 2 February 1769 after a day of audiences and died quickly; an aneurysm near the heart is generally believed to have been the cause. He was buried in the Vatican on 8 February, and in 1774 his remains were moved to a monument sculpted by Antonio Canova.
pope-cornelius: Emperor Decius, who ruled from 249 to 251, persecuted Christians rather sporadically and locally, but in January 250 he ordered all citizens to perform a religious sacrifice before commissioners or face death. Many Christians refused and were martyred, including Pope Fabian on 20 January 250, while others took part in the sacrifices to save their lives. During the persecution it proved impossible to elect a successor, and the papal seat stayed vacant for a year, with the church governed by several priests, including Novatian. When Decius left Rome to fight the Goths, the Roman clergy chose a new bishop. The more moderate Cornelius was unwillingly elected over Novatian and others in March 251.

Cornelius held, with Cyprian of Carthage, that Christians who had lapsed could be restored to communion through repentance shown in a period of penance. Novatian held that idolatry was unpardonable and that the Church had no authority to forgive apostates. Supporters of the stricter position had Novatian consecrated bishop and refused to recognise Cornelius. Both sides wrote to other bishops. Cornelius had the support of Cyprian, Dionysius and most African and Eastern bishops, while Novatian had a minority of the Roman clergy and laity. Cornelius convened a synod of 60 bishops that confirmed him as the rightful pope and excommunicated Novatian and his followers.

His letters give a picture of the Roman church. It had forty-six priests, seven deacons, seven sub-deacons, forty-two acolytes, fifty-two ostiarii and over 1,500 widows and persons in distress, and it fed over 1,500 people daily. From these numbers it has been estimated that there were at least 50,000 Christians in Rome in his time.

Decius was killed in battle with the Goths in June 251, and persecution resumed under his successor, Trebonianus Gallus. Cornelius was exiled to Centumcellae, where he died in June 253. The Liberian catalogue ascribes his death to the hardships of banishment, while later sources say he was beheaded. He was buried in a catacomb behind a Latin inscription reading Cornelius Martyr. One of his letters mentions the office of exorcist in the church for the first time.

His head was claimed by Kornelimünster Abbey near Aachen, and in the Rhineland he was venerated as one of the Four Holy Marshals in the late Middle Ages. His feast day is 16 September, shared with Cyprian; it was originally 14 September, the date on which, according to Jerome, both were martyred.
pope-eugene-iv: Gabriele Condulmer was born in Venice to a rich merchant family; his father was Angelo Condulmer and his mother Bariola Correr. His sister Polissena was the mother of the future Pope Paul II, and he was a nephew of Pope Gregory XII. On 30 December 1407, at twenty-four, he was made Bishop of Siena by his uncle, with a dispensation for his age. Siena's political leaders objected to a young foreigner and he resigned in 1408, the year Gregory made him a cardinal. He served as papal legate in the March of Ancona and at Bologna, and was elected pope unanimously on 3 March 1431.

His first quarrel was with the Colonna, relatives of his predecessor Martin V. The main struggle of his pontificate was with the Council of Basel, opened on 23 July 1431. On 18 December 1431 he dissolved it, but it refused to disband and renewed the Council of Constance's resolutions that a council stands above the pope. Under a compromise arranged by the emperor Sigismund he recognised the council in 1433.

Troops from Milan invaded the Papal States and a republic controlled by the Colonna was set up in Rome. On 4 June 1434 Eugene escaped down the Tiber disguised as a monk, pelted with stones, and reached Florence in October. In 1438 he convened a rival council at Ferrara; Basel deposed him on 25 June 1439 and elected Duke Amadeus VIII of Savoy as the antipope Felix V. On 6 July 1439 the bull Laetentur caeli proclaimed a union with the Eastern Orthodox Church, which proved temporary. Eugene entered Rome on 28 September 1443 after nearly ten years away.

In the bull Creator Omnium of 17 December 1434 he rescinded Portugal's right to conquer the Canary Islands, and he excommunicated anyone who enslaved newly converted Christians there, though he later tempered this at the king of Portugal's request. He first protected Jews, then in 1442 issued Dudum ad nostram, which restricted Jewish life but was not enforced in his lifetime.

Eugene died in Rome on 23 February 1447. His victory over Basel contributed to the collapse of the conciliar movement, though it was won by concessions to princes, so the papacy relied more on the Papal States for revenue. He re-established the University of Rome in 1431 and consecrated Florence Cathedral on 25 March 1436.
pope-francis: Jorge Mario Bergoglio was born on 17 December 1936 in Flores, a neighbourhood of Buenos Aires, the eldest of five children. His father, Mario José Bergoglio, was an accountant and an Italian immigrant from Piedmont; his mother, Regina María Sívori, was a housewife born in Buenos Aires to a family of northern Italian origin. The family left Italy in 1929 to escape the fascist rule of Benito Mussolini. At 21, after life-threatening pneumonia and three cysts, he had part of a lung removed.

Bergoglio entered the Society of Jesus as a novice on 11 March 1958, after three years at the archdiocesan seminary in Villa Devoto, and studied the humanities in Santiago, Chile. He took perpetual vows on 12 March 1960 and taught literature and psychology in Santa Fe and Buenos Aires. He was ordained in 1969 and was Jesuit provincial superior in Argentina from 1973 to 1979. In 1976 the Argentine Navy kidnapped two Jesuit priests, Orlando Yorio and Franz Jalics, during the Dirty War. Bergoglio is widely reported to have failed to protect them; a criminal complaint filed in 2005 was dismissed, but the debate over his conduct has continued.

He became archbishop of Buenos Aires on the death of his predecessor, Quarracino, on 28 February 1998, and was created a cardinal in 2001 by Pope John Paul II. He doubled the number of priests working in the city's shantytowns, which earned him the name villero bishop, and put the archdiocese's finances on a stricter footing. After the resignation of Pope Benedict XVI, the conclave elected him pope on 13 March 2013. He took the name Francis in honour of Francis of Assisi, and was the first Jesuit pope, the first from Latin America and the first from the Southern Hemisphere.

As pope Francis called for decentralised, synodal governance, made women full members of dicasteries of the Roman Curia and convened the Synod on Synodality. He was a behind-the-scenes broker, with the Government of Canada, of the restoration of diplomatic relations between the United States and Cuba announced on 17 December 2014.

His last public appearance was on Easter Sunday, 20 April 2025. He died on Easter Monday, 21 April 2025, aged 88, of a cerebral stroke. His funeral took place on 26 April, and on 8 May the conclave elected Robert Francis Prevost as Pope Leo XIV. Francis had appointed more than 80 per cent of the cardinals who elected his successor, and he formalised the Church's opposition to the death penalty in all cases.
pope-gregory-i: Gregory was born around 540 in Rome, recently reconquered by the Eastern Roman Empire from the Ostrogoths, into a wealthy noble family with close ties to the church. His father, Gordianus, was a patrician and senator who served for a time as Prefect of the City of Rome, and his great-great-grandfather had been Pope Felix III. Gregory was himself prefect of Rome at 30. On his father's death he turned the family villa into a monastery dedicated to Andrew the Apostle, later rededicated as San Gregorio Magno al Celio.

In 579 Pope Pelagius II chose Gregory as apocrisiarius, his ambassador to the imperial court in Constantinople, and he held the post until 586. The Roman delegation had gone to ask the emperor for military aid against the Lombards. Emperor Maurice had long decided to limit his efforts against them to intrigue and diplomacy, and the empire was occupied with the Persians in the East and the Avars and Slavs to the north. There is no evidence that Gregory's tenure accomplished much for the objectives of Pelagius.

He returned to his monastery in 585 and was elected by acclamation in 590, when Pelagius II died of the plague then spreading through Rome. Gregory wrote letters disavowing any ambition for the papacy, and one to Maurice asking him not to confirm his election, though the prefect of Rome intercepted it. He built a system of charitable relief for the poor of Rome, most of them refugees from Lombard incursions, holding that the wealth belonged to the poor and the church was only its steward. He sent missionaries to England, among them Augustine of Canterbury and Paulinus of York, and died on 12 March 604.

Gregory is the only pope between the fifth and the eleventh centuries whose correspondence and writings survive in enough quantity to form a comprehensive body. His Moralia in Job is one of the longest patristic works, based on talks on the Book of Job. His Pastoral Care became the definitive statement of the nature of the episcopal office. The Dialogues are four books on the miracles of holy men of sixth-century Italy, with the second devoted to a life of Saint Benedict.

John the Deacon wrote that Gregory revised the liturgy of the Mass, removing many things, changing a few and adding some. In his own letters Gregory says he moved the Pater Noster to just after the Roman Canon, where it still stands in the Roman Liturgy, and he established the nine Kyries at the beginning of Mass. He is honoured with Augustine, Jerome and Ambrose as one of the four Great Latin Church Fathers.
pope-gregory-ii: Gregory was born into a noble Roman family in 669, the son of Marcellus and Honesta. As a young man he was placed in the papal court and made a subdeacon under Pope Sergius I, later a deacon in charge of the library of the Roman Church and then a papal secretary. In 711 he accompanied Pope Constantine to Constantinople to deal with Rome's rejection of the canons of the Quinisext Council. Gregory handled the negotiations, and Emperor Justinian II agreed that the papacy could disregard whichever of the council's decisions it wished. He was consecrated on 19 May 715.

Gregory began by repairing Rome's Aurelian Walls, a task interrupted in October 716 when the Tiber flooded the city for eight days. He took a close interest in missions. In 716 Duke Theodo of Bavaria visited him, and Gregory sent delegates to help establish a church hierarchy there. In 718 the Anglo-Saxon missionary Winfrid approached him; he took the name Boniface and was commissioned in May 719 to preach in Germany. Gregory made him a bishop in November 722. He also restored Monte Cassino in 718.

He tried to keep on good terms with the Lombard king Liutprand. Around 721 he appealed to Charles Martel to drive the Lombards out, but Charles did not respond. Gregory and Liutprand later met at Sutri and reached the agreement known as the Donation of Sutri, by which Sutri and some hill towns in Latium were given to the papacy, the first extension of papal territory beyond the Duchy of Rome.

From about 722 Gregory was at odds with Emperor Leo III, who tried to raise taxes on the papal patrimonies in Italy to pay for an ongoing war. Gregory refused, and the people of Rome drove out the imperial governor. When Leo issued an iconoclast edict in 726, Gregory rejected it, and the Exarchate of Ravenna rose in revolt; Gregory dissuaded the armies from marching on Constantinople. Greek sources say he excommunicated Leo, but no western source confirms it.
Gregory died on 11 February 731 and was buried in St Peter's Basilica. His defiance of Leo prepared the way for the temporal power of the popes, and he is commemorated as a saint.
pope-gregory-ix: Ugolino dei Conti was born in Anagni, near Rome. Sources give his birth between about 1145 and 1170, and he is said to have been in his nineties, if not nearly a hundred, at his death. He studied at the Universities of Paris and Bologna. His cousin Innocent III made him Cardinal-Deacon of Sant'Eustachio in December 1198, and in 1206 he became Cardinal Bishop of Ostia and Velletri. He was Dean of the Sacred College of Cardinals by 1218 or 1219. At the request of Francis of Assisi, Pope Honorius III appointed him Cardinal Protector of the Franciscans in 1220.

Elected pope in 1227, he took the name Gregory because he assumed the office at the monastery of Saint Gregory ad Septem Solia. He continued the policy of papal supremacy of Gregory VII and Innocent III. In 1231 his bull Parens scientiarum, issued after the University of Paris strike of 1229, settled differences between the scholars and the local authorities by extending papal patronage; it has been called the university's magna carta. He also proclaimed a crusade against the Stedinger in October 1232 and endorsed the Northern Crusades.

Gregory began his pontificate by suspending Emperor Frederick II for delay in carrying out the promised Sixth Crusade, and excommunication followed. Frederick took Jerusalem, but Gregory distrusted him, and the war of 1228 to 1230 is known as the War of the Keys. After a truce, Frederick's defeat of the Lombard League in 1239 raised the prospect that he would dominate all Italy, and Gregory excommunicated him again and denounced him as a heretic. The struggle ended only with Gregory's death on 22 August 1241; his successor Innocent IV declared a crusade against the Hohenstaufen in 1245.
