The Acqua Felice aqueduct fed twenty-seven new fountains, new streets connected the great basilicas, four obelisks were erected, including the one in Saint Peter's Square, and the dome of St. Peter's was completed. Antiquities served as raw material: Trajan's Column and the Column of Marcus Aurelius became pedestals for statues of Peter and Paul, and the Septizodium of Septimius Severus was demolished for building materials. Reclamation of the Pontine Marshes reached more than 9,500 acres before it was abandoned on his death.

In 1588 the bull Immensa Aeterni Dei reorganised the Roman Curia, and he limited the College of Cardinals to seventy. In the same year the bull Effraenatam extended excommunication to contraception and to abortion at any stage. He renewed the excommunication of Queen Elizabeth I of England and promised a subsidy to the Armada of Philip II, payable only once the expedition had landed.

Sixtus fell ill with a fever on 24 August 1590 and died on 27 August. He was loathed by his political subjects as he lay dying, but later writers count him among the most important popes: impulsive, obstinate, severe and autocratic, yet open to large ideas and energetic in carrying them out.
pope-stephen-ii: Stephen was born in Rome, then part of the Exarchate of Italy within the Eastern Roman Empire, in 714. He was a Roman aristocrat. In 751 the Lombard king Aistulf captured the Exarchate of Ravenna and turned his attention to the Duchy of Rome. Stephen was selected on 26 March 752 to succeed Pope Zachary, following the recent death of the pope-elect, also named Stephen.

Relations between the papacy and the Eastern Roman emperors were strained in the mid-8th century because of the Isaurian dynasty's support for iconoclasm. Constantinople, itself beset by the Abbasid Caliphate to the south and the Bulgars to the north-west, could send no troops. Emperor Constantine V answered Stephen's repeated requests for help only with the advice to follow the ancient policy of Rome and set another Germanic people against the Lombards.

Stephen turned instead to Pepin the Short, king of the Franks, who had recently defeated an Umayyad invasion of Gaul. He travelled to Paris to plead in person against the Lombard and Muslim threats. On 6 January 754 he re-consecrated Pepin as king, and he anointed him at Saint-Denis in a ceremony that was evoked in the coronation rites of French kings until 1789. Pepin in return assumed the role of ordained protector of the Church.

At Quiercy the Frankish nobles consented to a campaign in Lombardy. Catholic tradition holds that Pepin there promised in writing to give the Church territories to be taken from the Lombards. This Donation of Pepin has not survived as a document, though later 8th-century sources quote from it. Pepin invaded Italy twice, and in 756 his army forced the Lombard king to surrender his conquests. Pepin conferred on the pope the territories of Ravenna, with cities such as Forlì, and the Pentapolis in the Marche, but left the Lombard kings their kingdom.

The Donation made the pope for the first time a temporal ruler over a strip of territory running diagonally across Italy from the Tyrrhenian to the Adriatic. The medieval popes could not exercise effective sovereignty over these mountainous lands, and the new Papal States kept the Lombard pattern of many small counties and marquisates, each centred on a fortified rocca. Charlemagne confirmed his father's donation in 774. Stephen II died on 26 April 757 and was succeeded by his brother Paul I. His pontificate marks the division between the Byzantine Papacy and the Frankish Papacy.
pope-sylvester-ii: Gerbert was born about 946, or at any rate between 945 and 950, in what was then the Duchy of Aquitaine. His exact birthplace is unknown. His parents took him to a nearby Benedictine abbey for instruction, and around 963 he entered the Monastery of St. Gerald of Aurillac. In 967 Count Borrell II of Barcelona took him to Catalonia to study mathematics. He studied under Bishop Atto of Vich and probably at Santa Maria de Ripoll, whose manuscripts came from Muslim Spain, especially Córdoba. In 973 Archbishop Adalberon appointed him a teacher at the cathedral school of Rheims.

Gerbert learned of Hindu–Arabic digits and applied them to the abacus, probably without the numeral zero. His pupil Richer recorded that he could calculate with it far faster than others using Roman numerals. He used an armillary sphere to teach astronomy, built a hydraulic organ with brass pipes at Rheims, and in 984 wrote to Abbot Eberhard of Tours about founding a large scientific library. His writings on arithmetic, geometry and astronomy were mainly teaching texts for his students.

After Adalberon died in 989, King Hugh appointed Arnulf as archbishop of Rheims. Arnulf was deposed in 991 for alleged treason and Gerbert succeeded him, but a synod in 995 declared the deposition invalid. Gerbert then taught Otto III, and in 998 Pope Gregory V made him archbishop of Ravenna. With imperial support he was elected pope in 999 and took the name Sylvester II, after Sylvester I, the adviser of Emperor Constantine I. He confirmed Arnulf at Rheims and acted against simony and concubinage among the clergy. In 1001 the Roman populace revolted and forced Otto III and Sylvester to flee to Ravenna. Otto died in 1002 on a third expedition to regain Rome.

Sylvester returned to Rome soon after the emperor's death, though the rebellious nobility remained in power. He died on 12 May 1003 and is buried in St. John Lateran. He was the first French pope. Later legends, found in William of Malmesbury and in a pamphlet by Cardinal Beno, a partisan of Emperor Henry IV, said that he stole a book of the dark arts from a Saracen philosopher, built a brazen head that answered yes or no, and made a pact with a demon.
pope-urban-ii: Urban II was baptised Eudes, or Odo, and was born into a noble family of Châtillon-sur-Marne in France. In 1050 he began his studies at the cathedral school of Reims. He became prior of the abbey of Cluny, and Pope Gregory VII named him cardinal-bishop of Ostia in about 1080. He was a prominent supporter of the Gregorian reforms, especially as legate in the Holy Roman Empire in 1084. Odo was elected by acclamation at a small meeting of cardinals and other prelates at Terracina in March 1088, after the short reign of Victor III.

From the start Urban faced Guibert, the former bishop of Ravenna, who held Rome as the antipope Clement III after the Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV took the city in 1084. Urban continued Gregory's policies with more flexibility and diplomacy. Kept away from Rome, he toured northern Italy and France, and synods renewed condemnations of simony, lay investiture and clerical marriage. He upheld the excommunication of King Philip I of France over his marriage to Bertrade de Montfort.

At the Council of Piacenza in March 1095 he received an ambassador from the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos asking for help against the Turkish tribes in Anatolia. At the end of the Council of Clermont, on 27 November 1095, he preached in the open air to a large crowd and called on them to take the Holy Land and the eastern churches from the Seljuks. He promised remission of sins to those who went, and the same indulgence applied to fighting the Moors in Spain.

No exact record of the Clermont speech exists. Five versions survive, written later and differing widely; Fulcher of Chartres, who was present, wrote his in about 1101. Urban's own letters speak more of liberating the eastern churches than of Jerusalem. Historians disagree about his motives: some point to reunion with the Eastern Church after the schism of 1054, others to his need for legitimacy against Clement III, others to fear of the Seljuks.

French armies removed Clement III from Rome in 1097. Urban died on 29 July 1099, fourteen days after Jerusalem fell but before the news reached Italy, and Paschal II succeeded him. Pope Leo XIII beatified him on 14 July 1881.
pope-urban-iv: Jacques Pantaléon was the son of a cobbler of Troyes. He studied theology and common law in Paris and became a canon of Laon and then Archdeacon of Liège. At the First Council of Lyon in 1245 he attracted the attention of Pope Innocent IV, who sent him twice on missions to Germany. On one of them he negotiated the Treaty of Christburg between the pagan Prussians and the Teutonic Knights. He became Bishop of Verdun in 1253, and in 1255 Pope Alexander IV made him Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem.

Pantaléon was at Viterbo seeking help for the Christians of the East when Alexander IV died. After a three-month vacancy, the eight cardinals chose him on 29 August 1261, and he was crowned on 4 September. He was the first pope elected without being a cardinal. A month before his election the Latin Empire of Constantinople had fallen to the Byzantines under Emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos, and Urban tried without success to stir up a crusade to restore it.

He took up the quarrel in Denmark between Jakob Erlandsen, Archbishop of Lund, and King Christopher I. After the king's death the regent Margaret Sambiria released the archbishop, and Urban agreed to a dispensation allowing women to inherit the Danish throne. The main questions were still open when he died.

His attention was chiefly on Italy, where Ghibelline cities favouring the Hohenstaufen faced Guelf cities favouring the pope. His captain was the condottiere Azzo d'Este. To counter Manfred, the heir of Frederick II, he supported Charles of Anjou, Count of Provence, in seizing the Kingdom of Sicily. Charles promised not to claim imperial lands in northern Italy or the Papal States and to pay an annual tribute of some 10,000 ounces of gold, while the pope would work to block the election of Conradin as King of the Germans.

Urban died in Perugia on 2 October 1264, before Charles reached Italy, and his successor Pope Clement IV kept to his agreements. He issued the bull Transiturus on 11 August 1264 and asked Thomas Aquinas to write the texts for the Mass and Office of Corpus Christi, which included the hymns Pange lingua, Tantum ergo and Panis angelicus. Two centuries after his death he became a character in the legend of the Minnesänger Tannhäuser, first attested in 1430, in which he said that forgiving the knight was as impossible as his staff growing leaves.
pope-urban-viii: Maffeo Vincenzo Barberini was born in April 1568 at Barberino Val d'Elsa, the son of the Florentine nobleman Antonio Barberini and Camilla Barbadoro. His father died when he was three, and his mother took him to Rome, where his uncle Francesco Barberini, an apostolic protonotary, took charge of him. He was educated by the Jesuits and received a doctorate of law from the University of Pisa in 1589. He served as papal legate to King Henry IV of France from 1601, became Archbishop of Nazareth in 1604, and was made a cardinal by Pope Paul V in 1606.

Barberini was elected pope on 6 August 1623 after the death of Gregory XV and took the name Urban VIII. His papacy covered 21 years of the Thirty Years' War. His military policy aimed less at restoring Catholicism than at securing his independence in Italy. The Duchy of Urbino was incorporated into the papal dominions in 1626, and in 1641 he began the Wars of Castro against Odoardo Farnese, Duke of Parma and Piacenza, whom he excommunicated. Castro was destroyed and its duchy joined the Papal States; he was the last pope to extend papal territory.

He opposed Copernican heliocentrism and ordered the trial of Galileo after the Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems appeared, in which the character Simplicio argues Urban's view. Galileo was summoned to Rome in 1633. Urban created 74 cardinals, among them his brother and two nephews, and his family amassed great wealth; Leopold von Ranke estimated 105 million scudi. His 1638 bull Commissum Nobis forbade the enslavement of natives living in the Jesuit Reductions of South America.

Urban was a patron of the arts and favoured the sculptor and architect Gian Lorenzo Bernini, who worked on the Palazzo Barberini, the baldacchino in St Peter's Basilica and the Fontana del Tritone. Bronze taken from the portico of the Pantheon prompted the saying that what the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did.

The papal debt rose from 16 million scudi at his election to 28 million by 1635 and 35 million by 1640. The cost of the Wars of Castro made him unpopular in Rome, and a crowd destroyed his bust on the Capitoline Hill after his death on 29 July 1644. His death is said to have been hastened by distress at the war's outcome. Giovanni Battista Pamphili succeeded him as Innocent X.
pope-zachary: Zachary was born in 679 into a family of Greek origin in the Calabrian town of Santa Severina. He was most probably a deacon of the Roman Church and as such signed the decrees of the Roman council of 732. He was chosen to succeed Gregory III on 3 or 5 December 741, and he was the last pope of the Byzantine Papacy.

Gregory III's alliance with the Lombard Duchy of Spoleto had put papal cities at risk when the dukes of Spoleto and Benevento rebelled. Zachary turned to King Liutprand the Lombard directly, and out of respect for him the king restored the territory the Lombards had seized and sent back captives without ransom. At the request of the Exarchate of Ravenna he persuaded Liutprand to abandon a planned attack on the city. The Liber pontificalis stresses his personal influence with Liutprand and with his successor Ratchis.

He corresponded with Archbishop Boniface of Mainz, confirmed the new bishoprics of Würzburg, Büraburg and Erfurt, and in 742 made Boniface papal legate to the Concilium Germanicum. In 745 he convened a synod in Rome to discourage the worship of angels. Asked by the Frankish Mayor of the Palace Pepin the Short whether it was better that the man with the royal power or the man without it should be king, he answered that it was better for the one who held the power, and soon afterwards the Frankish nobles abandoned the last Merovingian king, Childeric III. He also protested to the Byzantine emperor Constantine V about his iconoclastic policy.

Zachary built the original church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva near the Pantheon, over an ancient temple of Minerva, and restored the Lateran Palace. After Venetian merchants bought many slaves in Rome to sell to the Muslims of Africa, he forbade the traffic and paid the merchants their price, so that the slaves were freed.

He died on 15 March 752 and was buried in St Peter's Basilica. His elected successor, Stephen, died within days, so that Stephen II followed. The church historian Johann Peter Kirsch called him an excellent, capable, vigorous and charitable successor of Peter, and Peter Partner called him a skilled diplomat in a dark corridor of history.
popocatepetl: Popocatépetl is a stratovolcano in the eastern half of the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt, 70 kilometres south-east of Mexico City, from which it can be seen depending on atmospheric conditions. A high saddle, the Paso de Cortés, links it to its twin volcano Iztaccíhuatl to the north, and the two lie within the Izta-Popo Zoquiapan National Park. The cone is about 25 kilometres across at its base and has a steep-walled elliptical crater. Paleomagnetic studies put its age at about 730,000 years. Its glaciers shrank greatly in the 1990s, partly through warmer temperatures and largely through volcanic activity, and were gone by early 2001.

About 23,000 years ago a lateral eruption destroyed the volcano's ancient cone and sent an avalanche up to 70 kilometres from the summit. Since the mid-Holocene there have been three major Plinian eruptions, about 3,000, 2,150 and 1,200 years ago. The latter two buried the village of Tetimpa and preserved evidence of its preclassical culture. DNA analysis of teeth and bones suggests that a violent eruption in the mid to late first century CE may have caused the large migrations that settled Teotihuacan.

An expedition led by Diego de Ordaz made the first recorded European ascent in 1519, and the early sixteenth-century monasteries on its slopes are a World Heritage Site. More than fifteen major eruptions have been recorded since the Spanish arrived in 1519. After about half a century of dormancy, activity increased in 1991, and smoke has risen constantly from the crater since 1993.

The name comes from the Nahuatl words popōca, 'it smokes', and tepētl, 'mountain'. Mexicans call it El Popo, and in local lore it is Don Goyo, a spirit said to have met a villager of Santiago Xalitzina as an old man called Gregorio Chino Popocatépetl. He is held to warn the locals of eruptions, and on 12 March, the day of San Gregorio, they bring flowers and food to the volcano. In Tlaxcaltecan mythology Iztaccíhuatl was a princess who died of grief when she was falsely told that the warrior Popocatépetl had been killed in battle. The gods turned them into mountains, and Popocatépetl became a volcano.
popol-vuh: The Popol Vuh is a foundational sacred narrative of the Kʼicheʼ people of Guatemala, one of the Maya peoples. Its name is translated as Book of the Community or Book of Counsel, literally the book that pertains to the mat, because a woven mat served as a royal throne in ancient Kʼicheʼ society and symbolised the unity of the community. The story was preserved by oral tradition until about 1550, when it was written down.

Ximénez is generally thought to have borrowed a phonetic manuscript from a parishioner, a rendering of an oral recitation made near Santa Cruz del Quiché soon after Pedro de Alvarado's conquest of 1524. Adrián Recinos and Dennis Tedlock, comparing the genealogy at the end with dated colonial records, suggest a date between 1554 and 1558. The preamble states that it is written under the Law of God and Christianity because the old Popol Vuh can no longer be seen.

The text has no divisions in its manuscript, but popular editions follow the arrangement of Charles Étienne Brasseur de Bourbourg in 1861: a preamble and four books. Book One tells of the creation of animals and then humans; the first humans, made of earth and mud, crumbled, and the second, made of wood, were washed away in a flood, and the survivors became monkeys. The Hero Twins Hunahpú and Xbalanqué kill Vucub-Caquix and his sons in Book Two.

In Book Three their father Hun-Hunahpú and uncle Vucub-Hunahpú are killed at a ballgame in the underworld Xibalba. The twins, conceived after their father's death, defeat the Lords of Xibalba and become the sun and the moon. In Book Four humans are made successfully from maize, and the book follows the movement of the Kʼicheʼ. Depictions of the Hero Twins and other episodes appear on Maya ceramics, and a stucco frieze at El Mirador may show them.

In 1701 the Dominican priest Francisco Ximénez came to Santo Tomás Chichicastenango and transcribed the work, setting out the Kʼicheʼ and a Spanish translation in parallel columns. His manuscript passed to the University of San Carlos after the clerics were expelled from Guatemala in 1829–30. Carl Scherzer copied part of it in 1854, and in 1855 Charles Étienne Brasseur de Bourbourg took the volume to France. It reached the Newberry Library in Chicago through the collection of Edward E. Ayer, where Adrián Recinos rediscovered it in 1941. Translators include Delia Goetz, Munro Edmonson and Dennis Tedlock. In 2012 the text was declared intangible cultural heritage of Guatemala.
poppaea-sabina: Poppaea Sabina was born at Pompeii in 30 CE as Ollia, daughter of Titus Ollius and Poppaea Sabina the Elder. At some point, probably before her first marriage, she took her mother's name, perhaps because of her father's disgrace and suicide after the fall of the praetorian prefect Sejanus. Her mother later died by suicide after being baselessly accused of adultery in 47. Her maternal grandfather, Gaius Poppaeus Sabinus, had been consul in 9 CE. In 44, at the age of 14, she married Rufrius Crispinus, an equestrian who had led the Praetorian Guard, and bore him a son.

Poppaea then married Otho, a friend of the new emperor Nero. According to Tacitus she married him only to get close to Nero, while other ancient historians make Otho the cause of the relationship. Nero fell in love with her, and Otho was ordered away to govern Lusitania. A decade later he became emperor. Nero divorced his first wife Claudia Octavia, claiming she was barren, and married Poppaea twelve days later in 62 CE, when Poppaea was pregnant. Octavia was exiled and then executed. Poppaea's daughter Claudia was born on 21 January 63. Mother and daughter received the title of Augusta, but Claudia died in May that year.

Tacitus and Suetonius portray Poppaea as an ambitious, ruthless schemer. Tacitus depicts her as inducing Nero to murder his mother Agrippina in 59, yet modern scholars question this, since Nero did not marry her until 62. The modern historian Michael Grant is cautious about the assessment and notes that Tacitus's portrait echoes Sallust's. Josephus calls her a worshipper of the God of Israel who urged Nero to show compassion to the Jewish people.

The cause of her death in 65 CE is uncertain. Suetonius says Nero kicked her in the abdomen during a quarrel while she was pregnant. Tacitus calls the kick a casual outburst and rejects claims of poison, and Cassius Dio says Nero leapt on her but admits he did not know whether it was intentional. Modern historians, aware of these writers' bias against Nero, allow that she may have died of complications of miscarriage or childbirth. She received a state funeral, was embalmed, and was given divine honours with her daughter. Her story was the subject of Monteverdi's last opera, L'incoronazione di Poppea, in 1642.
popular-front-france: The Popular Front grew out of the economic crisis of the Great Depression, which reached France from 1931, together with financial scandals, the instability of the Chamber of Deputies elected in 1932, the rise of Adolf Hitler in Germany and the growth of violent far-right leagues in France. After the elections of 1932 the Socialists and the Radical-Socialists could not agree to form a cabinet together, and France was governed by a series of short-lived Radical cabinets. The Communist Party had run alone in 1932 and had accused the Socialists of social-fascism. Three months after the victory of the Spanish Popular Front, the French alliance won the general election of 3 May 1936 with 386 of 608 seats.

For the first time the Socialists won more seats than the Radical-Socialists, and Léon Blum became the first Socialist prime minister of France and the first Jew to hold the office. His cabinet had 20 Socialists, 13 Radical-Socialists and two Socialist Republicans, and included three women, who could not yet vote. The Communists supported it without taking ministries. A general strike in May and June 1936 led to the Matignon Agreements, which gave workers the right to strike and to collective bargaining and secured paid holidays, a 40-hour week and wage rises. Parliament passed 133 laws in 73 days, and Blum dissolved the far-right leagues.

The government soon met trouble. Higher wages were offset by rising prices, production stagnated, and businessmen sent funds overseas. When civil war broke out in Spain in July 1936 the cabinet was deeply divided; fearing the war would spread, Blum chose non-intervention with Britain and other states, while the air minister secretly sold warplanes to Madrid. With a Senate controlled by conservatives, Blum fell in June 1937 and Camille Chautemps took over. Blum returned in March 1938 and was succeeded by Édouard Daladier in April. The Communists broke with the coalition by voting against the Munich agreement, and the Popular Front dissolved itself in autumn 1938.

Many historians judge the Popular Front a failure in economics, foreign policy and long-term stability, and it left many ordinary French people disillusioned. Others stress that it began state intervention in economic affairs, which grew under the Vichy and postwar regimes into the modern French welfare state. Charles Sowerwine argues that it was above all a coalition against fascism, and that it blocked fascism's arrival in France until 1940. Its paid holidays also marked the beginning of mass tourism in France.
popular-front-of-estonia: Edgar Savisaar put forward the idea of a popular front during a live broadcast on Estonian television, the programme Mõtleme veel, on 13 April 1988, calling for support of Gorbachev's perestroika. At first the body went by the short-lived name Popular Front for the Support of Perestroika. Savisaar and Marju Lauristin are named as its founders, and the movement was formally established on 1 October 1988 at a crowded congress that became the culmination of the first phase of the Singing Revolution.

It was one of a number of popular fronts created almost at the same time in many parts of the Soviet Union, and resembled the Popular Front of Latvia and the Sąjūdis movement in Lithuania. The Baltic states differed from the other Soviet republics in having been parliamentary democracies between the world wars before their annexation by the Soviet Union in 1940.

The front held a series of crowded and widely publicised events that stressed both Estonian national pride and democratic values, and it produced large quantities of printed matter and newspapers. Its leaders appeared constantly in the media. In this way it made the idea of an independent Estonia, which had come to seem an impossible dream after decades of Soviet rule, acceptable to a mass public.

It was opposed by the Intermovement, which represented the pro-Soviet part of the population, including most of the Russian minority and other groups settled in Estonia in the Soviet era, and which was seen as hostile to Gorbachev's reforms. Over time a gap opened between leading members who at first sought only autonomy within a reformed Soviet system and the rank and file, who backed full independence. Savisaar's character also drew growing opposition, and his critics formed smaller organisations of their own.

As political parties took the place of mass movements in the early 1990s, the front became an anachronism, and it was dissolved in 1993. Several of the groups formed by its opponents became important in the politics of independent Estonia in the following decade. The front itself was to a large degree the precursor of the Estonian Centre Party, though at its start it had a far broader base of support.
popular-front-of-latvia: Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania were occupied by the Soviet Union in 1940 and 1941, by Nazi Germany from 1941 to 1944, and again by the Soviet Union from 1944 until 1991. Armed resistance under the name of the Forest Brothers continued until 1956. A new chance came in the 1980s, when Mikhail Gorbachev's glasnost allowed more freedom of speech. From 1986 Latvians organised around specific causes, and a protest that stopped the building of a fourth hydroelectric dam on the Daugava near Daugavpils led to the founding of the Environmental Protection Club. Demonstrations organised by Helsinki-86 were suppressed.

The breaking point came in summer 1988, when prominent Latvians declared support for greater autonomy, newspapers wrote of banned episodes of history such as the occupation of 1940, and the banned Latvian flag returned.

The Popular Front was founded on 9 October 1988 and was the largest of the new organisations. At first it asked for wide autonomy rather than independence. Supported by moderates in the leadership of the Latvian SSR, including head of state Anatolijs Gorbunovs, but opposed by hardline Communists, it grew to 250,000 members. Because 48 per cent of the population was not ethnically Latvian, it reached out to minorities. On 31 May 1989 it announced that independence had become the only option.

In the elections to the Supreme Soviet on 18 March 1990 a pro-independence coalition led by the Front won 138 of 201 seats. On 4 May 1990 the new body passed a law declaring Latvia's intention to restore independence. Dainis Īvāns, the Front's chairman, became deputy speaker, and his deputy Ivars Godmanis became prime minister. The Soviet government did not recognise this, and a military crackdown was feared. On 13 January 1991 unarmed people built barricades in Riga and guarded them, singing Latvian songs, which gave the movement the name Singing Revolution. Independence was recognised after the failure of the Soviet putsch in August 1991.

The Front then faced economic transition, and Latvia's GDP halved from 1990 to 1993. The Godmanis cabinet lost popularity and many politicians left to form new parties. In the parliamentary elections of June 1993 the Front received 2.62 per cent of the vote and no seats. It renamed itself the Christian People's Party, merged with the Christian Democratic Union, and dissolved on 9 October 1999. Its newspaper Atmoda appeared in Latvian and Russian from 1989 to 1992. Its former offices in Riga house the Museum of the Popular Front of Latvia.
popular-front-spain: The Popular Front, in Spanish Frente Popular, was an electoral alliance formed in January 1936 by left-wing groups of the Second Spanish Republic to contest that year's general election. It was led by Manuel Azaña. It included the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party, the Communist Party of Spain and two republican parties, Republican Left, led by Azaña, and Republican Union, led by Diego Martínez Barrio. It was supported by Galician and Catalan nationalists, the POUM, the socialist union UGT and the anarchist union CNT, although many anarchists urged abstention in the election.

The Comintern had decided in 1935 that communist parties should ally with other anti-fascist parties in popular fronts. In Spain the coalition united leftist republicans and workers' organisations to defend the social reforms of the first government of the Republic, from 1931 to 1933, and to free those held since the Asturian rising of October 1934. Its manifesto demanded the release of political prisoners, the rehiring of dismissed state employees and an independent judiciary. It also promised a new tenancy law and the restoration of regional autonomy, while rejecting nationalisation of land.

In the election the Popular Front defeated the National Front, a collection of right-wing parties. It received 4,654,116 votes against 4,503,524 for the combined right, and elected 278 deputies, 99 of them Socialists, against 124 for the right, 88 of them from the CEDA. The new government soon rehired workers dismissed for political reasons and carried out reforms in working conditions, education, land tenure, public health and child welfare. Azaña was elected President of the Republic in May 1936, but the PSOE stayed out of the government because of the opposition of Francisco Largo Caballero.

Political violence continued, with arson and attacks on right-wing parties and Church property that Azaña denounced, and clashes between Falangists and Communists and Socialists. By July there had been 269 political killings. The government moved commanders whose loyalty it doubted: General Francisco Franco was sent to the Canary Islands and General Emilio Mola to Pamplona.

In July 1936 conservative and monarchist generals launched a coup d'état that began the Spanish Civil War, which lasted until 1939. The government dissolved the army in loyal territory and armed groups organised by the unions and workers' parties, which defeated the rebels at first in Madrid, Barcelona, Bilbao and Valencia. The Republican army was reorganised in October. After a long war of attrition, Franco defeated the Republican forces and ruled Spain as a dictator until his death in 1975. The Popular Front was dissolved after the Republican defeat.
porcelain: Porcelain, also called china, is a ceramic material made by heating raw materials, generally including kaolinite, in a kiln to temperatures between 1,200 and 1,400 °C. Its strength and translucence, greater than those of other pottery, come mainly from vitrification and the formation of the mineral mullite at these temperatures. It is often regarded as the most prestigious type of pottery for its delicacy, strength and whiteness, and it is frequently glazed and decorated. It can be divided into three main categories: hard-paste, soft-paste and bone china. The term has no universal definition.

Porcelain was invented in China over centuries of experiment, starting with proto-porcelain wares of the Shang dynasty (1600–1046 BCE). By the Eastern Han dynasty (25–220 CE) glazed ceramics had developed into porcelain as the Chinese defined it, and by the late Sui and early Tang dynasties the requirements of whiteness and translucency had been met, in types such as Ding ware. Such wares were already exported to the Islamic world. Under the Song dynasty (960–1279) production became highly organised, and Jingdezhen has been the largest centre since the Yuan dynasty.

Portuguese merchants began direct sea trade with Ming China in 1517 and Dutch merchants in 1598, and blue-and-white wares reached Europe. Japan could not make its own porcelain until Korean potters, captured during the Japanese invasions of Korea (1592–1598), found clay near Arita. Japanese exports to Europe began around 1660.

Chinese porcelain was held in such esteem in Europe that china became a synonym for the Italian-derived word porcelain. In Saxony, Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhaus and Johann Friedrich Böttger produced the first hard, white European porcelain in 1708, and the Meissen factory was established in 1710. In 1712 the Jesuit François Xavier d'Entrecolles revealed many Chinese manufacturing secrets in letters published in Europe.

Factories followed at Vincennes, moved to Sèvres in 1756, and in England at Chelsea in 1743 and elsewhere. Thomas Frye patented a porcelain containing bone ash in 1749, the first bone china. The Imperial Porcelain Factory in Saint Petersburg was founded under an agreement of 1744 signed by Elizabeth of Russia. Porcelain is also used for electrical insulators, laboratory ware and tiles.
porfiriato: The term was coined by the Mexican historian Daniel Cosío Villegas. Porfirio Díaz was a liberal army general who had distinguished himself in the War of the Reform and against the French intervention, and he came to power in 1876 by rebelling against President Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada under the Plan of Tuxtepec. That plan called for no re-election of the president, so in 1880 Díaz handed office to his ally General Manuel González. In 1884 he abandoned the principle and returned to the presidency, which he held until 1911.

From his second term historians have characterised the regime as a dictatorship. After the elections of 1886 no opponents of Díaz sat in Congress, which approved amendments allowing re-election in 1887 and 1890. Díaz replaced independent regional leaders with loyal men, appointed jefes políticos who answered to the central government and commanded local forces, and drew rivals into business with foreign investors. This mix of conciliation, co-optation and repression, sometimes called the Pax Porfiriana, kept order for decades under the motto of order and progress.

A group of intellectuals known as the Científicos justified the regime with the positivism of Auguste Comte and the social Darwinism of Herbert Spencer. Railways connected local economies, and export agriculture and industry enriched urban elites and foreigners while the gap with the poor widened. Church and indigenous community lands were broken up, debt peonage and child labour spread, and peasants were often driven off land claimed by Díaz's allies. The state built secular schools and founded the Universidad Nacional de México under Justo Sierra, yet the 1910 census found only 33 per cent of men and 27 per cent of women literate. Elites embraced French fashion and architecture, and the Law of Monuments of 1897 placed archaeological sites under federal control.

The centennial of independence in September 1910, which coincided with Díaz's 80th birthday, proved the regime's last display. Francisco I. Madero, who had campaigned under the slogan Effective suffrage, no re-election, denounced the fraudulent 1910 election in the Plan of San Luis Potosí. Fighting broke out in Morelos and at Ciudad Juárez, Díaz was forced to resign and go into exile, and a decade of revolution followed. Historians increasingly see the Porfiriato as laying the foundations of post-revolutionary Mexico.
porfirio-diaz: Porfirio Díaz was baptized on 15 September 1830 in the city of Oaxaca, the sixth of seven children; his exact birth date is unknown. His father, José Faustino Díaz Orozco, was an illiterate workman employed by a firm of merchants, and his mother's mother was Mixtec. In 1845 he entered the seminary of Oaxaca to study for the priesthood, but he later changed to law, with the future president Benito Juárez among his mentors. He fought for the Liberals in the Reform War.

In the second French intervention Díaz fought at the Battle of Puebla in 1862. He was captured after the second siege of the city in 1863 and escaped. As commander in southern Mexico he resisted the French until Oaxaca City fell in 1865, and after a second escape he won the Battle of Miahuatlán on 3 October 1866 and retook Oaxaca City. In June 1867 he commanded the forces that took Mexico City.

When Juárez won the election of 1871 against Díaz, Díaz's supporters alleged fraud and rose in the Plan de la Noria, proclaimed on 8 November 1871. The Plan of Tuxtepec of 15 January 1876 opposed the re-election of President Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada, and Díaz took leadership of that rising. He took formal control of the presidency at the start of 1877 and won the election that year. In 1880 he stepped down in favour of his ally Manuel González, but in 1884 he abandoned the principle and held office continuously until 1911.

Díaz kept power by co-opting and coercing rival interests, and foreign investors from the United States, Britain, Germany and France were an important support of his regime. Railways financed from abroad opened remote regions to markets. Land surveys gave investors secure title, but they often wiped out the claims of communities that could not prove title, and survey companies kept one-third of the land they measured. Rural communities and small farmers lost their holdings. In 1910 Díaz allowed Francisco I. Madero to stand against him, then had him jailed during the election. Madero issued the Plan of San Luis Potosí calling for armed rebellion, and in May 1911, after the Federal Army suffered defeats, Díaz resigned in the Treaty of Ciudad Juárez.

Díaz went into exile in Paris, where he died of heart failure on 2 July 1915, aged 84. He was buried in the Cimetière du Montparnasse. Before his fall, an adulatory literature called Porfirismo portrayed him internationally as the statesman who had brought stability to Mexico. His legacy has been revised since the 1990s.
porkkala: Porkkalanniemi, in Swedish Porkala udd, lies at Kirkkonummi in Southern Finland. Its strategic value was great. Coastal artillery based there could fire more than halfway across the Gulf of Finland, and a power that also held the Estonian coast, only 36 km away at the closest point, could block Saint Petersburg's naval access to the Baltic Sea. The peninsula is also only 30 km from Helsinki, so a foreign power based there could put significant pressure on the Finnish government.

The Moscow Armistice of 19 September 1944, which ended the Continuation War, gave the Soviet Union the right to lease a naval base at Porkkala. It replaced Hanko, which the Soviets had leased as a naval base in 1940–41. A large area, taking in land from Kirkkonummi, Siuntio and Ingå and almost all of Degerby, was leased from 29 September 1944. About 7,200 Finnish inhabitants were evacuated within ten days. The lease was for 50 years, and the Paris Peace Treaty of 10 February 1947 confirmed the Soviet right to the area until 1994.

Beyond its military use the base served to apply political pressure on Finnish governments and to help build a Soviet espionage network. It was run by a military commander, with no Soviet civilian administration, and at its height held about 30,000 Soviet troops and some 10,000 officials and civilians. From 1947 Finnish trains between Helsinki and Turku could cross the area on payment of fees, with shutters closed and photography forbidden. The Soviet team for the 1952 Summer Olympics in Helsinki was housed on the base.

An agreement signed on 19 September 1955 returned the area early, and Finland took control on 26 January 1956. This is attributed to Finlandization, to coastal artillery becoming obsolete in the nuclear age, to the Soviet Union's renunciation of Stalinism under Nikita Khrushchev and to Finland's neutrality. The Finns found that about half the civilian housing and 80 per cent of the commercial property handed over in 1944 had been destroyed, and most of the evacuated population returned.

The Soviet airfield at Friggesby was demolished and returned to farmland, and by the end of the 1960s most traces of Soviet tenure had been erased. The area holds one of the main bases of the Finnish Navy, at Upinniemi, and its coasts are popular for birdwatching during the spring migrations of Arctic geese and other waterfowl.
poro: The Poro, also written Purrah or Purroh, was introduced by the Mane people, Mande elites who led large migrations from the Mali Empire into the southern coastal lands as early as 1000 CE. It is sometimes called a hunting society, and only men are admitted. In Sierra Leone two linked associations also exist: the Yassi, nominally for women though Poro members attend some of its ceremonies, and the Bundu, strictly for women, to which every member of the Yassi must also belong. Of the three, the Poro is by far the most important.

Even infants are briefly admitted, carried into the Poro bush and out again, and boys join at puberty in a rite of passage. In its civil role the society acts as a kind of governing body, making laws and deciding on war and peace, and its elders judge cases of alleged witchcraft. It meets in the dry season, between October and May, in a bush enclosure divided by mats and roofed by overhanging trees. There are three grades: chiefs and rulers, known as the big men, then priests, then the general membership.

The ceremonies are presided over by the Poro devil, a man in ritual dress who speaks to the meeting through a long wooden tube that distorts the voice. When women, children or outsiders take part the devil stays away, and he is unseen even by most members. Wooden masks worn in Poro masquerades represent a spirit world of benign and malevolent spirits. The society has its own rituals, language, tattooing and symbols, and an oath of secrecy keeps details scarce.

The Poro can lay its taboo on anything or anyone, and because no member defies it, a taboo laid on crops has caused great trouble; in 1897 the British colonial government passed an ordinance forbidding the taboo on all local produce. The society has kept political weight into recent times. In 2009 rock-throwing Poro members protested the choice of Elizabeth Simbiwa Sogbo-Tortu as the first female chief of the Nimiyama Chiefdom in eastern Sierra Leone and barred her from taking office. Charles Taylor is reported to have co-opted the society during his rule in Liberia.
porrentruy: Porrentruy lies on both sides of the Allaine River in Ajoie, the bulge in the north-western corner of Switzerland that extends into France, at the foot of the Jura Mountains. It is the seat of the district of Porrentruy. The first trace of human presence is a Mesolithic tool, and the first known settlement dates from the Roman era. Ruins of a Gallo-Roman temple were found in 1983, and a kilometre of the Roman road from Augst to Mandeure lies nearby.

The name first appears in 1136 as Purrentru and presumably comes from the Latin pons Ragentrudis, the bridge of Ragentrud, wife of the Frankish king Dagobert I. The Counts of Pfirt built a castle on a defensible hill and made it the capital of Ajoie. In 1281 they sold the territory to the Bishop of Basel, but the Counts of Montbéliard refused to hand over the town.

Bishop Henry of Isny asked King Rudolph I of Habsburg for support, and after six weeks under siege the count gave way. On 20 April 1283 the king asked the bishop to grant the town a charter. The bishop sold Ajoie back to Montbéliard in 1386, but the town was again subject to the bishop from 1461.

The Reformation in Basel led the bishopric to move its headquarters to Porrentruy in 1527. Under Bishop Jakob Christoph Blarer von Wartensee, who reigned from 1575 to 1608, the town reached the height of its importance, with the castle enlarged and a Jesuit college built, and this prosperity ended with the outbreak of the Thirty Years' War in 1618, when the town was repeatedly occupied, besieged and plundered. On 27 April 1792 French Revolutionary troops drove out the bishop.

Porrentruy became the capital of a dependent republic, which France incorporated in 1793 as the Département du Mont-Terrible. In 1815 the town was given to the Canton of Bern. In the 19th century politics was marked by conflict between Liberal-Radicals and Catholic Conservatives, and the Radicals held the mayor's office from 1860 until 1972. The Canton of Jura, created on 1 January 1979, chose Delémont rather than Porrentruy as its capital.

Porrentruy had 6,675 inhabitants in 2018, most of whom speak French. It houses the cantonal courts, the archives of the former episcopal see of Basel and the cantonal library. The old town, with Gothic, Baroque and neoclassical buildings, is part of the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites, and the castle, the Jesuit church and college and the Church of Saint-Pierre are listed as sites of national significance. The Porte de France, built in 1563, is the only medieval city gate left. In 1988 the town won the Wakker Prize for its architectural heritage.
port-arthur-tasmania: Port Arthur lies on the Tasman Peninsula, about 97 kilometres south-east of Hobart. The peninsula was a naturally secure site, surrounded by water that the administration rumoured to be shark-infested. The only link to the mainland was the isthmus of Eaglehawk Neck, 30 metres wide, which was fenced and guarded by soldiers, traps and dogs. Many attempts at escape were made all the same, and some succeeded. Martin Cash escaped with two others.

The settlement was named after George Arthur, the lieutenant governor of Van Diemen's Land, and began in September 1830 as a timber-getting camp. From 1833 until 1877 it received the convicts judged most hardened, the secondary offenders who had persistently reoffended in Australia. Security was among the strictest in the British penal system, yet the regime rested on the idea that prisoners could be reformed while punished. Boys, some as young as nine, were held apart at Point Puer, the second boys' prison of the British Empire, and put to stone cutting and construction.

The Separate Prison, completed in 1853 and extended in 1855, grew out of Jeremy Bentham's theories. Its wings could all be seen from a central hub, though individual cells could not. It marked a shift from physical to psychological punishment: food served as reward or penalty, and under the Silent System prisoners were hooded and kept silent. Many developed mental illness. Critics held that Port Arthur was as harsh as other penal settlements, or worse. The Isle of the Dead received those who died; of 1,646 recorded graves only 180, those of staff and military, are marked.

After the prison closed in 1877 much of the property was auctioned, though most was not sold until 1889. Buildings decayed, owners pulled some down, and fires in 1895 and 1897 and earth tremors did further damage. The town of Carnarvon replaced the prison settlement, and in 1927 the name Port Arthur was restored as tourism grew. Novels such as Marcus Clarke's For the Term of His Natural Life of 1874 kept the convict past before the public.

Since 1987 the Port Arthur Historic Site Management Authority has run the site. It was inscribed with the Coal Mines Historic Site on the World Heritage Register on 31 July 2010 as part of the Australian Convict Sites. On 28 April 1996 Martin Bryant murdered 35 people and wounded 23 at the site, which led to a national restriction on high-capacity semi-automatic shotguns and rifles.
port-au-prince: Port-au-Prince lies on the Gulf of Gonâve, whose bay acts as a natural harbour and has sustained economic activity since the Taíno. The city's layout resembles an amphitheatre, with commercial districts near the water and residential neighbourhoods on the hills above. The name means 'Prince's Port', but it is unclear which prince was meant: one theory points to Le Prince, a ship that arrived in 1706, though the islets in the bay were called les îlets du Prince as early as 1680.

The area was part of the Taíno chiefdom of Xaragua. Under Spanish rule the governor Nicolas Ovando, from 1503, had Taíno leaders killed at a feast, and violence and disease decimated the native population. The Spanish administration abandoned the region in 1606, and French filibusters arrived around 1650, setting up a hospital that gave the region the name Hôpital. Spain renounced its claims in 1697. Petit-Goâve was too malarial and Léogâne hard to defend, so Port-au-Prince was built in 1749, and in 1770 it replaced Cap-Français as capital of Saint-Domingue.

In 1804 it became the capital of independent Haiti. After the assassination of Jean-Jacques Dessalines in 1806 it was capital of the southern republic under Alexandre Pétion, and it became capital of all Haiti when the country was unified in 1820. American forces occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934. On 12 January 2010 a magnitude 7.0 earthquake destroyed most of the central historic area, including the cathedral and the National Palace; Haiti's government estimated the death toll at 230,000.

Port-au-Prince is the capital and most populous city of Haiti, with a population estimated at 1,200,000 in 2022. It is the seat of the State University of Haiti, established in 1920, and the Presidential Palace stands on the Champ de Mars. Its cultural sites include the National Museum, founded in 1938, the National Archives and the National Library. Each November the national cemetery fills with people celebrating Fet Gede, a Vodou festival of the dead.
port-louis: Dutch settlers used the site as a harbour from 1606 and called the area the Harbour of Tortoises. Under French government it became the administrative centre of Mauritius, then called Ile de France, and a major reprovisioning halt for French ships passing between Asia and Europe around the Cape of Good Hope. The port is named in honour of King Louis XV, and the French governor Bertrand-François Mahé de La Bourdonnais contributed to the development of the city. Because the Moka Mountain Range shelters it from cyclone winds, it was chosen to house both the main harbour and the fort.

The port kept its value during the British occupation of the island in the Napoleonic Wars, when it helped Britain control the Indian Ocean. Port calls fell drastically after the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, but rose during the canal's seven-year closure from 1967. Modernisation in the late 1970s helped it remain the central point for all imports and exports of Mauritius.

Port Louis is the capital and most populous city of Mauritius, with 147,066 inhabitants at the 2018 census. The main harbour is the only official port of entry and exit for sea vessels in the country, and ships must be cleared there before visiting any other anchorage. It is the biggest port facility in the Indian Ocean region, with specialised terminals for sugar, fish and containers.

Many buildings reflect the city's colonial history, among them French colonial buildings of the 18th century such as Government House, the Jummah Mosque, Saint James Cathedral, a Tamil temple and the five-tier Port Louis Theatre. The Aapravasi Ghat is the remains of the immigration depot built by the British government to import labourers from India, Eastern Africa, Madagascar, China and Southeast Asia to work on the island's sugar estates. The Intercontinental Slavery Museum deals with slavery and indentured labour.
port-moresby: Port Moresby lies on the shores of the Coral Sea, on the south-western coast of the Papuan Peninsula of the island of New Guinea. The place where the city was founded has been inhabited by the Motu-Koitabu people for centuries. When Europeans first came, the largest settlement, Hanuabada, consisted of five villages of Motu and Koita people, who were organised into units called iduhu, somewhat like clans. Port Moresby was already an important centre of trade, visited by distant tribes of New Guinea.

In February 1873 the crew of HMS Basilisk, surveying the southern shore of New Guinea, reached the harbour. Captain John Moresby named it for his father, Admiral of the Fleet Sir Fairfax Moresby. Missionaries of the London Missionary Society arrived in 1873 and 1874. In 1883 the Premier of Queensland ordered the police magistrate Henry Chester to take possession of the eastern half of New Guinea, and on 4 April the Union Jack was raised at Port Moresby. A protectorate over the south-eastern coast was proclaimed in October 1884, and Special Commissioner Peter Scratchley chose the site as the colonial capital.

In 1906 the Papua Act transferred Papua, with Port Moresby as capital, to direct Australian rule. In the Second World War it was a prime objective of Imperial Japanese forces in 1942 and 1943, and by September 1942 it was an important Allied complex of bases. General Douglas MacArthur had his headquarters there from November 1942 to October 1944. It was granted city status in 1972 and became the capital of independent Papua New Guinea in September 1975.

Port Moresby is the capital and largest city of Papua New Guinea, with 756,754 inhabitants at the 2024 census. Although surrounded by Central Province, it forms its own National Capital District, and the Motu and Koitabu landowners are represented by the Motu Koita Assembly. The National Parliament Building, opened in 1984, and the National Museum and National Library stand in the suburb of Waigani.
port-of-spain: Port of Spain measures about 10.4 square kilometres and lies in the north-west of the island of Trinidad, between the Gulf of Paria, the Northern Range and the Caroni Swamp. The Laventille Hills form its eastern boundary. The climate is tropical monsoon, with little seasonal variation, a wet season from May to December and a dry season from January to April. The city proper is small. It forms the western end of a continuous built-up area, the East-West Corridor, which runs about 24 kilometres east to Arima.

The Spanish founded the town as Puerto España. The first settlement stood near an Amerindian fishing village called Cumucurapo, meaning place of the silk cotton trees, in the area now known as Mucurapo. The name Conquerabia is also recorded for an Amerindian settlement here. It may have been a separate village, another name for Cumucurapo, or the result of a misunderstanding by early Spanish settlers, who set up a port called Puerto de los Españoles, later Puerto de España. In 1560 a Spanish garrison was posted near the foot of the Laventille Hills.

Queen's Park Savannah, once sugar land, was bought by the town council in 1817 from the Peschier family. After an election in 1887 Michel Maxwell Philip became mayor, a post previously held only by white men, which the historian Bridget Brereton wrote perhaps marked the emergence of the coloured man as a political force in Trinidad. The city was also the de facto capital of the short-lived West Indies Federation.

Port of Spain is the capital and chief port of Trinidad and Tobago, with a municipal population of 49,867 in 2017. It is a retail and administrative centre, with most government offices, and a financial centre for the Caribbean. The Trinidad and Tobago Stock Exchange, the Central Bank, the Red House and Independence Square are in the downtown district. Queen's Park Savannah, about 110 hectares, is the largest open space. The pre-Lenten Carnival is the city's main annual festival, and the city was among the hosts of the 2007 Cricket World Cup.
port-st-johns: Port St Johns lies about 220 kilometres north-east of East London and 70 kilometres east of Mthatha. The Mzimvubu River reaches the Indian Ocean there through a gorge known as the Gates of St John, flanked by sandstone peaks named after two British officers, Mount Thesiger at 342 metres and Mount Sullivan at 304 metres. Some of the most significant travertine deposits in South Africa are found nearby, and about 10 km west of the town sandstone is quarried for building. The climate is humid subtropical.

The town is thought to take its name from the Portuguese ship São João, although that ship was in fact wrecked at Port Edward; later seafarers mistook the mouth of the Mzimvubu for the site of the wreck. In the mid-19th century the Mpondo king Ndamase allowed a few white traders to settle at the river mouth. After his death in 1876 the Mpondo Great House at Lusikisiki tried to take over the area, and on 17 July 1878 his eldest son Nqwiliso ceded the western bank of the river to the Cape Colony in return for recognition as an independent ruler and a promise of protection.

The river mouth served as a port until the 1940s, when silting made the river too shallow for ships. From 1976 to 1994 the town was the principal port of the Republic of Transkei. Port St Johns was also the birthplace of the broadcaster Capital Radio 604.

Port St Johns is the main settlement of the Port St Johns Local Municipality in the O.R. Tambo District, in Pondoland. The 2011 census counted 6,441 inhabitants, about 90 per cent of them Xhosa speakers. It is a centre of tourism on the Wild Coast, reached by the R61 road, and the Pondoland Park, a forested area of 500 km2, stretches from the river mouth north towards KwaZulu-Natal.
port-vila: Port Vila lies on the west coast of the island of Efate, in Shefa Province, and is the capital and largest city of Vanuatu. Locally it is called simply Vila. The name of the area is Efil in the native South Efate language and Ifira in the neighbouring Mele-Fila language, of which Vila is a variant. Ifira is a small island in Vila Harbour where many traditional landowners live. The climate is tropical and maritime, with nearly constant trade winds, a wettest month in March and a driest in September.

Port Vila is the most important harbour and the centre of trade of Vanuatu. It is home to many languages: the daily lingua franca is Bislama, English and French are widely spoken, and many of Vanuatu's 138 indigenous languages are heard as people from rural areas move to the city.

Melanesian people have occupied the area for thousands of years. In 2004 an archaeological expedition at Teouma found a burial site of 25 tombs holding about three dozen skeletons of members of the Lapita culture; ceramics from the site were dated to the 13th century BCE. James Cook charted Efate in 1774 and named it Sandwich Island. His expedition did not land, but noted the good harbours and land suitable for European settlement.

In the late 19th century, when the islands were known as the New Hebrides, the economic balance began to favour the French by the 1890s, and they established large plantations. The French citizen Ferdinand Chevillard bought and cleared land around Port Vila for what was to be the largest French plantation on the island; it became instead the municipality of Franceville, which declared independence on 9 August 1889 and lasted only until June of the following year. After 1887 the territory was jointly administered by the French and the British, formalised in 1906 as an Anglo-French Condominium. During the Second World War Port Vila was an American and Australian airbase.

Port Vila had 49,034 inhabitants at the 2020 census, 16.3 per cent of the population of Vanuatu. The people are predominantly Melanesian, with small Polynesian, Asian, Australian and European populations. Christianity is the main religion in Vanuatu, and the city has a Roman Catholic cathedral, the Cathédrale du Sacré-Cœur, seat of the Diocese of Port Vila.

The Vanuatu Cultural Centre, which hosts the Vanuatu National Museum and the National Audiovisual Archives, stands at Saralana Park in front of the National Parliament. The city is one location of the University of the South Pacific, and is served by Bauerfield International Airport. It has been damaged by cyclones: Cyclone Uma in 1987 and Cyclone Pam on 13 March 2015, whose eye wall passed just east of the town.
porta-pia: Porta Pia was one of the northern gates in the Aurelian Walls of Rome and one of Pope Pius IV's civic improvements, named after him. It stands at the end of a new street, the Via Pia, and replaced the Porta Nomentana, a few hundred metres to the south, which was closed up at the same time. The new urban area could no longer reach the Via Nomentana through the ancient gate. According to Vasari, Michelangelo gave the pope three designs, beautiful but too extravagant, and the pope chose the cheapest. Construction began in 1561 and ended in 1565, after Michelangelo's death, and Giacomo Del Duca carried out the work.

It was Michelangelo's last architectural work. No trace survives of his three drawings, and it is not certain that the gate was built to the original plan. A bronze medal of 1561 by Gian Federico Bonzagna and an engraving of 1568 show it quite differently from its present form. Most experts consider that Michelangelo meant to give gates a picturesque and dramatic front, suited to their symbolic role as an entrance to Rome. The gate was set slightly behind the line of the walls and closed the long view along the Via Pia and what is now the Via XX Settembre. A second arch was opened around 1575 to ease traffic, which had grown after the nearby Porta Nomentana was closed.

The outer façade was completed in 1869 to neoclassical plans by Virginio Vespignani, who seems to have followed an engraving of 1568 closely. It has niches with statues of Saints Agnes and Alexander, by the will of Pius IX, who wished a memorial to his escape from danger when the audience chamber of the convent of Sant'Agnese collapsed during his visit on 12 April 1855.

On 20 September 1870 Bersaglieri soldiers entered Rome through a breach opened by artillery in the wall about a dozen metres west of the gate, and completed the unification of Italy. A marble and bronze monument stands at the breach. In front of the gate is a Monument to the Bersagliere, commissioned by Mussolini and erected in 1932 by Publio Morbiducci. The buildings between the two arches, once the customs office, house the Historical Museum of the Bersaglieri. On 11 September 1926 the antifascist activist Gino Lucetti threw a bomb at the car carrying Benito Mussolini here, without effect.
portland-cement: Portland cement developed from natural cements made in Britain from the middle of the 18th century. In 1756 John Smeaton experimented with combinations of limestones and additives, including trass and pozzolanas, for the lighthouse now known as Smeaton's Tower. James Parker patented Roman cement in 1796; it became popular but was largely replaced by Portland cement in the 1850s. Louis Vicat's artificial hydraulic lime is considered the principal forerunner of Portland cement. The name is recorded in a directory of 1823, and in his patent of 1824 Joseph Aspdin used it because the hardened cement resembled Portland stone, quarried on the Isle of Portland in Dorset. His product was nothing like modern Portland cement and has been called proto-Portland cement.

His son William Aspdin, who left his father's company, apparently produced calcium silicates by accident in the 1840s, set up a plant at Rotherhithe in 1843 and improved his cement in 1848. In 1853 he moved to Germany. Isaac Charles Johnson refined the product further and claimed to be its real father. In 1859 John Grant set requirements for the cement used in the London sewer project, which became a specification, and Frederick Ransome patented the rotary kiln in 1885, allowing a continuous process.

Portland cement is made by heating limestone and a clay source in a kiln to form clinker, at about 1,450 °C for modern cements, and then grinding the clinker with about 5 per cent gypsum. The gypsum prevents flash setting. Ordinary Portland cement is grey, and white Portland cement needs raw materials very low in iron and a hotter kiln.

Its most common use is in concrete, a composite of gravel, sand, cement and water that can be cast in almost any shape and used for roads, dams and structural elements. It is also used in mortars, plasters and grouts. A typical concrete sets in about six hours and reaches a compressive strength of 8 MPa in 24 hours and 41 MPa at three months. Manufacture releases carbon dioxide from the raw materials and from fuel, and its quarries and kilns have environmental effects.
portlaoise: The Annals of the Four Masters, written in the 1630s, call the site Port Laoighisi. The town grew around the Fort of Leix, or Fort Protector, whose construction began in 1548 under the Lord Deputy, Sir Edward Bellingham, to secure English control of the county after the exile of Gaelic chieftains the year before. The fort stood on rising ground, protected to the south and east by the River Triogue and an esker known as the Ridge.

An Act of Parliament in the reign of Mary I established the town proper, named Maryborough in her honour, and the county became Queen's County. The area had been a focus of the rebellion of Ruairí Óg Ó Mórdha, who lost his lands, which the Crown wanted settled by reliable landowners. For some fifty years the settlers fought a continual low-scale war against Gaelic chieftains who opposed the settlement, and the town was burnt several times by the end of the 16th century.

Maryborough received a market in 1567, and in 1570 a charter of Elizabeth I raised it to a borough. It sent two members to the Irish Parliament until 1800. Its Court House was built in 1805 and its County Gaol in 1830. In 1929, a few years after the foundation of the Irish Free State, the town was renamed Portlaoighise, later simplified to Port Laoise, and the county became County Laois.

Portlaoise is the county town of County Laois, in the South Midlands of the province of Leinster, 94 km west-southwest of Dublin on the M7 motorway. The Slieve Bloom mountains lie to the west and the Great Heath of Maryborough to the east. It had 23,494 inhabitants at the 2022 census. Remains of Fort Protector can still be seen in the town centre. The first aeroplane made in Ireland was assembled in the town, and its first flight was reported on 4 November 1909.
portmahomack: The Scottish Gaelic name, Port Mo Chalmaig, means the haven of Saint Colmóc. The village lies on a sandy bay on the northern coast of the Tarbat Peninsula, in the parish of Tarbat, about nine miles east of Tain. Its small harbour was designed by Thomas Telford, and the village is unusual in lying on the east coast while facing west. Tarbat Ness Lighthouse stands about three miles away at the end of the peninsula.

Shell middens point to settlement as early as one or two thousand years BCE, and the remains of an Iron Age broch lie a little to the west of the village. In 1949 the archaeologist O. G. S. Crawford speculated that a square fortification near Port a' Chaistell, described by a minister in 1822, might have been a Roman camp, though no trace of Roman settlement was later found there.

The excavations directed by Martin Carver around the redundant St Colman's church found an enclosure ditch, a burial ground with cist and head-support burials, the remains of a stone church and at least four monumental stone crosses. Over two hundred pieces of sculpture were recovered. The scholar Victoria Whitworth has suggested that the Book of Kells, whose display capitals resemble the sculptures, may derive from this monastery rather than from Iona.

Later conflicts touched the peninsula. The Battle of Tarbat Ness was fought around 1030 to 1040 between Thorfinn the Mighty, Earl of Caithness, and the King of Scotland, and in the 1480s men of the Clan Ross cornered a raiding party of the Clan Mackay in the Tarbat church and set it on fire. Cod, ling, halibut and other fish were taken in great quantities from the 17th century, and herring exports peaked between 1850 and 1890 before steam trawlers brought decline; grain exports from the harbour ended in the 1930s.

The village has a permanent population of between 500 and 600. The former parish church, whose oldest part may date from the 9th century, houses the Tarbat Discovery Centre with finds from the excavations, while some of the carved stones are shown in the Museum of Scotland in Edinburgh. Two storehouses by the harbour, built in the late 17th century and in 1779, survive as housing.
porto: Porto stands on the Douro River estuary in northern Portugal, about 280 kilometres north of Lisbon, and its western part reaches the Atlantic coast. It is the capital of the Porto District. Its historic core, with the Luiz I Bridge and the Monastery of Serra do Pilar, was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996, and has been a National Monument since 2001.

Before the Roman conquest the region was inhabited by the Gallaeci, a Celtic people, and findings suggest settlement at the mouth of the Douro as early as the eighth century BCE. As Portus Cale the town became a significant commercial hub under the Roman Empire, and its combined Celtic-Latin name has been cited as the origin of the name Portugal. In the Suebian and Visigothic periods it was a key centre for the spread of Christianity.

The Methuen Treaty of 1703 strengthened ties with England, and by 1717 English firms dominated the port wine trade. The Marquis of Pombal created a state-controlled wine company and demarcated the Douro, Europe's first protected wine region, which led in 1757 to the Revolta dos Borrachos, suppressed brutally by the authorities.

On 29 March 1809, during the Peninsular War, the Ponte das Barcas, a pontoon bridge, collapsed as civilians fled French forces, with an estimated 4,000 deaths. Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, then retook the city, crossing the Douro in wine barges. On 19 January 1919 monarchists declared the Monarchy of the North in Porto, which briefly served as the capital of the restored monarchy.

Porto is the second-largest city in Portugal, after Lisbon, with a metropolitan area of about 1.9 million people. Port wine takes its name from the city, since the cellars of Vila Nova de Gaia packaged and exported the fortified wine. In 2001 it shared the title of European Capital of Culture with Rotterdam.
porto-novo: Porto-Novo lies in the south of Benin on an inlet of the Gulf of Guinea, 13 kilometres from the Atlantic, from which it is separated by a lagoon. It stands about 30 kilometres east of Cotonou and 12 kilometres from the Nigerian border. Its commune covers 52 square kilometres. The city sits at the edge of the Dahomey Gap, which makes its climate drier than its nearness to the equator would suggest.

Porto-Novo was once a tributary of the Yoruba Oyo Empire, which offered it protection from the neighbouring Fon, who were expanding their power. The Yoruba called the city Ajashe, and the Gun called it Hogbonu. The first inhabitants were Yoruba-speaking, but a wave of migration from the region of Allada in the 1600s brought Te-Agbalin and his group to Ajashe in the late 16th century. In 1730 the Portuguese Eucaristo de Campos named the city Porto-Novo, because it resembled the city of Porto. It developed as a port for the transatlantic slave trade led by the Portuguese Empire.

In 1861 the British, who were active in nearby Nigeria, bombarded the city, and in 1863 the Kingdom of Porto-Novo accepted a French offer of protection. The neighbouring Kingdom of Dahomey objected to French involvement, and war broke out between the two states. In 1883 Porto-Novo was incorporated into the French colony of Dahomey and its dependencies, and in 1900 it became Dahomey's capital. The French sought to impose their language in every sphere of life and to stamp out the indigenous languages. Kings continued to rule in the city, officially and unofficially, until the death of the last, Alohinto Gbeffa, in 1976; from 1908 the king held the title of Chef supérieur.

Many Afro-Brazilians settled in Porto-Novo after returning to Africa following emancipation in Brazil, and Brazilian architecture and foods remain important to its cultural life. Under French rule, people often fled across the new border into British-ruled Nigeria to avoid harsh taxation, military service and forced labour. The border cuts through contiguous Yoruba- and Egun-speaking areas.

Porto-Novo is the official capital of Benin and the second-largest city, with 264,320 people at the census of 2013. The national parliament sits there, while the presidency and most other government institutions are in Cotonou. Its residents are mostly Yoruba and Gun. King Toffa's Palace, now a museum, and its surrounding district were added to UNESCO's Tentative List in 1996. The Da Silva Museum tells of the returning Afro-Brazilians, and the Alexandre Sènou Adandé Ethnographic Museum holds a large collection of Yoruba masks.
porto-santo-stefano: The town lies on the slopes of Mount Argentario, which dominates the whole area, on the north-western promontory of the peninsula in the Province of Grosseto. It is a little more than 40 kilometres south-east of Grosseto, about 12 km from Porto Ercole, the other major town of the municipality, and 150 kilometres north-west of Rome. It has two harbours, Porto Vecchio and Porto del Valle, and was once linked by a small railway line to Orbetello, closed in 1944.

Exposed to pirate raids, the settlement counted for little under the Aldobrandeschi and the Republic of Siena. Joining the State of the Presidi in the mid-16th century made it a place of great importance on the Argentario, and the Spanish Fort was built there; it now houses a permanent exhibition, Submerged Memories. Two Spanish lookout towers also survive, Lividonia and dell'Argentiera, the latter on the slopes of Mount Argentario. Like the other towns of the area, Porto Santo Stefano became part of the Grand Duchy of Tuscany in the first half of the 19th century.
After the cruise ship Costa Concordia capsized on 13 January 2012, many of its passengers and crew were brought to the mainland on the town's ferries from the Isola del Giglio.

The town is divided into four historical districts, Croce, Fortezza, Pilarella and Valle, each with its own coat of arms: a seagull above the cross of Saint Andrew for Croce, a golden Spanish fortress and horse for Fortezza, a golden vase and a dolphin for Pilarella, and an axe and the lighthouse for Valle. Every August the districts race against each other in the Palio Marinaro, a rowing regatta of 4,000 metres in boats called gozzi. The prize was first held in 1937 and was suspended from 1940 to 1944 because of World War II.
porto-torres: Porto Torres lies on the north-west coast of Sardinia, in the centre of the Gulf of Asinara, about 25 kilometres east of Cape Falcone and 15 kilometres from Sassari. It is a comune in the Metropolitan City of Sassari. The municipality is split into two parts of almost equal size: the town, with its industrial area and Roman ruins, on the flat Nurra plain, and the islands of Asinara and Isola Piana, which since 1997 form the Asinara National Park. Its full Latin name was Colonia Iulia Turris Libisonis, where Turris, tower, probably refers to a nuraghe or to Monte d'Accoddi.

Traces of human presence include the altar of Monte d'Accoddi, necropolises and, from the Bronze and Nuragic ages, the necropolis of Su Crucifissu Mannu, where two skulls show signs of surgery, possibly for relieving migraines and tumours or for religious reasons.

The town was founded in the 1st century BCE as Colonia Iulia Turris Libisonis, apparently by Julius Caesar, and was the first Roman colony on the whole island. Pliny calls it the only colony on Sardinia in his time, which suggests that there had been merely a fort before. The main road across the island ran from Caralis, Cagliari, to Turris, and a second road ran along the west coast. Remains include a temple dedicated to Fortune, baths, a basilica, an aqueduct and a bridge. It was an episcopal see in the early Middle Ages. The Romanesque basilica of San Gavino, built between 1065 and 1080, honours three saints said to have been beheaded in 303 under Diocletian and Maximian.

The city was inhabited until the 11th century, when most people moved to Sassari. In the Judicate of Logudoro its name became Torres. It was partly under Genoese hands until the early 15th century, when the Aragonese took it, and later it became part of the Kingdom of Sardinia. Torres was separated from Sassari in 1842, when the area around the basilica joined the fishermen's community by the port to form Porto Torres. It was bombed by the Allies on 18 April 1943.

Porto Torres is the second biggest seaport on the island after Olbia. The basilica of San Gavino, the largest Romanesque church in Sardinia, has two apses instead of the usual western facade and eastern apse, and its crypt holds several Roman sarcophagi; it was the main cathedral of the archdiocese of Sassari until 1441.
portobelo: Portobelo lies on the northern part of the Isthmus of Panama, in Colón Province, 32 km northeast of the modern port of Colón at the Atlantic entrance of the Panama Canal. It was chosen for its deep natural harbour. Tradition holds that Christopher Columbus named it Puerto Bello, meaning beautiful port, in 1502. After the English privateer Francis Drake died of dysentery in 1596, he was buried at sea in a lead coffin off Portobelo, and Drake Island at the mouth of the harbour commemorates him.

The Spanish explorer Francisco Velarde y Mercado founded Portobelo in 1597, and it quickly replaced Nombre de Dios as the major local port for Peruvian silver. With Veracruz it was one of the two Atlantic ports on the route of the Spanish treasure fleet, and the Spanish built fortifications to protect it. English privateers led by William Parker captured it in 1601. Henry Morgan did so in 1668 with 450 privateers and plundered it for 14 days; the English pirate John Coxon took it again in 1680.

In 1726 the Royal Navy under Admiral Francis Hosier blockaded the port to stop the treasure fleet returning to Spain; Hosier and many of his sailors died of tropical disease at Bastimentos. On 21 November 1739 a British squadron under Admiral Edward Vernon captured it in the War of Jenkins' Ear. More medals were struck for Vernon than for any other 18th-century British figure, and places across the British Isles were named Portobello, among them Portobello Road in London, a district of Edinburgh and the Portobello Barracks in Dublin.

The Spanish recovered Portobelo in 1741 after their victory at the Battle of Cartagena de Indias. British efforts to gain a foothold on the Spanish Main and disrupt the galleon trade failed. Afterwards the Spanish used small fleets trading at many ports, which made them less open to attack, and ships began to sail around Cape Horn to trade directly on the western coast.
