In the Middle Ages the town stood at a crossroads of trade routes and was part of the defence system of the emerging Hungarian state. Several authors derive the name from the Hungarian eper, meaning strawberry, and people of Prešov are traditionally called koňare, horse keepers.

The area was inhabited as far back as the Paleolithic period, and the oldest tools and mammoth bones found there are 28,000 years old. Continuous settlement dates from the 8th century, and Slavs arrived between the 4th and 5th centuries. The first written mention is from 1247, in the form Theutonici de Epuryes. After the Mongol invasion of 1241, King Béla IV of Hungary invited German colonists to fill gaps in the population, and Prešov became a German-speaking settlement. King Andrew III of Hungary granted it city rights in 1299, and Louis the Great raised it to a royal free town in 1347.

Prešov later belonged to the Pentapolitana, a community of five royal cities with Košice, Bardejov, Levoča and Sabinov. A town school is first mentioned in 1429 and the first coat of arms dates from 1453. The Prešov Greek Catholic Archeparchy was founded on 3 November 1815 by Emperor Francis II. After the Second World War the Prešov Orthodox Diocese was created by dividing the Mukachevo-Prešov Orthodox Diocese, and the Cathedral of St Prince Alexander Nevsky was built between 1946 and 1950 in the traditional Russian style. In the past Prešov was a typical multiethnic town in which Slovak, Hungarian, German and Yiddish were spoken.

Prešov is the seat of the Prešov Region and of Šariš, with a population of about 85,000. The old town has Baroque, Rococo and Gothic buildings, while housing estates of concrete panel buildings on the outskirts show Soviet influence. The city is the seat of the Roman Catholic Co-Cathedral of St Nicholas, the Slovak Greek Catholic metropolis and a diocese of the Evangelical Church of the Augsburg Confession. The University of Prešov includes Greek Catholic and Orthodox theological faculties. Its museums include the Museum of Ruthenian Culture and a collection of Judaica in the Prešov Synagogue, and its lively music scene has earned it the nickname Slovak Seattle.
prester-john: Prester John, in Latin Presbyter Ioannes, was imagined as a Nestorian patriarch and king who ruled a Christian nation lost among pagans and Muslims in the Orient, and who was said to descend from the Three Magi. The title Prester comes from the Greek presbyteros, meaning elder. The legend drew on reports of Saint Thomas the Apostle preaching in India, recorded in the third-century Acts of Thomas, and on embellished reports of the Church of the East in Asia. René Grousset suggested that it may have begun with the Kerait clan, thousands of whom joined that church shortly after the year 1000.

The narrative began in earnest in 1145, when the chronicler Otto of Freising reported meeting Hugh, bishop of Jabala, at the court of Pope Eugene III in Viterbo. He said that Prester John had recently won a great battle against the rulers of Media and Persia. Robert Silverberg links this to the victory of the Qara Khitai under Yelü Dashi over the Seljuks at the Battle of Qatwan in 1141.

About 1165 copies of a Letter of Prester John, probably forged, began to spread through Europe. It claimed to be addressed to the Byzantine emperor Manuel I Komnenos by a Christian sovereign and King of India, who lived in a palace of gems and gold and ruled from Persia to China. It was translated into many languages, including Hebrew, and circulated in ever more embellished form for centuries. Textual study of the Hebrew versions points to an origin among the Jews of northern Italy or Languedoc, and its author was most likely a Westerner. Pope Alexander III wrote to Prester John on 27 September 1177 through his physician Philip, of whom nothing more is recorded.

After 1221, when Jacques de Vitry reported a King David of India advancing against the Saracens, the legend was linked to the Mongols. Genghis Khan's foster father Toghrul, a Nestorian ruler of the Keraites defeated in 1203, was identified with the Prester, and Franciscan envoys such as Giovanni da Pian del Carpine and William of Rubruck travelled to the Mongols partly in hope of an eastern ally. As the Mongol Empire collapsed, Europeans placed the kingdom elsewhere, and from about 1250 it was increasingly located in Ethiopia. By 1520 Europeans knew the Ethiopian emperor as Prester John, though Ethiopians never used the name. In the 17th century Hiob Ludolf showed there was no native connection.
pretoria: Pretoria stands about 56 kilometres north-northeast of Johannesburg, at an altitude of about 1,339 metres. It lies in a warm, sheltered, fertile valley in the transitional belt between the plateau of the Highveld to the south and the lower-lying Bushveld to the north, surrounded by the hills of the Magaliesberg range, and straddles the Apies River. It is called the Jacaranda City for the roughly 60,000 to 70,000 jacaranda trees along its streets.

Pretoria was founded in 1855 by Marthinus Pretorius, a leader of the Voortrekkers, who named it after his father Andries Pretorius and chose a spot on the banks of the Apies as the new capital of the South African Republic. The elder Pretorius had become a national hero of the Voortrekkers after his victory over Dingane and the Zulus in the Battle of Blood River in 1838, and had negotiated the Sand River Convention of 1852, in which the United Kingdom acknowledged the independence of the Transvaal. Pretoria became the capital of the republic on 1 May 1860, superseding Potchefstroom.

In the First Boer War, Republican forces besieged the city in December 1880 and March 1881, and the peace treaty was signed in Pretoria on 3 August 1881 at the Pretoria Convention. In the Second Boer War the city surrendered to British forces under Frederick Roberts on 5 June 1900, and the conflict ended in Pretoria with the Peace of Vereeniging, signed on 31 May 1902 at Melrose House. That war ended the Transvaal Republic and began British hegemony in South Africa.

In 1910 the Boer republics of the South African Republic and the Orange River Colony were united with the Cape Colony and Natal Colony as the Union of South Africa. Pretoria became the administrative capital of the whole country, with Cape Town as the legislative capital and Bloemfontein as the judicial capital, and from 1910 to 1994 it was also the capital of the province of Transvaal. It achieved official city status on 14 October 1931 and remained the administrative capital when South Africa became a republic in 1961.

Pretoria is the executive capital of South Africa, seat of the executive branch and home to all foreign embassies. It forms the central part of the City of Tshwane Metropolitan Municipality. It is an academic and research centre, with the University of Pretoria, the University of South Africa and the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research. The Voortrekker Monument and Kruger House, residence of the president of the South African Republic, are among its museums and monuments.
pribina: Pribina was a West Slavic prince, born around 800, whose career is recorded in the Conversion of the Bavarians and the Carantanians, a work written in 870. According to a marginal note later absorbed into its text, Archbishop Adalram of Salzburg consecrated a church on his lands at Nitrava, usually identified with Nitra, around 827. It is the first church in Eastern Europe whose existence is documented in writing. It cannot be decided whether it was consecrated for Pribina, who was still a catechumen, or for his wife, who seems to have been of the Bavarian Wilhelminer family. Historians debate whether he held Nitra as a lieutenant of Mojmir I or as ruler of an independent principality.

Mojmir I, duke of the Moravians, drove Pribina across the Danube shortly after Ratpot took over the defence of East Francia's eastern marches, around 833. Ratpot presented him to Louis the German, who ordered him baptised at Traismauer and set him to serve in Ratpot's army. After a quarrel with Ratpot, Pribina fled with his son Koceľ to Bulgaria, but Malamir had made peace with the Franks and would not act for him. He moved to Lower Pannonia, ruled by Ratimir, and in 838 took refuge with Count Salacho of Carniola when Ratpot's army came against Ratimir. Salacho reconciled him with Ratpot.

Louis the German then made him ruler of Lower Pannonia under his own suzerainty, with lands near Lake Balaton on the river Zala. Pribina built a large fortress at modern Zalavár, known as Blatnohrad or Moosburg, to guard against the Bulgarians and the Moravians. His task was to gather the Slavs fleeing from various directions and keep them loyal to the Franks. His authority reached from the Rába in the north to Pécs in the southeast and Ptuj in the west.

Pribina had churches built in the region, and at his request the archbishop of Salzburg consecrated a number of them, among them one at Pécs. In 847 Louis converted his benefices near the lake, apart from those held from the archbishop, into personal property, and in 860 confirmed his donation of three hundred homesteads and vineyards to the monastery of Niederaltaich. His death is uncertain. He may have been killed in battle with the Moravians who supported Louis's son Carloman in a revolt, or captured by Carloman and handed over to the Moravians. Louis installed his son Koceľ as ruler of Lower Pannonia in 864.
pribislav-of-mecklenburg: Pribislav was one of three sons of the Obotrite chieftain Niklot, who was killed in 1160 during a joint campaign by Duke Henry the Lion of Saxony and King Valdemar the Great of Denmark. Most of the Obotrite lands were then divided among Saxon lords, and Pribislav and his brother Wertislav were left only the fortress of Werle on the River Warnow near Rostock, from which they kept up the fight against Henry.

In 1163 Niklot's sons raised a widespread revolt against Saxon rule. While Wertislav and much of the Slavic nobility were held prisoner by Henry during the siege of Werle, Pribislav destroyed many former Obotrite castles, among them Mecklenburg, where all the male defenders, settlers from Flanders, were killed. He retook Malchow and Quetzin, but Henry crushed the revolt with much bloodshed and had Wertislav publicly hanged at Malchow. Backed by a Danish fleet, the Saxon army defeated the Slavs at the Battle of Verchen in 1164, and Pribislav fled to Pomerania, from where he later raided the counties of Schwerin and Ratzeburg.

The Cistercian missionary Berno of Amelungsborn persuaded him to side with the Christians against the pagan Slavs, and Henry, in conflict with his own nobles and in need of an ally, restored him as Prince of Mecklenburg, Kessin and Rostock, while the County of Schwerin stayed in Saxon hands. As Henry's ally he fought the pagan Rani of Rügen. He founded the monastery of Doberan in 1171, endowed the Bishopric of Schwerin and went on pilgrimage to Jerusalem with Henry the next year.

He married Woizlava, daughter of Duke Wartislaw I of Pomerania, and arranged a marriage between his son Henry Borwin I and a daughter of Henry the Lion. He died on 30 December 1178 of a wound received at a tournament in Lüneburg and was buried in St. Michaelis Church there; in 1219 his son moved his remains to the newly completed Doberan Minster. His restoration founded a dynasty of Slavic origin that ruled Mecklenburg until 1918, while the lands of the Polabians and Wagrians to the west passed to Saxon lords.
pribor: Příbor lies on the Lubina River in the Moravian-Silesian Foothills, about 10 kilometres east of Nový Jičín and 20 kilometres south-west of Ostrava. Its highest point is 370 metres above sea level. The town has about 8,300 inhabitants. Its name means cutlery in modern Czech, but this is only a coincidence. If the Czech name is older, it probably comes from při boru or při zboru, meaning at a pine forest or at a ruin. If the German name Freiberg came first, it was originally rendered Vriburch or Freiburg and means free castle or castle with free access.

Count Frank von Hückeswagen founded the town in 1251, as a deed of the Moravian margrave Ottokar II confirmed in the same year, where it was called Vriburch. Its square was laid out on an old trade route to Poland, and the count built a solid castle. His descendants held the town until 1359, when it passed to the Bishops of Olomouc, who favoured it. Franz von Dietrichstein in particular granted it a number of privileges.

During the Thirty Years' War the town burned down three times, most destructively in the Swedish invasion of 1643, and it recovered in the second half of the 17th century. In 1694 Karl II von Liechtenstein-Kastelkorn founded a Piarist monastery and gymnasium, which also made education available to poorer people and made Příbor an important centre of education. From 1875 to 1938 the Czech Teacher Institute operated there and trained a number of significant teachers and figures of culture.

Příbor is one of the oldest towns in the region, and its historic centre is protected as an urban monument reservation. A regular square is lined with burgher houses, mostly Renaissance with Baroque alterations. The Baroque Piarist monastery now houses the town museum, a library and a primary art school. The most important of the town's four churches is the Church of the Nativity of the Virgin Mary, founded with the town, whose present brick building dates from the 14th century and has a tall slender tower. Sigmund Freud's birthplace is a museum with an exhibition about his life and work.
price-revolution: Prices in Western Europe rose roughly sixfold over 150 years, which amounts to about 1.2 per cent a year compounded. That is low by modern standards but high for the monetary system of the 16th century, which rested on silver. The inflation of about 1520 to 1640 is usually linked to the large influx of gold and silver from the Spanish treasure fleet. Starting in the 1540s, silver came from Zacatecas, Guanajuato and Taxco in Mexico and the mountain of Potosí in Peru, and Potosí's output rose in the 1560s after mercury deposits were found in the Andes.

Specie entering Spain raised its prices and caused a balance of payments deficit, which spread the metal to the rest of Western Europe. Earl J. Hamilton counted imports of around 210 million pesos in the 16th century, 160 million of them after 1550. Martín de Azpilcueta linked American silver to rising prices in 1556, and Jean Bodin made the case in 1568 against Jean de Malestroit, who blamed debased coin. Spain debased little until 1599, when Philip III introduced a purely copper vellon coinage.

Other causes are proposed. Population growth after the Black Death raised demand for food, and grain prices rose sooner and faster than others. Urbanisation and the enclosure of common land in England increased the pace of trade. Silver output in Bohemia, Germany and Hungary also rose to a peak in the 1530s.

Charles V borrowed heavily from the Fuggers, the Welsers and Genoese banking families to be elected emperor and to fund his policy, repaying them from American bullion. Bullion worth 15 million ducats reached the imperial treasury in his reign, and his interest rates grew from 17 to 48 per cent. Spain declared default in 1557, a year after his abdication, and had three bankruptcies by the end of the century.

Landowners with fixed rents suffered in Europe, though not in Spain, and people on fixed incomes, such as hidalgos and lower clergy, grew poorer, as wages lagged behind prices. In the second half of the century inflation made Spanish enterprise less competitive. Antwerp became the centre of the international economy, and Genoa flourished until the Crown's bankruptcies. Prices then stayed near their early 17th-century levels until the later 18th century.
pridi-banomyong: Pridi was born in Ayutthaya province on 11 May 1900 into a family of farmers, the second of five children. He became one of the country's youngest barristers in 1919, at nineteen, and in 1920 won a scholarship to study in France. There he began to assemble a group of fifty civil servants who wanted to turn Thailand's absolute monarchy into a constitutional one. He received a doctorate from the University of Paris in 1927, the year he co-founded Khana Ratsadon with like-minded Siamese students, and he returned to Siam to work in the Ministry of Justice.

On 24 June 1932 Khana Ratsadon, the People's Party, with Pridi leading its civilian faction, carried out a coup that ended 150 years of absolute monarchy under the Chakri dynasty. In 1933 his Draft National Economic Plan, calling for the nationalisation of land, public employment and social security, was rejected by royalists, who shut down parliament, and he was accused of being a communist and went into exile. He returned in 1934, founded Thammasat University and served as minister of the interior, of foreign affairs and of finance. As foreign minister he signed treaties revoking the extraterritorial rights of twelve countries.

As regent from 1941 to 1945 he refused to sign Plaek Phibunsongkhram's declaration of war on Britain and the United States and built the Free Thai Movement against the Japanese, though Nigel Brailey argues that his stance sprang mainly from hostility to Phibun. He became prime minister in 1946. On 9 June 1946 King Ananda Mahidol was found dead of a gunshot wound; a commission ruled that neither suicide nor murder was proved, and Pridi's opponents blamed him.

On 8 November 1947 a coup returned Phibun to power and Pridi was taken to Singapore. A counter-coup he attempted in 1949 failed, and he left for China, never to return to Thailand. In 1970 he went to France, and he died near Paris on 2 May 1983. His ashes were brought back to Thailand three years later. The charge that he was the mastermind of the king's death has since been regarded as politically motivated, and he won every libel suit he brought over it. UNESCO recognised the centenary of his birth, and Thammasat University has a library and an international college named for him.
prilep: Prilep lies in the northern part of the Pelagonia plain, in the south of North Macedonia, 74 kilometres from Skopje and 44 from Bitola. In antiquity the region belonged to Pelagonia and was annexed to the Macedonian kingdom during the 4th century BCE. Near the village of Čepigovo are the ruins of the ancient city of Styberra, which the Goths razed in 268 though it remained partly inhabited. The name first appears in Greek as Prilapos in 1014, and derives from Old Slavic words meaning stuck on the rock, after the hilltop above the town.

In 1014 Tsar Samuel of Bulgaria was said to have had a heart attack at Prilep on seeing thousands of his soldiers blinded by the Byzantines after the Battle of Kleidion. In 1041 the Byzantine emperor Michael IV defeated Petar Delyan's rebellion in the region. Byzantium lost the town to the Second Bulgarian Empire, but retook it. Serbian King Dušan took Prilep in 1334, and after 1365 it belonged to King Vukašin, co-ruler with Dušan's son Stefan Uroš V. After Vukašin's death in 1371 his son Marko ruled it, and rebuilt the citadel into an important stronghold.

Prilep became part of the Ottoman Empire in 1395 and stayed so until 1913, when the Kingdom of Serbia annexed it. Its bazaar began to develop in the 18th century, and one of the largest annual fairs in Macedonia was held there in the middle of the 19th. Bulgaria occupied the town from 17 November 1915 to 25 September 1918. It then joined the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes and, from 1929, the Vardar Banovina. In the Second World War it was occupied by the German Army on 8 April 1941 and by the Bulgarian Army on 26 April 1941, and local partisans attacked the police station on 11 October 1941. Communist partisans retook it definitively on 3 November 1944.

Prilep is a regional centre of tobacco growing and also produces white marble. The Markovi Kuli, the ruins of the fortress above the town, are among its medieval sites, along with the Treskavec Monastery, built in the 12th century in the mountains north of the town, which has frescoes of the 14th and 15th centuries. The dialect of Prilep, with those of Veles, Bitola and Ohrid, was chosen as a basis of the standard Macedonian language after the Socialist Republic of Macedonia was formed within Yugoslavia.
primary-chronicle: The Primary Chronicle, in Old East Slavic the Povest vremennykh let, takes its title from the opening line of the Laurentian text: these are the narratives of bygone years regarding the origin of the land of Rus', the first princes of Kiev, and the source from which the land of Rus' had its beginning. It covers the period from about 850 to 1110 and was compiled in Kiev in the 1110s. Medieval tradition credited the monk Nestor the Chronicler. Modern scholars consider it an anonymous compilation by several editors, because the internal evidence and Nestor's known works often contradict one another.

In 1116 the hegumen Sylvester of Kiev extensively edited the text and signed it; the new edition glorified Vladimir II Monomakh, patron of his monastery's village. A third edition followed two years later, centred on Monomakh's son Mstislav the Great. The authors drew on oral tradition, Rus'–Byzantine treaties, Norse sagas, and Byzantine chronicles such as those of John Malalas and George Hamartolos.

The narrative traces the Slavs back to a son of Noah and tells the founding of Kiev by Kyi, Shchek, Khoryv and Lybid. It relates the calling of the Varangians and the rise of the Rurik dynasty, Oleg the Wise's conquest of Kiev after the murder of Askold and Dir, and Olga's vengeance on the Drevlians, who had murdered her husband Igor. It describes the siege of Kiev by the Pechenegs in 968, the conversion of Vladimir the Great, and the succession crisis after his death, in which Yaroslav rose to power.

Christian themes run through the text, which is usually taken to reflect its monastic authors. In the Korsun legend, Vladimir captures the Greek city of Korsun in Crimea and demands the emperor's sister Anna in marriage; he is baptised before the marriage.

The original manuscript has not survived. The text is known from later copies, chiefly the Laurentian Codex of 1377, written at Nizhny Novgorod-Suzdal for Prince Dmitry Konstantinovich, and the Hypatian Codex of the 15th century. Because the manuscripts contain chronological errors, folklore and political revisions, historians treat its accuracy critically; Aleksey Shakhmatov showed in 1908 that it combines earlier accounts and documents.

It remains the main written source for the early history of the East Slavs, with corrections from the Novgorod First Chronicle. Samuel Hazzard Cross published an influential English translation of the Laurentian text in 1930, completed in a revised edition by Olgerd P. Sherbowitz-Wetzor in 1953, and by the early 21st century Primary Chronicle had become the common English name for the text shared by the main surviving manuscripts.
primera-junta: Its official name was the Provisional Governing Junta of the Provinces of the Río de la Plata in the Name of Lord Don Ferdinand VII, and it claimed to govern for the King of Spain while he was a prisoner of Napoleon. Juntas had sprung up in the Spanish cities that resisted the French invasion, and when the Supreme Central Junta of Spain dissolved itself in 1810, politicians in Buenos Aires such as Juan José Castelli argued that sovereignty had returned to the people. Many of them also resented the Spanish trade monopoly. An open meeting of the cabildo on 22 May 1810, pressed by the militias and a crowd in the Plaza Mayor, ended in the creation of the Junta on 25 May.

The Junta sat in El Fuerte, the fort that had been the viceroys' residence since 1776, where the Casa Rosada now stands. Cornelio Saavedra was its president, Mariano Moreno and Juan José Paso its secretaries, and its other members were Manuel Alberti, Miguel de Azcuénaga, Manuel Belgrano, Juan José Castelli, Domingo Matheu and Juan Larrea. From the start a radical faction led by Moreno faced a conservative wing behind Saavedra, each accusing the other of seeking power it was not meant to have.

The Royal Audience and the Cabildo opposed the Junta from its first day. When the Audience swore allegiance to the Council of Regency in Spain, its members and the former viceroy Cisneros were banished and shipped to the Canary Islands. Santa Fe, Entre Ríos, Corrientes, Mendoza and other places accepted the new government, but Montevideo, Paraguay and Upper Peru did not. In Córdoba the former viceroy Santiago de Liniers raised a counter-revolution; after his defeat Castelli had the leaders executed by 26 August. Historians still dispute the authenticity of the Operations plan, a secret programme attributed to Moreno.

By December 1810 the rivalry had reached its peak. Backed by deputies from the interior provinces who had not yet been admitted, Saavedra forced Moreno to resign on 18 December, and the deputies' entry turned the body into the Junta Grande. Britain, Spain's ally against Napoleon, stayed neutral while favouring its own trade.
primorsk-kaliningrad-oblast: Primorsk lies in the southwest of the Sambia Peninsula, on a bay on the northern shore of the Vistula Lagoon, about 30 km west of Kaliningrad. It belongs to Baltiysky District. The census of 2010 counted 1,956 inhabitants, against 2,150 in 2002 and 1,792 in 1989. Under its other names it appears as Fischhausen in German, Rybaki in Polish and Žuvininkai or Skanavikas in Lithuanian.

The site has been linked with Adalbert of Prague, who was sent with soldiers of Bolesław I the Brave of Poland to Christianize Prussia and was beheaded nearby in 997 by the pagan Sambians after he destroyed their sacred oak grove. In 1254 the Teutonic Order, with King Ottokar II of Bohemia, conquered Sambia during the Prussian Crusade. When the lands were divided, the Bishop of Sambia had a castle built here, called Schonewik. It was first mentioned in a deed of 1268 and is among the oldest in the region. A settlement was laid out from 1299, mostly by settlers from Stralsund, and it received a town charter in 1305. As the bishops' residence it was called Bischoveshusen, then Vischhusen from about 1325.

In 1454 King Casimir IV Jagiellon incorporated the region into the Kingdom of Poland, and after the Thirteen Years' War it was held by the Teutonic Knights as a Polish fief. In 1525 Bishop George of Polentz waived his rights and the residence passed to the Duchy of Prussia. On 12 February 1526 Duke Albert married Princess Dorothea of Denmark in the castle chapel. His mentally disabled son Albert Frederick lived in the fortress until his death in 1618, after which it decayed. From 1701 the town was part of the Kingdom of Prussia, and King Frederick I had the castle demolished and its stones used at the fortress of Pillau.

In 1818 Fischhausen became the seat of a district in the Province of East Prussia. Some Polish insurgents of the November Uprising, including Ignacy Domeyko and General Dezydery Chłapowski, were interned there in 1831. A railway from Königsberg to Pillau opened in 1865. In 1939 the town had 3,879 inhabitants. The Red Army captured it in a battle on 21–24 April 1945, and the medieval town was almost completely destroyed. It was renamed Primorsk, meaning by the sea, in 1946.

Primorsk lost its status as a district seat in 1947 and was demoted to an urban-type settlement in 2005. Its town status was restored in 2008. Its notable natives include the ophthalmologist Arthur von Hippel, the physicist Wilhelm Wien and the geneticist Arno Motulsky.
primoz-trubar: Primož Trubar was born in 1508 in the village of Rašica in the Duchy of Carniola, then under the Habsburgs. He attended school in Rijeka in 1520 and 1521 and in Salzburg from 1522 to 1524, then studied in Trieste under the bishop Pietro Bonomo, where he met Humanist writers, in particular Erasmus of Rotterdam. In 1527 the bishop made him a priest at Loka pri Zidanem Mostu. He enrolled at the University of Vienna in 1528 but did not complete his studies, and in 1530 he became a preacher in Ljubljana.

He lived there until 1565 and considered Ljubljana the capital of all Slovenes because of its central position. It is estimated that about 70 per cent of its 4,000 inhabitants attended mass in Slovene. He took the speech of Ljubljana as the foundation of what later became standard Slovene, adding a little of his native Lower Carniolan dialect. Leaning gradually towards Protestantism, he was expelled from Ljubljana in 1547.

In 1550, as a Protestant preacher in Rothenburg, Trubar wrote Catechismus and Abecedarium, the first two books in Slovene, printed that year at Schwäbisch Hall by Peter Frentz. Catechismus also contained the first Slovene music in print. In all he wrote 22 books in Slovene and two in German. On the exhortation of Pier Paolo Vergerio he translated the Gospel of Matthew in 1555, and by 1577 he had published the whole New Testament in three parts. From 1561 to 1565 he managed and supervised the South Slavic Bible Institute. He founded the Protestant Church of the Duchy of Carniola and was its first superintendent. His introduction of the Reformation led the Habsburgs to wage the Counter-Reformation, which a small Protestant community survived.

Trubar died on 28 June 1586 in Derendingen, then in the Holy Roman Empire and now part of the city of Tübingen, where he is buried. In 1952 a street in Ljubljana was renamed Trubarjeva cesta after him. He appeared on the 10 tolar banknote in 1992 and on the Slovene 1 euro coin in 2007. Slovenia proclaimed 2008 the Year of Primož Trubar for the 500th anniversary of his birth, and since 2010 8 June has been Primož Trubar Day.
prince-aimone-duke-of-aosta: Aimone was born in Turin as the second son of Prince Emanuele Filiberto, Duke of Aosta, and Princess Hélène of Orléans. His great-grandfather was King Victor Emmanuel II of Italy. He was granted the title Duke of Spoleto on 22 September 1904, was educated with his brother Amedeo at St David's College in Reigate, Surrey, and later studied at the naval academy in Livorno. He became a member of the Italian Senate on 1 April 1921. In 1929 he led an expedition to the Karakoram that concentrated on scientific work, and he received the Royal Geographical Society's Patron's Medal in 1932. In 1939 he married Princess Irene of Greece and Denmark, and their son Amedeo was born in 1943.

On 18 May 1941 Ante Pavelić, leader of the Ustaše, led a delegation to the Quirinal Palace to ask Victor Emmanuel III to name a member of the House of Savoy as king of Croatia. The Independent State of Croatia was a fascist puppet state partly under Italian and German control, whose leaders hoped a monarchy would give them legitimacy. Aimone was named king and took the regnal name Tomislav II. He first thought the nomination a joke by his cousin, but accepted from a sense of duty.

He was due to be crowned in Duvno but never went to Croatia. He objected to Italy's taking part of the Dalmatian coast, and an insurgency meant his safety could not be guaranteed. The Ustaše government had stripped the monarchy of most powers, so he held no real authority and acted from Italy and Hungary. Some sources call him king designate. He abdicated on 31 July 1943 on the orders of Victor Emmanuel III after Mussolini's dismissal. He inherited the title Duke of Aosta on 3 March 1942, when his brother Amedeo died in a British prisoner of war camp in Kenya.

In the last months of the Second World War Aimone commanded the naval base of Taranto, but he was dismissed for criticising the judges who found General Mario Roatta guilty of war crimes. He reached the rank of Squadron Admiral. After the birth of the Italian Republic he left for South America in 1947 and died suddenly on 29 January 1948 in a private suite at a hotel in Buenos Aires. The claim to the Aosta title passed to his son Amedeo.
prince-edward-island: Prince Edward Island lies in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, about ten kilometres across the Northumberland Strait from both Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. It has a land area of 5,686 square kilometres and is the only Canadian province consisting entirely of islands. Its bedrock is sedimentary. When the Pleistocene glaciers receded about 15,000 years ago a strip of land still joined the area to the mainland, and rising seas flooded it and formed the island. The Mi'kmaq call it Abegweit or Epekwitk, roughly land cradled on the waves.

The Mi'kmaq are the Indigenous inhabitants, and the island formed part of Mi'kma'ki, their homeland. Jacques Cartier was the first known European to see it, in 1543. In 1604 France claimed the Maritimes as the colony of Acadia and named the island Île Saint-Jean. The Mi'kmaq never recognised the claim but welcomed the French as trading partners and allies. It passed to Britain in 1763 and became a separate colony in 1769.

In the mid-1760s a survey led by Samuel Holland divided the island into 67 lots, allocated by lottery on 1 July 1767 to supporters of King George III. Ownership stayed with landlords in England, which angered settlers who could not gain title to the land they worked. Islanders spent decades trying to persuade the Crown to confiscate the lots. The Charlottetown Conference was held from 1 to 7 September 1864, but the island stayed out of Confederation in 1867. Facing railway debts, it joined Canada on 1 July 1873, and Canada financed a buy-out of the last absentee landlords.

Prince Edward Island is the smallest Canadian province by area and population but has the highest population density. Its capital and largest city is Charlottetown, and it is one of the three Maritime provinces. Farming is central to the economy, and the island produces about a quarter of Canada's potatoes. Surnames of its earliest settlers are still mostly Acadian, Scottish, Irish and English. Its nicknames include Birthplace of Confederation. A law of 1982 limits non-resident ownership of land, a legacy of the colonial land question.
prince-elector: The German practice of electing monarchs began when ancient Germanic tribes formed ad hoc coalitions and elected their leaders. While all free men originally voted, suffrage came to be limited to the leading men of the realm. At the election of Lothar III in 1125 a small number of eminent nobles chose the monarch and then submitted him to the remaining magnates for approval, and soon the right to choose was settled on an exclusive group of princes. A letter of Pope Urban IV in 1265 suggests that by immemorial custom seven princes held the right, namely those who had voted in the disputed election of 1257, which produced two kings.

Disputes followed over who held the Wittelsbach seat, the Count Palatine or the Duke of Bavaria, and over the right of the King of Bohemia to take part. The Golden Bull of 1356 settled the disputes. The composition then remained unchanged until the 17th century, except that in 1547, after the Schmalkaldic War, the Saxon electorate passed from the Ernestine to the Albertine branch of the Wettin family.

In 1623 Frederick V, the Elector Palatine, came under the imperial ban after the Bohemian Revolt and his seat went to the Duke of Bavaria. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 created a new post for the Count Palatine, raising the number to eight. A further post, for the Elector of Hanover, was created in 1692. In 1777 the number fell back to eight when the Elector Palatine inherited Bavaria. In 1803 new electorates were created for Württemberg, Baden, Hesse-Kassel and Salzburg, but the Holy Roman Empire was abolished in 1806 before any of the new electors could vote.

Electors ranked behind only the emperor, kings and the highest dukes, and held privileges not shared with other princes; the Golden Bull gave them the Privilegium de non appellando, barring their subjects from appeal to a higher imperial court. Each held a high office of the Empire: the Archbishop of Mainz was Archchancellor of Germany, the Archbishop of Cologne of Italy and the Archbishop of Trier of Burgundy.

Under the Golden Bull a majority sufficed, each elector had one vote, and elections were held regularly at Frankfurt from the 14th century. From the 16th century electors drafted a Wahlkapitulation, a contract that the king-elect swore to keep. All kings elected from 1438 to 1740 were from the Habsburg dynasty. After 1806 the former electors kept their lands, many taking the titles of king or grand duke, and Hesse-Kassel remained an electorate until 1866.
prince-eugene-of-savoy: Eugene was born at the Hôtel de Soissons in Paris on 18 October 1663, the youngest of five sons of Eugene Maurice, Count of Soissons, a French general officer, and Olympia Mancini, a niece of Cardinal Mazarin. From the age of ten he was brought up for a career in the church, but at 19 he chose a military career. Because of his poor physique and possibly a scandal involving his mother, Louis XIV refused him a commission in the French army and forbade him to enlist elsewhere. Embittered, he left France and entered the service of Emperor Leopold I, in whose army his elder brother Louis Julius had just fallen.

Eugene arrived at Leopold's camp in mid-August 1683, when the Ottoman army was besieging Vienna, and distinguished himself there at the age of 20. He commanded troops at Buda in 1686 and at Belgrade in 1688 and was a field marshal by 25. As commander-in-chief in Hungary he won the Battle of Zenta in 1697, which ended the Ottoman threat for nearly twenty years. In the War of the Spanish Succession he won victories in Italy, including Turin in 1706, and with the Duke of Marlborough won at Blenheim in 1704, Oudenaarde in 1708 and Malplaquet in 1709.

In 1716 Charles VI sent him to Hungary against the Turks. With about 70,000 men he attacked the Grand Vizier Damat Ali Pasha's army of some 200,000 on 5 August at Petrovaradin; the Vizier died of wounds. Eugene took Belgrade in 1717 and secured peace in 1718. As president of the Imperial War Council he later led a defensive campaign in the War of the Polish Succession, hampered by poor troops and a shortage of funds.

Eugene returned to Vienna in October 1735, weak and unwell, and died in his sleep in the night of 20-21 April 1736. His heart was buried with his ancestors in the Basilica of Superga in Turin and his body in St Stephen's Cathedral. He never married. A patron of the arts, he built the Stadtpalais in Vienna and, with the architect Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt, Baroque palaces including the Belvedere. Napoleon counted him among the eight great commanders of history, though later military critics have disagreed. An equestrian statue in Vienna calls him the wise counsellor of three emperors.
prince-frederick-charles-of-hesse: Frederick Charles Louis Constantine was born on 1 May 1868 at his family's Panker Castle, in Plön, Holstein. He was the third son of Frederick William of Hesse, Landgrave of Hesse, and his second wife, Princess Anna of Prussia. His father was a Danish military officer, and in the 1840s he had been one of the candidates of Christian VIII of Denmark to succeed to the Danish throne if the king's male line died out, but renounced his rights in 1851 in favour of his aunt Louise. Raised in Denmark, he settled in northern Germany in 1875, when the senior branch of Hesse-Kassel became extinct.

On 25 January 1893 Frederick Charles married his second cousin, Princess Margaret of Prussia, youngest sister of Kaiser Wilhelm II and a granddaughter of Queen Victoria. They had six sons, including two sets of twins. Two of them died in World War I.

The Parliament of Finland elected Frederick Charles King of Finland on 9 October 1918, using the Finnish form of his name, Fredrik Kaarle. With the end of World War I, his German birth and the abdication of Wilhelm II, which ended the monarchies of Germany, the arrangement was soon thought untenable by influential Finns and by Frederick Charles himself. Not much is known of the stance of the victorious Allied Powers.

He renounced the throne on 14 December 1918 without ever arriving in the country. His son Wolfgang had been designated crown prince, and a wedding to a Finnish lady was already in preparation. Finland's next elections were a victory for anti-monarchists, and parliament quickly adopted a republican constitution. The regnal name Väinö I, remembered by Finns, probably came from a newspaper column, not from the electoral document.

On 16 March 1925 Landgrave Alexander Frederick of Hesse abdicated as head of the House of Hesse, and Frederick Charles, his younger brother, succeeded him. He died on 28 May 1940, and his eldest surviving son, Philipp, succeeded him as head of the house.

According to certain family documents and correspondence, his successor as King of Finland would have been Wolfgang, not Philipp. Philipp was already the designated heir to the rights over the Electorate of Hesse, and was in the military and out of contact in 1918, while Wolfgang was with his parents and ready to travel.
prince-frederick-duke-of-york-and-albany: Frederick was born on 16 August 1763 at St James's Palace, London, the second son of George III and Queen Charlotte, a princess of Mecklenburg-Strelitz. His father chose an army career for him, and he was gazetted colonel on 4 November 1780. From 1781 to 1787 he lived in Hanover and studied at the University of Göttingen with his younger brothers. On 27 November 1784 he was created Duke of York and Albany and Earl of Ulster. In 1788 he opposed William Pitt's Regency Bill in the House of Lords, and in 1789 he fought a duel with Colonel Charles Lennox, firing no return shot after Lennox missed.

Promoted full general on 12 April 1793, Frederick commanded the British contingent of Coburg's army in Flanders. He won the Siege of Valenciennes in July 1793 but was defeated at Hondschoote that September. In 1794 he won at Beaumont and Willems and lost at Tourcoing, and the army was evacuated through Bremen in April 1795. He became field marshal on 18 February 1795 and effective Commander-in-Chief on 3 April 1795. His second field command, the Anglo-Russian invasion of Holland in 1799, ended with the Convention of Alkmaar on 17 October, and the rhyme The Grand Old Duke of York mocked him afterwards.

As Commander-in-Chief he carried through a large programme of reform, and he supported the founding of the Royal Military College, Sandhurst, in 1801. In the same year he issued a Royal Warrant for the Royal Military Asylum in Chelsea, for the orphaned children of soldiers. He resigned on 25 March 1809 after his mistress Mary Anne Clarke was accused of selling army commissions. Parliament acquitted him of taking bribes by 278 votes to 196, and he was reappointed on 29 May 1811.

After the death of Princess Charlotte of Wales in 1817 Frederick stood second in line to the throne, and he became heir presumptive on his father's death in 1820. He died of dropsy and apparent cardiovascular disease in London in 1827 and was buried in St George's Chapel, Windsor Castle. Fredericton in New Brunswick, the Duke of York Column in Waterloo Place and the Duke of York's Royal Military School were named for him or built in his memory.
prince-george-of-greece-and-denmark: Prince George was born on 24 June 1869 at Mon Repos palace in Corfu, the second son and child of George I of Greece and Olga Konstantinovna of Russia. In 1883, aged fourteen, he was sent to Denmark to enlist in the Danish navy, and there he became one of the best students of his class at the Danish Naval Academy. He was in the care of his grandfather Christian IX and his uncle Prince Valdemar, with whom he formed a lifelong attachment lasting until Valdemar's death on 14 January 1939.

In 1891 his uncle Tsar Alexander III asked him to accompany his cousin, the Tsesarevich Nicholas, on a voyage to Asia. On 11 May 1891, in Japan, the policeman Tsuda Sanzō struck Nicholas twice with a sabre, and George knocked him unconscious with his cane, an event known as the Ōtsu Incident. The Japanese emperor thanked him, but a version reaching Saint Petersburg named him as the assassin, until Nicholas silenced his detractors. In 1896 he was president of the Sub-Committee for Nautical Sports of the Hellenic Olympic Committee for the first modern Olympic Games in Athens and president of the judges.

In February 1897 he commanded a flotilla of six torpedo boats off Crete, sent to prevent Ottoman intervention when 2,000 Greek volunteers landed. The Great Powers occupied the island, and after the Greeks were crushed in the war of April 1897 they arranged autonomy under nominal Ottoman rule. In 1898, when Turkish troops had been ejected, George was made High Commissioner.

He was a staunch royalist and assumed absolute power, and he fell out with Eleftherios Venizelos, his minister of justice and leader of the movement for union with Greece. After Venizelos summoned a revolutionary assembly at Theriso in 1905, the pro-Prince parties won 38,127 votes against 33,279 in the 1906 elections, but in September 1906 George was forced to resign and was replaced by Alexandros Zaimis.

In 1907 George married Princess Marie Bonaparte, an heiress to the Blanc casino fortune, on 21 November. They had two children, Peter and Eugénie. He served as aide-de-camp to King George I until the king's assassination in March 1913. He died on 25 November 1957, aged 88, the last living child of King George and Queen Olga, and was buried at Tatoi Royal Cemetery. The coastal resort of Georgioupolis, between Chania and Rethimno, is named after him.
prince-gong: Yixin was born on 11 January 1833 into the Aisin Gioro clan as the sixth son of the Daoguang Emperor and the third son of Imperial Noble Consort Jing, of the Khorchin Mongol Borjigit clan. He studied in the imperial library and practised martial arts with his fourth brother Yizhu, and the emperor named the spear and sword movements he created. When Daoguang fell critically ill in 1850, his secret edict named Yizhu as successor and made Yixin a first-rank prince, though a rumour held that the edict had been tampered with. Yizhu became the Xianfeng Emperor and gave him the title Prince Gong of the First Rank.

In 1860, during the Second Opium War, British and French forces closed on Beijing and the Xianfeng Emperor fled to Rehe, appointing Prince Gong Imperial Commissioner with full authority. On 24 October 1860 he signed the Convention of Peking with British, French and Russian officials, then asked to be punished for signing an unequal treaty; the emperor replied that there was no need. In 1861 he set up the Zongli Yamen, the de facto foreign affairs ministry, and in 1862 founded the Tongwen Guan to teach technology and foreign languages.

After Xianfeng died in August 1861, Prince Gong, at odds with the eight conservative regents named in the will, joined the Empress Dowagers Ci'an and Cixi in the Xinyou Coup and had them arrested. The Tongzhi Emperor made him Prince-Regent. In 1864 Qing forces ended the Taiping Rebellion, and the court praised his leadership. In April 1865 an official accused him of monopolising power and taking bribes, and the empress dowagers stripped him of the regency. He kept the Zongli Yamen and a seat on the Grand Council, and supported Zeng Guofan, Li Hongzhang and Zhang Zhidong in the Self-Strengthening Movement.

Cixi came to distrust him, and in 1884, after the Grand Council could not decide whether to intervene when the French invaded Vietnam, she removed him from all positions. His brother Yixuan, Prince Chun, replaced him. In October 1894, during the First Sino-Japanese War, she recalled him to head the Zongli Yamen and the Admiralty and gave him command of the capital's defences. He died in May 1898 aged 67 by East Asian reckoning. The Guangxu Emperor attended the funeral and gave him the posthumous name Zhong. His tomb is in Changping District, Beijing, and his former residence in Xicheng District is a museum.
prince-henry-the-navigator: Henry was born on 4 March 1394, the third surviving son of King John I of Portugal, founder of the House of Aviz, and of Philippa, sister of King Henry IV of England. He may have been born in Porto. As early as 1410 or 1412 he had commissioned captains to explore the coasts beyond Cape Non. In 1415, at 21, he took part in the capture of the Moorish port of Ceuta, where he was knighted with his brothers Edward and Peter and made Duke of Viseu, the first time the title duke was used in Portugal. He relieved Ceuta again in 1418, and the two expeditions let him gather intelligence about the lands to the south from Muslim prisoners.

In 1419 Henry became governor of the Algarve, and in 1420 administrator of the Order of Christ, which funded his plans. His brother King Edward granted him all profits from trade in areas he discovered and the sole right to authorise expeditions beyond Cape Bojador. He was the main organiser of the disastrous expedition to Tangier in 1437, after which his younger brother Ferdinand stayed a hostage until his death. Henry promoted the colonisation of the Azores during Peter's regency.

Henry directed the development of the caravel, a lighter ship that could sail farther, and sponsored voyages, taking a 20 per cent tax on their profits. João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira found Porto Santo in 1418 and settlers reached Madeira in 1420. After fifteen failed expeditions in ten years, Gil Eanes passed Cape Bojador in 1434. The Portuguese reached the Bay of Arguin in 1443 and the Senegal River in 1444. Gold and slaves began arriving in Portugal, and by 1452 the gold allowed the minting of the first cruzado coins.

Henry died on 13 November 1460 and was buried in the Monastery of Batalha. No one called him Henry the Navigator in his lifetime or for three centuries: two nineteenth-century German historians coined the name, and British biographers popularised it. The idea of a school of navigators at Sagres is regarded by modern historians as a misconception, created in the 18th century. He employed some cartographers, but there was no organised centre of navigation science. By 1462 the Portuguese had explored the African coast as far as Sierra Leone.
prince-kitashirakawa-yoshihisa: Yoshihisa was born on 1 April 1847, the ninth son of Prince Fushimi Kuniie and Horiuchi Nobuko. He entered the Buddhist priesthood under the title Rinnoji-no-miya and served as an abbot in Edo. When the Boshin War brought down the Tokugawa shogunate and Satsuma and Chōshū forces took the city, he fled north with Tokugawa partisans.

In the north he became the nominal head of the Ōuetsu Reppan Dōmei, a short-lived alliance of almost all the domains of northern Japan led by Date Yoshikuni of Sendai. Some documents name him Emperor Tōbu and list the holders of the chief offices of a new northern court, with a planned era name of either Taisei or Enju, but historians are divided on whether he was ever actually named emperor.

In 1873 Emperor Meiji recalled all imperial princes serving as Buddhist priests to secular life, and Yoshihisa succeeded his younger brother, Prince Kitashirakawa Kasunari, as the second head of the princely house of Kitashirakawa. After military training in Germany he was commissioned a major general in the Imperial Japanese Army on his return in 1887. He married Shimazu Tomiko, adopted daughter of Shimazu Hisamitsu of Satsuma, on 10 July 1886; besides their son Prince Kitashirakawa Naruhisa he had five sons and five daughters by concubines. In 1893, as lieutenant general, he took command of the 4th Division.

During the First Sino-Japanese War he was moved to the 1st Division and took part in the invasion of Taiwan, where he contracted malaria and died outside Tainan on 27 October 1895, though rumours held that Taiwanese guerrillas had killed him. He was the first member of the imperial family known to have died outside Japan, and the first in modern times to die in war. Under State Shinto he was made a kami, enshrined at Yasukuni Jinja and in most Shinto shrines built in Taiwan under Japanese rule, and he was the sole deity of Tainan-Jinja.
prince-louis-of-battenberg: Louis was born on 24 May 1854 in Graz, the eldest son of Prince Alexander of Hesse and by Rhine and his morganatic wife, Countess Julia von Hauke. Because of that parentage he did not inherit his father's rank in the Grand Duchy of Hesse, and on 26 December 1858 he became Prince Louis of Battenberg when his mother was made Princess of Battenberg. His early years were spent in northern Italy and at his father's houses in Hesse. His mother spoke French to him and he had an English governess, so he grew up trilingual.

Although born in Austria, he enrolled in the Royal Navy at fourteen. He returned to Britain in May 1869, joined HMS Royal Alfred, and spent three and a half years in the Americas. In 1875–76 he served on HMS Serapis during the Prince of Wales's tour of India. Royal appointments slowed his progress, since promotions were seen as undeserved favours, and in the House of Commons members questioned his appointment to HMS Dreadnought. He married Princess Victoria of Hesse and by Rhine, a granddaughter of Queen Victoria, at Darmstadt on 30 April 1884.

In 1892 he invented the Battenberg Course Indicator, an analogue device for finding the course and speed to steer between ships. As rear admiral from 1 July 1904 he commanded the 2nd Cruiser Squadron, and his family connections helped to settle the Dogger Bank incident peacefully. As Second Sea Lord from December 1911 he improved conditions for ratings and created an Admiralty War Staff. He became First Sea Lord in 1912. Elements of the press, such as Horatio Bottomley, objected to a man of German origin being trusted with defence secrets, and once the war began his background forced his retirement.

At the behest of George V he gave up the title Prince of Battenberg on 14 July 1917 and changed his surname to Mountbatten. On 7 November the King made him Marquess of Milford Haven. He declined a dukedom as he could not afford the lifestyle expected of a duke. He sold Heiligenberg Castle in 1920 after losing his Russian investments.

He was promoted Admiral of the Fleet on the Retired List in 1921, and died on 11 September 1921 in London of heart failure after influenza, aged 67. His daughter Louise became Queen of Sweden, his son Louis served as First Sea Lord from 1954 to 1959, and Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, was his grandson.
prince-marko: Marko was born about 1335, the first son of Vukašin Mrnjavčević and his wife Alena. The family name comes from Mrnjava, whom the Ragusan historian Mavro Orbin described as a minor nobleman from Zachlumia. The earliest written reference to Vukašin, from 1350, calls him the appointed governor of Prilep for Emperor Stefan Dušan. In July 1361 Dušan's successor Uroš appointed Marko to head an embassy to Ragusa to negotiate peace. Peace was not reached, but Marko secured the release of detained Serbian merchants from Prizren and was allowed to withdraw silver his family had deposited in the city. That account holds the earliest undisputed reference to him.

Vukašin, co-ruler with Uroš, crowned Marko young king in 1370 or 1371. On 26 September 1371 Vukašin was killed and his forces defeated at the Battle of Maritsa, and when Uroš died in December 1371 Marko formally became king of the Serbian land. The Serbian nobles, who had become effectively independent, did not recognise him.

By 1372 Đurađ I Balšić had taken Prizren and Peć and Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović had taken Pristina, and by 1377 Vuk Branković held Skopje. Marko kept Prilep and ruled a small territory in western Macedonia, sharing power with his brother Andrijaš. He funded the Monastery of Saint Demetrius near Skopje, completed in 1376 and known as Marko's Monastery. He became an Ottoman vassal, though the date is uncertain and probably not immediately after Maritsa.

Marko died on 17 May 1395 fighting against the Wallachians at the Battle of Rovine. Although a ruler of modest historical significance, he became a major figure of South Slavic oral tradition, venerated as a national hero by Serbs, Macedonians and Bulgarians as a protector of the weak who confronted the Turks.

In Serbian epic poetry he is Kraljević Marko, prince or king's son, and the poems, composed by anonymous poets under Ottoman rule, bind together adventures that show his character. Bulgarian and Macedonian tales say a vila fostered him and gave him supernatural strength. Legends make him a giant who created the Demir Kapija gorge with a stroke of his sabre. Dramas, paintings and sculptures, among them Ivan Meštrović's Marko on Šarac, took up the figure.
prince-maximilian-of-baden: Maximilian was born in Baden-Baden on 10 July 1867, the son of Prince Wilhelm Max of Baden and Princess Maria Maximilianovna of Leuchtenberg, a granddaughter of Eugène de Beauharnais. He studied law and cameralism at Leipzig University and trained as an officer in the Prussian Army. After the death of his uncle Grand Duke Frederick I of Baden in 1907 he became heir to the grand-ducal throne of his cousin Frederick II, whose marriage remained childless, and he became president of the upper house of Baden's parliament.

He married Princess Marie Louise of Hanover and Cumberland in 1900. In 1914 he became honorary president of the Baden section of the German Red Cross, working for prisoners of war, and he spoke against the resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare in 1917.

After the Supreme Army Command told the government in late September 1918 that the front was about to collapse, Chancellor Georg von Hertling's cabinet resigned and Max was appointed Imperial Chancellor and minister-president of Prussia on 3 October 1918. He had reservations about the plan and said openly that he was no politician, but Wilhelm II convinced him to take the post. His government rested on the majority parties of the Reichstag, and for the first time included Social Democrats, among them Philipp Scheidemann and Gustav Bauer. He sought an armistice on the basis of Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points, and when Erich Ludendorff turned to continued fighting, Max had him dismissed.

A political amnesty was passed, and in late October the constitution was amended so that the chancellor answered to the Reichstag. As revolution spread in early November, Max urged Wilhelm II to abdicate. At noon on 9 November 1918 he announced the abdication of the emperor and the renunciation of the crown prince without waiting for their consent. He then resigned and handed the chancellorship to Friedrich Ebert in an unconstitutional move, and refused Ebert's request to stay on as regent.

Max returned to Baden and spent the rest of his life in retirement. He rejected a mandate to the Weimar National Assembly of 1919 and in 1920 founded the Schule Schloss Salem boarding school with Kurt Hahn. He published Völkerbund und Rechtsfriede, Die moralische Offensive and Erinnerungen und Dokumente. In 1928 he became head of the House of Zähringen as Margrave of Baden, and he died at Salem on 6 November 1929. Although regarded as a weak chancellor, he is seen as having played a vital role in the transition to a government based on the Reichstag majority, which made Ebert's government acceptable to some conservative forces in the bureaucracy and military.
prince-maximilian-of-wied-neuwied: Alexander Philipp Maximilian zu Wied-Neuwied was born in Neuwied on 23 September 1782, the grandson of the ruling count, after 1784 prince, Johann Friedrich Alexander of Wied-Neuwied. Born at the end of the Enlightenment, he became friends with two of its major figures: Johann Friedrich Blumenbach, a comparative anthropologist under whom he studied the biological sciences, and Alexander von Humboldt, who served as his mentor. He joined the Prussian army in 1800 during the Napoleonic Wars and rose to the rank of major in the Zieten Hussars. He was given leave in 1815.

Wied led an expedition to south-eastern Brazil from 1815 to 1817. In 1816 he found the Botocudos, about whom he gave exact details for the first time. Because of war among the tribes he had to abandon his original route, and he stayed for a time near some ruins he had come across. North of the Belmonte river he made his way through the woods and reached the province of Minas Gerais after many difficulties.

His health was poor, he was detained for four days on unfounded suspicions, and he was robbed of much of his collection of insects and plants. He embarked for Germany on 10 May 1817 and wrote Reise nach Brasilien and Beiträge zur Naturgeschichte von Brasilien. The album of the Brazil journey first showed Europe real images of Brazilian Indians.

In 1832 he travelled to the Great Plains of the United States with the Swiss painter Karl Bodmer, going up the Missouri River. He recorded the cultures of many Native American peoples with sympathy, notably the Mandan and the Hidatsa, who lived in settled villages on the river, and nomadic peoples such as the Sioux, Assiniboine, Plains Cree, Gros Ventres and Blackfoot. On his return he wrote Reise in das Innere Nord-Amerikas (1840).

Bodmer's watercolours of individuals, artefacts and customs are acknowledged as among the most accurate and informative ever made, and many were adapted as hand-coloured engravings to illustrate the 1840 publication. Wied collected many ethnographic objects and specimens of plants and animals, which are still kept in museums, notably the Linden Museum in Stuttgart. The orchid genus Neuwiedia was named for him, as were eight species of reptiles. He was elected a member of the American Philosophical Society in 1845 and died on 3 February 1867.
prince-of-wales: The first known use of the title Prince of Wales was in the 1160s, by Owain Gwynedd, ruler of Gwynedd, in a letter to Louis VII of France. Owain probably meant to claim pre-eminence over the other Welsh rulers of Deheubarth, Powys and Gwynedd. After his death in 1170 only Rhys ap Gruffydd of Deheubarth is known to have used it, in two charters of the 1180s. Gwynedd's rulers preferred styles such as Prince of North Wales, until Dafydd ap Llywelyn revived the title in 1245.

Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, Dafydd's nephew, used no other style from 1262 until his death in 1282: Prince of Wales and Lord of Snowdon. By 1263 he had induced the remaining native rulers to do him homage, and he built governing structures that made his authority effective across the Principality of Wales. Henry III of England recognised his title and authority in the Treaty of Montgomery of 1267.

Edward I of England conquered Wales between 1277 and 1283. Llywelyn was killed in 1282, and his brother Dafydd, who took up his title, was defeated and executed in 1283, after which the principality was permanently annexed. To finalise the conquest, on 7 February 1301 Edward invested his Welsh-born son Edward of Caernarfon as Prince of Wales, beginning the custom of granting the title to the heir apparent.

The title is neither automatic nor heritable. It merges with the Crown when its holder becomes king, and reverts to the Crown if he dies first, leaving the sovereign free to grant it to the new heir. Since 1301 the heir has generally also been made Earl of Chester, and the prince is typically Duke of Cornwall, a duchy created in 1337 by Edward III for his son Edward of Woodstock, the Black Prince.

Two later claimants tried to revive the Welsh title. Owain Lawgoch made an abortive invasion attempt in 1372. Owain Glyndŵr's supporters proclaimed him Prince of Wales at the start of his revolt in 1400, and in 1404 he had himself crowned and planned state institutions for a new principality. The rebellion began to fail by 1406, and he died in obscurity, probably around 1415. Henry Tudor, the future Henry VIII, received the title in 1504 after the death of his brother Arthur in 1502, and Charles Stuart, later Charles I, received it in 1616 after the death of his brother Henry Frederick in 1612. Edward, later Edward VIII, was invested at Caernarfon Castle in July 1911, the first such public investiture for centuries.
prince-rupert-of-the-rhine: Rupert was born in Prague in 1619, the third son of Frederick V of the Palatinate and Elizabeth Stuart, daughter of James VI and I. His father had just been elected king by the largely Protestant estates of Bohemia, a step the Catholic House of Habsburg saw as rebellion. After Frederick's defeat by Emperor Ferdinand II at the Battle of White Mountain in 1620, his parents were mockingly called the Winter King and Queen. The infant prince was nearly left behind in the flight from Prague until a courtier, Kryštof z Donína, tossed him into a carriage.

He grew up between the courts of The Hague and of his uncle Charles I. At fourteen he attended a Dutch pas d'armes, and he fought with Frederick Henry, Prince of Orange, at the siege of Rheinberg and in the campaign around Breda in 1637. He was later captured and imprisoned at Linz during the Thirty Years' War.

In August 1642 Rupert evaded the pro-Parliamentary navy, landed at Newcastle and joined the King at Leicester Abbey, where he was appointed General of Horse. By the end of September he had raised about 3,000 cavalry, and a charge at Powick Bridge, the first military engagement of the war, made him a hero to young Royalists. His practices drew criticism: he demanded two thousand pounds from Leicester as the price of not sacking it, conduct usual in Europe for which Charles reprimanded him. Quarrels with George Digby and the slighting of the Marquess of Hertford at Bristol undermined his position, and he was banished after surrendering Bristol.

He then served Louis XIV as a mareschal de camp, took the fortress of La Bassée in 1647 by negotiation and was shot in the head. In 1648 he joined the Royalist fleet under the Duke of York. After the Restoration he sat in the House of Lords as Duke of Cumberland, joined the Privy Council in 1662 and rose to command the Royal Navy in the Anglo-Dutch Wars. He also took up mezzotint, producing The Great Executioner in 1658, and after about 1674 experimented in a laboratory at Windsor Castle.

Rupert died of pleurisy at Spring Gardens, Westminster, on 29 November 1682 and was buried in Westminster Abbey in a state funeral. He left most of his estate equally to the actress Margaret Hughes and their daughter Ruperta. The historian Ian Gentles called him a famed warrior who won hardly any battles on land or sea, beloved by his men for his courage but bad tempered and a poor judge of character, and yet one of the most romantic figures in English history.
prince-shotoku: Prince Shōtoku was born, according to tradition, on 7 February 574. His own name was Prince Umayado, meaning prince of the stable door, because it is said that he was born in front of a stable. His father was Emperor Yōmei, and his mother was Princess Hashihito no Anahobe, Yōmei's younger half-sister. His parents were relatives of the ruling Soga clan, and he was involved in the defeat of the rival Mononobe clan. The main source for his life is the Nihon Shoki, and parts of his record are legend. The name Shōtoku first appears in the Kaifūsō, compiled in 751, more than a hundred years after his death.

According to tradition his aunt, Empress Suiko, appointed him regent in 593. He is said to have established a centralised government, and in 603 to have set up the Twelve Level Cap and Rank System at court. He is credited with promulgating the seventeen-article constitution. In 605 the Sui emperor sent a message addressed to the sovereign of Wa, and in 607 Shōtoku sponsored a mission led by Ono no Imoko, carrying a note from the sovereign of the land of the rising sun to the sovereign of the land of the setting sun. It contains the earliest known written use of a term meaning land of the rising sun for Japan.

He led a large national project to promote Buddhism and commissioned the temple of Shitennō-ji in Settsu Province, present-day Osaka, after his victory over the Mononobe. Documents at Hōryū-ji say that Suiko and Shōtoku founded it in 607, and excavations in 1939 confirmed that his palace, the Ikaruga no miya, stood in the eastern part of the present complex.

Shōtoku died on 8 April 622 and is said to have been buried at Shinaga in Kawachi Province. Tradition attributes to him the Sangyō Gisho, commentaries on the Lotus Sutra, the Vimalakirti Sutra and the Śrīmālādevī Sūtra. The first, the Hokke Gisho, is traditionally dated to 615 and regarded as the first Japanese text, which would make him the first known Japanese writer. Over successive generations a devotional cult arose around him for the protection of Japan, the imperial family and Buddhism, and religious figures such as Saichō and Shinran claimed inspiration or visions attributed to him. Legend says he could talk and walk at birth.
prince-vijaya: The Mahavamsa gives Vijaya a marvellous ancestry. His grandmother Suppadevi, daughter of the king of Vanga and a princess of Kalinga, was carried off by Sinha, the lion, whom some modern interpreters take to have been an outlaw living in the forest. Their son Sinhabahu escaped with his mother and sister, killed his father, founded the city of Sinhapura in the Lala country and married his sister Sinhasivali. Vijaya was the eldest of their thirty-two sons. Where Sinhapura lay is uncertain: it has been placed in Bengal, Odisha, Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh, among other places.

Made prince regent by his father, Vijaya became notorious with his followers for violent deeds, and prominent citizens demanded his death. Sinhabahu instead expelled them: their heads were half shaved and they were put on a ship, their wives and children being sent off on separate ships.

In the Mahavamsa's telling the kingdom was named Tambapanni, copper-red hands, because the red soil coloured the hands of Vijaya's men, and his people were called Sinhala after Sinhabahu. His ministers founded villages, among them Upatissagama. To be crowned he needed a queen of noble house, and the Pandya king of Madhura, identified with Madurai, sent his daughter with a hundred noble maidens, craftsmen and a thousand families of eighteen guilds, who landed at the port of Mahatittha.

Vijaya then sent Kuveni away, since his people feared supernatural beings. She went with their two children, Jivahatta and Disala, to the Yakkha city of Lankapura, where she was killed as a traitor. The children fled to Sumanakuta, and from them the chronicle derives the Pulinda, identified with the Vedda people. Vijaya, crowned, is said to have given up his evil ways and ruled in peace and justice.

Having no heir, Vijaya in old age sent for his twin brother Sumitta, but died before a reply came. His ministers governed for a year until Panduvasudeva, Sumitta's youngest son, arrived from Sinhapura to rule. The older Dipavamsa tells a similar story without Kuveni or the South Indian princess, and two other versions of the legend, one recorded by Xuanzang and one a Jataka painted at Ajanta, give the founding prince other names.

There is no archaeological evidence for the story. In Sri Lanka it is often treated as history and used in political argument: Sinhalese scholars such as K. M. de Silva have cited it for the Indo-Aryan origins of the Sinhalese, while Tamil authors such as Satchi Ponnambalam have dismissed it as fiction serving Sinhalese territorial claims.
princely-state: The princely states were the traditional monarchical states of India that had formed, under various degrees of pressure, subsidiary alliances with the East India Company. The British Raj took over these relationships after 1858. Some dynasties, especially those of Rajput princes, were long established, while others dated from the turbulent disintegration of the Mughal Empire in the 18th century. Some, mainly with Muslim ruling families, were of foreign origin: the rulers of Hyderabad were Turco-Persians and those of Bhopal Afghans. Only the Rajput states, Manipur and a scattering of South Indian kingdoms could trace their lineage to the period before the Mughal Empire.

India under the Raj consisted of British India and the princely states. By treaty the British controlled the external affairs of the states absolutely, while the states kept control of their internal affairs, subject to substantial British influence. Rulers bore titles such as Maharaja, Nawab, Nizam and Wadiyar, all of which the British translated as prince. Precedence was set by gun salutes of an odd number from three to 21; about 120 states were salute states, though more than 500 existed in all. The Chamber of Princes, established in 1920, gave the rulers a forum to voice their needs until 1947.

The doctrine of lapse, pursued most vigorously by the Governor-General the Marquess of Dalhousie, placed under Company control any state whose ruler died without a male biological heir. Dalhousie annexed seven states, among them Awadh, Nagpur, Jhansi and Satara. Resentment of these annexations contributed to the discontent behind the rebellion of 1857, and the doctrine ended with Company rule in 1858.

In 1920 the Indian National Congress asked the princes to establish responsible government. At independence on 15 August 1947, 565 princely states were officially recognised, covering 40% of the area of pre-independence India and 23% of its population. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and V. P. Menon persuaded the rulers of almost all of them to accede to India, and most others joined Pakistan. Hyderabad was annexed. Kalat declared independence and acceded to Pakistan on 27 March 1948, after which the Khan's brother revolted against the accession.
princes-stone: The stone is the reversed base of an Ionic column, which probably came from the nearby Roman city of Virunum, founded as the capital of the province of Noricum under Emperor Claudius (41-54). In the Middle Ages the coat of arms of the Duchy of Carinthia was carved on its upper surface. It stood north-west of the imperial palace of Karnburg on the Zollfeld plain, built by Emperor Arnulf of Carinthia, until 1862, when it was taken to the Landhaus of the provincial assembly in Klagenfurt.

After Carantania was absorbed into the Frankish Empire, the ceremony at the stone became the first part of the installation of the Dukes of Carinthia, followed by a mass at Maria Saal cathedral and the enthronement at the Duke's Chair, where the duke swore an oath in German and received the homage of the estates.

The peasant on the stone, speaking for the people in Slovene, asked who was coming forward, whether he was a just judge, freeborn and a defender of the Christian faith, and by what right he could take the seat. He was promised sixty denarii and a house free of tribute, gave the duke a light blow on the cheek and made way. The duke then mounted the stone with drawn sword and turned to face every direction while all sang the Slovenian Kyrie.

A seat used at the installation of Herman II of Sponheim in 1161 may have been the stone. About 1341 the chronicler John of Viktring described the rite at the accession of Meinhard II of Gorizia-Tyrol in 1286: the duke-to-be found a free peasant sitting on the stone, who would not give up his place until Meinhard had assured him that he was worthy and would rule justly.

Jean Bodin described the ceremony in 1576 as unrivalled in the world, though the Stone of Scone and the Lia Fáil were used in similar ways. Thomas Jefferson's initials appear beside the passage in his copy of Bodin, which gave rise to a myth that the rite inspired the United States Constitution; mainstream scholars dismiss the idea.

After Carinthia was divided following the First World War, the stone became shared and disputed heritage. Slovenia's decision in 2005 to show it on its 2-cent coin caused consternation in Austria, and in 2006 it was moved from the Carinthian State Museum, where it had been shown since 1905, to the Heraldic Hall of the Klagenfurt Landhaus.
princess-alice-of-the-united-kingdom: Alice Maud Mary was born at Buckingham Palace on 25 April 1843, the third child and second daughter of Queen Victoria and Prince Albert. Her sex was greeted with mixed feelings, and the Privy Council sent Albert a message of congratulation and condolence. Her education was devised by Albert's friend Baron Stockmar and included needlework, woodwork, French and German. She nursed her grandmother the Duchess of Kent in 1861, and when her father fell fatally ill in December 1861 she nursed him until his death, then spent six months as her mother's unofficial secretary. Her mother's search for a husband produced only two suitable princes, and Alice found neither acceptable.

Alice was engaged to Prince Louis of Hesse on 30 April 1861. Parliament granted her a dowry of 30,000 pounds, which Albert thought would not allow her to do great things in the little realm of Hesse. They married on 1 July 1862 in a private ceremony at Osborne House, which the Queen called more of a funeral than a wedding. Her life in Darmstadt was unhappy because of impoverishment, family tragedy and worsening relations with her husband and mother. She became friends with the theologian David Friedrich Strauss, whose views on the Bible she shared, which led Empress Augusta to call her a complete atheist.

Alice took an interest in nursing, especially the work of Florence Nightingale. When Hesse sided with Austria in the Austro-Prussian War of 1866, she managed field hospitals while heavily pregnant. Her Princess Alice Women's Guild took over much of the running of the state's military hospitals. She founded the Alice-Hospital in Darmstadt in 1869 and the Alice Society for Women's Training and Industry. Her husband became Grand Duke Louis IV in 1877, and she became grand duchess, with greater duties that strained her health.

Her youngest son Friedrich, who had haemophilia, died on 29 May 1873 after falling from a window, and Alice never recovered from the loss. In November 1878 diphtheria struck the Hessian court. She nursed her family for over a month before falling ill herself, and died on 14 December 1878, the first of Queen Victoria's nine children to die.

Her daughter Alix married Tsar Nicholas II and passed on the gene for haemophilia to the Tsarevich Alexei; Alix and her family were killed by the Bolsheviks at Ekaterinburg in 1918. Her daughter Elisabeth, who had married Grand Duke Sergei Alexandrovich, was killed the day after. Her grandson Louis Mountbatten was the last Viceroy of India. The Alice-Hospital continued to flourish long after her death.
princess-juliana-international-airport: The airport began as a United States military airstrip during World War II. The first commercial flight landed on 3 December 1943. In 1944 the future Queen Juliana of the Netherlands visited the island using the airfield, which was later named in her honour. It sits alongside Simpson Bay Lagoon on the Dutch side of Saint Martin, in the country of Sint Maarten.

As air travel and tourism grew, the airport was upgraded several times. In 1964 it was remodelled and relocated, with a new passenger terminal and control tower, and further improvements followed in 1985 and 2001. A three-phase masterplan of 1997 aimed to modernise it. Phase I, completed in 2001, widened and strengthened the runway, upgraded the taxiways and apron and renovated the old terminal.

The airport has a single asphalt runway, 2,300 metres long and 45 metres wide, designated 10/28. Its terminal was designed to handle 2.5 million passengers a year.
