Phase II of the masterplan brought a new radar facility and control tower, in service from 29 March 2004, and a new terminal that opened in 2006. The control tower and radar also give approach control to several nearby airports, including those on Anguilla, Saint Barthélemy, Saba and Sint Eustatius.

The airport is the island's main aviation gateway, serving both the Dutch and French sides of Saint Martin, and the main hub for the smaller Leeward Islands. The final approach to Runway 10 passes directly over Maho Beach, where aircraft cross the sand at low altitude. This approach has become a popular attraction for aviation enthusiasts, and warning signs are posted because of the jet blast from departing aircraft.

For decades KLM flew a Boeing 747 from Amsterdam to Sint Maarten, and its low approach over Maho Beach drew crowds. KLM replaced the 747 with an Airbus A330, and the last scheduled 747 flight arrived on 28 October 2016.

Hurricane Irma later tore much of the roof from the terminal. The airport served humanitarian and reconstruction flights, and commercial service resumed within weeks using temporary facilities. The terminal was later rebuilt.
princess-milica-of-serbia: Milica was the daughter of Prince Vratko Nemanjić, remembered in Serbian epic poetry as Jug Bogdan, a great-grandson of Vukan Nemanjić, Grand Prince of Serbia, of the elder collateral branch of the Nemanjić dynasty. She was a fourth cousin once removed of Dušan the Mighty, Emperor of Serbia. Her only brother, the župan Nikola, was buried in 1379 in the Monastery of St. Nicholas in Kuršumlija. Through her, the children of her marriage to Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović descended from the Nemanjić line.

She and Lazar had eight children. Of the daughters, Jelena married Đurađ II Balšić and later Sandalj Hranić Kosača, Mara married Vuk Branković, Dragana married Emperor Ivan Shishman of Bulgaria, and Olivera married Sultan Bayezid I after the Battle of Kosovo as a pledge of peace.

In November 1389, soon after Lazar's death, the Hungarians under Sigismund took a series of northern fortresses and reached as far south as Kragujevac; scholars disagree on how the fighting ended. Vuk Branković, who had accepted Lazar as his overlord, tried to overthrow Milica, and he and the Hungarians were close to an alliance. When the Ottomans reached her border in the summer of 1390, she accepted Ottoman suzerainty and allowed the Turks free passage. Some scholars believe her slander of Branković may have shaped the early accounts of his treachery at Kosovo.

She founded the Ljubostinja monastery around 1390 and took vows there around 1393 as the nun Eugenia (Jevgenija), later abbess Euphrosine. With Euphemia, the former Vasilissa of Serres, she travelled to Bayezid's court in 1398/99, and in 1403 she went to the sultan at Serres to argue for Stefan in a dispute between her sons and Branković.

She wrote prayers and religious poems, among them A Mother's Prayer, issued with her sons at the Dečani monastery in 1397, and a lament for her husband, My Widowhood's Bridegroom. She died on 11 November 1405, was buried at Ljubostinja and was canonised by the Serbian Orthodox Church.
princess-wencheng: Princess Wencheng belonged to a minor branch of the imperial clan of the Tang dynasty. Both Chinese and Tibetan sources agree that she was not a daughter of the Chinese emperor. In Tibet she is also called Gyasa, meaning Chinese wife. In 634 King Songtsen Gampo sent an envoy to Luoyang, and on hearing that the Turks and the Tuyuhun had marriage alliances with the Tang he proposed a marriage. The Tang refused, and the envoy told Songtsen that they had first accepted but that the Tuyuhun had changed their decision. Songtsen attacked the Tuyuhun and the Dangxiang.

Songtsen stationed large numbers of troops on the western border of Songzhou, in modern Sichuan, and demanded a princess in marriage or else he would lead 50,000 troops against it. In 638 the Tibetans attacked Songzhou and took two prefectures, but withdrew after Tang counterattacks. Tibetan sources claim victory, and Chinese sources claim it for the Tang. In 640 Songtsen made a new proposal, which the Tang accepted to prevent further attacks. In 641 Wencheng left for Tibet with Gar Tongtsen Yulsung and married Songtsen Gampo.

According to the Old Book of Tang, Songtsen received her at Bohai Lake and built a palace for her. She disliked the Tibetan custom of painting faces red, and he banned it. The Tang monk Xuanzhao, passing through Tibet, was warmly received by her. Tibetan histories say she found Tibet shaped like an indigenous demoness, Srinmo, lying on her back, and that temples were built to suppress her. She oversaw the building of the Ramoche Temple and, with Songtsen's wife from Nepal, helped him with national affairs and the growth of Buddhism.

Tibetan sources call her Rgya-Mo-Bzav, the goddess from the Central Empire, and hold her to be a manifestation of White Tara, as Songtsen's first wife, the Nepali princess Bhrikuti, is of Green Tara. Tradition says the seated statue of Sakyamuni she brought is enshrined in the Jokhang. A thangka she embroidered is kept at Tradruk Temple in Nêdong. Chinese classical literature treated her as an insignificant figure, while from about 1928 Republic of China nationalist writing made her a transmitter of technology. Since the 2000s the Chinese state has presented an opera about her in Lhasa, which many observers say misrepresents Tibetan history.
princeton-university: The institution began in Elizabeth, New Jersey, in 1746 as the College of New Jersey, one of the nine colonial colleges established before the American Revolution. Its formative years were shaped by the Log College, a seminary founded by the Reverend William Tennent at Neshaminy, Pennsylvania, in about 1726. No legal connection existed, but many of its pupils and adherents later supported the college; Princeton historians reject the older view that it was the college's predecessor.

After the death of President Jonathan Dickinson the college moved in 1747 to Newark, where the parsonage of his successor Aaron Burr Sr. stood. Governor Jonathan Belcher granted a second charter on 14 September 1748 after the first was disputed by Anglicans, and gave the college his library of 474 volumes.

Nassau Hall, begun in 1754 and finished in 1756, was the first seat of the New Jersey Legislature in 1776 and was involved in the Battle of Princeton in 1777. The Congress of the Confederation met there from 30 June to 4 November 1783. A fire gutted its interior in 1802, and a large student riot in 1807 led to the resignation of President Samuel Stanhope Smith.

Woodrow Wilson, an alumnus and professor, became the 13th president and introduced the preceptorial system in 1905, adding small-group teaching to lectures. In 1906 the university became nonsectarian. Wilson kept the college closed to Black students. The college had officially become a university in 1896. After 1945 it desegregated and expanded its research, and it explicitly prohibited the admission of women from its founding until 1969.

Undergraduates complete independent work, including a senior thesis, and first- and second-year students live in one of seven residential colleges. Customs include the Reunions parade of alumni, called the P-rade, and the belief that a student who leaves through the FitzRandolph Gates before graduating will not graduate. Alumni include the presidents James Madison and Woodrow Wilson and the vice presidents Aaron Burr, George M. Dallas and John Breckinridge. Albert Einstein, who belonged to the Institute for Advanced Study, lectured and visited often and became associated with the university.
principality-of-lucca-and-piombino: The principality joined two territories. The new Principality of Lucca covered the lands of the old republic, which France had occupied since late 1799. The Principality of Piombino had been occupied in 1804 and given by Napoleon to his sister Elisa in March 1805, with the title of Duchess of Portoferraio. From July 1805 the two were ruled as a single monarchy and a client state of Napoleonic France.

Elisa held the real power. Her husband, Felice Pasquale Baciocchi, was formally made Prince of Lucca at the request of the people, who hoped to keep at least a semblance of independence from France. In 1806 the lands of the former Duchy of Massa and Carrara and the former Este Garfagnana were added.

Napoleon himself wrote the constitution on 22 June 1805, setting up a Council of State to advise the prince and a legislative Senate. The French franc was the currency, and only a few local coins were struck. On 3 March 1809 Napoleon made Elisa Grand Duchess of Tuscany, ruling from Florence over a region annexed to the French Empire two years earlier from the former Kingdom of Etruria. Lucca and Piombino then became part of the grand duchy and so a territory of the French Empire, with a special status and a prefect, Antoine-Marie-Pierre de Hautmesnil, though never a French department.

In 1814 Austrian troops occupied Lucca, ending French rule as Napoleon fell. The Congress of Vienna gave Piombino to the Grand Duchy of Tuscany and Elba to the exiled Napoleon. Lucca became a state again as the Duchy of Lucca, granted to Maria Louisa, Infanta of Spain and former Queen of Etruria, in place of Parma, which went to Napoleon's wife, Marie-Louise. She accepted only after the Treaty of Paris of 1817 promised Parma to her son Charles Louis after Marie-Louise's death.
principality-of-regensburg: The principality was first created as an ecclesiastical electorate for Archbishop Karl Theodor von Dalberg, the Elector-Archchancellor of the Empire, after the French annexed Mainz, his former see, following the Treaty of Lunéville. Most of its land had belonged to the Prince-Bishopric of Regensburg. It also took in the lordships of Donaustauf, Wörth and Hohenburg, the former free imperial city, and St. Emmeram's Abbey with the abbeys of Obermünster and Niedermünster inside the city. Dalberg also held the new Principality of Aschaffenburg on the Main.

Because Dalberg took over the electoral dignity of Mainz, the state is known in German as the Kurfürstentum Regensburg, and because the archiepiscopal rank of Mainz passed to Regensburg, in English also as the Archbishopric of Regensburg. Bavarian claims on the city delayed his installation as archbishop until 1 February 1805. With the end of the Holy Roman Empire in 1806 the principality lost its electoral status and joined the Confederation of the Rhine, and the Napoleonic Code was introduced in 1809.

In the War of the Fifth Coalition Austrian troops occupied Regensburg on 20 April 1809, and three days later French troops shelled and stormed it. Under the Treaty of Paris Dalberg gave the city up to the Kingdom of Bavaria, which formally incorporated it on 22 May 1810.

In return Dalberg received Hanau and Fulda, which he joined with Aschaffenburg to form the Grand Duchy of Frankfurt. He kept the title of Archbishop of Regensburg until his death in 1817. After the Bavarian Concordat the see was reduced to a suffragan diocese of Munich and Freising.
principality-of-reuss-younger-line: The Principality of Reuss-Gera, officially called the Principality of Reuss Junior Line after 1848, was a sovereign state in what is now Germany, ruled by members of the House of Reuss. It was one of the successor states of the Imperial County of Reuss. The counts Reuss, with their capitals and residences at Gera, Schleiz, Lobenstein, Köstritz and Ebersdorf, were all raised to the rank of prince in 1806. Their successor branch heads shared that title, while the cadets were each styled prince as well, so that every male of the family was properly Prince Heinrich, with a Roman numeral, Reuss, J.L.

The territories of four separate branches of the Junior Line were amalgamated between 1824 and 1848. By then the senior branch of Gera held sovereignty, while the surviving cadet branches kept their rights of succession to the princely throne. In 1905 the principality had an area of 827 square kilometres (319 square miles) and a population of 145,000, with Gera as its capital. When the German Empire collapsed at the end of the First World War, the reigning prince lost his crown along with all the other monarchs of Germany. In 1919 the territory of the Junior Line merged with that of the Elder Line as the People's State of Reuss, which became part of the new state of Thuringia on 1 May 1920.

The House of Reuss followed a unique system of naming and numbering its men. Every male member bore the name Heinrich, followed by a Roman numeral. Most noble houses number only the ruling head, in the order of reigns, but the Junior Line gave a number to every male family member, beginning again with the first son born in each century. The sons within one family need not bear sequential numbers, since all kinsmen share the same sequence. The sons of Prince Heinrich LXVII Reuss of Schleiz, for example, were named Heinrich V, Heinrich VIII, Heinrich XI, Heinrich XIV and Heinrich XVI. As a result, some heads of the Junior Line carried the highest numbers of any European ruling family.

Marriage rules were strict. When Prince Heinrich XXVI Reuss married Countess Viktoria von Fürstenstein in 1885, their children were not allowed to bear the princely title and were called Counts of Plauen, though they stayed in the line of succession to the two Reuss thrones. The designation Junior Line was dropped in 1930.
principality-of-wales: Llywelyn ap Gruffudd began as one of several princes of Gwynedd Uwch Conwy, which Henry III of England had forced the brothers to share by the punitive treaty of 1247. After victory over his brothers in 1255 he reconquered the areas of Gwynedd that England held, and in 1257 large parts of mid-Wales from the Marcher Lords. He allied with Simon de Montfort against Henry III. By the Treaty of Montgomery in 1267 Llywelyn was granted the title Prince of Wales and the homage of lesser Welsh princes, in return for his own homage to the king and a fee of 24,000 marks in instalments.

Disputes with his brother Dafydd and with English lords led to renewed war with Edward I in 1276, and the Treaty of Aberconwy in 1277 confined Llywelyn to Gwynedd Uwch Conwy. He died in battle in 1282 in a revolt that Dafydd had begun. Dafydd took the title, resisted briefly, and was captured and executed in 1283. The Statute of Rhuddlan of 1284 "annexed and united" the principality to the English crown. From 7 February 1301 the crown's lands in north and west Wales were granted to Edward I's son Edward of Caernarfon, and thereafter they went to the heir apparent, with the title Prince of Wales.

Edward built a ring of stone castles, including Beaumaris, Caernarfon, Conwy and Harlech, and founded English boroughs beside them. English criminal law replaced Welsh, though Welsh law remained in civil cases. Madog ap Llywelyn rose in 1294–95 and Owain Lawgoch's supporters in 1372 to 1378. Owain Glyndŵr was crowned at Machynlleth in 1404 and was ultimately unsuccessful. The Laws in Wales Acts of 1535 and 1542 ended the principality as a legal entity.

The native principality took in about three-quarters of the area of modern Wales. By 1271 it had a population of about 200,000, as much as 10 per cent of it town-dwellers, and unfree slaves had long disappeared there. Lesser lords swore fealty to the prince directly, and the prince paid tribute to the king, with £11,500 paid between 1267 and 1272. Cattle were its main export, with flannel second, and it imported salt, wine, wheat, iron and weapons. After the conquest the royal lands were organised in shires, with North Wales administered from Caernarfon and West Wales from Carmarthen.
principate: The term comes from the position of princeps senatus, the most influential member of the Roman Senate in the Republic, which Sulla abolished and Augustus revived in 28 BCE. Princeps, meaning leading or first citizen, had applied to nobles who distinguished themselves in service to the Republic. After the Battle of Actium and the defeat of Antony and Cleopatra, Octavian gained power step by step while courting the Senate and the people and presenting himself as a restorer of the Republic.

On 13 January 27 BCE he made a show of returning power to the Senate. On 16 January the Senate gave him the title augustus and asked him to take command of the provinces again, which he accepted for ten years, and with them control of most of the legions.

Historians Werner Eck and Sarolta Takács trace the authority Augustus created to three sources: powers of office delegated by the Senate and people, his immense private fortune, and the patron-client relationships he built across the empire. Together these formed his auctoritas. After a second settlement in 23 BCE, when he gave up the consulship, he held a proconsular imperium greater than that of all other proconsuls throughout the empire and the power of a tribune for life, which let him convene the Senate and people and veto their actions. In 12 BCE he became pontifex maximus, a title that emperors kept until 476 CE.

The forms of oligarchic self-rule inherited from the Republic, under the motto of the Senate and People of Rome, masked the reality of autocratic rule. After the fall of the Julio-Claudian dynasty in 68 CE, Vespasian gave the position a legal basis in the lex quae dicitur de imperio Vespasiani, and the military role of the imperator gradually overshadowed the civilian ideal of the princeps.

The nineteenth-century German scholar Theodor Mommsen proposed the periodisation of Principate and Dominate. He saw the Principate as a constitutional system, a diarchy in which power was shared between the princeps and the Senate, that broke down in the third century under Diocletian. Since the early twentieth century scholars have increasingly rejected this view.

Historians following Ronald Syme regard the Principate as a variant of monarchy, and they no longer find diarchy a useful concept. Jochen Bleicken considers the scheme unsuitable because its legal basis is flawed and it suggests that the earlier imperial period was freer. The term is nonetheless still used for the first phase of the Roman Empire, from Augustus to the end of the Crisis of the Third Century.
principia-mathematica-newton: In January 1684 Edmond Halley, Christopher Wren and Robert Hooke discussed the inverse-square law. Hooke claimed to have derived it and all the laws of planetary motion but produced no derivation, and Halley, who could derive the law only for the circular case, resolved to ask Isaac Newton. The first book was presented to the Royal Society at the close of April 1686. Hooke made priority claims, and Newton, who hated disputes, threatened to suppress the third book; Halley tactfully persuaded him to go on. The Society had just spent its book budget, so Halley paid for the publication himself, and the book appeared in summer 1687.

The Principia is written in Latin in three books. Book 1, De motu corporum, concerns motion without a resisting medium and begins with lemmas on the method of first and last ratios, a geometrical form of infinitesimal calculus. Book 2 largely concerns motion through resisting mediums, and Newton was a pioneer of fluid mechanics there. Book 3, De mundi systemate, applies universal gravitation to the Solar System. It shows by stages that the inverse-square law holds for the satellites of Jupiter and then for all bodies, treats the irregularities of the Moon's motion and the motion of comets, offers the first theory of the precession of the equinoxes and estimates the share of the Sun and Moon in the tides.

Newton published two further editions: in 1713, edited by Roger Cotes for Richard Bentley, and in 1726, under Henry Pemberton. The later editions added four Rules of Reasoning in Philosophy and a General Scholium. Andrew Motte made the first English translation in 1729. Alexis Clairaut wrote in 1747 that the book marked the epoch of a great revolution in physics, and Joseph-Louis Lagrange and Pierre-Simon Laplace gave it extreme praise. It is generally considered one of the most important works in the history of science. A picture of a page of the book was carried by the Voyager spacecraft in 1977.
printing-press: A printing press applies pressure to transfer ink onto paper, cloth or a similar surface. Johannes Gutenberg, a German goldsmith, invented the movable-type press around 1440 by combining four existing technologies: the screw press, movable type, the codex book and mechanised paper production. The Chinese artisan Bi Sheng made the first movable type in the 11th century, in baked clay, and the oldest surviving book with metal movable type is the Jikji of 1377, from the Korean state of Goryeo. None of these East Asian methods spread widely, because a Chinese text needed thousands of characters, whereas Gutenberg's press used the Latin alphabet with a small set. Gutenberg added a hand mold for casting type and an oil-based ink suited to metal type.

A compositor set individual metal letters into lines, which were arranged in a frame called a galley and then in a forme resting on the bed. The type was inked with leather pads called ink balls, a dampened sheet was laid over it, and a long lever, the bar, drove a screw that pressed the platen onto the paper. All of this was done by hand, and the basic design of the wooden handpress stayed largely the same for over three centuries. Lord Stanhope built an iron press by 1800 that printed a sheet in one pull. In 1814 The Times began printing on steam-driven presses built by Friedrich Koenig.

By the end of the 15th century around 270 European cities had printers, and by 1500 presses in Western Europe had produced over 20 million copies. Between 1518 and 1520 printers in Germany distributed 300,000 copies of Martin Luther's works. The press spread rapidly because it was portable and printers could move to a neighbouring city when one authority tried to curb them. Jesuit missionaries set up a press at Goa in 1556, and Juan Pablos set one up in Mexico City in 1539.

The historian Elizabeth Eisenstein described the press as an agent of change. Books became cheaper, authors came to be more closely associated with their works, and books increasingly appeared in vernacular languages rather than Latin. Church and secular authorities introduced licensing and banned books, with limited success. The press is now generally treated as one of several causes of the Reformation rather than the only one.
pripet-marshes: The Pripet Marshes, also called the Pripyat, Pinsk, Polesie or Rokitno Marshes, lie in Polesia along the forested basin of the Pripyat River and its tributaries, between Brest in the west, Mogilev in the northeast and Kyiv in the southeast. Most of the region is in Belarus and part is in Ukraine. They cover roughly 269,400 square kilometres and extend about 480 kilometres from west to east and 225 kilometres from north to south. The marshes change greatly in size through the year, since melting snow in spring and autumn rain cause extensive flooding as the river overflows.

Dense woods are interspersed with marshes, moors, ponds and streams. Open sedge and reed spaces alternate with almost impenetrable shrub thickets, and on dry islands there are deciduous or pine forests. In the spring flood the swamps are almost completely covered with water, and local people often cross them by boat. The region has 827 species of vascular plants and 246 recorded bird species, and it is a wintering area for migratory birds that nest in Scandinavia, Finland, the Baltic states and Russia.

For most of the year the marshes were virtually impassable to large military forces, which shaped strategic planning in the region. Like most other wetlands in Europe, they were once regarded as unhealthy and a source of sickness. Drainage of the eastern part began in 1872, and by the late 19th century it had destroyed 1.5 million hectares of wetland for pasture and farmland.

At the start of the First World War the marshes separated the Austro-Hungarian Fourth Army from the XII corps. The Third Army Corps of the Imperial Russian Army entered the gap before the Second Army's transfer from Serbia was complete, and the Russians soon captured the railhead at Lemberg, capital of Austrian Galicia. The wetlands remained one of the principal obstacles on the Eastern Front for the rest of the war.

In the Second World War they divided the central and southern theatres and sheltered Soviet and Polish partisans. German armies invading the Soviet Union skirted them to the north or south, and German troops dreaded them. In 1942 about 1,000 Jews escaped from the Łachwa Ghetto after an uprising, and about 600 of them found refuge in the marshes. The German administration planned the Pripet Plan, led by Konrad Meyer, to drain the marshes, remove their inhabitants and settle German colonists, but Hitler cancelled it late in 1941, fearing Dust Bowl conditions. A plan to drain the wetlands was also made in 1952 under Soviet administration.

The Pripet Marshes are the largest wetland area in Europe. The Chernobyl exclusion zone lies about 356 kilometres east-southeast of their geographic centre, and the town of Pripyat is not to be confused with the marshes.
priscillian: Priscillian was born around 340 into the nobility, possibly in Gallaecia in north-western Hispania, and was well educated. About 370 he began a movement in favour of asceticism. He urged the study not only of the Bible but of apocryphal books, which he valued as helpful in telling truth from error rather than as inspired. His eloquence and severely ascetic example won over bishops, among them Instantius and Salvianus. He taught that the perfect in body, mind and spirit were celibate or, if married, continent, while holding out hope of pardon to those who could not reach full perfection.

Bishops opposed to him, notably Hyginus of Corduba and Hydatius of Augusta Emerita, accused his teachings of being gnostic. A synod at Caesaraugusta in 380 condemned practices such as eating the Eucharist at home instead of in church, women praying alongside men, fasting on Sundays and withdrawing to the mountains during Lent; it did not name Priscillian. He was then elected bishop of Ávila and consecrated by Instantius and Salvianus. His rival Ithacius of Ossonoba obtained an edict from the emperor Gratian against false bishops and Manichees, and Priscillian went to Rome to plead his case, but neither Pope Damasus I nor Ambrose of Milan received him. Through the magister officiorum Macedonius the edict was withdrawn, and he returned to his see.

In 383 Magnus Maximus rebelled against Gratian, who was assassinated, and Maximus made Augusta Treverorum his residence. There Ithacius brought his case. Priscillian was tried by a secular court on charges that included sorcery, a capital offence, was made to confess to obscene doctrines and nocturnal meetings, and was executed by the sword around 385 with five companions. Maximus is also said to have wished to enrich his treasury from the confiscated property of the condemned.

The execution is seen as the first case of secular justice intervening in a church matter and the first killing of a Christian by other Christians for heresy. Pope Siricius, Ambrose and Martin of Tours protested, largely on the ground that a civil court should not decide an ecclesiastical case. Priscillian was honoured as a martyr, especially in Gallaecia, and Priscillianism lasted in Hispania and Gaul until the second half of the 6th century; the second synod of Bracara Augusta condemned it again in 563.

His writings were thought lost until Georg Schepss found eleven tracts at the University of Würzburg in 1885; four of them describing the trial appear to be by a close follower. It is hard to separate what Priscillian himself taught from what his enemies, and later groups called Priscillianist, ascribed to him.
priscus: Priscus of Panium was born in Panion, in Thrace, between 410 and 420, and wrote in Greek as a historian and rhetorician. After his journey to the court of Attila he spent an interlude in Rome and then travelled to Alexandria and the Thebaid in Egypt. About 456 he appears for the last time in the East, attached to the staff of Euphemios, the magister officiorum of Emperor Marcian. He died after 472.

He accompanied Maximinus, the head of the embassy sent by Emperor Theodosius II to Attila. At the Hunnic court he met a Greek merchant dressed in Hunnic fashion, who had been taken when Viminacium on the Danube was sacked about 441 or 442. The man had been the slave of the Hunnic nobleman Onegesius, had won his freedom and had chosen to settle among the Huns. Priscus debated with him the quality of life and justice in the Byzantine Empire and in the barbarian kingdoms.

He also described a dinner at one of Attila's houses, built of decorative polished wood with no thought of defence. He brought gifts for Attila's wife, Kreka, who had three sons. The Roman embassy was seated at the end of the table farthest from Attila, who sat on the middle couch with his honoured chiefs on his right. The food came on silver and gold plates, yet Attila used only a wooden cup and dressed plainly. When evening came, torches were lit and songs of his victories were sung.

The mission itself failed. Unknown to Priscus's party, it served as a respectable front while Constantinople tried to bribe one of Attila's advisers to assassinate him. Attila learned of the plot, and it shaped how he dealt with the ambassadors.

Priscus wrote an eight-volume history in Greek, known as the History of Byzantium, though that was probably not its original title. It probably ran from the accession of Attila to the accession of Emperor Zeno, from 433 to 474, but survives only in fragments. Byzantine writers used it heavily, among them Evagrius Scholasticus, Cassiodorus, Jordanes and the author of the Souda, and it was excerpted in the Excerpta de Legationibus of Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus (r. 913-959).

His style is straightforward, and his work is regarded as a reliable contemporary account of Attila, his court and the reception of the Roman ambassadors. He is counted among the classicizing historians: although he wrote in the Christian era, his work is almost completely secular and follows an historiographical tradition reaching back to the fifth century BCE.
pristina: Pristina lies on an alluvial plain in the regions of Llap and Kosovo, across the Gollak Hills in central and eastern Kosovo. The area has been inhabited since the Neolithic, and the earliest recognised traces were found at Gračanica, Matiçan and Ulpiana. In antiquity it belonged to the Dardanian Kingdom, and the nearby settlement of Ulpiana represents the heritage of the classical era. The origin of the city's name is unknown; Eric P. Hamp connected it with an Indo-European word for a ford and a word cognate with English stone.

After the division of the Roman Empire the area stayed within the Byzantine Empire between the 5th and 9th centuries. It was ceded to the First Bulgarian Empire in the middle of the 9th century, fell again to the Byzantine Empire in the early 11th century, when it was part of a theme called Bulgaria, and passed several times to the Second Bulgarian Empire. The Kingdom, later Empire, of Serbia held it through the 13th and 14th centuries. King Stefan Milutin founded the nearby Gračanica monastery in 1315, and Pristina is first recorded in 1342, as a village, in the reign of Stefan Dušan.

In 1455 it had a small population of 300 households. In the following century it became an important mining and trading centre because of its position near Novo Brdo, known for its trade fairs and for goatskin, goat hair and gunpowder. During the Austro-Turkish War of the late 17th century, townspeople under the Catholic Albanian priest Pjetër Bogdani pledged loyalty to the Austrian army, and he supplied a force of 6,000 Albanian soldiers. According to Noel Malcolm the town then had a majority of about 15,000 Muslims, probably Albanian.

Albanians pillaged and partly burned Pristina in May 1901. Serb forces took it on 22 October 1912, and Bulgaria occupied it in 1915. In 1948 it was chosen as the capital of the province of SAP Kosovo within Yugoslavia, and it remained the capital after Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008.

Pristina is the capital and largest city of Kosovo, with 227,466 residents at the census of 2024, most of them Albanians. It holds the Parliament, the courts and the residences of the president and prime minister. The University of Pristina, founded in the 20th century, is the largest and oldest in the city, and the National Theatre of Kosovo dates from 1946. Of 426 protected monuments in Kosovo, 21 are in Pristina, many of them from the Byzantine and Ottoman periods.
prithvi-narayan-shah: Prithvi Narayan Shah was born on 7 January 1723 in the Gorkha Palace, the first child of Nara Bhupal Shah and Kaushalyavati Devi. His education began at the age of five under the Brahmin astrologers Mokchyeshwor Aryal and Bhanu Aryal, and Queen Chandra Pravawati shaped his character. In 1737 he was married to Indra Kumari Devi, daughter of Hemkarna Sen of Makwanpur. He succeeded his father at the age of 20. Before his campaigns the country held 54 small states, the Baisi and Chaubise Rajya among them, and Gorkha was a minor regional power. He travelled incognito to Varanasi to learn about India, and his father-in-law Abhiman Singh obtained firearms and ammunition for him there.

His first attack on Nuwakot, in 1743, failed. Nuwakot lay between Gorkha and Kathmandu and was a gateway to the trade with Tibet. After making neutral alliances with Lamjung, Tanahun and Palpa he attacked from three directions, and its army was routed in 1744. He was defeated at Kirtipur in 1757, losing his commander and prime minister Kalu Pande, and took it only on a third attempt, in 1765. Chaukot fell after a blockade and a battle in which the Gorkhalis lost 332 men. He conquered Makwanpur, which brought a clash with Mir Qasim, the Nawab of Bengal, whose army under Gurgin Khan was ambushed and destroyed.

Shah then encircled the Kathmandu Valley with an economic blockade and occupied the Kuti Pass, halting trade with Tibet. Jaya Prakash Malla of Kathmandu appealed to the East India Company, which sent Captain George Kinloch in 1767. Floods, hunger and Gorkhali attacks ruined the expedition. Shah entered Kathmandu unopposed on 25 September 1768, during the Indra Jatra festival, and by the end of that year had reduced the cities still holding out. He allowed the old king Ranjit Malla of Bhadgaon safe passage to Benaras. He founded the Nepal Army in August 1762 with five permanent companies.

Shah died at Devighat, Nuwakot, in January 1775 on his birthday. His eldest son, Pratap Singh Shah, succeeded him, while Regent Bahadur Shah and Queen Rajendra Laxmi pushed the unification west and east. Late in life he gave instructions at Nuwakot that were compiled as the Divyopadesh, which describes Nepal as a yam between two boulders, the Qing dynasty and the British in India. It also urged economic self-reliance and a boycott of imported cloth. He expelled the Capuchin missionaries and called his realm the true land of the Hindus. Prithvi Jayanti marks his birth, and a highway and a campus in Pokhara bear his name.
prithviraj-chauhan: Few inscriptions survive from Prithviraj's reign, and none was issued by the king himself. Much of what is known comes from medieval chronicles that are not entirely reliable. Prithviraja Vijaya is the only surviving literary text from his reign, while Prithviraj Raso, which popularised him as a great king, contains many exaggerated accounts. Prithviraj was the son of the Chahamana king Someshvara and Karpuradevi, a Kalachuri princess, and was born in Gujarat. The year 1166 was calculated by Dasharatha Sharma from the astrological positions given in Prithviraja Vijaya. When Someshvara died in 1177, Prithviraj was about eleven years old and ascended the throne with his mother as regent, assisted by a council and the chief minister Kadambavasa.

His first military success was the suppression of a revolt by his cousin Nagarjuna and the recapture of Gudapura, possibly modern Gurgaon. Madanpur inscriptions of 1182 claim that he laid waste Jejakabhukti, the Chandela kingdom of Paramardi. Before 1187 he made peace with Bhima II, the Chaulukya king of Gujarat. The Prithviraj Raso tells that he eloped with Samyogita, daughter of the Gahadavala king Jayachandra, but no other source supports this, and the Gahadavala records are silent.

Muhammad of Ghor had captured Multan in 1175 and was defeated by the Chaulukyas in Gujarat in 1178. He then conquered Peshawar, Sindh and Punjab and moved his base to Punjab, which brought him into conflict with Prithviraj. Leading a coalition of Rajput kings, Prithviraj defeated the Ghurid army near Taraori in 1191. In 1192 Muhammad returned with an army of Turkish mounted archers and defeated the Rajput army on the same battlefield.

Most medieval sources say Prithviraj was taken to Ajmer, where Muhammad planned to keep him as a Ghurid vassal, and was later killed for rebelling. Accounts of his end differ: Hasan Nizami says he was caught conspiring and beheaded, while the Hammira Mahakavya says he refused food and died in captivity. Muhammad installed the Chahamana prince Govindaraja at Ajmer.

Later portrayals differ. Jain stories of the 14th and 15th centuries, such as the Prabandha-Chintamani, present him as an inept king responsible for his own downfall, whereas the Prithviraj Raso, patronised largely by Rajput courts, makes him a great hero. The defeat at Tarain is seen as a landmark in the Islamic conquest of India, and the Ghurid victory was presented as a milestone leading to the Delhi Sultanate.
privilegium-maius: The House of Habsburg had ruled the Duchy of Austria since 1282, but the Golden Bull of 1356, issued by Emperor Charles IV, left the Duke of Austria out of the seven prince-electors who chose the king. Rudolf IV sought to raise the standing of his house and its lands: as Charles IV had made Prague the centre of his rule, Rudolf did the same for Vienna, granting it privileges, launching building projects and founding the University of Vienna. In the winter of 1358/1359 he ordered the forgery, a modified and expanded version of the Privilegium minus with which Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa had made Austria a duchy in 1156.

The Privilegium Maius was the main document of a set of five forged charters, some purporting to come from Julius Caesar and Nero to the Roman province of Noricum, others from later rulers, among them charters dated 1058, 1228, 1245 and 1283. It claimed for the dukes the inseparability of their territory, inheritance by the first-born, their own jurisdiction and legislation without appeal to the emperor, and the right to display certain symbols of rule. It also mentioned, once and as an honorary designation, a newly coined title of Palatine Archdukes ranking with the electors, which became the basis of the title Archduke of Austria. The original Privilegium minus was lost at about the same time.

Charles IV refused to confirm the document, though he accepted some of its claims, and the poet and scholar Petrarch, his adviser, identified it as a forgery. The first Habsburg to use the title of archduke was Ernest of Iron, ruler of Inner Austria from 1406 to 1424, and from the 15th century all Habsburg princes were styled archdukes. Frederick III's confirmation of 1453 made the document imperial law, and he added the power of ennoblement for his family as hereditary rulers of Austria, a right normally reserved to the emperor.

Over time the Austrian archdukes took an almost royal position and displayed it with special insignia, and the House of Habsburg and Austria came to be seen as a single unit. The family published editions of the documents and forbade discussion of their authenticity. The privilege lost its meaning with the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire in 1806, and in 1852 the historian Wilhelm Wattenbach proved it a forgery.
privilegium-minus: The deed belongs to the conflict between the House of Hohenstaufen and the House of Welf. In 1138 King Conrad III of Germany deposed the Bavarian duke Henry the Proud and gave Bavaria to the Austrian margrave Henry Jasomirgott. Conrad's nephew Frederick, elected King of the Romans in 1152, probably with the support of his cousin Henry the Lion, son of Henry the Proud, wanted the quarrel ended before his campaign to Rome, where he was crowned emperor on 18 June 1155.

After a secret meeting near Regensburg on 5 June 1156, a diet at Regensburg on 8 September saw Henry Jasomirgott renounce Bavaria, which passed to Henry the Lion. To make up for the loss, Austria was raised to a duchy with the consent of the princes, led by Duke Vladislaus II of Bohemia. The deed was issued on 17 September 1156.

Austria was given to the House of Babenberg as an inheritable fief, and inheritance was also possible through the female line. If the duke had no children he could designate a successor, the libertas affectandi, though this right was bound for life to Henry Jasomirgott and his wife Theodora Komnene, who were childless. The duke had to attend the Imperial Diet only when it met in Bavaria, and owed the emperor troops only for wars in lands near Austria.

Its name sets it apart from the Privilegium Maius, a 14th-century forgery made for the Habsburg duke Rudolf IV of Austria. When the last male Babenberg, Frederick II, Duke of Austria, died in 1246, the female line gave rise to rival claims: those of Gertrude of Babenberg and her husbands, and that of King Ottokar II of Bohemia, husband of Margaret of Babenberg, who held the duchies until Rudolf I of Germany deposed him in 1276. The Pragmatic Sanction of 1713 drew in part on its provisions, and 1156 is sometimes given as the date of Austria's independence from Bavaria.
prizren: Prizren lies on the banks of the Prizren River in the foothills of the Šar Mountains in southern Kosovo, and its municipality borders Albania and North Macedonia. Excavations in the Prizren Fortress show that the site was inhabited from the Middle Bronze Age, around 2000 BCE, to the late Iron Age. The city has traditionally been identified with Theranda in Roman Dardania, although recent research suggests that Theranda may have stood at present-day Suva Reka. The fort was rebuilt under the Eastern Roman emperor Justinian.

The present town is first mentioned in 1019, in the time of Basil II, as Prisdriana. Byzantine rule ended there when the Serbian Nemanjić dynasty took the fort and the town, and in 1219 Prizren's church separated from the Patriarchate of Constantinople. The old town grew below the fortress, where Ragusan traders were based. Stefan Dušan founded the Monastery of the Holy Archangels and was buried in it; the city briefly served as capital of the Serbian Empire under him.

From 1371 regional feudal rulers held it, among them the Mrnjavčević, Balšić and Branković families. The Ottomans took Prizren on 21 June 1455 and made it the capital of the Sanjak of Prizren, later part of Rumelia Eyalet and a larger city of the Kosovo vilayet. The League of Prizren was created there in 1878 to seek the national unification and autonomy of Albanians within the Ottoman Empire.

Serbian forces captured the city in the First Balkan War in 1912, and it passed into the Kingdom of Serbia. The takeover was bloody, with 400 people dead in the first few days, and reports later emerged of widespread killings of Albanians. In 1946 it became part of the Autonomous Region of Kosovo and Metohija within the People's Republic of Serbia.

Prizren is the second most populous city and municipality of Kosovo, and the constitution designates it the country's historical capital. Albanian, Bosnian and Turkish are used as official languages of the municipality, as well as the two official languages of Kosovo. It is regarded as the most culturally and ethnically varied city in Kosovo, with Albanian, Bosniak, Turkish and Romani communities.

The city is known for its heritage of mosques, churches and old buildings, among them the Sinan Pasha Mosque, the Monastery of the Holy Archangels and Our Lady of Ljeviš, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Dokufest film festival is held there.
probus-emperor: Probus was born in Sirmium in Pannonia Inferior, the son of Dalmatius. The Historia Augusta gives his father's name as Maximus and says his personal wealth was modest. He entered the army around the age of 25 and rose rapidly. The emperor Valerian appointed him a military tribune at a very young age, and he justified the choice with a victory over the Sarmatians on the Illyrian frontier.

He became one of Aurelian's highest-placed lieutenants and reconquered Egypt from Zenobia in 273. In 275 Tacitus made him supreme chief of the east with extraordinary powers, and after Tacitus died in 276 the troops in Asia Minor elected Probus emperor in his camp.

Florian, the half-brother of Tacitus, had also proclaimed himself emperor, but he was killed by his own soldiers after an indecisive campaign against Probus in Cilicia. Probus referred his claim to the Senate in a respectful dispatch, and it ratified it. In 277 he defeated the Goths on the lower Danube. In 278 he campaigned in Gaul against the Alemanni and Lugii, while his generals cleared the province of Frankish and Burgundian raiders. He then crossed the Rhine, repaired the fortifications of Hadrian between the Rhine and Danube, and accepted the submission of nine major tribes, which pledged recruits for his army.

By demanding a tribute of manpower he set a precedent for bringing foreign soldiers into the empire as auxiliaries on a large scale. In peacetime he set soldiers to useful works, such as planting vineyards in Gaul and Pannonia. In 280 and 281 he put down three usurpers, Julius Saturninus, Proculus and Bonosus, and in the winter of 281 he held a triumph in Rome. He left Rome in 282 to prepare a campaign against Persia.

Accounts of his death differ. According to Joannes Zonaras, the commander of the Praetorian Guard, Marcus Aurelius Carus, was proclaimed emperor by his troops; troops Probus sent against him changed sides, and his remaining soldiers killed him at Sirmium in September or October 282. Other sources say soldiers who objected to civic work such as draining marshes rebelled against him. Carus became emperor and had the killers put to death.

Edward Gibbon, drawing largely on the Historia Augusta, treated Probus as the last of the benevolent constitutional emperors of Rome. His successor Carus did not seek the Senate's confirmation of his title, and Diocletian later undermined its authority. Probus's victories continued the line of soldier emperors from Illyria begun by Claudius Gothicus.
proclamation-of-the-german-empire: Whether a united Germany would include Austria had divided the German states since the Napoleonic Wars. Otto von Bismarck, the Prussian minister president, held that unity was possible only without the Habsburg monarchy. The Austro-Prussian War of 1866 dissolved the German Confederation of 1815, and after the victory at the Battle of Königgrätz Bismarck formed the North German Confederation without Austria, which adopted a constitution and became a state a year later.

The candidacy of Prince Leopold of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen for the Spanish throne, backed by Bismarck, led France to threaten war. Although the candidacy was withdrawn, Napoleon III sent his ambassador Vincent Benedetti to Bad Ems to demand that King Wilhelm I renounce any future claim, which Wilhelm refused. France declared war on Prussia on 19 July 1870, and the southern German states joined Prussia under their defensive alliances.

Victories in August and September 1870 made the southern princes willing to join the North German Confederation. By the November Treaties, Baden, Hesse-Darmstadt, Württemberg and Bavaria entered it on 1 January 1871, when a new constitution renamed the country the German Reich. On 9 and 10 December 1870 the Reichstag had voted to offer the imperial title to the Prussian king. The date of 18 January recalled the coronation of Elector Frederick III of Brandenburg as Frederick I of Prussia in 1701.

German troops paraded round the palace while Paris was under siege. In the Hall of Mirrors, whose ceiling glorified Louis XIV as a conqueror of German cities, regimental delegations raised their battle-torn banners. A service at a field altar ended with the hymn Nun danket alle Gott. Bismarck read out the proclamation, and Frederick I, Grand Duke of Baden, Wilhelm's son-in-law, called out "His Majesty, Kaiser Wilhelm", avoiding the constitutional title German Emperor, which Wilhelm would not accept.

Several rulers, among them those of the Grand Duchy of Hesse, the Duchy of Brunswick and Lippe, were not represented. The accounts of Wilhelm, Bismarck and the historian Albert von Pfister, present as a soldier, agree that a field altar stood in place of a throne, though they stress different aspects of the ceremony. These contemporary reports are considered more authentic than later portrayals, notably those in schoolbooks between 1918 and 1945, which were shaped by the defeat of the empire in the First World War. The founding day of 18 January became a day of celebration.
proclamation-of-the-peoples-republic-of-: The Chinese Civil War between the Nationalist government and the Chinese Communist Party was fought intermittently from 1927. The party had earlier proclaimed a state of their own, the Chinese Soviet Republic, at Ruijin on 7 November 1931, within the scattered territories they held; its government moved north to Yan'an during the Long March, and it was abolished in 1937. Hostilities paused from 1937 to 1945 while the Second United Front fought the Japanese invasion, and in the final phase, from 1945 to 1949, the party gained the upper hand.

Mao Zedong at first suggested keeping the name Republic of China under new leadership, but the overseas Chinese entrepreneur Tan Kah Kee objected and urged a clean break, and the committee accepted Zhang Xiruo's proposal of People's Republic of China. On 21 September 1949 Mao announced the new state in a speech to the first plenary session of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference.

At 15:00 Beijing Time on 1 October, Mao spoke from the top of the Tiananmen Gate. His proclamation said that the conference had enacted the organic law of the Central People's Government, elected him its chairman, with Zhu De, Liu Shaoqi, Song Qingling, Li Jishen, Zhang Lan and Gao Gang as vice chairmen, and chosen Beijing as the capital. The government council adopted the Common Program as its policy, named Zhou Enlai premier and foreign minister and Zhu De commander-in-chief of the People's Liberation Army, and declared itself the sole legal government of all the people.

The parade that followed, commanded by Nie Rongzhen and inspected by Zhu De, involved around 16,000 officers and personnel; no earlier Chinese government had held a public review of troops. Liu Bocheng, who had watched a parade on Red Square in Moscow, proposed the Soviet format.

The Soviet Union recognised the new state on 2 October 1949, the first country to do so, and other communist states followed, among them Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary, North Korea, Poland and Mongolia. Many Western countries, the United States among them, continued to recognise the Republic of China on Taiwan, and both governments claimed to be the legitimate government of all China. Chiang Kai-shek called the new government a puppet regime of the Soviet Union. The People's Republic moved quickly to consolidate its power and nationalise industries, and 1 October became its National Day.
proclamation-of-the-republic-brazil: After the Paraguayan War parts of the elite turned against the monarchy. Pedro II had no sons, and many feared that his heir, Isabel, Princess Imperial of Brazil, would leave the country in practice to her French husband, Prince Gaston, Count of Eu. The arrest of two bishops in the 1870s, after they followed Pope Pius IX against the Freemasons, strained relations with the Catholic Church. Officers resented civilian control and slow promotion, and the positivism of Auguste Comte spread through the military schools. A Republican Manifesto of 1870 and the Itu Convention of 1873 gave republicans a programme.

The Golden Law of 1888, signed by Isabel as regent, abolished slavery without compensation, and many former slaveholders joined the republican cause as revenge. The Viscount of Ouro Preto, head of the last imperial cabinet from 7 June 1889, proposed reforms to save the monarchy, but conservative deputies vetoed them.

The coup, planned for 20 November, was brought forward after a rumour on 14 November that Benjamin Constant Botelho de Magalhães and Deodoro da Fonseca had been arrested. At dawn on 15 November Deodoro, who was ill, led a few hundred soldiers in Rio de Janeiro, apparently intending only to remove Ouro Preto; he was moved further by word that his old rival Gaspar da Silveira Martins would head the next cabinet.

General Floriano Peixoto refused Ouro Preto's order to resist, saying that in Paraguay they had faced enemies but here all were Brazilians, and the cabinet was deposed. The only man wounded was the Baron of Ladario, Minister of the Navy. That evening José do Patrocínio drafted the proclamation of the Republic of the United States of Brazil.

The next day Major Frederico Solon de Sampaio Ribeiro ordered the imperial family to leave for Europe; it was allowed back only in 1920 by President Epitácio Pessoa. A provisional government under Deodoro abolished the life-term Senate and the Council of State and dissolved the Chamber of Deputies. Monarchist risings followed and were put down: in January 1890 an attempt by several regiments left more than 100 casualties, and 21 participants were executed. The Federalist Revolution of 1893 to 1895 cost about 10,000 lives, and the War of Canudos ended in 1897 when the army overran the settlement and killed nearly all its inhabitants.
proconsul: The Latin word prōconsul is a shortened form of prō consule, meaning one acting on behalf of the consul, and it appears on inscriptions from 135 BCE. The office was created to deal with a constitutional peculiarity of the Roman Republic: only a consul could command an army, but two consuls served at a time, each for one year, and could not normally serve two terms running. If a campaign was under way when a consul's term ended, his command could be prorogued, which kept continuity.

Ancient historians describe Quintus Publilius Philo as the first proconsul. His army was besieging Neapolis when his consulship expired, and the people voted that he should conduct the campaign in place of a consul.

A proconsul held full consular authority outside Rome, though Cicero noted that he lacked the right to take the auspices. Proconsulships were in practice often treated as extensions of a consul's term. Two proconsuls of the Republic had never been consul: Scipio Africanus, made proconsul by vote of the Popular Assembly to lead the expedition against the Carthaginians in Spain, and Lucius Manlius Acidinus.

As Rome annexed territory, proconsuls and propraetors became its provincial governors, assigned the provinces by lot, the proconsuls those with the most troops. Sulla made the governorships annual in 81 BCE and required a governor to leave the province within thirty days of his successor's arrival. In 67 BCE Pompey received an unprecedented multiyear proconsulship to deal with piracy.

Augustus replaced the armies loyal to individual commanders with a standing imperial army. Proconsuls lost military authority but kept the prestige of the title. He kept the border provinces, where most legions stood, under his own control, and the governors of senatorial provinces were chosen by lot, with the result ratified by the Senate. A passage in the New Testament notes that cases might be judged by a proconsul. An early fifth-century document, the Notitia Dignitatum, lists three: for Asia, Achaea and Africa.

Although proconsul was an official title only in ancient Rome, the word has been applied to modern British, American and French officials with delegated authority. Writers such as Carnes Lord discuss figures like Leonard Wood in Cuba, Lucius D. Clay in Germany and Paul Bremer in Iraq in 2003 within the framework of proconsular authority.
procopius: Apart from his own writings, the main source for Procopius's life is an entry in the Suda, a Byzantine encyclopaedia written after 975. He was a native of Caesarea in Palestine and would have received a conventional upper-class education in Greek classics and rhetoric, perhaps at the school at Gaza. He may have studied law, possibly at Berytus or Constantinople, and became a lawyer. He knew Latin, as was natural for a man with legal training.

In 527, the first year of Justinian's reign, Procopius became legal adviser to the general Belisarius. He served with Belisarius on the eastern front until the defeat at the Battle of Callinicum in 531, and he witnessed the Nika riots of January 532, which Belisarius and Mundus put down with a massacre in the Hippodrome. In 533 he went with Belisarius against the Vandal kingdom in North Africa and took part in the capture of Carthage. He then rejoined him for the war in Italy, lived through the Gothic siege of Rome, which lasted a year and nine days, and saw Belisarius enter Ravenna in 540.

His relations with Belisarius appear to have cooled after that, and when Belisarius returned to Italy in 544 Procopius appears no longer to have been on his staff. The date of his death is not certain. Many historians place it in 554, but an urban prefect of Constantinople named Procopius is recorded in 562, and some scholars think he may be the historian.

His History of the Wars, in eight books, is his most important work. The first two books cover the conflict with Sassanid Persia, including the war of Khosrau I in 540 and the great plague from 542. The next two cover Belisarius's campaign against the Vandal kingdom, and the final four the war in Italy against the Ostrogoths. The eighth book brings the history to 553.

The Secret History claims to report the scandals Procopius could not include in his official history for fear of angering the emperor, the empress and the generals. It portrays Justinian as cruel, venal and incompetent. It was discovered in 1623 in the Vatican Library, and scholars differ on how far it shows his real feelings. On Buildings, in contrast, is a panegyric on Justinian's public works, probably written at his behest.
progressive-liberal-party: The party was founded on 23 November 1953 by William Cartwright, Cyril Stevenson and Henry Milton Taylor, and was the first national political party in the Bahamas. Earlier that year Cartwright and Stevenson had travelled to London to cover the coronation of Elizabeth II, meeting members of the British Labour Party there, and had visited the Jamaica Labour Party and the People's National Party in Jamaica. The party opposed racial discrimination, corruption and poor administration under a restricted, property-based franchise, and called for wider voting rights, including votes for women. In 1956 it won about a third of the vote and six seats, forming the first organised opposition bloc in the House of Assembly.

Lynden Pindling, who had joined a few months after the founding, became its parliamentary leader. In 1962 the party won the largest share of the vote but fewer seats, which it blamed on unfair constituency boundaries. On 27 April 1965, later called Black Tuesday, Pindling threw the Speaker's mace out of a window of the House of Assembly in protest, and the party boycotted the House for almost nine months. In 1967 it won 18 of the 38 seats, tying the United Bahamian Party, and with the backing of Randol Fawkes and Alvin Braynen formed the first black-led government.

Early independence was the issue of the 1972 election, which the party won with 29 of 38 seats, and the Bahamas became independent on 10 July 1973. In government it favoured stronger state control of the economy, more Bahamian ownership of business and the replacement of foreign workers by Bahamians. In the 1980s a Commission of Inquiry into drug trafficking reported corruption in the police and at cabinet level, and the issue split the party: Hubert Ingraham, dismissed by Pindling, later led the Free National Movement, which won 33 of 49 seats in 1992.

Pindling retired in 1997, after the party had won only six seats, and Perry Christie led it back to office in 2002. It lost in 2007, returned in 2012, and in 2017, amid corruption scandals and the delayed opening of the Baha Mar resort, fell to four seats. Under Philip Davis it won 32 of 39 seats in 2021, during the COVID-19 pandemic, and on 12 May 2026 won 33 of 41 constituencies, the first back-to-back victory by a Bahamian party since 1997.
prohibition-in-the-united-states: Drinking had been contested in America since the colonial period. The American Temperance Society, formed in 1826, had reached 1.5 million members by 1835. The dry crusade continued from the 1840s, led by Protestant denominations, and in the late 19th century it linked saloons with political corruption. Maine's law of 1851 banned the manufacture and sale of liquor, and twelve states followed before its repeal in 1856. The Woman's Christian Temperance Union gave the movement a national grassroots base, and after 1900 the Anti-Saloon League coordinated it.

The Senate proposed the Eighteenth Amendment on 18 December 1917, and it became part of the Constitution when a 36th state approved it on 16 January 1919; the country went dry on 17 January 1920. The Volstead Act set the rules for enforcement and defined the banned drinks. Religious use of wine was permitted, and private possession and consumption were not illegal under federal law, though many local laws were stricter. Enforcement lacked a central authority, some states such as Maryland and New York refused to enforce the amendment, and the terrain, ports and long borders with Canada and Mexico made smuggling hard to stop.

Many of the wealthy stockpiled liquor before 1920, while small portable stills were on sale within a week of the ban. Within six months over 15,000 doctors and 57,000 pharmacists held licences to prescribe or sell medicinal alcohol. A black market grew up, and organised crime has been argued to have gained a financial basis from it. In Cicero, Illinois, the gang leader Al Capone operated despite the police.

Before the Volstead Act about 14% of federal, state and local tax revenue came from alcohol, and when the Great Depression struck, governments wanted that income. Captain William H. Stayton's Association Against the Prohibition Amendment, founded in 1918, was the largest of nearly forty groups working for repeal. The Twenty-first Amendment repealed the Eighteenth on 5 December 1933, the only time in American history that an amendment was passed to repeal another. It lets states restrict or ban alcohol, and dry counties remain.

Its effects are disputed. One review concluded that Prohibition probably reduced per capita alcohol use and harm at first, but that the benefits eroded as a black market grew. Rates of cirrhosis fell, while another study found consumption fell to about 30 percent of its earlier level and later rose to 60–70 percent. The historian Lisa McGirr argues that it expanded the powers of the federal state and fell hardest on African Americans, immigrants and poor whites.
prokop-the-great: Prokop was born around 1380 into an eminent, partly German-speaking family of Prague, German patrician on his mother's side. He received the tonsure early in life, became a married priest, studied in Prague and then travelled for several years abroad. At first he belonged to the Utraquists, the moderate wing of the Hussites. On returning to Bohemia he continued to officiate as a priest but became the most prominent leader of the advanced Hussite or Taborite forces in the later part of the Hussite Wars.

Prokop was not the immediate successor of Jan Žižka as leader of the Taborites, as has often been stated, but he commanded their forces when they won their great victories over Germans and Catholics at Ústí nad Labem in 1426 and Domažlice in 1431. The defeat of the crusaders of the Holy Roman Empire at Domažlice led to peace negotiations at Cheb in 1432 with representatives of the Council of Basel.

He also led Taborite raids into Hungary and Germany. In 1429 a large Bohemian army invaded Saxony and the territory of Nuremberg, but the Hussites made no attempt to hold German land, and on 6 February 1430 Prokop agreed the Treaty of Kulmbach with Frederick I, burgrave of Nuremberg. He was the most prominent member of the embassy that reached Basel on 4 January 1433.

After fruitless talks he returned to a Bohemia in new turmoil. The Taborites besieging Plzeň revolted against him, and he withdrew to Prague. The Bohemian nobility, Catholic and Utraquist, formed a league against radicalism, and with their help the citizens of the Old Town seized the New Town of Prague, which Prokop failed to defend. With Prokop the Lesser he retreated eastward, and on 30 May 1434 the army of the towns met the nobles' army between Kourim and Kolín at Lipany. The Taborites were decisively defeated, and both Prokops died in the battle. In July 1917 the fourth rifle regiment of the Czechoslovak legions was named after him.
proletariat: The word comes from the Latin proletarius, a social class of Roman citizens who owned little or no property. The name presumably originated with the census held every five years, which registered citizens and their property and fixed their military duties and voting privileges. Those who owned 11,000 assēs or fewer fell below the lowest category for military service, and their children, called prōlēs, were listed instead of property, hence proletarius, a producer of offspring. Their only contribution to the commonwealth was their children, the future citizens who could colonise conquered territories.

The proletarii were the lowest class in the Comitia Centuriata, largely deprived of voting rights. Voting began with the highest social ranks, so a majority could be reached early and their votes never taken.

In the early 19th century liberal scholars in Western Europe noted the similarities between the growing industrial working class and the Roman proletarians. In 1839 the French philosopher Felicité Robert de Lamennais compared workers to the slaves of Rome in De l'esclavage moderne, published in English as Modern Slavery. The Swiss economist Jean Charles Léonard de Sismondi was the first to apply the term to the working class created by capitalism, and Karl Marx most likely met it in his writings.

Marx used the term for a class with no significant ownership of the means of production, whose only means of subsistence is to sell its labour power for a wage. In his theory capitalism rests on the exploitation of the proletariat by the bourgeoisie: the goods the workers produce belong to the capitalist, who sells them, and wages absorb only part of the price. Marx argued that the conflict of interest between the two classes gives workers common interests across national boundaries, and that the proletariat would displace capitalism through a dictatorship of the proletariat, leading to a communist society.

Marxist theory defines the borders of the proletariat only vaguely. Above it lie the lower petty bourgeoisie, such as small shopkeepers, and below it the lumpenproletariat, a class Marx considered retrograde, made up of the poorest outcasts living outside legal employment.

During the Chinese Communist Revolution the concept stressed a proletarian class consciousness, developed through political education by the Chinese Communist Party, rather than social attributes such as being an industrial worker. This allowed the revolution to address the relative weakness of China's industrial working class. The socialist states that followed the Russian Revolution championed an official version of proletarian culture.
pronoia: By the 11th century Byzantine aristocrats held honorific titles and power at the emperor's gift, and competition for them was fierce. The most desired grants involved governing and collecting taxes in parts of the empire. By the reign of Constantine IX, in the middle of the century, some aristocrats had begun to assert sovereignty over regions, collecting taxes for themselves and often plotting rebellion.

In the late 11th century Alexius I tried to reform the aristocracy by distributing Roman territory among its members. This also removed them from Constantinople and made it harder for them to challenge the emperor directly. Most of the pronoiai Alexius granted went to members of his own Comnenus family. His measure legitimized the holding of land by aristocrats and brought it under centralized state control.

The limits of a pronoia were recorded in an imperial document called a praktika. Its holder was a pronoiarios, and those who worked the income stream, such as farmers on the land, were called paroikoi. The grant could be land, its money value or the income it produced, and could also cover water and fishing rights or customs collection. Several people might hold different rights to one piece of territory.

A pronoia gave the grantee possession, not ownership, which remained imperial. When monasteries or other institutions received grants, these were in effect permanent, since the institutions continued. The paroikoi were not serfs as peasants were in western Europe: they owed no particular loyalty or service to the pronoiar, who was often not a native of the land granted.

Manuel I Comnenus extended pronoiai to army officers in place of a regular salary, so that holders became something like tax collectors who kept part of what they raised. After the Crusaders captured Constantinople in 1204 the system continued in the Empire of Nicaea, where John III Ducas Vatatzes gave pronoiai to the church and to noblewomen, which had not been done before.

Michael VIII Palaeologus, after recovering Constantinople in 1261, audited the pronoiai so that their values matched reduced conditions. Under the Palaeologan emperors pronoiars could more easily be organized into military units, and Andronicus II Palaeologus used the money raised from them to finance expeditions against the Bulgarians. There were only a few thousand pronoiars, and the impoverished empire could not afford a full army or navy. Pronoiars began to extract rents from the paroikoi. After the fall of Constantinople in 1453 the Ottomans kept their own version, the timar system, which they had borrowed from the Eastern Romans.
prosthesis: The word prosthesis comes from the Ancient Greek prosthesis, meaning "addition, application, attachment". Prostheses originate in the ancient Near East around 3000 BCE, with the earliest evidence in ancient Egypt and Iran. The earliest recorded mention of eye prostheses is the Egyptian story of the Eye of Horus, in which Thoth restores the plucked-out left eye of Horus. The earliest archaeological evidence, from about 3000 to 2800 BCE, is an eye prosthesis buried with a woman at Shahr-i Shōkhta in Iran, probably of bitumen paste covered with a thin layer of gold.

A prosthesis may restore the function of a missing body part or serve a cosmetic purpose. The part may be lost through injury, disease or a condition present at birth. Limb prostheses replace arms or legs at various levels of amputation, and organ prostheses include artificial hearts and kidneys. Cosmetic prostheses have long been used to disguise injuries and disfigurements. A prosthetist prescribes, designs and manages the device, usually beginning with a plaster cast of the affected limb.

The Egyptians were early makers of foot prostheses, as a wooden toe found on a mummy shows. In South Asia the Rigveda, about 1200 BCE, tells of the warrior queen Vishpala. Roman bronze crowns have also been found, but their use may have been more aesthetic than medical.

An Italian surgeon recorded an amputee whose artificial arm allowed him to remove his hat, open his purse and sign his name. Ambroise Paré, considered the father of modern prosthetics, improved both amputation surgery and design; among his inventions was an above-knee device, a kneeling peg leg and foot with a fixed position, an adjustable harness and a knee lock. Pieter Verduyn made the first non-locking below-knee prosthesis. After the Second World War the National Academy of Sciences urged more research, and government funding set up programmes in the armed forces and the Veterans Administration. Elaine Scarry argues that every artifact extends the body, as chairs supplement the skeleton and tools the hands.
protagoras: Protagoras was born in Abdera, in Thrace, opposite the island of Thasos, around 490 BCE. According to Aulus Gellius he first made his living as a porter, until the philosopher Democritus saw him carrying a load of small pieces of wood tied with a short cord so accurately that Democritus took him for a mathematical prodigy, and took him into his household to teach him philosophy. Protagoras became well known in Athens and a friend of Pericles.

His dates are not recorded but are worked out from surviving writings. In Plato's Protagoras he says he is old enough to be the father of Socrates, Prodicus or Hippias, and in the Meno he is said to have died at about 70, after forty years as a practising sophist. His death is therefore placed about 420 BCE, though the story of his trial for impiety on which assumptions rest appears to be fake.

Plato credits Protagoras with inventing the role of the professional sophist. He taught subjects related to virtue and political life, and above all whether virtue could be taught. Plato has him claim to teach the proper management of one's own household and of public affairs. The titles of his books, such as Technique of Eristics, show that he also taught rhetoric and argument. Aristotle records that he was criticised for claiming to make the weaker argument stronger.

His best-known statement, from his lost work Truth, is that of all things the measure is Man. Plato took it to mean that there is no objective truth. Protagoras seems to have meant that each person's experience shapes their judgments, so that two people may truly find the same weather cold and hot, but he held that views are not of equal worth: a sophist teaches students to tell the useful from the harmful. Plato and Aristotle both argued against him.

Of his lost work On the Gods, Protagoras is reported to have written that he had no means of knowing whether the gods existed, because of the obscurity of the subject and the brevity of human life. According to Diogenes Laërtius this angered the Athenians, who expelled him and burned his books in the marketplace; Cicero also mentions the destruction. The classicist John Burnet doubts the account, since both writers lived centuries later and contemporaries do not mention such persecution. Very few fragments of his writing survive.
protectorate-general-to-pacify-the-east: The protectorate, known in Chinese as the Andong Duhufu, was created beside the Ungjin Commandery in the former Baekje lands, and was said to have been garrisoned with 200,000 soldiers. It was meant to oversee nine commanderies, 42 prefectures and 100 counties holding an estimated 697,000 Goguryeo households. Emperor Gaozong of Tang also proposed a Great Commandery of Gyerim for Silla, which King Munmu of Silla refused. Emperor Taizong of Tang had promised Silla Baekje and the lands south of Pyongyang in return for its help, but he died before Goguryeo fell and Gaozong broke the promise.

The people of Goguryeo revolted in 669, and the Tang deported tens of thousands of households to empty lands south of the Yangtze and Huai rivers; most sources give between 28,200 and 38,300 households. From 670 to 675 Goguryeo loyalists allied with Silla, among them Go Yeonmu and Geom Mojam, fought the Tang inside and outside the protectorate, and in 676 Silla took all the land south of the Taedong River. The seat was moved to Liaoyang in 676 and to Xincheng, in modern Fushun, in 677. The deposed Bojang of Goguryeo, made commander there, plotted with the Mohe people to revive his kingdom and was banished in 681.

After the rebellion of the Khitan Li Jinzhong in 697, the protectorate was reduced in 698 to the Andong Area Command, and in 699 Tang troops left Liaodong. Its rank was restored in 705, when the seat moved to Youzhou, west of present-day Beijing; it moved again to Pingzhou in 714 and to the old city of Liaoxi in 743. In 736 the Tang formally recognised Silla's rule south of the Taedong. Sources date its end to 756, 758 or 761, when, according to the Old Book of Tang, it held only 5,718 households.

According to Kim Jong-bok, neither Silla nor Parhae occupied Liaodong after the Tang abandoned it. Silla did not advance beyond the Taedong River, and in 827 it mobilised 10,000 people to build a wall along the river against Parhae's attacks. Kim argues that Liaodong became a buffer zone between the Tang and Parhae, which explains the relative peace among the Tang, Parhae and Silla in contrast with the Goguryeo period; Parhae responded only in 924, after the Khitans had taken Liaoyang.
protestant-reformation: Europe suffered a series of calamities from the early 14th century, culminating in the Black Death, which killed about a third of its population. Humanism, with its slogan ad fontes, back to the sources, brought enthusiasm for textual criticism: Lorenzo Valla showed that the Donation of Constantine, a basic document of papal authority, was a medieval forgery. Many of Luther's ideas were anticipated by Wycliff, Hus, Erasmus and others, and scholars now see the Reformation as in important respects a continuation of trends within late medieval Catholicism.

Pope Leo X announced a new plenary indulgence in 1515 to finance the building of St Peter's Basilica, and the friar Johann Tetzel sold indulgences in Germany with unusually aggressive methods. The Reformation is usually dated from Martin Luther's publication of the Ninety-five Theses in 1517.

Printing carried the new ideas quickly: Luther was responsible for about one fifth of all works printed in Germany in the first third of the 16th century. Huldrych Zwingli led reform in Zürich from 1522, and John Calvin shaped the Continental Reformed tradition. Radical reformers such as the Swiss Brethren demanded believers' baptism and a church free of the state. The Peasants' War of 1524 and 1525 drew on the new excitement against authority. In April 1525 Albert of Brandenburg-Ansbach turned the Teutonic Order's Prussia into a hereditary duchy, and the Reformation was introduced in Electoral Saxony on Christmas Day 1525. At the Diet of Augsburg in 1530 the Protestants presented the Augsburg Confession, written by Melanchthon.

Elsewhere the kings of Denmark and Sweden took the lead in Scandinavia. In England, William Tyndale's New Testament had more than 15,000 copies in secret circulation by about 1535, and under Edward VI Thomas Cranmer's Book of Common Prayer replaced the Mass with a vernacular liturgy.
