Disputes in Germany led to the Schmalkaldic War, and later came the French Wars of Religion and the revolt in the Netherlands, where more Protestants were persecuted between 1523 and 1555 than in any other country.

The Catholic response, the Counter-Reformation, included new orders, above all the Jesuits, whose establishment Paul III sanctioned in 1540. The Council of Trent met from December 1545 to 1563, reaffirmed that apostolic tradition was as authentic a source of faith as the Bible, and stressed good works in salvation, rejecting two important elements of Luther's theology. Historians often use the plural to stress that the movement was not uniform but the result of parallel movements: Lutheranism, Calvinism, the Radical Reformation and the Catholic Reformation. It is considered one of the events that signified the end of the Middle Ages, and the end of the Reformation era is disputed among scholars.
protestant-union: The Protestant Union, also called the Evangelical Union, the Union of Auhausen, the German Union or the Protestant Action Party, was a coalition of Protestant German states. Frederick IV, Elector Palatine, formed it on 14 May 1608 to defend the rights, land and safety of each member. It included both Calvinist and Lutheran states.

Two events led to its formation. In 1607 the Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II and Duke Maximilian I of Bavaria reestablished Catholicism in Donauwörth. By 1608 a majority of the Imperial Diet had decided that the renewal of the 1555 Peace of Augsburg should depend on the restoration of all church land appropriated since 1552. The Protestant princes met at Auhausen and formed the coalition under Frederick IV. In response the Catholic League was organised the following year, headed by Maximilian.

Members included the Palatinate, Neuburg, Württemberg, Baden-Durlach, Ansbach, Bayreuth, Anhalt, Zweibrücken, Oettingen, Hesse-Kassel and Brandenburg, and free cities such as Ulm, Strasbourg, Nuremberg, Worms and Speyer. Its guidelines bound each member to keep good faith, to join no other alliance, to keep a secret correspondence on dangers and to come at once to the aid of any member attacked. The union was not to affect disagreements on points of religion, and no member was to allow attacks on another in books or from the pulpit.

It was weak from the start, since several powerful Protestant rulers, notably the Elector of Saxony, did not take part, and it suffered strife between its Lutheran and Calvinist members. In 1610 it intervened in the War of the Jülich Succession.

In 1619 Frederick V of the Palatinate accepted the crown of Bohemia against Emperor Ferdinand II. On 3 July 1620 the Union signed the Treaty of Ulm, declaring neutrality and declining to support him. In January 1621 Ferdinand II put Frederick V under an imperial ban, and the Palatinate lost the Upper Palatinate to Bavaria. The Union protested at Heilbronn in February, but Ferdinand ordered it to disband its army. Its members complied under the Mainz accord in May, and it was formally dissolved on 14 May 1621. A separate union, the Heilbronn League, appeared twelve years later and fought the emperor under the guidance of Sweden and France.
protestantism: Protestantism follows the theology of the Protestant Reformation, a movement that began in the 16th century with the aim of reforming the Catholic Church of perceived errors and abuses. It began in the Holy Roman Empire in 1517, when Martin Luther published his Ninety-five Theses in reaction to abuses in the sale of indulgences. Luther argued against buying or earning forgiveness and claimed instead that salvation is a gift God gives to those who have faith.

The name comes from a protest. Six princes of the Holy Roman Empire and the rulers of fourteen Imperial Free Cities issued a protest against the edict of the Diet of Speyer in 1529 and were the first to be called Protestants. Lutheranism spread into Denmark–Norway, Sweden, Finland, Livonia and Iceland, and Calvinist churches spread in Germany, Hungary, the Netherlands, Scotland, Switzerland, France, Poland and Lithuania. The separation of the Church of England from the Catholic Church under King Henry VIII began Anglicanism.

Protestants hold to justification by faith alone, the priesthood of all believers, and the Bible as the highest authority for faith and practice. They reject papal supremacy, and early Protestants rejected transubstantiation. Lutherans affirmed a corporeal presence of Christ in Holy Communion, along with Catholics, while the Reformed affirmed a real spiritual presence.

The movement soon divided into branches: Lutheranism, Anglicanism, Calvinism or Reformed Christianity, and later Methodism, which grew from a revival within the 18th-century Church of England under John Wesley, and the Baptists, who hold that baptism should be given only to professing believers. The Radical Reformation, which had no state sponsorship and faced intense persecution from both Catholics and mainstream Protestants, gave rise to Anabaptism, whose descendants include the Amish, Hutterites and Mennonites.

The Reformation affected marriage and family, education, the political and social order, the economy and the arts. Protestant churches reject a celibate priesthood and allow their clergy to marry. Freedom of conscience gained priority after Luther refused to recant at the Diet of Worms in 1521, and Rhode Island, Connecticut and Pennsylvania combined democratic constitutions with freedom of religion. Protestants founded hospitals, schools and aid organisations, and in the 19th century many took part in the abolition of slavery, prison reform and woman suffrage. Estimates of the number of Protestants worldwide range from 600 million to 1 billion, because scholars disagree on which denominations count.
proto-sinaitic-script: The Proto-Sinaitic script is a Middle Bronze Age writing system known from about 30–40 inscriptions and fragments from Serabit el-Khadim in the Sinai Peninsula and two from Wadi el-Hol in Middle Egypt. Together with about 20 Proto-Canaanite inscriptions it is called Early Alphabetic, and it is the common ancestor of the Paleo-Hebrew alphabet, the Ancient South Arabian script and the Phoenician alphabet, from which the Greek and Latin alphabets descend. According to the common theory, Canaanites or Hyksos who spoke a Canaanite language repurposed Egyptian hieroglyphs to make a different script. The hieroglyph for pr, house, was adopted to write the first consonant of baytu, the Semitic word for house.

At Serabit el-Khadim the mountain held turquoise mines and a temple of the goddess Hathor, visited by repeated expeditions over 800 years. Many workers came from the Nile Delta and included numerous speakers of an early Northwest Semitic language. Most of the inscriptions are scratched on rocks near the mines and along the roads to the temple, among far more numerous hieratic and hieroglyphic texts. Four were found in the temple, on two small statues and on either side of a small stone sphinx.

Edward Henry Palmer copied inscriptions in Wadi Magharah in the winter of 1868–1869, but his text was not published until 1904. In the winter of 1905 Hilda and Flinders Petrie found a series of inscriptions at Serabit el-Khadim. Petrie recognised hieroglyphic characters but saw that the script was not Egyptian, and he assumed the turquoise miners had devised it from borrowed linear signs.

In 1916 Alan Gardiner argued that the signs were early forms of the Semitic letters. Assigning b to the house sign, he read a recurring word as lbʿlt, to the Lady, meaning Hathor. Another word, mʿhbʿlt, was read as Beloved of the Lady, and this reading was accepted after the phrase was found beneath a hieroglyphic inscription reading Beloved of Hathor, Lady of Turquoise. In the 1950s and 1960s William Albright published interpretations that derived the Canaanite alphabet from hieratic.

The two Wadi el-Hol inscriptions, found in 1999 by John and Deborah Darnell on a road linking Thebes and Abydos, are dated between 1900 and 1800 BCE. They suggest the script arose in Egypt and that Proto-Sinaitic writing developed from the mid-19th to 18th centuries BCE. The principal debate is between an early date, around 1850 BCE, and a late date, around 1550 BCE, which decides whether the script is Proto-Sinaitic or Proto-Canaanite and so whether the alphabet was invented in Egypt or in Canaan. Proto-Canaanite is clearly attested only after the Bronze Age collapse. Other proposed Early Alphabetic texts include inscribed clay cylinders from Umm el-Marra, about 2300 BCE, and a sherd from Lachish of the 15th century BCE.
protogeometric-style: The style emerged after the Late Bronze Age collapse, in the Greek Dark Ages, as the first expression of a reviving civilisation. It was produced in Attica and Central Greece, led by Athens, and from Athens it spread to several other centres. It followed the development of a faster potter's wheel, and its vases are markedly more accomplished technically than earlier Dark Age pottery.

Its dating has been refined by radiocarbon dating and Bayesian models applied to Lefkandi, Kalapodi and Corinth, which Toffolo and colleagues used in 2013 to place the transition from Sub-Mycenaean to Protogeometric in the second half of the 11th century BCE. The archaeologist Alex Knodell divides the Protogeometric period itself into three sub-periods, and the style was succeeded by the Geometric style.

The decoration is purely abstract. Broad horizontal bands often run round the neck and belly of a vessel, together with the concentric circles. Many other simple motifs occur, but much of the surface is usually left plain, unlike many pieces of the later Geometric style.

Both the red and the black colours were made from the same clay, levigated and fired in different ways, and firing faults sometimes produced a change of colour within a single band. As potters learned to control this variation, the way opened to the three-phase firing technique that became characteristic of Greek pottery.

Potters also took up new shapes influenced by Mycenaean ones, among them the belly-handled amphora, the neck-handled amphora, the krater and the lekythos. Attic artists reworked these vessels on the fast wheel, making them taller and so increasing the area available for decoration.
proton: The idea of a national car was conceived in 1979 by Mahathir Mohamad, then Deputy Prime Minister, to strengthen the Malaysian automotive industry. The Cabinet approved the National Car Project in 1982, and Proton was established on 7 May 1983, wholly owned by the government through Khazanah Nasional, with Mahathir as its head. The name is a backronym for Perusahaan Otomobil Nasional, National Automobile Enterprise. Between 1983 and 1984 Proton approached Mitsubishi Motors and arranged a joint venture, and the result was the Proton Saga, launched in July 1985.

Mitsubishi Motors and Mitsubishi Corporation supplied most of the platforms, engines, parts and expertise, trained Proton's staff in Japan, and provided its managing director from 1988 to 1993, Kenji Iwabuchi. Management passed gradually to Malaysians in the 1990s. All Proton cars launched between 1985 and 2000, except the Tiara, were based on Mitsubishi vehicles. The Saga captured a 47 percent share of the Malaysian market in 1986, with 24,148 cars sold, and a peak share of 74 percent in 1993. Sales in Malaysia fell from 404,000 units in 1997 to 163,851 in 1998 during the Asian financial crisis, but Proton kept a majority share into the early 2000s.

The Proton Waja, launched in August 2000, was the company's first indigenously designed model, although it still used a Mitsubishi engine. In 2006 Perodua, the second Malaysian carmaker, overtook Proton in sales. Proton owned Lotus Cars from 1996 to 2017. Mitsubishi had sold its stake to Khazanah Nasional by 2005, and in 2012 DRB-HICOM fully acquired Proton. In May 2017 DRB-HICOM announced the sale of 49.9 percent of Proton to Geely, signed in June 2017, and Lotus ceased to be a Proton unit. In 2024 Proton announced a research centre at the Geely Automobile Research Institute at Hangzhou Bay.

Proton is headquartered in Shah Alam, Selangor, with further facilities at Proton City in Perak. It first exported cars in December 1986, to right-hand-drive markets such as New Zealand, the United Kingdom and Singapore. An attempt to enter the American market in November 1988 failed to meet strict US regulations. The Wira of 1993 was the first Proton built in both left- and right-hand drive, which opened Continental Europe in October 1994, and at its peak the company sold in over 70 countries.
Its Petronas EON Racing Team won the 2002 Production World Rally Championship with the driver Karamjit Singh. Its first SUV, the Proton X70, launched in 2018, was based on the Geely Boyue.
providence-rhode-island: Providence lies at the head of Narragansett Bay, at the mouth of the Providence River, which is formed in the middle of the city by the confluence of the Moshassuck and Woonasquatucket rivers. Its limits enclose a small area of about 20.5 square miles, of which roughly a tenth is water. Like Rome, it is one of many cities claimed to stand on seven hills. The city grew up before the automobile, and its streets run irregularly, radiating from old gathering places such as Market Square.

Roger Williams settled Providence in June 1636. As a minister in the Massachusetts Bay Colony he had advocated the separation of church and state and condemned the colonists' confiscation of land from the Indians, and for these and other opinions described as diverse, new and dangerous he was convicted of sedition and heresy and banished. He and his companions first settled at Rumford, then moved down the Seekonk River, around Fox Point and up the Providence River to the meeting of the Moshassuck and Woonasquatucket. They named the settlement after God's merciful Providence. It grew into one of the original Thirteen Colonies.

Williams founded the First Baptist Church in America there in 1638, and the Old State House served as the state's capitol from 1762 to 1904. Providence developed as a busy port and was one of the first cities in the country to industrialise, becoming noted for textile manufacturing and then for machine tools, jewellery and silverware. Its population peaked in the 1940s, just before the nationwide movement to the suburbs.

Providence is the capital and largest city of Rhode Island and the county seat of Providence County; its population was 190,934 at the 2020 census. The State House houses the General Assembly and the offices of the governor. The East Side has the largest contiguous area of buildings on the National Register of Historic Places in the U.S., many of them from before the Revolution. The city has Italian, Portuguese and Irish neighbourhoods, and is home to Brown University, the Rhode Island School of Design, Providence College and other institutions of higher education.
providenciales: Providenciales, known locally as Provo, lies in the northwest Caicos Islands. The island has an area of 98 square kilometres and had a population of 23,769 in 2012, the latest year for which the government published an island-by-island census. It is the third largest island of the Turks and Caicos in area and holds a majority of the population. The western half is mostly barren wilderness and contains Chalk Sound National Park, a bay about 5 kilometres long whose uniformly turquoise water is studded with tiny islets. Northwest Point Marine National Park takes in nearby reefs and saline lakes that attract breeding and migrant waterfowl.
The rugged hills and ridges are carpeted with prickly pear cactus and scrub. The island lies close to a migration route of the humpback whale and is surrounded by uninhabited cays.

The British Loyalist Thomas Stubbs owned the Cheshire Hall plantation, which grew sisal and cotton, from the 1790s until 1810, and its ruins remain. There are also remnants of Caribbean piracy at Osprey Rock and Sapodilla Hill. Before the island became a tourist destination it had three small centres of population: Blue Hills, The Bight on Grace Bay, and Five Cays.

As recently as 1964 Providenciales had no wheeled vehicle, roads, water, telephones or electricity. The original developer, Provident Ltd, ran shuttle flights from Florida twice a week in a World War II DC-3, as part of a real estate buying programme. Its Third Turtle Inn, built in 1967, was the only hotel. Resort hotels, an 18-hole golf course and many luxury condominiums were later built, and the island became popular with retirees from around the world, which set off a boom in residential development.

Most resorts stand along the 8-kilometre Grace Bay. Long Bay Beach on the southern, windward side is largely undeveloped and a kiteboarding destination. The Leeward Highway runs east to west from Downtown to Leeward, and most services lie near it. Downtown and Kew Town are near Providenciales International Airport, and Wheeland is in the northwest. Larger communities have grown at Leeward, Long Bay and Chalk Sound.
province-of-albacete: The Province of Albacete lies in central Spain, in the southern part of Castile–La Mancha, in the southeast of the Central Plateau. Its capital, the city of Albacete, is 262 kilometres by road southeast of Madrid. The province borders the provinces of Granada, Murcia, Alicante, Valencia, Cuenca, Ciudad Real and Jaén. Its main river is the Júcar, which crosses the northeast and is known for its deep gorges and trees. The highest point is La Atalaya, at 2,083 metres in the Sierra de las Cabras.

The territory has been inhabited since ancient times, as cave paintings in the Cueva del Niño and the Cueva de la Vieja show. In Roman times it was divided among Carpetania, Celtiberia, Contestania, Bastetania and Oretania. The Romans built a significant settlement at Libisosa, and under the Visigoths Tolmo de Minateda grew in prominence. In the Muslim period numerous farmhouses, castles and watchtowers were built to fight off invaders. On 25 April 1707 the Battle of Almansa was fought near Albacete, in which Philip V triumphed and established the House of Bourbon on the Spanish throne.

In 1822 the short-lived Province of Chinchilla was created from municipalities of La Mancha, Cuenca and the Kingdom of Murcia, with its capital at Chinchilla de Monte-Aragón, very close to Albacete. It became the basis on which Javier de Burgos created the Province of Albacete in 1833. After the Constitution of 1978 the province left the Murcia region and joined Castile–La Mancha, whose Statute of Autonomy was approved in 1982.

The province covers 14,931.74 square kilometres and has 87 municipalities and seven judicial districts, with a population of 390,751. Besides the capital, towns of more than 10,000 inhabitants are Hellín, Villarrobledo, Almansa, La Roda and Caudete.
province-of-brandenburg: The Province of Brandenburg was set up in 1815 from the core of the Kingdom of Prussia, taking in most of the historic Margraviate of Brandenburg, apart from the Altmark, and Lower Lusatia. The margraviate went back to Albert the Bear of the House of Ascania, who established it in 1157, and Charles IV's Golden Bull of 1356 confirmed the electoral dignity of its margraves. In 1415 it passed to Frederick of Nuremberg, the first Hohenzollern to rule it, and it became the core of the Brandenburg-Prussian state. After the Napoleonic Wars the Congress of Vienna of 1815 divided Prussia into ten provinces, and Lower Lusatia and the area around Belzig and Jüterbog were taken from the Kingdom of Saxony, which had allied with Napoleon.

The province was headed by an Oberpräsident and was divided into two governorates, Potsdam in the northwest and Frankfurt (Oder) in the southeast. Its government sat first at Potsdam, moved to Berlin in 1827, returned to Potsdam in 1843 and settled in Charlottenburg in 1918. Berlin, originally part of the province, grew into a metropolis from the 1830s. It became an autonomous city district on 1 April 1881 without wholly leaving the province, and was formally separated on 1 October 1920. The Greater Berlin Act of 1920 also took Charlottenburg and many other districts, so Brandenburg lost half its population and two-thirds of its tax base.

Serfdom was abolished by the Prussian reforms of 1807, but the outer rural regions kept the large estates of the Junker nobility, on poor soil and with little but brown coal in Lower Lusatia. Theodor Fontane portrayed provincial life in his Wanderungen durch die Mark Brandenburg. Under the Nazi regime the province held the concentration camps of Sachsenhausen and Ravensbrück, and in 1945 it was the scene of battles at the Seelow Heights, Halbe and Berlin. The Neumark east of the Oder-Neisse line was ceded to Poland, and the rest formed the state of Brandenburg in the Soviet zone, dissolved in 1952 and re-established in 1990.

The 1905 census counted 3,531,906 people, 97 per cent of whom gave German as their mother tongue. Sorbians made up 1 per cent, mostly in Lower Lusatia, and Polish speakers 1.3 per cent. A provincial Landtag was set up in 1824 in an advisory role, elected by estates, and the provincial ordinance of 1875 strengthened self-rule and made it indirectly elected. A universal, direct and equal franchise was first used in 1921.
province-of-castellon: The province is bordered by the provinces of Valencia to the south, Teruel to the west and Tarragona to the north, and by the Mediterranean Sea to the east. Its western side lies in the mountainous Sistema Ibérico area. Penyagolosa, the highest mountain of the province and the second highest in the Valencian Community, is regarded as one of the most emblematic Valencian mountains.

The Greenwich Meridian passes through the province, and commemorative monuments mark it at La Pobla Tornesa, Castellón and Almassora. At Castellón it crosses the 40th parallel, and the exact point can be visited at the Meridian Park. The province is divided into 135 municipalities and, historically, into eight comarques: Alcalatén, Alt Maestrat, Alto Mijares, Alto Palancia, Baix Maestrat, Plana Alta, Plana Baixa and Ports.

Besides Castellón de la Plana, the major cities are Vila-real, Borriana, La Vall d'Uixó and Vinaròs. Traditionally the economy rested on citrus fruit and vegetables, notably at Nules and Benicarló. From the 17th century the province developed a ceramic and tile industry, centred on Onda, L'Alcora, Nules, Castellón de la Plana and Vila-real, and most Spanish tile producers are now concentrated there. Furniture and chemical industries are also present, and there is a large oil refinery at Castellón de la Plana.

Older industries such as footwear at La Vall d'Uixó, fishing at Castellón and Vinaròs, and textiles at Vilafranca and Morella have given way to services and tourism. Seaside resorts include Benicàssim, Orpesa, Vinaròs, Borriana and Peníscola. Inland, the monumental towns of Morella, Vilafamés, Sant Mateu and Segorbe draw visitors, as do mineral springs at Montanejos, Benassal and Catí.
province-of-hanover: During the Austro-Prussian War the Kingdom of Hanover tried to stay neutral, as did some other members of the German Confederation. After Hanover voted on 14 June 1866 in favour of mobilising confederation troops against Prussia, Prussia took this as just cause for war. The kingdom was soon dissolved and annexed. Otto von Bismarck then used the private wealth of the dethroned House of Hanover to finance his continuing efforts against Ludwig II of Bavaria. The territory became the Province of Hanover, first of the Kingdom of Prussia and later of the Free State of Prussia.

In August 1946 the British military administration recreated the State of Hanover on the basis of the former kingdom. Three months later it was merged with Oldenburg, Brunswick and Schaumburg-Lippe into the new state of Lower Saxony, with the city of Hanover as capital.

The province was divided into six regions, first called Landdrosteien (high bailiwicks): Aurich, Osnabrück, Stade, Lüneburg, Hildesheim and Hanover. On 1 April 1885 they were reorganised as Regierungsbezirke, the standard Prussian governorates, and subdivided into urban and rural counties, the old Amt structure being disbanded.

The boundaries shifted at times. Wilhelmshaven, an urban county from 1919, was ceded to Oldenburg in 1937. In the same year Harburg-Wilhelmsburg went to Hamburg and Cuxhaven, previously part of Hamburg, joined the province. In 1941 Goslar passed to Brunswick and Holzminden came from it.

The central Prussian government appointed the heads of the province, called Oberpräsident. The first was Otto Graf zu Stolberg-Wernigerode from 1867 to 1873, and Rudolf von Bennigsen served from 1888 to 1897. Gustav Noske of the SPD held the post from 1920 to 1933, followed by two members of the NSDAP, Viktor Lutze and Hartmann Lauterbacher. Hinrich Wilhelm Kopf of the SPD held it in 1946. The elected provincial parliament, the Provinziallandtag, chose the executive, the Landesdirektor.
province-of-hesse-nassau: The Province of Hesse-Nassau was a province of the Kingdom of Prussia from 1868 to 1918, and then of the Free State of Prussia until 1944. It came into being through the annexations of Hesse-Kassel, Nassau and Frankfurt in 1866, after the Austro-Prussian War, and was organized by decrees of March 1867 concerning municipal constitutions. It was officially formed by a Royal Decree of 7 December 1868, which merged the two administrative districts of Kassel and Wiesbaden.

The province combined the formerly independent Hesse-Kassel, the Duchy of Nassau and the Free City of Frankfurt with areas gained from the Kingdom of Bavaria and from the Grand Duchy of Hesse, including part of the former Landgraviate of Hesse-Homburg. Its capital was Kassel, and it was divided into the two administrative regions of Kassel and Wiesbaden. Its largest part surrounded the province of Upper Hesse in the Grand Duchy of Hesse, called the People's State of Hesse from 1918.

On 1 April 1929 the Free State of Waldeck became part of Hesse-Nassau after a popular vote and joined the Kassel region. In 1935 the Nazi government in effect abolished all the German states, so the provinces held little meaning. Even so, on 1 July 1944 Hesse-Nassau was split into the provinces of Kurhessen, with its capital at Kassel, and Nassau, with its capital at Wiesbaden.

On 19 September 1945, after the end of World War II, the two provinces were merged again and combined with most of the neighbouring People's State of Hesse to form Greater Hesse, which became the modern state of Hesse in 1946. Parts of Nassau went to Rhineland-Palatinate.

The Oberpräsident, or High Commissioner, was the chief administrator of a Prussian province. He was appointed by the King on the advice of the Prussian Minister for the Interior and administered the province with the help of a provincial council appointed by the Prussian government.

The flag of Hesse-Nassau was identical to that of the Netherlands, whose royal house originates from the Duchy of Nassau. The coat of arms had three parts for the three entities that formed the province: a crowned lion striped silver and red on blue for the Electorate of Hesse, a crowned golden lion on a blue field strewn with billets for the Duchy of Nassau, and a silver eagle with golden talons on red for the Free City of Frankfurt.
province-of-hohenzollern: The two principalities belonged to the Catholic branch of the Hohenzollern family, in Swabia, the ancestral home of the house to which the kings of Prussia belonged. Their ruling houses had hereditary treaties with Prussia going back to 1695 and 1707. When their future came into question during the German Revolutions of 1848–1849, King Frederick William IV was at first reluctant to take them over, until his adviser Rudolf von Stillfried-Rattonitz warned that otherwise the princes would turn to the House of Württemberg, Prussia's hereditary enemy. The treaty of annexation was signed on 7 December 1849, the day both princes abdicated, and Prussia took possession of Sigmaringen on 6 April 1850 and of Hechingen on 8 April.

The Hohenzollern Lands formed a governmental district, a Regierungsbezirk, which was not a true province but had almost all a province's rights. With about 65,500 people in 1850 they were smaller and less populous than any full Prussian province. The district president ranked with the governors of the provinces and the district was represented in the Prussian State Council, but many functions, including military affairs, higher education and medicine, fell to the nearby Rhine Province.

From 1875 a district parliament, the Kommunallandtag, was elected for local self-government. The court of appeal sat in Arnsberg, about 450 km to the north, until 1879 and afterwards in Frankfurt am Main. In 1925 four of its seven upper bureaus, the Oberämter, were combined into the two new Oberämter of Hechingen and Sigmaringen.

During the Austro-Prussia War of 1866 troops from Württemberg, fighting on the losing Austrian side, occupied the district from 27 June to 6 August. In 1918 it became a province of the Free State of Prussia. After the Nazi seizure of power in 1933 provincial functions were in effect suspended, and the district belonged to the Gau of Württemberg-Hohenzollern under Wilhelm Murr, though it formally remained a Prussian district.

After World War II the area lay in the French occupation zone, and the military government joined it with southern Württemberg in the state of Württemberg-Hohenzollern, with Tübingen as capital. The districts of Hechingen and Sigmaringen survived the merger into Baden-Württemberg in 1952, but the old boundaries disappeared in the district reform of 1973. Most of the area now lies in the Sigmaringen and Zollernalbkreis districts.
province-of-posen: The province comprised most of the historical region of Greater Poland. The land is mostly flat and drained by the Noteć in the north and the Warta in the centre, with hundreds of small lakes left by glaciers. Agriculture was the main industry, growing rye and other grains, sugar beets, potatoes, and some tobacco and hops. Posen was always majority Polish, with roughly 60 to 70 per cent Polish speakers, together with German and Jewish minorities. Almost all the Poles were Roman Catholic and most Germans Protestant. Its area was 28,962 square kilometres, and its population grew from 820,176 in 1816 to 2,099,831 in 1910.

Prussia gained the territory in the partitions of Poland of 1772 and 1793. After the Napoleonic Wars the Congress of Vienna restored the western part of the Duchy of Warsaw to Prussia in 1815 as the semi-autonomous Grand Duchy of Posen, with an advisory parliament, Polish as the official language and a viceroy, Antoni Radziwiłł. After the failed November Uprising of 1830 it lost much of this status.

A first Greater Poland uprising in 1846 failed when its leaders were arrested. The second, in 1848, was a rising against inclusion in Germany; on 26 April 1848 Frederick William IV divided the Grand Duchy, and when the insurrection went on, Prussian troops defeated the Poles and all of it became the Province of Posen. It joined the North German Confederation in 1866 and the German Empire in 1871.

Bismarck regarded the Poles as enemies of the Reich. In 1872 he began his Kulturkampf in Posen by taking inspection of Catholic schools from the clergy, and the Polish peasants rallied behind their priests. German became the sole language of government business in 1876. In 1906 some 100,000 schoolchildren went on strike against whipping for refusing to answer in German. The Prussian Settlement Commission, founded in Posen in the 1880s, was given 100 million marks to buy Polish estates and let them to German farmers. These measures failed and heightened the Poles' national identity.

A third Greater Poland uprising began on 27 December 1918, after a speech by Ignacy Jan Paderewski in Posen, and by mid-January the insurgents held most of the province. An estimated 3,000 to 3,500 people died before an armistice on 16 February 1919.

Under the Treaty of Versailles, effective 10 January 1920, the captured territory became the Poznań Voivodeship of Poland; the remainder, where Germans were the majority, about 2,200 square kilometres, was joined in 1922 with West Prussia as Posen-West Prussia. More than half of the German speakers in the ceded regions emigrated. In 1939 Nazi Germany annexed the area as Reichsgau Wartheland, and after the Second World War all of it came under Poland and its German population was expelled.
province-of-quebec-1763-1791: The colony grew out of the British conquest of New France in the Seven Years' War. After the capitulation of Montreal in 1760 it was placed under military government, and civil government began only in 1764. In the Treaty of Paris of 1763 France gave up its claim to Canada, choosing instead to keep the small and profitable island of Guadeloupe. Under the Royal Proclamation the new province held the cities of Quebec and Montreal and the land around them, reaching neither the Great Lakes nor Rupert's Land.

The Quebec Act restored French customary law, the Coutume de Paris, in private matters alongside English common law, and allowed the Catholic Church to collect tithes. Its new boundaries ran from the Appalachian Mountains to the Mississippi River and from the Ohio River north to the lands of the Hudson's Bay Company. The seigneurial system also survived the conquest.

The Treaty of Paris of 1783, which ended the American Revolution, ceded the lands south of the Great Lakes to the United States, but Britain kept its posts there. Through Detroit, Fort Niagara and Fort Michilimackinac it went on supplying its troops and the Western Confederacy of indigenous nations until the posts were handed over after the Jay Treaty of 1794.

Loyalist refugees from the American Revolutionary War brought a substantial English-speaking Protestant population, settling mainly in the Eastern Townships, Montreal and the Pays d'en Haut west of the Ottawa River. The Constitutional Act divided the colony at that river so that the western part could have English law and an English-speaking majority.

The province had no elected legislature. The governor ruled directly with the advice of counsellors: a council to advise him on all affairs of state was created in 1764, and the Quebec Act set up a Council for the Affairs of the Province of Quebec for legislation. The governors were James Murray, Guy Carleton, later 1st Baron Dorchester, Sir Frederick Haldimand, and Carleton again from 1786.

From 1763 to 1764 the province was divided into the judicial districts of Montreal and Quebec, and a Trois-Rivières District was formed in 1790. In 1788 four districts were created in the western reaches of the Montreal District, among them the Western District, first known as Hesse District; they became the colony of Upper Canada.
province-of-saxony: The Province of Saxony, also called Prussian Saxony, was a province of the Kingdom of Prussia and later the Free State of Prussia from 1816 until 1944. It was formed from territories ceded or returned to Prussia in 1815 by the Congress of Vienna: most of the northern territories of the Kingdom of Saxony, the former French Principality of Erfurt, the Duchy of Magdeburg, the Altmark, the Principality of Halberstadt and some other districts.

The Prussian lands beyond the Elbe, the Altmark, the Principality of Halberstadt, the County of Wernigerode and the western part of the Duchy of Magdeburg, had belonged to the Kingdom of Westphalia from 1807 to 1813 before Prussia regained them. Saxon territory gained after the Battle of Leipzig in 1813, confirmed in 1815, included Wittenberg, Merseburg, Naumburg, Mansfeld, Querfurt and Henneberg. Lands given to Prussia after the Reichsdeputationshauptschluss included Erfurt, the Eichsfeld, the former imperial cities of Mühlhausen and Nordhausen, and Quedlinburg Abbey.

The province had an irregular shape. It surrounded enclaves of Brunswick and some Ernestine duchies, had several exclaves, and was almost bisected by the Duchy of Anhalt. Its majority was Protestant, with a Catholic minority of about 8 per cent in 1905. It sent 20 members to the Reichstag and 38 delegates to the Prussian House of Representatives. It was one of the richest regions of Prussia, with highly developed agriculture and industry. Before 1944 it was divided into three administrative regions, the Regierungsbezirke of Magdeburg, Merseburg and Erfurt. In 1932 it was enlarged with the regions around Ilfeld and Elbingerode, formerly part of the Province of Hanover.

On 1 July 1944 the province was divided along the lines of its three regions. The Erfurt region was merged with the Schmalkalden district of Hesse-Nassau and given to Thuringia, the Magdeburg region became the Province of Magdeburg, and the Merseburg region became the Province of Halle-Merseburg. In 1945 the Soviet military administration combined Magdeburg and Halle-Merseburg with the State of Anhalt into the Province of Saxony-Anhalt, with Halle as its capital, and in 1947 it became a state.

The East German states were abolished in 1952 and recreated in 1990 as the modern states of Thuringia and Saxony-Anhalt. The old borders lasted longest in the church, since the Church Province of Saxony in the Evangelical Church remained in existence until 2008.
province-of-westphalia: The province was formed and awarded to Prussia at the Congress of Vienna in 1815, after the Napoleonic Wars, and combined territories that Prussia already held with a range of formerly independent principalities. The new province brought Prussia a large Catholic population, a significant change for a state that had been almost entirely Protestant.

Areas long under Prussian rule, such as Minden-Ravensberg and the County of Mark, welcomed the return, and in Siegerland the Protestant majority eased acceptance. The former prince-bishoprics of Münster and Paderborn and the Duchy of Westphalia were sceptical, and the Catholic nobility was mostly hostile. Twenty years later Jacob Venedey called the Rhenanians and Westphalians Musspreußen, have-to-be-Prussians.

Hopes of a constitution, voiced by bourgeois Westphalians such as Johann Friedrich Joseph Sommer and Benedikt Waldeck, faded with the censorship of the Restoration period. German nationalism became a force in the province only in the 1840s. The Revolutions of 1848 brought a burst of political activity, but their failure was accepted with little resistance. Later the Centre Party dominated the Catholic parts of the province, its heartland, and the Soest Programme of 1870 was one of its founding documents.

From the start of the nineteenth century parts of the province were the first areas of Germany to industrialise, led by the coal mining and metalworking of the Ruhr. The population grew from 1.78 million in 1871 to over 3.6 million in 1905, and in the Arnsberg district, the centre of industry, it rose by over 400 per cent between 1818 and 1905. From around the 1870s companies drew workers from the eastern provinces of Prussia and beyond. The first miners' strike in the Ruhr took place in 1872.

In the March 1933 elections the Nazi party won 28.7 per cent in the largely Catholic Münster district, against 44 per cent across Germany. The Jewish population of Westphalia fell from about 18,000 in 1933 to a little over 7,000 in 1939, and deportations began on 10 December 1941. Prisoners of war and forced labourers worked in the province, and according to some estimates over 65,000 soldiers, mostly Soviet, died at Stukenbrock alone.

After the Second World War the province lay in the British Occupation Zone, and in July 1945 the British appointed Rudolf Amelunxen as its Oberpräsident. In 1946 it was combined with the northern part of the Rhine Province and the Free State of Lippe to form North Rhine-Westphalia. The Regional Federation of Westphalia-Lippe, established in 1953, carries on the task of the old provincial federation.
province-wellesley: Seberang Perai spans the entire mainland portion of the Malaysian state of Penang, on the Malay Peninsula, and is separated from Penang Island by the Penang Strait. It borders Kedah to the north and east and Perak to the south, and covers about 748 square kilometres, about the size of Singapore. The terrain is mostly flat and alluvial, apart from hills along the eastern border with Kedah, where Mertajam Hill, at 545 m, is the highest point.

The northern coast is sandy and exposed to the Malacca Strait, while the southern coast is muddy and covered with mangroves, sheltered by Penang Island. The name was Province Wellesley until it was changed. Seberang Perai is believed to come from a local expression for the northern banks of the Perai River, since seberang means the other side in Malay.

The area bears evidence of human habitation in the Neolithic era. The site of Guar Kepah, with human remains in shell middens, is the only known example of coastal adaptation among Neolithic humans in Malaysia. The area was once part of the Bujang Valley civilisation, and the Mahanavika Buddhagupta plaque and the Cherok Tok Kun megalith at Bukit Mertajam indicate significant Hindu influence between the 5th and 6th centuries.

In 1800 the British East India Company annexed a strip of the mainland from Kedah for 4,000 Spanish dollars. The agreement, negotiated by George Caunter for Lieutenant-Governor George Leith, gave the Company permanent sovereignty over both Penang Island and the new territory, named Province Wellesley after the Governor-General of India, Richard Wellesley. The Perai River became the border with Kedah. Throughout the 19th century the province was administered from George Town, and the Municipal Ordinance of 1913 set up town boards for Butterworth and Bukit Mertajam and a rural board for the rest.

Agriculture brought immigrants from China and India, and roads and railways led to new towns such as Butterworth and Bukit Mertajam. RAF Butterworth was opened a few months before December 1941, and was attacked by Japanese bombers on 9 December and abandoned by the Royal Air Force on 15 December, four days before Penang fell to the Japanese.

The 2020 census recorded 946,092 people in Seberang Perai, about 54 percent of the population of Penang. Malays accounted for 49 percent, ethnic Chinese for nearly 33 percent and Indians for almost 10 percent. After independence in 1957, development spread from George Town. The Port of Penang moved to the municipality in 1974, and the Perai Free Industrial Zone was created in 1980. Two road bridges and a ferry link it to George Town. Seberang Perai is known as the rice bowl of Penang, and it was made a city in 2019.
provins: There are signs of human occupation in the area as early as the Paleolithic. In Roman Gaul Provins stood at the crossroads of two regional corridors, one from Soissons to Troyes and one running south towards Sens. By the 9th century the town was minting its own coin, the denier provinois, and Charlemagne had sent his missi dominici there.

Under the protection of the Counts of Champagne, Provins hosted one of the largest Champagne fairs, crucial to the medieval economy. In the upper town the fair was held twice a year, in May and November, while the lower town had a yearly market in September. The town also became a banking centre, and the denier was widely accepted throughout Europe. The fairs continued from 1120 until 1320.

King Philip IV visited several times in the late 13th century and devastated the town with harsh taxes, which ended its prosperity and caused residents to flee. The town was besieged repeatedly and changed hands frequently from the 14th to the 16th centuries, and this instability reduced its importance. On 3 August 1429 the recently crowned Charles VII attended Mass at Saint-Quiriace there with his court and Joan of Arc. Largely untouched by the Industrial Revolution, Provins remained a small market town in the 19th century.

Provins lies in the Seine-et-Marne department in the Île-de-France region and is the sous-préfecture of its arrondissement. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001. Its 12th-century fortifications survive, including the Caesar Tower and the city walls, and many buildings of the upper town date from the 12th century, when they housed merchants' residences, shops and counting houses. Of the fair towns of the County of Champagne, Provins is the only one that has kept much of its medieval character.

The collegiate church of Saint-Quiriace was built by Henry I of Champagne to display the head of Judas Cyriacus, brought from Jerusalem, and its 12th-century construction was never completed. Two sets of caves lie under parts of the town: one probably used in the Middle Ages to store food and extract fuller's earth, the other deeper, with Bronze Age and Iron Age graffiti. Provins is a centre of cultivation of the Provins rose, Rosa gallica, from which jam, honey and sweets are made.
prudentius: Aurelius Prudentius Clemens was born in 348 in the Roman province of Tarraconensis, the northern part of the Iberian Peninsula. He practised law with some success and was twice a provincial governor, perhaps in his native country, before the emperor Theodosius I summoned him to court.

Towards the end of his life, possibly around 392, he retired from public life to become an ascetic. He fasted until evening, abstained entirely from animal food, and wrote poems, hymns and controversial works in defence of Christianity. He later collected the Christian poems written in this period and added a preface, which he himself dated 405.

His poetry was influenced by early Christian authors such as Tertullian and Ambrose, as well as by the Bible and the acts of the martyrs. The Cathemerinon, or Book in Accordance with the Hours, has twelve lyric poems on times of the day and church festivals. The Peristephanon, or Crowns of Martyrdom, has fourteen on Iberian and Roman martyrs, some suggested to him by sacred images in churches or by the inscriptions of Pope Damasus I. Two hymns from the Cathemerinon, including Corde natus ex parentis, are still in use today.

His other works include the Apotheosis, which attacks those who deny the Trinity and the divinity of Jesus, and the Hamartigenia, which attacks the dualism of Marcion. The Books Against Symmachus oppose the pagan senator Symmachus, who asked that the altar of Victory, removed by Gratian, be restored to the Senate house. The Dittochæon has 49 quatrains meant as captions for the murals of a basilica in Rome.

The Psychomachia, or Battle of Souls, describes the struggle of faith, supported by the cardinal virtues, against idolatry and the corresponding vices. It joined elements of Hellenic epic with inner psychological conflict, and became the inspiration of medieval allegorical literature; C. S. Lewis judged its influence greater than its artistic merit. By joining Christianity with classical culture, Prudentius remained one of the most popular medieval authors, and as late as the 13th century Henri d'Andeli set him beside Horace and Statius.
prussian-academy-of-sciences: The Academy was established in Berlin on 11 July 1700, four years after the Prussian Academy of Arts. Prince-elector Frederick III of Brandenburg founded it as the Electoral-Brandenburger Society of Sciences on the advice of Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, who became president, with the theologian Daniel Ernst Jablonski as vice-president. It was not funded directly from the state treasury: Frederick granted it a monopoly on producing and selling calendars in Brandenburg, a suggestion of Leibniz.

When Frederick was crowned King in Prussia in 1701 it was renamed the Royal Prussian Society of Sciences. Unlike other academies, which focused on a few topics, it was the first to cover both sciences and humanities. A statute of 1710 divided it into two classes for sciences and two for humanities, an arrangement that lasted until 1830.

Under Frederick II of Prussia the Academy changed greatly. In 1744 the Nouvelle société littéraire and the Society of Sciences were merged, and in 1746 it was renamed the Académie royale des sciences et belles-lettres. In the 18th century, when French was the language of science and culture, it was a French-language institution, and Frederick made French official. Its members included Immanuel Kant, Jean-Baptiste le Rond d'Alembert and Étienne de Condillac. Leonhard Euler was a member from 1741 to 1766, and Frederick invited Joseph-Louis Lagrange to succeed him as director.

Before 1740 the Academy had been overshadowed by bodies in London and Paris, and it went through two decades of crisis at mid-century marked by scandals and rivalries, among them the quarrel between Voltaire and Pierre-Louis de Maupertuis, its director from 1746 to 1759. By 1789 it had gained international repute.

From about 1812 it was called the Royal Prussian Academy of Sciences. On 25 November 1915 Albert Einstein presented his field equations of general relativity to it. Under Nazi rule from 1933 it was subjected to Gleichschaltung, and Jewish members were expelled in 1938.

After World War II the Academy reopened on 1 July 1946 as the German Academy of Sciences at Berlin and was renamed the Academy of Sciences of the GDR in 1972. After German reunification it was disbanded and the Berlin-Brandenburg Academy of Sciences and Humanities took its place under a treaty of 1992. Its members also included Montesquieu, Voltaire, Denis Diderot, Hermann von Helmholtz and Max Planck.
prussian-crusade: Polish princes had fought the Prussians for two centuries, using the aim of conversion to Christianity to seek control over them, while the Prussians raided Chełmno Land and Masovia for slaves. Bolesław I's missionary Adalbert of Prague was killed in 997 and Bruno of Querfurt in 1009. In March 1217 Pope Honorius III allowed the Cistercian bishop Christian of Oliva to preach a crusade against the Prussians, who had by then invaded Chełmno Land and plundered 300 churches. A crusade in 1222 and 1223 left little behind, and the knights of the Order of Dobrzyń were mostly killed. In 1226 Christian asked the Teutonic Order for help, and Emperor Frederick II granted it Chełmno Land and any future conquests in the Golden Bull of Rimini.

In 1230 Hermann von Salza sent Conrad von Landsberg with seven knights and 70 to 100 squires and sergeants to Masovia. The Order fortified the Vistula, with castles at Culm and Thorn by 1232, and was joined each year by German, Polish and Pomeranian crusaders. In 1233 and 1234 it founded Marienwerder and won a battle on the frozen Sirgune River, and it later founded Elbing and Balga. Pope Innocent IV divided Prussia into four dioceses in 1243. The First Prussian Uprising of 1242, backed by Duke Swantopelk of Pomerelia, ended in the Treaty of Christburg in February 1249, which gave converts civil liberties and considerable autonomy.

In January 1255 an army of 60,000 under King Ottokar II of Bohemia conquered Samland in less than a month. The knights founded Königsberg, named for the Bohemian king, and those Sambians who resisted were exterminated en masse. After the Samogitian victory at Durbe in 1260 the Prussians rose again, in the Great Prussian Uprising of 1260 to 1274, and destroyed most of the Order's Prussian castles in the early 1260s. German reinforcements arrived from 1265. The crusaders killed or forced the surrender of each tribe's war leader and exterminated the native population en masse if it refused to convert.

After the uprising many Prussians lost rights given at Christburg and were reduced to serfdom, and many fled to Lithuania or Sudovia. The Order rebuilt its castles in stone or brick, and the Sudovians surrendered in 1283. Prussian risings in 1286 and 1295 were short-lived, and by the end of the century the Knights controlled Prussia through their monastic state. The Prussians were gradually subjected to Christianization and cultural assimilation over the following centuries, and their language, culture and pre-Christian religion were erased by physical and ideological force.
prut: The Prut rises on the eastern slope of Mount Hoverla in the Carpathian Mountains, in Ukraine's Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast. It first flows north, turns north-east near Yaremche and south-east near Kolomyia, and after reaching the border between Moldova and Romania bends further south-east and then south. Its upper reaches, as far as Delyatyn, are mountainous, and near Yaremche it drops over the waterfall of Probiy. The lowest part of its basin is strongly marshy, and ships can travel from the mouth up to Leova. The basin covers 27,540 square kilometres, and Chernivtsi is the largest city on its banks.
Herodotus lists the river, as Porata or Pyretus, among the five rivers of the Scythian country that swell the Danube. In 1538 the army of Suleiman crossed it during the campaign of Karaboğdan.

In the Russo-Turkish War of 1710-1711 the army of Peter the Great, allied with Dimitrie Cantemir, the ruler of Moldova, met the Ottoman army under Grand Vizier Baltaci Mehmed Pasha. The Russian camp between Stănilești and the river was completely surrounded. Talks began on 21 July 1711 and the Treaty of the Prut was signed on 23 July. Cantemir went into exile in Moscow, and Greek Phanariotes from Istanbul came to rule Moldova. On 1 August 1770 Pyotr Rumyantsev defeated a larger Ottoman army at the Battle of Kagul on the river, and in 1821 Alexander Ypsilantis crossed it at Sculeni to start a rebellion in the Danubian Principalities, which set off the Greek War of Independence.

The river has been a frontier several times. Before the First World War it divided Romania from the Russian Empire, between 1918 and 1939 it ran partly through Poland and Greater Romania, and after the Second World War it marked the border between Romania and the Soviet Union. Today it forms 31 kilometres of the border between Romania and Ukraine and 711 kilometres of that between Romania and Moldova. The Stânca-Costești Dam, operated jointly by Moldova and Romania, stands on it.
przemysl: Przemyśl lies on the navigable San River, in an area connecting mountains and lowlands known as the Przemyśl Gate. Open lines of transport and fertile soil gave it importance, and trade routes link it to Central Europe. It is the second-oldest city in south-eastern Poland after Kraków, dating back to the 8th century, when a fortified gord of the Lendians, a West Slavic tribe, stood on the site. In the 9th century it became part of Great Moravia, and its name most likely dates from that period.

The region was contested between Poland, Kievan Rus and Hungary. Mieszko I annexed the Lendian lands in 970 to 980, and Nestor the Chronicler recorded the city's capture by Vladimir I of Kiev in 981. It changed hands several times in the 11th century, and in 1085 became the capital of a semi-independent Principality of Peremyshl under Kievan Rus'. An Orthodox eparchy was founded there before 1218, and from 1246 it was under Mongol suzerainty. In 1340 Casimir III of Poland retook it, and its charter on Magdeburg rights was confirmed in 1389.

The city prospered as a trade centre in the 16th century, with a population of Poles, Jews, Germans, Czechs, Armenians and Ruthenians. The Old Synagogue dates from 1559 and a Jesuit college from 1617. The Swedish invasion of the Deluge and the general decline of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth ended this prosperity in the mid-17th century. In 1772 Przemyśl passed to Austria with the First Partition of Poland. Between 1888 and 1914 it was made a first-class fortress with 44 forts. The Russians besieged it in October 1914, and it surrendered on 22 March 1915 after the fortifications were destroyed; the Central Powers retook it on 3 June 1915.

In November 1918 Poles and Ukrainians fought for the city, and Polish forces crossed the San on 11 and 12 November. In September 1939 the German army took it, and the border between Germany and the Soviet Union ran along the San through the city until June 1941. Over 500 Jews were murdered in and around the city that September. A ghetto was established on 15 July 1942, holding some 22,000 people, and until September 1943 almost all its Jews were sent to Auschwitz or Belzec. Major Max Liedtke and Albert Battel were later named Righteous Among the Nations by Yad Vashem. After 1945 the border lay about 15 kilometres east of the city.

Przemyśl is in the Subcarpathian Voivodeship. Its Old Town is listed as a Historic Monument of Poland, as is the Przemyśl Fortress. Sights include the castle built by Casimir III in the 14th century, the cathedral and the Carmelite church.
przemysl-ii: Przemysł II was born on 14 October 1257 in Poznań, the only son of Duke Przemysł I of Greater Poland and Elisabeth of Wrocław, and was born after his father's death. His uncle, Duke Bolesław the Pious, took guardianship of the duchy, and after his mother died in 1265 Przemysł and his sisters were raised in their uncle's care. In 1272 he was named nominal commander of an expedition against Brandenburg that captured the fortress of Strzelce Krajeńskie. He married Ludgarda, a granddaughter of Barnim I of Pomerania, in 1273, as part of an alliance with Pomerania.

In 1273 he became independent Duke of Poznań, though the circumstances are unclear. One document suggests he was held under house arrest in the castle of Gniezno and escaped without help. He then allied with Henry Probus, Duke of Wrocław. On the death of Bolesław the Pious in 1279 he also obtained the Duchy of Kalisz and ruled all Greater Poland.

In these years he worked with Jakub Świnka, whom he saw consecrated as Archbishop of Gniezno on 18 December 1283, to unite the Piast principalities. In 1281 Henry Probus broke the rules of hospitality by imprisoning him at a meeting and forcing political concessions. A rebellion by Sędziwój Zaremba in 1284 cost him the castle at Ołobok for a time. Under the will of Henry Probus he received the Duchy of Kraków in 1290, with the title of High Duke of Poland, but he lacked the support of the local nobility and withdrew from Lesser Poland, taking the royal crown and regalia from Wawel with him.

He allied in 1293 with Władysław the Elbow-high and Casimir II of Łęczyca against King Wenceslaus II of Bohemia, who held Kraków. After Mestwin II died in 1294, Przemysł inherited Pomerelia under the Treaty of Kępno of 1282. This made him the strongest ruler of the Piast dynasty and enabled his coronation as King of Poland at Gniezno on 26 June 1295, performed by Jakub Świnka. He was the first Polish ruler to hold the hereditary royal title after a long period of high dukes and two nominal kings.

Only nine months after his coronation, on 8 February 1296, Przemysł was murdered during a failed kidnapping attempt by men of the Margraves of Brandenburg, with some help from the noble families of Nałęcz and Zaremba. Brandenburg had meant to seize him, not to kill him. He was the last male of the Greater Poland line of the Piast dynasty. His death brought rapid intervention by those who wished to take over his lands, and by March Greater Poland was torn between Władysław the Elbow-high and Henry III of Głogów.
przemyslaw-of-raciborz: Przemysław was the fourth son of Władysław, Duke of Opole-Racibórz, and his wife Euphemia, daughter of Władysław Odonic, Duke of Greater Poland. On their father's death he and his brother Mieszko I received the districts of Racibórz, Cieszyn and Oświęcim, which they ruled together as co-dukes until 1290.

In 1285 Przemysław and his brothers, except Bolko I, supported Bishop Thomas II Zaremba in his struggle with Henry IV Probus, Duke of Wrocław, and the bishop found refuge in Racibórz. In 1287 Henry IV made a retaliatory expedition that besieged the town and almost destroyed it. In 1290 the duchy was formally divided: Przemysław kept the main town of Racibórz and Mieszko I took Cieszyn and Oświęcim. A year later Przemysław, Mieszko I and Bolko I paid homage to King Wenceslaus II of Bohemia, and Przemysław very likely became his vassal. In 1299 he granted Racibórz its urban privileges and founded a Dominican monastery there.

Przemysław died on 7 May 1306 and was buried in the Dominican monastery in Racibórz. Between 1289 and 1291 he had married Anna, daughter of Duke Konrad II of Masovia, and they had at least three children: Leszek, Anna, who married Duke Nicholas II of Opawa in 1318, and Euphemia. Constance, who ruled in Wodzisław Śląski until her death in 1351, is also believed to have been their daughter. Leszek, as the only son, inherited the whole duchy except Wodzisław Śląski, which went to Przemysław's widow Anna as her dower.
psalm-104: The psalm opens in Hebrew with barachi nafshi, bless my soul. Grogan notes that it follows the creation narrative of Genesis 1, and vanGemeren finds a chiastic structure in it. The opening verses describe God as a king moving through his royal dwelling, covering himself with light as with a garment and spreading out the heavens like a tent. Verses 5 to 9 tell of the founding of the earth and make even the deep a work of God, not something existing before him as in Babylonian creation mythology. Later verses turn to the waters, the animals and birds, and the regularity of the created world.

Verse 26 names Leviathan as just another of God's creatures, an object of entertainment rather than a challenge to his authority, as surrounding Canaanite tribes believed. Verses 27 to 30 stress that every creature depends on the creator's continuing care. The close returns to the praise of the opening and ends with the wish that sinners be consumed out of the earth. The psalm holds the first occurrence of Hallelujah in the Old Testament.

Hebrews 1:7 quotes verse 4. Many observant Jews recite the psalm on the New Moon, and verses of it stand in several daily prayers. In the Eastern Orthodox Church it is read daily at the start of Vespers, often understood as Adam's song outside the closed gates of Eden. In the Catholic Easter Vigil it answers the reading of the creation story from Genesis, and in the Book of Common Prayer it is appointed for the evening of the twentieth day of the month and for Evensong on Whitsunday.

The psalm resembles the Egyptian Great Hymn to the Aten of Akhenaten, written some 400 years earlier. Grogan, Craigie and Zimmerli point out that in the psalm the sun and the rest of creation are not gods but creations, and Grogan calls it implicitly antipagan. Mark S. Smith observes that enthusiasm even for indirect influence has been tempered in recent decades, though Egyptologists such as Jan Assmann and Donald Redford argue for it. Settings include John Dowland's in Thomas Est's psalter of 1592, Heinrich Schütz's for the Becker Psalter of 1628, Bach's cantata BWV 187 of 1726 and Philip Glass's opera Akhnaten.
psalm-23: The theme of God as a shepherd was common in ancient Israel and Mesopotamia. King Hammurabi, in the conclusion to his law code, wrote: I am the shepherd who brings well-being and abundant prosperity. This imagery was well known to the community that created the psalm, and it was easily taken into its worship. The heading ascribes the psalm to King David, who is said in the Hebrew Scriptures to have been a field shepherd as a youth, but some scholars do not accept this and propose other possibilities, commonly dating it to the post-exilic period.

The psalm begins in the King James Version with the words The LORD is my shepherd, and in Latin is known by its first words, Dominus regit me. It portrays God as a good shepherd feeding and leading his flock, and the rod and staff of verse 4 are shepherd's tools. Commentators read the green pastures and still waters as the care of a shepherd who knows that each sheep must be led personally, since sheep without a shepherd die of predators or starvation.

Harold Kushner takes verse 4, I will fear no evil, for thou art with me, as the key to the whole, finding in it the promise that no one has to face the pain of the world alone. J. Douglas MacMillan relates the table prepared in verse 5 to an old practice of feeding sheep from little raised tables, and the anointing with oil to oil poured on wounds to repel flies. Some see Psalms 22, 23 and 24 together as shepherd psalms.

The psalm is used in both Jewish and Christian liturgies. In Judaism it is traditionally sung during the third Shabbat meal, and it is commonly recited in the presence of a deceased person and at the funeral service. For Christians the image links David with Jesus, called the Good Shepherd in the Gospel of John. Orthodox Christians usually include it in the prayers of preparation for the Eucharist, and in the Catholic Church it is assigned to the Liturgy of the Hours and sung as a responsorial at Masses for the dead.

After the Reformation it was rendered in English metrical versions, including one by Thomas Sternhold in 1565 and the hymn The Lord's My Shepherd from the 1650 Scottish Psalter, traditionally sung to the tune Crimond. The King James Version of 1611 remains the best-known English text. In the 20th century the psalm became strongly associated with funerals in the English-speaking world, although the Book of Common Prayer does not include it in its burial service.
psammuthes: Psammuthes, also written Psammuthis, is the Hellenized form of the Egyptian name Pasherienmut. He is named in three epitomes of Manetho's Aegyptiaca, those of Africanus, Eusebius and the Armenian version of Eusebius, and in the Demotic Chronicle. These sources do not agree on the order of the kings of the dynasty, and it is unclear whether he came before or after Hakor. Manetho and the Demotic Chronicle both give him a reign of one year, and the highest date in the archaeological record agrees: a Mother of Apis stele that records his Year 1, fourth month of Peret.

The Egyptologist John D. Ray proposed that the throne passed to Hakor on the death of Nepherites I in 393 BCE, and that in Hakor's second year a usurper, Psammuthes, seized power and deposed him. On this view Hakor regained the throne before the second year of Psammuthes, and then dated his monuments from his first coronation, pretending the usurper had never existed.

Some monuments naming him survive: the Mother of Apis stele from the Serapeum at Saqqara, a block from Akhmim and other finds from the Theban region. He is generally credited with ordering a chapel at Karnak, which Hakor later usurped and finished, although Hakor may instead have begun it before his deposition and restored it during his second reign.

In 2022 and 2023 a joint mission of Nottingham Trent University and the University of Hawaii, directed by Jay Silverstein and Robert Littman, excavated at Tell Timai the remains of a temple of the Twenty-ninth Dynasty with a monumental inscription dedicated to Psammuthes. Thmuis, as the site was then called, was an extension of Mendes, at that time the political capital of Egypt. The temple appears to have been looted and razed after Artaxerxes III reconquered Egypt. It was rebuilt under Ptolemy II, with part of it dedicated to Arsinoe II in her Isis aspect, and this second temple appears to have been destroyed in the Great Rebellion mentioned on the Rosetta Stone.
psamtik-i: In 671 BCE the Assyrian king Esarhaddon invaded Egypt against the Kushite rulers of the Twenty-fifth Dynasty and set up twelve Delta kinglets, a Dodecarchy, allying with Necho I of Sais, the most powerful of them. In 665 BCE the Kushite king Tantamani invaded Lower Egypt again. Necho I died in battle and his son Psamtik fled to Syria. In 664 BCE Ashurbanipal, Esarhaddon's son, retook Memphis, sacked Thebes and expelled Tantamani, and Psamtik returned with the Assyrian force and was installed as ruler of Sais and Memphis.

Psamtik I was the first pharaoh of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty, ruling from Sais between 664 and 610 BCE. According to Herodotus, the other kinglets chased him from Memphis into the Delta swamps after he fulfilled an oracle by pouring a libation from a bronze vessel. From 662 BCE he made contact with Gyges, king of Lydia, who sent Ionian Greek and Carian mercenaries, with whom he reconquered Memphis and defeated the other kinglets. He placed mercenaries in garrisons at Daphnae and Elephantine, and by 657 BCE he held the Delta.

In 656 BCE he sent an expedition to Thebes that made the God's Wife of Amun, Shepenupet II, adopt his daughter Nitocris I as heiress. In 655 and 654 BCE he fought Libyan tribes and put a garrison at Marea. Herodotus describes a twenty-nine year siege of Ashdod, though its dating is uncertain. After Ashurbanipal died in 627 BCE the Assyrian Empire unravelled. The Scythians reached as far south as Judah, and Psamtik persuaded them with gifts to turn back.

Psamtik died in 610 BCE and was succeeded by his son Necho II. Herodotus reports that Psamtik tried to find the origin of language by giving two newborn children to a shepherd, who was told to let no one speak to them. When one child cried bekós, Psamtik concluded that the word was Phrygian, the Phrygian word for bread, and that Phrygian was the original language. No other source confirms the story.

In March 2017 Egyptian and German archaeologists found a colossal quartzite statue about 7.9 metres tall at Heliopolis, in Cairo. It was first thought to depict Ramesses II, but an inscription with one of Psamtik's names identified it as his.
psamtik-ii: Psamtik II, known to the Greeks as Psammetichus, was a king of the Saite-based Twenty-sixth Dynasty and the son of Necho II. His prenomen, Nefer-Ib-Re, means beautiful is the heart of Re. A stela from Thebes dated to the third year of his reign records a heavy defeat inflicted on the kingdom of Kush, and the Egyptian army marched as far south as the Third or even the Fourth Cataract. It was the first confrontation between Egypt and Nubia since the reign of Tantamani.

The Karnak stela says that Nubians rose against the army at Pnubs and capitulated before a single arrow was loosed, and that four thousand two hundred men were brought back as prisoners. A Greek graffito on the colossal statue of Ramesses II at Abu Simbel records that those who sailed with the king came as far as the river permits, the foreign-speaking troops, Greeks and Carians, led by Potasimto and the Egyptians by Amasis. The campaign weakened Kush, and the Nubian rulers moved their capital south from Napata to Meroe, although most historians agree this was not the only reason. Elephantine remained Egypt's southern border, and the names and royal emblems of the Kushite 25th Dynasty kings were hacked out of their monuments in Egypt.

Psamtik was also a builder. A pair of obelisks more than 21.79 metres high stood in the temple of Heliopolis, and Augustus later had one of them, today the Obelisk of Montecitorio, brought to Rome in 10 BCE. At Philae he built a kiosk, the oldest known monument on the island, and at Hibis in the El-Kharga Oasis he founded a temple of Amun, Mut and Khonsu, whose decoration was completed only under the Persian king Darius I and possibly Darius II.

Psamtik II died in 589 BCE and was succeeded by his son Apries, born to Queen Takhut. Another of their children, Ankhnesneferibre, served as God's Wife of Amun until the Persian conquest of 525 BCE. According to Herodotus, ambassadors from Elis visited the king, and the wise men of Egypt told them that the Olympic Games should admit only strangers, since the Eleans would favour their own townsmen.
psamtik-iii: Psamtik III, called Psammetichus or Psammenitus by the Graeco-Romans, was the son of the pharaoh Amasis II and one of his wives, Queen Tentkheta. He succeeded his father in 526 BCE, when Amasis died after a long and prosperous reign of some 44 years. According to Herodotus, who documented most of what is known about his reign and life, he had a son named Amasis and a wife and daughter whom no source names.

Psamtik ruled Egypt for no more than six months. A few days after his coronation rain fell at Thebes, a rare event that frightened some Egyptians, who took it as a bad omen. The young and inexperienced pharaoh faced a Persian invasion led by King Cambyses II, whose army crossed the Sinai desert with the help of the Arabians.

In the spring of 525 BCE a battle was fought near Pelusium, a city on Egypt's eastern frontier, and the Egyptians were defeated. Psamtik and his army withdrew to Memphis, which the Persians captured after a long siege, taking Psamtik himself. Shortly afterwards Cambyses ordered the public execution of two thousand of the principal citizens, including, according to some sources, a son of the fallen pharaoh.

Herodotus describes Psamtik's captivity in Book III of his Histories. Psamtik's daughter and the daughters of the Egyptian noblemen were enslaved, while his son and two thousand sons of noblemen were sentenced to death, in retaliation for the killing of a Persian ambassador and the two hundred crew of his boat. An old man who had once been the king's friend was reduced to beggary. All of them were paraded before Psamtik, who showed grief only at the sight of the beggar.

His compassion led to his being spared, though his son had already been put to death. He was then taken into the entourage of the Persian king at Susa. After a while he tried to raise a rebellion among the Egyptians. When Cambyses learned of it, Herodotus reports, Psamtik drank bull's blood and died at once. He was the last pharaoh of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty.
pshavi: Pshavi lies chiefly among the southern foothills of the Greater Caucasus, along the Pshavis Aragvi River and the upper reaches of the Iori River. It borders Khevsureti to the north, and the two regions were historically grouped together under the name Pkhovi. To the east lie the western fringe of Tusheti and the northernmost tip of the Pankisi Gorge, to the south the Zhinvali Reservoir and the Georgian Military Road, and to the west Mtiuleti and Gudamakari.

The region falls into three valley systems. The historical heartland, Pshavi proper, has about ten villages stretching east from the meeting of the Pshavis Aragvi and Khevsuretis Aragvi rivers to Ukanapshavi, centred on the village of Shuapkho. Lower Pshavi, with about thirty villages and its main village at Magharoskari, runs south along the Pshavis Aragvi to the Zhinvali Reservoir, taking in the Chargali, Sharakhevi and Sondiskhevi valleys. A half-dozen more villages lie along the upper Iori.

Pshavi is now part of the Mtskheta-Mtianeti region. Its population has fallen sharply through a rural exodus that began in the 19th century, and many former villages are now only a few houses; an early 20th-century census counted 210 households in Pshavi proper and 368 in Lower Pshavi. In 2016 the Georgian government began to consider giving the region Protected Landscape status.

The Pshavs speak a dialect of Georgian close to that of the Khevsurs. Nominally Georgian Orthodox, they have, like other mountain peoples, kept some pre-Christian beliefs, which a few still profess in a syncretic form at the region's many shrines. Luka Razikashvili (1861 to 1915), known as Vazha-Pshavela, a lad from Pshavi, was born in Chargali, where his home is a house museum.
pskov: Pskov stands on the Velikaya River in north-western Russia, about 20 kilometres east of the Estonian border. Its name was originally Pleskov, which may be loosely translated as the town of purling waters. The earliest mention, under 903, records that Igor of Kiev married a local lady, Olga, later Saint Olga of Kiev. Pskovians sometimes take that year as the city's foundation, and in 2003 they marked its 1,100th anniversary.

The first prince of Pskov was Sudislav, the youngest son of Vladimir the Great. In the 12th and 13th centuries the town adhered politically to the Novgorod Republic. The Teutonic Knights took it in 1241, and Alexander Nevsky recaptured it several months later. To secure their independence from the knights the Pskovians elected a Lithuanian prince, Daumantas, known in Russia as Dovmont, as their leader in 1266. He fortified the town, and the core of the citadel still bears the name Dovmont's town.

Novgorod formally recognised Pskov's independence in 1348, and it became the capital of the Pskov Republic. Its most powerful force was the merchants who traded with the Hanseatic League. The veche promulgated a law code, the Pskov Charter, which was one of the principal sources of the all-Russian law code of 1497. The Kremlin withstood twenty-six sieges in the 15th century alone, and a local school of icon-painting flourished.

The Grand Duchy of Moscow annexed the city in 1510. Three hundred families were deported to central Russia and merchants and military families from Muscovy were settled there. In the Livonian War it withstood a prolonged siege in 1581 and 1582 by a Polish-Lithuanian army of 50,000 under King Stephen Báthory, defended mainly by civilians. It also withstood a Swedish siege in 1615. Peter the Great's conquest of Estonia and Livonia ended its traditional role as a border fortress.

Pskov is the administrative centre of Pskov Oblast and preserves much of its medieval walls, built from the 13th century onwards. Within the Krom, the medieval citadel, stands Trinity Cathedral, founded in 1138 and rebuilt in the 1690s, which holds the tombs of the saint princes Vsevolod and Dovmont. The Churches of the Pskov School of Architecture were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019.
psusennes-i: Psusennes is the Greek form of Pasibkhanu or Pasebakhaenniut, which means The Star Appearing in the City. His throne name, Akheperre Setepenamun, means Great are the Manifestations of Ra, chosen of Amun. He was the son of the High Priest Pinedjem I and of Duathathor-Henuttawy, a daughter of Ramesses XI, and so a grandson of Ramesses XI through his mother. His brother Menkheperre was High Priest of Amun at Thebes, and the two appear to have worked in close cooperation. Psusennes married his sister Mutnedjmet and also Wiay, and his daughter Isetemkheb married Menkheperre.

The length of his reign is not certain. Different copies of the records of Manetho give him either 41 or 46 years, and the editors of the Handbook to Ancient Egyptian Chronology estimate 46. Two anonymous Year 49 dates from Thebes and Kom Ombo have been given to Menkheperre, who is documented in a Year 48 record, but Aidan Dodson and Thomas Schneider assign Year 49 to Psusennes.

Pi-Ramesses, on the Pelusiac branch of the Nile, suffered when the river silted up and drought made river transport to the city difficult. Psusennes moved the centre of government to Zaon, Greek Tanis, on the Tanitic branch. He turned Tanis into a full capital, surrounding its temple with a brick temenos wall. The sanctuary of Amun was made of blocks salvaged from Pi-Ramesses, many still bearing the name of Ramesses II, and obelisks of Ramesses II were brought from the old city. He built the enclosure walls and the central part of the Great Temple, dedicated to Amun, Mut and Khonsu, which Siamun completed.

His successor Amenemope may have been his son. Another son, Ankhefenmut, was buried in his tomb with his name and titles erased, which suggests he fell from favour. Pharaoh Amenemope and General Wendjebauendjed were also buried in the tomb, and Shoshenq II and two anonymous royal individuals were reburied there after their own tombs were inundated with water.

Pierre Montet found the tomb at Tanis, known as NRT III, in February 1940, intact, the only royal tomb of Egypt found unrobbed.
