It is distinct from Pular, the Fula variety of Guinea and the Fouta Djallon, though the two are to some extent mutually intelligible.

Pulaar has 21 noun classes, marked by suffixes, which often reflect a noun's meaning: the ɗam class covers liquids and the nge class bovines such as the cow, naage, a trace of the herding life of the Fulɓe. Its counting is quinary-decimal, so that seven, jeeɗiɗi, joins the words for five and two. Verbs take -t, -d, -n and -r suffixes, normally in that order, which mark meanings such as retaliation, reversal, repetition and intensity.

Pulaar has lost ground to Wolof and French. A study of 1987 to 1988 found its use declining among younger bilingual speakers in northern Senegal, and the scholars John Hames and Fiona McLaughlin link this to the economic and cultural weight of Wolof. In Mauritania, Hames argues, the government of President Moktar Ould Daddah favoured Arabic education, and a law of 1965 made Arabic compulsory in primary and secondary schools.

The Association pour la Renaissance du Pulaar taught literacy in Mauritania, with more government funding after Ould Daddah's overthrow in the late 1970s, but its work was reduced after the coup of 1984. After the Manifesto of the Oppressed Black Mauritanian appeared in 1986, crackdowns on Pulaar speakers and teachers increased, and the activist Djigo Tafsirou was arrested and possibly died in detention. In Senegal Pulaar was admitted as an official language by presidential decree in 1971.
pulakeshin-i: Pulakeshin was the son and successor of Ranaraga and a grandson of Jayasimha, the earliest historically attested ruler of the family. Records of the later Kalyani Chalukyas name his father as Vijayaditya, but historians set these aside, since the Vatapi Chalukya records name Ranaraga explicitly. The name appears in inscriptions as Polekeshin, Polikeshin and Pulikeshin; J. F. Fleet and D. C. Sircar read it as a Sanskrit-Kannada hybrid meaning tiger-haired, while K. A. Nilakanta Sastri derived it from Sanskrit words for great and lion.

As the first sovereign ruler of his line, he has been called the real founder of the dynasty. His earliest inscription, issued at Badami under the title Vallabheshvara, records the Ashvamedha, but the early records give no details of his campaigns, and Sircar suggested that the dynasty's military successes in this period belonged to his son and commander-in-chief Kirttivarman I. Inscriptions give him titles such as Satyashraya, Rana-vikrama, Shri-prithvi-vallabha, which marked paramountcy, and Dharma-maharaja. A stone tablet at Amminabhavi of 566-567 records his grant to the shrine of the deity Kalideva on the occasion of a solar eclipse.

The epigraphic evidence shows him following the Vedic religion. The Mahakuta Pillar inscription of his son Mangalesha lists the Agnishtoma, Vajapeya, Ashvamedha, Hiranyagarbha and other Shrauta sacrifices, and the Nerur inscription credits him with knowledge of the Manusmriti, the Puranas and the Ramayana. Nilakanta Sastri took the title Dharma-maharaja to mean that he promoted the Vedic faith against Buddhism and Jainism.

He married Durlabha-devi of the Bappura lineage, whom the Mahakuta inscription compares to Damayanti; the Aihole inscription's mention of Indukanti most likely names another queen. He was succeeded first by Kirttivarman I, whose own Badami inscription implies an accession in 566-567, and then by Mangalesha. A prince named Pugavarman is sometimes taken for another son, though he may have been Mangalesha's.
pulakeshin-ii: Pulakeshin was a son of the Chalukya king Kirttivarman I. He appears to have been a minor when his father died, and his uncle Mangalesha succeeded to the throne. Inscriptions of the later Chalukyas of Kalyani claim that Mangalesha returned the kingdom when Pulakeshin grew up, but Pulakeshin's own Aihole inscription contradicts this, and he seems to have overthrown his uncle. Historian K. V. Ramesh suggests that Ereya was his name before his coronation. His hereditary epithet Satyashraya, refuge of truth, often stood for his name, and later rulers called the dynasty Satyashraya-kula.

Facing many enemies after the war of succession, he won over Govinda and defeated Appayika, besieged Banavasi and ended the Kadamba dynasty, giving most of its land to his Alupa vassals, and received the submission of the Gangas of Talakad, whose ruler Durvinita married a daughter to him. He besieged Puri, the capital of the Mauryas of Konkana. The Aihole inscription credits him with subjugating the Latas, the Malavas and the Gurjaras, and after his victory over Harshavardhana he took the title Parameshvara.

In the east the rulers of Dakshina Kosala and Kalinga accepted his suzerainty. He captured Pishtapura, fought a battle near Kunala lake, now Kolleru Lake, conquered the Vishnukundina kingdom and appointed his younger brother Kubja Vishnu-vardhana as its governor. According to the Persian historian Al-Tabari he sent presents and letters to the Sasanian emperor Khosrow II about 625 CE. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, who visited in 641–642, described him as a man of farsighted resource and astuteness.

Pulakeshin was a Vaishnavite but patronised other faiths. The Jain poet Ravikirtti, who composed the Aihole inscription, built the Meguti temple at Aihole in his reign, work began then on the Shaivite shrines called the Upper, Lower and Malegitti Shivalaya, and Xuanzang counted over 100 Buddhist monasteries in his empire with more than 5,000 monks. The Aihole inscription describes an empire bound by the oceans on three sides, though there is no evidence that he annexed the Chola, Kerala or Pandya kingdoms. The order of succession among his sons is unclear.
punakha: Punakha is the administrative centre of Punakha dzongkhag, one of the 20 districts of Bhutan. It lies at an elevation of 1,200 metres above sea level, about 72 km from Thimphu, a journey of about three hours by car. Unlike Thimphu, it is quite warm in winter and hot in summer. Rice is the main crop along the valleys of the Pho Chhu and Mo Chhu, the two main rivers of Bhutan, and Dzongkha is widely spoken in the district.

Punakha was the capital of Bhutan and the seat of government until 1955, when the capital was moved to Thimphu. Its great fortress, Pungthang Dewachen Phodrang (Palace of Great Happiness), better known as Punakha Dzong, was constructed under the command of Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal and is believed to have taken about two years to complete. It is the winter residence of Bhutan's Central Monastic Body, led by the Je Khenpo, and houses the most sacred relics of the Southern Drukpa Kagyu school, including the Rangjung Kasarpani, and the sacred remains of Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal and Tertön Padma Lingpa.

In 1907 the dzong was the site of the coronation of Ugyen Wangchuck as the first King of Bhutan. Three years later a treaty was signed at Punakha by which the British agreed not to interfere in Bhutanese internal affairs, while Bhutan allowed Britain to direct its foreign affairs. The dzong has suffered repeatedly. It was partially destroyed by fire in 1780, 1789, 1802, 1831, 1849 and 1986, and it experienced an earthquake in 1897 and a flood in 1994. Standing at the confluence of the two rivers, it is vulnerable to flash floods caused by glacier lakes, and flood damage is recorded in 1957, 1960 and 1994.

A covered wooden cantilever bridge over the Mo Chhu was built together with the dzong in the 17th century and was washed away by a flash flood in 1957 or 1958. A new bridge of traditional construction, with a free span of 55 metres, was begun in 2006 and completed in 2008 with help from Germany. The valley is known in Bhutan for rice farming, both red and white, and the village of Ritsha, with its two-storey houses of pounded mud on stone foundations, is often called the rice bowl of Bhutan. Punakha Domchoe, held in the first month of the Bhutanese year, is an important festival combining ritual with a display of horsemanship and sword play.
punctation-of-olmutz: The German Confederation, dominated by Austria, had been dissolved in the Revolutions of 1848 and partially succeeded by the Frankfurt Assembly. After the assembly failed, Prussia took the initiative in early 1850 with the Erfurt Union, a federation of most of the German states under its own lead. The two powers were thus in conflict over the leadership of Germany.

A dispute between the Elector of Hesse and his subjects gave the Austrian chancellor Felix zu Schwarzenberg the occasion to isolate Prussia further. Austrian and allied armies advanced into the Electorate of Hesse, and on 8 November 1850 the Prussian army came close to war with Bavaria, an ally of Austria, near Fulda-Bronnzell. In the Warsaw negotiations of October 1850 Tsar Nicholas I of Russia had already taken Austria's side, which was part of the reason why Prussia decided to give in.

The agreement, also called the Agreement of Olmütz, came out of a conference held in the town, now Olomouc in the Czech Republic, and closed the Autumn Crisis of 1850. Prussia gave up its claim to lead the German states and submitted to Austrian leadership of the restored confederation. It agreed to demobilise, to take part in the intervention of the German Diet in Hesse and in Holstein, and renounced any resumption of the Erfurt Union. Austria for its part agreed to call a conference of ministers to discuss a reform of the confederation.

The ministerial conference that Austria had promised met in Dresden the following year and ended without result, so that the confederation continued unreformed under Austrian leadership. The name of humiliation was given to the treaty because many saw in it a capitulation of the Prussians to the Austrians.
pune: Pune lies on the western margin of the Deccan Plateau at about 560 metres above sea level, on the leeward side of the Sahyadri range, and is about 149 kilometres by road south-east of Mumbai. The old city, with its many peths, stands on the east bank of the Mutha river, while the cantonment areas of Khadki and Camp were laid out by the British. The earliest reference to the town is a Rashtrakuta dynasty copper plate of 937 CE, which names it Punya-vishaya. Copper plates of 858 and 868 CE show an agricultural settlement called Punnaka on the site, and the Pataleshwar Caves, a rock-cut temple complex, date from the same era.

The Seuna Yadavas of Devagiri held Pune from the 9th century to 1327, and Muslim sultanates held it until the late 1600s. In 1599 the Ahmadnagar Sultanate granted it as a jagir to Maloji Bhosale, who passed it to his son Shahaji. Shahaji chose the town as the residence of his wife Jijabai and young son Shivaji, the future founder of the Maratha empire, and the Lal Mahal, where Shivaji spent his youth, was completed in 1640. Baji Rao I, appointed Peshwa in 1720, moved his base to Pune in 1728 and began Shaniwar Wada, finished in 1730, which turned a kasbah into a city.

After the Peshwas were defeated at the Battle of Khadki on 5 November 1817 the British seized the city and placed it under the Bombay Presidency. They built a large military cantonment to the east, while the old city kept narrow lanes and districts divided by caste and religion. Pune became the monsoon capital of the Governor of Bombay, and the Southern Command of the Indian Army was established there in 1895.

Pune is the administrative headquarters of Pune district in Maharashtra, with 3,124,458 people in the city at the 2011 census. Marathi is the official and most spoken language. The University of Pune, now Savitribai Phule Pune University, was founded in 1949, the National Chemical Laboratory in 1950 and the National Defence Academy in 1955. Among historic sites are Shaniwar Wada and the Aga Khan Palace, where Mahatma Gandhi was interned during the Quit India movement. The first rules of modern badminton were drawn up in Pune in 1873.
punic-wars: For a century before the First Punic War the Roman Republic had expanded in southern Italy, and by 270 BCE, when the last Greek cities of Magna Graecia submitted at the end of the Pyrrhic War, it had conquered all of peninsular Italy south of the Arno. Carthage, with its capital in what is now Tunisia, ruled a maritime empire that covered southern Iberia, much of the North African coast, the Balearic Islands, Corsica, Sardinia and the western half of Sicily. The most reliable source is the Greek historian Polybius, whom modern historians accept largely at face value despite his favourable treatment of Scipio Aemilianus.

The First Punic War began in 264 BCE over control of the Sicilian city of Messana, when Rome had a strong army but no navy. It lasted twenty-three years and was fought mostly on and around Sicily. After Carthage was defeated in 241 BCE it paid large reparations and Sicily became the first Roman province. Hamilcar then took his army to Iberia in 237 BCE and built a largely autonomous state in the south-east, with silver mines and manpower.

The Second Punic War began in 218 BCE after Hannibal captured Saguntum. Hannibal crossed the Alps and campaigned in Italy for fourteen years, repeatedly defeating Roman legions. A Roman invasion of Africa in 204 BCE led to his recall, and he was defeated at Zama in 202 BCE. The treaty of 201 BCE stripped Carthage of its overseas territories, imposed an indemnity and forbade it to wage war without Rome's permission. The Third Punic War began in 149 BCE, after Carthage, harried by the Numidians under Masinissa, raised an army against the treaty. Elements of the Senate led by Cato the Elder had long wished to destroy Carthage.

In 146 BCE the Romans stormed Carthage, sacked it, slaughtered or enslaved its population and demolished the city. A curse was placed on anyone who might resettle the site, which was confiscated as public land. The remaining Carthaginian territory became the Roman province of Africa, with Utica as its capital, a major source of grain for Rome. Punic cities elsewhere, such as those in Mauretania, kept their own government and culture, and the Punic language continued to be spoken in North Africa until the 7th century CE.
punisa-racic: Račić was born on 12 July 1886 in the village of Slatina, near Andrijevica, in the Principality of Montenegro. In 1902, aged sixteen, he entered the service of the politician Nikola Pašić, who regarded him as a son and encouraged his ambitions. He was active in Serbian nationalist circles and claimed to have organised attempts on the lives of King Ferdinand I of Bulgaria, King Constantine I of Greece and Emperor Wilhelm II of Germany.

After the First World War he gained a reputation for suppressing pro-Bulgarian movements in Macedonia. Until 1928 he led the Association of Serbian Chetniks "Petar Mrkonjić", which built a large network across Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he is reported to have had ties to the Karađorđević dynasty. He was elected to parliament on 27 September 1927.

On 19 June 1928 Račić and twenty-three colleagues demanded that Stjepan Radić be examined for mental illness or punished for calling Serbian ministers plunderers and bandits, and Račić and Toma Popović shouted threats against Radić in the chamber. Serbian newspapers such as Politika, Samouprava and Jedinstvo had called for the murder of Croat politicians.

The next evening, after the deputy Ivan Pernar accused him of plundering Muslim homes in Macedonia, Račić drew a handgun at the podium. He shot Pernar and Ivan Granđa, who survived, then Đuro Basariček as he aimed at Svetozar Pribićević, then Radić, and finally Radić's nephew Pavle at point-blank range. Radić died on 8 August 1928; before his death he alleged that the shooting had been planned within the Radical club.

Five people were killed in clashes with police in Zagreb in the following ten days, and the shooting destroyed popular support for the kingdom in Croatia. Račić, treated as a hero through much of Serbia, gave himself up and was sentenced to 60 years, reduced at once to 20. He served most of it under house arrest in a comfortable villa with three servants, a leniency likely owed to his Chetnik connections, and was released on 27 March 1941.

The Ustaše later used the shooting as one of their excuses for the genocide and persecution of Serbs during World War II. Račić was killed by the Yugoslav Partisans on 16 October 1944, during the liberation of Belgrade from the Axis powers.
punjab: Punjab is a geographical, ethnolinguistic and historical region in the north-west of South Asia, within modern Pakistan and north-western India. Its name comes from the Persian panj, five, and āb, water, and means the land of five waters: the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Sutlej and Beas, all tributaries of the Indus. The Mahabharata names a region Panchanada, and the ancient Greeks called it Pentapotamía. The Rigveda knew a land of seven rivers, Sapta Sindhu, which also counted the Indus and the Kabul. Its boundaries are imprecisely defined: in the sixteenth-century Mughal Empire the term meant a smaller area between the Indus and the Sutlej.

Settlements grew along the five rivers as early as the Indus Valley civilisation, which flourished from about 3000 BCE. Indo-Aryan migrations passed through the region in waves between 1500 BCE and 500 BCE, and the bulk of the Rigveda was composed there between about 1500 and 1200 BCE. Local kingdoms known as Mahajanapadas arose. In the ninth century the Odi Shahi dynasty from Gandhara, called the Hindu Shahis, ruled western Punjab along with Kabulistan. The Mughals gained power in the early sixteenth century and gradually controlled the whole region from their capital at Lahore, until the dynasty weakened in the eighteenth century and Afghan rulers took the region.

Maharajah Ranjit Singh founded the Sikh Empire, which lasted from 1799, when he captured Lahore, until 1849, when it was conquered in the Second Anglo-Sikh War. It stretched from the Khyber Pass in the west to western Tibet in the east and from Mithankot in the south to Kashmir in the north, with Lahore as its capital. It had about 3.5 million people in 1831 and was the last major region of the subcontinent annexed by the British Empire. The British Punjab Province was one of the largest provinces of the British Raj. After the Partition of British India in 1947 the region was divided into West and East Punjab, and in 1966 India divided East Punjab into Punjab, Haryana and Himachal Pradesh.

Lahore is the largest city and historic capital, and other major cities include Faisalabad, Rawalpindi, Multan, Amritsar, Ludhiana and Chandigarh. The Punjabi people speak Punjabi, written in the Gurmukhi script in India and in Shahmukhi in Pakistan. Muslims are the majority in Pakistani Punjab and Sikhs in Indian Punjab, with Hindu, Christian, Jain and other communities. Islam arrived through southern Punjab in the eighth century and became the majority religion by the sixteenth, largely through Sufi missionaries. Agriculture has been central to the economy, and wheat, rice, cotton and sugarcane are grown; the Green Revolution of the mid-1960s to the mid-1970s made the region a major food producer.
puno-region: Puno lies in the south-east of Peru and is the fifth largest department of the country, after Cuzco, Madre de Dios, Ucayali and Loreto. It is bordered by Bolivia to the east and by the departments of Madre de Dios, Cusco, Arequipa, Moquegua and Tacna. Its capital, the city of Puno, stands on Lake Titicaca in the Altiplano, or high sierra, on the Collao Plateau. The Andean mountains make up 70 per cent of the territory and the rest is covered by Amazon rainforest.

The western part of Lake Titicaca, the world's highest navigable lake, lies in the department. Its islands include Taquile, Suasi and Amantaní, known for weaving and pre-Columbian constructions. The Uros live on floating islands made of totora reeds and travel in boats of the same material. The Titicaca National Reserve protects extensive stretches of reeds and many species. The climate is cold and dry with a four-month rainy season, while the rainforest is warm.

In ancient times the Collao plateau was inhabited by Aymara groups, among them the Collas, Zapanas, Kallahuayos and Lupacas, and the Quechuas came later. The area was the territory of the Tiahuanacos, between 800 and 1200 CE, who were the highest cultural expression of the Aymara people in what is now Peru and Bolivia. The Incas took over these lands in the fifteenth century. The chronicler Inca Garcilaso de la Vega places the legend of Manco Cápac and Mama Ocllo, who emerged from the waters of Lake Titicaca to found the Inca Empire, in these ancient times.

Under Spanish rule Puno was the obligatory route for travellers to Potosí in Bolivia, and the Spanish, drawn by mining, left an important colonial legacy. In 1668 the viceroy, the Conde de Lemos, established San Juan Bautista de Puno as capital of the province of Paucarcolla; it was later called San Carlos de Puno after Charles II of Spain and became capital of the Intendancy of Puno. The department was created by the Reglamento Provisional de Elecciones of 26 April 1822. In 1870 the Arequipa to Puno railway was installed and navigation began on Lake Titicaca.

The department is divided into 13 provinces and 107 districts, and is run by a regional government. Indigenous people are the majority. In the 2007 census the language first learnt by most residents was Quechua (38.01 per cent), followed by Spanish (34.81 per cent) and Aymara (26.93 per cent). The Quechua spoken is the Cusco-Collao variety.
puntarenas: Puntarenas is a city on the Pacific coast of Costa Rica and the seat of the Puntarenas canton, which is the first canton of the province of the same name, so the city is also the provincial capital. The city comprises the districts of Puntarenas, Chacarita and El Roble. The name joins punta and arenas, meaning point and sands, and is first recorded in February 1720, when the pirate John Clipperton noted in his journals that he had come to a Punta de Arena, the needle-like strip of land on which the city stands. The province is the most extensive in the country, with its largest section in the south, far from the city.

The first European to reach the site was Gil González Dávila in 1522. The Gulf of Nicoya served as an entryway to the interior of Costa Rica, but the port of Puntarenas was not developed until 1840, when coffee production in the highlands reached exportable volumes. In 1845 the Congress of the Republic declared it a duty-free port, with the exception of cognac and hard liquor.

At first the coffee came down to the port in oxcarts along a trail through the mountains. In 1859 a stretch of railway was completed between Puntarenas and Esparza, one of the country's earliest Spanish settlements, founded in 1574. The line was eventually built through to San José and opened in 1910.

The railway kept the Pacific port at the centre of the regional economy throughout the 20th century. The old port facilities aged and could not take the much larger ships of modern fleets, so in the 1980s a new port was built to the south at Caldera, where ships had anchored in colonial times and which had been the first port site used since 1522.

Puntarenas has some 100,000 inhabitants with its surrounding neighbourhoods. Its Pacific beaches attract tourists, especially surfers, and regular ferries cross to the Nicoya Peninsula. Seafood such as ceviche characterises its cooking.
puntland: Puntland occupies the north-eastern portion of Somalia, about 212,510 square kilometres or roughly one third of the country. It borders Somaliland to the west, the Gulf of Aden to the north, the Guardafui Channel and the Indian Ocean to the east, Galmudug State to the south and Ethiopia to the south-west. Cape Guardafui forms the tip of the Horn of Africa, and Ras Hafun is the easternmost point on the African continent. The Golis Mountains, Galgala and Al Madow are among its mountains.

The climate is semi-arid and warm, favouring pastoralism, and no area receives more than 400 millimetres of rain a year. The name derives from the Land of Punt mentioned in ancient Egyptian sources, whose exact location is still unknown. Many studies place Punt in present-day Somalia, while others place it elsewhere.

The Majeerteen Sultanate was founded in the mid-18th century and rose to prominence the next century under Boqor Osman Mahamuud. Centred on Alula, it controlled much of northern and central Somalia in the 19th and early 20th centuries and ruled the towns of Alula, Bargaal, Bosaso and Hafun. It traded widely and made treaties with foreign powers. A struggle between Boqor Osman and his cousin Yusuf Ali Kenadid nearly destroyed it; Kenadid was forced into exile in Yemen, then returned in the 1870s with Hadhrami musketeers and established the Sultanate of Hobyo in 1878.

After the Somali Civil War began in 1991, a constitutional conference was held in Garoowe in 1998 over three months. Political leaders, traditional elders, business people and civil society representatives took part, and the autonomous Puntland State of Somalia was established to provide services and security and to facilitate trade. Abdullahi Yusuf Ahmed was its founding president. A new regional constitution was passed on 15 June 2009, and in January 2009 the short-lived quasi-state of Maakhir was incorporated into Puntland. Control of the Sool, Sanaag and Ayn provinces in the west has been disputed with Somaliland.

Puntland is a federal member state of Somalia with its capital at Garoowe, and Bosaso is its commercial capital. Its president and vice president are elected by a unicameral parliament. About 39 per cent of its people were estimated to be nomads in 2016, and the population is mainly Somali, with the Darod especially well represented and a number of Mehri residents. Islam is the main religion.

The coastline is 1,600 kilometres long and rich in fish. Livestock, fishing, frankincense, myrrh, gum arabic and trade are the main sources of income, and the key trading centres are Bosaso and Galkayo. Puntland also has its own security force and its own public broadcaster, Puntland TV and Radio, founded in April 2013.
punto-fijo-pact: On 23 January 1958 President Marcos Pérez Jiménez fled Venezuela for the Dominican Republic, and a group of military leaders took control. His government had been a dictatorship that relied on oil revenues to pay for a vast campaign of urbanisation and modernisation, and the United States had supported it as a reliable source of oil. Venezuela had been under dictatorial rule for nearly all its history since independence in 1830. With oil prices falling and the mood after the coup unsettled, the parties feared that a disputed election would harm the country, and they sought a way to bind themselves to accept the coming presidential vote.

Three representatives of each party signed, among them Rómulo Betancourt of Acción Democrática, Rafael Caldera of COPEI and Jóvito Villalba of the Unión Republicana Democrática. The parties promised to respect election results, prevent the dominance of any single party, work together against dictatorship, and share a basic programme of government. The winners were to consider bringing members of the other signatories into national unity governments. The pact also guaranteed obligatory military service and better salaries, housing and equipment for the armed forces.

The pact allowed the uncontested election of Betancourt, who became the first president in 20th-century Venezuela elected by universal suffrage to finish his term; Caldera later became president too. In 1962 the Unión Republicana Democrática refused to sign the Costa Rica agreement excluding Cuba from the Inter-American system and left the governing coalition.

Acción Democrática and COPEI came to rely on shared oil revenues to hold power through patronage and clientelism. When oil income fell sharply in the 1980s, public trust in them declined; the Caracazo riots of 27 February 1989 followed sudden rises in transport and fuel prices. In 1993 Caldera was elected president for another party, Convergencia, and in 1998 Hugo Chávez campaigned on breaking the two-party system. The pact is often credited with the most stable period in the republic's history, and criticised for enabling an inflexible two-party system.
pura-kehen: Pura Kehen stands at the foot of a wooded hill in Cempaga, about 2 kilometres north of the centre of Bangli. Bangli, whose name is said to come from bang giri, red forest or red mountain, was one of the nine kingdoms of Bali, and its regency was founded by the Gelgel Kingdom of the Majapahit dynasty. The temple is named in three copper inscriptions, of the late 9th, early 11th and 13th centuries, each under a different name and each tying it to the village of Bangli.

In the earliest the Brahmans who kept it called it Hyang Api, god of fire. By the early 11th century it was Hyang Kehen, from the Balinese keren, flame, and served as the official temple where royal officials swore oaths before the fire god Agni, using a vessel wound with four serpents, the bejana sarpantaka. Those proven unfaithful were held to bring a curse on themselves and their descendants. The name Pura Kehen appears in the 13th-century inscription.

The temple rises from south to north over a hilly outcrop in three courtyards. Terraced steps with statues of figures from the Ramayana lead to the outer court, whose central gateway is a paduraksa, a form usually kept for the entrance to the inner sanctum. There stands a sacred banyan tree at least 400 years old; the people of Bangli believe that a broken branch foretells a death, a king's, a brahmin's or a commoner's according to the side on which it breaks. Pavilions hold the gamelans.

A candi bentar gateway leads to the middle court of shrines and offering preparation. The inner court holds the 11-tiered meru, dedicated to the temple's protecting god, and a padmasana lotus shrine to Brahma, Shiva and Vishnu. Porcelain plates set in its wall include scenes of rural England with a watermill and a four-horse coach.

The feast of Pagerwesi is held every six months to honour Hyang Widhi and his manifestations, and the Ngusaba Dewa, or Karya Agung Bhatara Turun Kabeh, falls on Purnama Kalima in early November. Smaller ceremonies honour Saraswati and other gods.
pura-luhur-uluwatu: The temple stands on the south-western tip of the Bukit Peninsula in Pecatu Village, South Kuta, in Badung Regency. It is the only Balinese sea temple, or pura segara, that is also one of the nine directional temples, and it is dedicated to Sang Hyang Widhi Wasa in his manifestation as Rudra. The name joins ulu, edge, and watu, rock: the temple is built at the edge of a cliff 70 metres high that projects into the sea. In folklore the rock is part of the petrified barque of Dewi Danu.

A Kecak dance based on the Ramayana is performed on the cliff side every day at 6 pm, against the sunset. Long-tailed macaques live at the temple and snatch visitors' belongings, which they can usually be persuaded to give back for fruit or nuts. Studies of these monkeys suggest that they learn this bartering and pass it on to their young.

A small temple is claimed to have existed on the site earlier, but the structure was significantly expanded by a Javanese sage, Empu Kuturan, in the 11th century. Dang Hyang Nirartha, another sage from East Java, is credited with introducing the padmasana shrines, and it is said that he attained moksha here, an event known locally as ngeluhur, to go up. This gave the temple its epithet Luhur, height.

In 2009 a spatial planning regulation, Bali Provincial Regulation No. 16, set a zone of 5 km from the temple's outer wall in which no building was allowed except for Hindu religious facilities, so that both settlements and tourist buildings were outlawed. This conflicted with the customary law, awig-awig, of the Pecatu village community, which protected the temple forest within a radius of 350 m. Applying the state law would have meant demolishing many existing buildings.

At least seven lawsuits were brought by individuals, groups and customary communities of Pecatu, and the Supreme Court rejected the appeals in 2010 and 2013. In 2015 the provincial government issued Regulation Number 8, which set three types of protection for temples, each with a core, a buffer and a utilisation zone. Uluwatu was classed as type II, with a core zone of up to 1 km, a buffer zone from 1 to 2.5 km and a utilisation zone from 2.5 to 5 km.
pura-taman-ayun: The temple was built in 1634 by the king of Mengwi, Gusti Agung Putu, also known as Cokorda Sakti Blambangan, as a family temple (pura kawiten) to honour the spirits of his ancestors. Over the centuries it underwent several restorations and renovations. According to Henk Schulte Nordholt, it was renovated in 1750 by an architect named Hobin Ho, and the last major renovation took place in 1937.

The name means beautiful garden, and the complex is the second-largest temple in Bali. It stands in the middle of the town of Mengwi, 19 km north of Denpasar. The compound covers 6.9 hectares, a rectangle oriented north to south and surrounded on the west, south and east by a large body of water like a moat; a bridge on the south side leads in.

Like other holy temples it has three sections: the outer courtyard (jabaan or Nista Mandala), the middle courtyard (jaba tengah or Madia Mandala) and the inner sanctuary (jeroan or Utama Mandala), each divided from the next by a split gate, the candi bentar. The inner sanctuary, reserved for worshippers and ringed by a smaller moat, holds the highest structures, shrines of two up to eleven tiers, where Hindu gods and the ancestors of the Mengwi dynasty are venerated.

Water shapes both the look of the temple and its work in the local subak irrigation system. Besides the moats there are ponds, basins and fountains, and the temple's waters are said to feed three subaks in the Badung Regency. On 6 July 2012 it became one of the five sites of the World Heritage Site named Cultural Landscape of Bali Province: the Subak System as a Manifestation of the Tri Hita Karana Philosophy, with a buffer zone of 51.3 hectares around the compound.

A wing of the complex holds an art gallery and a theatre showing the temple's history as told by the Mengwi royal family. It is linked to the outer courtyard by a wantilan, an open pavilion first used for cockfighting and now for gatherings and musical performances. Close to the south-west corner stand the Ogoh Ogoh Museum, with figures of demons carried in the Ngrupuk parade on the day before Nyepi, and the Yadnya Museum, with replicas of Balinese Hindu rituals.
purana-qila: Excavations by the Archaeological Survey of India under B. B. Lal in 1954–55 and 1969–72 found Painted Grey Ware dating to about 1000 BCE, and later finds show habitation through the Mauryan, Shunga, Kushana, Gupta, Rajput, Delhi Sultanate and Mughal periods. Alexander Cunningham identified the site with Indraprastha, and into the early 20th century it was known as Pandavon Ka Qila, Pandava's fort. Matching such literary traditions to archaeological remains is, however, almost always methodologically impossible.

The fort began as the walls of Dinpanah, the new city of Delhi that the Mughal emperor Humayun was building. Sher Shah Suri, founder of the Sur Empire, strengthened its fortifications, completed its walls and called his fort Shergarh. How much each ruler built is disputed, as the primary sources differ: Abbas Sarwani says both forts were unfinished at Sher Shah's death, and Tarikh-i-Khan-Jahan credits Salim Shah Suri with a wall defending Dinpanah.

On 7 October 1556 the Hindu king Hem Chandra Vikramaditya, who had defeated Akbar's forces at the Battle of Delhi, was crowned in the fort; a month later the Mughals defeated him at the Second Battle of Panipat. In the 1920s Edwin Lutyens aligned the central vista of New Delhi with it. During the Partition of India in 1947 it held a camp for Muslims bound for Pakistan, with between 150,000 and 200,000 refugees by September; the camp ran until early 1948.

During the Second World War the British interned Japanese civilians there: by December 1942 the Purana Quila camp held 2,115, most from Singapore, in tents that gave little protection from winter cold or summer heat. From the 1970s its ramparts became a setting for theatre, beginning with three productions of the National School of Drama directed by Ebrahim Alkazi.

The walls rise to 18 metres and run for about 1.5 km, with three double-storeyed sandstone gateways: the Bara Darwaza facing west, still in use, the south or Humayun Gate, and the Talaqi Gate. Each is flanked by semicircular bastions and decorated with marble inlay, blue tiles, jharokhas and chhatris. Of the buildings inside, little survives besides the Sher Mandal and the single-domed Qila-i-Kuhna Mosque of 1541, a Friday mosque with five horseshoe arches and the best preserved building of the fort.
puranas: Tradition credits Vyasa, the narrator of the Mahabharata, with compiling the Puranas. An old account holds that there was originally a single Purana: the Vishnu Purana says Vyasa entrusted his Puranasamhita to his disciple Lomaharshana, who passed it to disciples whose collections, together with his own, formed the Mulasamhita from which the later eighteen Puranas were derived. Many scholars instead consider the Mahapuranas the work of multiple authors over several centuries.

The word purana appears in the Vedic texts, for example in the Atharva Veda. The texts existed in oral form before they were written down, so the date of a written copy does not give the date of origin. Ludo Rocher states that no Purana can be given a specific date as a whole; Wendy Doniger assigns approximate dates, such as c. 250 CE for the Markandeya Purana and c. 450 CE for the Vishnu Purana.

The eighteen Mahapuranas, the major Puranas, are traditionally divided into three groups of six according to the three qualities of existence: purity, passion and inertia. Each group centres mainly, but not only, on one deity. There are also eighteen Upapuranas, or minor Puranas, though lists disagree on which titles belong among them. The Skanda Purana, with 81,000 verses, is the largest. Together the texts run to over 400,000 verses.

Several Puranas name five characteristics of a Purana: the creation of the world, its further creation and cosmology, the genealogies of gods, sages and kings, the cosmic ages of each patriarch, and accounts of royal dynasties. The Bhagavata Purana adds five more. In practice the range is wider. Some, such as the Agni Purana and Matsya Purana, treat subjects from astronomy and cosmetics to philosophy and festivals, while the Skanda, Padma and Bhavishya Puranas are largely pilgrimage guides.

The Puranas are classed as Smriti and do not have the authority of scripture in Hinduism. Scholars have nevertheless seen in them a process of cultural synthesis, in which the beliefs of many local traditions were woven into the Vedic and Brahmanic fold. Greg Bailey describes them as records of cultural adaptation over some 2,000 years.

Their manuscripts differ greatly. A palm-leaf manuscript of the Skanda Purana found in Nepal, dated to 810 CE, is entirely different from the versions in circulation since the colonial period, and later finds suggest major rewritings before the 12th century and again in the 15th to 16th centuries. Because the texts record neither authors nor dates and are inconsistent with one another, Rocher states that attempts to use them as history have had limited success unless supported by inscriptions, archaeology and other independent evidence. Horace Hayman Wilson published an English translation of the Vishnu Purana in 1840.
purandar-singha: Purandar Singha was born in 1807 at Silmari in British-ruled Bengal, a great-great-grandson of the Ahom king Rajeswar Singha. His grandfather and his father Brajanath Gohain had conspired against reigning kings and lived there as exiled princes in poverty. In 1818 Ruchinath Burhagohain, who held King Chandrakanta Singha responsible for bringing in the Burmese, invited Brajanath to claim the throne, and their force entered the capital Jorhat on 17 February 1818. Brajanath had coins struck in his own name, but the mutilation of one of his ears barred him from kingship, since an Ahom king had to be without blemish. His son, then ten years old, was acclaimed instead.

Real authority lay with Brajanath and Ruchinath, who removed the officers suspected of loyalty to Chandrakanta. A Burmese army of 30,000 sent by King Bodawpaya defeated the Assamese on 17 February 1819; Purandar, his father and Ruchinath fled to Guwahati with the valuables of the royal treasury, worth 3.5 million rupees. After a second defeat on 11 June 1819 they escaped to Bengal. The Governor-General Lord Hastings refused to help. They recruited soldiers in Goalpara, Bengal and Bhutan, armed with the aid of a British trader, Robert Bruce, and fought both Chandrakanta and the Burmese before withdrawing in 1822.

After the Treaty of Yandabo of 24 February 1826 the British held the Brahmaputra valley. Sensing discontent, they considered in 1832 restoring Upper Assam as a tributary princedom and chose Purandar over Chandrakanta; some historians think they expected a long-exiled prince to be the more grateful and submissive. From April 1833 he ruled from Jorhat, without Sadiya and Matak, for a tribute of 50,000 rupees. Within three years he fell behind in his payments and asked for a reduction. An enquiry by Captain Francis Jenkins found corruption and oppression, and the king himself amassing a personal fortune.

The kingdom was placed under direct British control in September 1838. Purandar stayed in Jorhat and refused the pension of 1,000 rupees a month granted in October 1838, hoping that a petition to the Governor-General would restore his state; it was turned down. When officials and adventurers dug into the royal tombs, the maidams, at Charaideo in search of treasure, he first protested and then opened many tombs himself. He died on 1 October 1846 and was entombed at Jorhat, at the place now called Raja Maidam.
purandara-dasa: Purandara Dasa was born into a Kannada Deshastha Madhva Brahmin family; his father was a diamond merchant, and he himself traded in gold, silver and jewellery before giving his wealth away to become a Haridasa, a servant of Vishnu. His birthplace has long been disputed. Some placed it at Purandaraghatta in Karnataka or at Purandaragad near Pune, the latter now regarded as a mistake that ties his pen name to a military camp. In 2018 a five-member committee set up by the Government of Karnataka reported that Tirthahalli was the likeliest place, at Araga in the Vijayanagara Empire.

He followed the Dvaita philosophy of Madhvacharya and took his Haridasa initiation from Vyasatirtha at Hampi. Manuscripts written by Tallapaka Chinanna, grandson of the poet Annamacharya, record that the two met at Tirumala and sang devotional songs together before Sri Venkateshwara. His songs, in the local Kannada language, carried the teachings of the Bhagavata Purana to ordinary people and often criticised the faults of society. In one, comparing cows of different colours and sugarcane of different shapes, he argued that birth alone cannot decide whether a person is high or low. His son Madhvapati gave 1564 as the year of his death; the year of his birth is uncertain.

Musicologists call him the Sangeeta Pitamaha, or grandsire, of Carnatic music. He made the raga Mayamalavagowla the basic scale for teaching and arranged graded lessons, among them swaravalis, janti swaras, alankaras, lakshana geetas, prabandhas, ugabhogas, sooladis and kritis. He set his words to the ragas of his day, brought folk ragas into the mainstream and used colloquial language. His sooladis are regarded as the standard for raga lakshana, and scholars credit him with standardising the varna mettus. A legend holds him to be an incarnation of Narada. India issued a stamp in his honour on 14 January 1964, the 400th anniversary of his death.
purepecha-empire: The kingdom was founded in the early 14th century in the lake basins of the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt, between the Lerma and Balsas rivers. According to the Relación de Michoacán, written around 1540 by the Franciscan Jeronimo de Acalá from the narratives of Purépecha noblemen, a leader named Tariácuri set out to gather the communities around Lake Pátzcuaro into one state. Around 1300 he made the first conquests and installed his sons Hiripan and Tangáxuan as lords of Ihuatzio and Tzintzuntzan, while he ruled from Pátzcuari.

By Tariácuri's death, around 1350, his lineage, the Vacúxecha or eagles, held every major centre around the lake. Hiripan and later Tangáxuan I extended the conquests to the Lake Cuitzeo area, set up an administrative bureaucracy and divided the tribute of conquered lands among lords and nobles.

Under King Tzitzipandáquare some conquests were won and lost again to rebellions or Aztec pressure, but by 1460 the kingdom reached the Pacific coast at Zacatula, the Toluca Valley and present-day Guanajuato. After the Aztec defeat of the 1470s the ruler fortified the eastern border with military centres such as Cutzamala and settled Otomi and Matlatzinca refugees there on condition that they defend it. From 1480 the Aztec ruler Ahuitzotl backed attacks by allied peoples, which King Zuangua repelled. Between 1480 and 1510 the Purépecha occupied parts of Colima and Jalisco for their saltpetre mines, until local resistance in the Saltpeter War drove them out.

After the fall of the Aztec Empire, King Tangáxuan II exchanged envoys with the Spaniards. In 1522 Cristóbal de Olid reached Tzintzuntzan and the Purépecha army, perhaps as many as 100,000 men, chose not to fight. Tangáxuan submitted but kept wide autonomy, so that the people paid tribute to him and to Cortés alike. Nuño de Guzmán, allied with the noble Don Pedro Panza Cuinierángari, had the king executed on 14 February 1530. In 1543 the land officially became the governorship of Michoacán.

The king was called Irecha, a title the Spaniards rendered as Cazonci, and the capital stood at Tzintzuntzan, the place of hummingbirds, on Lake Pátzcuaro. The kingdom included Nahuas, Otomi, Matlatzincas, Mazahuas, Chichimec groups and others besides the Purépecha. Its people worshipped many deities, among them Kweráwahpiri, goddess of rain, and Xarhátanha, goddess of maize. The historian Robert West called the Tarascans and their neighbours the foremost metallurgists of pre-Conquest Mexico: they worked copper, silver and gold and made bronze needles, fishhooks and axeheads.
purgatorio: Purgatorio follows the Inferno and precedes the Paradiso. Allegorically it represents the penitent Christian life, and in describing the climb Dante discusses the nature of sin, examples of vice and virtue, and moral questions of politics and the Church. Virgil is his guide until the last four cantos, where Beatrice takes his place. The poem holds that all sins arise from love: perverted love directed to others' harm, deficient love, or disordered and excessive love of good things. The journey begins on the shore of the mountain at 6 am on Easter Sunday 1300 and takes three and a quarter days.

Dante places Purgatory on an island-mountain in the Southern Hemisphere, at the antipodes of Jerusalem, raised by rock displaced when Lucifer fell. Its lower slopes, which commentators call Ante-Purgatory, hold the excommunicate, among them Manfred of Sicily, and the late-repentant, such as Belacqua and Pia de' Tolomei of Siena, murdered by her husband. Above them seven terraces purge the seven deadly sins: pride, envy, wrath, sloth, avarice, gluttony and lust. On each the souls meet examples of the opposite virtue, always including an episode from the life of the Virgin Mary, and on the terrace of lust every soul must pass through a wall of flame.

Prayer runs through the cantica: Dante receives eleven requests for prayer, and Forese Donati has climbed most of the mountain within five years of his death through his wife Nella's prayers, while Statius has spent over 500 years there. At the summit lies the Earthly Paradise, where Matilda leads Dante to an allegorical procession, Virgil departs and Beatrice demands Dante's first personal confession of the Comedy.

Scholars have long debated the size and shape of the mountain. In the Renaissance Antonio Manetti and Alessandro Vellutello proposed models that Galileo Galilei refuted, and later estimates put its height between 11.4 and 192 km. Dante's treatment of homosexual souls as capable of salvation was lenient for its time and is often left out of later illustrations. Franz Liszt's Symphony to Dante's Divina Commedia of 1856 has a Purgatorio movement, Chaucer referred to the poem, and Gustave Doré, John Flaxman, Dante Gabriel Rossetti and William Blake depicted its scenes.
puritans: The Elizabethan Religious Settlement of 1559 established the Church of England as a Protestant church and closed the English Reformation. Under Elizabeth I the church was widely considered Reformed, and Calvinists held the best bishoprics and deaneries, yet it kept cathedrals, choirs, a formal liturgy in the Book of Common Prayer, traditional vestments and bishops. The Puritans were dissatisfied with this limited reform. The word Puritan began as a term of abuse, dated by Thomas Fuller to 1564, and the people it described called themselves the godly, saints or God's children.

They adopted a covenant theology and in that sense were Calvinists. Divided in church polity between episcopal, presbyterian and congregational views, some wanted the established church reformed throughout, while others favoured separation. At the Hampton Court Conference of 1604 James I largely sided with his bishops.

Under Charles I the Puritans became a political force. Opponents of the royal prerogative allied with reformers who saw the church moving in the wrong direction and objected to growing Catholic influence at court. By the late 1630s they were allied with the commercial world, with parliamentary opposition and with the Scottish Presbyterians, and the First English Civil War of 1642 to 1646 brought them to power. Some Puritans left for New England between 1629 and 1640, supporting the founding of the Massachusetts Bay Colony. The migration ceased by 1641.

At the Restoration of 1660 and under the Act of Uniformity of 1662, the Church of England returned to its pre-war form. Historian Edmund Calamy estimated that about 2,400 Puritan clergy left it in the Great Ejection of 1662. They were thereafter included among Dissenters.

In colonial New England, Puritan leaders worked for universal literacy so that people could read the Bible. In 1642 Massachusetts required heads of households to teach their children and servants to read. In 1647 Parliament banned Christmas, Easter and Whitsuntide. New England Puritans were intolerant of Quaker, Anglican and Baptist beliefs, and those of Massachusetts Bay were the most active persecutors of Quakers.

Puritanism was never a formally defined division of Protestantism, and the term was rarely used after the turn of the 18th century. Congregationalist churches are descended from the Puritans, and their beliefs appear in the Savoy Declaration. Many Dissenters formed the basis of later Congregationalist, Baptist and Presbyterian traditions. Writers such as John Milton, John Bunyan and Anne Bradstreet are still read.
pushmataha: Pushmataha's early life is poorly documented and his parents are unknown; a legend made him spring fully armed from an oak struck by fire from a cloud. Most historians place his birth near the future site of Macon, Mississippi. At 13 he fought against the Creek, and between 1784 and 1789 he took part in wars with the Osage and Caddo west of the Mississippi River, raids driven by the depletion of Choctaw deer-hunting grounds and by competition over the fur trade. His knowledge of these lands, later Arkansas and Oklahoma, served him in later negotiations with the United States.

By 1800 he was mingo of the Okla Hannali, or Six Towns district, in the south of the Choctaw lands, known for his eloquence in council. He negotiated the Treaty of Mount Dexter on 16 November 1805. In 1811 he argued against Tecumseh's plan, and the joint Choctaw-Chickasaw council refused the alliance. In the war he raised 500 warriors and was commissioned in the United States Army; with 150 Choctaw he fought under Brigadier General Ferdinand Claiborne at the Battle of Holy Ground on 23 December 1813, and in 1814 he joined General Andrew Jackson's force against the Creek.

Elected paramount chief after the war, he resisted the Protestant missionaries who arrived in 1818 while taking up cotton gins and new farming methods, and spent much of his military pension on Choctaw schools. He negotiated the treaty of 24 October 1816 and the contested Treaty of Doak's Stand of 18 October 1820, signing the latter only after securing guarantees that squatters would be evicted from reserved lands.

In 1824 he led a delegation with the chiefs Apuckshunubbee and Mosholatubbee to Washington to seek the removal of white settlers from Choctaw lands in Arkansas, or compensation. He met President James Monroe, spoke to Secretary of War John C. Calhoun, met the Marquis de Lafayette and sat in his army uniform for a portrait by Charles Bird King. He fell ill with croup and died on 24 December 1824; as he had asked, he was buried with full military honours as a brigadier general in the Congressional Cemetery. Oklahoma later named Pushmataha County after him.
pushyamitra-shunga: Pushyamitra Shunga, also written Pushpamitra, was the founder and first ruler of the Shunga Empire, which he established to succeed the Maurya Empire. He took power after assassinating the last Mauryan emperor, Brihadratha. He is said to have driven out the Greeks in a Shunga-Greek war and to have ruled for 36 years. The Buddhist Ashokavadana names him as the last Mauryan emperor, which appears to confuse him with Brihadratha. Inscriptions of the Shungas have been found as far as Ayodhya, and the Divyavadana says his realm reached Sakala, now Sialkot in Pakistan.

He performed the Vedic Ashvamedha sacrifice to legitimise his rule, as the Dhanadeva-Ayodhya inscription records. Michael Witzel states that the Manu Smriti, which stresses orthodox faith in statecraft, was first compiled under his rule, and Kaushik Roy sees it as a Brahmanical reaction to the rise of Buddhism and Jainism. His history is also recorded in Banabhatta's Harshacharita.

Buddhist texts accuse Pushyamitra of persecuting Buddhists. The earliest, the Ashokavadana of the 4th or 5th century CE, says his advisers told him he could rival Ashoka's fame by destroying Buddhism. He tried to destroy the Kukkutarama monastery, then offered a hundred coins for every monk's head at Sakala, and was killed by a Buddhist yaksha. Later texts, among them the Vibhasa, the Arya-Manjushri-Mula-Kalpa and Taranatha's history of the 16th century, tell similar stories with different places and deaths. Many historians regard them as exaggerated.

Scholars are divided. John Marshall found evidence of damage to Buddhist sites at Takshashila and thought the Sanchi stupa vandalised in the 2nd century BCE, and others date damage at Kaushambi and Deur Kothar to his time. H. Bhattacharya suggested political motives, since Buddhists may have favoured his Indo-Greek rivals. Others reject the claim. Etienne Lamotte notes that the legends disagree on where he campaigned and died, and that the dinara named in the Ashokavadana was not in general use before the 1st century BCE. Romila Thapar and Eric Seldeslachts find no firm evidence, and the Buddhist monuments of Bharhut and Sanchi were improved under Shunga rule, though N. N. Ghosh dates Bharhut to later Shunga kings. Pushyamitra was succeeded by his son Agnimitra.
puster-valley: The Puster Valley is one of the largest longitudinal valleys in the Alps, running east to west between Lienz in East Tyrol, Austria, and Mühlbach near Brixen in South Tyrol, Italy. It lies in the western part of the Periadriatic Seam, which separates the Southern Limestone Alps from the Central Eastern Alps. Half of the valley drains westward to the Adriatic through the Adige, the other half eastward to the Black Sea through the Danube, with the watershed on the shallow Toblacher Feld. The Rienz flows west and the Drau east into East Tyrol. Its towns lie between 750 and 1,180 metres above sea level, and the largest side valley is the Tauferer Ahrntal.

The valley has been inhabited since prehistoric times, and Iron Age finds are known. The Romans called its Illyrian inhabitants Saevates, and used the Rienz valley as a main road to the north-eastern regions of the Empire. It belonged to the province of Noricum, and over four centuries its people took on Roman customs, language and the Christian religion. In the 5th century Goths, Baiuvarii and Slavs came down into the area, and the Baiuvarii won out over the Slavs, who left traces in the place names of East Tyrol.

From the 10th century it formed the Pustrissa countship, first mentioned in 974. Emperor Henry IV ceded it to the Bishop of Brixen in 1091, and the Hapsburg took possession of it in the 16th century. After the Austrian defeat at Austerlitz and the Treaty of Pressburg in 1805 the region passed to Bavaria, and Tyroleans under Andreas Hofer repeatedly fought Bavarian rule. After Napoleon's fall it rejoined Austria, and after the First World War the South Tyrolean part was assigned to Italy. The Puster Valley Railway opened in 1871.

The South Tyrolean part forms the Puster Valley District, founded in 1969 from 26 municipalities, with an area of 2,071 square kilometres and more than 73,000 people. Bruneck is its main town. The 2001 census recorded German as the native language of 80.96 per cent of its people, Ladin of 13.40 per cent and Italian of 5.64 per cent.
putna-monastery: The monastery stands on land crossed by the river Putna, which rises in the Obcina Mare mountains of Bukovina, in what was medieval Moldavia. Burials found deep beneath the foundations of its oldest buildings show that hermits lived on the site before Stephen the Great built there. The monastery is also the starting point of the Via Transilvanica, a long-distance walking trail.

Stephen the Great, who is said to have founded a church after each important victory, began the monastery on 10 July 1466, after the battle in which he took the citadel of Kilia, as an offering of thanks to God; its church was dedicated to the Virgin Mary. A chronicle of the time records that he bought the village of Vicovu de Sus for 200 zloty and gave its land and revenue to the monastery.

The building took three years, and its consecration waited a further year while the Moldavians were fighting other battles. On 3 September 1470 Metropolitan Teoctist consecrated it in the presence of Stephen and his family, and it became the chief religious site of the area. The present church was largely rebuilt between 1653 and 1662 by Vasile Lupu and his successors: it keeps the ground plan of a Moldavian church of the 15th and 16th centuries but has many features of 17th-century architecture. The long-held belief that a Greek architect named Theodor designed it rested on a reading of the Kilia chronicles since shown to be wrong.

Stephen's tomb is a place of pilgrimage, and his icon veils and tombstones are held up as fine examples of Moldavian art of his time. Also buried there are Bogdan III the One-Eyed, Maria of Mangup, Maria Voichița and Metropolitan Teoctist I. The oldest embroidery in the collection, from the end of the 14th century, is an epitaphion of silk and gold thread made by Euphima, a Serbian nun who was the daughter of Vojihna, and her daughter Euprasijka.
putrajaya: Putrajaya is an enclave within the state of Selangor on the west coast of Peninsular Malaysia. It covers 4,931 hectares, divided into 20 precincts. The central Core Island, Nusa Perdana, holds the ministerial headquarters, civic squares, courts and ceremonial boulevards, while the outer precincts hold housing, schools, shops and recreation grounds. The master plan reserved nearly 40 per cent of the territory for parks, water bodies and landscaped open space, including the Putrajaya Lake and its wetlands. The city was named in honour of Malaysia's first prime minister, Tunku Abdul Rahman Putra Al-Haj; putra means prince or son and jaya success or victory in Sanskrit.

The site was originally Prang Besar, established in 1921 as a rubber estate by British veterans of World War I, which grew from 800 acres to 8,000 by taking in surrounding plantations. In the late 1980s the federal government sought to gather ministries scattered across congested Kuala Lumpur into a dedicated administrative capital. Prang Besar was chosen over an alternative site at Janda Baik in Pahang because it lay midway between central Kuala Lumpur and the planned Kuala Lumpur International Airport at Sepang. The federal government acquired about 11,320 acres from the Selangor state government.

The city was conceived in the 1990s by Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad and the Kuala Lumpur mayor Elyas Omar as a garden city and intelligent city. Construction began in August 1995, one of the largest infrastructure undertakings in Southeast Asia, at an estimated cost of US$8.1 billion, with designs mostly by Malaysian firms. The Asian financial crisis of 1997 moderately slowed it. Much of the monumental architecture draws on regional Islamic motifs, including Arabesque, Persian and Central Asian styles. The Prime Minister's Department moved there in 1999, and most federal civil servants followed between 2000 and 2005. On 1 February 2001 Selangor formally ceded the territory, which became Malaysia's third federal territory after Kuala Lumpur in 1974 and Labuan in 1984.

Putrajaya is the administrative centre of Malaysia and houses the executive and judicial branches of the federal government, the judiciary having moved there in 2003. Kuala Lumpur remains the national capital under the federal constitution, and continues to be the seat of the Yang di-Pertuan Agong and of Parliament. Local administration lies with the Putrajaya Corporation, a statutory body under the Prime Minister's Department.
puuc: The word puuc comes from the Maya term for hill. Because the Yucatán is mostly flat, the name was extended to the large karstic range of hills in the southern part of the state of Yucatán, which reaches into northern Campeche and western Quintana Roo. Besides Uxmal, Kabah, Sayil and Labna, the region holds Xlapak, Kiuic, Bolonchen, Chunhuhub, Xculoc and many smaller ruins. The explorer Teobert Maler, who surveyed the zone closely, described the area around the site of Dolores as full of ruins.

The Puuc style began at the end of the Late Classic period and reached its widest extent in the Terminal Classic. Its builders set carefully cut veneer stones into a concrete core, an advance on the earlier Maya practice of stacking larger stones in lime and mud mortar for support. The core-and-veneer technique allowed somewhat larger and more stable interior rooms, and many Puuc corbelled vaults still stand even where most of their facing has fallen away.

The shift from earlier Classic architecture to Puuc masonry is well documented at Oxkintok. The style also spread beyond the hills, south to Edzná and east to Chichen Itza. The Chunhuaymil project gathered data on the surviving Puuc architecture of 19 archaeological sites in an area of 100 square kilometres.

The Puuc Biocultural State Reserve, also called the Kaxil Kiuic reserve, was designated in 2011 and covers 1358.93 km2. It protects both the region's archaeological sites and its wildlife, which includes 247 species of birds, 63 of mammals, 52 of reptiles and 14 of amphibians, among them five species of large cats such as the jaguar.
puxian-wannu: Puxian Wannu was a Jurchen from Xianping. He first served the Jin as Director of the Shangjiu Bureau, in charge of the horses of the court and the army. In 1206 he was deputy to the Grand Commander Wanyan Saibu in the Jin invasion of the Song dynasty, and at Zhenshui he led his troops round to strike the Song army from the rear; some twenty thousand Song troops were killed. The Jin ruler Wanyan Jing then made him Pacification Commissioner of Xianping and sent him to Liaodong.

When Genghis Khan invaded in 1211, the Jin army was routed at Yehu Ridge, and Puxian Wannu withdrew to Xianping. The Jin court moved its capital to Kaifeng, and Khitan leaders such as Yelü Liuge rose in the northeast proclaiming the restoration of the Liao. Ordered repeatedly to suppress them, he won some battles and lost others. In 1215, the year the Mongols took Zhongdu, he called the Jurchen chieftains to a council at Xianping, argued that the court could no longer defend Liaodong, and with their support declared independence as Heavenly King of a state named Great Zhen, with the reign title Tiantai.

In 1217 he moved to the Tumen River basin, renamed his state Eastern Xia and set his capital, called Nanjing, around Yanji. His domain reached from the Laoyeling Mountains south into present-day North Korea and east to the Sea of Japan. He seems to have submitted to the Mongols again, and in 1218 Mongol and Eastern Xia armies entered Goryeo together to destroy the Khitan remnants.

In 1222, while Genghis Khan was campaigning in the west, he revolted against the Mongols once more, and after Goryeo refused to open trading posts on the border he invaded it several times. In 1233 Güyük, the son of Ögedei, attacked Eastern Xia with a large army and took five of its capitals in succession. With his fall the Jurchen remnants in Manchuria surrendered, beginning almost two hundred years of Mongol rule there. Persian sources such as the Jami' al-tawarikh mention him under another name.
puyang: Puyang lies on the northern shore of the Yellow River in north-eastern Henan. It borders Anyang to the west and Xinxiang to the south-west, and the provinces of Shandong and Hebei to the east and north. Its climate is a warm temperate continental monsoon one, with a dry, windy spring, a hot and rainy summer and a winter with little snow or rain. The surrounding land is farmed, and the adequate sunshine suits crops.

A burial site of the Yangshao culture in the area has a depiction believed to be an ancient cosmogram of the round Heaven and the square Earth. In 1987 a group of clams arranged in dragon patterns was unearthed there and dated to more than 6,400 years ago. It earned the city the name of the First Dragon of China, and a Chinese research association has named Puyang the Hometown of Chinese Dragons. Many Chinese scholars regard it as one of the important birthplaces of Chinese civilization.

The Classic of Poetry, the earliest collection of verses in China, includes poems that depict the countryside of Puyang. Wu Qi, the military strategist, Shang Yang, the statesman, and Lu Buwei, the thinker, are among the historical figures from the city.

In the Three Kingdoms era Puyang was Cao Cao's headquarters in Yan Province from 191 until 196 CE, and the battlefield of the Battle of Yan Province from 194 to 195. Under the Qing and the Republic of China it was a county of Daming Prefecture in Zhili province; in 1928 Zhili was abolished and Puyang joined Henan. In August 1949 it was taken from Henan into the experimental province of Pingyuan, and in November 1953 it was finally returned to Henan.

Puyang is a prefecture-level city that administers one district and five counties. Its 2020 census recorded 3,772,088 people. It has four national cultural relics protection units, among them the Qicheng relics, and a larger number of provincial and local sites, including the Cangjie mausoleum site and the Nanle Confucius temple. Petroleum and natural gas are its main mineral resources, and the Zhongyuan Oilfield and other petrochemical enterprises are established there.
puyi: Puyi was born in Beijing on 7 February 1906, the son of the Manchu prince Zaifeng, Prince Chun, and of Youlan, daughter of Ronglu, an ally of Empress Dowager Cixi. His uncle, the Guangxu Emperor, was his predecessor. In 1908 Cixi chose him to succeed the childless Guangxu, and he ascended the throne at the age of two with his father as regent. After the garrison at Wuhan mutinied on 10 October 1911, the general Yuan Shikai was sent to crush the revolt but could not, since opinion had turned against a dynasty that many believed had lost the mandate of heaven.

Empress Dowager Longyu, regent from 6 December 1911, endorsed the edict of abdication on 12 February 1912 under a deal brokered by Yuan. Under the Articles of Favourable Treatment Puyi kept his imperial title and remained in the northern half of the Forbidden City. The general Zhang Xun restored him to the throne from 1 to 12 July 1917, and from 1919 the Scottish scholar Reginald Johnston tutored him. On 5 November 1924 the warlord Feng Yuxiang abolished his title and expelled him from the palace, and in 1925 he moved to Tianjin.

After the Mukden incident of 18 September 1931 the Japanese Kwantung Army proposed that he head a Manchurian state. He was installed as Chief Executive of Manchukuo on 1 March 1932 and crowned Emperor of Manchukuo, with the regnal title Kangde, on 1 March 1934. On 9 August 1945 the Soviet Union entered Manchukuo and its armies overwhelmed the Kwantung Army.

The Soviets took Puyi to Siberia, and in 1946 he testified at the Tokyo War Crimes Tribunal. He was repatriated to China in 1950 and, after his release in 1959, published an autobiography ghostwritten by Li Wenda and worked as a gardener and then as a researcher. Red Guards burned copies of his book during the Cultural Revolution, but Premier Zhou Enlai protected him. Puyi died in Beijing on 17 October 1967, aged 61, of kidney cancer and heart disease.
pyinbya: According to the Burmese chronicles, Pyinbya was a son of King Saw Khin Hnit of Pagan, born in 817 or, by another reckoning, 802. Before his accession he was lord of Pyinbya, a village of Pagan, and was known as Pyinbya Mintha. He succeeded his brother, King Khelu, in 846. The chronicles count him as the 33rd king of a dynasty founded in the early 2nd century, but they do not agree on his regnal years or on the years of his birth and death; the oldest of them, the Zatadawbon Yazawin, is considered the most accurate for the Pagan period.

The chronicles date the founding of the city of Pagan to 23 December 849 and a settlement at Taungdwin to 857, perhaps the southern limit of his young kingdom. Mainstream scholarship sees Pagan as founded by the Mranma, or Burmans, of the Nanzhao Kingdom, and as the first known Burman settlement in the Irrawaddy valley. It arose after raids by Nanzhao into the upper valley, from the 750s to the 830s, had left the Pyu states severely weakened and many Mranma warriors and their families in the region. The site lay close to the Chindwin river and just west of a richly irrigated rice plain, and may have been meant to help Nanzhao pacify the countryside.

The chronicles say Pyinbya died in 876, at the age of 59, and was succeeded by his son Tannet. Pagan remained one of several competing city-states until the late 10th century, when it grew in authority and grandeur. Two hundred years after Pyinbya founded the city, his great-grandson Anawrahta created the Pagan Empire, the first unification of the Irrawaddy valley and its periphery.
pyongyang: Pyongyang lies in the west-central part of North Korea on a flat plain, about 50 kilometres east of Korea Bay, an arm of the Yellow Sea. The Taedong River flows southwestward through the city, about 109 kilometres upstream from its mouth. The Pyongyang plain is one of the two large plains on the western coast of the Korean peninsula, the other being the Chaeryong plain, each of about 500 square kilometres.

The name comes from the Sino-Korean words for flat and land. In native Korean the city was called Buruna or, less commonly, Barana, which may mean land of the field. Its other historic names include Ryugyong, Kisong, Hwangsong, Rakrang, Sŏgyong, Sodo, Hogyong, Changan and, under Japanese rule, Heijō. Early in the 20th century missionaries called it the Jerusalem of the East, because it was a stronghold of Protestant Christianity, especially during the Pyongyang Revival of 1907.

In 1955 archaeologists excavated prehistoric dwellings in a large ancient village at Kŭmtan-ni in the Pyongyang area, dating to the Jeulmun and Mumun pottery periods. According to legend the city was founded in 1122 BCE on the site of the capital of the traditional king Tan'gun. Korean historiography beginning with the 13th-century Samguk yusa links it to Asadal, or Wanggeom-seong, the first capital of Gojoseon. Historians reject this because earlier Chinese works such as the Records of the Grand Historian mention a much later Joseon, so the link may have been asserted by North Korea for propaganda, though Pyongyang did become a major city in old Joseon.

Wanggeom-seong, on the site of modern Pyongyang, served as the capital of Gojoseon from 194 to 108 BCE and fell in the Han conquest of 108 BCE. Emperor Wu of Han ordered four commanderies set up, with Lelang Commandery at the centre and its capital, called Joseon, at the location of Pyongyang. Pyongyang was also the capital of Goguryeo and later served as a secondary capital of Goryeo. Until 1946 it was the provincial capital of South Pyongan Province.

Pyongyang is the capital and largest city of North Korea, a directly administered city with a status equal to the provinces. It became the de facto capital after the state's founding in 1948 and was declared the official capital by the 1972 Constitution. The 2008 census counted 3,255,288 people. The city was devastated in the Korean War and quickly rebuilt with Soviet assistance. Kim Il Sung University, the country's oldest, was founded there in 1946. The best-known local dish is Pyongyang raengmyŏn, thin buckwheat noodles in a cold meat broth with watery kimchi and a slice of sweet Korean pear.
pyotr-ilyich-tchaikovsky: Tchaikovsky was born on 7 May 1840 in Votkinsk, a small town in Vyatka Governorate near the Kama River. His father, Ilya Petrovich Tchaikovsky, was a lieutenant colonel and engineer in the Department of Mines and managed the Ironworks in Kamsko-Votkinsk. Although musically precocious, he was educated for a career as a civil servant, since there was little opportunity for a musical career in Russia and no institutional music education. On 10 June 1859, aged 19, he graduated as a titular counselor, a low rung on the civil service ladder, and spent three years in the Ministry of Justice. He then entered the new Saint Petersburg Conservatory, from which he graduated in 1865.

The Western-oriented teaching he received at the conservatory set him apart from the nationalist composers of The Five, Mily Balakirev, César Cui, Modest Mussorgsky, Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov and Alexander Borodin, who thought conservatories unnecessary. Tchaikovsky and his fellow students were caught between them and Anton Rubinstein, who defended professional training. His successes came infrequently and with great effort, and he was lifelong sensitive to criticism; Nikolai Rubinstein attacked the First Piano Concerto in private fits of rage. Hans von Bülow premiered it and championed other works. From 1867 the publication of his songs and piano music for the home market helped his popularity.

In March 1884 Emperor Alexander III conferred on him the Order of Saint Vladimir, which carried hereditary nobility and a personal audience with the Tsar. In 1885 the emperor requested a new production of Eugene Onegin at the Bolshoi Kamenny Theatre, signalling that his music was replacing Italian opera as the official imperial art, and awarded him a lifetime annual pension of 3,000 rubles. In his last years he grew at ease with the Belyayev circle around Rimsky-Korsakov. In 1892 he was voted a member of the Académie des Beaux-Arts in France, and in 1893 the University of Cambridge gave him an honorary Doctor of Music degree.

Tchaikovsky died in Saint Petersburg on 6 November 1893, aged 53, and was interred in Tikhvin Cemetery at the Alexander Nevsky Monastery. His death is attributed to cholera, caused by drinking unboiled water at a local restaurant. In the 1980s there was academic speculation in Britain that he killed himself, and Roland John Wiley wrote that we do not know how he died and may never find out. His music has remained popular, though critics were initially divided: some Russians thought it insufficiently Russian, while some Europeans praised it for offering more than exoticism.
pyotr-krasnov: Pyotr Nikolayevich Krasnov was born in Saint Petersburg on 22 September 1869 (10 September, old style), the son of Lieutenant General Nikolay Krasnov and grandson of General Ivan Krasnov. In 1888 he graduated from the Pavlovsk Military School and joined the Ataman regiment of the Life Guards. In 1902 the army newspaper Russkii Invalid published his articles from a trip to Mongolia, China and Japan, among them one on the Japanese army that a staff officer called poorly founded, hasty and far from the truth.

In the First World War Krasnov commanded the 2nd Combined Cossack Division from 1915 to 1917. In the summer of 1916 it was the first unit to break through Austro-Hungarian positions at the Battle of Lutsk, and he was wounded in the leg. In September 1917 he took command of the 3rd Cavalry Corps. After the October Revolution, Alexander Kerensky appointed him commander of the 700 Cossacks who marched on Petrograd. Bolshevik troops surrounded them at Gatchina on 15 November, and Krasnov was taken prisoner but soon released by Leon Trotsky, after which he made his way to the Don.

In May 1918 he was elected Ataman of the Don Cossack Host at Novocherkassk. He negotiated with the Germans occupying Ukraine and, with their support, equipped an army that drove the Soviets from the Don region in May and June 1918. By the middle of June a Don Army of 40,000 men, 56 guns and 179 machine guns was in the field. The historian Richard Pipes described him as an opportunist and an adventurer, and his German orientation made the Allied governments distrust him. On 19 February 1919 he left for Western Europe, and Afrikan P. Bogaewsky succeeded him as Don Ataman. He lived in Germany, then in France from 1923, where he helped found the anti-communist Brotherhood of Russian Truth, and he wrote novels.

During World War II Krasnov sought an alliance with Nazi Germany, motivated in part by Soviet repression of the Cossacks and the Russian Orthodox Church. After the invasion of 22 June 1941 he spoke regularly on Radio Berlin in Russian, in antisemitic broadcasts that presented the German advance as a liberation, and he worked with officials of Alfred Rosenberg's ministry for the occupied eastern territories.

The British handed him to the Soviets on 28 May 1945. He was held in the Lubyanka prison in Moscow, tried by the Military Collegium of the Supreme Court and sentenced to death with Andrei Shkuro and others. He was hanged on 17 January 1947. In 1997 Russia's Military Collegium confirmed that he had been justly convicted and was not to be rehabilitated, and in 2008 the council of Don atamans refused a petition for his rehabilitation, citing his collaboration with Germany.
